# TO THE MOST SERENE PRINCE
# LORD CHARLES EMANUEL,
## GRAND DUKE OF SAVOY
### MY LORD.

---

<margin>NATIONAL LIBRARY OF ROME, VITTORIO EMANUELE</margin>

**THERE GO FORTH**, Most Serene Lord, these books of mine regarding **Painting** under the glorious name of Your Highness, as the singular and—among all the Princes of this age—the most generous protector of all the <term>liberal Arts|In the Renaissance, these were the intellectual disciplines (like grammar, logic, and music) considered worthy of a free person, as opposed to "mechanical" manual labor.</term>. Among these arts, there is no doubt that Painting—not only in its Theory and contemplation, but also in its most worthy practice and exercise—should be numbered; as I have discussed at length in several places within these books. Especially since there have been, at various times, both Princes and Kings who have not disdained, having sometimes set aside their scepters, to take up the brush and, with the greatest delight, handle the ruler and the stylus <note>original: "la rega, & lo ſtile." These are the physical tools used for drawing and measuring in geometric compositions.</note>. 

Nor have I been induced to dedicate these books to you solely for this reason—that Your Highness, emulating the Great Augustus <note>A reference to the first Roman Emperor, Augustus, who was famously a patron of the arts and letters.</note> in this regard as in all others, so loves and prizes all the liberal Arts, and particularly takes such high pleasure in this very art of Painting—but also from considering within myself how marvelously the soul of Your Highness is composed and adorned with all those parts from which this most noble art is itself composed. These are the very subjects treated and discussed throughout these pages, namely: **Motion** (which I also call **Decorum**), **Color**, **Light**, **Perspective**, and **Proportion**. 

For one sees in Your Highness, to the supreme astonishment of everyone, the <term>motions|original: "moti." In Renaissance art theory, this refers both to physical movement and the "motions of the mind"—the outward expression of inner emotions through gesture and posture.</term> in this so slippery age of youth, and amidst so many delights and comforts of a most ample state, always regulated by reason and continually directed, as if toward a final goal—

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the page is "de'", indicating the next page begins with the word "dei" or "degli" (of the).</meta>

<summary>This page contains the dedication of Lomazzo's treatise to Charles Emmanuel I of Savoy, praising the Duke's patronage and metaphorically linking the Duke's personal virtues to the five core principles of painting: Motion, Color, Light, Perspective, and Proportion.</summary>
<keywords>Charles Emmanuel I of Savoy, Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo, dedication, patronage, liberal arts, Theory of Painting, Decorum, Color, Light, Perspective, Proportion, Renaissance art theory</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the formal dedication by Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo to Charles Emmanuel I, Duke of Savoy. <margin>NATIONAL LIBRARY OF SAINT MARK, VENICE</margin>

of your royal thoughts, to the public good, and to the health of the people, committed by divine power to your care and government. From this, it follows that in all your actions, Your Highness always works with such regard for every circumstance of place, time, and person: which is that <term>decorum|The Renaissance concept of 'decorum' (propriety) meant that every element of an artwork or a social action must be appropriate to the subject, setting, and status of the individuals involved.</term>, which above all things, like a celestial frieze, adorns human actions. In Your Highness are discovered various and most splendid colors of heroic virtues; your most rare comportments shed an eternal light. The perspective of your providence is most sharp; which, looking with such straight lines at the three parts of time <note>A reference to the past, present, and future—the hallmark of a wise ruler.</note>, produces marvelous effects. And from all these things results in Your Highness a harmony equal in proportion to that which the great African <note>Scipio Africanus the Younger, who appears in the "Dream of Scipio" at the end of Cicero’s *On the Republic* (*De Re Publica*).</note> heard in the heavens in the writings of Cicero; indeed, superior in such a way that it can truly be called a harmony proceeding from the very breath of the Holy Spirit. 

But without doubt, my gift is too small for so great a Prince. Despite this, because it comes from a person who cannot give you anything greater, and is born from a most ardent desire to honor Your Highness as much as you deserve, I hope that you will not only not despise it, but will be greatly pleased by it; in imitation of blessed God, who welcomes small offerings due to the great devotion of those who intend to honor Him with them. I humbly beseech you, therefore, to deign to receive it gratefully; and wishing you continual prosperity and exaltation, with all submission and reverence, I kiss your most serene hands. 

From Milan, the 23rd of June, the year 1584.

Of Your Highness,

->The most humble servant,<-
->Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo.<-

**To our beloved son Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo of Milan.**

# POPE GREGORY XIII

*Beloved son, health and Apostolic Blessing. You have recently explained to us that through your long nights of study and labor, and for the common benefit of many, you have composed a work entitled On Painting, which contains the theory and practice of painting. Having already had this work examined and approved by our beloved sons, Brother Giulio Ferrari of Cremona—then the Inquisitor at Milan—and also by the Vicar of our beloved son Cardinal Carlo Borromeo <note>Carlo Borromeo (1538–1584) was the Archbishop of Milan and a leading figure of the Counter-Reformation; he was later canonized as a saint</note>, titular priest of Saint Praxedes and Governor of the Church of Milan in spiritual matters by Apostolic dispensation, you now intend to commit it to the press. However, you fear that after it has been published, it might be printed and sold by many others without your knowledge or permission, which would result in no small loss and detriment to you. You have therefore humbly petitioned us to deign to assist you with a timely remedy out of our Apostolic kindness. We, therefore, wishing to provide for your protection in these matters, to compensate you for a portion of your labors, and to favor you with special grace, are moved by your petitions in this regard. By the tenor of these presents and by Apostolic authority, we grant and allow that within ten years from the date of this document, the aforementioned work may not be printed, sold, held for sale, or offered in any way by anyone without your consent, except by those to whom you have granted such permission in writing. We therefore forbid all and singular printers and booksellers, both within and outside of Italy, located in lands mediately or immediately subject to the Apostolic See <note>This refers to the Papal States and any territories where the Pope held direct or indirect political jurisdiction</note>, under penalty of the sentence of automatic excommunication and a fine of two hundred gold <term>ducats|The gold ducat was a standard trade coin of the Renaissance, known for its high purity and consistency</term> of the chamber—half of which shall be applied to the Apostolic Chamber and the other half to you—to be incurred by the very act of contravention without any further judicial declaration or decree as often as the offense occurs, and to be exacted without remission, along with the loss of such books: that within this ten-year period they shall not print the aforementioned work or any part of it without your express permission, nor give it to others to print except to you or to those whom you have assigned the printing of the work...*

<summary>This page contains a formal Papal Privilege granted by Pope Gregory XIII to Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo, providing him with a ten-year exclusive right to print and sell his treatise on painting. It establishes severe ecclesiastical and financial penalties for unauthorized reproduction, highlighting the legal protections for authors in the 16th century.</summary>
<keywords>Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo, Pope Gregory XIII, Carlo Borromeo, copyright history, printing privilege, Renaissance art theory, Milan, Apostolic Chamber, excommunication</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the text of the Papal Brief issued by Pope Gregory XIII to Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo. The previous page ended mid-sentence, establishing the legal right for Lomazzo to publish his work. This page details the enforcement of that right and the legal overrides (derogations) common in 16th-century official documents.</meta>

...or those you have commissioned, should dare or presume to sell the printed <note>original: <term>impressum vendere</term></note> work, or hold it for sale, or offer it, or otherwise possess it. Furthermore, we command all our venerable brothers—the Archbishops, Bishops, and their Vicars, or their general officials in spiritual matters—as well as the Legates, Vice-legates, Governors, Judges, Magistrates <note>original: <term>Potestatibus</term></note>, Police Captains <note>original: <term>Baricellis</term>; local law enforcement officers in the Papal States</note>, and all others whom this may in any way concern, that as often as they are requested by you or on your behalf, they must assist you with the protection of an effective defense. 

They are to enforce these provisions by our authority at your simple request against any who are disobedient or rebellious, using <term>ecclesiastical censures</term> <note>spiritual penalties such as excommunication</note> and other appropriate legal or practical remedies. They may even call upon the aid of the secular arm <note>original: <term>brachij secularis auxilio</term>; this refers to calling upon civil authorities or physical force to enforce the decree</note> if necessary. 

This grant stands notwithstanding any Apostolic constitutions or ordinances, or any statutes and customs even if confirmed by oath or Apostolic approval. It overrides any prior privileges or Apostolic letters, even those issued by our own accord <note>original: <term>motu proprio</term>; a document issued by the Pope on his own initiative</note>, with certain knowledge, from the fullness of our power, or in a formal assembly <note>original: <term>consistorialiter</term></note>. Even if these prior laws require specific and express mention to be set aside, and though they otherwise remain in effect, for this occasion only we specially and expressly override them, as well as anything else to the contrary.

->Given at Rome, at Saint Peter's, under the Ring of the Fisherman <note>original: <term>annulo piscatoris</term>; the signet ring used for papal briefs</note>, on the 28th day of January, 1584, in the twelfth year of our Pontificate <note>the duration of a Pope's reign</note>.<-

->A. Saulius.<-

<meta>catchword: Of</meta>

**D**ON SANCHO de Guevara and Padilla, Castellan of Milan, of His Majesty’s Secret Council, Governor of this State, and his Captain General in Italy, etc. Since Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo has set forth to us that with much labor and personal expense he has compiled a treatise on the art of Painting, and because it does not seem right to him that after his hard work others should take both the honor and the profit, he has petitioned us to grant him a <term>Privilege</term> <note>a legal grant, similar to a modern copyright, giving an author exclusive rights to their work</note> in such a way that no one else but him may print, nor sell, nor have others sell the said work. 

We, desiring to help and favor all virtuous people, and particularly those who labor for the public benefit, have granted this in the manner written below. Therefore, by the authority we hold, we grant a broad Privilege, so that no person of whatever condition, status, or preeminence—except for the said Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo, or his successors, or those who have cause from him—may, for the next fifteen years, print, or have printed, or sell if printed, or have sold such a treatise, under the penalty of losing all copies found and a fine of fifty <term>scudi</term> <note>a gold or silver currency used in Italy at the time</note> for every violation. This fine is to be applied in thirds: to the <term>Royal Chamber</term> <note>the state treasury of the Duchy of Milan</note>, to the accuser, and to the petitioner. And we command everyone whom this concerns, or shall concern, to observe and ensure the observation of this present grant for the said time. Given in Milan under the witness of our hand and our seal on the 2nd of October, 1582.

->Don Sancho de Guevara y Padilla.<-

Seen by Filiodonus. <note>original: <term>Vidit Filiodonus</term></note>

Montius.

<summary>This page contains a formal legal privilege granted by Don Sancho de Guevara, the Spanish Governor of Milan, protecting Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo's intellectual property rights for fifteen years. It establishes the penalties for unauthorized printing or sale of his treatise on painting.</summary>

### BY SIR GIULIANO GOSELINI.

> **H**e so equaled nourishing Nature,
> *Giving so much strength and life to colors,*
> *That she, conquered and mocked by his brush,*
> *Took his eyes from him. Ah, too cruel a fate.* <note>Lomazzo began to lose his sight in 1571 and was completely blind by age 33. This forced him to turn from painting to writing art theory.</note>
> *But with internal sight he possesses Painting,*
> *Woven into such clear and true history;*
> *That she has risen to much greater esteem,*
> *And he no longer cares for the light that was taken.*
> *From the heavens and the stars he draws movement and light,*
> *And from the <term>First Idea</term> <note>original: "prima Idea." In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the perfect, divine form of an object existing in the mind before it is physically created.</note> he derives the forms*
> *Of drawing and coloring for Art.*
> *And how, though blind, he descends—and by what paths—*
> *From the <term>Empyrean</term> <note>the highest part of heaven, thought in the 16th century to be the realm of pure fire and the dwelling place of God</note> to the Abysses, and enlightens others,*
> *Learn here, reader, in these learned and illustrious pages.*

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the series of introductory commendatory poems for Giovan Paolo Lomazzo’s "Treatise on the Art of Painting." Like the previous poem by Gosellini, these sonnets by Gherardo Borgogni and Giovanni Filippo Gherardini celebrate Lomazzo’s dual mastery of practical painting and theoretical writing, specifically focusing on the paradox of his blindness.</meta>

<meta>catchword: Of</meta>

## By Sir Gherardo Borgogni.

> **Y**ou, already with your works divine and fair,
> Giving life to wooden panels and to colors, <note>original: "legni" (woods). This refers to the poplar panels commonly used as supports for paintings in Renaissance Italy.</note>
> Rose glorious to the highest honors,
> To walk as an equal with Zeuxis and Apelles. <note>Zeuxis and Apelles were the most famous painters of ancient Greece. In the Renaissance, comparing a contemporary artist to them was the highest possible compliment.</note>
> Now, so that everyone sings and speaks of you,
> You reveal soul-stirring treasures in living pages;
> And as a faithful guide to the most worthy Painters,
> You travel with your name to this region and that.
> If double praise is due for twin-fold worth,
> O wise Painter; who could reach the mark,
> So high and sublime, of your great merits?
> You wield the brush among the rarest masters, and you live
> Within your work; nor shall the passing of the hours
> Take away the first glories of your talent.

---

## By Sir Giovanni Filippo Gherardini.

> **H**e saw, and he painted: and no age
> Ever possessed works of the brush more rare.
> Blind, he then wrote pages so prized and dear,
> That one can no longer hope for more.
> His hand then gave life to stones and to wood;
> And made art triumph over nature:
> Now anyone who pays heed here is amazed
> At how loftily his style teaches this.
> But however much a great desire pricks another,
> I fear they shall not reach such a goal,
> Unless they saw then, and painted alongside him,
> And who now contemplates with him, and writes while blind. <note>This concludes the common Renaissance trope that only a practitioner who has "seen" the secrets of art can truly write about them, even if—like Lomazzo—they have lost their physical sight.</note>

<summary>This page contains two commendatory sonnets praising Giovan Paolo Lomazzo. The poets emphasize that his transition from a master painter to a blind art theorist has granted him a "double glory" and an unparalleled intellectual depth.</summary>

<keywords>Gherardo Borgogni, Giovanni Filippo Gherardini, Zeuxis, Apelles, art theory, blindness, paragone, Renaissance poetry, painting techniques</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues the sequence of commendatory verses preceding Giovan Paolo Lomazzo's "Treatise on the Art of Painting, Sculpture, and Architecture" (1584). Following the previous poems by Borgogni and Gherardini, these verses by Lodovico Gandini further explore the "ut pictura poesis" (as painting, so is poetry) theme, focusing specifically on the paradox of Lomazzo's blindness.</meta>

# By Sir Lodovico Gandini.

->To the Author.<-

**P** *ainting, which every man so greatly delights in,*
*Is called mute poetry:* <note>This refers to a famous ancient aphorism attributed to Simonides of Ceos: "painting is silent poetry and poetry is speaking painting."</note>
*But let it also be called*
*Poetry that speaks;*
*Since within your style all of it is discerned*
*So well adorned with eternal words.*

---

->By the same.<-

**S** *peaking painting*
*We call Poetry.*
*Eloquent Poetry*
*We say is Painting:*
*Painting therefore and Poetry are equals.*
*But how much more are they equal,*
*If to this <note>To poetry.</note> light was given through his pages by*
*Homer, who was without lights;* <note>original: "senza luci". In Italian verse, "lights" is a standard metaphor for eyes. Homer, the father of Greek epic poetry, was famously blind.</note>
*And you, deprived of lights,* <note>Lomazzo lost his sight in 1571 at age 33; this "deprivation" is a recurring theme in the book's introductory poems to emphasize his inner vision.</note>
*Give light to this <note>To painting.</note> with your pen?*

---

->By the same.<-

**P** *ainters once had lights;* <note>They had physical eyesight.</note>
*But they did not paint with light:* <note>Here, "light" refers to the intellectual and theoretical clarity that Lomazzo’s writing provides to the practice of art.</note>
*Now they shall not only have lights,*
*But they shall paint with light.*
*Who offers them this light?*
*Your shining work, though you are deprived of lights.*
*Most high Painter, overflowing with light.*

Bernardini <note>Likely referring to the printer or a member of the production circle.</note>

<summary>This page features three short poems by Lodovico Gandini celebrating Lomazzo’s ability to "illuminate" the art of painting through his writing despite his blindness. The verses play on the dual meaning of "light" as both physical eyesight and intellectual/artistic guidance.</summary>

<keywords>Lodovico Gandini, Lomazzo, blindness, ut pictura poesis, art theory, Homer, light and sight, metaphors for eyes</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the series of commendatory Latin verses praising Giovan Paolo Lomazzo. Following the Italian verses by Gandini on the previous page, this page features contributions by the physician and poet Bernardino Baldini and the scholar Sigismondo Fogliano. The "catchword" at the bottom right, "In," indicates the first word of the following page.</meta>

### By Bernardino Baldini, on the book of Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo, the blind painter.

> **W**ho painted the parts of the world so learnedly? Was it Argus? <note>In Greek mythology, Argus Panoptes was a giant with a hundred eyes, symbolizing total vision.</note>
> No; this man lacks eyes; Argus saw with a hundred lights. <note>original: "centeno lumine". Poets often used "lights" as a metaphor for eyes.</note>
> Was it Tiresias the seer, who, though void of light,
> Observed things that no man understood? Nay,
> He is another distinguished Tiresias, named Paul. <note>Lomazzo's first name was Giovanni Paolo; the poet plays on the name Paul.</note>
> For who besides Tiresias has peered so sharply
> Into the things that Paul has brought forth so skillfully in his golden book?

### Sigismondo Fogliano on the book of Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo.

> **H**ow a blind man can carry a light before those who see,
> And render the celestial dwellings with his brush;
> This history-filled book of the painter Lomazzo demonstrates,
> Who, though deprived of light, saw the gods <note>original: "superos", referring to the inhabitants of heaven or the divine realm.</note> in his mind.
> Just as Paul <note>The Apostle Paul, who was famously blinded by divine light on the road to Damascus before his spiritual eyes were opened.</note> could not learn the mysteries
> Unless his eyes were darkened when he was snatched up to heaven;
> So that this second Paul might see the seats of the gods with his mind alone,
> Light was given to his mind, once it was taken from his eyes.

<summary>Two Latin poems praising Lomazzo by comparing his blindness to the prophetic vision of Tiresias and the divine revelation of St. Paul, arguing that his loss of physical sight granted him superior intellectual and spiritual "light."</summary>
<keywords>Bernardino Baldini, Sigismondo Fogliano, Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo, Argus, Tiresias, St. Paul, blindness, inner vision, divine light, artistic theory</keywords>

### In praise of the work of Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo,
### A poem by Willem Huysmans of Antwerp.

**W**hatever was once hidden in the art of Apelles, <note>Apelles of Kos (4th century BCE) was the most famous painter of ancient Greece, renowned for his realism and technical perfection.</note>
-> Which could have remained concealed from even the most famous men; <-
And whatever Apelles painted with his skillful brush, <note>original: "penicillo", literally a "little tail," referring to the fine-haired brushes used by artists.</note>
-> Which no one else fostered with equal dexterity: <-
This, these seven volumes <note>Lomazzo’s treatise is famously divided into seven books, covering subjects like proportion, emotion, and light.</note> reveal through watchful study,
-> Under the auspices of your noble name, high Charles. <note>Charles Emmanuel I (1562–1630), the Duke of Savoy, to whom Lomazzo dedicated this work.</note> <-
The wavy sea contains nothing, nor the earth, nor the heavens
-> Which either pole covers with its slanted rotations, <-
That he has not expressed to perfection <note>original: "ad unguem", literally "to the fingernail." This Roman idiom refers to a sculpture finished so smoothly that a fingernail cannot feel any joints or imperfections.</note> with extraordinary effort,
-> With an artistic hand accompanying Nature. <-
The human mind hides nothing in its silent depths
-> Of which the face does not possess certain seeds. <note>A reference to Lomazzo's second book, which deals with "Actions and Gestures," explaining how internal emotions are visible on the face.</note> <-
Give way, Roman painters, give way, Greeks!
-> This work comes forth, pleasing for many reasons. <-
But in what way, Paul, with what Muse <note>original: "camœna", a Latin term for the spirits of song and poetry.</note> shall I celebrate you?
-> Our Thalia <note>Thalia was the Muse of comedy and pastoral poetry; here, the poet uses her to represent his own poetic voice.</note> stands amazed at your gifts. <-
Nature made you lynx-eyed <note>Reference to Lynceus, an Argonaut in Greek myth who possessed such sharp vision he could see through the earth.</note>, but a dreadful
-> Accident made you blind; <note>Lomazzo went blind in 1571 at age 33, after which he dictated his theoretical works.</note> yet nature does not hinder you, nor does the accident. <-
Those things which a lynx-eyed man once penetrated with sharp vision,
-> You surpass, Paul, with the light of your fine genius. <-

# SONNET BY THE AUTHOR OF THE WORK.

**T** *HE Great Creator established the formed proportions* <note>original: "Fondo... le formate misure"; The author uses a "F" drop cap to begin the poem, framing God as the ultimate architect or geometer.</note>
*for the elements within the first bodies;*
*Placing souls thereafter in living beings,*
*where color was formed through motion.*
*Then spreading His splendor over them,*
*by which they shone distinctly from one another,*
*And in beholding the rays and the outlines,*
*which show the primal honor of such an art.*
*Through both styles* <note>Likely referring to the "two sisters" of painting and sculpture.</note> *He has granted us the gift*
*of arranging these things, with stories and forms*
*of all that exists from the heavens down to the smallest speck.*
*Therefore, I humbly ask His forgiveness*
*if I do not know how to teach the path as the ancients did,*
*or as the moderns, among whom I have arrived like one blind.*

# STANZAS BY THE SAME AUTHOR.

*Virtue and art are extinguished and lost,*
*those which the two sisters* <note>original: "due suore"; referring to the sister arts of Painting and Sculpture.</note> *once sent to the heavens;*
*Therefore, I have moved to this region*
*to restore them with labor and zeal:*
*Celebrating those who, through works on paper, were born*
*with these arts, and through heat and frost*
*held them as their deities; and to them I write,*
*under the great Charles Emmanuel, my Divine Patron.* <note>Charles Emmanuel I (1562–1630), Duke of Savoy, known for his extensive patronage of the arts and sciences.</note>

*Where perhaps at times those parts will be seen,*
*which were once extinguished by a cruel fate;*
*As in that which recorded the ornate and beautiful*
*works of marble, metal, and painting,*
*that existed in the world; and in the treatise that Apelles* <note>Apelles of Kos was the most famous painter of ancient Greece. Since his works are lost, he represents the pinnacle of artistic achievement that the author seeks to emulate or describe.</note>
*provided for art and its distinct principles,*
*and of the others who raised them up and were once*
*masters of them, each confident in their execution.*

# SONNET BY THE AUTHOR FROM TOLEDO.

<margin>E</margin> **T**he formed forges <note>original: "fucine"; a metaphor for the divine workshop where the physical world was crafted.</note> of the elements
Were the great wonder of the first physical bodies;
Touching then the souls smiling above,
He granted restraint and color through motion.
Thereafter, pouring out His splendor,
To realize many great and intent designs,
And upon seeing the rays and the outlines,
They created the first honor of existence.
Truly, He fixed a soul's gift within that state,
Adorning it with paintings, histories, and forms
Of everything from the heavens down to the smallest point.
I humbly seek pardon upon this shore
If I do not know as much as the ancients; in so many forms
He hides me, yet unites me with Giulio <note>Likely Giulio Romano (c. 1499–1546), a master of Italian Mannerist art and architecture.</note>.

# PREFACE OF THE WORK,
## IN WHICH IS TREATED
### THE EXCELLENCE AND THE ORIGINE,
#### *And progress of Painting.*

<margin>
NATIONAL LIBRARY ROME
VITTORIO EMANUELE
</margin>

***A**mong the most precious and excellent gifts from the goodness of God, scattered with a most generous hand over the human race, without doubt, the most precious and excellent has been the gift of that power of our soul which we call intellect. For it is, in short, the instrument and the means by which our life is maintained and preserved, and men come to understand, and consequently to desire, their ultimate end. This is most clearly proven. Because it cannot be denied that with this intellectual power men first understood and investigated all the needs of human nature, and where its corruption and total ruin consist; and then provided all those means that were necessary to maintain and preserve it. Hence we see that our intellect, having noticed that if that radical moisture <note>term: radical moisture (original: humido radicale); in medieval and Renaissance medicine, this was the vital fluid or "oil" thought to sustain the lamp of life.</note> which natural heat <note>term: natural heat (original: calor naturale); the innate heat believed to reside in the heart that drives metabolism.</note> continually consumes and destroys were not repaired, the corruption and destruction of man would certainly follow, it first imagined the most useful art of agriculture, and its companions and, so to speak, its ministers, with which the earth—which was previously sterile and barren—would be rendered fruitful, and would come to produce abundantly all those things with which this weak human nature could be preserved. Similarly also, because our bodies, naked as they had been produced by nature, were variously harmed by the intemperance of the air; it ingeniously rediscovered the art of weaving and manufacturing clothes, not only for the shielding and defense of bodies from the injuries of the heavens <note>The "injuries of the heavens" refers to harsh weather like rain, wind, or extreme temperatures.</note>, but also for ornament and decorum. And to this same end, it has rediscovered in short all the mechanical arts <note>term: mechanical arts (original: arti mecaniche); the practical, manual crafts such as masonry, smithing, and carpentry.</note> together with the daring science of navigation. Thus, seeing that human nature was fragile and subject to innumerable infirmities,*

<vocab>Painting, Intellect, Art of agriculture, Mechanical arts, Science of navigation, Human nature</vocab>

<summary>This opening proem establishes the intellect as a divine gift essential for human survival, attributing the invention of agriculture, weaving, and the mechanical arts to man's need to preserve his fragile physical nature. It sets the stage for defining Painting as a similarly noble pursuit derived from this intellectual capacity.</summary>
<keywords>Intellect, Divine Gifts, Human Nature, Agriculture, Weaving, Mechanical Arts, Navigation, Radical Moisture</keywords>

## PREFACE.

<margin><unclear>Stamp: FROM THE LIBRARY OF CARDINAL AZZOLINI, ROME</unclear></margin>

*...by experiencing the virtues of herbs and other natural things, it discovered the art of medicine. And understanding man to be by his nature a social animal, it began with art to congregate them together; and so that they might better preserve themselves in this way of living, it ordained the sciences of Economics <note>term: Economics (original: Economica); in this period, this refers to "Oeconomia," the art of managing a household or family estate, rather than modern finance.</note> and Politics; and it also induced them to divide the fields equally among them, seeing that in this way they would be more diligently cultivated. And finally, knowing that for all created things there was one creator, ruler, and governor of the whole world and the ultimate end of man, it began to stir our will to love and desire Him.*

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Since this intellectual power has therefore been the cause of the invention of so many beautiful arts and sciences; and being the instrument through which our soul unites in this life to its ultimate end through grace, and in the next through glory; it remains most clear what I proposed at the start: that it is, among all the other gifts of God, the most noble and distinguished gift. However, although it is so excellent and useful to the human race, it nonetheless has need of ministers and servants to help it; and among other things it has need of that other power of our soul which we call memory. For, as the philosophers teach us, it is necessary for anyone who wishes to understand to turn toward the phantasms <note>term: phantasms (original: fantasmi); these are mental images or impressions derived from the senses which the intellect "reads" to form thoughts.</note> that are within the memory; hence it can be said that memory serves the intellect as the treasurer of its treasures. Because everything that the intellect understands, it stores and guards in the memory; and from there it retrieves it when it wishes to understand it another time. And even though the intellectual memory is the same thing as the intellect, the same intellect nonetheless requires another different power—namely, the bodily memory—to perform its operation of understanding. But because this bodily memory also could not contain all things (for it is like a vessel which, once it is full, spills out whatever else is poured into it), it likewise has need of other things, and principally of the most noble art of painting, which was discovered by the same intellect for its own aid. For (as has been said) the intellect needs the memory to return anew to understand what it has already understood; and the memory, because it cannot remember everything, needs something to help it and someone to wake it: and among the most fit and suitable instruments to perform this, painting is the most principal. This is demonstrated clearer than the sun. Because if it is true, as...*

<sig>v</sig>

<summary>This page argues that the human intellect, though divine and noble, requires 'bodily memory' to function, and identifies the art of painting as the primary tool used to assist and 'awaken' human memory.</summary>

<header>PREFACE</header>

## PREFACE

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*...as it is very true that the use of writing was introduced so that the arts and sciences, discovered with such great study and labor by ingenious men, would not be lost; because the physical power of memory could not contain the images and likenesses <note>original: "idoli, & simolacri"; in this context, these refer to mental representations or "phantasms" of objects rather than religious idols.</note> of as many things as there are in the world—being infinite in potential—nor as many propositions as are contained in all the arts and sciences. Thus was imagined that most skillful invention of letters and characters, by which all the concepts of our mind come to be fully declared, and all the sciences are preserved in books for the benefit of posterity, eternal and immortal. If it is true, I say, that inks and writings were discovered to preserve the memory of the sciences, it follows most clearly that painting is the instrument within which the treasure of memory is enclosed, since writings are nothing other than the painting of light and dark.* <margin>The Egyptians</margin> *Hence we see that the Egyptians, with the painting of animals and other things, declared all their sciences and secrets, both sacred and profane; so much so that painting among them was like a treasury <note>original: "erario"; a public treasury or storehouse for wealth.</note> where they stored the riches of their high sciences for eternal memory. From this, we have subsequently drawn great utility, both in things pertaining to Philosophy and to astrology, by means of Plato, Pythagoras, and other philosophers who sailed as far as Egypt to learn them, and who later became the teachers of all Europe. The ancient Romans likewise, in imitation of those peoples, formed their emblems with paintings of men and animals, which they used to place in private and public places; concealing beneath them not only the greatest secrets of moral and natural things, but also the sharpest professional stimuli to incite hearts toward magnanimous and generous undertakings—of which custom some vestiges are still seen in Europe in our own times. Not only emblems or hieroglyphs, but the glorious deeds of illustrious men were explicitly painted by command of the Roman people in public places, to excite men to emulate such glorious feats. Thus, in various locations in Rome, as examples of fortitude, one could see in one place a painting of Horatius Cocles <note>A legendary Roman hero who famously defended the Sublician Bridge alone against the Etruscan army.</note> who, with an undaunted spirit, defended the Sublician Bridge alone against a massive army of Tuscans; and in another place, Marcus Marcellus, who, by cutting off the head of Britomartus <note>Viridomarus (here Britomaro), a leader of the Gauls defeated by Marcellus in 222 BCE.</note>, the Captain of the Gauls, threw the entire enemy army into flight and confusion. As an example of military discipline, Papirius the Dictator—* <note>Referring to Lucius Papirius Cursor, a Roman dictator famed for his strict adherence to military discipline.</note>

<sig>A 2</sig>
<meta>sholu <unclear>handwritten note at bottom left</unclear></meta>
<meta>re, quan-</meta>

<summary>This page argues that writing and painting were invented to supplement the limits of human memory, preserving knowledge for future generations. It highlights the Egyptian use of hieroglyphs and the Roman use of historical paintings and emblems as tools for both education and moral inspiration.</summary>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Figures and histories of all the Gods were also painted, as some remains <note>original: "vestigi"; literally "vestiges" or archaeological ruins.</note> of them can still be seen in Rome today; by these paintings, the Romans were kindled and set on fire with the love of religion and divine worship. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Now, there is no need to discourse at length on the use of this painting among the Greeks; because everything that has been said about the esteem and value in which it was held by the Romans was done in imitation of those same Greeks. They, having recognized the immense utility of painting, always held it in the highest honor and esteem; so much so that they spared no expense in purchasing whatever they found excellent in it. Thus we read of King Attalus, who bought a panel by Aristides the Theban painter for one hundred talents <note>A talent was a massive unit of currency; one hundred talents would represent a kingly fortune, emphasizing the extreme value of art.</note>; and of King Candaules, who paid as much in gold for a panel by Bularchus, where in a modest space the destruction of the Magnesians was painted. To conclude, the rewards with which the Greeks honored painters (as all their histories testify) and the many excellent paintings that the Romans brought back from them during the time when the Empire flourished most, show us clearly in what high regard they held this most noble art.

I do not say that images are the total cause of such great effects, for this would be an impious opinion; but I say that painting moves the eye, and the eye guards all the <term>simulacra</term> <note>original: *simolacri*; these are mental images or likenesses of objects that the senses transmit to the mind.</note> and the images of things it sees in the memory, and presents those to the intellect, which then understands the truth and falsehood of those things; and having understood them, it represents them to the will; which, seeing things as evil, abhors them, and seeing them as good, loves them, and by natural inclination follows after them. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But because I would not want this discourse of mine to generate boredom in the minds of the readers, I will not go on wandering further in this most spacious field of the praises of painting, as it is my intention to strive for brevity, as has been easily recognized up to this point. And while one could discourse at length about its purpose, I wanted only to say that it was the means by which the greatest things were acquired. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;It is not, however, to be passed over in silence that painting is one of those things which are desirable for their own sake. And the soul takes a much greater pleasure when it then discerns the <term>symmetry</term> <note>original: *simmetria*; the harmonious proportion and balance of parts in a work of art.</note> of a good and skillful artist in a figure, and notices that wonderful art with which he makes an immobile and unfeeling figure appear to our eyes to move, and jump, and run, and call out, and strike with its hands, and move its whole life forward, backward, to the right, and to the left. ...an army, and an entire province: and finally that our intellect has reached this limit in its investigation, having desired through art to imitate **formative nature** <note>original: *natura formatrice*; the creative power of nature that gives shape to all things.</note>, the maker of the elements, plants, trees, animals, and man. But because it is necessary—not only for the understanding of what we have already said, but also for what will follow—to understand the difference or conformity that exists between painting and sculpture, I shall briefly declare my opinion regarding this; so that, perhaps, the sculptors do not claim for themselves those praises which are proper to painting, and we others [painters] remain deprived of the fruit of our labors.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For there has always been a dispute between sculptors and painters as to which of the two arts was more excellent; and many have judged differently, some in favor of sculptors, and others in favor of painters, such as myself. Whenever I have happened to reason about such a matter, I have always defended this side; because I intended to bring to light this work, in which I then wanted to treat the subject more amply, with the hope that this discourse—as much for its novelty as for the reasons that would be brought forward—should not displease the readers. And primarily, to have a more certain resolution of all this, it is necessary to consider the agreement and difference of these two arts; because in this way it can be known much more clearly in the following chapter (where I will then reason about it particularly) which of them is of greater value and excellence. This seems to me to be something that should not have been omitted in any way by those who have treated this question.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I say then, that painting and sculpture are contained under one and the same art, by that rule which says: *those things that agree in a third, agree among themselves.* <note>A principle of logic (syllogism) suggesting that if two things share a common category or essence, they share a nature.</note> And even if it might appear to someone that by this rule, one would also come to conclude that a man, for example, was a horse, since both agree in a third—namely, in being animals—this is most false. They agree only in the part that both are animals, but they are different in species. And the same could be said of painting and sculpture; nevertheless, it must be understood with judgment that, just as between one man and another one cannot say there is any essential difference because both are **rational men** <term>rational men</term> <note>original: *huomini rationali*; in Renaissance philosophy, "reason" was the defining essence of humanity.</note>, so it is with sculpture and painting...

*...they cannot be called essentially different from one another; because both tend toward the very same end of representing individual substances* <note>original: "sostanze indiuidue"; referring to specific, existing things in the physical world rather than abstract concepts.</note> *to our eyes, and both do so equally by following the geometric quantity of those individuals; and thus one, like the other, equally toils to represent the beauty, the decorum, the motion, and the contours of things; and finally, both are intent on nothing other than portraying things from nature as similarly as they can. For let us suppose that a King commissions a painter and a sculptor to both make a portrait of him; there is no doubt that both will have in their intellect the same* **idea** *and* **form** <note>The author is using "idea" in the Platonic sense—the perfect mental concept that precedes the physical work.</note> *of that King, and will proceed in their minds with the same discourse of reason and art; and in short, will have the same proposal and goal of making the portrait as similar as possible to the person of the King. The means will also be the same, because both will strive to imitate the person of the King, preserving his same geometric quantity—which is, for example, ten faces* <note>A traditional Renaissance system of proportion where the total height of a figure is measured as ten times the length of the face.</note> *—and preserving all his contours, neither more nor less, than those of the King. And thus they will observe the quantity and contour of his forehead, his nose, his eyes, his mouth, and finally of his whole life; and then the portrait will remain exactly like the body of the King. So it is that these two craftsmen proceed by the same art in their mind and intellect.*

*Then, before they set to work upon the material, they first design* <term>disegno</term> <note>In Italian art theory, "disegno" means both the physical act of drawing and the intellectual "design" or intent behind the work.</note> *on paper or on something else everything that they had conceived in their mind; and the expressive design of the idea of both agrees in everything that must express the likeness, which is the essence of these arts. And perhaps they will only be different in some accidental thing; because one of them will make the legs or the arms with a different position and motion, even if both had been prescribed a certain attitude and position by the King, such as standing straight, in which he wished to be portrayed. It is true that one paints and the other carves, but this is nonetheless a material difference, which does not create a different species of art or science. The essential difference alone is what makes a different and diverse species of science, which is not found between painting and sculpture; and thus it is no specific difference to make the portrait of the King in stone, or in wood, or in metal, or on a panel, or with a brush, or with a chisel, because all these differences are material. *...[who] carves the King in marble were to say to the person portraying him in wood that they were not a sculptor because they used wood while he used marble; it would be exactly the same if the sculptor told the painter that he was not part of his art because he uses marble while the painter works on a panel or canvas, or because one uses a chisel and the other a brush.* If the difference of the material alone does not, therefore, create a difference in the art, we must also necessarily say that those who make a portrait of the same thing on a panel and the other in marble cannot be called different species of artists. And although the sculptor represents the entire body of the King with all its contours—something the painter does not do—it should not be said that they are different in art, since even "more or less" <note>The author is using a logical principle: a difference in degree (more or less detail) does not change the essential nature or "species" of an activity.</note> does not create an essential difference. Thus, it would not be a conclusive reason to say, "this figure is in full relief <note>High relief or a fully three-dimensional statue.</note>, and this one in half-relief <term>bas-relief</term>, therefore only the first is a sculptor and the other is not." Likewise, one cannot say: "the painter makes only a single view in a figure, and the sculptor makes them all, therefore their arts are different." Because if the painter makes only one view, it is because he works on a flat surface. So if he represents only a half-figure, or if at one time he shows it from the back and another in profile, this happens because of the imperfection of the material—which is flat—and not because of an imperfection in the art. And so I conclude resolutely that it is the very same art with which one portrays a figure in marble, wood, silver, or gold, and that with which one portrays on panel, paper, or a wall. *...[Athen]ian <note>Likely a reference to Eumarus of Athens, whom Pliny the Elder credits with first distinguishing gender in painting.</note>, who began to distinguish the male from the female. Cimon of Cleonae* <note>An early Greek painter credited with developing perspective and anatomical detail.</note> *greatly enlightened this art, discovering **foreshortening** <term>scorzi</term> in figures, and painting faces with such skill that they looked in all directions; furthermore, he demonstrated how to represent the folds in garments, and the muscles and veins in bodies. Just as in the time of our fathers, Bernardino Luini* <note>A North Italian painter (c. 1480–1532) known for his Leonardesque style.</note> *was also accustomed to say that a painter without perspective was as much a painter as a doctor without grammar is a doctor.*

...so many sciences and so many arts, that one not only needs to be a free man <note>In the Renaissance, a "free man" referred to someone of social standing who practiced the "liberal arts," rather than someone performing manual or servile labor.</note>, but also wealthy, to be able to provide oneself with the necessary books and have the means to pay the teachers who might instruct him. # Division of the whole work.

**T**HERE are two ways and modes of proceeding in an orderly fashion in any science or art; one of which is called the order of nature, and the other is called the order of doctrine <note>In Renaissance philosophy, the "order of nature" usually refers to the way things actually come into being, while the "order of doctrine" refers to the way they are best taught to a student.</note>. Nature proceeds in an orderly way by beginning from the imperfect and ending in the perfect, and by beginning from singular things and ending in universals. And if the human intellect were to proceed in understanding things in the same way and order in which they were produced by nature itself, this would truly be the most excellent way in the world to understand. For we would begin to know all things through their first and immediate principles, and we would also know these not as mere ideas, separate from particular things (as some have said), nor as things only imagined and placed within the human intellect (as others have wished), but as those very principles which joined together in the formation of particular things; we could almost see them with our own eyes and point to them with our fingers. This is the most beautiful and certain way of knowing of all others. For who does not see that when our intellect begins its operation of understanding through particular things, it begins to know these same particulars through their matter and their form? These are their first and immediate principles—not placed in the "concave of the moon" <note>A phrase referring to the celestial spheres of Aristotelian cosmology; the author means principles are not abstract, distant concepts but are physically present in the world around us.</note>, nor imagined only by the intellect and stored within it as if in a container, but principles that have concurred to constitute and form the composite "Peter," for example, or "John" <note>Peter and John (Pietro and Giovanni) were standard names used by philosophers of the time to represent "any individual person" in a logical argument.</note>. And in this same Peter or John, these principles can almost be pointed out with a finger. And what proof, then, or what knowledge can be more evident and more certain than that which is drawn from the thing placed before one’s eyes? This is not only my thought, but that of the Prince of Philosophers <note>A standard title for Aristotle.</note> himself, who writes that first principles can be proven through the senses, meaning that sensory proof is more certain than intellectual proof. And from this it follows that a thing will, by its nature, be knowable when it is such that it can be seen with the eyes and felt with the other senses. And this is the reason why Aristotle, at the very beginning of the *Physics*, says that particulars are knowable by their nature; if we could comprehend and understand them all, we would be most wise. *...their infinite number in potentiality can only be known by He who is infinite in actuality <note>The author refers to God, who is "infinite in act" (complete and perfect), whereas created things are "infinite in potentiality" (there is no limit to how many could theoretically be created).</note>. For although some celestial creature <note>Likely referring to angels.</note> might perhaps be capable of understanding those particular things that are actually created and produced, nevertheless, because there are not so many particulars created in the world that a much greater number could not be produced—which depends solely on the freedom of God and His providence—therefore this potentiality (or to speak more clearly, all the particulars that have been created and produced, together with those that will be recreated and produced in the world) can only be known by God through His prescience <note>Foreknowledge</note>. And Aristotle alluded to part of this when he said that particulars were "known to nature," perhaps meaning the Prime Mover of nature, which is God Himself.*

*Particulars, then, are knowable by their own nature; for as much as they possess **actuality**, so much do they possess (as the philosophers say) **knowability**. And they exist actually because their matter is no longer pure potentiality but is actualized by its form, and its form no longer remains in the "womb of matter" but resides within it, actualizing it. And although this refers properly to individuals of **substance** <term>substance: the essential nature of a thing, like "a human" or "a tree"</term>, it is also understood proportionally of individuals of **accidents** <term>accidents: non-essential properties that "happen" to a substance, such as color, size, or position</term>.*

*It remains clear, then, that if we do not understand particulars, it is not because they are unintelligible by nature, but rather it happens through our own deficiency, because we cannot comprehend their infinite multitude. And therefore our intellect should not begin to understand things through the order of nature, since it cannot comprehend all particulars (which are infinite), but it must begin with the **order of doctrine**, of which our intellect is capable. This is because this order proceeds from universal things to particulars, which can be easily known by us, since our intellect is of such a nature that it properly understands the universal—being a power of the spiritual soul, and therefore delighting in universal things separated from matter and made in some way spiritual through the work of the **active intellect** <term>Active Intellect: in Renaissance philosophy, the faculty of the mind that abstracts general concepts from specific, physical examples</term>.*

*For this reason, since I wish to treat the art of painting in this book, I have chosen to follow the **order of doctrine**. And because one could err in this if I were to start from too high a level—for instance, if I wanted to begin by defining for the reader what **quality** is and how many species it has, or declaring what **habit** <term>habit: a stable quality or learned skill, like the ability to paint</term> and **disposition** are, or what a **figure** is...*

<summary>The author explains that while God can understand every specific detail of the universe, human limitation requires that we learn through "doctrine"—moving from general rules to specific examples. He applies this logic to his treatise on painting, choosing to teach the art through universal principles rather than starting with every individual detail.</summary>

...figure or form; and to demonstrate how painting, through various considerations, is understood under these species of **quality** <term>quality: in Aristotelian philosophy, one of the categories of being, describing the nature or "how" of a thing</term> (a matter that belongs more to the logician and the philosopher than to the painter). For this reason, following the precept of Horace who warns us not to begin the history of the Trojan War from Leda’s two eggs <note>original: "le due uoua di Leda." In his *Ars Poetica*, the Roman poet Horace advises starting an epic "in the middle of things" rather than with the birth of Helen of Troy from an egg, which he considered too distant a starting point for the story of the war.</note>—that is, when treating a subject, one should not take a starting point too remote from the matter at hand—I will begin instead with the **definition** of painting. This is its first and most immediate principle, as well as the most general and proper that can be considered.

Then I will show its **genus** <term>genus: the broad category a thing belongs to (e.g., "art")</term>, which is the first part of the definition; and finally, all the **differences** <term>differences: the specific characteristics that distinguish a thing from others in the same category (e.g., what makes painting different from sculpture)</term> that enter into the definition to limit its genus—which is a type of quality called **art**—and to constitute this most specific type of quality called painting.

Because the differences that make painting a particular art, distinct from all other arts in the world, are five—namely **proportion, motion, color, light,** and **perspective**—I will treat each of these differences separately in its own book in order. Thus:

*   The first book will contain a treatise on **proportion**, which is the first difference of painting.
*   The second on **motion**.
*   The third on **color**.
*   The fourth on **light**.
*   The fifth on that part of **perspective** which is necessary to the painter.

In these five books, I will follow the aforementioned "order of doctrine," which begins with the most universal and immediate principle of painting (its definition) and then proceeds to the five parts that constitute it.

However, considering that not everyone who begins to learn this art will be able to pick the fruit from this tree because it is too high—meaning that by treating the essential and principal parts of painting generally in these first five books, these general concepts might be too far removed from our senses for everyone to discern which universal principle applies to this or that particular thing—I, who greatly desire the progress and benefit even of those who are just beginning to learn this art, have decided to add a **sixth book**. In this book, I will treat **practically** what is taught **theoretically** in the first five; for this is also the proper order of teaching: that practice follows theory. And because those who begin to work practically need more than just the rules

This begins from heaven and goes down into hell, demonstrating the manner in which one must paint **God** and the **Angels**, as well as the forms and garments in which the ancients depicted the **Planets**, the **elements**, and other things. To achieve this, it was necessary to read and re-read an infinite number of books, disregarding my own private gain or convenience in order to bring benefit and service to those of my profession. It is only right—as I also pray them with all my heart’s affection—that they welcome and cherish these labors of mine, undertaken for their service and to expand this art. Let them consider how little help and light I was able to receive from the labors of others; this matter has been touched upon by so few that I could almost say, without arrogance, that I have been the first who has begun to write about it with such skill and method, easing the path so that others may walk it more swiftly in the future.*

## On the Definition of Painting. Chapter I.

**PAINTING** is an Art which, with proportionate lines and colors similar to the nature of things, following the light of perspective, imitates the nature of physical objects in such a way that it not only represents volume and relief on a flat surface, but also motion, and visibly demonstrates many affects and passions of the soul to our eyes. <note>In the Renaissance, "passions of the soul" (affetti) referred to the outward physical manifestation of internal emotions, which painters were expected to master.</note>

To clarify this definition, we must understand that in all natural things one finds "matter," which corresponds to the "genus," and "form," which corresponds to the "difference." <note>Lomazzo is using Aristotelian logic here. To define something, one must identify its broad category (genus) and the specific quality that distinguishes it from others in that category (difference).</note>

Thus, logicians say that the genus is that which declares the essence of things, and the difference is that which declares the form and essential quality of those same things.

Therefore, according to this doctrine, since I have wished to declare what painting is with the aforementioned definition, it is necessary to demonstrate its genus and its differences, by which it is distinguished and made diverse from all other sciences and arts.

The genus of painting, then, is art.

And that painting is an art is proven by the definition of "art" itself, which in short is nothing other than a right and regulated reason for the things that are to be made. <note>This is a classical definition of art derived from the Latin "recta ratio factorum" (the right reason of things to be made), emphasizing that art is an intellectual process of following rules, not just manual labor.</note>

It is also proven because all natural things are the rule and measure for the majority of the sciences and arts in the world; since they are made by God with supreme wisdom, they consequently possess within themselves all possible perfections of which they are capable. Therefore, they can serve as the correct rule for artificial things. From this, it follows clearly that painting is an Art, because it takes these natural things as its rule; it is an imitator—and so to speak, the "ape of nature"—whose quantity, relief, and color it always seeks to imitate. <note>original: "simia de l'istessa natura." The "Ape of Nature" was a common Renaissance trope used to describe the artist’s ability to mimic reality so closely that it rivaled God's creation.</note>

It achieves this with the help of Geometry, Arithmetic, Perspective, and Natural Philosophy, with such right and correct reason that it could not be more so.

But because among the arts some are "liberal" and some are "mechanical," it will not be out of place to briefly touch upon which of these painting should be numbered. <note>The "Liberal Arts" (like Grammar or Logic) were considered intellectual pursuits worthy of free men, while "Mechanical Arts" were seen as manual labor or trades. This was a major debate for Renaissance artists seeking higher social status.</note>

If this question had to be decided by authority, it would be determined quickly, for Pliny openly calls it a Liberal Art. <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman author whose "Natural History" was a primary source for Renaissance art history.</note>

But it can also be easily proven by reason.

For even though the painter cannot achieve his goal without using both hand and brush, it is nonetheless clear that in this exercise one takes on so little toil and fatigue that there is no free man in the world who would not find such an exercise pleasing and infinitely delightful.

<summary>Lomazzo defines painting as an intellectual art that imitates nature through the rules of perspective and logic. He argues that painting is a "Liberal Art" rather than a mere manual craft, emphasizing its foundation in geometry, arithmetic, and the study of human emotion.</summary>

Therefore, we read that **King Francis I of France** many times delighted in taking the stylus in hand and practicing drawing and painting. Many other Princes, both ancient and modern, have done the same; among whom we must not remain silent regarding **Charles Emmanuel, Duke of Savoy**, who—just as in every heroic virtue—likewise in this and other liberal arts, imitates and happily equals that great King Francis, his maternal grandfather, to the amazement and wonder of the whole world. They practiced these arts because they saw that in such exercise there is nothing servile or mechanical, but all is free and noble. <note>In the Renaissance, "mechanical" arts were considered lower-class manual labor, while "liberal" arts were the intellectual pursuits of free men and nobility.</note> And in truth, what free man or Prince would there be in the world who would not take delight in imitating God and Nature with the brush as much as he can? 

Furthermore, it is clear that the Geometer also uses his hands, drawing lines, circles, triangles, quadrangles, and other similar figures; yet no one has ever said that Geometry was a mechanical art just because that manual work is so slight and light that it would be absurd to say anyone became of servile condition because of it. The same logic applies to painting, in which a man tires himself so little that it cannot be said in any way that, if he is noble, he is debased by practicing it. If we also consider that painting is subordinate and subject to <term>perspective</term> (the science of light and sight), Natural Philosophy, and Geometry itself—all of which are undoubtedly liberal sciences—and furthermore that it has certain conclusions which it proves with self-evident and immediate first principles, we must necessarily conclude that it is a liberal art. 

Which specific liberal art it is among the many that exist can easily be drawn from the definition provided above. For it was first said that it represents the bulk and relief of physical things on a flat plane, excluding none, whether natural or artificial; for it is clear that the painter also depicts palaces, temples, and all other things made by hand and by art. 

Then it was said that it represents the figure on a plane, and thus it is distinguished from <term>sculpture</term>—not essentially, as we said in the preface, but "accidentally" <note>Lomazzo uses the Aristotelian sense of "accidental," meaning a quality that does not change the essential nature of a thing, such as the medium used.</note> due to the diversity of the matter with which these two arts represent natural things. Sculpture also imitates nature, but it does so by taking a body already created by God <note>meaning a three-dimensional material like stone or wood</note>, whereas the painter does it on a flat plane and surface. This is one of the primary reasons why painting should be esteemed as more ingenious and of greater excellence than sculpture: because through pure art, on a plane where there is nothing but width and length, it demonstrates and represents to the eye the third dimension, which is relief and thickness; and thus it makes a body appear in the

...on a flat surface where naturally it is not found. <note>The author is referring to the illusion of three-dimensional depth (perspective) created on a two-dimensional plane.</note> Furthermore, it is added in the definition that painting demonstrates and represents **bodily motions** to the eye. On the other side, one sees the Saints, who in a certain way seem to be just finishing their resurrection, ascending through that air to be placed at the right hand of Christ. In another part, one truly seems to see the Angels descending from heaven with the standard of the Holy Cross, and in yet another, the same Angels carrying blessed souls to the place at the right hand of **GOD**. To conclude, there is no bodily motion—whether forward or backward, to the left or to the right, upward or downward—that is not seen expressed in this skillful and admirable painting.

This is especially true in Christ, in whom one sees such kindled anger and indignation that he seems to blaze and strike like lightning; and in the Saints and the damned, in all of whom, pale and confused, the fear and terror they have of the wrathful judge is visibly discerned. In short, many motions of both the body and the soul are seen in this painting by the divine **Buonarroti**, and by the excellent **Raphael of Urbino**, and other ancient and modern painters—such as love, hate, sadness, joy, and any other motion of the soul one might wish for.

...of the figures along with the manner and proportion they require; showing, for example, in the Pharsalian War <note>The decisive battle in 48 BCE where Julius Caesar defeated Pompey the Great.</note> **Julius Caesar** in a pose that he perhaps did not strike, or putting him in the vanguard <note>The foremost part of an advancing army.</note> where he might have actually been in the rearguard, or painting him addressing and exhorting his men to fight as brave soldiers—something he might not have actually done. Beyond this <note>Meaning beyond the "poetic license" to alter historical details for dramatic effect.</note>, the painter is constrained to proceed in all his works with proportion and art. For before he outlines and draws a man, it is necessary that he knows his size and stature; for it would be a very great error to make a man of ten faces <note>A "face" was a standard unit of measurement in Renaissance art theory, based on the length of the human head; a standard figure was usually 8 to 10 "faces" tall.</note> who should be eleven or twelve. It is also necessary that he knows what proportion the forehead has to the nose, and the nose to the mouth and the chin, and the whole face to the neck; in short, he must seek to know the proportion of all things, both natural and artificial.

And because it seems almost impossible for one man alone to know all of this, the most prudent **Apelles** <note>A celebrated painter of ancient Greece, active in the 4th century BCE, known for his technical perfection.</note>, after he had painted something he wanted to be perfect, used to put it out in public and hide himself behind it. He would listen to what was judged regarding the proportion and art of his painting; and according as each person judged those things of which they had knowledge and experience, he would go about reforming the work. Conversely, he also rejected the judgment of those who wanted to judge parts that did not belong to their profession. This happened with a cobbler <note>A shoemaker.</note> who, not content with having discussed the foot of one of his figures, also wanted to give judgment on the other parts; to him, **Apelles** said, *let the shoemaker not go beyond his shoe.* <note>original: "ne sutor vltra crepidam." This famous Latin proverb warns people not to offer criticism outside their field of expertise.</note>

Besides this, the painter also has to use these proportionate lines with a certain method and rule, which is nothing other than that which **Nature** herself uses and proceeds with when making a composition. In such a composition, **Nature** first presupposes **matter** <note>In the Aristotelian sense, "matter" is the raw, unformed substance of a thing.</note>, which is something without form, without beauty, and without boundaries; and then into that **matter**, she introduces **form**, which is something beautiful and defined. So does the painter, who takes a panel which on its face has nothing but a surface or a plane without beauty, whose parts have no ends or boundaries; and he beautifies and defines it by outlining and drawing on it a man, a horse, or a column; and by shaping or polishing all its contours. In short, he imitates with lines the nature of the thing he paints, as much in width as in length, bulk, and thickness. 

And because a precept of **Michelangelo**'s is very relevant in this place, I will not fail to report it simply, leaving the interpretation and understanding of it to the prudent reader. It is said, then, that **Michelangelo** once gave this advice to Mar- <note>The text breaks off mid-name, likely referring to the painter Marcello Venusti.</note>

<summary>The author explains that while painters have license to adjust historical details for impact, they must strictly follow the rules of proportion and anatomy. He uses the philosophy of Matter and Form to describe the act of painting as an imitation of Nature's creative process.</summary>

--- Page 65 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of artistic theory, transitioning from the anecdote of Apelles to the specific technical advice attributed to Michelangelo. It focuses on the "serpentine" and "pyramidal" forms as the essence of grace in movement.</meta>

...[Mar]co of Siena <note>Marco Pino (c. 1521–1583), a Mannerist painter who moved from Siena to Rome and studied under Michelangelo.</note>, a painter and his disciple, that he should always make the figure **pyramidal**, **serpentine**, and multiplied by one, two, and three. And in this precept, it seems to me, consists the entire secret of painting. For the greatest grace and charm that a figure can possess is that it appears to move, which painters call the <term>fury of the figure</term> <note>original: "furia de la figura"; this refers to the lifelike energy, spirit, or dynamic tension within a depicted body.</note>.

And to represent this motion, there is no form more suited than that of a flame of fire, which, according to **Aristotle** and all the Philosophers, is the most active element of all, and the shape of its flame is the most suited to motion of all. This is because it has a cone and a sharp point with which it seems to want to break through the air and ascend to its sphere <note>In Aristotelian cosmology, fire naturally moves upward toward its "natural place" or sphere above the air.</note>. So, when the figure has this form, it will be most beautiful. 

This form can also be used in two ways: one is where the cone of the pyramid, which is the sharpest part, is placed at the top, and the base, which is the widest part of the pyramid, is placed at the bottom like fire. Then, one must show in the figure a breadth and width, such as in the legs or the clothes at the bottom, and at the top it must be thinned in the manner of a pyramid, showing one shoulder and making the other recede and <term>foreshorten</term> <note>original: "scorzi"; a technique used to create the illusion of an object receding strongly into the distance.</note>, so that the body twists, and one shoulder is hidden and the other is projected and revealed. 

The figure being painted can also stand in the manner of a pyramid that has its base and widest part turned toward the top, and the cone toward the bottom. In this way, the figure will show width in the upper part, either by showing both shoulders, extending the arms, showing one leg and hiding the other, or in some other similar way, as the wise painter judges will suit him best. 

But because there are two kinds of pyramids—one straight, like the one near Saint Peter's in Rome, which is called the <margin>pyramid of **Julius Caesar**</margin> <note>Now known as the Pyramid of Cestius; in the Renaissance, it was popularly but incorrectly believed to be the tomb of Julius Caesar.</note>, and the other in the shape of a flame of fire—and this latter one **Michelangelo** calls <term>serpentine</term> <note>original: "serpentinata"; the S-shaped spiral pose that became a hallmark of Mannerist art.</note>, the painter must accompany this pyramidal form with the serpentine form, which represents the tortuosity of a living snake when it moves, which is the true form of a wavering flame of fire. This means that the figure should represent the shape of a capital letter **S**, either upright or reversed, like this: **∫**; for then it will have its beauty. 

And this form must be observed not only in the whole, but also in each of the parts.
