...the logic of proportion, which we will treat extensively in this book. For taking the part from the knee to the foot, the thickest part is in double proportion to the thinnest; and the thighs are in triple proportion compared to the narrowest part. Now, returning to our definition, it remains for us to explain that part where it is said that painting represents things with **color** similar to natural things. In this, one must consider that since the painter is a craftsman, he must proceed according to the method of **Nature**, which first presupposes (as all the natural philosophers say) the **matter** of things, and then gives them **form**. But because the making and creating of the substances of things belongs, as the theologians say, to an infinite power—which is not found in any pure creature—it is necessary for the painter to take something in place of matter, and this is **proportionate quantity**, which is the matter of painting. Painters should consider this deeply: that "proportionate quantity" means the same as <term>disegno</term> <note>original: "disegno"; in Renaissance theory, this term encompasses both the physical act of drawing and the intellectual concept or internal design of a work.</note>, and this same *disegno* is the substantial matter of painting. And therefore, let them be warned that however excellent and miraculous they may be in coloring, if they do not have *disegno*, they do not have the matter of painting, and consequently, they are deprived of its substantial part. 

It is not denied, however, that the power of coloring is very great. For just as individual men, if they consisted of nothing but matter (in which it is clear they all agree), would all be one and the same thing, and that difference so pleasing to our eyes among so many particular men would not be seen in the world—a difference made by the <term>seven individuating circumstances</term> <note>original: "sette particolarità che chiamano i Filosofi individuanti"; these are the philosophical "accidents" (form, figure, place, time, lineage, country, and name) that distinguish one individual from another of the same species.</note>, which are seven substantial accidents that cause individuation and singularity in substance, and are the cause of so much diversity and beauty—so if the painter were only to draw a proportionate man, just and equal to nature, because many men are found equal in quantity, certainly by quantity alone that man would not be recognized. But when, beyond the *disegno* and the proportionate, just, and equal quantity, he adds the **similar color**, he then gives the final form and perfection to the figure. He makes it so that everyone who sees it discerns which man it is, and can say, for example, that it is the **Emperor Charles V**, or **Philip** his son; that he is a <term>melancholic</term> man, or a <term>phlegmatic</term>, <term>sanguine</term>, or <term>choleric</term> one <note>These refer to the four humors or temperaments believed to govern human health and personality in Renaissance medicine.</note>; that it is the figure of a man who loves, who fears, of a youth full of shame and blushing. In conclusion, the figure will have all its natural perfection, so that he who [is depicted] will be immediately recognized in it...

This is seen very clearly. For the sculptor toils in nothing else but making the figure have the same <term>quantity</term> <note>original: "quantità"; in this context, it refers to the physical dimensions, volume, and mass of the object.</note> as the natural figure which he imitates; thus, what the sculptor properly does is to make the figure *equal* to the natural one. This cannot be said to be making it perfectly *similar* to it; for the philosophers <note>This refers to Aristotelian physics and logic, which distinguished between "quantity" (size/number) and "quality" (attributes like color or heat).</note> say that in quantity one does not properly find "similarity," but only in <term>quality</term> <note>original: "qualità"</note>, and the color that the painter employs is a quality. 

Because of this, the painter gives the figure its proper appearance, making it resemble the natural original, which is a most true and most proper "quality." And although one thing is said to be "similar" to another when it has the same quantity, it is nevertheless said improperly; for speaking properly, it should be called *equal* and not *similar*. This is because, as I have said, similarity is only found in quality, and the sculptor only deals with quantity, in which only *equality* is found. 

But the painter, in his <term>drawing</term> <note>original: "disegno"; here referring to the structural plan or linear composition.</note>, not only seeks to give the right and true quantity to the figure and make it equal to the natural original, as the sculptor does, but he further adds the quality, which is color. He gives the figure both quality and similarity, which, as I said just before, the sculptor cannot give.

## On the Division of Painting. Chapter II.

**P**ainting is divided into theory and practice. Theory provides general precepts that everyone who wishes to become excellent and famous in this art must observe. Practice provides rules of <term>prudence</term> <note>In this context, "prudence" refers to the artist's practical wisdom and ability to make good judgments when applying rules to specific, real-world problems.</note> and judgment, teaching how one must put into operation what has been stated and imagined generally. This I have reserved for the sixth book, which is titled "On Practice." And because <term>History</term> <note>original: "Hiſtoria"; in art theory, this refers to narrative painting—the depiction of significant historical, biblical, or mythological events—which was considered the highest form of art.</note> is also necessary to the painter, as I have said elsewhere, following the same order of prudence, I have compiled another book for it, which is the seventh.

Theory is divided into five parts: the first treats proportion; the second, the position and situation of the figure; the third, color; the fourth, light; and the fifth, perspective. Proportion is divided into two parts: one is called the proportion proper to the thing one wishes to represent and paint; the other is called proportion to the eye, or in perspective. For example, a man of average stature is nine or ten faces in length. His proper proportion is that the face, relative to the whole body, stands in a <term>ninefold</term> <note>original: "nouenaria"</note> or <term>tenfold</term> <note>original: "decupla"</note> proportion. Regarding this proper and natural proportion or measure of things, I shall treat it in this book. 

The other proportion is with respect to the view, and it is different. Because according to how far and distant the thing is from the eye, the eye itself judges the proportion that the head or face has with the entire body. Thus, if a sculptor makes a statue of a man ten faces high, following the proper and natural proportion, and then places it in a high location, the eye will naturally judge that statue to be disproportionate without a doubt. And the reason is, because when a statue is placed in a high position, and the person seeing it is in a low position, the head, the face, and the higher and superior parts reach the eye at an **acute angle**, while the legs and the lower and inferior parts reach it with a more **obtuse angle**; therefore, everyone who sees it will conclude that it has a small head, face, and upper parts compared to the legs and lower parts. 

And the philosophical and perspectival reason is that when that statue represents itself in all the surrounding air—which is <term>diaphanous</term> <note>A technical term for transparent, often used in historical texts to describe air or water that allows light and images to pass through.</note>—by means of certain <term>visual species</term> <note>In ancient and Renaissance optics, "species" were thought to be invisible "likenesses" or "images" that objects shed into the air to travel to the viewer's eye. original: "spetie visuali"</note> (which are like the images seen in a mirror when a person looks into it), those species reach the eye within **visual lines** made in the shape of a **pyramidal figure**, with the cone and the angle of the figure touching our eye. 

Thus, the further away an object stands, the more acute is the cone or angle of the pyramid, and the object appears smaller; and the closer the object stands to the cone of the pyramid <note>Meaning closer to the eye, where the vertex of the pyramid is located.</note>, the more obtuse and large the angle becomes, and consequently, the object appears larger. 

Now, the painter does not have to observe both of these proportions in his figure; indeed, it is impossible for him to observe them. And if he wishes to become excellent, he must take care **never to give a figure its own proper and natural proportion**, for that would be a very great error. Indeed, all those painters and sculptors who have given their works the proper and natural proportions of the object have erred greatly and against the rules of painting; as, for example, if a living man is ten "faces" <note>A "face" (the distance from the hairline to the chin) was a standard unit of measurement in art theory for determining the proportions of the human body.</note> in length, and they paint or sculpt him likewise as ten faces.

I mean to say that if the place is high and the view is low, he must make the head and the higher parts of the figure somewhat larger than is natural. Because in this way, the eye that sees it will judge it to be proportioned.

I have observed many skilled painters who, with very good reason—this being the duty of the art—represent the Pope, the Emperor, the Soldier, and every other person with the <term>decorum</term> <note>In Renaissance art theory, *decorum* (propriety) meant that every figure should be depicted in a way that suits their age, sex, social standing, and the specific situation.</note> that reason dictates they should have. In this, the painter shows himself to be an expert in his art, representing not the action that the Pope or Emperor might have happened to be doing by chance, but what he ought to have been doing, out of respect for the majesty and dignity of his station. 

And this is the method and the order of prudence, which must be observed not only in this aspect but in all others—namely in proportion, by helping and supplying the defects of Nature with Art. Thus, if an Emperor is disproportionate, the painter should not express all of that disproportion in the portrait; and if he is too pale, he must help him with a little liveliness of color, but in such a way and with such moderation that the portrait does not lose its likeness, and so that the defect of Nature is skillfully covered with the veil of art. And in these movements <note>The "movements" or "motions" refers to the expressive actions and underlying vitality of the figures.</note> Leonardo, Raphael, Michelangelo, Polidoro, and Gaudenzio <note>Leonardo da Vinci, Raphael Sanzio, Michelangelo Buonarroti, Polidoro da Caravaggio, and Gaudenzio Ferrari—all titans of the High Renaissance and Mannerist periods.</note> were rare masters.

Color, together with light, is likewise considered in two ways: naturally and in perspective, just as we have said regarding proportion. Natural illuminated color is that which a man or the thing one wishes to represent naturally possesses; and we call it "natural" in this context not according to the strict definition of the Philosophers, but after the manner of painters. For example, that part of a natural body that looks straight ahead and stands opposite the Sun has three degrees of red color and receives another three degrees of light from the Sun. Now, if the painter wishes to represent this part exactly as it is seen in nature, he will do so by applying three degrees of red color and another three of light color <note>Likely referring to white or a tint used for highlights.</note> with which he will express the light; and thus he will naturally represent the color and the natural light.

Color illuminated through the art of perspective is that which is similar to the natural, but it is not achieved by taking three degrees of red and three of light to express the three degrees of red and three of light found in nature. Instead, it is achieved by considering the distance and the remoteness of the place from which the painting is to be seen. Therefore, if the location is very high, the painter will mix with the red color three and a third degrees—or more or less, depending on the amount of light that is lost due to the distance of the place—so that the painting will thus come to be exactly like the natural. To put it in a word: he will mix as much more light color with the red as the painting loses in clarity from being too high. For this reason Titian and the most talented Polidoro, by perfectly understanding this secret of light in perspective, gave such great relief and vigor...

...rial to his paintings. Now, of these two ways of coloring, the painter will follow that of perspective, for that same reason I just alleged when speaking of proportion. And so, if he wishes to paint three or four men, one behind the other, it will be necessary for all of them to have, <term>for example</term> <note>original: "verbi gratia"</note>, four degrees of color, and all receive four degrees of light; but it will also be more necessary, in order to represent that man who stands further away, to mix in so much less bright color as he loses that light by being seen from a distance. Because although such men receive equal degrees of color and light, nevertheless the color and light of the one who is further away comes to the eye with a sharper <term>angle of the pyramid</term> <note>This refers to the "visual pyramid," a concept in Renaissance optics where light rays travel from the object to the eye, forming a pyramid shape. A "sharper" or more acute angle means the object is further away and occupies less of the visual field.</note>; and thus he cannot be seen as clearly as the one who is closer; and the eye judges that he has less light because he cannot be seen with such clarity.

Nor is this at all contrary to what I have already said: that when a painting is to stay in a high place, one must increase the brightness as much as the eye loses due to the distance of the location. Because when many figures are painted in a single picture or canvas, one behind the other, if the picture is in a distant and high place, the painter will put more bright color in the figure that is feigned to be closer to the eye, according to how much clarity it loses by the distance of the location. But he cannot represent the other man in the same plane—who is feigned to be further away—unless he diminishes the light. And therefore, if he gives three degrees of bright color to the figure he feigns to be nearest, he must give less light to the figure behind him for the reason stated. 

But this will be treated at greater length in the <term>Book of Lights</term> and in the <term>Book of Perspective</term>. In this first book, we will treat the <term>natural proportion</term> and the specific proportion of things, both natural and some artificial: not because the painter must follow this proportion—since he must always have the proportion of perspective and visual lines proposed to the eye—but because it is necessary to first understand this natural and proper proportion of things to know then how to portray it and transfer it to the view and perspective of the eye, as will be treated in the book of perspective.

# PREFACE #

...or members of the thing seen: such that what delights and pleases us, delights and pleases for no other reason than that it possesses within itself the order of proportion, which consists in the measurement of the parts; and therefore all human inventions possess as much beauty and goodness as they are more ingeniously proportioned. Therefore, following Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman author of 'De architectura,' whose writings were the foundation of Renaissance architectural and artistic theory.</note>, whoever wishes to proceed with reason in his works must necessarily know the nature and power of proportions. Having understood this with beautiful and subtle discernment, he will not only be an excellent judge of the works of the ancients and moderns, but also an inventor and craftsman of rare and excellent things in his own right. Now, from proportion follow and result infinite and important effects, the principal of which is the majesty and beauty in bodies called <term>Eurythmia</term> <note>From the Greek *eurythmos*, meaning "well-proportioned." Vitruvius used it to describe the graceful and harmonious appearance of a work's parts.</note> by Vitruvius. For whenever a well-composed thing is seen, it is said to possess beauty; and by "proportion," in short, nothing else is meant than the due beauty in all things, which brings to the eyes all those delights and pleasures that can be perceived through that sense and penetrated with the eye of the intellect.

<margin>1</margin>
How important this beauty and majesty in bodies is can be seen more than clearly in matters belonging to divine worship. From the majesty and beauty of sacred images—instilled in them by this <term>Eurythmia</term> and <term>symmetry</term> <note>In classical art theory, symmetry refers to the harmonious "commensurability" or proportional relationship between all parts of a work, rather than just mirror-image balance.</note>—it is a marvelous thing how much piety, religion, and reverence toward God and His Saints increases in our souls. This is as we read of the Jupiter <note>original: "Gioue"</note> sculpted by Phidias <note>original: "Fidia"</note> in Elis; it so increased the religious devotion of those peoples. This will occur all the more in us Christians. For whenever we see this majesty expressed in a Christ, will we not undoubtedly be more inflamed to the contemplation and consideration of Him, and to adore Him? And in a Virgin Mary, will we not be more incited to prayer and to pleas for our sins? Therefore, knowing the excellence and dignity of this proportion—so pleasing to the sight and such a sweet demonstrator of beautiful things—the ancient Zeuxis <note>original: "Zeusi," a famous Greek painter of the 5th century BCE.</note> persuaded all of Greece, when it was at its height, that paintings in which this majesty was perceived should be given to Princes and to sacred temples. They were considered things that could not be valued with a price, being the works of those who were held as Gods among men; for they represented almost everything that the Great God had manufactured, and moreover, they added beauty where nature had failed by always choosing the finest of visual delights. Nor is proportion the principal ornament of painting alone, but of all the arts; for (as Vitruvius says) since it is contain—

It is indeed true that the painter (as Leon Battista Alberti <note>Leon Battista Alberti (1404–1472) was a foundational Renaissance humanist, architect, and principal theorist of art who argued that painting should be based on mathematics and the study of nature.</note> asserts), because he considers it most perfectly in relation to the human body, possesses greater dignity than the others who concern themselves with it. For this reason, the ancients, honoring painting above all as the mistress of this proportion, called almost all other artisans "craftsmen" <note>original: "fabri"</note>, but did not place the painter in that number.

## *On the necessity and definition of Proportion.*
### *Chapter I.*

**N**ot without reason did the Ancient Greeks—at the time when painting was continually receiving perfection and approaching its peak through the work of Simantes, Euphenides, Aristides, Eupompus of Sicyon, and Pamphilus of Macedon (an illustrious painter and master of Apelles, who was the first to join the knowledge of good letters <note>A reference to a liberal arts education, including literature and philosophy.</note> with painting)—guide themselves by reason and art more than any of their predecessors. They considered how all things formed without proportion and measure could in no way possess harmony, nor represent beauty and grace to judicious onlookers. They used to say that it was impossible to make a good painting, or even a tolerable one, without the help of Geometry and Arithmetic, and that it was therefore necessary to know them. And King Philip of Macedon <note>Philip II, the father of Alexander the Great, who was a patron of the arts.</note> likewise approved of this. And it is more than true (letting the purely practical <note>original: "puri prattichi." The author is dismissing those who paint by habit or intuition alone without understanding the underlying mathematical theory.</note> chatter on) that whoever has no knowledge of these two disciplines, as I said in its place, cannot possibly know the probable or true proportions and measures of bodies; the necessity of which proportions will be made known in this book. For it is clearly understood that painting without this is like a piece of marble roughed out without measure or reason; just as, for example, columns that are too thin, or thick, or short, or long, are still columns, and dwarfs, hunchbacks, and the crippled are still men. This third book, then, will contain nothing other than the universal proportion of the principal things, from which all others derive. To begin which, it is necessary to consider...

-># BOOK ONE.<-

<margin>C 2</margin>
<meta>Catchword: hanno</meta>

[con]sider <note>Continuing the word "considerare" from the previous page.</note> what the power of this proportion is, and of the parts that belong to it.

Proportion is nothing other than a consonance and correspondence of the measurements of the parts among themselves and with the whole in every work that is made; and this consonance is called "commodulation" <note>original: *commodulatione*; from the Vitruvian term *commodulatio*, referring to the internal mathematical symmetry of a structure.</note> by Vitruvius. For a "module" <note>original: *modulo*; a standard unit of measure used to establish the proportions of an entire building or figure.</note> is the name given to that measurement which is taken first, by which both the parts and the whole are measured. This is what (leaving aside for now its types, which I will distinguish in their proper places), having been lost for so long, caused the just and true form of man to go misunderstood. Consequently, no building ever emerged that possessed reason, despite great expense and much material; and the painters themselves, not understanding what they were doing, made disproportionate figures instead of proportionate men. This is evidenced by the buildings, temples, statues, and paintings made throughout the world—and especially in Italy from the time of Constantine the Great <note>Emperor Constantine (reigned 306–337 AD); Lomazzo identifies his reign as the beginning of a "Dark Age" for classical art standards.</note> until the time of Giotto in Tuscany <note>Giotto di Bondone (c. 1267–1337), the artist credited with reviving the imitation of nature.</note> and Andrino of Edessa of Pavia in Lombardy <note>Andrino di Edessa (14th century), a painter from Pavia whom Lomazzo regarded as a key figure in the Lombard tradition.</note>.

And this, finally, is that which, being understood, so satisfies the judgment that one not only learns of oneself to do what one wishes, but to recognize the beauty of statues and figures, both of the ancients and the moderns. Without it, the painter is not only unworthy of the name of "Painter," but is like one who believes he can support himself upon the water, only to be submerged. For, in short, it is impossible to form anything that possesses harmony or suitability within itself if there is no proportion and measurement of the parts, rationally numbered and understood.

Now, this most excellent part of painting I shall strive to teach to those students in whom the rational soul performs its operations by means of well-disposed and proportionate bodily organs. For these students will delight in knowing the power of nature through art; and with diligent study—doing marvelous things by means of the primary rays of the divine light and the proportionate means of virtue—they will penetrate so far that they will immediately recognize anything disproportionate as something contrary to them. To this perfection, on the contrary, those who have disproportionate and intemperate bodily organs can never attain, for they have also corrupted their judgment. I speak of some who, not knowing the virtue of proportion, seek nothing but that cursed, charming surface of colors applied in their own way; and so they go about all day plastering so many canvases and facades throughout the world, to the great laughter of those who understand, and with sorrow that Art should be so mistreated by such clumsy and ignorant men; for just as in this part they do not...

He argues that true artistic judgment is impossible without understanding proportion, which he links to the health of the "rational soul" and its bodily organs.</summary>

## Of the External Members of the Human Body. Chapter V.

**F**or greater clarity, I will come in this place to name all the members, or rather external parts, that form the human body, as these are of greater necessity to the painter than the rest for understanding the proportions which will be treated in the following chapters. Now the highest part—to begin from here—is commonly called, as everyone understands, the head, and by some the *capo*, and by such also the Pumpkin <note>original: "Zucca"; a colloquial or slang term for the head used in the Renaissance.</note>, the summit of which is called the sinciput <note>original: "sincipite"; the front of the skull from the forehead to the crown.</note>. That place on the head where the hair turns in a circle is called the vertex; and the root of the hair above the forehead, the center; the anterior part where the hair begins to grow is called the forelock; the parting of the hair that begins here and goes to the vertex—whether in males in the Nazarene fashion <note>original: "al modo Nazareno"; referring to hair parted down the middle, similar to traditional depictions of Jesus of Nazareth.</note> or in females—is called the parting line <note>original: "scriminale".</note>; the long hair of women is called tresses; curled hair, locks; straight-hanging hair, *zazzare* <note>original: "Zazzare"; a long, bob-like hairstyle popular in the Renaissance.</note>; gathered hair, a tuft; twisted hair, frizzy; those that are full of curls, ringlets; and the mane of hair at the nape of the neck is called the *cuticagna* <note>original: "cuticagna"; the scalp at the back of the head.</note>. 

The forehead contains the entire space from the roots of the front hair down to above the eyebrows. The temple <note>original: "Polso"; literally "pulse," referring here to the anatomical temple where the pulse is easily felt.</note> is the highest point of the parts of the forehead that ends at the hair; the "melon" <note>original: "melone"; a term for the rounded protrusion of the frontal bone above the eyebrows.</note> is that swelling above the eyebrows on the forehead; the temple area terminates between the forehead, the *polso*, and the ear. The Ear is that circle contained within the space between the temples and the upper cheek to the root of the hair on the side of the head; its lower part is called the earlobe <note>original: "grasello".</note>, and the hole through which sound enters is the ear canal <note>original: "mirenga".</note>. The eyebrows are those thick hairs where the forehead ends below; and that space in the middle that separates one eyebrow from the other is called the glabella. The upper eyelid is that small part that surrounds the eye from above. The Eye is that which is contained by the upper and lower eyelids. The black of the eye is that round image in the middle of this little circle...

The upper part of the hand extends from the bracelet to the first joints of the fingers and is called the **comb** <term>pettine</term> <note>Referring to the metacarpus, the bones forming the structure of the hand</note>. The joints of each finger are three, except for the thumb which has only two, and the spaces between one and the other are called **internodes**, or **articles**, of which there are two per finger, except the thumb which has only one. In that space or article which is from the last joint of the fingers to their tips is the **nail**; the boundary of which is called the **crown** (I speak of where the flesh or skin attaches). The hand ends from the wrist or bracelet down to the tips, or let us say the extremities, of the fingers. 

The leg contains these parts: first the **hip** or **haunch** <note>original: "anca ouero galone"</note>, which begins from the joint of the torso and ends with the legs; it is called the upper part of the **thigh**, which is that which extends to the beginning of the **knee**. The **inner thigh** <term>vargo</term> is the part inside the thigh, below the genitals; the **groin** <term>anguinaglia</term> is the front part of the thighs. The **knee** begins from the ball of the back <note>the patella/kneecap</note>, which is at the end of the thigh, and extends until below that, to the beginning of the...

## On the proportion of the human body of ten faces in length and width. Chapter V.

**I**t is only right that, following the order of the ancient Greeks, this body—whose proportions and harmonies I particularly intend to treat—should be made similar to and in proportion with every other artificial body that is the most beautiful to be found in nature, in which are included all artificial proportions and harmonies, both greater and lesser. This will be seen in this chapter and in those that follow. For this reason, I have wished to place this [system] before the others, as their foundation, which by right reason contains them all within itself. This figure, then, is first divided into **ten faces** <note>A classical system of measurement where the length of the human face—from the chin to the hairline—serves as the basic unit; a body "ten faces" high was considered the ideal "heroic" proportion</note> or parts, one of which is contained (I speak of its length)...

Thus each of these resonates to each of the others in a **sesquialter proportion**, which is called a **Fifth**. 

Furthermore, one of these spaces is as large as the distance from one **nipple** <term>capitello delle mammelle</term> to the other, and it is the same distance from each of these to the pit of the throat, whereby they form an **equilateral triangle**. The circumference of the head from the eyebrows to the nape of the neck behind is in **double proportion** with the whole head. The circumference of the waist down to its depth—that is, from the front to the back—is in **triple sesquialter proportion** <note>A 3.5:1 or 7:2 ratio</note>, and can also be made in unison with the length of the trunk or torso of three "faces." ## On the slender proportion of the male body of ten faces.

### Chapter VI.

**T**his proportion of a long and thin body must be regulated (with due measure, however) in imitation of the form of the body of <term>Mars</term> <note>The Roman god of war</note>, god of battles among the heathens, as he who—due to heat and dryness—has a body conforming to this: that is, long and slender. This will also serve for any body that possesses his nature: that is, the impetuous, choleric, cruel, warlike, discordant, bold, reckless, and those quick to anger. These are all vigorous and strong, for no other reason than the thickness of their bones, stripped of a multitude of flesh. Therefore, they must have hard bodies, harsh joints with prominent connections, and very wide nostrils because of the heat that dilates them; and such must be the eyes, the mouth, and the other orifices, as will be described more minutely in its proper place, it being enough here to speak of the proportion. This body is divided in length—that is, from the top of the head to the soles of the feet—into thirty equal spaces, which for now I call degrees, and each of these is divided into ten equal spaces, which I call <meta>catchword: mando / I call</meta>

### On the proportion of the young body of nine heads.
### Chapter VIII.

**I** judge that if Francesco Mazzolino <note>better known as Parmigianino (1503–1540), famous for his "Mannerist" style of elongated figures</note> had never painted any
figure of another type—that is, the crude, heavy, and melancholic—that he
would have been considered a wonder of the world, since he so excellently represented slender figures, guided by a refined desire, just as
he himself was. Thus, clearly, if he had represented only
Apollos, Bacchuses, Nymphs, and the like, he would have with the greatest judgment introduced his so-beloved slender proportion, and at times
exceedingly lithe. But having likewise represented it
in Prophets—as in his *Moses* in Parma—and in a Madonna upon
an <term>Ancona</term> <note>a large, often multi-paneled altarpiece</note> with certain Angels nearby in the same city, and in other similar figures contrary to such proportion, he has given an example
to all other painters of how one must avoid this error, which
he himself could easily have avoided. For since he was judged
in a certain way to be the spirit of Raphael of Urbino <note>meaning he was seen as the artistic successor to Raphael’s grace</note> by that same painter—or rather the light of art—he could have taken him as an example, just
as he, who represented so many figures, introduced as many proportions
conforming to their various natures or roles. For this reason his
old men are seen as weary and bowed, the young men as agile and slender according to their nature, and so on for all of them. From this example, it can be understood that the painter must not restrict himself to one and the same proportion in all his figures; because
besides demonstrating no historical truth, it represents the
greatest flaw there is in art: that is, figures that appear to be
twins,

And so that one may be warned of this error and understand this proportion, as it is the one used for young men who possess beauty, such as those who are slender and graceful, with a certain noble manner of fierce spirit: Raphael of Urbino expressed it in the *Saint George Killing the Serpent*, which is seen in the Church of Saint Victor of the Friars in Milan; and in the *Saint Michael* found in France at Fontainebleau; and in 그 Saint George which he formerly made for the Duke of Urbino on a panel. But to treat it exactly, by way of precepts, one must first know that the slender, youthful body of <term>nine heads</term> <note>a system where the total height of the body is nine times the height of the head, creating a tall, elegant figure</note> is, from the top of the head to the tip of the chin, the ninth part of its length. And from here upward, through the straight line of the face, it is one-tenth (I speak as far as the root of the hair); and even one-eleventh, as I have observed in the *Saint Michael* of Raphael, and also in the ancient *Apollo* <note>the Apollo Belvedere, a famous Roman marble statue considered the pinnacle of aesthetic perfection during the Renaissance</note>. 

But however it is done, this space is divided into three equal parts: one for the forehead, another for the nose, and the other down to the chin. It is indeed true that in the space of eleven parts—because of a certain tuft of hair that is shown—the forehead is less than a third part; and this rule was held, as is seen by the statues, by all of Greek antiquity. Truly, a low forehead represented something better and more graceful than a high one.

### On the proportion of the male body of eight heads. Chapter IX.

**B**ecause in every work, the entire body of a figure and the whole <term>narrative composition</term> <note>original: "Istoria", a term used by Renaissance theorists to describe a complex scene with multiple figures telling a story</note> together are always the principal concern, as the logic of the individual parts must relate back to it; therefore, let no painter think that however well he can execute a single thing in a work—beyond what is required by the logic of the whole—he will gain any praise for it. Rather, he can be certain of reporting nothing but shame for this; for it is certain that by letting one part dominate another, the latter is offended, and the larger part likewise suffers, because the other parts cannot look toward the correct order. 

And so many excellent painters, both ancient and modern, having realized they were carried away by an excessive desire to do well, have left their works unfinished, unable to remedy them except by destroying what (however admirable it was) they had done. Witness to this is that most famous ancient painter **Euphranor** <note>A celebrated Greek sculptor and painter of the 4th century BCE</note>, who, while painting the twelve Gods in Athens, made the figure of **Neptune** so excellent—in proportion, in colors, and in every other aspect—that when he later wanted to paint the figure of **Jupiter** with an even more beautiful appearance, having exhausted all his mental energy on the first figure, he was unable not only to make Jupiter succeed, but even the other Gods. 

**Zeuxis** <note>A legendary Greek painter famous for his extreme realism</note> also felt ashamed because of the "naturalness," so to speak, of his grapes and the failure in the boy. <note>This refers to the story where Zeuxis painted grapes so realistically that birds flew down to peck at them; however, Zeuxis was unhappy because he felt that if he had painted the boy holding the grapes just as well, the birds would have been too afraid to approach.</note> Among the moderns, **Leonardo [da] Vinci**, that most stupendous painter, while painting a Last Supper of **Christ** with the **Apostles** in the refectory of **Santa Maria delle Grazie** in Milan, and having painted all the Apostles, made **James the Great** and **James the Less** with such beauty and majesty that when he later wanted to depict Christ, he could never bring that holy face to completion or perfection, despite being most singular [in his talent]. 

Desperate and unable to do anything else, he went to consult with **Bernardo Zenale** <note>An Italian painter and architect (c. 1460–1526) who worked in Milan and was a friend of Leonardo</note>, who, to comfort him, said: "Oh Leonardo, this error you have committed is so great that no one but God can remove it. For it is not in your power, nor anyone else's, to give greater divinity and beauty to any figure than what you have given to James the Great and the Less; so be of good cheer, and leave Christ thus unfinished, because you will not make Him—"

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence, likely continuing Zenale's advice on the following page: "you will not make Him [as beautiful as the Apostles]." Catchword: ser (likely "serà" or "servirà").</meta>

### On the proportion of the virile body of seven heads. Chapter X.

**P**ythagoras, the greatest Philosopher, bears ample witness to the truth of the rules regarding the proportion of bodies. By means of these rules, by discerning the proportion of **Hercules** from that of the other Gods, he discovered how great the size of his body was, and consequently by how much he surpassed other men. He did this by considering (as **Aulus Gellius** <note>A 2nd-century Roman author who recorded this legend of Pythagoras in his *Attic Nights*.</note> writes) the size of Hercules' feet. With these feet, Hercules had measured out the <term>stadium</term> <note>A Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet.</note> in Achaia before the temple of **Olympian Jupiter**, where the **Olympic games** were celebrated every five years. This stadium was exactly 625 feet long, just like the other stadia of Greece, and yet it was of greater total length than the others were <note>Pythagoras reasoned that because Hercules' foot was larger than a standard man's, a track of 625 "Herculean" feet would be longer than a track of 625 standard feet, allowing him to calculate Hercules' exact height.</note>. From this example, it is clearly understood that a single proportion cannot serve everyone, as they are as different from each other as bodies are different by nature. 

And therefore, I will proceed to treat the proportion of the well-squared body of seven heads, with strong, robust, and prominent limbs. This body is first in length, from the top of the head to the sole of the foot, seven heads. That is: from the top of the head to the tip of the chin [is one head]; and from the chin to the pit of the throat is one-tenth and one-eleventh [of the total height]; to the top of the shoulder two-elevenths; to the tip of the chin one-seventh; to the top of the forehead one-tenth, which is divided into three equal spaces, of which one makes the forehead, the other the nose, and the third from below [the nose] to the chin. ### *On the Proportion of the Female of Ten Faces. Chap. XI.*

**A**lthough nature, that most wise mistress, is ordinarily accustomed to vary in such a way that every individual is different in beauty and proportion, it is nonetheless clearly seen through experience that she demonstrates her art with greater skill and study in certain beautiful individuals that she creates. Thus I—since art, following the example of nature itself, must also always seek to imitate the most perfect things—wishing to treat the proportion of the female, will not extend myself to treat the proportion of all women produced by nature, which would be impossible; but I will treat only the most beautiful proportions found in the most graceful and beautiful women. And to begin, the proportion of the female in general from the summit—from the head to the sole—is sixty parts, that is, degrees of five minutes each, which then total three hundred. The specific measurements are first: from the top of the head to the tip of the shoulder, which is the same as the <term>collarbones</term> <note>original: "clauicole"</note>, are ten degrees; and from here to the top of the <term>shoulder blades</term> <note>original: "scapule"</note>, that is where the neck ends at the sides, there are eight; and to the end of the chin, seven and two minutes. From here to the root of the hair, which is the whole face, are six degrees; of which the forehead has two up to the eyebrows, the nose has another two; and the other two are from there to the chin. From the hairline to the <term>crown</term> <note>original: "vertice"</note>, there is one degree and one minute; and the rest from here to the top of the head is four minutes. But here it must be noted that these proportions are not meant as circumferences, but only as diameters in width and depth, in thickness, and divisions of lines in length. Now following what has been started, I say that from the <term>pit of the throat</term> <note>original: "fontanella"</note> to the waist are eleven degrees; and below the breasts, seven degrees; at the <term>nipples</term> <note>original: "capitelli," literally 'little capitals'</note>, six; at the armpits, four; and at the top of the chest, two. From the waist to the <term>genitals</term> <note>original: "natura"</note> are nine degrees; to the bottom of the belly, seven. To the top of the thigh, six; and to the navel, three. I will now begin to treat them in the same order as the previous two, so that no one thinks these proportions are made by chance. ### *Proportion of the Female of Ten Heads.* Chapter XII.

**T**he proportion of the female of ten heads in length is as follows. From the top of the head to the sole of the foot is ten times the distance from the top of the head to the tip of the chin; and the midpoint happens to be above the <term>genitals</term> <note>original: "la natura"</note>, and it is composed thus. ## On the Proportion of the Woman of Nine Faces. Chapter XIV.

**N**ot without reason did Vitruvius, in the first book of his *Architecture*—where he distributes the styles of temples according to the nature of the Gods and assigns their respective orders—decide to dedicate the Ionic work to the Goddess Juno. He chose this because it is less heavy than the Doric and less graceful and slender than the Corinthian. Being a prudent man, he considered that this Goddess is by her nature not as heavy as the "Great Mother" <note>Cybele, often associated with the sturdier Doric order</note>, nor as lithe and perfectly beautiful as Venus; nonetheless, she holds the highest rank for a matronly beauty full of majesty. 

Therefore, I too attribute this proportion of nine faces to her specifically; it is less slender than the "Venusian" proportion, yet it is the most beautiful among the matronly types, in which one must represent both majesty and grace. This same proportion can also be adapted for queens of middle age, and likewise for any female body that ought to display a dignified beauty and gravity. For this reason, it is most properly suited to the Virgin Mother of our Savior. 

The measurements are as follows: From the top of the head to the mouth is one of the nine parts of her total length; the same distance is found from the top of the forehead to the chin; thus, the distance from the top of the head to the forehead is the same as that from the chin to the mouth. From the eyes to the <term>hollow of the neck</term> <note>original: "fontanella," the suprasternal notch at the base of the throat</note> is one of the nine parts, and just as much from there to the <term>breastbone</term> <note>original: "forcata," literally the 'fork,' referring to the area below the breasts</note>, and from the breasts to the navel, and from the navel to the <term>genitals</term> <note>original: "natura"</note>. From the genitals to the knee are two more "faces"; and from the middle of the knee to the narrow part of the leg above the heel are another two faces, and up to this point there are eight faces. The ninth face is composed of the combined spaces between the heel and the sole, the hollow of the neck and the chin, and the hairline and the top of the head. 

The width is also composed of nine faces in this manner: first, by extending the arms, the distance from the hollow of the neck to the tip of the middle finger is half the total, which is four and a half faces; the other side is the same, so that in total they equal nine faces. But these are then divided so that two faces are measured from one <term>collarbone</term> <note>original: "chiaue delle spalle," literally the 'keys of the shoulders'</note> to the other, so that there is one face per side from the center to the bone; and for the arm, from the collarbone to the fold of the elbow, there is likewise one...

### On the proportion of the Female of nine heads. Chapter XIV.

**Al**though many other proportions of bodies could be described, which are of little importance because they are not the primary types, I have nonetheless decided to omit them—both because they are, as I said, of little importance, and also to avoid causing boredom to the readers. It seems to me that it is now time to conclude these main and regular proportions and come to the others, starting first with this one of nine heads, which is entirely slender and full of grace. Since this represents the "third beauty" <note>Renaissance art theory often categorized beauty into three types: the majestic (Juno), the wise (Minerva), and the graceful/lithe (Venus or Diana).</note>, beyond Minerva, it can also be adapted to Diana, because of her speed and agility, and to all the Nymphs of the springs, and to the Muses, though they differ in dress according to their roles. 

In this proportion, from the top of the head to the chin is one-ninth part of its <term>width</term> <note>original: "larghezza." In the context of "nine-head" proportions, the author likely means the total height of the figure, or is comparing the head height to a specific horizontal axis.</note>. From the chin upward to the hairline above the forehead, the face can be made to be a tenth part of the whole body, or even an eleventh, as best pleases the painter. This space is divided into three equal parts: the first occupies the forehead, the second the nose, and the third the remainder down to the chin. 

Furthermore, from the top of the head to the highest part of the <term>shoulder blade</term> <note>original: "scapulario"</note> is one part in fifteen or sixteen; and to the <term>hollow of the neck</term> <note>original: "fontanella," the suprasternal notch at the base of the throat</note> is one in six. From the hollow of the neck to the top of the chest is one in thirty; to the <term>armpits</term> <note>original: "ditelle"</note> one in sixteen; to the <term>nipples</term> <note>original: "papille," also referred to here as "capitelli" or capitals, an architectural term</note> one in eleven; below the breasts one in nine; and at the waist two parts in eleven. From here to the navel is one in twenty-six; to the <term>hip joint</term> <note>original: "chiaue della coscia," literally the 'key' of the thigh</note> one in ten; to the bottom of the belly two in seventeen; to the <term>genitals</term> <note>original: "natura"</note> one in seven; to the end of them one in twelve or thirteen; to the lowest part of the buttocks one in eleven or twelve. 

To the middle of the thigh is one in twelve; from the sole of the foot to the base of the heel is one in forty-two; and to the <term>instep</term> <note>original: "collo di esso piede," the 'neck' of the foot</note> one in twenty-six. From the heel to the middle of the knee is one in four; to the end of the knee one in twenty-six; below it, one in thirty; to the base of the outer <term>calf muscle</term> <note>original: "polpa esteriore"</note> one in eleven; to the inner calf one in nine. 

The arm, from the top of the shoulder to the elbow, is two parts in eleven; and from here to the tip of the middle finger is one in four; then the hand to the <term>wrist joint</term> <note>original: "giūtura"</note> is one in eleven. One can also make the hand a tenth part, like the face, because the hand must always be as long as the face in all bodies—especially in slender ones, and even longer, as the works of learned painters and sculptors bear witness. 

The width of this body, facing forward at the hairline, is one part in eleven; at the middle of the forehead, one in ten; at the eyebrows, one in eleven; at the ears, one in ten; at the nose, one in thirteen; the throat, one in twenty-one; the top of the shoulder blade, one in nineteen; the hollow of the neck, two in thirteen; and from one <term>collarbone</term> <note>original: "chiaue delle spalle"</note> to the other, one in...

### On the proportion of the Female of seven heads. Chapter XV.

**R**easonably, the ancients made the Goddess Vesta <note>Vesta was the Roman goddess of the hearth, often associated with Cybele or the "Great Mother" Earth.</note> seven heads tall, because this proportion is entirely grave and matronly; and thus they attributed it to the great mother Earth, as she is the one who gives birth to all things. It is indeed true that this proportion can also be suited to some other Goddess who is similar in gravity to the Earth; likewise, it will also suit women and matrons who are among the most graceful. ### *On the proportion of the child of four heads. Chapter XVIII.*

**T**he final proportion of the human body is a length of four heads; I mean that the fourth part of its body is the head, measured from the top of the head to the end of the neck-fold <note>original: "palarco" or "palearco," referring to the fleshy fold or dewlap under an infant's chin</note>, that is, under that thickness that ends with the stomach. And from the top of the head to the top of the forehead is one of twenty-four [parts]; to the vertex <note>the crown of the head</note>, one of sixteen; to the eyebrow and the top of the ears, one of eight; to the bottom of the neck-fold, one of four. But from the vertex to the end of the chin is one of six. The midpoint between the eyebrow and the chin is the nose, and the length of the ear; and this space of the nose is divided into three equal parts: one is for the nostril, the second is from the nostril to nearly the middle of the eye, and the third is from there to the eyebrow. The space from the nose to the chin is divided into five: two are above the mouth, and the other three are from the mouth to the chin. And the line of the mouth ends behind at the base of the nape <note>original: "gnucca," the back of the neck</note>, and that of the chin...

The width of the neck below the chin is one of nine; and this is divided into three equal spaces, of which the middle one is between one eye and the other; and the nose is the [same as the] width of the mouth. The diameter from one shoulder to the other is one of four, but from one joint <note>original: "chiaue"</note> of the arm to the other are two of nine. ### *On the specific external parts of the Horse,*
### *and their names. Chapter XIX.*

**F**or a better understanding of the proportions, it seems expedient to me that the names of the limbs of this animal be set down first; because otherwise, besides the matter remaining obscure, one could easily take one thing for another—especially since the names of these parts are not very well known, and are named differently by different people. And so the reader, to avoid error, shall be guided by these names that I shall set down as the horse's own, according to the good Italian authors.
And to begin from the head: those hairs that spread over the forehead are called *crini* <note>hairs</note>, and the whole bundle of them is called the *ciuffo* <note>forelock</note>; and likewise those that hang on either side of the ears, along with those that extend from the summit of the head to the beginning of the back along the neck, are called by the same name, *crini*, though more properly they are called the *coma* <note>original: "coma," a Latin-derived term for a head of hair or a mane</note>. At the summit of the forehead and the beginning of the upper jaws, the ears are born; the space between them at the top is called the summit of the head, and at the bottom, the summit of the forehead. The raised area around the brow of the eyes is called the *conca* <note>literally "the shell," referring to the orbital ridge or eye socket</note>, and the point formed by both eyelids on the inside of the eye is called the inner angle, and the other toward the jaw is called the outer angle. The upper jaw is that which terminates with the lower one, and with the neck...

...the neck above, and with the throat below: the lower part ends with the **bars** <note>The "bars" (barre) are the sensitive, toothless spaces in a horse's mouth where the bit rests.</note>, and with the front part which is the nose, of which the hole is called the **nostril**, and also **nasca** <note>original: "nasca," an archaic Italian term for the nostril or nose.</note>, which is its proper name. The **bar** is that raised part around the mouth where the bit is placed; the **muzzle** or **whiskers** is that which ends from the nose to the upper lip; under the mouth is the lower lip; under which is the **chin-groove** <note>original: "barbozzo," the area where the curb chain of a bridle rests.</note> which ends with the bars and the lower jaws. The neck extends from the summit of the head at the back to the spine, and in front it is called the **throat**; the beginning of the chest is called the **hollow of the breast** <note>original: "fontanella," literally "little fountain," referring to the indentation at the base of the neck.</note>; and its beginning is under the jaws. The **shoulder** is on the sides between the chest, the neck, the back, and the ribs, and the beginning of the arm. The **chest** goes from the hollow of the breast to end under the belly between the arms. Those hollows on either side of the chest where the upper arm unsheathes are called the **keys of the arms** <note>Likely referring to the points of the shoulders or the axillary region.</note>. The arm extends from the shoulder, from the chest, and from the "key" down to the knee, and the knee down to the lower part of the leg, which then also ends at the joint. This joint, down to the hoof, is called the **horn** <note>original: "corno," referring to the keratinous hoof wall.</note>; the hairs are called the **coronet**; behind the horn it is called the **heel**; those hairs that are above, after the joint and the cleft, are called the **pastern hair** <note>original: "pastorello."</note>; and all of this from the leg to the sole which is under the horn, where the shoe is placed, is called the **hand**; and on the back legs, it is called the **foot**.

The **back** ends from the vertex where the mane grows at the end of the neck down to the **croup**. The croup begins from the start of the **dock** <note>original: "tronco," the muscular part of the tail.</note> above, and ends with the buttocks and the flanks; the **ribs** are contained on the sides between the back, the shoulders, and the hips; and under those, the lower part is called the **ventre** or indeed the **belly**, which ends from the lower part of the chest down to the member. The **dock** is the beginning of the tail, under which stays the hole from which the excrements exit, placed in the middle of the buttocks, which finish down at the beginning of the hips, or what one might call the rear heels. The front beginning of the leg is called the **point of the hip**, which finishes at the thighs; the interior part of the hips under the testicles is named the **vargo** <note>An archaic term for the groin or inner thigh area.</note>. Everyone understands what the testicles and the member are and where they are; the **thigh** finishes at the head of the **hock**; which "head" is specific to the back legs at the "knee" <note>The author is clarifying that the hock is the equivalent of the knee for the hindquarters.</note>, and the hock itself extends from there to the joints; the hairs after the joints are called, as in the front legs, the **pastern hair**, since they are similarly composed at the feet with the horns (or rather hooves) and soles; but (as I have said before) the front ones are called **hands**, which for beauty's sake should be round, and those behind are called **feet**, which should be somewhat long, but proportional and not mismatched with the hands. Finally, for a greater understanding of the whole, let us leave—

...with the tail attached to the dock <note>The "dock" (tronco) is the living part of the horse's tail from which the hair grows.</note>. It must be noted that proportions are understood in two ways: one will be by parallel lines from the top of the head down to the sole of the foot, descending in order from member to member down to the hoof, both from the front and from the back, giving the lengths, widths, and thicknesses of the members. The other will be the exact measurement of the lengths from member to member—on the face, the back, and in profile—as will be understood by reading. Now I will treat the first type of <term>proportions</term> <note>Proportions in this context refer to the mathematical relationship between different body parts to achieve an ideal aesthetic.</note>, and the second in the next chapter.

The parts that the horse needs to have in general to be beautiful and well-proportioned are these: the top of the head should be as high from the ground as a well-proportioned man is tall, and not a point more or less; otherwise, the smaller ones would look like donkeys, and the larger ones like elephants or similar creatures. Thus, the viewer would be deprived of that pleasure he takes in seeing a handsome man and a fine <term>horse</term> <note>original: "cavallo"</note> together. 

But following my purpose, and beginning from the feet as horsemen do—who judiciously affirm that a horse, however good its coat may be, is not good if it is poorly proportioned, as **Grisone** <note>Federico Grisone was a famous 16th-century Neapolitan nobleman and one of the founders of classical dressage.</note> and other experts also affirm—the horn of the hooves should be wide, round, and hollow; the heel ample; the coronets <note>The area just above the hoof where the hair begins.</note> thin and hairy; the **pasterns** <note>original: "pastarelli," the part of the leg between the fetlock and the hoof.</note> short; the joints thick; the legs straight and well-spaced; the arms sinewy; the **cannon bones** <note>original: "cannuoli," the long bone above the pastern.</note> short, equal, and correct; the knees large, lean, and flat. The **muscles of the shanks** <note>original: "lacerti de gli stinchi"</note> above the knees, when the horse stands square, are much wider from one to the other at the top than they are at the bottom. The shoulders must be long, spacious, and filled with flesh; the chest should be broad and round; the neck should not be short, but rather long and thick toward the chest, arched in the middle, and thin near the head. 

The ears should be small, sharp, and upright with a correct length; the forehead should be lean and broad; the eyes large; the hollows of the eyebrows full and projecting outward; the jaws thin and lean; the nostrils open and flared, so that within them one can almost see the red of the interior. The mouth should be large; and finally, the whole head together should be well-matched, long, dry, and so to speak, **mountainous** <note>This likely refers to a "chiseled" look where the bone structure and veins are clearly visible through the skin.</note>, so that the veins show in every place. But that length is of such proportion that, compared to its width, it seems long, but compared to the neck and the rest of the body, it is short. The mane should be long and curled; the tail long down to the ground with its dock thick and of correct measure, well-placed between the thighs or buttocks. The back should be short, and such that it does not curve either upward or downward; the loins should be round and flat toward the spine, which should be **channeled** <note>original: "acanellata," referring to a "double-muscled" back where the spine sits in a groove between the muscles.</note>, and...

& double; the ribs should be wide and long, with a slight slope from the back rib to the point of the hip. The belly should be long, large, and properly tucked under the ribs. The flanks should be full; the croup round and level, slightly sloping with a groove in the middle, and with a great breadth across from point to point. The thighs should be long and spacious with well-formed bones, and with much flesh inside and out; the hocks broad, lean, and extended; the <term>sickle-curvatures</term> <note>original: "falci"; referring to the curve of the hind legs</note> curved and spacious like those of a deer, and the testicles with a small member. And note that all its members must correspond to the size of the body in the manner of a deer, being a little higher behind than in front. 

All these particularities are understood to belong to the horse that is the most beautiful, slender, and agile in every limb, and of such a horse I intend to describe the just and true proportion, imitating <term>Leonardo da Vinci</term> <note>Leonardo (1452–1519) was famous for his extensive anatomical studies of horses, particularly for the Sforza monument.</note>, who was excellent and unique in sculpting and painting horses, as is seen in his anatomy, and also <term>Raphael</term> <note>Raffaello Sanzio (1483–1520), the High Renaissance master.</note>, and <term>Gaudenzio</term> <note>Gaudenzio Ferrari (c. 1471–1546), a Northern Italian painter and sculptor known for his lifelike equine figures in the Sacro Monte chapels.</note>, who were likewise excellent in this regard. For others could also be described, such as <term>cobs</term> <note>original: "bertoni"; likely referring to heavy, docked-tail horses</note> and similar fat and coarse ones, or those too thin, as if their limbs were unhinged, such as certain stray Turkish horses and those of other nations. But these I will omit, and I will expand only upon the first type, by whose example all other proportions of horses can be set right according to the rule that will be stated.

## On the proportion of the Horse in front and behind. Chap. XX.

**F**rom the top of the head to the sole of the forefeet is one single part, and the head, from that same top to the end of the muzzle, is two parts out of seven of that length. The head, from one outer part of the ears to the other, is one twenty-third or twenty-fourth; the top of the conchae one ninth; the outer corners of the eyes the same. From one inner corner of the eye to the other is one fourteenth; the width of the neck at the beginning of the throat is one twelfth or fourteenth; the face one twenty-second or twenty-fourth.

However, if anyone makes them known and familiar to themselves, there is no doubt that they will be able to paint or otherwise form a horse perfectly in all its actions; just as, on the contrary, having no knowledge of them, they could never do anything plausible or pleasing to their own taste or that of the experts; it being clear that <term>science</term> <note>original: "scienza"; in this context, it refers to a disciplined, theoretical understanding of art based on natural laws.</note> consists only in difficult things. Now from here we shall move on to architecture, and we shall see how and in what manner it too, in all its orders, proceeds with reason and proportion. But first, we shall see how it should be understood according to the opinions of the ancients and the moderns, some more and some less founded on reason; upon which Architecture was founded, and from which excellence is founded anew by those who understand it best.

### *On the proportion of the orders of Architecture in general. Chap. XXII.*

**I**N all things, it naturally appears that without goodness there can be no beauty, nor conversely goodness without beauty. Likewise, in every manufactured thing, convenience and utility cannot be provided unless beauty is joined to them—that is, if the due proportion is not present; because utility and convenience are obtained from nature and from art. [...dim/tire] the vision, and they offend it by dilating it too much; on the contrary, thick, dense, and cramped things, just as they are coarse and obstructive, likewise also dim and offend the eyes. However, this delight is more or less according to the judgment of the person moved by them, who is allowed to enjoy them only as much as he has practiced himself in beauty and the knowledge of proportions. For it is most certain that even if a <term>material man</term> <note>original: "huomo materiale"; a person focused only on physical reality without intellectual or artistic training.</note> feels pleasure and delight upon seeing a beautiful thing, he cannot feel it perfectly as another would who has knowledge of beauty.

And from this it follows that all beautiful and well-made things please everyone universally as useful and delightful things; but not equally, nor in the same manner, especially since everyone is different by nature from others. Hence we see that any intelligent person who has ordered or built anything, whether by <term>composition</term> <note>original: "compositione"; the art of arranging different elements together.</note>, arrangement, or proportion, has been different and diverse from others, even though their works are plausible, good, and beautiful. This is what all the principal architects, both ancient and modern, have done; as I shall clearly make known in the book on compositions, especially concerning the composition of the <term>orders</term> <note>original: "ordini"; the classical styles of architecture, such as Doric, Ionic, or Corinthian.</note>, members, and buildings, it being sufficient in this place to speak of the variety of established proportions.

In this, I conclude that in all works two <term>intelligences</term> <note>original: "intelligenze"; here used to mean fundamental conceptual principles or modes of understanding.</note> are required, without which a good or beautiful <term>building</term> <note>original: "fabrica"; a structure, or the act of construction.</note> can never be made: namely, in what way one must give proportion to the work in regard to itself, and secondarily in what way it must be given in regard to the eye with which the building is made adorned. Just as through its inherent proportion it becomes useful because of the strength of the parts that result from it.

As for the first, I say that it [internal proportion] cannot be arranged without the other [proportion for the eye], just as this one likewise cannot stand without that. Otherwise, the disunion of the whole would follow; for if one attended only to giving proportion to the thing in regard to itself, it would certainly follow that, not having [the other]...

## FIRST [BOOK].

...the other part, the thing, even if it is well-proportioned in itself, would not be rendered useful or beautiful; for example, on a wall or a column that is covered with letters or minute <term>histories</term> <note>original: "istorie"; in this context, it refers to narrative scenes or reliefs depicting historical or mythological events.</note> from the top to the bottom, if the letters or histories are proportionate in relation to themselves, they will be equal. Consequently, the result will be that those at the top will lose too much [to the distance] and will appear small, offending the eyes; they could not be read like those at the bottom, nor could the small figures of the stories be discerned. Thus, the utility of that painting would cease, and it would clearly be seen that there is neither the proportion of utility nor of beauty. Therefore, it is seen that the ancients used to form the letters at the top longer than the lower ones, according to the <term>logic of seeing</term> <note>original: "ragione del vedere"; what we now call optical refinement or perspective correction.</note>; whereby the proportion of the thing in itself was represented all at once, appearing equal to the sight, and from this was drawn the utility and the delight of reading and seeing the letters. This is seen most clearly in Rome, on the historiated <term>Column of Trajan</term> <note>A Roman triumphal column finished in 113 AD, famous for its spiral relief that wraps around the shaft; the figures at the top are carved larger than those at the bottom so they appear uniform to a viewer on the ground.</note>, where the figures seem equal, and yet they are longer at the top than at the bottom.

But to demonstrate this in more important things in the actual buildings themselves: who does not know that if one made the <term>orders</term> <note>The classical styles of architecture (Doric, Ionic, Corinthian, etc.).</note> one above the other in sequence, according to the proportion in which they are to be shown but without the logic of perspective, it would result in them appearing exceedingly low due to the receding of the facade above the horizon? This would happen despite them having their own proper proportion, because they lacked this other proportion discovered through the way of seeing things according to the logic of regulated distance. From this, the <term>projections</term> <note>original: "sporti"; parts of the building that jut out.</note> and reliefs of the architraves, pedestals, and cornices would be seen to excessively occupy the upper parts; and the columns would have no beauty suitable to the sight. In figures as well, both in relief and in painting, placed on high, if one observes nothing but their natural proportion and does not accompany it with this [proportion] of perspective, it is clearly seen that the men appear to the sight as dwarves and deformed.

For which reason I hold that the ancients, in those very great statues and colossi like that of <term>Rhodes</term> <note>The Colossus of Rhodes, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, a massive bronze statue of the sun god Helios.</note>, in order to make them correspond to the eye without offense, did not make them otherwise proportioned according to natural proportion—because the head, being so high, would have appeared as thick as a heel—but rather, by composing and tempering together both modes of proportion, they went on increasing the limbs measurably as one ascended to the top. This they also use in the highest columns, in obelisks, and in short, in all things; and the reason for doing this is one of those secrets contained in <term>drawing</term> <note>original: "disegno"; a fundamental concept in Italian art theory encompassing both the physical act of drawing and the intellectual design/conception of a work.</note> and in the art of seeing; wherefore by others it

can be understood, except by one who is a master of these two parts <note>The "two parts" refers to the "proportion of the thing in itself" and the "proportion of appearance" discussed on the previous page.</note>. As for the second way, I say that if one still wished to arrange a thing without the proportion of itself, but only according to how it must appear to the eyes from a certain distance, it would easily collapse or could not have the strength to sustain itself for a long time. Because in this way, by itself, one seeks to see things perfectly as if they were equally proportioned beneath the sight; for it would follow that as things are raised higher, it would be necessary to make them excessively wider and longer, even to the point of the <term>visual cut</term> <note>original: "taglio ordinato"; refers to the intersection of the visual pyramid with the picture plane or the surface of the object.</note> determined by the sight and the distance. And then one member would not support the other, both because of being widened and because of being raised, and consequently the thing could neither be enjoyed nor seen with delight. Likewise in painting, if it were governed solely by this [optical rule] without anything else behind it, the most meager and disconcerted things in the world would be produced. Therefore, one must take care to proceed in all things with these two ways: to give proportion, as I have said, to the thing according to itself, and according to the appearance proportioned to the sight; otherwise, nothing of value can be made. For, in short, the coupling and the mixture of these two proportions is what causes that much-praised <term>grace</term> <note>original: "gratia"; a central concept in Renaissance art theory referring to a quality of beauty that transcends mere rules and mathematical measurements.</note> in the appearance of things, which is known only by the learned and admired by the ignorant.

And so the ancients, having noted this, established that one <term>order</term> <note>The classical orders of architecture (Tuscan, Doric, Ionic, Corinthian, and Composite).</note> should follow another in an organized way as the structure went higher, so that it would acquire this grace, beauty, and utility. For this reason, one sees in the **Colosseum** the **Composite** placed highest above the others; and after that the **Corinthian** above the **Ionic**, being less high; and after the **Ionic**, and finally the **Doric** as the lowest and set opposite the eyes; and with the same rule all the other members follow in order as is seen.

Now, returning to the architects who, in one and the same order, have used different proportions (as is apparent from the remains of the ancients collected in <term>Serlio</term> <note>Sebastiano Serlio (1475–1554), an Italian Mannerist architect whose influential treatise "Tutte l'opere d'architettura et prospettiva" helped codify the five orders.</note>, and from the measures described by **Petrucci**, and from those designed by **Iacomo Barozzo** <note>Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola (1507–1573), author of "Canon of the Five Orders of Architecture," one of the most successful architectural textbooks in history.</note>), it is seen that they vary among themselves. For **Petrucci**, in the pedestals, wants the surface of the **Tuscan** <term>stylobate</term> <note>The continuous base or platform supporting a row of columns.</note> to be a perfect square, as it is a stronger figure than the others; and that of the **Doric** to be of diagonal proportion; the **Ionic** <term>sesquialtera</term> <note>A ratio of 3:2.</note>; the **Corinthian** <term>super-particular two-thirds</term> <note>original: "sopra partiente due terzi"; likely referring to a ratio of 5:3.</note>; and the **Composite** of double proportion <note>A ratio of 2:1.</note>. He wants the **Tuscan** column to be six diameters of its base high; the **Doric** seven; the **Ionic** eight; and so he goes on discussing the others and their members according to how he treats each order more particularly. But **Barozzo**, finding a new, ingenious, and resolute invention, measures this order in another way; and in this manner, he has imagined as a general rule to make the pedestal a third part of the height of all columns, including the base and capital.

To which I respond that (as I already said at the beginning of this book) among the **Dorians**, not knowing what proportion to give to columns, they imagined a well-formed and robust man—as a very clear and reliable model for all things—to be six feet in height; and thus they raised the **Doric** column to six diameters of the lower part of the shaft. But after a time it happened that the **Ionians**, wishing to make columns that had both strength and proportion, converted the proportion of that Doric column from feet into heads, deriving from man this logic: that a robust, strong, and well-squared body was seven heads in height. And thus, what was six diameters [based on] feet, they made seven heads [high]; and they dedicated this proportion and order particularly to **Hercules**, and later also to **Mars** and **Minerva** for a certain strength without delicacy that they imagined was in them—making, therefore, no delightful ornament, but leaving it solid and pure. And this first column of six feet was also followed by the **Tuscans**, decorating it with rustic members, and they called it **Tuscan** after themselves.

The same **Ionians**, considering also that the most beautiful but matronly proportion in human bodies is eight heads in length, by this example raised the second column to the same number of diameters; but with more ornaments and beauty than the first, calling it **Ionic**. Considering its nature, they dedicated it to **Juno**, and also—due to a certain kind of severity and the robustness of the hunt—to **Diana**, and to **Father Liber** <note>original: "padre Libero"; an ancient Italian god of wine and fertility, often identified with Bacchus.</note> for other similarities.
