## On the proportion of the Tuscan order. Chapter XXIII.

**T**he Tuscan Order, which is also called "rustic," is used only in fortresses and city gates, as it is stronger than the others, and also less decorated, being only of a thick and rough-hewn form. Its proportion—which I will briefly describe here without searching for barbaric or Greek names for the members, but using those that our architects commonly use for greater clarity—is as follows. First, the Column is seven parts high including the base and capital, according to Vitruvius; and one part is its width at the bottom of the shaft. The base is half the width of the Column in height; dividing it into two equal parts, one is given to the <term>plinth</term> <note>original: "ciocco"; the square or round bottom block of the base.</note>. Dividing [the remainder] into three, two are given to the <term>torus</term> <note>original: "baſtone"; a large, rounded convex molding.</note>, and the other to the <term>cincture</term> <note>original: "cinta"; a small ring-like molding.</note>. Its <term>projection</term> <note>original: "ſporto"; how far the molding extends outward from the column.</note> is made in this way: Make a circle as wide as the column is thick at the bottom, and placing it in a square, and drawing a circle outside over the four corners, the projection is formed. And only in this order, as Vitruvius says, the plinth of this base is round, because all others must have it square. The height of the capital is the same as the base, which is divided into three parts: one is given to the <term>abacus</term> <note>The flat, square slab at the very top of a capital.</note>; the second is divided into four parts, three of which are given to the <term>echinus</term> <note>original: "uouolo"; the rounded, cushion-like part of the capital.</note>, and the fourth to its <term>fillet</term> <note>original: "liſtello"; a small flat band.</note>; the remaining third part is given to the <term>necking</term> <note>original: "fregio"; while this usually means "frieze," in the context of a capital, it refers to the neck-like space below the moldings.</note>. The <term>astragal</term> <note>original: "tondino"; a small semi-circular molding.</note> with its small square, or <term>neck-ring</term> <note>original: "collarino".</note>, and half of the necking are divided into three parts: the necking has two, and the square has one; of which the projection shall be as much as its height, and the astragal as much as both of them together. The column or shaft, at the top part, is diminished by a fourth part. And thus the capital above, is...

...touches the upper ruler called the <term>fillet</term> <note>original: "listello"</note> and square, and another to the lower. The projection of the base is half of its height; and thus the plinth is on every side one and a half times the thickness of the column.

But because <term>Vitruvius</term> <note>A Roman architect and engineer (1st century BC) whose "Ten Books on Architecture" became the foundational text for Renaissance architects.</note> has divided this order into <term>Modules</term> <note>A standard unit of measure used in classical architecture to determine the proportions of a building, usually based on the radius or diameter of the column at its base.</note>, we will proceed in this way, as <term>Petrucci</term> <note>Likely referring to a contemporary commentator or editor of Vitruvius.</note> has also done; making the column two modules thick, and the height—including the base and capital—fourteen [modules]. Therefore, since the base is one module high and the capital another, the trunk or shaft of the column ends up being twelve modules long.

Now, the height of the capital is divided into three parts: one of which is for the abacus, also called the <term>Plinth</term> <note>The flat, square slab forming the uppermost member of a capital.</note>, which contains the reversed molding called the <term>cyma</term> <note>original: "cimasa"</note>, which is the third part of said abacus. The second part is for the <term>echinus</term> <note>The rounded, cushion-like molding below the abacus.</note>, also called the <term>ovolo</term>, with the small steps or fillets, of which there are three, each being a fourth part of the ovolo. The third part is given to the frieze called the <term>hypotrachelion</term> <note>The "neck" of the column capital, located between the shaft and the echinus.</note>, the height of which is one-sixth less than the column at the <term>lower shaft</term> <note>original: "imo scapo"</note>, that is, the bottom part. The width of the capital at the upper part is, on each face, two modules and one-sixth of another.

And because, according to some moderns, the described proportion of Vitruvius is considered very meager, a richer and more beautiful one is introduced in imitation of ancient works in this manner: having made three parts of the capital as I said, the Plinth or abacus is divided into three parts; one of which is given to the <term>cyma</term> <note>original: "cimatio"</note>, or reversed molding, with its fillet (as was also said above), but it is also divided into three parts, with one belonging to the fillet and two to the cyma.

The ovolo is similarly divided into three parts that form it, and the other third is given to the steps or <term>annulets</term> <note>original: "annuli" — small rings or bands encircling the column capital.</note>; which being three, and this part divided into as many subsections, results in one for each. The frieze [is] as has been said; and the projection—called by some the <term>proiettura</term>—of every member is equal to its height. The bead molding beneath the frieze, as well as the necking called the <term>apophyge</term> <note>The slight curve where the column shaft meets its base or capital.</note>, is half of the frieze; and the bead is double the necking.

The epistyle, called the <term>architrave</term>, which is placed above the capital, is one module high—that is, the twelfth part of the shaft—and it is divided into seven parts, one of which belongs to the band called the <term>taenia</term> <note>A small, flat band at the top of an architrave.</note>. The <term>guttae</term> <note>original: "gocciole" — small, drop-like ornaments hanging beneath the triglyphs.</note> or bells, with the fillet beneath the band, are one-sixth of a module; this is divided into four parts: three are taken by the guttae and one by the ruler or fillet; and there must be six guttae hanging beneath the <term>triglyphs</term> <note>Vertically channeled blocks in a Doric frieze.</note>, with two for each <insert>part</insert>. The length <note>In this context, the vertical height.</note> of the triglyphs is one and a half modules, and its width one module; which is divided into twelve parts, of which one part is left on each side for the half-channels, and of the ten parts...

the remaining six [parts] are given to the flat surfaces of the <term>triglyphs</term> <note>Vertical blocks with three channels, a signature feature of the Doric frieze.</note>, that is, two for each; and four for the two small channels in the middle that divide them. From one triglyph to the other, the space is one <term>module</term> <note>A standard unit of measurement in classical architecture.</note> and a half; this space is a perfect square and is called a <term>Metope</term>. If one wishes to introduce elegance there, plates and ox heads are placed in the manner seen among the ancients; who, having sacrificed bulls where they used a plate <note>These decorative elements, known as bucrania (ox skulls) and paterae (libation bowls), represent the remains of ancient religious sacrifices hung on temples.</note>, later placed similar things around the Temple as ornament. Now, above the triglyphs, their <term>capitals</term> have a height of one-sixth of a module, and above them is placed the <term>corona</term> or <term>dripstone</term> <note>The projecting part of a cornice that shields the wall from rain.</note> with the two <term>cyma moldings</term> <note>original: "cimatij"; S-shaped architectural moldings.</note>, one above and the other below; the whole of which, divided into five parts, three make the dripstone, and two the cyma moldings. But the height of the whole is half a module, and above the dripstone the <term>cyma</term> called the <term>upright ogee</term> <note>original: "gola dritta"; a molding that is concave at the top and convex at the bottom.</note> is half a module high, plus one-eighth part of it for its small square [fillet] above. The projection of the dripstone is two-thirds of a module, on the underside of which, above the triglyphs, the drops <note>Small, peg-like ornaments (guttae) found under the triglyphs.</note> are drawn, and also between one triglyph and the other, lightning bolts in the metopes. The projection of the <term>reversed ogee</term> <note>original: "gola rovescia"; a molding that is convex at the top and concave at the bottom.</note> is equal to its height, and so it is for all the other members except the dripstone, under which, in place of the cyma molding, the <term>dentil</term> <note>Small, tooth-like blocks used as decoration in a cornice.</note> is also placed. The channels or <term>flutes</term> <note>original: "strie"</note> of the <term>column</term> of this order must be twenty in number, carved in such a way that from one channel to the next, a straight line is drawn which will be the side of a square. Once the square is formed, by placing the compass with one point at its center and the other touching both ends of the line and drawing an arc, it will make its correct hollow, which will be the fourth part of a circle. The pedestal, called the <term>stylobate</term>, is as wide as the plinth of the column base; and its net height is found by drawing a square from its width, then a diagonal line from corner to corner; however long that line is, that is its height. This height is divided into five parts, adding one part for its cyma molding and members, and another for the base; and thus, proportionally, the pedestal comes to be seven parts, just like the column; which together present a graceful appearance to the viewer. And here I shall conclude, leaving to the curious the investigation of the beautiful inventions and manners of the ancients concerning this order with their various proportions, as can be seen in **Rome**: at the **Julian Prison** <note>Likely referring to the Mamertine Prison or nearby structures in the Roman Forum.</note>, in the **Theater of Marcellus**, at the **Forum Boarium**, and in **Verona** at the **triumphal arch**, and in many other most beautiful fragments of various kinds found throughout Italy. I will only advise that the column should be tapered at the top by as much as the projection of the necking and the astragal, because this is as wide as the lower shaft.

### ***On the proportion of the Ionic order. Chapter XXVII.***

**T**he Ionic Column is generally made eight diameters high, including the base and capital, and in this almost all modern architects agree; although Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the 1st-century BC Roman architect whose treatise *De architectura* became the foundational text for Renaissance architecture.</note> wishes it to be eight and a half. Each of these diameters is the specific diameter of the <term>lower shaft</term> <note>original: "imo scapo"; the bottom-most part of the column's cylindrical body.</note>. The base is half of this width in height. The <term>plinth</term> <note>original: "ciocco"; the square block at the very bottom of the base.</note> is a third part of the height of the base. The remainder is divided into three parts: one is given to the <term>Torus</term> <note>A large, convex, ring-shaped molding.</note>, also called a "staff" and a "upper bead"; and the other part below this Torus is divided into six parts, of which one is given to the <term>astragal</term> <note>A small, semi-circular convex molding.</note> or bead; and its small round part is half of said astragal. The <term>fillet</term> <note>original: "quadretto"; a small, flat, rectangular molding.</note> under the Torus is as large as the astragal; and the remainder goes to the <term>Trochilus</term> or <term>scotia</term> <note>A deep, concave molding that creates a shadow; "Trochilus" is the Greek term.</note>. The third remaining part is also divided into six parts: one is given to the lower astragal, and its fillet is half of it; and just as much is placed below, above the plinth; the rest is given to the lower scotia. The <term>projection</term> <note>original: "proiettura" or "sporto"; how far the molding extends outward from the shaft.</note> is on each side one-eighth and one-sixteenth part [of the diameter], and thus the plinth is on each side a quarter and an eighth part wider than the thickness of the column. I shall not cease also in this place to report the opinion of Vitruvius regarding this base; who requires, in the third [chapter] of the third book, that it be (as I have said) half the diameter of the lower shaft, and that it be divided into three parts, of which one belongs to the plinth, and the other two are made into seven parts. Of these, three belong to the <term>torus</term> <note>original: "bastone".</note>, and the other four for the two <term>scotias</term> <note>original: "canetti".</note> and astragals; and he wants the fillets to be arranged in this way: that the said four parts be equal, and each of them should have an astragal with its fillets. The astragal is one part, and the fillet is half. The lower scotia appears larger than the one above because its projection spreads further out than the other, and yet they are of the same measure. Now, leaving the base since enough has been said of it, I come to the capital, which is in height a third part of the width of the column. The face of the <term>abacus</term> <note>The flat slab forming the top of a capital.</note> in width is as much as the lower shaft, but divided into eighteen parts, one part is added to the two sides—that is, half per side—which then comes to nineteen parts in total. But withdrawn into the interior part by one and a half parts per side, a curved <note>original: "cetera".</note> or perpendicular line must be drawn which is nine and a half parts; and of those, one and a half is given to the abacus, and the eight parts below the abacus are given to the <term>scroll</term> <note>original: "cartoccio".</note> called a vine-tendril, and also a <term>volute</term> <note>The iconic spiral scroll of the Ionic capital.</note>. From the abacus downward, four parts are left; and giving one part below them to the **eye** <note>original: "occhio"; the circular center of the volute's spiral.</note>; so that from it downward...

...example of the necking, or <term>apophyge</term> <note>The curved transition between the column shaft and the capital or base</note>; and the <term>ovolo</term> <note>A rounded, convex molding, often decorated with egg-and-dart patterns</note>, and then from the top of the <term>astragal</term> <note>A small, ring-like molding</note> to the bottom of the vault. But setting this aside, if the column is between twelve and fifteen feet in height, it requires the architrave to be half the width of the lower <term>shaft</term> <note>The main body of the column; the "imo Scapo" refers to the diameter at the very bottom</note>; if from fifteen to twenty feet, the height is divided into thirteen parts, and one of these is given to the architrave; if from twenty to twenty-five feet, it is divided into twelve and a half parts, and one is given to the <term>epistyle</term> <note>Another name for the architrave, the lowest part of the entablature</note>; and if from twenty-five to thirty feet, it is divided into twelve parts, and one goes to the architrave; and so, if the column is of greater height, the architrave is made according to the proportional share. This is done so that when looking upward through the air, which diminishes one's sight, the work does not appear meager; whereas, conversely, when viewed close to the eyes, it appears rich and large in its proportions.

Once the architrave is formed according to its height, it is divided into seven equal parts, and one part shall be the <term>cyma reversa</term> <note>An S-shaped molding with the convex curve at the top</note>, the projection of which is equal to its height. The rest is divided into twelve parts, of which three go to the first <term>fascia</term> <note>The flat, horizontal bands that make up the architrave</note> called the lower one, four to the second called the middle, and five to the third called the upper. The thickness of this <term>epistyle</term> at the bottom is equal to the top of the <term>shaft</term>, and the thickness at the top is equal to the lower <term>shaft</term>.

Regarding the <term>frieze</term> <note>The middle section of the entablature, between the architrave and the cornice</note>, if one wishes to ornament it, it should be a fourth part higher than the architrave; but if it is made plain and solid, it should be a fourth part smaller. The <term>cyma reversa</term> above the <term>frieze</term> is one-seventh the height of said <term>frieze</term>, and its projection is equal to its height. The <term>dentil</term> <note>A series of small, rectangular blocks resembling teeth</note> above is as high as the <term>middle fascia</term> of the architrave, and its projection is equal to its height. Its face height is twice its width, and the space between the <term>dentils</term> is one-third less than their width. The <term>cyma reversa</term> above them is one-sixth of their height. The <term>corona</term> <note>The flat, projecting part of the cornice that sheds water</note> called the <term>drip</term> with its <term>cyma reversa</term> is as high as the <term>middle fascia</term> and the <term>dentil</term> together. The projection of the <term>drip</term> with the <term>dentil</term> is equal to the height of the <term>torus</term> <note>A large convex molding</note> or <term>frieze</term> with its <term>cyma reversa</term>. The <term>cyma recta</term> <note>An S-shaped molding with the concave curve at the top</note>, which is called the <term>sima</term>, is as high as the <term>drip</term> plus an eighth part more. Its fillet is a sixth part of it, and the projection is equal to its height.

Concerning the <term>pedestal</term> <note>The support or base for the column</note>, its face is as wide as the <term>plinth</term> <note>The square block at the very bottom of the column base</note>; and the height of the <term>die</term> <note>The central block of the pedestal, also called the "netto"</note> is in a <term>sesquialteral</term> <note>A ratio of 1.5 to 1, or a square and a half</note> proportion—that is, a square and a half. It is divided into six parts, one of which belongs to its base, and another to the cornice above; so that just as the column is eight diameters high, the <term>pedestal</term> comes to be the same height, and thus they agree in proportion. One must note, however, that these <term>Ionic</term> proportions are general rules. For according to the judgment of the craftsman, one may increase or decrease...

...example of the ancients, of whom many Ionic works are still seen, and most notably at the Theater of Marcellus <note>An ancient open-air theater in Rome, built in the closing years of the Roman Republic</note>, and in many other places, though they vary somewhat among themselves. Of these, Petrucci <note>Likely Giovan Battista Pedrezzano, a Venetian publisher who produced editions of Serlio's work</note> has included drawings of the most beautiful parts in his book called *of Serlio*, where he introduces another type of proportion for the <term>architrave</term>, <term>frieze</term>, and <term>cornice</term> <note>The three parts of the entablature, the horizontal structure resting on the columns</note> that is truly most beautiful. In this method, the total height—which comprises the architrave, frieze, and cornice together—is one-fourth of the column's height; Vignola <note>Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola, a prominent 16th-century architect</note> follows this same rule, as he does for all the other orders. 

Now, to return to our place, this fourth part is divided into ten: three parts make the architrave (divided as we described in the other section); three more make the frieze; and the remaining four make the cornice. The cornice itself is also divided into six parts: one goes to the <term>dentil</term> <note>A series of small, rectangular blocks forming a molding</note>; one to the <term>cyma reversa</term> <note>A molding with an S-shaped profile, convex at the top and concave at the bottom</note> that supports the <term>modillions</term>; two to the modillions <note>Ornate brackets or blocks placed under the projecting part of the cornice</note> themselves; one to the <term>corona</term> <note>The flat, vertical face of the cornice, often called the 'gocciolatoio' or drip because it sheds water</note>; and the last to the <term>cyma recta</term> <note>An S-shaped molding that is concave at the top and convex at the bottom</note>. The width of the modillions is equal to their height including their <term>cap</term>, although some keep them narrower; the distance from one to the next is half as much again, or even double, or somewhere in between those two. The <term>projection</term> <note>How far the molding sticks out from the wall</note> of the entire cornice is, at minimum, equal to its height. These are the very words of Petrucci, who reports that he took the proportions of this cornice from the example in Rome at Santa Sabina <note>A 5th-century Roman basilica known for its preserved classical columns</note>. But let us come to the Corinthian order—entirely graceful and beautiful, intended to provide delight and pleasure with both reason and utility. I must not fail to note, however, that the Ionic column at the top aligns with the first vault on the front side, directly at the level of the eye looking across.

### On the proportion of the Corinthian order. Cap. XXV.

**T**he Corinthian order was introduced, as I have said before, in imitation of virginal delicacy. Because virgins, due to the tenderness of their age, are slender of limb and therefore suited to produce more graceful and pleasing effects. As a general rule, the column has a height of nine <term>diameters</term> measured at the lower <term>shaft</term> <note>The main body of the column; 'imo Scapo' refers to the thickness at the base</note>; its base is half of that diameter. This base is divided into four parts: one is given to the <term>plinth</term> <note>The square block at the very bottom; 'ciocco' in the original</note>, and the remaining parts are divided into five. One of these five is given to the upper <term>torus</term> <note>A large, rounded molding; 'bastone' in the original</note>, which is one-fourth smaller than the lower one. The rest is divided into two equal parts: one is given to the lower <term>scotia</term> <note>A concave, hollow molding; 'cavetto' in the original</note> with its <term>astragal</term> <note>A small, ring-like molding</note>, or bead, along with the two <term>fillets</term> <note>Small, flat, rectangular moldings; 'quadretti' in the original</note>. The astragal should be one-sixth of the scotia, and each fillet is half the size of the astragal; however, the fillet above the lower torus is two-thirds of the astragal. The other part is divided such that the astragal is one-sixth of the whole, its fillet is half of that astragal, and the other fillet under the upper torus...

There must be eight middle leaves, and just as many on the bottom. The width of the abacus is measured along the diagonal line from corner to corner, and across two diameters of the lower shaft; which, when placed in a square with a larger circle drawn outside touching the four corners, and another square made outside that circle divided by diagonal lines, will show these lines to be two column-widths in length, according to Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman author of 'De Architectura', whose work was the foundation for Renaissance architectural theory</note>. But from one corner to the other of the larger square at the bottom, a base of a perfect triangle is made, at the bottom angle of which is the point for carving the top, or abacus; which is done so that at the center of the larger square at the bottom (which is also the upper base of the triangle), in that space from the larger circle to the smaller one, four parts are made; one of which remains below the smaller circle; and here, taking a compass and placing one point on the tip of the triangle at the bottom, and the other on the said point of the fourth part below the smaller circle toward the larger one, and circling to where the curved line intersects the two sides of the triangle, there it will form the limit of the horns of the capital on the right and left sides of the larger square; and thus the abacus will fall in a plumb line with the block of the base, and drawing a line from the projection of the <term>astragal</term> <note>A small, semi-circular molding, often called a "bead"</note> under the capital up to the horn of the capital, the projections of the tips of the smaller and larger leaves and the volutes will join exactly here; such that this capital will be

But I do not know for what reason **Vignola** <note>Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola (1507–1573), an influential Italian architect</note> made the projections of the larger leaves extend further out than the horns <note>The pointed corners of the abacus</note>; because of this, and for other reasons, they appear too short and pulled inward. I have often heard excellent architects call these capitals of his **docked capitals** <note>original: "capitelli bertoni"; a term for animals with cropped ears or tails</note>, as if they had their ears cut off. Regarding the **architrave**, **frieze**, and **cornice**, since **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman author of 'De architectura'</note> makes no mention of them, except for the **modillions** <note>Decorative brackets under the cornice</note> which serve all other orders as they do this one, I will follow the teaching of **Baldassarre** <note>Baldassarre Peruzzi (1481–1536), an architect and painter known for his study of antiquity</note>.

First, one divides the height of the column, including its base and capital, into four parts; one of these parts makes up the architrave, frieze, and cornice. This fourth part is then divided into ten units:
*   Three units go to the **architrave**, which is divided like that of the **Ionic order**.
    *   Under the middle **fascia** <note>A flat, horizontal band</note> is a **bead** <note>original: "tondino"; a small convex molding</note> measuring one-eighth of that middle fascia.
    *   Under the upper fascia is another bead measuring one-eighth of that upper fascia.
*   The next three of the ten units are given to the **frieze**.
*   The remaining four units make up the **cornice**.

The cornice is shared among nine units:
*   One unit for the **cyma reversa** <note>original: "gola rovescia"; an S-shaped molding</note> above the frieze.
*   Two for the **ovolo** <note>original: "uouolo"; a convex, egg-shaped molding</note> with its small square fillet.
*   Two for the **modillion** <note>The ornamental bracket supporting the upper part of the cornice</note> with its own cyma reversa.
*   Two for the **corona** <note>The flat, vertical face of the cornice that "crowns" the order</note>.
*   The final two for the **cyma recta** <note>original: "gola dritta"; an S-shaped molding that is concave at the top and convex at the bottom</note> and its **cymatium** <note>The crowning molding</note>, which should be one-fourth the height of the cyma recta itself.

If one creates a large cornice without modillions, it is done as follows: First, the architrave measures half the diameter of the column. The frieze, because it is decorated, is one-fourth larger than the architrave. The cornice (without the cyma reversa above the frieze) is as high as the architrave. Thus, the total height is less than one-fifth of the column’s height. If the column is fluted, it is done like the **Ionic**, though the flutes should be filled <note>A technique called "cabling," where the lower part of the groove is filled with a convex molding</note> from the bottom third downward.

The **pedestal** is as wide as the **die** <note>original: "ciocco"; the central block of the pedestal</note>. This width is divided into three parts; two of these are added to the three, making its height (not counting its moldings), which is called the **superbipartient two-thirds proportion** <note>original: "proportione sopra bipartiente duas tertias"; a mathematical ratio of 5:3</note>. The moldings are made by this rule: the height of the clear pedestal <note>The "naked" or main block of the pedestal</note> is divided into seven parts; one of these is given to its base and another to its cap. This results in nine parts, which correspond to the nine parts of the column, and thus they come together proportionately.

And although this is the general rule for the **Corinthian order**, the members vary in other ways, just as the ancients used them out of necessity; and not only the members, but also the proportions vary in some way, just as the entire order itself varies according to...

### Of the proportion of the Composite Order. Chap. XXVI.

**T**he **Composite Order**, called **Latin work** <note>original: "opera latina"</note>, and also **Italic** by the Romans (who, as I said above, were its inventors), maintains the column height, including the base and capital, at ten diameters. Its base is half as high as the diameter of the **lower shaft** <note>original: "imo ſcapo"; the bottom of the column</note>, and it follows the Corinthian style; therefore, it is proportioned just as I have described for that base. The column is fluted in the same manner as the Corinthian; it can also be striated like the Ionic. The capital is made like the Corinthian, but with the scrolls or rather the **volutes** <note>original: "cartocci"</note> larger than the Corinthian **helices** <note>original: "Clauicoli"; the small stalks or scrolls under the abacus</note>. The **architrave** is as high as the thickness of the column at the **upper shaft** <note>original: "ſommo ſcapo"; the top of the column</note>, and the **frieze** or rather the **zoforo** <note>original: "Zolforo"; a term for a frieze often decorated with animals or figures</note> where the **modillions** <note>decorative brackets</note> are located, is of the same height. The **cyma reversa** <note>original: "gola roueſcia"; a wave-shaped molding</note> of the modillions is one-sixth part of them. The projection of the modillions is equal to their height. The **drip-stone** <note>original: "gocciolatorio"; the corona or projecting part of the cornice</note>, with its cyma reversa, is as high as the architrave; divided into two parts, one is given to the cyma reversa and the other to the drip-stone. Its projection is equal to its height. The **pedestal** is twice as high as its width, in a double proportion; this refers to the **die** <note>original: "piano netto"; the flat central block of a pedestal</note>, which, having its height divided into eight parts, gives one to its base and another to its cap. Thus, the column being ten parts, the pedestal corresponds to it with the same number of parts. And this is (in general) the proportion of this order called **Composite**, because it is composed of the other orders and is variously adorned with different members of animals and bindings. This can be seen among many other things in **Trastevere** <note>A district in Rome</note> in a capital which is composed of Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian; having the **abacus** and the Doric cyma reversa, while the channel and the flutings are Ionic, and the **astragals** <note>small bead-like moldings</note> and leaves are Corinthian. Similarly, the base is highly ornate, being Doric in its two **tori** <note>original: "baſtoni"; large convex moldings</note> and Corinthian in its two **scotias** <note>original: "Canetti"; concave moldings</note>, the astragal, and other delicate carvings. Beyond this, at the **Basilica of the Forum Transitorium** <note>Also known as the Forum of Nerva in Rome</note>, one sees a capital that holds a winged horse with foliage in place of the helices, just as all the rest is very well accompanied from the shoulders back, which denotes it as Composite. Thus, many other diversities are found in this order, in which **Albrecht Dürer** created strange bizarries in his **Gate of Honor** <note>original: "porta dell’honore"; referring to the 'Triumphal Arch of Maximilian I', a massive woodcut masterpiece</note> released in print, though few examples are actually found. Now, for the rule of diminishing all columns generally in all orders, taking the rule from the...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of architectural orders, specifically detailing the geometric method for the "diminution" or tapering of column shafts, moving from the Tuscan order to the Ionic, Corinthian, and Composite.</meta>

->BOOK<-

regarding the tapering of the **Tuscan column**, which tapers from the top of the **upper shaft** <note>original: "sommo scapo"; the top diameter of the column</note> by one-fourth part, it is as follows: The shaft of the column is divided into three equal parts; the entire lower third remains plumb <note>perfectly vertical, without tapering</note>, and the two remaining thirds are divided into four equal parts by transverse lines. Then, above the bottom third part, a semicircle is drawn, and from the lines hanging from the outer edges of the capital, one-eighth part is retracted on each side—which in total will be one-fourth part—below the **apophyge** <note>original: "apofigi"; the curved part of the shaft where it meets the capital or base</note> or **cincture** <note>original: "cimbra"; the ring-like molding at the top or bottom of the shaft</note>. Here, two **cathetus lines** <note>original: "linee catete"; perpendicular lines</note> are drawn over the semicircle, and the part of the semicircle that remains from that line to the outer edge of the column is divided into as many equal parts as there are in the upper two-thirds of the column. This being done on the right and left sides, lines are drawn from the two sides of the semicircle: the first to the first marked above, the second to the second, and the others to the others marked on the column. Thus, beginning from the top of the shaft to draw a line on each side that touches the intersections of the lines where the column was divided with those straight lines that depart from the sides of the divided semicircle as described; and descending to the very end of the top of the lower third of the column, the true profile of it will be made.

And this rule serves all the others, as **Petrucci** <note>likely Federico Petrucci, an architectural commentator</note> asserts, even though **Vignola** <note>Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola (1507–1573), a highly influential architectural theorist</note> maintains that it is not good for anything except the Tuscan and **Doric column**, which, because it rises higher, is tapered by one-fifth part. But leaving this aside, the **Ionic column** of fifteen feet or less tapers by one-sixth part at the upper shaft; and if it is taller (though this rarely occurs), it tapers according to the proportion taken from this, as **Vitruvius** <note>the ancient Roman author of "De architectura"</note> says. The **Corinthian** tapers from sixteen feet of height downward by one-sixth part. The **Composite**, from the middle of the shaft between the bottom of the block and the upper shaft, is tapered in a diligent manner by as much as the overabundance or projection from the **astragal** <note>original: "tondino"; a small convex molding</note> to the upper shaft; the amount of which is projected outward as much as the height of its **necking** <note>original: "collarino"; the part of the column between the shaft and the capital</note>, just as was said regarding the Corinthian order. 

And whoever wishes to taper it otherwise, without straying too far, may do so. Because in this order one has a certain license <note>artistic freedom</note> that is not had in the others, as is also seen in the **fluting** <note>original: "strie"</note>, as many have taught. And because columns are also made about a third of the way up more swollen and thick <note>referring to "entasis," the slight convex curve in the shaft</note> than they are at the **lower shaft** <note>original: "imo scapo"</note>, especially the Corinthian and Ionic, the method of doing this with beautiful proportion was shown by **Vignola** in the last of his orders as his own invention; where he also shows how to make **twisted columns** <note>original: "colonne torre"; literally "towered columns," referring to the spiral or Solomonic columns</note> in the likeness of those of the **Temple of Solomon**.

## On the proportion of intercolumniations, and of the columns according to them, and their tapering, and of their appearances. Chapter XXVII.

Now we must consider the proportion of the <term>intercolumniations</term> <note>The space between two adjacent columns</note>, which in some temples are narrow and in others are wide; thus they carry different appearances, creating various effects of sweetness, beauty, greatness, and majesty. According to these proportions, Vitruvius has distinguished the types or manners of intercolumniations. The first he calls **Pycnostyle** <note>From the Greek meaning "thick-set" or "crowded"</note>, which means of thick and narrow columns; this occurs when one column is separated from the next by a space of one column and a half. By the "thickness" of the column, we mean the diameter of its lower shaft. The second manner is called **Systyle**, and it is that in which the intercolumniation is two column diameters wide; in this space, the <term>plinths</term> <note>original: "ciocchi"; the square blocks at the base of the columns</note> are as large as the distance between two plinths. The third species is called **Diastyle**, and it is when one can place the thickness of three columns within the intercolumniation. The fourth is named **Araeostyle**, and it is when the spaces between the columns are more distant than they ought to be. The last is called **Eustyle**, which is the most excellent of all in terms of utility, beauty, and firmness, being founded on the soundest reasoning. In this style, the spaces between the intervals must be two and a quarter column-diameters wide; however, the middle intercolumniation, both in the front and in the back, must be made three diameters wide. Thus, in Vitruvius's own words, it will have a graceful appearance, the entrance will be without hindrance, and the walkway around the <term>cella</term> <note>The inner chamber of a temple that houses the cult statue</note> will be spacious. 

The universal rule, therefore, shall be: if the facade of the place has four columns, divide it into eleven and a half parts, excluding the side margins and the projections of the bases. If it has six columns, divide it into eighteen parts; and if eight, into twenty-four and a half parts. From these parts—whether for a front of four, six, or eight columns—take one part, and that shall be the <term>module</term> <note>A standard unit of measure in classical architecture based on the column's diameter</note> for the thickness of the column. Every intercolumniation, except for the middle one, will then be two modules and a quarter, and the middle intercolumniation, both front and back, will be three modules. The heights of the columns will be eight and a half modules; thus, by such a division, the spaces will have their proper proportion. But in the **Araeostyle** species, the columns are raised differently, for their width is one-eighth of their height; in the **Diastyle**, the height is measured in eight and a half parts; in the **Systyle**, in nine and a half; and in the **Pycnostyle**, in ten. But the height of the column—

...column of the **Eustyle**, just as in the **Systyle**, it is divided into nine and a half parts. And one of these parts is the diameter of the <term>lower shaft</term> <note>original: "imo scapo"; the thickness of the column at its base</note>; and thus, this part is used to determine the ratio of the <term>intercolumniations</term> <note>the spaces between columns</note>. Because if the intercolumniations increase in proportion, the diameters of the shafts must also increase. For (as **Vitruvius** says) in the **Araeostyle** <note>a style with very wide spacing</note>, where the intercolumniation is very broad, if the diameter were only a ninth or tenth part of the height, the column—being so isolated—would appear thin and would be weak. This is something that would not appear so in the narrow intercolumniations of the **Pycnostyle** <note>original: "Piedistilo"; here referring to the "thick-set" style mentioned on the previous page</note>, for which thin columns can be raised. Therefore, it is necessary to shape the proportions of the bodies according to the type of work being produced; otherwise, one would depart from the true order of proceeding in works for the sake of beauty and utility.

And so it is seen that those who have regard for this, in works where the intercolumniations are square, they place very wide pilasters of <term>rustic work</term> <note>stonework left with a rough, textured surface</note>; and in intercolumniations of <term>sesquialter</term> <note>a 3:2 ratio</note> proportion, or similar, they place very strong **Tuscan** columns; and in the narrower ones, **Doric** columns; in narrower still, **Ionic**, and in the narrowest of all, **Corinthian**. However, as a general rule, one must take care where the spaces are wide to keep the columns very thick, and where they are narrow, very thin. Consequently, **Corinthian** columns will not be suitable in wide spaces, nor **Tuscan** columns in narrow ones. All of this is to be understood not only regarding well-made columns, but also regarding everything that is fit to support weight, such as pilasters, <term>herms</term> <note>original: "termini"; pillars topped with a head or bust</note>, balusters, long <term>modillions</term> <note>ornamental brackets under a cornice</note>, and the like.

In addition to this, it must also be noted that according to the height of any column, because of the loss of size that occurs relative to one's sight, it must be <term>diminished</term> <note>tapered</note> at the top; unless it rises so high that it appears tapered of its own accord. And so, following the subtle doctrine of **Vitruvius**, if the column is first fifteen feet long, let the lower diameter be divided into six parts, and let the top of the column below the <term>apophyges</term> <note>original: "apofigi"; the curved transition between the shaft and the base or capital</note> have five of them. And if the lower **shaft** is between fifteen and twenty feet, let it be divided into six and a half parts, of which five and a half are given to the upper **shaft**. If it is from twenty to thirty feet, the lower **shaft** should be one-seventh part larger than the upper **shaft**. But if it is from thirty to forty feet high, let the lower **shaft** be divided into seven and a half parts, and let the top have six and a half. If it is from forty to fifty feet, the proportion should be diminished even less. In that case, the lower **shaft** is only one-eighth larger than the top. Thus, by reason of proportion, it is diminished nearly half as much as the first. This is the true and just proportion of the intercolumniations with the columns, and of the columns with one another, and likewise of their elevations,

...or divisions <note>original: "perdimenti"; likely a variant of "partimenti," meaning compartments or sections</note>, or whatever we wish to call them. But because all buildings, palaces, and temples must be proportioned and adorned in all their internal parts and places, in conformity with their aspect—that is, the facade of said temples or palaces—and according to their example, all structures, whether poor or rich as they may be, must be regulated. For it would not be right for a building to be ornate on the outside and rough on the inside, or of one <term>order</term> <note>the specific style of architecture, such as Doric or Ionic</note> on the outside and another on the inside, which would cause the proportions of the members, intervals, <term>porticos</term> <note>porches supported by columns</note>, and window-placements to become disjointed. 

Therefore, for the sake of explanation, it should be known that the ancient Greeks ordained seven principal **aspects** <note>the general layout or plan of a temple’s exterior</note>, which they named according to the richness or poverty of the columns, so that the remainder of the building would be constructed according to their proportion. 

The first they called (as **Vitruvius** writes) <term>in antis</term> <note>original: "ante"; a temple where the side walls extend to the front, framing the columns</note>, which means "face in pilasters," where small pilasters are made in the corners; these are still called <term>antae</term> by their name, being square buttresses, and in the middle are two columns that project outward, above which is the <term>pediment</term> <note>original: "frontispitio"; the triangular gable at the top of a temple front</note>. 

The second they called <term>prostyle</term> <note>original: "prostilo"</note>, that is, "face in columns." This is because, in front of the corner pilasters mentioned before, it holds columns that follow the order of those in the middle, and it has a pediment similar to the first; this aspect is the first addition made to the simple style already mentioned, being understood only on the facade. 

The third aspect they called <term>amphiprostyle</term> <note>original: "Ampfiprostilo"</note>; because it adds to the second type a similar rear part with columns and a pediment, and it can be said to have "two heads," or both fronts in columns. 

The fourth was called <term>peripteral</term> <note>original: "Periptepros"</note>, that is, "around the side," or encircled by columns. It has six columns in the front and back, and eleven on the sides, counting those at the corners; these are placed in such a way that the spaces between one column and the next surround the walls up to the final rows of columns, allowing one to walk around the perimeter. 

The fifth aspect they called <term>pseudodipteral</term> <note>original: "psendodipteros"</note>, that is, a "false aspect of two orders." It is made so that there are eight columns on the front and back, and fifteen on the sides including the corner ones. But the parts of the <term>cella</term> <note>the inner chamber or "sanctuary" of a temple</note> are aligned with the four central columns of the ends, so that the space between the walls and the outermost rows of columns is the width of two <term>intercolumniations</term> <note>the space between columns</note> plus the thickness of one column base. 

The sixth aspect they called <term>dipteral</term> <note>original: "dipteros"</note>, and it has two rows of columns all around, creating a double portico; it has eight columns in the front and back, but on the sides around the temple it has two rows of columns, as I have said. 

The final aspect, which they named <term>hypaethral</term> <note>original: "hipetros"</note>, that is, "under the air" <note>meaning open to the sky</note>, is uncovered and has ten columns at each end; in the rest it is similar to the dipteral, but in the...

### *How also the measurements of ships, temples, buildings, and other things are drawn from the human body.* Ch. XXVIII.

**O**therwise, from the human body—a perfect work of God—is drawn 그 measure with which everything is minutely measured, called the <term>braccio</term> <note>literally "arm"; a common unit of length in Renaissance Italy, roughly 23-27 inches depending on the city</note>. This is with very great reason since it is drawn from the arm of the man, and its third is drawn from the <term>palm</term>; because three palms make one *braccio*, and a man is also three *braccia* long and three wide <note>This refers to the "Vitruvian Man" concept where a man with arms outstretched fits within a square of equal height and width</note>. Another sort of *braccio* was also found in the human body which land-surveyors use, and it is called the <term>foot</term>, and also the <term>pace</term>, drawn from the human foot and the step. It was devised for the ground so that there would be no need to bend down to measure it, and it was divided into twelve parts, because six "thick fingers" make a foot, and two feet make a pace, and a pace makes twelve fingers, that is, twelve <term>inches</term> <note>original: "onze"; though literally "ounces," in this context it refers to the division of the foot into twelve inches</note>. And thus the *braccio* was devised for measuring height, and the foot for measuring downward. And just as the pace is divided into twelve as I have said, so also the *braccio* is divided into twelve fingers, or rather inches; which then are further divided by thirds and halves, and more or less as occurs. Beyond this, the ancients drew the palm, with which the whole was measured, from that of the man; and it was of three palms of four fingers each, which come to make twelve fingers. Next, because four palms make one foot in a man (as **Vitruvius** says), they made feet of just as many palms. So that sixteen fingers came to make four palms, that is the <term>cubit</term>, and they made it to be in propor-

...<term>sesquialter</term> <note>original: "sesquialtera"; a ratio of 3:2, where one value is one and a half times the other</note> proportion to the foot—that is, six palms, or twenty-four fingers—and each of the fingers they divided into four minutes. From the head, which is an eighth part of the body, they then derived the mile of eight stadia, with which the entire world is measured, along with the distances between us and each star, and their sizes. Each stadium was one hundred and twenty-five paces, and every pace was five feet, so that the mile came to be one thousand paces, five thousand feet, twenty thousand palms, eighty thousand fingers, and three hundred and twenty thousand minutes, and twelve hundred thousand and eighty thousand seconds <note>totaling 1,280,000 seconds; these "minutes" and "seconds" are units of length rather than time</note>. Furthermore, Ships, Boats, Galleys, and the like are modeled after *Noah’s Ark*, which was drawn from the human body. For it is read that God himself taught *Noah* how to build the *Ark*, as he who had built the entire machine of the World most wisely, and had gathered all the perfection of it in a higher way within man, whereby one is called the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>original: "mondo grande"; the "great world" or the universe</note> and the other the <term>microcosm</term> <note>original: "mondo picciolo"; the "small world" or man as a reflection of the universe</note>. 

And therefore those who measured this small world divided the body into six feet, and the foot into ten degrees, and the degrees into five minutes, which made a total of sixty degrees and three hundred minutes; to these they compared as many other geometric cubits, by which the Ark was described by *Moses*. For just as the human body is three hundred minutes in length, fifty in width, and thirty in height, so likewise the Ark was three hundred cubits in length, fifty in width, and thirty in height. According to this rule, the *Greeks* later built the magnificent *Ship Argo*; and their custom went so far that, not content with their proportion, they also wished to suggest its origin by making it in relief with very large human heads and <term>mascarons</term> <note>original: "mascaroni"; decorative carvings of faces or masks</note> that represented the eighth part of their length; and at the end with various coils of tails and the final parts of feet, denoting that there was the end of the body of the mascaron or human head; and on the sides with very large arms adorned with various carvings. 

This practice continued to expand, so that ships were built in the form of animals, yet according to the said ratios, with heads of lions, eagles, and with other strange coils and whimsical details. Those who desire to know of these should read the histories of the *Greeks*, the *Egyptians*, and the *Romans*; there they will find how great they were in this, reading of the golden ship of *Cleopatra* with silver rudders, and of that of *Gaius Caligula* made of ivory and gold, with masts of ivory likewise worked in gold, with sails of silk and woven gold, and similarly with the ropes and all other belonging things; which I leave behind to come to the *Temples*, they too being taken from the form of man. From the round and circular form of man, the method was derived for making temples round in their floor plan, and also for raising them high according to their diameter; in this manner is the Rotunda in Rome, called the **Pantheon**, founded by *Marcus Agrippa*, which on the inside is divided in the middle at the level of the diameter or the <term>pettine</term> <note>original: "pettine"; literally "comb," here referring to the horizontal line or "waist" of the sphere</note>, so that the vault from there upward becomes a semicircle. The **Temple of Bacchus** similarly in Rome was raised from this roundness to its greatest height, which is that of the *Tiburio* <note>The crossing tower or drum of a dome</note>, in double proportion to the circle, or rather the floor plan of that same *Tiburio*. One finds at Tivoli, above the river Aniene, the very ancient **Temple of the Goddess Vesta**, which is built in this circular form, and is just as high on the outside and inside as the circular plan, having a height of <term>sesquialter</term> <note>A 3:2 ratio</note> proportion.

Other ancients also imagined building temples from the square form. Thus, the **Temple of Janus** was once built in the *Forum Boarium* in a square shape, as were many others that are outside of Rome; and that wonderful square portico constructed by the Greeks with one hundred columns, which was ascended by stairs located in the corners. From this, the moderns, having opened their eyes, have also set their hands to such a plan or square form, as **Poggioreale** in Naples bears witness.

Beyond this, from the <term>sesquialter</term> proportion which is found in our body from the <term>fontanella</term> <note>original: "fontanella"; the suprasternal notch or the hollow at the base of the throat</note> to the <term>pettignone</term> <note>original: "pettignone"; the pubic bone or groin area</note>, and from there to the chest, the ancients with the greatest sagacity drew another form for temples, as can be gathered from the **Temple of Peace** in Rome—where that massive marble column is still seen—and also from the **Temple of Piety**. 

And to come to the arches, some of the ancients took the plans of the torso—that is, the distance from the <term>fontanella</term> to the <term>pettignone</term> with its depth, which is exactly the third part—and also of this entire space, adding up to the nose with the same depth, as is seen in the temples <note>Though the author says "temples," he is referring to the Triumphal Arches</note> of **Titus**, **Septimius**, **Trajan**, **Constantine**, and many others that are of <term>sesquialter</term> and double proportion; that is, of a width of four times the <term>sesquialter</term> proportion or figure, which is also six. From the proportion of the foot, likewise, the form of other rare buildings was derived, as can be recognized among ancient works from the **Port of Ostia**. 

Similarly, from the plan of the human head, from the contour of the hand which form two types of oval figures, and also from the line of the <term>fontanella</term> to the <term>pettignone</term>, and from the diameter of the body in the middle of that which forms another oval, the ancients drew the form of their theaters, as can be understood in the **Colosseum of Titus** <note>The Flavian Amphitheatre in Rome</note>, in the **Arena of Verona**, in the **Theater of Pola** in Dalmatia <note>Modern Pula, Croatia</note>, and in the courtyard of the temple of...

In imitation of these ancient models, the Moderns have learned to design temples that are oval, short, and oblong, as well as those that are circular, pentagonal, hexagonal, octagonal, square, and cruciform. Many such designs can be seen drawn by <term>Baldassarre Peruzzi</term> <note>The text reads "Petrucci," but refers to the famous Sienese architect and painter Baldassarre Peruzzi (1481–1536)</note> in the fifth book of **Serlio** <note>Sebastiano Serlio, an influential architecture theorist of the Renaissance</note>. But because no certain rule has yet been established for the construction of **Cruciform Temples** (an invention, I believe, of the Germans <note>original: "Todeschi"; the author likely refers to the Gothic style, which favored the Latin cross plan</note>, and much used by **Bramante**, as is seen in his plan for the **Temple of Saint Peter** in Rome, and that of **Saint Satiro** in Milan by his disciple), I hold this view: this form will possess all the more proportion and beauty the closer it approaches the form of the human body.

A man standing upright represents the height of the entire temple—I am speaking of the <term>Tiburio</term> <note>The crossing tower or drum that supports a dome</note> or the cupola, down to the plumb line of his feet. From that point at the feet, which is the center of the cupola, to the great door, the logic of the square requires an equal distance; that is, another "man's length," as if he were stretched out upon the ground. And this width, through which one enters and exits by the great door, is exactly as wide as the <term>Tiburio</term>. The top of the <term>Tiburio</term>, where it begins to turn into a vault, represents the collarbones <note>original: "clauicole"</note> of the human body.

And because these collarbones are two "faces" wide <note>A "face" is a Renaissance unit of measurement based on the length of the human face; Vitruvius noted a well-proportioned man is ten "faces" tall</note>, and there are ten "faces" in the human body, it follows that the Temple—or rather the <term>Tiburio</term> with its lantern and everything else down to the floor—should be five diameters of that same <term>Tiburio</term>, or ten "faces." Likewise, the aisle where one walks, from the door to the plumb line of the center of the <term>Tiburio</term>, should be the same width for the same reason. The wings <note>The transepts</note>, following the logic of the floor plan and the width of the <term>Tiburio</term>, must also be of the same width, as must the **Choir**, or the head of the Temple.

### *Where all proportions originate. Chapter XXIX.*

**T**he Greeks, in imitation of the most ancient peoples, rediscovered the true and venerable proportion, in which nothing but extreme beauty and grace could be discerned. They presented this in the triangular mirror to Venus, the Goddess of celestial beauty, from whom all others derive. But leaving the mirror aside, we shall demonstrate it in the triangular figure, specifically in the <term>isosceles triangle</term> <note>The original uses *triangolo issopleuro* but defines it as having "two equal lines and the third unequal," which describes an isosceles triangle rather than an equilateral one</note>, which is a triangle that has two equal lines and a third unequal one, in a pyramidal shape. You shall therefore divide the smallest line of this triangle—which is the base of the pyramid—into ten equal parts. This will be done with ten equally distant lines drawn to the apex of the pyramid. Then, on this line of ten "faces" <note>A "face" was a standard unit of measurement in art theory, representing the length of a human face</note>, you will take the width of the aforementioned proportion of the woman, which is divided into so many parts. You will follow these proportionately in each of the ten faces from the front, then in profile, and in the back, along with the arms. In this way, you will draw the widths of the members to their contours, and they will correspond in the front, profile, and back views upon another paper traced from that very same one. This is the true and singular proportion of beauty. But if you wish to create another, shorter proportion, you shall draw another line—like that of the ten faces—closer toward the "eye" <note>The vanishing point or apex of the diagram</note>, so that it comes to be high from the lateral line to the bottom one, with the measure of ten parts reduced into nine. Then, on the lines of the faces drawn toward the eye (which are ten in the line of nine), you will draw the width of the members to that equality of the first, and thus it will become shorter and thicker. This you shall do for the front, profile, and back on another paper traced from this one.

**I**f you also wish to make one of eight or seven, you shall follow the same path with the same width as the principal one. Indeed, with the same rule, you can draw figures of nine and a half or eight and a half faces, as it seems best to you. If you wish to make a female figure eleven or twelve faces long, you shall draw the highest lateral line from the eye, and the bottom one further out...

## *On the power of proportion, and how through it one may introduce the proper dimensions in colossi. Chapter 30.*

**B**ecause it can never be that figures appear to our eyes as large as they actually are, even when they are perfectly proportionate. As the rays of the proportions travel to the **Cone of the Pyramid** <note>In Renaissance perspective theory, the "visual pyramid" describes how light travels from an object to the eye (the apex). Objects appear smaller as they recede or as the angle of the "cone" narrows</note> which is the eye, and the line of the facade—which acts like a mirror—is interposed there, the eye will never be able to see the figure as long as it truly is through this Pyramid. This is even more true because the eye barely perceives a single point, or nothing at all, as it spreads its rays to find the parts of the figures; the further these parts extend, the more they lose their perceived proportions. Therefore, a way has been found so that they may be understood by their proportions as measured in effect, rather than just how they are seen by the eye. And because these proportions were thus ordained by the great painter, the **Best and Greatest** <note>Referring to God as the ultimate architect and artist</note>, many Heroes followed after. Among the Babylonians there were Nimrod, Belus, and Semiramis; among the Egyptians, Amasis and Sesostris; and many among the Greeks and Romans. These figures wished to transfer these human proportions into greater size, such as **colossi** as tall as towers. In such works, because our eyes must be raised to such a great height, the heads would seem tiny in comparison to the feet, as will be discussed in the sixth book. Therefore, to determine their heights and proportions, one shall draw a right square on paper with two crossed diameters, resulting in four equal squares. In one of those squares, one will place a cube, and above that, nine more shall be added, making ten in total. This shall be the height of the human figure. ...the diameter as it is, one of the ten parts shall be marked, and all of these together shall be called a **squared figure** <note>original: "figura squadrata"; this refers to a rectangular prism or "block" used as a geometric shorthand for the human body's proportions, where the width is one-tenth of the height</note>. Let this described figure serve as a rule for the colossi <note>Colossi are statues of significantly larger than life-size scale</note> that one wishes to make. 

Thus, in the event that one wishes to make a colossus ten parts higher, you shall add another ten parts above the already squared figure. And because the diameter of the figure is one part in ten, and the base above it is just as much, it will be necessary to place another ten parts next to it, and another ten above those. Then, because at the bottom the square will not be complete but for a half, a half-figure will remain; to finish this, one will add as many parts as the aforementioned, so that this colossus will result in being eight parts of the figure, being double in height. 

And to verify what I have said, if you wish to double the **cube** or **die** <note>original: "cubo ouer dado"; a "die" refers to a single gaming cube</note>: if you place one die upon another, it is necessary to place six others in the said square, arranged two by two, which results in the doubling of the cube; there will then be eight dice in total to double the first. And here, with such orders and proportions—as I shall also explain later regarding both the circle and the square—one can grow and multiply all **regular and irregular geometric bodies**. 

Now, for the knowledge of the particular heights and thicknesses of such colossi, one must know that the aforementioned squared figure is taken at ten parts (or faces) high and one in diameter. This diameter is placed within a **geometric circle**, around which a perfect square is made that finds the four diametrical roundnesses <note>The four points where the circle touches the sides of the square</note> of the circle and the square. 

And wishing to double the diameter, one will draw a **diagonal line** from one right angle to the other; and according to that diagonal line which divides the square in half, four perfect parts of a right square are made. Then, within that square, a circle is formed that touches its four diametrical parts; and this will be the doubling of the other circle and square. Whereupon this diameter is raised ten parts, just like the squared figure; which, when compared again to the first figure, remains half of this one in both width and height. 

If you wish to make it four times larger than the first figure, you will draw the diagonal line to this second square, extending it exactly into the third square and making its circle. Thus, step by step, you will make whatever colossi you wish with these rules, noting that the doubling of the aforementioned diameter is the most important factor, increasing it thereafter within the squared figure. 

With this method, you can make all the diameters that please you, and you can also find by this rule how many natural figures <note>That is, standard life-sized human figures</note> go into the colossi. # ->BOOK ONE.<-

**O**ne man being the unit, the colossus would therefore be eighteen men high, plus two feet, which constitute a third of a man. Now, speaking of the eighteen figures and setting the two feet aside for elsewhere: if one takes the aforementioned **squared figure**—which is ten faces <note>original: "faccie"; a standard unit of artistic measurement where the height of a person is divided into ten head-lengths or "faces"</note> high with its diameter at the bottom being one of those ten parts (representing the human figure)—then to make a colossus eighteen figures high, there will be eighteen figures at the bottom of the square at the base with their diameters. Thus, one says eighteen times eighteen makes three hundred and twenty-four, and that is how many diameters there will be. Then, taking those eighteen figures upright one above the other at the bottom, and multiplying the three hundred and twenty-four diameters by the eighteen figures in height, the result will be five thousand eight hundred and thirty-two. This is the number of [standard-sized] figures that go into making the said colossus.

But as for the two feet that make up a third of a human figure, you shall distribute this quantity into eighteen parts, because that is how many figures are in the height of the colossus; you shall increase each of the eighteen parts by one above each figure, dividing one of the eighteen parts into ten to raise the ten faces of the human figure. By increasing in this manner, as I said above, you will multiply the said colossus for each part by one hundred and ten feet. You shall also use this rule to find the natural proportion in the great golden colossus that Nebuchadnezzar <note>The Babylonian king mentioned in the Book of Daniel (3:1), who erected a massive golden image</note> ordered to be made, sixty cubits <note>An ancient unit of length based on the forearm</note> in height and six in width. Because if four cubits make one man, he would come to be fifteen men high; and multiplying by fifteen at the base, there would be two hundred and twenty-five diameters, which represent that many figures; and then multiplying those diameters by the fifteen in height, they result in three thousand three hundred and seventy-five figures in total.

In short, one must take the greatest care in making and proportioning them correctly according to what has been discussed. And you shall always ensure that the sighting-hole—or whatever iron tool it may be—with the strings attached to it, projects onto the facade what will be described in practice regarding the colossus proportioned according to the view <note>This refers to the practice of "optical corrections," where a statue's proportions are distorted so that it appears correct to a viewer looking up from the ground</note>.

# SECOND BOOK,
## ON THE SITE, POSITION,
## DECORUM, MOTION, FURIA,
### & grace of figures.

->*By Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo, Milanese Painter.*<-

->**On the force and efficacy of motions. Chapter I.**<-

<margin>N</margin>ON-etheless, there is no doubt that all those motions seen in figures that resemble natural motions possess the greatest grace; and conversely, those that depart from the natural are entirely devoid of any grace, being discordant with nature in the same way that out-of-tune strings are on an instrument. And not only do these motions, so vividly expressed from the natural, bring grace to a figure; but they also produce the same effect that natural ones usually do. For just as naturally one who laughs, or cries, or performs any other action, moves most others who see him to that same affection <note>affection: in this period, "affection" (affetto) refers to a deep emotional state or psychological movement</note> of joy or sorrow—as that man once said:

> *if you wish me to weep, you must first feel grief yourself; then your misfortunes will affect me;* <note>original: "si vis me flere dolendum est primum ipsi tibi, tunc tua me infortunia ledent" — a famous quote from the Roman poet Horace's *Ars Poetica*, advising that an artist must truly feel an emotion to evoke it in an audience.</note>

so, and not otherwise, a painting represented (as I was saying) with motions portrayed from life will without doubt make one laugh with the one who laughs, think with the one who thinks, lament with the one who cries, rejoice and be glad with the one who is happy. And beyond this, it will make one marvel with the one who marvels, desire a beautiful young woman as a wife upon seeing her naked, feel compassion for the one who suffers, and even be moved to eat upon seeing someone eating precious and delicate foods, fall asleep seeing someone who sleeps sweetly, be moved in the soul and almost enter into a furia <term>furia: a technical term in Renaissance art for a sense of intense, divine energy or martial spirit in a figure</term> with those who are seen fighting courageously in battle, expressed with their proper and appropriate motions; be moved to indignation and nausea by those seen doing something filthy and dishonest; and infinite other similar effects. Which truly are of no less mar-

<margin>I</margin>
Wonder and astonishment to the world are those marvels of the ancient musicians who, by playing as they pleased, were accustomed to incite men to fury and indignation, or to inspire them toward love, arms, honorable deeds, and other such passions. Equal to these are those other marvelous and stupendous works of **mathematical motions** <note>mathematical motions: In the Renaissance, "mathematics" included the study of mechanics and engineering. Here, Lomazzo refers to what we would now call "automata" or early robotics.</note>, which are recounted of those truly wise ancients: making figures move by themselves, like those of **Daedalus**, which (according to Homer’s account) went into battle on their own; or like the **Tripods of Vulcan** mentioned by Aristotle; or the golden statues of servants that moved by themselves and served guests at the table during the banquet of **Iarchas the Gymnosophist** <note>Iarchas: Lomazzo likely refers to the Indian sage Iarchas from the life of Apollonius of Tyana, though the text says "Iarba." The Gymnosophists were "naked philosophers" of India famous in classical lore for their wisdom and supposed magical inventions.</note>; or those most ancient statues of **Mercury** in Egypt that spoke; and finally many other similar wonders.

In our own times, **Leonardo da Vinci** also created such things. According to what his disciple **Francesco Melzi**—a very great miniaturist—told me, Leonardo used to make birds out of a certain material that flew through the air. Once, in the presence of **Francis I, King of France**, he made a **Lion** of admirable craftsmanship walk of its own accord across a hall, and then stop and open its chest, which was found to be entirely filled with lilies and various flowers. This was a source of such wonder to that King and all those present that they could then easily believe that the wooden dove of **Archytas of Tarentum** once flew; or that a bronze **Diomedes** (as Cassiodorus reports) sounded a trumpet; or that a serpent of the same metal was heard to hiss; or that certain birds sang; or even that the bronze head of **Albertus Magnus** spoke to **Saint Thomas Aquinas**, who broke it because he believed it was a work of the Devil—though it was, in fact, a mathematical creation and labor, as is now admitted.

But to resume the argument I had set aside: I say that because these motions are so powerful in moving the soul when they are expressed in a way that appears natural, one must principally—and above all others—imitate **Leonardo** to achieve this most excellent and important faculty. It is told of him that he never depicted a motion in a figure without first desiring to see it for a time in real life through his own study. This was for no other reason than to extract from it a certain natural liveliness; then, by adding the power of art, he made his painted men appear better than the living. It is recounted by men of that time who were part of his household that, wanting once to make a painting of some peasants laughing (though he did not eventually paint it, but only drew it), he chose certain men he judged suitable for his purpose. Having become familiar with them, he arranged a banquet for them through the help of some friends; and as he was **sitting with them**...

<page-num>107</page-num>
<header>FIRST BOOK</header>

...following him <note>Leonardo’s servant or companion</note>, he began to tell the craziest and most ridiculous stories in the world, so that he made them laugh until their jaws dropped <note>original: "alla smașcellata"; meaning unbridled, side-splitting laughter</note>, even though they did not know what they were laughing at. From this, by diligently observing all their gestures alongside those ridiculous words that remained impressed in his mind, he later retired to his room after they had departed. There, he drew them so perfectly that those looking at the drawings were moved to laughter no less than the stories of Leonardo had moved the guests at the banquet. 

They also say that he took great delight in going to see the gestures of the condemned when they were led to their execution, in order to note the knitting of their eyebrows <note>original: "incarnamenti di ciglia"</note> and the movements of their eyes and bodies. Following this example, I would judge it a most expedient thing for a painter to delight in seeing fistfights, observing the eyes of knifefighters, the strains of wrestlers, the gestures of actors, and the charms and flatteries of <term>women of the world</term> <note>Lomazzo refers here to courtesans or prostitutes, who were studied by artists for their performative grace and artifice.</note>, in order to become instructed in every detail. 

For these are the spirits—or rather the very soul—of painting. Therefore, let no one fail to attend to these concerns to keep the brain awake; for whoever does not attend to them is, without doubt, cold and dead in **invention** <note>In Renaissance art theory, "invention" refers to the original conceptualization and storytelling of a work.</note>, and will struggle for ten years to create a single pose for a figure that, in the end, is worth nothing. Thus we see that, to avoid falling into such a notable defect, all the great inventors have for the most part been the most subtle investigators of natural effects, delighting (as I have said) in seeing them often, and remaining continually occupied in this practice through deep thought and study. 

From this, a man comes to acquire a skill so refined that he uses it as if it were a second nature, vividly representing all the poses and movements that suit his purpose. This is exactly what our **Cesare Sesto** acquired, if we look at his truly miraculous drawings, in which the attitudes are seen to be so appropriate and suited to the subject that nothing more could be added. For this reason, he was very dear to, and held in high esteem by, **Raphael of Urbino**. It is also told that Raphael was often accustomed to say jokingly that it seemed a great thing to him that, being such close friends as they were, they nonetheless showed not the slightest "respect" <note>The sense here is that they did not defer to one another out of politeness, but competed fiercely and honestly in their craft.</note> for each other in the art of painting. These were truly the words of <term>virtuosi</term>; for they competed together with such sweet emulation that, if it were still found in our times, it would make the world blessed. But to our misfortune, in its place has succeeded a cruel envy that gnaws at us and pierces the heart at the excellence and valor of others, and causes us to mock and insolently scorn the ignorance and ineptitude of others.

He contrasts the productive, friendly rivalry of Raphael and Cesare Sesto with the "cruel envy" of his own day.</summary>
