## On the Necessity of Motion. Chapter II.

**I**n this place, it is reasonable that we should subsequently treat motion itself—that is, with what art the painter must appropriately give motion to a figure. This must be done according to the nature of the proportion of the form and the matter; for as I have said, the spirit and life of art consist precisely in this. For this reason, painters are accustomed to call it sometimes <term>fury</term> <note>original: "furia"; referring to a state of intense creative passion or divine inspiration.</note>, sometimes <term>grace</term> <note>original: "gratia"; the quality of effortless elegance and beauty.</note>, and sometimes the excellence of art. And this is not without reason, since this part is the most difficult to achieve in all of art, and also the most important and necessary to know. 

Through this, painters make known the difference between the dead and the living; the fierce from the humble; the mad from the wise; the sorrowful from the joyful; and, in short, all the passions and gestures that a human body can show and perform, distinct among themselves. These are called by the name "motion," for no other reason than that they are a certain expression and outward demonstration in the body of those things which the soul suffers internally. For the internal motions of people are known no less through this way than through words; indeed, even **more** so, because this is performed by the body itself, which acts neither more nor less than what is commanded by the <term>rational soul</term> <note>In the philosophy of the time, the "rational soul" was the highest part of the human soul, responsible for reason and will.</note>, whether turned toward good or toward evil according to its perceptions. 

And from this it follows that those painters who understand these things (though they are rare) ensure that one sees in their paintings those marvelous and secret works of nature, moved by that <term>motive virtue</term> <note>original: "Virtù motiua"; a contemporary medical and philosophical term for the power that enables the soul to move the physical limbs.</note> which, continually remaining hidden in the heart, demonstrates itself outwardly in the body and sends out its "branches" through the exterior members, which move accordingly. From this are born those greatest wonders, the effects and demonstrations of figures that are seen to be as different from one another as the passions of their souls are different; some of which will be treated to some extent in this book. 

Now, the knowledge of this motion is that which, as I said a little above, is considered so difficult in art and esteemed as a divine gift. For it is through this part specifically that painting is compared to poetry. Just as it is necessary for the Poet—along with the excellence of his intellect—to have a certain desire and an inclination of will by which he is moved to compose poetry (which the ancients called the **fury of Apollo** and of the muses), so too it is fitting for the Painter. Along with the other parts required of him, he must have the knowledge and the power to express the principal motions as if it were born within him and grown with him from his <note>original: "dalle faſcie"; literally "from the swaddling clothes," meaning from earliest infancy.</note> cradle. Otherwise, it is a difficult, indeed impossible thing to possess this art perfectly.

<summary>Lomazzo explains that "motion" (the outward expression of internal emotion) is the most vital and difficult element of painting, distinguishing the living from the dead. He argues that this ability is a divine gift, likening the painter's inspiration to the "fury" of ancient poets.</summary>
<keywords>motion, artistic expression, rational soul, motive virtue, fury of Apollo, grace, artistic inspiration, psychology of art</keywords>

Just as we see through experience, there have been many excellent **Painters**—and many are still found today—who have been held in the highest esteem by everyone for their painting. These are the ones who represent figures with beautiful colors, well-understood limbs, and very well-proportioned <term>anatomical connections</term> <note>original: "legature d'anatomia"; referring to the way joints and muscles are linked to show movement.</note>, and who have diligently illuminated them with good <term>chiaroscuro</term> <note>original: "chiaro, & scuro"; the technique of using strong contrasts between light and dark to give the illusion of three-dimensional volume.</note>. 

But because, despite all the care and patience they have used, they were never able to successfully acquire this faculty <note>The faculty of "motion" or "spirit" discussed on the previous page.</note>, they have left their works subject to the criticism of posterity. This is solely because the poses and **gestures** of their figures are poorly expressed, having been taken from the <term>inventions</term> <note>original: "inuentioni"; in Renaissance art theory, this refers to the creative concept or original composition of a work.</note> of others—that is, from those who were born with this unique grace. They then arranged these figures according to how they themselves imagined they should stand. They imagine these gestures and motions in the figures, but when these are removed from the original purpose and effect for which they were created, they cannot be judged as good, for they lack a proper correspondence to the circumstances of the scene.

And so, these unfortunate "diligent" painters—who are otherwise skilled in the craft of painting—however much they might imitate the gestures and acts of other inventors, can never make any of their <term>histories</term> <note>original: "istoria"; a narrative painting depicting a scene from the Bible, mythology, or history, considered the highest form of art.</note> appear well-composed. This is because such a composition can only be the work of those who bring it to life all at once, guided and pushed by a pure intelligence and a **natural fury** <note>original: "furia naturale"; a state of inspired, rapid creativity, often likened to divine madness.</note>. 

It is indeed true that those who possess this gift of invention usually cannot, on the other hand, have the same patience for the labor as the others do. This happens for no other reason than the constant inventions and <term>caprices</term> <note>original: "capricci"; sudden, imaginative, and playful artistic whims.</note> that assault their minds. Because of this, as soon as they have sketched a body and formed a gesture, infinite others of a different sort are born in their imagination. Thus, because of the extreme delight they feel in the act of invention, they cannot find the patience to finish any work they have started.

But the truly capable and excellent painters are not only helped by nature but are also perfected in **art**. They seek to choose the best gesture for every intended effect, restraining that overabundant natural fury with the deliberate reason they hold in their mind. With this balance, they finish the figure with delight and pleasure, always ensuring that in every limb one can see a certain "fury" that conforms to the main motion. 

And for this reason, they alone come to win the prize in this profession. This success is not granted to the "furious" ones because of their impatience, nor to those first "diligent" ones because they have no knowledge of this motion and cannot express it while working—whereas the naturally furious painter will demonstrate it with just four strokes. For this reason, the diligent painter remains inferior, just as both of them yield by a long margin to the inventor who rationally accompanies the gift of nature with the study of art. I will...

I am, however, of the opinion that it is possible—though not with that same natural vehemence, fury, and ease—to acquire this faculty of such great importance and necessity. Without it, paintings can be said to be neither alive nor dead. This is achieved through the power of studying motion <note>original: "moto"; in this context, it refers to both physical movement and the outward expression of internal emotion.</note> and the other categories of art, and through knowledge of the logic and cause from which it arises. For from this, one comes to derive a certain hidden intelligence that is very accessible. When this intelligence is put into practice with patience, and combined with the knowledge of the other categories, there is no doubt that it can make a judicious inventor <note>original: "inuētore"; the artist's ability to conceive and compose a scene.</note> out of one who had neither natural inclination nor ease for it. I say such an inventor—guiding himself solely by reason—will arrive at a greater degree of perfection than those others born with fury and motion, but who are devoid of study and patience.

As an example, if someone reads diligently and considers, part by part, the history of the **Passion of our Lord**, they will undoubtedly derive the true rule and idea with which they must represent the motions of **Christ**, the **Apostles**, the **Jews**, and whoever else took part in that cruel tragedy. In this way, they will move the souls of the viewers to pity, tears, sorrow, and indignation no less with painting than we are moved by the reading of that history. Thus, the artist will know how to depict in the Jew the violent, offensive, ugly, mocking, agitated, and twisted motions; and in **Christ**, who is entirely patient, restrained and bowed motions, so that they come to show us—as if in a very clear mirror—that singular humility and patience with which He primarily reconciled us to the Eternal Father.

However, although these things can be clearly drawn from the reading of histories, they can nonetheless, for greater ease, be taken and imitated with the greatest success from accidental examples in living people. They can then be expressed through art and the study devoted to it. Art makes the depth of its study visible and shining within the work, exciting and moving the <term>affections</term> <note>original: "affetti"; the internal emotions or states of mind that an artist seeks to portray through outward gestures.</note> of pity and sorrow, as in a painting of the Passion, or other emotions as required by the story the painter chooses to represent.

Regarding the way and manner of giving these motions according to the diversity of the passions and the affections that can move souls at various times and on various occasions, I hope in God to show clear examples in this book. This is despite it being a part so difficult that it can only be drawn from the hidden sources of <term>natural philosophy</term> <note>original: "Filosofia naturale"; the study of nature and the physical universe, which at this time included the study of human psychology and the soul's impact on the body.</note>. Therefore, it would be a work more suitable for a seasoned man than a youth; for which reason, not without some blushing, I set myself to treat it, especially since it has never truly been untangled until now by **Painters**, even though it is of such...

necessity and need. But if, as I have said, this part has never been fully or sufficiently treated or taught in the past, and if I do not fully open and level the promised path, at least this labor of mine should not be despised; for I will at least provide a free field for everyone to exercise their intellect easily, and with a certain order and rule. This rule shall be most secure and very singular, since by it so many excellent Painters have governed themselves. By imitating history, these artists have understood form and given to their paintings the appropriate <term>motions</term> <note>original: "moti"; the movements of the body that reveal the "passions of the soul" or internal emotions.</note>, proportioned, carried, and guided by reason, accompanied by natural frenzy. 

Among these, the first was **Raphael of Urbino**, who with supreme majesty divinely formed his works; **Polidoro** <note>Polidoro da Caravaggio (c. 1499–1543), known for his dramatic chiaroscuro frescoes on Roman facades.</note>, whose paintings are seen to be so full of frenzy and excellence; **Andrea Mantegna**, who was most acute and diligent in this; and **Leonardo da Vinci**, in whose works no error was ever discerned regarding this part. Of this, among all his other things, the most clear proof is the wonderful **Last Supper** of **Christ** and his **Apostles**, which can be seen painted in the refectory of **Holy Mary of Grace** <note>Santa Maria delle Grazie</note> in **Milan**. In this work, he expressed the motions of the passions of the souls of those Apostles in such a manner—in their faces and in all the rest of the body—that it may well be said that the truth itself was not at all different from this representation. That work has been one of the most marvelous works of painting that was ever made at any time by any painter, however excellent, in oil <note>original: "oglio"</note>—a method of painting of which **John of Bruges** <note>original: "Giouanni da Brugia"; referring to Jan van Eyck, whom Vasari and others of this period credited with the "invention" of oil painting.</note> was the inventor at that time. 

For in those Apostles, one can see individually admiration, terror, grief, suspicion, love, and similar passions and affections in which they all then found themselves; and finally, in **Judas**, the treachery conceived in his soul, with a countenance exactly like that of a traitor. Thus, Leonardo clearly demonstrated how perfectly he understood the motions that the soul is accustomed to cause in bodies. Because these are a most necessary part for the Painter, they will be treated throughout almost this entire book. **Michelangelo** was also most astounding in this regard, and as one who knew it to be extremely difficult, he applied to it very long and continuous study. For this reason, one sees in his paintings the most difficult motions, expressed outside of common usage, yet all tending toward a certain fierceness and <term>terribilità</term> <note>original: "terribilità"; a quality of awe-inspiring power and emotional intensity.</note>. 

Nor should we omit the great **Titian**, who by practicing the difficulties of these motions has deservedly obtained the name of a most primary Painter. His figures bear witness to this, in each of which shines a certain motor force that seems to incite everyone to imitate him, wherefore someone once well said of him that he...

Furthermore, there are the stories of **Saint Roch**, made by him at **Vercelli**, along with many other works in that city. In short, all of **Lombardy** is adorned and filled with the works of this excellent man. Regarding him, I do not want to omit a saying about the art of motions that he frequently had in his mouth: that every painter delights and takes pleasure in stealing the inventions of others, but that there is then a great risk of being discovered and recognized as a thief. This great painter, although he can rightly be compared—for Prudence, Wisdom, and valor—to those named in the third Book of **Architecture**, was nonetheless omitted by **Giorgio Vasari** in the *Lives* <note>Vasari's "Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects," the foundational work of art history which favored Florentine and Sienese artists.</note> he wrote of Painters, Sculptors, and Architects. This was for no other reason (to avoid giving him a more ugly mark) than that he intended only to exalt his **Tuscany** to the heavens. But let us come now to the motions caused by the reasons that shall be stated; and first, for clearer understanding, let us begin to treat the <term>passions of the soul</term> <note>original: "passioni dell’animo"; the internal emotional states that trigger physical movement.</note> by which the Body moves and produces its particular effects.

## Of the passions of the soul, and their origin and difference. Chapter III.

**T**he passions of the soul are nothing other than certain motions that proceed from the apprehension <note>original: "apprensione"; in this context, the way the mind perceives or grasps an object or idea.</note> of any thing. This apprehension is of three kinds: sensual, rational, and mental; and according to these three, the passions also exist within the soul. Because sometimes they follow sensual apprehensions, and then they regard good or evil in the form of convenience or inconvenience, pleasantness or offensiveness; and these are called natural passions. Sometimes they follow rational apprehensions, and they regard good and evil in the manner of virtue and vice, of praise and blame, of the useful and the useless, of the honest and the dishonest; and these are called rational passions. Sometimes they follow mental apprehensions, and regard good and evil by the reason of the just and the unjust, of the true and the false, and then they are called intellectual passions. 

The lower powers <note>Refers to the faculties of the "sensitive soul" in Aristotelian and Scholastic philosophy, which humans share with animals.</note> are then divided into the <term>concupiscible</term> <note>original: "concupiscibile"; the faculty through which the soul is drawn toward what is pleasing or avoids what is harmful.</note> and the <term>irascible</term> <note>original: "irascibile"; the faculty through which the soul resists obstacles or fights for a difficult good.</note>, and both one and the other regard what appears good or evil in different ways. Because the concupiscible faculty sometimes considers good and evil absolutely, and thus causes love, or even lust, and conversely hate; or it considers the good as absent, and thus are born cupidity and desire; or it considers evil as absent, but near, and thus generates horror, flight, and abomination; or it regards good and evil as present, and then from the former comes delight, joy, and pleasure, and from the latter sadness, anguish, and pain. 

The irascible power considers good and evil under the reason of the difficulty of acquiring and obtaining it, or fleeing and avoiding it. From this is born sometimes confidence, and consequently hope, and at other times, audacity; sometimes distrust, and thus despair, fear, or dread. Often this irascible power is also moved to vengeance, and this occurs only because of a past evil, such as an injury or offense received; and thus is generated anger. 

From this discourse it remains clear that there are eleven named passions or, if we wish to say, affections in the soul: love, hate, desire, horror, joy, sorrow, hope, despair, audacity, fear, and anger. From these, in order, are born as many motions as can be introduced into bodies through all our art. Therefore, it is necessary to pay close attention to the motions, so that they are represented in such a way that they do not obscurely hint at the roots from which they come, and denote the causes by which they are produced; and according to these, they should be introduced and disposed in the bodies. Doing otherwise, one would do nothing other than...

### How the body changes through the passions of the soul. Chapter IV.

**I**t is a most clear thing, and known through continuous experience and manifest to everyone, that the soul—according to the different passions by which it is overwhelmed through sensual perceptions <note>original: "apprensioni sensuali"; the way the mind grasps information through the five senses.</note>—similarly alters and transforms the imagination and the body in various ways with a perceptible transformation; changing the accidents <note>In the philosophy of the time, "accidents" were non-essential qualities like color, temperature, or moisture.</note> in the body, and producing different qualities in the limbs. And so, in joy the spirits <note>original: "spiriti"; in Renaissance medicine, these were subtle fluids or vapors that carried life and sensation through the body.</note> are pushed outward; in fear they contract; in shame they move toward the brain. Moreover, in joy, the heart gradually expands outward; in displeasure it gradually withdraws inward, and similarly in anger and fear. 

But suddenly, anger or the desire for revenge induces heat, redness, a bitter taste, and an influence of the belly <note>likely referring to a sudden digestive reaction or "nervous stomach."</note>; and fear induces cold, heart palpitations, loss of voice, and paleness. Sadness causes sweat and a cerulean <note>a bluish-gray or sickly pale color</note> whiteness. Compassion causes a certain sadness which often attacks and harms the one who sympathizes and is moved to mercy. This is usually seen in lovers closely tied by the knot of love, where what one suffers, the other suffers as well. 

Anxiety induces dryness and blackness. How many colors—now red, and now pale—the desire of love arouses can be seen in lovers, especially during their encounters. And all these passions, when they are most vehement, sometimes bring death; as happened to Sophocles <note>The Greek playwright was said to have died of joy after winning a competition.</note>, and to Dionysius the Tyrant of Sicily <note>Dionysius I, who reportedly died after hearing his play won a prize at Athens.</note>, upon receiving news of a doubtful victory; a thing that has happened to many others through sadness as well, besides other evils and accidents that arise from such passions when they assault the soul with vehemence. Various examples of this can be seen in histories, which I will not stop to recount here as they are more curious than necessary for our purpose. 

I will only say how much a great anger, joined with a magnanimous boldness, can do and work, with the example of Alexander the Great; who, being overtaken by enemies in India, was seen to cast fire and light from his body. The same is read of the father of Theodoric <note>Theodemir, King of the Ostrogoths.</note>, who through a similar vehement affection sent out sparks of fire from his heart, as if from a burning coal, which went flying and...

Now, by representing all these passions and affects in the histories <note>original: "istorie"; in Renaissance art theory, this refers to narrative paintings depicting a specific scene or story, considered the highest form of art.</note> that we paint, using their appropriate and proper movements, we come to create that great variety which so delights and pleases—enticing and drawing our souls to itself with a sweet force. This is something so powerful and effective that one reads of a certain musician who boasted of having the power to make men go mad with sound, and then return them to their former state.

### In which bodies the passions of the soul have more power. Chapter V.

**E**ven though these described passions of the soul have a place universally in everyone through the aforementioned perceptions, we must not imagine that they show themselves externally in bodies in the same way, or that they cause the same movements. This is because each passion shows itself outwardly and moves the body only as much as that body corresponds to it. And just as the passions are varied and diverse among themselves—for which reason they generate different movements in bodies—likewise, as each body is of a different temperament <note>original: "temperatura"; the specific balance of the four humors in an individual's body.</note>, it must necessarily act differently. Consequently, the passions will show themselves in a person with all the more force as he—being the instrumental cause through his constitution and temperament—is more similar and conforming to their nature.

To see this more clearly, we know that every body is composed of four humors <note>The "Four Humors" were the basis of ancient and Renaissance medicine: blood, phlegm, yellow bile (choler), and black bile (melancholy).</note>, which represent the four elements: phlegm, which represents water; melancholy, which represents earth; choler, and blood, of which one represents fire and the other air. Now, according to how each body is tempered and primarily constituted by one of these four humors, one will always see that the acts and gestures within that person are exactly like the acts—or to put it more properly, the qualities—of the element to which his prevailing humor corresponds. 

Thus, if he is melancholic <note>In this period, "melancholy" was not just a mood but a physical state caused by an excess of black bile, associated with the earth.</note>, and therefore of the earthy element, one will see in him drooping, heavy, and constrained actions, just as one sees the earth itself to be drooping, heavy, and constrained. Consequently, his movements will be anxious, tiresome, sad, rigid, stubborn, and the like; all of which tend downward, and therefore move the limbs by making them hang and bow down, and also huddle together just as the cold of winter usually does. And therefore, in these bodies, anxiety will appear much more powerful...

...anxiety, horror, and despair, because they possess a certain natural principle within them due to the dryness and blackness <note>Dryness and blackness are the qualities of "black bile," the humor associated with the element of Earth and the Melancholic temperament.</note> that it likewise induces; this is because the movements of water are also downward-tending, although not as much as those of the earth, and they are less restricted. **Phlegm** <term>flegma: the cold and moist humor associated with water</term>, to which water corresponds, creates in the bodies where it prevails timid, simple, humble, and merciful movements, which then cause the limbs of the body to tend somewhat downward and to dilate. And thus, fear—or rather dread—corresponds to phlegm because of the paleness it infuses, as does sorrow because of the cerulean <note>original: "bianchezza cerulea"; a pale, bluish-white color associated with sickness or coldness.</note> whiteness it displays. 

Air has its movements tending upward, but not excessively, as they are tempered and not at all dilated or twisted like those of fire. Because air is a pleasant element, the movements of the **blood** <term>sangue: the warm and moist humor associated with the Sanguine temperament</term> in bodies conform to it; that is, they are tempered, modest, gracious, royal, merciful, and cheerful. For this reason, they move the limbs temperately, not allowing them to be agitated, nor to hang, nor to twist, nor to dilate. To these movements, the aforementioned passions of the soul correspond perfectly: namely love, from which arise delight and pleasure, desire, joy, and hope—all passions of cheerfulness and a tranquil mind, enemies of anxiety, despair, and hatred. Therefore, they push our spirits outward, contrary to what the movements of water and earth do, which restrict them. 

Fire, finally, has movements very different from the others. For, as is visibly understood in a flame, they naturally tend toward extreme height, and as they approach it, they all go about twisting. (In wanting to represent this, the ancient poets feigned ***Vulcan, the God of Fire, to be Lame*** <note>In mythology, Vulcan (Hephaestus) was cast from Olympus and walked with a limp; here, the author uses this as a metaphor for the flickering, "interrupted" movement of a flame.</note>) yet he does not continue growing and climbing upward with a single, steady motion, but rather an interrupted one, moving bit by bit with agitation. Therefore, similar to these are the movements of **choler** <term>colora: yellow bile, the hot and dry humor associated with the element of Fire</term> in bodies. These are violent, impetuous, arrogant, bold, and fierce; and for this reason, they also cause the limbs of the body to agitate, twist, lift, stir, and overflow. Since the passions of hatred, audacity, and anger are very much in conformity with these movements, they will appear perfectly in such bodies, as they are the passions that enlarge the limbs through heat and inflame the flesh with redness—especially the eyes—swelling all the limbs impetuously. 

Now, here the diligent **master of motion** <term>motista: an artist or theorist specialized in the depiction of physical movement and gestures</term> must take care: whenever he recognizes a certain **humor** <term>humore: one of the four bodily fluids believed to determine temperament</term> to be superabounding in a body, he must make that body perform the movements corresponding to that passion, according to the conformity it holds with the very humor that prevails. By observing this, he will not depict lazy, humble, or weak movements in a magnanimous soldier, which would...

...come to the fearful and the penitent. Neither in the most holy Pope nor in the sacred Emperor should one see movements that are restricted, rough, horrid, or harsh—movements suitable only for the wicked, the base, and the harmful. Generally, in all people, one should avoid movements that do not belong to their character in any way. Anyone who considers these reasons carefully will surely understand the foundation for reasonably creating as many movements and gestures as can be imagined and performed. 

This is because no part of any body exists that does not harmonize with all the others, just as the others do with it. From the surface of the limbs, which act as the "instrument" of the soul, follows the color; and according to the color follow the taste, hearing, voice, sight, desires, activities, movements, habits, speech, and everything else. Thus, one will never find a **Martial body** <term>corpo Martiale: a body type dominated by the influence of the planet Mars, corresponding to the "choleric" temperament</term>—characterized as lean and tall, with prominent, hard limbs, strong joints, and thick bones—that does not also have a somewhat dark skin tone, though tinted with a "scorched" redness. Such a person has a low forehead, wide eyes of a flaming and yellow color, thick eyebrows, and wide, open nostrils that seem to "blow smoke in abundance" <note>Lomazzo uses this vivid imagery to describe the hot, dry nature of the choleric temperament, which was thought to produce excessive heat and "vapors" through heavy breathing.</note>. They have a large mouth, thick red lips, fine teeth, small ears, a prominent chin, and pronounced cheeks and jaws. Their hair is dark but tends toward an inflamed red, appearing curly, rough, and ringed. 

Furthermore, such a person will always have a harsh, sharp, loud, and violent voice. They delight only in laborious things, such as carrying arms and exercising the body in wrestling and similar activities. They would rather hear narrations of terrible deeds than pleasant ones. Such a person is exceedingly sensual, impatient, restless, intolerable, and agitated in their gait, along with infinite other similar manners and inclinations. 

When someone perfectly understands the habits of one type of person, they can very easily—and almost by an infallible rule—judge and make conjectures about others. This is because all natural things, through a specific logic, form, proportion, nature, and movement, have certain correspondences between them. Whenever these are well understood and penetrated with the "sure philosophical escort," there is no doubt that all the gestures and movements imaginable in bodies can be understood and judiciously put into practice. 

If this understanding and knowledge is necessary for any artist, it is especially necessary for the **painter** <term>pittore</term>. No one can deny that if a figure does not vividly show its internal affection and passion through external movements—which must not be hidden but revealed—it remains most imperfect and loses all its <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword is "lode," meaning "praise" or "merit."</note>...

Because the painter has set out to always imitate nature and to approach it as closely as possible, it clearly follows that since we see man always somewhat driven by some **passion of the soul** <term>passione dell’animo: the internal emotions or mental states that "move" a person</term>, and always following a movement in accordance with that passion—showing it and letting it shine through like a clear mirror—so too must it be done in painting. ## How the body also changes by way of imitation.

### Chapter VI.

**T**he passions of the soul also change the body through the power that the passionate human soul has to transform the body. This power is moved by a powerful imagination, just as happens in a state of great wonder or shock because of something seen or heard. In this, one must take care above all to make the other movements that follow in consequence proportionate to the movement of the **principal passion** <note>The dominant emotion driving the scene, such as fear or joy.</note> depicted in the figure, according to the force with which it moves them. In this way, we will not see as many discords as are seen in many painted places. Where this proportion and correspondence of movements is lacking—along with the principal effect that must be represented in the figure according to the requirements of the story—it can truly be said that they appear more like things in dreams or things made by chance without consideration, rather than demonstrations of a true history or representations imagined with proper reasoning and figures introduced with proportionate logic. 

But because there are many of these effects that primarily cause movement, I will provide some examples to give some clarity. Through these, I hope to provide such light to the professors of this art that they will understand that no figure can be represented in any history that is not moved by the power of some other thing; just as that figure is moved by another which, being the primary one, is itself moved by the principal movement of the passion or the spectacle. And so we see that one who recounts a wonderful event to others, he principal—

...mind moves itself, according to the nature of what it relates; and the listeners, some more and some less, are moved with it by those same motions, making similar effects with their bodies. This occurs in all cases, because we see different effects: fierce in warlike words; sad in painful ones; compassionate in those of pity; ridiculous in the capricious; and in the happy, carefree and content. Just as we see, for example, in one who tells some **witticism** <term>facetia: a clever joke or humorous anecdote</term> while laughing, he incites the others to laugh as well.

But man is moved far more by seeing than by hearing; from which it follows that it is necessary—even in the expression of **movements** <term>moti: both physical gestures and the "movements of the soul" or emotions</term>—for the **painter** <term>pittore</term> to be all the more accurate and exquisite. He must observe the aforementioned rules and warnings as a strict law. For there is none among us who does not experience within himself that, upon seeing another die or suffer, he is entirely moved and saddened for the dead, and it seems that he suffers for the one who struggles. Seeing someone's leg or arm cut off, he flinches and twists his own body toward the side where the other is wounded, as if he feels something of that pain.

And so, if we wish to discuss all the other effects that a human body can produce, we will always find in them a certain power and almost **hidden force** <note>This refers to the concept of "similitude" or "sympathy," where the soul naturally mirrors the state of those it observes.</note> which, by way of **likeness** <term>similitudine</term>, induces others to contract some of that state and move according to it. From this, the philosophers maintain that no one should wonder if the body and the **soul** <term>animo</term> of one can be similarly affected by the soul of another. For the soul is much more powerful, strong, and fervent, and more vigorous in movement than are the **vapors** <note>In Renaissance medicine, "vapors" were subtle substances produced by the blood that influenced the mind and spirits.</note> that exhale from bodies. Nevertheless, there is no lack of means by which the body submits no less to the soul of another than to its own body. Therefore it is said that man, solely through his **disposition** <term>affetto</term> and habit, operates upon another man.

Thus we are warned that we must flee and entirely depart from the company of men of **corrupt and lost morals** <term>costumi corrotti</term>; because the soul of such people, as if with a pestilent and contagious breath, infects whoever stands near them. Conversely, one should embrace the company of the good and well-mannered, for one draws marvelous benefit from them.

But returning to our principal subject, I say that although all the said changes can take place in all bodies through likeness, they nevertheless have a much greater place in those where there is a certain natural and intrinsic **conformity** <term>conformità</term> of both soul and body. For this reason, we will see a rigid and horrid **Saturnine** <note>A person dominated by the "cold and dry" humor of black bile, influenced by the planet Saturn; typically gloomy or melancholic.</note> person not so easily moved to pity by some horrendous spectacle as a **Jovial** <note>Influenced by Jupiter; typically cheerful, benevolent, and sanguine.</note>, pleasant, and clement person would be. Nor will a terrible **Martial** <note>Influenced by Mars; typically bold, angry, or "choleric."</note> man be terrified at the sight of some homicide, as will...

## BOOK 2

the timid **Lunar** <term>Lunare: a person whose temperament is dominated by the influence of the Moon, typically thought to be moist, changeable, and phlegmatic</term> person; indeed, though he may be moved somewhat by force, he will at the same time show a certain kind of sparking, like one who reacts upon seeing something that is of his own nature. In this way, in short, all other bodies are moved, more or less according to the conformity they have with one another, and also according to the times, the age, and the activities. For the child will move in one way, the youth in another, the man differently, and likewise otherwise the old man, and otherwise the decrepit, as is clearly seen—without me expounding further—every day in natural occurrences.

Therefore, the **painter** <term>pittore</term> must not be negligent in the consideration of these things, which are the very spirit of the art. Instead, he must continually speculate upon them, it being a matter of the greatest subtlety and difficulty, as is manifestly seen from the small number of painters who have succeeded excellently in this part. This is because, as I said recently, all the passions of the soul—from which outward movements arise in bodies—operate in them more or less depending on whether they have lesser or greater conformity with the **four humors** <term>humori: the four bodily fluids (blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm) believed to control health and temperament</term> of each individual, which are also called **elements** <note>In Renaissance thought, the four humors corresponded to the four elements: Fire, Air, Water, and Earth.</note>.

Hence we see that for this reason, with such subtlety and study, the nature of these humors and their "friendship" or "enmity" toward one another have been investigated by **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century mathematician and astronomer</note>, the Arabs, the Hebrews, the Egyptians, and other ancients, along with **Albertus Magnus** <note>A 13th-century German Dominican friar and philosopher</note> and infinite other modern philosophers and mathematicians. They have maintained that all these passions and movements come from the **superior bodies** <note>The planets and stars</note> by a certain natural inclination. However, this is not by necessity, for we others who have the light of faith well know that it is in the power of man to turn them either to good or to evil. For this reason, I will go on reporting and describing in order the movements which the said wise men observed to be caused by these superior bodies; because, consequently, one will come to know more systematically the movements of men, according to how they are subject to some of them, for the reasons already cited. For greater clarity, I will add more below and will begin with the first and highest, naming them all with their particular names and surnames drawn from the Indians, the **Orphics** <note>Followers of the mystical teachings attributed to the mythical poet Orpheus</note>, and other ancient poets.

### *How all motions can by accident occur in everyone, though differently. Chapter VIII.*

**U**p to this point, we have reasoned about the motions that arise both by cause of the elements and from the humors and passions; and further, for a more perfect knowledge, we have discussed the motions that arise from the celestial bodies <note>The planets</note>, and how they are different from one another through the various dominions they have over men and the various effects they influence and cast upon them. Now it remains to speak in particular of some principal properties of such motions, taking a natural example (as I have always used to do until now) and guiding myself by the understanding of the planets, as those from which the various effects and influences descend into these inferior bodies. And if these specific details of motions are expressed, they will serve to demonstrate certain passions of the soul in every body. But because these particular motions are, as we have said, specifically found in those whose activities are conformed to them, it follows that in this place we demonstrate how they also occur "by accident" <note>In a philosophical sense, "by accident" means a trait or state that is not essential to one's nature but is triggered by external circumstances.</note> in any man, of whatever condition or profession he may be. This entire explanation arises through the five senses, acting as the instrumental causes of our apprehensions: such as by **sight** in seeing the beautiful and the ugly; by **hearing** in sensing sounds, as well as good and evil, such as praise and blame; by **smell** in sniffing the fragrant, the fetid, the strong, and the sha...

...to; for taste, there is savoring: sweet, sour, bland, fatty, salty, astringent <note>The original Italian *stitico* here refers to a binding or dry flavor, like that of an unripe fruit or a strong tannin.</note>, pungent, bitter, oily, strong, unpleasant, and as Aristotle says, hard and soft. Finally, for touch: feeling cold, heat, moisture, dryness, and also rough, light, arid, slippery, heavy, hard, soft, greasy, thin, and other similar qualities from which are caused all the acts and <term>motions</term> <note>In Renaissance art theory, *moti* (motions) refers to physical gestures that reveal the inner state or "passions" of the soul.</note> that can be made in a body, though they are greater and more apparent in one than in another. Because we know that just as these qualities are diverse among themselves and are distinctly attributed to planets, so the motions proceeding from and caused by them come to be diverse, just as the objects, voices, smells, flavors, and materials are diverse; and also as the senses, the apprehensions, and the passions are diverse. Now, although in all men there is a certain particular instinct that inclines them either to good or to evil—according to how he, as the free and absolute lord and arbiter of his affections, chooses for himself and finds more pleasure—according to which instinct he generally operates and moves, it nonetheless remains that through each of these external senses (without which he can do nothing, and indeed would not even exist), he moves in different ways. He is fit to receive within himself all motions, building within his soul the passions according to the apprehensions made by these senses, and thus he reflects those motions within himself, even if they are not in conformity with his particular instinct, which ordinarily inclines and governs him in his actions. 

And that this is so, we read of David, the most Holy King of the Hebrews, having lustful motions for Bathsheba when he saw her washing herself naked from the Royal Palace, and likewise motions of cruelty in commanding that Uriah be killed; and yet he was continent and most merciful. And Solomon, his son, the wisest of all, was given over as a prey to the senses and conquered by the flatteries of harlots to become an idolater—a thing so distant and repugnant to his natural instinct. And thus, looking through histories, one finds in some brave and unconquered Princes acts of fear and cowardice; in merciful men, cruelty; in pious men, acts of vengeance and hatred; in the chaste, luxury; in the bold, timidity—of which examples all histories are full. One finds transportations from joy into sorrow, from weeping into laughter, from avarice into liberality, and similar things of which it would be long to speak, and also hardly necessary; given that every day we see living examples among people in the various occurrences of rapture, pain, slaughter, love, dishonesty, theft, homicide, hatred, vengeance, betrayal, tyranny, insolence, and other similar evils; and on the contrary as well, of piety, pardon, loyalty, clemency, liberality, honesty, victory, honor, religion, temperance, peace, and respects,

# SECOND BOOK

...respects, and similar things. For example, the thief, in the presence of people, in order to hide the constant fear he has of being recognized and discovered as a thief, will make motions of audacity and loyalty; secret prostitutes, <note>The original *meretrici* refers to sex workers; "secret" implies those who operated outside of regulated brothels, often in higher social circles.</note> such as those of the courts, in the presence of other matrons and ladies, will present themselves with motions that are entirely virtuous, restrained, and full of respect. These are, however, their "habits" <note>In this context, *habiti* (habits) refers to an outward disposition or a practiced character rather than clothing.</note> or their disposition used to cloak themselves, so as not to let themselves be recognized for who they are and to flee the shame and the harm that would follow. Just as the thief also covers his defects under contrary cloaks to shield himself from the deserved punishment of the gallows.

Here, then, the painter can understand how—besides being bound to demonstrate the habitual <term>passions</term> <note>From the Latin *passio*, meaning "suffering" or "undergoing"; in early modern art theory, these are the emotions or states that the soul "undergoes."</note> of the soul through proper motions and gestures, as has been said—he must also represent those that come by accident <note>The term "by accident" (*per accidente*) refers to temporary emotions triggered by specific circumstances, as opposed to a person's permanent character.</note>. In this consists a great part of the difficulty of this art: showing diverse affections and passions in a single body. This was a thing much observed among the ancient painters, though with difficulty, as they were men who did not want to omit anything nature could show that they did not also represent with their art.

With even more order, one reads that **Euphranor** <note>A famous Greek sculptor and painter of the 4th century BCE.</note> made, in his portrait of **Alexander**, the face and countenance of **Paris** <note>The Trojan prince Paris was also known as Alexander; the author is referring to a famous lost painting where Euphranor captured the complex nature of this mythological figure.</note>, in which one could recognize at once that he was the judge of the **Goddesses**, the lover of **Helen**, and the killer of **Achilles**. One reads that **Parrhasius of Ephesus** painted the **Idol of the Athenians** <note>The *Demos*, a personification of the Athenian people.</note> in such a way that it showed itself to be angry, unjust, and inconstant, yet also placable, clement, merciful, lofty, glorious, humble, fierce, and fleeting. One reads of **Theon**, who showed in **Orestes** both fury and sorrow together; and of that other painter who represented in **Ulysses** his feigned madness. And of **Aristides of Thebes**, who, in the wounded woman dying while nursing her child, expressed the pain and the fear she had that, her milk having failed, the child would suck her blood. Of him it is written that he was the first to express these disturbances of the soul, and he was then followed and imitated by all other painters.

I also find myself in possession of a small terracotta head of a **Christ** while he was a child, by the hand of **Leonardo da Vinci** himself. In this, one sees the simplicity and purity of the child, accompanied by a "certain something" that demonstrates wisdom, intellect, and majesty; and the air, which is yet that of a tender child, also seems to have the character of a wise old man—a truly excellent thing.

## **On the motions of melancholy, timidity, malice, avarice, slowness, envy, blushing, and anxiety. *Chapter IX.***

**I**t is right, since we have treated in general all the <term>motions</term> <note>The term "motions" (*moti*) refers to the physical movements, gestures, and facial expressions that reveal the inner state of the soul.</note> and which bodies they particularly suit, and how they can occur in everyone by accident, that we now treat each one in particular. Therefore, beginning with <term>melancholy</term> <note>In the Renaissance, melancholy was one of the four "humors" or bodily fluids believed to govern temperament. It was associated with deep thought, sorrow, and creative genius.</note>, it produces actions that are pensive, dismal, and full of sadness. If one wished, for example, to express it in our first parents, Adam and Eve, after committing the sin of disobedience, they would be made with downcast eyes, fixed on the ground, with the head bowed, the elbow upon the knee, and the hand under the cheek, seated in a suitable place, such as under some shady tree, or among rocks and caves. This is also where one would place Hagar, when, pregnant with Ishmael and cast out by Abraham's wife, she had taken refuge in a solitary place, and there she remained all grieving, weeping and lamenting with her head bowed, until the Angel descended from Heaven to comfort her in such a guise. And in this way should be expressed the adulteress, Peter, and David after he had denied Christ <note>The author likely refers to Peter’s denial and David’s own acts of repentance (such as for Bathsheba) as examples of profound regret and melancholy.</note>, and others like them. Ariosto also partially shadowed this in the character Sacripante, in the first Canto, when he said:

> *Pensive for more than an hour with head held low*
> *The grieving Knight remained, my Lords.*
<note>original: "Pensoso più d'un'hora à Capo basso / Stette Signori il Cauaglier dolente." from Ludovico Ariosto’s epic poem *Orlando Furioso*.</note>

And in the Second:

> *And he had moist eyes, his face low,*
> *And showed himself pained and weary,*
<note>original: "Et hauea gl'occhi molli, il vifo basso, / E si mostraua adolorato, è lasso,"</note>

Timidity produces weak, trembling actions, without any vigor, as seen in the Apostles when they took flight and were in disarray when Christ was taken; or on the ship, when they saw Peter walking upon the waves of the sea; and likewise in Peter himself when, in the presence of the handmaid of the palace, he denied Christ. It is seen generally in all those who fear some impending ruin, as one reads in Virgil regarding Aeneas, because of the fortune of the sea that threatened him with shipwreck; or those fleeing the enemy, like Absalom, his Father <note>The author refers to King David fleeing from the rebellion of his son Absalom.</note>, or Lot and his daughters fleeing from the five burning cities. In all of these, one wants to express languid, suspended, confused motions, deprived of vigor. For one who flees fearfully, the actions that Ariosto gives to Angelica are perfectly adapted, when he says:

> *And often she turns her pale face back*
> *For it seems to her that Rinaldo is at her shoulders.*
<note>original: "E speffo il vifo fmorto adietro volta / Che le par che Rinaldo habbi alle spalle."</note>

It also happens that it must be expressed in a certain way in great Princes who have been friends to it, such as in the Emperors Vespasian, Galba, and the like. 

Slowness makes a man lazy and sluggish in every action, and his acts are: resting himself, moving the arms and all the rest of the limbs tardily, not widening or moving the legs much, and once placed in a position, remaining there a good while, just as do the forgetful, porters, and peasants. This is also shown in philosophers and great wise men, in a certain way through study and contemplation, making them place their hands gravely in their beards; likewise, it is shown in the elderly, and especially...

Envy—a most cruel pain of the soul caused by the good of others—makes all the limbs withdraw, as if contracting; it clouds the eyebrows, clenches the teeth, pulls back the lips, and twists the face with a certain passionate gaze, as if in the act of wanting to understand and spy on the deeds of others, and always talking more about others. This should be expressed, for example, in **Cain**, when seeing his brother sacrifice the good sheep to God, he is inflamed with indignation and the envy to kill him. It would have a most beautiful effect to paint him with a finger in his mouth between his teeth, which is an evident sign of an indignant soul determined to cause offense and take revenge. Likewise, it should be expressed in the face of **Lucifer** while he induces our ancient Mother to sin in the Terrestrial Paradise, and to conclude, in all those who, spurred by envy, seek to offend and remove others from the happy state in which they see them placed.

Coarseness <note>Italian: *Rozezza*. This refers to a lack of refinement, civility, or "grace" in movement, often associated with lower social classes or uneducated individuals.</note> makes gestures without grace or gentleness, but rather in a certain headlong and agitated manner, provided it achieves its intent, without any other regard or respect that is proper. This is the characteristic attitude of mountain peasants, laborers, and commoners, who do not know at all what civil practice or propriety is. Nevertheless, it is also demonstrated at times in great men and in many princes, such as those we read were Cincinnatus, Lucius Dentatus, and Sertorius among the Romans; and among the Barbarians, the King of the Cimbri, Genseric, Attila, Tamerlane, Selim, Barbarossa, and many others who, being modern, can be known by everyone. 

Anxiety makes for unpleasant, tiresome, and nauseating gestures, such as praying, fawning, flattering, annoying, and bothering with various gestures and bows—without any grace—toward the one from whom a benefit is expected, never ceasing to ask, nor having any respect or consideration for the suitability of place or time. This is perceived principally in the *pizzoccheri* <note>A term for members of a lay religious movement, sometimes used here to imply a type of fawning or hypocritical outward devotion.</note>, beggars, and the avaricious. It is a peculiar vice in indiscreet peasants, and is found in the anxious and many others of similar condition. 

Sadness <note>Italian: *Mesticia*. A heavy, gloomy sorrow or dejection.</note>, although it is little less than the same thing as melancholy, if one wished to represent it gracefully in someone, in my judgment it could be painted as **Ariosto** paints it in **Angelica** in the eighth Canto <note>Referencing Ludovico Ariosto's epic poem *Orlando Furioso*, Canto 8, stanza 37.</note>, where he says, *stunned, and fixed upon the shifting sand,*

> ->*As if accusing the Great Mover who had*<-
> ->*Turned all events to her harm.*<-

# **On the movements of fortitude, fidelity, justice, devotion, majesty, and constancy. Chapter X.**

**F**ortitude of the soul, which was the specific gift of **Abraham, Jacob, Joshua, and Moses**, generates movements representing **Constancy**, generosity, **Majesty**, and daring. Therefore, some consider whether fickle, light, or similar movements are appropriate or fitting for such characters. The other kind of fortitude, which belongs to the body—though it is joined together with that of the soul—was specific to **Achilles, Hector, Ajax, Hercules, Samson**, and a thousand others. It produces fierce, robust, powerful, and unconquered actions. For this reason, these figures do not expand or scatter themselves as if they were weak and light. Thus, one see that strong men are well-squared in their stature, with firm and steady steps, terrible in appearance, and rarely with their arms flailing in the air or their heads bobbing.

**Fidelity** produces pure, plain, and loyal actions, without any mixture of other movements. These are seen mostly in continent, moderate, and reasonable men. From this, it arises that such people are always gathered within themselves; they rarely open their mouths to speak, and they do not involve or incline themselves indiscriminately to all things, but only to those that suit their taste, refusing others freely <gloss>liberamente</gloss> without any pretense. We read that this was done by those celebrated faithful of God, **Noah and Abraham**, the first Patriarch; and among the gentiles <note>In this context, "gentiles" refers to non-Christian figures from classical mythology and history.</note> by **Argia** and **Polynices**, **Dido** and **Sychaeus**, **Brutus** toward his country, **Hypermestra** with her new husband, and among the Romans, **Marcus Atilius**, along with many others. According to the demands of the promised faith made on various occasions, different gestures must be attributed to them, although in the end, they differ little or not at all.

**Justice**, being—as the **Platonists** say—a masculine virtue, produces virile, magnanimous, bold, and moderate actions; yet they are more severe than pleasant or sweet. Truly, a just man should not show this pleasantness or ease in his actions, but rather a soul gathered within itself and entirely devoted to the consideration of the matter. This is because pleasantness brings with it a certain softening and a hint of flattery, from which either pity arises, or which similarly twists the soul from the right path and, in short, corrupts Justice. Hence, the **Ancient Egyptians** used to represent Justice without ears, wishing to give us to understand

This Justice, if ever it were to be perfectly represented in the face of *Christ*, should be shown on the final day of Judgment, just as *Pietro Perugino* and *Gaudenzio* at Varallo <note>Gaudenzio Ferrari (c. 1471–1546), a painter and sculptor known for his work at the Sacro Monte of Varallo.</note> represented it in their "Judgment," and above all as *Michelangelo* demonstrated it. **Devotion** performs gestures in many ways, according to the many manners and modes of praying. For as one reads in *Virgil*, in the second book of the *Aeneid*, where he has *Anchises* thank *Jove* during the burning of Troy upon seeing a flame surround the head of his grandson *Ascanius*; and in the fourth book, where *Iarbas* complains to *Jove* his father upon seeing *Dido* taken from him by *Aeneas*, it is clearly taught to us that to pray devotedly to the celestial Gods, one must stand with hands raised to Heaven. 

To pray to the Marine Gods, one must have the hands turned toward the Sea, as the same author advises us in the fifth book of the *Aeneid* in the person of *Cloanthus* <note>Original: "Cleante."</note> when he prays to obtain victory in the ship race. To pray to the Infernal Gods, one must kneel over a pit dug into the earth. To ask for peace, one must extend the right hand unarmed, as one reads in *Virgil* in many places in the final book of the *Aeneid*, whom *Ariosto* later imitated in the Eighteenth Canto <note>Referencing "Orlando Furioso."</note>, where he says:

> ->And raising the bare hand, without weapons,<-
> ->An ancient sign of truce and of peace.<-

## BOOK TWO

Abraham, when commanded to observe Circumcision, threw himself on his knees with his face to the ground, as Moses also did for a certain time on Mount Sinai. And Hezekiah prayed to the Lord with his face toward the wall; Elijah put his head between his knees, and other similar ways of praying are read. It is enough that, besides these, there are also specific acts of devotion such as standing with the face turned toward the ground—as Christ did in the garden—and with the head tilted to one side, as many most holy members of religious orders do. Others include raising the face to Heaven with arms open, and sometimes even crossed, as Kings do; beating the chest; raising hands to Heaven with only one knee on the ground; curling the fingers of the hand near the chin with the face bowed; spreading the arms with the head bowed; stretching out flat on the ground—that is, face down—and other such ways used by us Christians in all places where we wish to pray to the Lord in a humble and devout act. Indeed, I would praise it if, in all the aforementioned manners, the eyes were kept turned toward that image before which one prays; just as we do toward the **Sacred Host** <note>The bread consecrated in the Eucharist, believed by Catholics to be the body of Christ.</note> when it is raised high by the Priest for greater humility.

I could refer to other gestures of devotion from various nations, such as those of the naked Sages of Meroë <note>Meroë was an ancient city in modern-day Sudan.</note>, called <term>Gymnosophists</term> <note>From the Greek for "naked philosophers"; a group of ancient Indian or African ascetics who practiced nudity and meditation.</note>; the **Salii** priests <note>Roman priests of the god Mars known for their ritual dances.</note>, for whom jumping in armor was a devout gesture in honor of Mars; and the **Corybantes**, who worshiped the goddess Cybele, the great mother of the Gods, with the sounds of drums. And so it is with many others. One even sees, until the present time, the Turks worshiping <term>Mahomet</term> <note>The text uses "Macone," an archaic Italian term for Muhammad, reflecting the historical Christian misconceptions of Islamic practice as idolatrous.</note> by turning and showing their backs to him, and their Great Lord <note>Referring to the Sultan.</note> by prostrating entirely on the ground with their faces down, and other foolish and ridiculous ways that I do not report, as they are not relevant to our purpose. 

It suffices that, in general, these motions of devotion should be quiet, peaceful, humble, stable, and somber rather than cheerful. This is proper to contrition and the weeping for sins, and to praying to God, where acts and manners devoid of laughter, joviality, and fickleness are required. 

The acts of **Majesty** belong with those of honor, nobility, magnanimity, liberality, and excellence. All of these united together should be represented in Popes and Emperors—especially when seated on chairs and Tribunals—and likewise in Kings and other great personages who hold the highest rank among others. Finally, **Constancy** makes acts strong, stable, and firm in what one has deliberated to do; and therefore, the constant man does not bend according to the will of others, but according to his own thought, which must be represented in his face: as in Job, who stood firm and intrepid...

Whenever it occurs to paint these figures, one must always represent this constancy as invincible in their actions.

This is because all other passions incline somewhat toward one another, except for this one; and therefore, the constant man alone should be portrayed with movements distinct from all others. To ensure he alone is the spectacle and the wonder of the story, he can be represented in the manner one reads of certain ancients who were most persistent in their particular humors <note>In the Renaissance, "humors" referred to a person's temperament or bodily fluids that dictated their personality.</note>. Regarding this, as Pliny narrates, some were hated by the world because they overstepped and transformed the virtue of constancy into <term>rozzezza</term> <note>Roughness or a lack of social refinement; a primitive or unpolished manner.</note>, biting at everyone and going about in an ill-mannered way. Such is told of a certain Crassus, who was never seen to laugh, for which reason he was called **Agelastus** <note>From the Greek "agelastos," meaning "the one who does not laugh."</note>; of Zoroaster, who never cried; and of Socrates, most famous for his wisdom, who was always seen with the same expression—neither more cheerful nor more disturbed—so that in him one could not judge any passion or thought. Among all the philosophers, there was Diogenes the Cynic <note>The philosopher famous for living in a tub and rejecting social conventions.</note>, from whom the others later took their name; and Pyrrho, Heraclitus, and Timon. All of these, through this excessive constancy—or rather, obstinacy—remained very distant from the natures and customs of others.

## SECOND BOOK

despising everyone with gestures that are terrible, threatening, and insolent, such as those that ought to be expressed in the **Giants** against **Jove** <note>Jupiter/Zeus, king of the gods, who fought the Giants in the Gigantomachy.</note>, and in **Nimrod**, the founder of the great Tower <note>The Tower of Babel.</note>, and in the giant **Goliath** slain by **David**. **Robustness** <term>Robustezza: physical strength and hardiness</term> produces actions that are vigorous, hard, and rigid, such as looking fiercely and standing firmly upon the legs, and always keeping the torso well-composed—that is, not allowing the limbs to go slack as weak bodies do, which tend to droop downward; on the contrary, these are elevated and tend upward. They do not speak with a feigned voice, but freely and with gravity; they move rarely and only with a certain purpose, and when they do move, they terrify those who watch them. For these reasons, **Antaeus**, the most ancient King, was called the son of the **Earth** <note>A mythological giant who gained strength whenever he touched the ground.</note>, because of his limbs and his vigorous and robust movements; just as it was with **Typhon** the giant, for fear of whom the poets fabled that the Gods transformed themselves into various shapes. **Hercules of Thebes** similarly possessed this disposition, as did **Milo of Croton** <note>A celebrated Greek athlete of the 6th century BCE.</note>, and **Lysimachus** <note>A general of Alexander the Great.</note> of Alexandria, who killed the Lion. 

**Ferocity** makes the countenance conform to the rest of one’s movements: proud, terrible, wild, cruel, and severe, as **Ariosto** <note>Ludovico Ariosto, author of the epic poem Orlando Furioso.</note> gracefully expressed in part in the final Canto regarding **Rodomonte**, where he says:

> Without dismounting, without bowing his head,
> And without any sign of reverence,
> He shows he despises **Charles** by his gesture, <note>Charlemagne, King of the Franks.</note>
> And the high presence of so many Lords,

and in other places regarding this same **Rodomonte**, and **Mandricardo** <note>Another Saracen knight in Ariosto's poem, known for his pride and ferocity.</note>, who must always be shown with hands ready to strike others, pulled back into themselves, with a severe brow, without laughter or pleasantness, in such a manner that everyone appears terrified by them, not daring to fix their gaze upon them; they should look askance without moving their eyes, or doing so only slowly, flaring the nostrils, huffing, and opening the mouth somewhat, as if in the act of wanting to always offer insult and provoke battle with their hands—in the act of threatening and offending—and finally with harsh and horrible movements of the body. 

**Horror** produces shuddering movements full of terror; and therefore it causes one to tremble, to flee, to be frightened, to pant, and to lose vigor and the color of the face, as in **Thisbe** when she perceives the lioness at the fountain <note>A reference to the tragic story of Pyramus and Thisbe; she fled upon seeing a bloody-mouthed lioness.</note>, or in that armed servant who, by the mere sight of **Marius** <note>Gaius Marius, a Roman general. Harshness makes gestures rigid, hard, and crude, in which no nobility, piety, pleasantness, or love is seen. And therefore it causes one to knit the brows, to move slowly and without grace, to twist the mouth when speaking, to look with disgust at those who fix their eyes upon them, and thus to become perverse and stubborn toward the advice of others—as are the Tartars, Scythians <note>Ancient nomadic peoples often cited by Renaissance authors as the ultimate examples of "uncivilized" or "barbaric" behavior.</note>, and as were once the Goths, Vandals, and those barbarian nations that assaulted and ruined Italy and half the world without pity, and without any respect for things human or divine; and after them the old Lombards <note>original: "Longobardi"</note>, who came from the deserts of Scythia—rude men, barefoot, fierce, without the art of warfare, without the ornament of arms or horses, of beastly customs, with muffled, disheveled, and terrifying faces; as is also written of **Tamerlane**, the most cruel Tartar, of the **Laestrygonians** <note>A tribe of man-eating giants from the Odyssey, also depicted in later epic poetry.</note> whom **Ariosto** depicts, and of **Polyphemus** <note>The famous one-eyed Cyclops from Greek mythology.</note>.

This terribleness appears even greater when, near the terrible person, one sees the bystanders who fear and tremble, and who are in doubt of doing anything that might offend or displease him. A passion shines more brightly when compared to its opposite, because it will have more force, depending however on the subject being represented. <term>Obstinacy</term> <note>original: "L'Ostinatione"; refers to a stubborn refusal to change one's mind, viewed here as a physical and moral vice.</note> makes movements persistent, capricious, hard, inexorable, and immutable, causing one to suffer any discomfort rather than change their opinion, raging in the manner of a bear or a lion. Such was Pharaoh, King of Egypt, while he suffered so many plagues and damages through Moses, which he could have avoided by setting the people of Israel free. In addition to this, it makes a man stay within himself and care for nothing other than what he thinks; it makes him fold his arms and press them to his chest, keeping his eyes cast down toward the ground rather than lifted high. He leans firmly against whatever is there, such as his back against a wall, or his arms or elbows on a chair—or whatever seat he finds himself in—with his legs crossed or drawn inward, with his feet or one knee over the other, and other similar movements that are seen every hour in those who are obstinate and persistent.

<term>Disdain</term> <note>original: "Lo sdegno"; a mix of indignation and contemptuous anger.</note> causes a slight shaking of the head, a fierce widening of the eyes, and a mouth with a bitter smirk; it makes one raise the arm somewhat with the hand turned open, and lift the nose as if something stinks, and other similar movements. These are seen constantly, mostly in the Germans, because of their inherent suspicion, which they take over any small thing that causes them disdain. This vice is also characteristic of the Spaniards. Indeed, they suddenly fall into disdain when things do not go exactly according to their wishes. This is because they rarely achieve what they want, both because others do not hold them or their affairs in the high esteem they arrogantly claim for themselves, and also because they are ordinarily avoided by everyone due to that natural and hateful quality of theirs: the desire to stand above and command everyone.

<term>Impiety</term> makes movements inhuman, cruel, and fierce—entirely contrary to those of the kind, pleasant, and discreet. These traits were heavily noted in Cambyses <note>Cambyses II, King of Persia, often depicted in historical texts of this era as a model of madness and cruelty.</note> and Cyrus, the grandson of Astyages, King of the Medes, and in many others who took a most great but bestial delight in the blood, slaughter, and death of others.

<term>Injury</term> <note>original: "L'ingiuria"; here meaning the act of insulting or wrongfully harming another through speech or gesture.</note> makes movements unjust, offensive, slanderous, and insulting. Thus, it causes one to lunge with impetus and look fiercely at the person being infuriated, threatening them and making scorns and outrages—as we read the wicked Jews did to Jesus Christ, and other barbarians did to the holy martyrs.

**Pride** is understood in both a good and a bad sense. Praiseworthy pride—that is, the splendor and loftiness that seeks status—produces noble and principal movements, as seen in those who, through a certain burning desire for greatness and honor, aspire to high station and the command of affairs. And those nobles who use these manners with judgment and discretion truly become accomplished in all their dealings. Pride in the bad sense—which is the more proper and also the more common meaning—produces imperious, arrogant, and insolent movements that cause the limbs to swell and the head to be held high, yet without stability or gravity. Finally, it shows in every act a disdain and <term>contempt</term> <note>original: "contempto"; here meaning a willful disregard for the value of others' opinions.</note> for the advice of others, as we read of Rehoboam, son of Solomon, who, by scorning the counsel of the elders, was driven from his kingdom; of Nebuchadnezzar; of Enceladus, Briareus, and the other <term>Giants</term> <note>Mythological figures who attempted to overthrow the gods.</note> at Phlegra against Jove.

**Vanity** produces gestures that are out of place but accompanied by a certain self-satisfaction, so that they possess more of delight and thoughtlessness than of any actual resolve; therefore, they are light and disjointed, such that they move those who see them to laughter and incite them to mockery. This is clearly seen in certain "floaters" and vainglorious people who persuade themselves that no one looks at or thinks of anything other than their own foolish, insipid, substanceless, hateful, and truly vain deeds. Therefore, in their actions, they tend to always show off, flutter about, gloat, twist themselves, fuss, preen, and boast, as one see certain people of low character doing. We read that Xerxes, King of Persia, was most vain, as was his father, since they set about lowering hills, leveling mountains, joining sea to sea, and uniting Sestos and Abydos—disjointed cities—with a bridge; and among the Romans, Gaius <note>Referring to the Emperor Caligula.</note> in designing impossible buildings. Finally, **daring** produces movements that are spirited, audacious, and fierce...

### Chapter XII.

**T**he acts, or rather gestures, of **honor** include giving and receiving, sitting and standing in primary places, and being admired and revered by others in a principal position—such as in spacious, reserved, and eminent locations like chairs of state, tribunals, pulpits, and the like. Beyond this, honor makes a man composed, without moving aimlessly, but rather with the greatest consideration and purpose. It makes one hold the body upright, with the face held high rather than low; it does not allow for placing knee over knee, nor crossing the legs, nor even holding the hands behind the back, nor picking at one's ears, nor performing other similar acts, as **Giovanni della Casa** notes in his *Galateo* <note>A famous 16th-century courtesy book on manners and etiquette</note>. Instead, it requires holding the limbs apart from one another—such as the feet and the knees—with the arms magnificently extended and the hands free, not constricted. For instance, one should not place one hand inside the other, nor wring the fingers, nor cross the arms, as these are vile acts, and therefore worthy of being avoided by all honorable persons. Such people wish to possess a serene air full of grace, and a dignified and majestic bearing when their status requires it, as seen in **Popes**, **Emperors**, and the like.
