...that everywhere they hold the first place.

**Command** <note>original: "Commandamento"</note> creates various movements suited to the quality of the thing being imposed. For instance, in **Nero**, when he commands that fire be set throughout all of **Rome**, or that **Peter** and **Paul** be put to death, he would turn his face and severe eyes toward those to whom he signals and commands the deed. However, the most expressive and common act of commanding is to clench the hand while extending the ring finger <note>In the gestural language of the era, the ring finger—the "annulare"—was sometimes used in specific oratorical or authoritative signals.</note> straight out, with the arm also held straight toward the one who must obey; this is the general manner of command used by severe **Princes** and **Majesties**.

One must consider, however, that just as instructions vary, so too do the movements of commanding. If someone commands pleasant things, they should be represented with a joyful face and pleasing, laughing gestures. In this manner, **Heliogabalus** <note>A Roman emperor known for his decadent and eccentric lifestyle.</note> would be shown while he commands that tables and banquets be prepared for the harlots of **Rome**, and has public money given to them, calling them his "fellow soldiers" <note>original: "comilitoni"</note>; and likewise those who have themselves served at the table during drunken revels, such as **Albinus of France**, **Vitellius the Roman**, **Lucullus in the Apollo** <note>Refers to Lucius Licinius Lucullus, a Roman famous for his banquets; the "Apollo" was his most lavish dining hall.</note>, and the like.

If, on the contrary, one commands something sorrowful, he should appear pensive and melancholy, with gestures lacking a certain boldness. This is how the elderly **Jacob** would be represented during the famine, while he commands his sons to go to **Egypt** to buy grain; and in even more grieving actions, **Abraham** when he commands **Isaac** his son to climb upon the altar to be sacrificed to **God**.

The movements must then show themselves full of majesty in **God**, when He commanded Father **Adam** that he should not taste the fruit of the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil.

They should be severe and terrible in **Moses**, when he commanded the people of **Israel** that the [Golden] Calf be destroyed, and that the sons of **Levi** should carry out the most cruel slaughter which they performed upon that people.

And they should be merciful in **Christ**, when he commanded that so many thousands of people be fed with three loaves and four fish <note>The author likely refers to the miracle of the loaves and fishes, though the biblical count varies (five loaves/two fish or seven loaves/a few fish).</note>, and when he humbly commands the **Apostles** to let their feet be washed and dried by him.

And so, in all other cases, one must take great care so that both the one who commands and the one who is commanded have their proper, conforming, and corresponding movements; for it would not look right for one to command in one manner while the other appeared to obey in another.

**Nobility** <note>original: "La nobiltà"</note> produces refined and courteous acts, yet always accompanied by a certain height and dignity. These should appear delightful and honored, but with a specific respect, greatness, and severity with which a nobleman always conducts himself. Therefore, he is never seen moving his limbs or making any gesture without cause; in short, he always imitates...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 142 regarding how internal virtues and honors manifest through specific physical gestures and bodily movements.</meta>

<page-num>143</page-num>

->SECOND [BOOK]<-

...through those acts and movements which we have said are caused by honor. **Magnanimity**, which is nothing other than greatness of spirit, creates acts that are bold, ready, and strong, accompanied by nobility, grandeur, and majesty. Furthermore, it makes the face alert and the appearance magnificent, so that it simultaneously generates fear, reverence, and love in those who look upon it. It ensures the hands are always occupied with worthy, generous, and important deeds, not allowing for any vile things or gestures whose actions might be sordid and abject. But whoever desires to perfectly know its other gestures should read those of **Alexander of Macedon**, **Pompey the Roman**, **Julius Caesar**, **Hannibal of Carthage**, **Charles of Lorraine** <note>Likely referring to Charles III, Duke of Lorraine (1543–1608), known for his statesmanship.</note>, **Matteo Visconti** <note>A powerful lord of Milan in the 13th and 14th centuries.</note>, and **Giacomo Trivulzio** <note>Gian Giacomo Trivulzio (1440–1518), a famous Italian military commander known as "the Great."</note>, who were for this reason surnamed "the Great" <note>original: "Magni"</note>—that is, great in spirit and unconquered <note>original: "inuitti"</note>.

**Liberality**, being entirely contrary to avarice, makes the countenance cheerful and joyful; it makes the acts worthy, fluid, and not restricted, and the hands free and always ready to give and to graciously share one's goods with others. **Excellence** makes the acts somewhat grave and considered, such as bowing, reaching, or raising the arms and legs, and turning the face and body always toward worthy and important occasions; it also involves turning the head in coordination with the body, in such a way that the whole person appears to be applied with great consideration to what they are doing. 

**Benignity** <note>A quality of kindness and gentleness, especially toward those of lower status.</note> makes the countenance and the acts pleasant, merciful, and gracious. It makes one turn the face without disdain or pride toward the person with whom one speaks, however lowly or poor they may be; it causes the face to be lowered rather than raised. Likewise, the arms, legs, and hands, along with the rest of the body, do not move with any violence or impetus, but with a sweetness and delight for the beholder. It is also expressed in this specific act: with arms open, elbows at the sides, and hands raised with the palms facing outward, the body and head bowed somewhat and tilted more to one side, so that the limbs seem to harmonize with the quality of one's merciful words. 

**Discretion**, which is the proper modesty in all things, makes the acts gentle, reserved, and wise, like those of people who discern the true from the false and good from evil. For this reason, such people do not give in to the whims of individuals, but by tempering them, they quiet them; thus they are severe and rigid against those who are stubborn and refuse to be satisfied by what is right, and conversely, they are pleasant and sweet toward good, just, and reasonable men. Therefore, discretion causes one to threaten one person and to caress or embrace another; all of these movements are accompanied by the countenance and regulated according to the requirements of the business at hand, as is seen in **Princes** and **Judges**, to whom the causes of private citizens are submitted for judgment. **Joy** makes one strike the... <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "mani" from the original manuscript indicates the sentence completes on the next page as "strike the hands," referring to clapping.</note>

### *On the motions of charm, grace, beauty, elegance, gentility, courtesy, flattery, blandishments, adulation, loving-kindness, embracing, kissing, lasciviousness, indecency, festivity, pomp, singing, dancing, play, joy, tranquility, delight, solace, and sweetness. Chapter XIII.*

**C**harm <note>original: "vaghezza"—a term implying both beauty and the longing or desire it inspires in the viewer.</note>, which is nothing other than a desire and a longing for something that delights, creates acts of admiration, wonder, and contemplation of the things seen. It is like a vain man who is peacocking with a thousand leaps, bows, movements, and whims; or like another who gazes longingly at his beloved, standing in a thousand ways and poses to admire and contemplate every part of her, until the neighbors, noticing it, laugh at him. Or, generally, it is like any other person who, according to the pleasure they take in something they are doing, nods their head—just as a **painter** does when he considers and admires one of his own paintings. 

**Grace** makes a man stoop to all things presented before him by necessity with charm, and with delightful and delicate gestures. Beyond this, it makes one accept gifts with a cheerful countenance, reward others willingly, give with majesty, and thank others kindly and with sweet [words].

[...manners to] obtain all that one craves and desires. In short, the graceful person represents themselves no differently than the companions of **Venus**, who are for that reason called the **Graces** <note>In Greek and Roman mythology, the three Graces (Aglaia, Euphrosyne, and Thalia) personified charm, beauty, and creativity.</note>. Furthermore, this quality causes one to receive people into one's home with a thousand charms, delights, and pleasing welcomes; and finally, all actions that can be performed in the finest manner will be done by these graceful types, just as the opposite is done by the graceless. 

**Loveliness** <term>venustà</term> <note>original: "venustà"—a term derived from the goddess Venus, implying a divine or ideal beauty that inspires love.</note> makes one's actions attractive, noble, graceful, and beautiful, as it is a quality that cannot exist without beauty of the body and grace in one's movements; however, such actions only manifest themselves in perfectly beautiful bodies. From this, such people are called "loveliness-filled" <note>original: "venusti"</note>, which is to say, perfect in both form and motion. Thus, they are likewise very well-suited to achieving what they want: especially through prayers, like **Esther** <note>The biblical Queen Esther, who used her beauty and grace to plead for the lives of her people.</note>; through charms, like **Tamar** <note>Likely referring to the biblical Tamar who used a disguise to secure her rights (Genesis 38).</note>; and even through command, as **Venus** did with **Mars**, of whom it is said:

**Gracefulness** <term>leggiadria</term> <note>original: "leggiadria"—a lightness or elegance of movement often associated with youth and agility.</note> makes one's actions lovely and agile, mixed with grace. For this reason, these movements are desired in all things, as they generate admiration and are the true ornament of objects. It makes the graceful youth or maiden appear in the most pleasing and well-coordinated attire possible—as much for their own suitability as for the delight of the eye, which is satisfied only by beauties and well-made things. Therefore, these graceful motions can hardly shine through in an ugly or disordered body. 

**Nobility of spirit** <term>gentilezza</term> <note>original: "gentilezza"—in the Renaissance sense, this refers to a refined, noble character rooted in virtue rather than just social rank.</note> makes one's actions graceful, courteous, noble, and virtuous. For as **Boccaccio** <note>Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375), the famous Italian author who argued in his works that true "gentilezza" comes from virtue, not bloodline.</note> says, nobility first came into the world through virtue; therefore, it cannot dwell in a base heart, even if the person is born noble, rich, and powerful. As the same author adds, all things can be left as an inheritance except for virtue, health, and nobility of spirit. Because of this, a person can only be called and held as "noble" insofar as they practice nobility through their actions, words, and deeds. 

**Courtesy** makes one's actions kind, humane, generous, skillful, and moderate, and it makes the face joyful and serene. We see, therefore, that these courteous people make anyone who interacts with them fall in love with them, binding them with such tight knots that they can never be untied, nor can they do anything in their presence that is less than honest and praiseworthy.

This is done so that what is desired can be better imprinted upon the one being flattered, drawing them toward a specific intent or design. # SECOND [BOOK]

[...the] state of one who flatters, in order to lead and persuade another more easily. One should show a varying face—now cheerful, now sad, now somewhere between the two, and quite often even shameful—according to what the weaving of the deceit requires. **Allurements** <term>blanditie</term> <note>original: "blanditie"—derived from the Latin *blanditia*, referring to charming or fawning speech and actions intended to flatter.</note> are specifically endearments paired with flattery, performed through nods, jokes, touches, games, pinches, and gestures of the hand and body, such as those seen in dances. This is not done without the greatest passion from those "caught in the lime" <note>original: "impaniati"—a metaphor referring to birds caught with birdlime (a sticky substance); here it refers to men hopelessly ensnared by charms.</note>, for as soon as the ladies have made them aware of it, they raise them high, only to later make them "do the snail's jump" <note>original: "salto della lumaca"—an idiomatic expression meaning to be deceived, rejected, or cast down after being led on.</note>. 

**Flattery** <term>adulatione</term>, being truly a "painting" of faked gestures that goes about imitating natural ones—not to actually be natural, but to serve its own ends and comforts—makes all its gestures faked, false, and simulated. It is like one who makes a profession of imitating the gestures, acts, and words of his superiors, never deviating from them in any way; yet he does all this without the slightest spark of virtue, but solely with the goal of his own profit and interest. Furthermore, it causes one to honor, revere, and praise the person from whom profit and honor are expected, ingratiating oneself with them little by little, gaining confidence and security under the color of respect and affection. This affection vanishes as soon as the "friend" falls from his high standing and is abandoned by Fortune, at which point the flatterer turns his back just as Fortune did. This is seen in the account by **Lucian** <note>Lucian of Samosata, a 2nd-century satirist who wrote "Timon, or the Misanthrope."</note> regarding a flatterer of the incredibly wealthy **Timon**, who fell from supreme happiness into such extreme misery that he had to work the earth to sustain his life. On this subject, **Ariosto** <note>Ludovico Ariosto, author of the epic poem *Orlando Furioso*.</note> wrote most gracefully when discussing the King of the Moors abandoned by his strongest warriors:

->*If the wretched state then turns to gladness,*<-
->*The flattering crowd turns its foot toward it;*<-
<note>original: "Se poi si cangia il tristo in lieto Stato, / Volta la turba adulatrice il piede;"—from *Orlando Furioso*, Canto 19. The verse suggests that flatterers follow the shift of fortune.</note>

**Kindheartedness** <term>amorevolezza</term> makes one’s acts pure, sincere, and full of goodness, such as throwing one’s arms around the neck, kissing, squeezing hands, smiles, bows, welcomes, and similar gestures that must be represented in art—as in the **Visitation of Elizabeth and the Virgin Mary** <note>The biblical meeting between Mary, pregnant with Jesus, and her cousin Elizabeth, pregnant with John the Baptist.</note>. And sometimes it must be accompanied by a joyful and tender weeping, as seen in **Joseph**, when in **Egypt** (after many welcomes and endearments) he made himself known to his eleven brothers, throwing his arms around **Benjamin's** neck with a thousand kisses and acts of tenderness and love. Such behavior is sought in all those between whom there is love by nature or by choice: such as between two friends, between relatives, between husband and wife, between father and son, between son and mother, and between lover and lover.

# BOOK TWO

...and in these, a certain method and order are observed. For depending on the state and the rank of the people, one must approach an **embrace** <term>abbracciamento</term> differently. As an example: between a superior and an inferior, the former will embrace the upper part of the body, and the latter the lower part. This was very well noted by the most exquisite Ariosto <note>Ludovico Ariosto (1474–1533), the famous Italian poet of the epic *Orlando Furioso*.</note> in the eighteenth Canto regarding Norandino and Gryphon, saying:

->Gryphon, seeing the King, who had turned kind,<-
->Come toward him to throw his arms around his neck,<-
->Left aside his sword and his ill intent,<-
->And embraced him humbly beneath the hips.<-

And in another place in the twenty-fourth Canto:

->And they embraced him where a superior is embraced<-
->With bare head and with bended knee;<-

Therefore, in these embraces, one must take great care to observe **decorum** <term>decoro</term> <note>The artistic and social principle of appropriateness; ensuring a figure's actions match their status and the situation.</note>. Embraces of force belong to wrestlers <term>Lottatori</term> and the like; as one reads of **Hercules**, who, tightly embracing **Antaeus** <note>In Greek mythology, the giant Antaeus was invincible as long as he touched the earth; Hercules defeated him by lifting him up in a crushing bear hug.</note> by the loins, held him so firmly against his chest that by sheer force, drawing the breath from his body, he deprived him of life.

And here the artist must be careful in describing a struggle not to make it so that one holds the other so tightly that he frees himself when it is not plausible, or that one suffers and shows he cannot defend himself in a situation where, by reason of the oppression, he cannot suffer or remain underneath. Let this suffice as a general warning.

There is also another embrace of force without the resistance of the other [initially], such as when the Romans abducted the **Sabine women**, or when **Pluto** stole **Proserpina** <note>Refers to the mythological "Rape of Proserpina," where the god of the underworld abducts the daughter of Ceres.</note>. In these, one must show violent, strong, and agitated actions in the one who abducts while met with opposition; and in the victims—according to their courage and spirit—some more and some less, one should show desperate, defensive, sprawling, and tearful actions, and in such cases, fearful ones as well.

**Lascivious embraces** are also of many types, and they should always be represented with this caution: that the hands, as the instruments of the embrace, should end on the softest parts of the body, such as the ears, lips, cheeks, throat, and other places that out of decency <term>honeſtà</term> should remain unmentioned. If one were to end the embrace on other parts, such as the elbows, shins, knees, shoulders, or the like, it would be an inept thing and worthy of blame, because there is no delight in it. I remind the painter to consider this part diligently; yet I also warn that I do not praise him if he expresses them too overtly, for the sake of modesty and decency.

Embraces should then be loving, sweet, and humane, accompanied by sweet glances. And these, having...

...always reaching with the sweep of the arm to touch the hands in the aforementioned places, they must be represented in various ways. But regarding the manner in which they should be represented, there is no need to provide a rule here; for every person has knowledge of this from nature. Thus, by oneself and without the precepts of others, one can understand how to appropriately express them with the brush. I will say this much: one must always keep an eye on the position in which the embraced parties find themselves. For one embraces in one way while standing, in another while lying down, and in another while sitting. One must also have regard for the will of both parties, whether it is mutual. For if one does not consent, instead of an **embrace** <term>abbracciare</term>, he must show offense, opening the arms, scratching, crying out, biting, and performing other such acts which must always be expressed according to what is read in the histories <note>In this context, "histories" refers to "history painting," the genre of painting depicting scenes from the Bible, mythology, or classical history.</note> one wishes to depict.

The **kiss** <term>baſcio</term> likewise causes the bodies to make different gestures according to various circumstances. For if one kisses a dead person, such as a son, one makes sorrowful, desperate, and tearful movements, such as clutching, struggling, scratching oneself, raising the hands, spreading the arms, bowing down, tossing about, twisting, wringing the hands, shaking, fainting, rolling the eyes, crying out, and the like, as can easily be seen every day from life. If one kisses as a sign of love, and as a way of welcoming friends or relatives, they kiss each other's cheeks mutually. But if, out of reverence, an inferior kisses a superior, he now kisses the hands, as with Lords; now the clothing; and now the feet, as with the **Pope**; and now the knee, as with the **Emperor**. And thus they perform gestures now of reverence, now of joy and courtesy.

If one kisses lasciviously, either on the lips, or in the eyes, or elsewhere, lascivious movements result, such as embraces, jests, laughter, the rolling of eyes, falling, tossing, pressing together, clinging to one another, and the like. There are also fraudulent and feigned kisses, such as those of prostitutes, procurers, and traitors <note>A likely reference to the "Kiss of Judas."</note>. **Lasciviousness** <term>laſciuia</term> performs acts according to its name—that is, lascivious glances, sweet embraces, soft kisses, and also acts of force, trials of life, and transformations, such as those of the Gods of which **Ovid** writes at length in the *Metamorphoses* <note>original: "Metamorfofi"</note>. ...in woman it seems that **lasciviousness** <term>lasciuia</term> <note>In this context, "lasciuia" refers to sensuality or erotic grace in an artistic sense, rather than purely negative "lust."</note> reigns much more naturally; I will speak of her, showing in what manner she must be painted. Her limbs, then, should be shown uncovered, and especially those most apt to excite desire, such as the breasts, the tip of the tongue in the act of kissing, the legs, or a bare arm—but not entirely and openly, so that there remains something yet to be desired. For this reason, we see that the ancients represented their **Venuses** <note>A reference to the "Venus Pudica" (Modest Venus) type of classical sculpture, where the goddess covers her nakedness with her hands or drapery.</note> as nude but not at all shameless or fully exposed, but rather with a certain way of bending and covering themselves with a small cloth; and in this manner, they kindled greater desire in the beholders, of which some vestige remains in Delos and Paphos. 

Infinite other acts of lasciviousness could be recounted here, or at least hinted at—and though it might perhaps be necessary for the instruction and warning of the painter, who often must express them either to please Princes and lords or even by his own whim—I have judged it better to omit them. It is impossible for such a discussion not to include something obscene that might contaminate good morals. 

Yet, so that this part is not entirely lacking in this treatise of mine—where I have sought to collect most exquisitely everything pertaining to this art—I wish to mention only two passages from approved writers, from which one may learn, as from a living example, how lascivious acts should be expressed in both women and men. One is in that amorous history of **Clitophon and Leucippe** <note>A famous ancient Greek romance by Achilles Tatius, known for its vivid descriptions of art and emotion.</note> by a Greek author, which was later translated into Latin by Signor **Annibal Croce** <note>Annibale Croce (d. 1577) was a Milanese nobleman and secretary to the Senate, known for his Latin translation of Achilles Tatius.</note>, who was secretary of the Most Excellent Senate of Milan and a man of most beautiful letters; the other is by **Master Sperone** <note>Sperone Speroni (1500–1588), a leading Italian humanist and philosopher whose "Dialoghi" were highly influential.</note> in his first dialogue titled *On Love*. 

Impropriety produces acts that are filthy, nefarious, shameful, and infamous, which should be used in no place or time. Because these are merely demonstrations of the most shameful parts and most dishonest effects—for which God sent fire from Heaven, burned men and houses, and destroyed them, and **Lot** barely had time to flee while his wife remained—I will say no more of them. 

**Festivity** <term>La festa</term> produces distinct and particular acts. In the festivals of Hymen <note>The Greek god of marriage ceremonies.</note>, the god of weddings and marriages, one performs movements and acts such as banquets, jokes, music, dances, games, kisses, and the like, according to the custom and rite of the Peoples. It is enough that whatever the act of celebration may be, it must not contain any melancholy or the appearance of a grave and pensive man; rather, it should be full of jubilee and joy. 

There are also other festive movements, as seen in those who rejoice for some good news of happy success, or of victory, or other things, in which occurrences the movements are represented now more festive and cheerful, and now less so, according to the importance of the good fortune. Pomp makes the acts splendid, haughty, majestic, and full of pride and ostentation, like one who, being better adorned than others, shows himself in a brave and principal manner. 

Singing, according to whether the voices are deeper <term>graui</term> or higher <term>acute</term>, makes the movements sometimes more vehement and sometimes more calm. For it is seen that the musician now swells his cheeks, now dilates them, and now constricts them; sometimes he thrusts out his lips, very often turns his eyes lasciviously, and sometimes fixes his gaze intently; now his face becomes flushed, and now it does not. This diversity of movement is not only caused by the variety of the tones of the voices, but also by the different dispositions of those who sing, who—depending on how well-disposed their organs <note>Refers here to the physiological "organs" of the throat and mouth used for vocalization.</note> are—sing some with ease and others with effort. 

One must also consider the movements of those who listen, who are sometimes moved to fury and impetus—as one reads of **Alexander the Great** at the Phrygian sound of that musician of his, by which he was marvelously inflamed for battle—sometimes to melancholy, sometimes to joy, sometimes to continence, and sometimes to other emotions, as is found written to have been the case among the ancients. For this reason, they also had a specific kind of music accommodated to each emotion. 

And in this matter, because I see many have fallen into error, I do not want to fail to warn that when painting anyone playing a wind instrument, such as **Angels**, one should not paint them in an act that does not appear to swell the cheeks, as if they were giving no breath to the instrument. Rather, let them be seen in an act that represents what they are doing, as **Michelangelo** well observed in his *Judgment* <note>The *Last Judgment* in the Sistine Chapel, where angels blow trumpets to wake the dead.</note> with the Angels who sound the Trumpets, and **Andrea Mantegna** in his—so to speak—bacchanals, in the figure who plays two bagpipes, and in the Tritons who sound the conch shells <term>buccine</term> <note>Ancient Roman trumpets or large shells used as horns.</note> which are distributed in prints. ...having read, or heard it told by others, that Minerva—simply because she once saw herself with puffed-out cheeks while playing the cornett—was so ashamed that she threw it away; and the young Alcibiades, while playing a fife, or whatever it may have been, saw Socrates, who took it up to play and puffed out his cheeks, distorting his whole face, hiding his eyes, and furrowing his brows, and likewise threw it away. 

Dancing can be said to have as many types as there are nations and peoples in the world, and consequently, these cause distinct and different movements. Thus, the **German** leaps and embraces in various manners; the **Frenchman** kisses, throws his arms around the neck, and holds arm-in-arm; the **Savoyard** bows lasciviously to the sound, makes a reverence, and then leaps, now strongly, now softly, and then embraces and leaps while embraced together; the **Spaniard** walks with gravity hand-in-hand, conversing of love; the **Flemish** dances partly in a wheel <note>A circular formation or "round dance."</note> and partly with leaps of the back; and the **Italian**, almost like an actor, leaps with great effort, twistings, and kicking of legs, lifting himself high, hurrying his steps and then slowing them down; he has his specialized sequences <term>ricercate</term> of five steps, seven, nine, twelve, and fifteen, which he adapts to the sound, whether it be broad or narrow, deep or high; yet always with charming gestures, such as glances, carriage of the body, bows, reverences, and other similar lures and fuels of love. 

There is no lack of other usual gestures to be seen in dances, in which vigor, speed, nimbleness, and theatricality are demonstrated, as in those who represent themselves with weapons in hand and go in a circle, leaping with mastery, vibrating their weapons in the **Moresca** <note>A stylized sword dance popular in the Renaissance, often depicting a mock battle between Christians and Moors.</note> fashion with various actions of parrying and the like, always adapting everything to different sounds of the Cymbal <note>Likely referring to a dulcimer or a rhythmic percussion instrument here.</note> or whatever other instrument is used. Others, with bells on their heels, with incredible dexterity and without theatrical gestures, exert all the force, gestures, and movements that can be made with the body, which to the onlookers—not being accustomed to or practiced in such a <term>paleſtra</term> <note>original: "paleſtra"; a Greek term for a wrestling school or gymnasium.</note>—seems a miraculous spectacle. 

Games also cause various gestures and acts, as among the ancient Romans in the games, or rather in the tragedies of the **gladiators**, and in our own day, as is seen in **fencers**. ### *On the movements of prudence, cunning, malice, shrewdness, sleight of hand, theft, honesty, modesty, quiet, and exercise.*

->Chapter XIV.<-

**P**rudence induces in men grave, collected, and composed acts, though these vary according to the different arts and actions in which prudence is exercised. She assigns to each person the most fitting and convenient manner, so that she clearly shines forth and makes herself known in the prudent man. For if the act were inconvenient, it would be an act of ignorance; the movements of ignorance are entirely contrary to those of Prudence. In prudent men—such as orators, theologians, philosophers, prophets, and the like—all movements are grave, retired, and full of majesty. For this reason, one does not see them throwing their arms about while standing or sitting, nor tossing their legs here and there like actors, nor exerting the force of their bodies like wrestlers. Neither do they laugh dissolutely, nor twist their waists like nymphs, nor perform other similar gestures and acts that are all contrary to their professions. Instead, they choose to maintain a certain tempered severity of brow and gravity, holding tablets and books, and sometimes—as a sign of contemplation—placing their hands in their beards, which are deftly fingered. Polidoro <note>Polidoro da Caravaggio (c. 1499–1543), a Renaissance artist known for his chiaroscuro facade paintings</note> frequently used this gesture for priests and ancient sages. The most judicious Michelangelo, who was very perceptive in this regard as in all others, did the same in his admirable *Moses* at the tomb of Pope Julius in Rome at Saint Peter in Chains <note>original: "Santo Pietro in Vincola," the church of San Pietro in Vincoli</note>. He likewise used this in the face of the Prophet Jeremiah in the Vatican, where he painted the Judgment <note>The artist refers to the Sistine Chapel; while Jeremiah is on the ceiling, the "Judgment" refers to the Last Judgment on the altar wall</note>; for Jeremiah, he placed the...

[in]solence, when it occurs in some history to paint them, *Sulpicia* <note>Likely referring to Sulpicia, the wife of Lentulus, who was celebrated as a model of wifely devotion in ancient Rome.</note>, and *Virginia the Roman* <note>A legendary figure whose death at the hands of her father to preserve her virtue led to the overthrow of the decemviri.</note>, *Miriam* the sister of *Moses*, when with the other Hebrew virgins she stands sweetly singing and praising God for the recovered liberty of the people of Israel—all these virgins and martyrs, and above all others the glorious Mother of our Lord. She is at times painted by certain clumsy and thoughtless artists with lascivious gestures and clothing, looking at those who behold her, just as they are accustomed to do with other virgins; an error in my judgment that is notable and worthy of the greatest reprimand.

For such women ought to cast their eyes toward the ground with the greatest <term>honesty</term> <note>original: "honestà"; in this period, it refers to moral integrity, decency, and a modest outward appearance.</note> and shamefastness. And in males, one must also very often represent and make this honesty shine forth, as in the ancient *Joseph the Hebrew*, in our Saints, and especially in *Saint John the Evangelist*, who was no less clear and illustrious for this virtue than he was beautiful and dear to *Christ*, the source and master of that same honesty.

*Modesty* makes acts discrete, tempered, <term>moderate</term> <note>original: "mediocri," meaning the "golden mean" or middle path between extremes, a classical virtue.</note>, and well-mannered, as if never showing in any place, time, or occasion affection or passion of the soul.

Therefore, it does not enter into terrible gestures, nor fearful ones, nor severe ones, nor those too pleasing, but stays within the humble and moderate.

And such people are always seen to be circumspect and balanced, with a certain equanimity possessed by few, which therefore renders them more honored and dear among others; just as, on the contrary, the immoderate are despised and hateful to everyone.

*Quietude* makes movements peaceful and tranquil; on the other hand, it also makes them idle and melancholy in those who never involve themselves in anything, nor have the daring to join the practices and commerce of people, but remain withdrawn, solitary, idle, and melancholy in the manner of a stone or a mole.

The first movements are like bows, prayers, alms, and the like, which good religious people and Catholic laymen use—enemies of clamor and noise—and also scholars, who, having retired far from the common crowd in honest solitude, make a profession of virtue and wisdom.

*Exercise* <note>original: "l’esercitio," referring here to physical activity, practice, or the active life.</note> makes acts and gestures diverse, according to the diversity of the exercises.

And just as the minds and intentions of the actors are diverse, so too are the acts and movements equally diverse and different from one another.

For this reason, *Mercury*, the father and author of all exercises, is feigned by the poets to be the messenger of the Gods, for no other reason than that he is fit to participate in and achieve all their particulars through his exercise and movement.

Generally, these movements are sharp, frequent, patient, quick, accurate, and diligent; but in particular, among scholars and lovers of letters and of painting, they should be—

...frequented, practical, attentive, quiet, diligent, and without noise among musicians and players, according to the manner of the song and the sound—swelling, twisting, lascivious, grave, apt to rise, move, and hurry according to the various tones and concords of bodily harmony; nor should one forget the sculptors and all other professors of art who exercise themselves with labor, appearing more or less fatigued, always representing to you acts of heat and sweat. From which a consequence is drawn, among many other reasons, that these arts are of less esteem and value than others, since their exercise requires bodily labor, even though among them sculpture is the most noble and excellent, as it closely approaches painting and joins it in imitating natural things. 

In this manner <term>Leonardo Vinci</term> <note>Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519). The author refers to Leonardo's "Paragone," a series of arguments comparing the arts, which was later compiled into his *Treatise on Painting*.</note> goes on discussing and arguing in a book of his that I read in years past, which he wrote with a tired hand <note>original: "mano stanca." He says that the more an art brings with it bodily labor and sweat, the more it is vile and less prized. For such an art is no less subject to coarse materials than to subtle ones—that is, to the imaginations of the mind, which can in no way be expressed where there is an interruption of something contrary to them. 

This is clearly seen to be the case in sculpture, where there is the intervention of marble, iron, and other similar materials of bodily labor and noise; all things that are enemies of study, which can never be so applied and focused that it is not greatly interrupted for this reason, and the work results in large part less beautiful and perfect than what the craftsman had conceived and imagined in his <term>Idea</term> <note>In Renaissance theory, the "Idea" is the perfect internal mental concept of a work of art that exists in the artist's mind before they begin physical production.</note> before he took up the chisel. 

So it cannot in any way be denied that this art of sculpture—being a tangle of stones, labors, and similar inconveniences, and consequently being an enemy to imagination and contemplation—yields in excellence and value to <term>painting</term>. Painting, by contrast, is an art far removed from labors, from noises, and from coarse materials. This is precisely the quality of the <term>liberal arts</term> <note>The "Liberal Arts" were the intellectual disciplines (like grammar, logic, and rhetoric) considered worthy of a free person, as opposed to "mechanical arts" involving manual labor.</note> and sciences. Therefore, above all others, painting is much more suited to expressing in figures all things imagined, however marvelous they may be in the Idea. For the painter can retire to a quiet place, remote from all the noises that can distract and interrupt him; and there, in that solitude and quiet, with a very subtle style or with the pen, he can go on silently expressing what he has conceived in his mind and bring it to a happy completion, without the defect of the material hindering him.

<summary>This page recounts Leonardo da Vinci’s argument for the superiority of painting over sculpture, emphasizing that painting's intellectual and quiet nature aligns it with the liberal arts, whereas sculpture's physical labor and noise hinder the artist's imagination.</summary>

<keywords>Leonardo da Vinci, Lodovico Sforza, Paragone, painting vs sculpture, liberal arts, artistic Idea, Renaissance art theory, bodily labor</keywords>

I

And since <term>modeling</term> <note>original: "plastica"; the art of shaping soft materials like clay or wax.</note> is the sister of painting—as the ancients affirm—and because it is an art of less noise and toil than the labor of working in stone, it was chosen by <term>sculpture</term> <note>original: "scoltura"; here specifically meaning the carving of hard stone or marble.</note> to be its mother, so that she might serve as an example and guide for its works. Sculpture uses modeling’s clay models—which are closer to the imagination—and then measures them with a compass to introduce into the marble the figures of men, horses, or whatever else is desired. From this, one can conclude and even infer that sculpture is nothing more than a laborious imitation of modeling, and a practice of carving marble with diligence and over a great length of time. Furthermore, sculpture elevates itself and becomes perfect only in as much as it approaches modeling. Because modeling possesses no less <term>design</term> <note>original: "disegno"; refers to both the physical drawing and the underlying intellectual concept of the work.</note>, composition of muscles, and outlines (though without the outer "skin" of color) than <term>painting</term> does, it is considered its sister. Thus, it follows that painting becomes the aunt of sculpture and the sister of modeling. 

Because I have always taken, and still take, great delight in this art—as evidenced by my various whole horses, legs, and heads, as well as human heads of Our Lady, complete and fragmented figures of Christ children, and a good number of heads of old men—I can say that modeling possesses a very great ease compared to the art of painting or fine drawing. For example, in modeling one makes a round ball, whereas in drawing, one must first circle it with a compass, and then on that same flat plane, go about shading and highlighting it with reflections and shadows so that it appears round like the modeled ball. 

Here one can recognize the great difference between making a <term>relief</term> <note>A three-dimensional work that projects from a background.</note> and representing one on a flat plane. Indeed, if one wishes to submit to the rules of <term>perspective</term> <note>The mathematical system for representing three-dimensional space on a two-dimensional surface.</note> and represent in order the "losses and gains" <note>An artistic term for foreshortening—the way objects appear to shrink or expand based on their angle to the viewer.</note>, the depths, and the prominence of limbs, it is a most certain thing that such patience and intelligence are required that it is almost impossible to do, let alone difficult. One would undoubtedly give up the task if the labor were not mitigated and compensated by the great delight one takes in seeing things stand out from the paper or panels as if they were natural. Therefore, in my humble judgment, I deem this exercise alone to be the most excellent and divine in the world, since the artist demonstrates himself to be almost another God. And these are, for the most part, the very words written by **Leonardo** in his aforementioned book, which are followed by many others on this subject that I have chosen to interject here, as it is a fitting place to discuss the arts, so that with the authority of such a great man, philosopher, and archi-

### ***On the <term>movements</term> <note>original: "moti"; in Renaissance art theory, this refers to the 'motions of the soul,' where outward physical gestures and expressions reveal internal emotions or spiritual states.</note> of credulity, fear, humility, fickleness, servitude, reverence, shame, mercy, and simplicity.***

-> Chapter XV. <-

**I** The gestures and acts of <term>credulity</term> <note>original: "credulità"; here meaning the state of belief or the readiness of the soul to accept faith, rather than the modern sense of being gullible.</note> are primarily performed before the thing in which one believes, as it is the object in which one’s faith is placed and situated; such as before the Gods, Idols, or deities that the ancient <term>gentiles</term> <note>original: "gentili"; referring to pre-Christian Greeks, Romans, and other polytheistic peoples.</note> adored, and also very often before men themselves. However, since the types of faith are diverse, the acts are not always performed in one single way; rather, even within a single faith they vary according to the various subjects of the believers. And so, according to the most ancient custom before the flood, the gestures of Adam, Abel, and the others before their sacrifices likely had to be of one manner, different from that used by Noah with his family while thanking God with a sacrifice after he had emerged from the ark. And similarly different from this was the manner of Jacob and his sons when, on the journey they were making to Egypt, Joseph prayed to God while making a sacrifice. Thus we must assume that the sorrowful and pious gestures of the unhappy people of Israel in Egypt were different while they were praying to the Lord to free them from the barbaric servitude of Pharaoh. In other countenances and acts the same people probably had to adore God before the Golden Calf, and again differently after they were saved from that most cruel slaughter—to their wonder and great amazement—around the Most Holy Tabernacle together with Moses, upon which was the glory of God. Thus we can imagine the credulous and <term>continent</term> <note>original: "continenti"; meaning self-restrained, chaste, or somberly composed.</note> acts of the young Tobias for three continuous nights with his bride on their knees; of the three youths in the fiery furnace; of Margaret in the boiling oil; of Catherine on the wheel; and of the other unconquered martyrs, who, according to the most fervent affections and the more burning devotions of their hearts, gave outward acts and signs of their faith. Distinct and different acts of faith and credulity are likewise those that we Christians use before the relics of the Holy Bodies, Crosses, and images of Christ and the Saints, where with eyes fixed and intent upon them, we pray in many ways—all however filled with holy humility and devotion—sometimes kissing them, and sometimes touching them with our fingers, and reverently bowing to them.

-> S E C O N D [B O O K] <-

...commanding them. Beyond this, because of the belief one has in the words of such men, one stands in their presence with admiration, without moving, except for some small motions that imitate and conform to those of the person in whom one believes. This is seen with a Preacher, in whose presence one remains attentive with eyes fixed upon him, continuously imitating all his movements and his carriage. It is also seen in the presence of saints by those who had obtained health or another signal grace from them; they stand in an act astonished and motionless with wonder, due to the certain opinion they held of their Holiness. From this opinion, it very often followed that they even obtained the resurrection of the dead—as we read of Paul who raised Patroclus <note>original: "Patroclo"; according to the apocryphal *Acts of Paul*, Patroclus was a young cupbearer to Emperor Nero who fell to his death from a window while listening to Paul preach and was subsequently resurrected by the Apostle.</note>, and I know not what others, and of many stupendous miracles performed by Peter—all of which are signs and acts of belief. If this belief were perfect and resolute in us, as it was in those happy and fortunate souls, there is no doubt that we too would be capable of performing miracles. But as that belief has failed over time, the power and virtue to perform wonders and supernatural things has failed along with it.

Fear produces acts—beyond those we have touched upon elsewhere—that are pale and trembling, as if the <term>spirits</term> <note>original: "spiriti"; in Renaissance physiology, these were subtle vapors or fluids that circulated through the body to provide life, movement, and sensation. Fear was thought to draw these spirits inward toward the heart, leaving the extremities cold and pale.</note> were failing and fainting within us, as seen in Adam and Eve while they are being driven out of the earthly paradise by the Angel. Furthermore, fear does not allow one to take a vigorous means of defense; instead, through weak actions and faces turned only toward a screen or toward flight, it makes one turn their back, or bend over if they cannot flee to avoid being harmed. Brave soldiers in the <term>lists</term> <note>original: "steccato"; the fenced or palisaded arena used for judicial duels and tournaments.</note> do not wish to do this for the sake of their honor, choosing instead an illustrious and glorious death.

Different are the movements of the same passion of fear in one who has erred, and is captured and led before the judge. For such a person stands with a twisted neck, a bowed head, and with sorrowful eyes turned toward the ground, entirely overcome, fearing and trembling at the deserved punishment he sees hanging over him.

Humility performs its acts in two ways: namely, those that are benign, clement, and humane; and those that are wretched and abject. The former are exemplified by those who, when honored, show themselves to be benign, and those who, moved by nothing other than an innate goodness and purity of soul, help others or show them honor, having regard and consideration for their merits. And all these gestures belong properly to Christ upon the donkey, and again when he washes the feet of the Apostles; likewise to John the Baptist toward Him while he baptizes Him in the Jordan, to Mary Magdalene while she lies prostrate at His feet weeping bitterly, to the Centurion when he prays that He deign to enter his house, and so to many others.

-> D I S C O R S O  I I <-

...that are read; such as those of the ancient fathers toward the most ancient Patriarch <note>Abraham, who is considered the father of many nations in the Judeo-Christian tradition.</note>, when God appeared to him saying that he should resolve to undergo great trials, because he would become the father of an infinite people. The other mode of humble gestures belongs to those who attend only to vile and little-honored things, which do not suit their condition and status at all. Examples include Nero, when he himself carried earth upon his shoulders at the Isthmus <note>A reference to Emperor Nero’s failed attempt to dig a canal across the Isthmus of Corinth in 67 AD, an act seen by aristocrats as demeaning manual labor.</note>; Vitellius, when he gave himself over to gluttony; or, above all others, Sardanapalus <note>A legendary king of Assyria often depicted in art as a symbol of decadence and effeminacy.</note>, while he stayed in the most secret part of his palace mingled among the women with the distaff and the spindle.

Volubility makes the actions varied, mobile, and uncertain, like one who has no firmness in himself, performing in a short time diverse movements of the hands, feet, legs, arms, and head without knowing what he is doing: playing, laughing, exulting, and going about skipping in strange ways. These are all contrary to the steadiness and the actions of a sensible and thoughtful man. These gestures are proper to drunkards, the mad, the enraged, and the flighty, who, if they were represented with actions other than those I have described, would undoubtedly not seem to be such people. For example, Saul <note>The first King of Israel, who in the Bible suffered from a "distressing spirit" and was soothed by David's harp.</note> would not appear to us to be possessed—as he truly was when he heard the sound of David, by which he was usually calmed—if shown in another countenance and act. And were it not for the fact that dancing acquires grace from the sound of music, I would say that among the most fitting acts for representing a madman would be the act of dancing. For it is clearly seen that if one watches someone dancing from a distance so that the sound cannot be heard, one cannot see a more inept or ridiculous thing.

Servitude makes the actions accurate, alert, and intent upon the task at hand, as was seen in the maidens of Semiramis <note>A legendary queen of Babylon.</note> when the news of Babylon was brought to her. They were all standing around occupied in serving her: some with mirrors and combs, some with jewels or chains, others with similar tools and ornaments, arranging one of her braids which at that moment was found loose. But because there are as many acts and gestures of servants as there are their offices and duties—such as adorning, dressing, shoeing, and carrying household goods and food—I will not dwell on this part, as it would be too long. It is enough only that I remind the painter that when representing someone who serves in whatever duty is desired, he should be careful not to make gestures unsuitable to that effect. For instance, one should not turn the face in a different direction from where the hands are working, as we see some poorly-observant artists have done in many paintings. In these, one sees <term>Christs</term> <note>Depictions of Jesus Christ in the scene of the Mandatum, or the washing of the feet.</note> who, while washing the feet of the disciples, have their eyes turned elsewhere; or Mary Magdalenes and Virgin Marys placed in the bath to be washed, without the washer looking at them...

...as if it were of no importance to look at the movement of the hands, or as if they had eyes in their fingernails <note>A metaphor for figures who seem to be looking at their own hands without purpose, or whose gestures are disconnected from their sight and intent.</note>; and [the same is seen in] the Maries who support the Virgin who has fainted before Christ on the Cross, who, by making joyful faces, seem not to care for her, turning their heads either upward or in directions contrary to the action they are performing. For this reason, it is necessary, as I have said, to always keep an eye on the hands, and if the effect being represented is one of strength, the whole body should show strength in every part—and especially in that part where the effort or weight lies. If it is an effect of joy, let the figure be entirely festive, but with respect and moderation, so that laughter does not overflow (which is the privilege of patrons alone). If it is of melancholy, let the figure show itself sad and full of weeping, tears, and sorrows, matching the grief with skill to that of the patron and his misfortune.

And so, to conclude, according to the primary effects given to the figures, one must accommodate and proportion all the actions, studiously observing this: do not make the servant have more majesty and gravity than the master. For it is fitting to give majesty to the master alone, and in the servant, as the lowest, these qualities should decline according to their rank. Through this, paintings will maintain their <term>decorum</term> <note>Decorum is a central concept in Renaissance art, meaning the "appropriateness" of a style or gesture to the subject's social status and the scene's emotional weight.</note>, as this is perhaps one of the most important and necessary considerations in the art. For one cannot create a "history" <note>An "istoria" or history painting: a large-scale narrative work depicting a significant scene from the Bible, mythology, or history.</note> where the gestures of servants do not enter, as seen in the story of the Three Magi and in all others; therefore, let no one fail to consider this well.

Reverence induces one to perform all those acts toward another by which one imagines they can show that they appreciate, love, and hold them in esteem as worthy of observance and honor—such as bowing, yielding one's place, prayers, humility, ceremonies, and similar reverent acts, devoid of pride and arrogance. We see these gestures typically represented before those from whom someone seeks a favor or grace. We read of this regarding the King of Sodom, who, having heard of the great victory of Abraham against the five kings, went before him with the greatest reverence on his knees, begging him to grant him the prisoners whom those defeated kings had previously led away from Sodom. [We also see it] in the wretched sons of Jacob, who, in order not to return to their father without Benjamin (who had been made a prisoner), reverently and with the humblest gestures they could, begged Joseph to grant him to them; and in Esther, who with great reverence and humility presented herself before King Ahasuerus <note>The Persian King Xerxes I, husband of Esther in the biblical narrative.</note>, praying for the life of Mordecai; and in the Queen of Sheba <note>original: "Regina de i Sabei"</note>, who, to hear the wisdom of Solomon, came before him with great reverence, infinite presents, and honors; and in the three Kings of the East called the Magi, who came from the other end of the world to visit...

...and to adore the Savior <note>original: "Saluatore"</note>, presenting themselves before him with bent knees, and offering him Gold, Myrrh, and Incense; and likewise for their family members to do so before their own Lords, and to Christ himself. This is often neglected and has rarely been observed in the past. But let this error pass along with the infinite others committed in this profession <note>The profession of painting</note>, which go unnoticed due to the lack of consideration given to the subtle importance of these things; artists instead follow only a certain coarse, general path without thinking any further.

Shame <term>vergogna</term> <note>Lomazzo treats "vergogna" not just as embarrassment, but as a specific category of modest, downward-looking gesture essential for certain figures.</note> creates gestures like those of one who fears to err, or who believes they have made an error. Therefore, these figures are timid and circumspect, with a certain modesty and honesty. This is also proper to virgins who are suddenly seen naked, like Andromeda when she was tied to the rock and was seen by Perseus—depicted in the manner described by Achilles Tatius of Alexandria <note>original: "Achille Statio Aleſſandrino"; a 2nd-century Greek author whose romance "Leucippe and Clitophon" influenced Renaissance art theory.</note>. Under the name of Angelica, the poet Ariosto depicts the shame she felt, saying:

> *When lowering over her beautiful naked body*
> *The Lady [turned] her eyes shamefully.*

Thus the ancients intended the act of shame to be the lowering of the eyes; for this reason, they painted Venus naked in such a manner, as Landino <note>Cristoforo Landino, a famous Renaissance commentator on Dante and Horace.</note> demonstrates regarding a certain passage of the Third Satire of Horace <note>original: "Oratio"</note> in the First Book. Leonardo da Vinci observed this as well, making Leda entirely naked with the swan in her lap, who shamefully lowers her eyes. But without searching for other historical examples, just as looking upward and around is a sign of audacity and impudence, so looking down is a sign of timidity and shame. Therefore, young women of marriageable age ought to hold their eyes in such a manner, matching them with the rest of their posture. This is how the Virgin should be represented when she is greeted by the Angel [at the Annunciation], and in every other of her actions.

Mercy <term>miſericordia</term> creates compassionate and pious acts; it causes one to take on something of the movement of the poor and afflicted, which moves the viewer to feel compassion. The figure should be represented as faint, pale, ragged, sorrowful, sick, and wounded, with wretched and bowed gestures and acts. They should have sorrowful, tearful looks full of melancholy, with the bowing of the head, twisting of the neck, reaching out of hands, spreading of arms, and similar signs that demonstrate the misery in which they find themselves. For this reason, joy and laughter are extinguished in the merciful person. They are represented in the guise of the fervent Martha, the hostess who served the sick and the crippled in her house, moved by pure compassion; or like many others from the Old Testament, or in the guise of Saint Eligius <note>original: "Santo Eligio"; the patron saint of goldsmiths, known for his extreme charity and for ransoming captives.</note>, or the personification of Charity and Mercy often painted in holy places and hospitals. Such a figure was once painted above the door on the facade of the Hospital of Charity in Milan.

Milan, *Bernardino Luini* <note>original: "Bernardino Louino"; a prominent North Italian painter and follower of Leonardo da Vinci.</note>; in which, although he expressed the likeness of a young woman with a cheerful but gentle face—who instead should have been a matron with a grave expression, whose name was celebrated and illustrious for her mercy and piety—nevertheless, in the rest, he depicted the poor figures below so well (the twisted, the wounded, the lame, the ragged, with such specialized detail) that they can truly be judged as the most beautiful and well-made that have ever been painted by anyone else.

There is also the stupendous Charity that was painted for *Francis I* <note>original: "Francesco Valesio"; King Francis I of France, a major patron of the Italian Renaissance.</note>, King of France, by *Andrea del Sarto* with children around her, and she, all merciful and charitable, consoles them all. Simplicity <term>semplicità</term> <note>In Renaissance art theory, "simplicity" refers to a natural, unstudied grace or purity of character reflected in outward behavior.</note> creates actions that are pure, straightforward, and free, like those of children and young girls without malice; and therefore they are cheerful, disheveled, simple, graceful, and without any sense of prudence or gravity—such as holding in their hands and playing with fruits, balls, cats, dogs, birds, flowers, and similar trifles. In this, one must take great care not to fall into the error of making a child do what they cannot know, such as reading or playing an instrument, or what their age and strength do not permit. By observing this, one will easily come to represent in them those puerile tendernesses like the crossing of legs, twisting of the body, bowing of the head, hands over the mouth, and the like, which I will pass over to avoid being too long. It is enough only to speak of another sort of simplicity by which the purity and loyalty of the mind is demonstrated, as for example was said of *Apelles* <note>The most famous painter of ancient Greece, often cited as the ultimate model for Renaissance artists.</note>: that just as he was stupendous in art, so he was simple and pure by nature; and among the moderns, *Raphael*, *Gaudenzio* <note>Gaudenzio Ferrari, a 16th-century painter and sculptor from the Valsesia region.</note>, and others whom I leave aside, to move further on to treat the other movements that remain for us.

### *On the movements of pain, wonder, death, madness, laziness, despair, annoyance, caprice, patience, and epilepsy.*

#### Chapter XVI.

**H**aving spoken in general and in particular about the natural and accidental movements of the body that proceed from the soul as the motivating cause, it remains in this place to add the particular movements of the passions and accidental apprehensions, which could not be treated under the rule of the others. And these are of no less necessity than the others to anyone who desires to proceed with reason in his paintings and to imitate the truth of nature as his model and example. The first passion, therefore, is pain, which

E 1

...which, according to the torment being suffered, causes the body to move in painful gestures. Describing this through the figure of Prometheus bound to the rock with the vulture pecking at his liver, Achilles Tatius <note>original: "Achille Statio"; refers to the 2nd-century Greek novelist Achilles Tatius, who famously described a painting of Prometheus in his novel *Leucippe and Clitophon*.</note> says that he would pull back his belly and side, and to his own detriment, draw in his thigh. Because of this, he drew the bird back toward his liver, while on the other side, his other foot extended the straight nerves down to the tips of the toes, also showing pain in the rest of the body by arching the eyebrows, tightening the lips, and baring the teeth. 

Pain furthermore causes the body to contort into various knots and twists the eyes, as happens when one is afflicted by poison or a snake bite. This was excellently expressed by the three ancient Rhodian masters—namely, Hagesander, Polydorus, and Athenodorus—in the much-celebrated *Laocoön* <note>The *Laocoön and His Sons* is a monumental Roman marble sculpture, rediscovered in 1506, showing the Trojan priest and his sons being crushed by sea serpents.</note> with his sons, where one statue is seen in the act of grieving, the other dying, and the third feeling compassion; it is now found in the Belvedere in Rome. 

Little different from such movements should be those of Saint Sebastian while he is being shot with arrows, and little different—except in certain specific parts—should be those of Saint Stephen being stoned, and Saint Peter nailed to the cross, and generally of the other Martyrs, in whom the movement must be expressed according to the type of torment. For one movement is caused by fire, as in Saint Lawrence, another by iron, as in Saint Bartholomew, and so one can reason for all the others. 

From this arises the fact that in the afflicted and sorrowful, one sees a delightful variety of withdrawn limbs, sagging arms, arched eyebrows, twisting, closed eyes, tightening and opening of the mouth, tremors, cries, agitations, inflammations, fears, sweats, and groans; not only from the pain of one's own torment, but also from that of others, such as grief over the death of a son, a brother, or other loved and dear persons. Pain also causes fainting, screaming, bewilderment, weeping, opening the arms, despairing, clenching the hands, and similar effects; as should be done for the father Jacob, when his sons presented him with Joseph’s blood-stained cloak as a sign that he had been killed by a wild beast. 

And with similar gestures, the painter must represent the sorrowful Virgin Mother of our Lord, while she is present to see her son raised up, pierced upon the hard wood of the Cross amidst so many torments and outrages. Similarly, those unhappy Hebrew mothers of the innocent children must be represented diversely among themselves, while they see their little ones being cruelly torn and killed in their own arms; these examples can be taken from the prints <note>original: "carte"; likely referring to the famous engravings by Marcantonio Raimondi based on Raphael's designs.</note> of the *Innocents* by Raphael.

It cites the Laocoön sculpture and Raphael’s work as prime examples of how to portray the suffering of martyrs and biblical figures.</summary>

...by Baccio Bandinelli <note>Baccio Bandinelli (1493–1560) was a leading Florentine sculptor and rival of Michelangelo, known for his work on the expression of human anatomy.</note>. Wonder creates its own specific movements, as *Ariosto* <note>Ludovico Ariosto, author of the epic poem *Orlando Furioso*.</note> demonstrates in part when he says:

-> I want to tell you—and it causes wonder— <-
-> To press the lips and arch the eyebrows. <-

And *Petrarch*:

-> Which makes others tremble with wonder, <-

It makes a person attentive, fixed, and immobile as a stone to listen to a strange and never-before-heard occurrence, just as *Ariosto* well described the wonder-struck and astonished paladins in the presence of *Rodomonte*:

-> They leave their food, and leave their words, <-
-> Only to hear what the warrior wants to say. <-

This <term>affect</term> <note>In Renaissance art theory, an "affect" (affetto) is the outward physical expression of an internal emotion or state of mind.</note> also applies to those who suddenly happen to see someone cruelly wounded or killed, and in short, to seeing anything else that is extraordinary and miraculous. Such must have been the state of those in Rome when they saw fire born from the earth, or the *Vestal Virgin* <note>Referring to the Vestal Tuccia, who proved her chastity by miraculously carrying water from the Tiber to the Temple of Vesta in a sieve.</note> carrying water in a sieve; and *Porsena* with the others standing by when they saw *Mucius Scaevola* burn his own hand; or the *Egyptians* and *Magi* in the presence of *Pharaoh* while the Rod of *Aaron* changed into a serpent. At such miracles, everyone always stands watching most attentively, almost as if outside of themselves, in the same manner that the Roman people would have been seen when *Simon Magus* <note>A sorcerer who, according to apocryphal tradition, attempted to fly to prove his divinity but fell and died at the prayers of Saint Peter.</note> fell headlong through the air and broke his neck. 

In such a scene, one should see a most numerous crowd gathered and squeezed together, a confused whispering and low murmuring between one person and another, a looking and pointing at the marvelous event with brows devoid of laughter but full of stupor. One should see them bewildered and suspended by a certain melancholy, with a desire to understand, to chatter, and to interpose themselves by force everywhere—poking their faces in and leaning among others who are crowded together, thus completing the cluster and expanding the circle. This is done with the pointing of fingers and hands, the spreading of arms, the protrusion of bellies, bowing, twisting, fixed gazes, and other similar acts that the ingenious painter can imagine for himself. 

Death, which is nothing other than a deprivation of life or the separation of the soul and the body, manifests its actions in a body in many ways. For if it comes suddenly, as to those who are killed, it makes the eyes roll upward so that half the pupil is hidden above, and the mouth opens, as *Virgil* excellently demonstrates in the fourth book of the *Aeneid*; and it causes different effects when, on the contrary, it comes slowly after one has long suffered, or when it comes through...

# BOOK 2

...another circumstance. These things must be very well understood by the painter. For if he has to represent *Pallas* <note>In Virgil's *Aeneid*, Pallas is a young prince killed by Turnus.</note> killed by *Turnus*, or *Turnus* by *Aeneas*, he should not make their limbs entirely thin and dry, as if they had died after a long and serious illness—unless they were already thin and abstinent in life, like *Saint John the Baptist* and *Saint Mary Magdalene* in the desert. But if someone has died from a lingering illness, he should be represented as gaunt and thin; and likewise if he has been dead for some time, like the resurrected *Lazarus* and others of whom historians have written. 

And in this matter, one must consider that just as the <term>movements of the soul</term> <note>The "moti dell'animo" refer to the internal emotions that manifest as external physical actions.</note> move the body according to their powers, so too the movements caused by death make the body immobile like earth, depriving all the limbs of strength and vigor. As *Daniele Ricciarelli* <note>Daniele da Volterra (c. 1509–1566), a Mannerist painter famous for his *Descent from the Cross* in the church of Trinità dei Monti in Rome.</note> judiciously observed in a Christ taken down from the Cross, which he painted in Rome in the Church of the Trinity; and *Michelangelo* in the marble dead Christ in the lap of his mother which is in Saint Peter’s in the Vatican; in these, one sees the true movements that death produces, seeing all the limbs falling and without any vigor to support themselves anymore. 

This must be most diligently noted, to avoid falling into the errors of those who give the limbs of the dead movements of vigor, and in a certain way make them perform an act of self-support by their own power. 

**Madness** creates foolish, vain acts, and in short, acts contrary to any movement that could proceed from reason and mindfulness; such as inappropriate leaps that make groups of people laugh, twisting of the body, gestures of the hands, turning of the arms, the head, and the whole body, laughter, scoffs, and other strange movements of the mouth and eyes—not unlike what *Ariosto* successfully describes in his *Orlando*, with acts of strength without cause and dangerous. 

And these are also seen in those who are oppressed by <term>burnt choler</term> <note>In the humoral theory of the time, "burnt choler" (colera adusta) was yellow bile that had become overheated, leading to violent mania or deep melancholy.</note>; it causes them, even if they are not insulted by anyone, to become bitterly angry, shout loudly, throw themselves at whoever they encounter, and harm themselves and others. 

But those in whom <term>burnt blood</term> <note>Similar to burnt choler, this was a medical condition where the blood was thought to become "scorched," leading to erratic or boastful behavior.</note> superabounds, exceed greatly in laughter, and above all they boast of great things, make promises about themselves, and with dances and songs they make a great celebration; whereas those burdened by the black dregs of the blood <note>A reference to "black bile," the humor associated with melancholy.</note> are always melancholy, and they imagine certain dreams for themselves, which frighten them in the present and make them fear for the future. To those who are overwhelmed by such passions, it also often happens that they throw their hands now to their head and now to their beard, they pull out their hair, and perform other similar follies. ...ness <note>The text begins mid-word with the suffix *-dagine*, completing the word *infingardagine* (sloth or laziness) from the previous page.</note> makes actions slow, coarse, and without reverence, such as leaning on whatever is convenient with the arms and legs, as is seen every day in peasants, kitchen servants, guards, rascals, and the like. From the observation of these actions, it follows that in a historical painting, the noble person is recognized all the more through such comparisons, especially when their form and clothing match the gestures of sloth. 

Despair produces actions signifying a certain deprivation of hope and happiness, such as wringing the hands or tearing at one's own limbs and clothes over a corpse whom one never hopes to see alive again; like Thisbe over Pyramus, when she miserably kills herself by throwing her whole body onto the point of a sword; or because of some notable misfortune suffered in war, like Saul, who in his despair has his three sons killed in his presence and finally kills himself; or for some loss of well-being or delight, like Cleopatra for Mark Antony, who for that reason poisons herself with snakes; and Dido for Aeneas, when—as Virgil describes—she miserably burns herself on a great pyre after plunging a dagger into her chest along with all her joys and treasures; or like Cato of Utica <note>A Roman statesman who committed suicide to avoid living under Caesar's tyranny.</note> and Mithridates, to avoid falling into the hands of the enemy; or like Nero, out of remorse for the enormous crimes he committed, expecting cruel punishments; and the Roman Lucretia, to avoid living in dishonor; or like Ahithophel <note>A counselor to King David who betrayed him and later hanged himself.</note> and Judas Iscariot, who for this reason hanged themselves by the throat. ->*Weeps, cries out, beats herself, scratches, and tears,*<-

And through many disastrous events from which various <term>movements</term> <note>In art theory, "movements" (moti) are the external physical gestures that reveal the internal state of the soul.</note> of despair arise, such as drowning or throwing oneself down from mountains. All these movements must appear deliberate, and of such a kind that the desperate person, by fulfilling their intent, may find some relief from their bitterness. 

Spitefulness <note>Original: *molestia*. Here referring to a malicious or troublesome disposition.</note> causes actions contrary to others; for they offend and annoy, as those which aim at nothing else but to oppose, offend, and provoke others. These are things commonly seen in the insolent, the annoying, the ignorant, and the envious; such as were Cain toward Abel, Ham against his brothers, Ishmael toward Isaac, Esau toward Jacob, Saul toward David, Absalom toward Amnon <note>The text reads *Aman*, but refers to the biblical story of Absalom and his brother Amnon.</note>, and many others named in history, who never ceased to plot, offend, and annoy.
