...-ful, cheerful, loving, liberal, greedy, and troublesome they show themselves to be. These gestures are also characteristic of those who, in the manner of **actors** <note>original: "istrioni"; referring to stage performers who specialized in mimicry and physical comedy.</note>, use movements suited to their roles to feign being a child, a **bravo** <term>bravo: a swaggering soldier or hired bully often depicted in Italian art and literature</term>, a humble man, a cruel one, an old man, a woman, and the like. They leap about in various ways and mock the crowd by imitating their actions in a jesting manner, which simultaneously provokes laughter, annoyance, and wonder. **Patience** produces humble gestures, devoid of any defense; in short—to avoid expanding where it is not necessary—they are such as are seen expressed in the **Passion of Christ**. For this reason, painters are obliged to represent this quality in Christ through every trial where He is offended and mocked by the Jews: especially when He is depicted being whipped at the column, shown to the people <note>The "Ecce Homo" scene where Pilate presents Christ to the crowd.</note>, and being crowned with thorns; and while He carries the Cross to the mountain, and is nailed upon it and raised into the air. In these moments, He never showed a sign of defense, nor of fleeing, nor of shunning His martyrdom. So too have those most holy **Martyrs** done for His love during their torments, massacres, and deaths; they stand humble in their suffering with their eyes now turned toward Heaven in hope, and now downward in humility, yet expressing their state through all their external limbs according to the pain they endured. Finally, the movements of **Lunatics**—such as we read in the **Gospel** regarding the one who was cured by Christ—are, in short, like those of a man who is beside himself and knows not what he thinks or wishes to do. Therefore, to express such people, it will first be necessary to make their hair disheveled or mangled, their eyes squinting or distorted, their nostrils fouled, their lips swollen and twisted in strange ways, and their teeth foaming, being more exposed on one side than the other. Their arms, hands, and legs should be trembling, so that they continually seem about to fall, in the manner of a man whose strength is failing; they should shake their heads and writhe and toss their whole bodies, with a dull, pale, or livid complexion. And in a similar way, one can represent the man mentioned in the Gospel who was also **possessed** <note>original: "spiritato"; a person possessed by a spirit or demon.</note>, using the gestures described above, though somewhat more vehement. There is another sort of these people who, according to **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine."</note> and other physicians, are called **Epileptics**. Among these, three types are found: some who, keeping the body straight, extend their arms and legs straight and tense; others who curve forward so that their feet come to touch their face; and others who, by curving backward, make their heels touch their head. Thus, according to the truth of the history, they shall be represented now in one way and now in another.

### On various other very necessary movements. Chapter XVIII.

**B**eyond the movements explained quite extensively until now, for the understanding of others that may be relevant, there are still others of no small importance. These are governed by the most beautiful and appropriate actions a human body can make, both because of the effect the person is then producing, and because of the quality of the seasons and the things tasted through the senses. To do this with praise, one must make a selection of the best and most suitable movements in all acts and effects, investigating them subtly and drawing them from the circumstances in which the person represented finds themselves. As, for example, **Leonardo da Vinci** once did in the Cartoon of **Saint Anne** <note>This likely refers to the "Burlington House Cartoon," a famous preparatory drawing by Leonardo.</note>, which was later transferred to France and is now found in **Milan** in the possession of the painter **Aurelio Luini** <note>Aurelio Luini (c. 1530–1593) was a Milanese painter and son of Bernardino Luini; he was a contemporary of the author.</note>. Many drawings of it are in circulation, where he expressed in the **Virgin Mary** the happiness and the joy she felt seeing such a beautiful child born as **Christ** was, and considering herself made worthy to be His Mother; and in **Saint Anne** similarly the joy and contentment she felt, seeing her daughter as the Mother of God, and herself blessed. 

And also in the panel seen in the **Chapel of the Conception** in **San Francesco** in **Milan** <note>This refers to the *Virgin of the Rocks*. The chapel belonged to the Confraternity of the Immaculate Conception.</note>—which will also be discussed in the book on lights—where one sees in **Saint John the Baptist**, while kneeling with joined hands he bows to **Christ**, the movement of obedience and boyish reverence. In the Virgin, one sees the movement of a joyful contemplation while she gazes at these acts; and in the angel, the movement of angelic beauty in the act of considering the joy that would result to the world from that mystery. In **Christ** the child, divinity and wisdom are shown; and thus the **Virgin** stands kneeling, holding **Saint John** with her right hand and extending her left outward in foreshortening <note>original: "in scorto"; an artistic technique used to create the illusion of an object receding strongly into the distance.</note>. Likewise, the **Angel** holds **Christ** with his left hand, who, while sitting, looks at **Saint John** and blesses him. 

Other painters, who have been lights of this art, have observed other movements, such as contemplation in raising the eyes to **Heaven**, admiring the angelic sounds, while leaving the instruments and other earthly sounds below on the ground. These movements were expressed in the singular panel of **Saint Cecilia**, who was painted by **Raphael** with four other Saints, which is found in **Bologna** at **San Giovanni in Monte**. And also the agony and the pain in those who are afflicted, which **Antonio da Correggio** expressed in **Christ** praying in the garden <note>The *Agony in the Garden*, a masterpiece of light and emotion by Correggio.</note> with admirable skill in his city. And likewise **silence**, **panting**, **sweating**, **puffing**, **sleeping**, **blowing suddenly**...

And let this suffice for examples. For if one wished to go about collecting all the examples to demonstrate how, in every effect, one must choose the proper <term>actions<note>original: "atti". In Renaissance theory, "actions" are the specific physical gestures used to convey the internal state or "movements" of the soul.</note></term>—without which a painting can have no value—it would be difficult to reach the end. 

One must also pay attention to the **seasons**; for **Summer** makes movements open, weary, and full of sweat and redness; **Winter** makes them restricted, withdrawn, and trembling; **Spring**, cheerful, vigorous, prompt, and of good color; and **Autumn**, hesitant, and more inclined toward melancholy than otherwise. 

However, if one were to paint a **fatigued man**, regardless of the season (though somewhat more in summer than in other seasons), he must always be represented with his limbs <term>strained<note>original: "rilouati", likely meaning muscles that are prominent or bulging due to exertion.</note></term>, oppressed, and jutting out, full of sweat and inflammation. This is especially true for those who carry loads, pull weights, or hasten to jump, walk, play with arms, fight, and perform similar exercises. 

**Sleep**, then, does not show any movement of vigor or strength, but appears as if it were a body extinguished of life. Therefore, take care not to do as some are accustomed to: creating attitudes and poses for those who sleep in which it is neither likely nor even possible that a person could actually fall asleep; as is sometimes seen in figures placed across rocks, benches, and the like, represented with limbs that are supporting themselves and exerting force. In this, it is clearly seen that such painters do not know how to observe <term>decorum<note>original: "decoro". The artistic principle that every element—pose, setting, clothing—must be appropriate to the subject and its status.</note></term>. 

From **tastes**, also, their own movements are born, as we experience every hour: a bitter and sour taste makes the eyebrows arch and moves other parts of the face, while a sweet and pleasant taste smooths...

...open the face, as a good smell likewise does; whereas, on the contrary, a foul one makes us plug our nostrils, look askance, and turn our backs, with furrowed brows, eyes nearly shut, and the mouth drawn inward. From hearing and touch, other distinct movements are similarly caused in our bodies. For example, from a sharp and noisy sound, there arises a sudden trembling and fright; from touching hot things, there arise fast and quick movements; and from touching cold things, withdrawn movements full of trembling, as happens to those who touch ice or snow in winter. I conclude the same regarding sight, because looking at excessively bright things causes the vision to be dazzled, and the man withdraws and shields himself; looking at dark things, the eyes sharpen by turning downward and nearly closing, in the same manner that painters often do when they wish to see from up close what effect a painting will have from a distance. And here I will put an end to the most important simple <term>movements</term> <note>Lomazzo uses "moti" (movements) to describe how internal emotions are physically manifested in the body and face.</note>, to come to the multiple movements.

## *Of friendship and enmity, of movements and their pairings.*
### Chapter XVIII.

**B**ecause beyond all the movements that have been declared in general and in particular—those which are expressed in order in figures—it is also required that, according to the logic of their friendship and enmity, one considers in what way two, three, or four can be coupled together and demonstrated in a single body, and shine forth in the face. This is as the good ancient and modern painters have done, though few possess this knowledge easily. According to the stated logic of the roots of the <term>passions of the soul</term> <note>The internal emotional states that drive physical action.</note>, and of the <term>four humors</term> <note>The ancient medical theory that human health and temperament were governed by four fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> and their suitabilities, we shall proceed, making their branches sprout forth from those trunks. 

Firstly, it is found that they are enemies and cannot be united together in the same subject: anxious, weary, sad, stubborn, and rigid movements with those that are temperate, modest, graceful, noble, clement, and cheerful. Nor can timid, simple, humble, pure, and merciful movements be united with those that are violent, impetuous, arrogant, bold, cruel, and fierce. On the other hand, the anxious, weary, sad, stubborn, and rigid will be "friends" with the timid, simple, humble, pure, and merciful; and they will also couple—though not with such ease and sympathy—with the violent, impetuous, arrogant, bold, cruel, and fierce. The temperate, modest, graceful, noble, clement, and cheerful can agree with the timid, simple, humble, pure, and merciful, and also with the...

...bold, fierce, magnanimous, liberal, graceful, and lustful. Thus, from one to another, in all the other <term>movements</term> <note>original: "moti." Lomazzo uses this term to describe the physical manifestation of internal emotions in the body and face.</note>, one can easily find their similarities and discords. Once this is known and understood, the movements are then easily coupled together and represented in the face in the manner appropriate to the <term>narrative</term> <note>original: "iſtoria." In Renaissance art theory, this refers to the complex storytelling or historical scene depicted in a painting.</note> and to the effect by which they are moved.

As an example, consider **Abraham** when he believes he must sacrifice his son to God: there is pity, sorrow, and obedience; and in **Isaac**, these same effects are mixed with trembling and pain. Beyond this, there are some movements that are the greatest of enemies to each other, yet both are friends to a third, and for this reason, they can be joined together. For it is seen that boldness and fear are enemies to one another, and yet both are friends to honesty and to lust. These two likewise do not agree together—rather, they are opposites—nonetheless, joy and liberality are friends and compatible with both, as are even malice and loyalty, even though these two are enemies to each other.

Cruelty and pity are likewise most contrary to one another, yet they can agree with lust, with joy, and with chastity. Grace and cowardice, though discordant, are joined in humility. Love and hate, such great enemies, are reconciled and made friends in contentment. Honor and shame are coupled in joy. Joy and melancholy can be united with pity, lust, cruelty, loyalty, liberality, religion, prudence, and the like. Stability and fickleness, which are repugnant to one another, find a place together in lust, cruelty, pity, and honesty. Pain, the enemy of rest, joy, avarice, and liberality, accompanies various vices. Fury and temperance join with loyalty and liberality; arrogance with modesty and with joy; boldness and strength, and shamelessness and shame, with liberality, strength, and obstinacy; justice with ignorance, lust, honesty, and joy with religion.

Besides these, justice, honor, grace, prudence, constancy, clemency, boldness, liberality, and joy are all mutual friends to one another. But lust is a friend to boldness, liberality, and joy, and not to the others. Honesty is a friend to all. Hardness and melancholy are friends to constancy, and boldness to hardness. We see, moreover, that fear and sweating do not stand together, yet they unite in sorrow. Paleness is contrary to blushing, yet they join in a friendly way in that same sorrow. Thus among the vices, insolence and laziness are discordant, yet they agree with lust. Fierceness is contrary to timidity, yet both unite with fickleness.

...obstinacy, the enemy of volubility, is accompanied by fierceness, cruelty, ignorance, pride, lust, insolence, and the like; pride and baseness are joined to rigidity and hatred; impetus, fury, and rage—all enemies of sloth—agree with it in hatred, and also in vengeance, slaughter, and death. Misery and vainglory, though contrary to each other, agree in madness and ignorance; loftiness, vanity, and contempt with betrayal, hatred, and rigidity. Finally, among the vicious and blameworthy <term>movements</term> <note>original: "moti." Lomazzo refers to the outward physical expression of internal passions.</note>, the insolent, fierce, cruel, daring, obstinate, impious, and coarse are friends with one another, and they cannot coexist with the timid, the base, the miserable, the lazy, and such like. And these latter can accompany the volatile, the ignorant, the vain, the lustful, the filthy, and others who then pair with the first group we mentioned. And so, by accompanying the movements with reason according to this friendship and enmity that we have said is found among them, one will come to represent whatever one desires, not only with ease but also with praise for the painter. 

For example, if one represents **Jupiter** while he embraces and caresses the **daughter of Inachus** <note>This is Io, a priestess of Hera whom Jupiter (Zeus) fell in love with.</note>, even though he would be, by his nature and by the occasion, pleasant and cheerful, he will nonetheless mix and almost blend **Majesty**, **daring**, and **lust** into that cheerfulness and pleasantness. If he were expressed otherwise, he could not easily appear to be Jupiter, since one can indeed caress a young girl, but with a base and dishonest gesture; this would not be appropriate—rather, it would be an extremely unbecoming thing to represent in such a God.

## Of certain movements of Horses. Chapter XIX.

Beyond the aforementioned movements that a horse can naturally make according to its limbs, there are others of no less importance. To understand these, the principles treated in the practical section will be useful. Now I say that a horse moves for no other reason than to produce some effect, and therefore it moves according to these intentions, as well as according to the events that follow afterward. Here one must open one's eyes very wide, because the entire science of making horses depends on this. To make such consideration familiar to oneself, one must largely make use of the labors already completed by others—in painting and sculpture as well as in writing—to more easily investigate the acts and effects of horses from nature, and to arrange them with due reason as is fitting. For it is well known that in difficult matters, it is very important to steady oneself and open one's eyes following the examples provided.

To make [the horse] bite the rich, foamy bit, and if it is necessary to have a valet hold him by the hand, one shall give him motion in the manner that <term>Tasso</term><note>Bernardo Tasso (1493–1569), an Italian courtier and poet, father of Torquato Tasso.</note> taught in the first Canto of his *Amadigi* when he says:

> The steed is graceful, entirely jet-black,
> With a star on its forehead, and three white-socked feet,
> It bit the foamy, beautiful bit at every hour
> And whinnying, makes itself heard from afar;
> It inflates its nostrils, snorts, is quick and slender,
> It wheels around the little dwarf,
> It cannot stay in one place, but with one foot
> It strikes and smites the earth from time to time.

I conclude, finally, that for every kind of motion, one can find examples among the good poets, both Latin and <term>Tuscan</term><note>Lomazzo uses "Tuscan" to refer to the literary Italian language.</note>, which I will not collect here as it would be a task not only long, but infinite. Let it suffice to have mentioned these few, according to what I promised above to do; so that one might know in what way, above all, one must give horses the appropriate movements, corresponding to the actions they perform. <term>Leonardo</term><note>Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519), whose studies on horse anatomy for the Sforza monument were legendary.</note> principally designed a great part of these, he who in this area has been the leader among the moderns; and among the ancients, he perhaps surpassed <term>Nealces</term><note>Nealces was a Greek painter of the 3rd century BCE, famously said to have created the effect of horse froth by throwing a sponge at his canvas in frustration.</note> the painter, who, being unique in his skill, painted a tired horse and wished to show the foam at its mouth, just as we read. In this way, they should be represented in actions that make them appear to whinny, jump, and frisk at the sound of trumpets; and in moments of terror and danger, one must give them the look and motion of fear and dread. 

This is seen in the horse of <term>Saint George by Cesare da Sesto</term><note>Cesare da Sesto (1477–1523) was a Milanese painter and a close follower of Leonardo da Vinci.</note> as it approaches the Dragon, in which one sees vividly and divinely expressed that impetus with which it forces itself to pull back its foot and flee the horrible sight of the Dragon; and yet, by sheer force, it is held back by the Saint until he ends his magnanimous enterprise. I once owned a drawing of this, along with various others by Leonardo, who in this matter was no less excellent than he was in all else—as can be seen, among other things, from a horse in <term>plastic relief</term><note>original: "rilieuo di plastica." This refers to a model made of a malleable material like clay, wax, or stucco.</note> made by his hand, which the sculptor <term>Cavalier Leone Aretino</term><note>Leone Leoni (c. 1509–1590), a famous sculptor and medalist from Arezzo who owned many of Leonardo's drawings and models.</note> possesses.

being, so to speak, some lazy and others fast according to the qualities of the body that moves them, according to the **passion** <note>In this context, "passion" refers to an intense internal emotion or driving impulse, such as rage or fear, that dictates movement.</note> by which it is overtaken, and also according to the habit and constitution of said body. Of which painting I once owned a drawing, which was very dear to me. 

And to properly investigate and understand the nature of such animals, and to commit their effects and movements to memory, I judge it expedient (leaving aside those of ancient <term>reliefs</term><note>original: "pile antiche," referring to ancient sarcophagi or stone carvings.</note>) to read the **poets** who touch upon them gracefully in comparisons and examples, as can be seen in **Homer**, **Virgil**, **Ovid**, **Horace**, **Catullus**, and others, all of whom have been imitated by the famous **Ariosto** in his never-sufficiently-praised *Furioso*, where I remember having read in the Second Canto, regarding two dogs fighting together, this stanza:

## On the movements of hair. Chapter XXII.

**I**n all those ways in which I have said the human body moves—that is, upward and downward; here and there; forward and backward—so too does the hair move, even winding around itself in circles. Faces with hair turned upward are made when one wishes to represent a person terrified by some frightening sight or other great danger. Also for those who have a <term>bad physiognomy</term> <note>Physiognomy is the historical "science" of judging a person's character or soul based on their outward physical features.</note>, the locks or flat hairs that are called <term>ruffled</term> <note>original: "rabuffati," referring to disheveled or standing-on-end hair.</note> are made turned upward. One also sees tresses gathered together on high, and also scattered hair, when they are imagined to be in a high place where some wind might blow from below, or a flame burns that moves them—as is seen in those who are being burned, for the flame pushes the hair upward. Hair turned downward is that which we see scattered, falling over the shoulders, as of one who combs it or wishes to arrange their braids; or as of those who naturally always wear it so, as **Christ** and the **Apostles** used; and others according to the ancient custom of the Greeks, Hebrews, and Persians. Thus, falling down, they are proper...

...also proper to poor beggars and scoundrels. Those [locks of hair] that turn here and there occur when one depicts a wind blowing from the side, striking the face and causing the hair to flutter through the air on the opposite side; or when the person leans to the side to perform some action. They move forward and backward also because of the breeze or the wind that blows; for if it blows from the front, the hair is scattered behind; and if from behind, it is scattered forward. This same effect is also caused by leaning either forward or backward, because hair has this quality: unable to support itself, it always falls toward the lower part. Therefore **Christ**, when he washes the feet of the **Apostles**, requires such an arrangement of hanging hair, and likewise the **Magdalene** when she lies wrapped at the feet of the **Savior**. 

However, they also turn forward and backward because of running and flight, as seen in a **Daphne** when she flies from **Apollo**, and in **Absalom** while he flees from his father. <note>In the Bible, Absalom's long hair became a fatal liability when it caught in a tree during his flight.</note> Nor does it seem right to remain silent on the fact that the hair of **Christ** should not be shown as if it were styled, nor should it appear very thin around the forehead. For such things belong to those who comb themselves often and keep themselves clean; to which Christ did not attend, nor did the Apostles.

But passing to the final movement of the hair—when the locks turn in a circle among themselves <note>referring to curls or ringlets</note>—I judge that there are as many types as there are roles of those to whom they are attributed. Because the philosopher and the theologian, for the sake of their gravity, require—as **Michelangelo** very well observed in his **Moses**—to have thick and slow-moving <term>locks</term> <note>original: *berre*, meaning thick clumps or tufts of hair</note>; and locks made in this way are also required for the beard. In this manner, the actions, gravity, role, form, clothing, and age are judiciously matched. 

In a strong man like **Hercules**, the locks should be thick and well-intertwined, turned in various directions with a very beautiful manner, yet not fine, but rather harsh and thick; for fineness is suited to the weak. A poor man or an old man without vigor should have them long, sparse, and such that they can barely be perceived, in the manner of one who is half-bald, like **Saturn**. 

A Lord full of majesty, like **Jupiter**—who should almost resemble the form of **Christ**—should have the <term>locks</term> of his hair neither too long nor too short, but so matched that they do not offend by any particular fault; such as being too similar to those of Hercules or those of Saturn. Sparse, somewhat wide, and full <term>locks</term> are required for children, such as **Cupid**, and for young virgins—that is, young girls. Harsh, twisted, well-defined <term>locks</term> that surround and adorn the low forehead, are...

Hair gracefully knotted together, or arranged in braids in various ways, with some ribbons <note>original: "benacci," likely meaning ribbons or small bands</note> in the gaps and contours, is characteristic of famous courtesans; and therefore the mirror is given as a character attribute to Venus, as the instrument for achieving this work. And one must proceed with this same rule when painting beards; which I will not discuss here, only advising that in this part concerning the hair, craftsmen must apply every effort and employ all their art, to allow their overall worth to be judged from it. 

And primarily one must represent the glistening highlights and their reflections <note>original: "ricacciamenti"</note>, for hair is naturally oily <note>original: "ontuosi"</note>, so that it shines more than the flesh. Furthermore, they should not be rendered to be viewed from up close, but from a distance, without visible brushstrokes, but with highlights blended <term>impastati|A technique where paint is applied thickly or blended smoothly so individual strokes disappear into a "paste"</term> with that grace which the leading painters have swiftly expressed in this regard; such as Antonio da Correggio, Giorgione of Castelfranco, Titian, Raphael, Polidoro, Leonardo, Gaudenzio, Andrea del Sarto, Perino del Vaga, Rosso, Mazzolino, and Boccaccino; and among sculptors, who have in this imitated the manner of the ancients, like those who made the Laocoön, Michelangelo, Donatello, Baccio Bandinelli, Andrea and Jacopo Sansovino, Pierino da Vinci, Giambologna, and Fontana; and in medals, the singular Giacomo da Trezzo; and in engraving them in prints, the divine Albrecht Dürer and Lucas van Leyden <note>original: "Luca da Holanda"</note>, Marcantonio Bolognese, and Cornelis Cort <note>original: "Cornelio Fiamengo" (Cornelis the Fleming)</note>.

### *On the Movements of All Sorts of Drapery.* Cap. XXII.

**T**he movements of drapery <term>panni|Cloth or fabric, often referring to the clothing on a figure</term>, that is, of their folds—or if we prefer to say pleats—must flow in all directions, no differently than branches from a tree trunk; and so arrange it that one fold is born from another, just as one branch emerges from another, or wave from wave; so that there is no part of the cloth in which one does not see almost...

--- Page 222 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of artistic decorum from the previous page, shifting the focus from the styling of hair to the depiction of movement in drapery and how it must correspond to the specific qualities of various fabrics.</meta>

<page-num>185</page-num>
<header>->SECOND BOOK<-</header>

...all the same movements. Now, these movements must be moderate, easy, and free, without interruptions, and should show grace and ease rather than the wonder of affected study and great effort. And because movements serve all sorts of fabrics, just as they do the body, it is right that they should be different from one another, just as the fabrics themselves are different. And therefore, they must be lighter in thin fabrics, such as cendals <note>original: "cendali," a lightweight, thin silk fabric</note>, linens, veils, and the like, in which the folds are tiny, and they lift, and trembling, and almost pleasantly waving, they swell slightly, dilating and billowing like a sail where the movement of the wind takes more force. They also go to find the naked form <note>original: "nudo," referring to the anatomical structure of the body beneath the clothes</note> everywhere, as is clearly seen in peasants; on the side from which the wind blows, one sees the thin clothes stretched over the naked form, and on the other side they flutter. The same happens with ties, belts of cloaks, and similar things; all of which movements appropriately belong to, and must be given to, the garments of Nymphs and other Goddesses, to whom lightness is suited.

Heavy movements must be adapted to sturdy fabrics, where the folds are rare and thick, so that they can only take movement slowly; and therefore they fall downwards, and find the naked form with difficulty because of the thickness that supports itself. And these movements are seen principally in brocades, in felts, in thick leather, and the like; in which the air cannot have much force. Therefore, their folds make their movements according to how they are handled and pressed by those who wear them, such as under the arms and under the knees due to the opening and unbending of the legs and arms, yet always making thick, hard, and firm folds, without minuteness or weakness; in such a way that on top of them, other thin fabrics could be placed for support without crushing them.

Moderate movements, which are neither heavy nor light, are those seen in the folds of fabrics such as rascia <note>original: "raſcia," a sturdy, twilled wool fabric often produced in Florence or Venice</note> and other fine wool cloths, which therefore allow themselves to be moved suitably by the air and guided by human limbs for their convenience; and so, making very beautiful and moderate folds, they follow the naked form very well, and also go gracefully and charmingly playing around the loins. And from here **Raphael, Michelangelo, Leonardo, Gaudenzio <note>Gaudenzio Ferrari, a prominent painter and sculptor of the Piedmontese school</note>, Albrecht Dürer**, and the other most excellent ones, have taken their method and manner of giving movement to their drapery <term>panneggiare|The art of depicting the folds and arrangement of clothing in art</term>, as if from the most beautiful examples, to use them generally in the cloaks of Saints and in the pavilions <note>original: "padiglioni," referring to large decorative hangings or tents often depicted in religious or royal scenes</note> that are fashioned from such cloths. To these are added other movements, which are called turns and traverses <note>original: "volti, & trauerſi," referring to complex, overlapping, or cross-wise folds</note>, and are proper to...

damasks, satins, *ormesini* <note>original: "ormesini," a thin, lightweight silk fabric originally from Hormuz</note>, and the like, in which one sees the folds crossed and broken among themselves by the diverse tensions of the cloth. From this, the Venetians have derived their manner of <term>panneggiare</term> <note>panneggiare: the artistic technique of rendering the folds and flow of drapery</note> and making folds that are very distant and contrary to the aforementioned movements followed by Raphael and the others. This style truly should not be observed anywhere but in portraits, where it seems not only to look good, but is almost necessarily required. But in history paintings <note>original: "historie," narrative scenes depicting significant historical, biblical, or mythological events</note>, in my opinion, it should not be used as a rule; and if it must be represented in any particular place, it should not be done entirely, but only imitated and almost hinted at with grace, in such a way that it does not appear affectedly taken from natural clothes without grace and order—a practice which many, in my judgment, are often accustomed to use with little reason. 

Other movements could also be considered, such as those of velvets, thin leathers, and the like, which are all different from each other; but since what has been said is sufficient for the understanding of such movements, I will not extend my discussion further; advising the painter only that in this part, no less than in others, he should invest study, time, and effort. For from this, no less than from other elements, depends his perfection and excellence; because these movements of cloth are so close to the living person that it is sensibly understood—and one can almost touch it with the hand—that the movements of a garment are capable of making a figure seem crippled and clumsy, moving the viewers to both disgust and laughter. 

This was the case with certain draperies used by our great-grandfathers two hundred years ago, which appear to be nothing other than striped folds, and, so to speak, made like candles; a style also used by some moderns who consider themselves talented, making moreover long and continuous movements through the folds in the manner of hanging pipes, without any other grace. Another flaw is also perceived in the cloths of the old painters, which appear made in a certain way like scales, which they derived from models of men dressed, I believe, in paper. The matter was then brought to perfection with very great effort by Bramante and Andrea Mantegna, and afterwards it was also further corrected and polished a little more by Albrecht Dürer and Lucas van Leyden <note>original: "Luca d'Olanda"</note>.

# *On the movements of trees, and of all that moves. Chapter XXIII*

**F**inally, the movements in every single thing that moves must be expressed with judgment, according as is appropriate to the thing to which they are given: now light, now slow, now mobile, and now otherwise.

**A**nd first, in plants, when they are struck by the wind, the thinner branches—and therefore also the lighter ones—must be represented as if they are striking against each other, yielding and bowing toward the side opposite to where the wind blows, much more so than the solid and therefore heavy ones, while the trunk remains strong and firm. The branches that grow from there begin to bend, and the others that rise from those bend even more, so that the same lightness is shown in the leaves. It is certainly true that not all trees move in the same way; for the Willow <note>original: "Salce"</note> moves and shakes extremely, while the Pine never does, or very little; and one could discuss all others in this way. But here it must be noted that young plants with tender trunks begin to shake from the bottom of the trunk, along with their branches and foliage.

Grasses also, and flowers, and fruits have their own trembling movements according to the wind and the breeze that blows, and also according to how they are weighed down by something—as for example, an ear of wheat <note>original: "spica di formento"</note> by a bird, which would not only make it twist but would pull it to the ground. This was well-noted by a certain peasant in the time of the Greeks to a particular painter—I do not recall if it was Aristides or Pamphilus <note>Aristides of Thebes and Pamphilus were celebrated painters of ancient Greece, known for their technical precision</note>—who had painted such a thing: a bird atop an ear of wheat without making the ear twist in the slightest.

Likewise, the movements of inanimate things—such as the trembling of feathers, wings, and plumes; the twisting of ropes and bindings; the flying of straw, dust, and similar things—must be shown according to the violence being done to them. This is so that no one, however clumsy they may be, is given a handle <note>original: "ansa," meaning an opportunity or excuse</note> to criticize and bite at a painting that is otherwise excellent. This happened a short time ago with a medal by a good sculptor <note>This likely refers to Leone Leoni’s 1561 medal of Michelangelo</note>, who, on the reverse side where he had portrayed Michelangelo, had depicted a poor man led by a dog on a leash <note>original: "corda," a rope or cord</note>. The leash was seen entirely stretched and straight like a stick, without any slack at all. This gave even a child the occasion to mock it, saying that if that dog had pulled that rope so strongly, he would either have choked himself or would not have been able to go any further. This caused such laughter among some painters who were with me that they nearly burst.

Many other similar movements are found in paintings that make people laugh; these would not escape the hands of painters so easily if, in every thing that is painted, its nature <note>original: "essere," its state of being or essence</note> were considered, however small it might be. This was the practice of the accurate Leonardo <note>Leonardo da Vinci</note> and Cesare da Sesto <note>A prominent pupil of Leonardo</note>, from whose hands no work ever emerged that was not entirely perfect. And thus, even in the smallest little herbs, one sees their forms rendered perfectly,

...[were] shaped and moved according to their own logic. **Albrecht Dürer** <note>original: "Alberto Durero"</note> had this same beautiful concern no less than the others, as can be fully understood in his prints and paintings. In these, one sees the proper motion given even to the tiniest hairs of the beard, as in the portrait of the **Duke of Saxony**, who was also later portrayed by **Titian** <note>original: "Ticiano"</note>. This is seen again in the fur of the dog in the print of **Saint Eustace**, in the horses of the print of the Knight <note>original: "carta del senso, & della morte"; likely referring to Dürer’s famous engraving 'Knight, Death and the Devil'</note>, and in the leaves of the large **Adam** and **Eva**. 

In the sea, one must likewise express its movements by representing the various agitations of the waves; and similarly in rivers, and in ships and boats—those leaps of the waves tossed by the storm <note>original: "fortuna," often used to mean a sea storm in this period</note>, and the struggle the ship makes against them. In waters that fall from a height, one must also represent their motion, especially when, striking upon cliffs or rocks, those sprays are seen leaping back into the air, soaking everything around them. 

In the air, let its movements be given with judgment to the clouds—now compressed by the winds, and now driven furiously by hail, lightning bolts, thunderclaps, rain, and other such things that are generated in the region of the air. Finally, one cannot create anything in which motion does not, in some way, have to be represented. 

But since this has been discussed so much that, in my opinion, it is enough, I will bring an end to these motions in the most burning motion of the flames, glowing with the desire to always move forward toward the end; no differently than they do before our eyes, even when struck and agitated in various directions by the wind, always growing and strengthening themselves.

# BOOK THREE
## ON COLOR,
### By Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo, Milanese Painter.

->On the Virtue of Coloring. Chapter 1.<-

There is no doubt that all things, when they are well-formed and guided by design <term>design: from the Italian 'disegno,' meaning both the physical drawing and the intellectual concept behind a work</term>, and then colored according to their proper order, take on the very same appearance that nature itself displays in that motion or gesture. For even dogs, upon seeing other dogs painted, bark at them from behind, as if calling or challenging them, believing them to be alive solely by their appearance—just as they do when seeing themselves in a mirror. It is told that a dog did exactly this, ruining a painted one that Gaudenzio <note>Gaudenzio Ferrari (c. 1471–1546), a major Northern Italian Renaissance painter known for his emotive and naturalistic style.</note> had painted on a panel of Christ Carrying the Cross in Cannobio. One also reads that birds have flown toward other perfectly represented birds, like those partridges that flew toward the Partridge painted by Parrhasius <note>A famous painter of Ancient Greece (5th century BCE), renowned for his skill in contour and illusion.</note> upon a column on the Island of Rhodes.

Historians recount that a dragon was once painted in Rome during the Triumvirate <note>A political regime in ancient Rome; likely referring to the era of Augustus, Mark Antony, and Lepidus.</note> so naturally that it caused birds to stop their singing. Even more marvelous was that painting in the Theater of Claudius Pulcher <note>Appius Claudius Pulcher, a Roman official in 79 BCE known for introducing realistic painted scenery to the Roman stage.</note>, where it is said that crows flew right into it, deceived by the appearance of the fake roof tiles, and tried to fly out through those fake windows, to the great wonder and laughter of the onlookers. 

It is a story known to everyone how Zeuxis <note>A legendary Greek painter (5th century BCE) often cited in debates about artistic realism.</note> painted certain clusters of grapes so naturally that birds flew into the theater square to peck at them; and how he himself was later deceived by the veil <note>original: "velo"; refers to the famous competition where Parrhasius painted a curtain so realistically that Zeuxis asked for it to be drawn aside.</note> that Parrhasius had painted over those grapes. I also recall that great marvel of the horse painted by the hand of Apelles <note>The most celebrated painter of antiquity (4th century BCE), court artist to Alexander the Great.</note>, to the confusion of some rival painters; as soon as living horses saw it, they began to neigh, snort, and stamp their feet as if inviting it to battle. This same Apelles painted that wonderful Alexander with a thunderbolt in his hand, which showed such great relief <term>relief: the illusion of three-dimensionality and physical presence on a flat surface</term>. In Rome in our own day, in Trastevere <note>A district of Rome known for its Renaissance villas and artistic heritage.</note>, one can see certain small children painted by Baldassarre of Siena <note>Baldassarre Peruzzi (1481–1536), a master of perspective and illusionistic painting.</note>;

<summary>Lomazzo begins Book Three by arguing that color, when combined with good design, creates a perfect imitation of nature (mimesis). He cites numerous classical and contemporary anecdotes of animals and humans being deceived by the lifelike quality of paintings.</summary>

...beds that seem to be made of stucco <note>Stucco is a type of plaster used for decoration; here, Lomazzo refers to painted objects that appear to have three-dimensional relief.</note>, such that they have sometimes deceived painters themselves. These examples, along with all the others one reads concerning the **power of coloring**, can easily be accepted as true, since even in modern times **Andrea Mantegna** <note>Andrea Mantegna (c. 1431–1506), a major Renaissance painter known for his mastery of perspective and anatomical detail.</note> deceived his master with a fly painted upon the eyebrow of a lion; and a certain other painter depicted a Parrot so naturally that it silenced the song of a real Parrot. The same occurred in a panel painted by **Cesare da Sesto** <note>Cesare da Sesto (1477–1523), a painter from Lombardy and a follower of Leonardo da Vinci.</note> of the **Baptism of Christ**, in which Bernazzano created the landscapes; he painted some birds upon the grass so naturally that, when the panel was placed outside in the sun, several birds flew around them, believing them to be alive and real. This panel is now found in the possession of Lord Prospero Visconti <note>A prominent Milanese nobleman and collector of the late 16th century.</note>, a Milanese knight adorned with fine letters.

But it is almost superfluous to go about collecting these minor wonders, as the **power of coloring** <term>power of coloring: translated from 'virtù del colorire,' referring to the specific skill and theoretical capacity of using color to create the illusion of life and depth</term> is a far greater marvel; for it represents the difference between every animal, whether it be of the earth, water, or air, and distinguishes the men of every region. Furthermore, in the same man, it shows the passions of the soul and almost the voice itself, displaying his complexions <note>In the Renaissance sense, 'complexions' referred to the balance of the body's humors, which dictated a person's temperament and health.</note> as if they were natural. Among the elements, it shows wicks, flames, waters, springs, clouds, lightning, and thunder; and stones—and in each of these are contained nearly all the virtues of coloring, which I shall remain silent upon in this place, concluding only this: that so great is the power of coloring that there is no corporeal thing created by God that cannot be represented by it as if it were real.

And this boast that can be given to painting in this regard, I judge to be one of the greatest and most illustrious that can be given to any art. Moreover, this art raises itself above the others and shines all the more because it works through the eyes, the principal sense, and represents beauty and all things according to how God ever created them. Nor does it only express things in figures as they are, but it also shows certain interior motions, almost painting and placing before the eyes the affections of the soul and their effects. From this, one infers that this art also benefits religion; since through it, one comes to represent not only the images of Saints and Angels, but even that of

### On the Necessity of Coloring. Chapter II.

**S**ince it is now time to color the design <term>disegno: a central concept in Italian art theory that encompasses both the physical act of drawing and the intellectual "design" or spark of an idea</term> of which we have treated until now, and to do so in the most perfect painting possible, we must treat in this book of colors and of their natural "friendships" and "enmities" <note>Lomazzo uses these terms to describe color harmony and contrast, as well as how certain pigments react chemically when mixed.</note>, both in their substance and their appearance. We shall also discuss their suitability, how they are mixed together, their proportions, and how they are necessary in all types of painting—and finally, which colors are appropriate for flesh tones. 

But in this treatise, I will not dwell on describing every color in detail, but only the principal ones. To do otherwise would create confusion, and would moreover be an endless task. Regarding the principal colors, I will touch upon their effects and their most important mixtures. I will omit—so as not to cause obscurity, and especially as it is not very relevant to our purpose—the parts of the world where all natural colors originate, or from what materials the artificial ones are made. 

And because the quantities of the mixtures cannot be fully grasped (since their number is infinite), I will mention only some of the main ones; for by the example of those, the others are governed. I will not, however, fail to warn that this part of painting [coloring] is nothing by itself without the help of the others. But if they are all joined together, they will show marvelous things, and demonstrate all the strength and—

design <term>disegno: both the physical act of drawing and the intellectual spark or "design" of an artistic idea</term> more perfectly expresses the intention of the talented painter; there, one does not find that confusion and dazzling glare of colors that is usually seen in the works of clumsy and ignorant painters.

But to arrive at the necessity of coloring (which is my primary purpose in this chapter), I say that without it, painting cannot be fulfilled nor receive its perfection; for it is coloring that perfectly expresses and gives, so to speak, the spirit to all things designed through the power of the other genres. And these things will acquire all the more grace and perfection the more excellently and with greater art they are colored. Thus, through the work and virtue of colors dispensed with good judgment in paintings, one will see—for example, in those faces drawn as grieving in the manner mentioned when we discussed the movements of the soul <term>moti: "movements" or "motions" of the soul; the Renaissance theory that internal emotions must be expressed through outward physical gestures and facial expressions</term>—eyes of a pale color; in the insane, a color completely devoid of red; in the wrathful, an inflamed color; in the tearful, eyes swollen with tears and red; in the sad and afflicted, a sallow color tending toward black. 

And so it is with herbs, flowers, plants, fruits, animals, stones, cloths, hair, and everything else—giving each its particular color drawn from nature, and also from the imagination, according to the things said and those that will be said about this. All the things of the world will be shown as if they were natural; expressing even the sun's rays, the stars, the night, the dawn, thunder, clouds, lightning, comets, the evening, the clear sky, rains, winds, and sea storms, with all the other things that must be brought to perfection according to the design already made by the painter, provided they are understood through what has been said and will be said of the other parts necessary to this art, from which is derived the knowledge of how to give lightness and darkness <note>The author is referring to the principles of light and shadow, often called *chiaroscuro*.</note> to colors.

->*What color is, and its species, and from where colors are caused.*<-

### Chapter III.

**C**olor, as Aristotle <note>Lomazzo relies on the Aristotelian tradition, which viewed color as a physical property of the "skin" or boundary of an object when acted upon by light.</note> says, is the extremity of a thing judged or visible in a bounded body, or rather it is a visible quality bounded at the extremity of an opaque body, which before it is illuminated is visible in potential, and by the benefit of light is seen in action. For color is caused by light in an opaque and dense body, with the primary qualities working together. There are seven species, or manners, of colors. Two are extremes, and like parents of all the others; and five are intermediate. The extremes are black and white; and the five intermediate are pale, red, purple, and green <note>The text here lists only four of the five intermediate colors; in the Aristotelian system used by Lomazzo, the fifth is typically blue (*azzurro*).</note>

<summary>Lomazzo argues that color provides the "spirit" and emotional truth to a drawing, enabling the painter to depict everything from human suffering to atmospheric phenomena. He then introduces the Aristotelian definition of color as a quality of light interacting with opaque bodies.</summary>
<keywords>coloring, disegno, moti, emotions, Aristotle, light, white, black, intermediate colors, art theory</keywords>

...green. Regarding the origin and generation of colors, coldness is the mother of whiteness, and a multitude of light concurs to produce it. Heat is the father of blackness, and it arises from a small quantity of light and a great amount of heat. Red is made from the mixture of white and black <note>This reflects the Aristotelian theory of color, which held that all colors were mixtures of light (white) and dark (black) in different proportions, rather than the modern primary color theory</note>. Violet, or pale color, is made of much white and a little red. Saffron—that is, yellow—is made of much red and a little white. Purple [purpureo] is made of much red and little black; and green from a little black and much red <note>original: "verde di poco nero è molto roffo." This unusual derivation of green from red and black is a specific hallmark of certain medieval and Renaissance natural philosophies</note>. And this shall perhaps suffice for the foundation and origin of colors. Now I will move on to treat their material substance.

### *What the materials are in which colors are found.*
### Chapter IV.

**A**mong the material colors that are generally used in these times, many are known, all of which have their own particular hues. First, those that make white are gypsum <term>gieffo: specifically "gesso," a sulfate of lime used for priming</term>, white lead <term>biaca: a highly toxic pigment made from lead carbonate, prized for its brightness</term>, "white," and crushed marble. There is also another thing that allows colors to remain "in fresco" <note>A technique where pigments are applied to wet lime plaster, becoming part of the wall itself</note> in the same way one paints when the lime is fresh: and this is one of the rare inventions found in the practice of the art—that is, finely crushed eggshells. One mixes all colors with this, more or less according to their needs; and this white, which cannot be "brushed away," when finely ground is good for coloring flesh perfectly in fresco.

The colors that make yellow are the "gialolino" <term>gialolino: lead-tin yellow, a staple of the Renaissance palette</term> from the furnaces of Flanders and Germany, dark orpiment <term>oropimento: a deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</term>, and ochre. Those that make "turchino" [deep blue] are the azures, such as ultramarine <term>oltramarino: the most expensive blue, made from ground lapis lazuli imported "from beyond the seas"</term>, "Hungarian" blue <note>likely azurite, a copper carbonate mineral</note>, and others; and also the smalts, like that of Flanders, which is the best of all. 

Those that make green are the various greens, "azures" <note>likely referring to malachite or blue-greens</note>, verdigris <term>verderame: a green pigment formed by the action of acetic acid on copper</term>, "verdetto" (which is called "Saint" [santo] but leans toward yellow), and also green earth and "Barilla green." 

"Morello" of iron and that of salt make a dark violet-purple [morello], and furthermore, there is calcined vitriol, sky-blue [cilestro], and dark indigo. Those that make red are the two cinnabars—namely, the mineral and the artificial <term>cenapri: vermilion (mercury sulfide), found naturally or synthesized</term>—and the red earth called "maiolica." 

Blood red is made by all the "lakes" <term>lacche: transparent pigments made by fixing organic dyes, like those from insects or plants, onto an inorganic base</term>; and orange [ranzato] is made by red lead [minio], and also "burnt orpiment," which is called gold color. And this is the alchemy of the Venetian painters <note>A reference to the famous "Colorito" of Venice, where artists like Titian used complex layering and experimental pigments to achieve glowing effects</note>. 

The dark shadow for flesh is made from "bell-earth" [terra di campana], from the earth of Umbria called "salzalo" <term>terra d'ombra: Umber, a natural brown earth pigment containing iron and manganese</term>, from burnt green earth, from asphaltum [spalto], from mummy <term>mumia: a pigment literally made from ground-up ancient Egyptian mummies, used for its transparent brown qualities</term>, and other similar things. Finally, those that make black are burnt oil, the shells...

...of coloring; which is called pastel, which is made with points composed particularly of powdered colors, of which all [colors] can be composed. This is done on paper, and was much used by Leonardo da Vinci, who made heads of Christ and the Apostles in this way—excellent and miraculous works on paper. ### Of the friendships and enmities of natural colors. Chapter VI.

Colors also have among themselves their own natural Friendships and enmities. Because of this, we see that if one takes a certain kind of color and mixes it with another, they both "die" together, so that no sign of either one is seen. And that this is true we find through experience: that gypsum <term>gesso: a mineral pigment made from calcium sulfate</term> is a friend to all colors, except for verdigris <term>verderame: a vibrant but reactive green pigment made by exposing copper to vinegar vapors</term>; white lead <term>biaca: lead carbonate, the primary white of the Renaissance</term> is similarly a friend to all, but is an enemy of "dry white" <note>original: "bianco secco," likely referring to Bianco di San Giovanni, a lime-based white used in fresco</note>. Dry white is only a friend to marble and yellows, except for that of Germany <note>likely lead-tin yellow, which was often sourced from German-speaking regions</note>. Orpiment <term>oro pimento: a bright yellow pigment made from arsenic trisulfide, notorious for reacting with other pigments</term> and calcined vitriol <note>vitriol heated until it changes color, often used to create reddish or violet tones</note> are friends to the blues, enamels <term>smalti: ground cobalt glass used as a blue pigment</term>, blue-greens, green earth, iron violet <note>morello di ferro</note>, Maiolica, *salzalo*, Campanian earth, charcoal, and scale black <note>nero di scaglia: black pigment made from the scales of oxidized metal</note>; but it is an enemy of grain <note>likely "grana," a red dye derived from insects</note> and others. Orpiment is an enemy of all colors, except for gypsum, ochre, blues, enamels, blue-greens, green earth, iron violet, indigo <term>endico: a deep blue plant dye</term>, maiolica, and lake <term>lacca: a transparent pigment made from organic dyes</term>. Ochre is a friend to all; the "little yellow" of Germany <note>gialolino di Lamagna: another name for lead-tin yellow</note> likewise to all except dry white. Orpiment and calcined [vitriol] are friends to the blues, and enamels are friends to all. Blue-green <note>likely malachite</note> is a friend to all, except for verdigris; verdigris is a friend to all except orpiment, gypsum, dry white, crushed marble, *barillo* green, cinnabar <term>cinabro: natural mercury sulfide, a bright red</term>, and minium <term>minio: red lead</term>. The "little green" <note>verdetto</note> is compatible with all, except for orpiment. Green earth is compatible with all, and likewise violet <note>morello</note>. Indigo is an enemy of dry white and a friend to all others; artificial cinnabar <note>vermilion</note> is an enemy of lime, verdigris, and orpiment. Maiolica and minium are friends to all, except that minium is an enemy of verdigris, dry white, orpiment, and the "little green." Umbers are friends to all, and likewise all blacks, except for burnt ivory <term>auolio arso: ivory black</term> and resin smoke <term>fumo di ragia: lampblack made from burning resin</term>, which are suited for oil colors. One finds...

### Which colors and mixtures one color makes with another.
### Chapter VII.

**R**egarding the mixing of colors, I will not expand on speaking about it distinctly in respect to all the different ways of working; instead, I will only reason about those that belong to working in oil. From this, one can then draw a rule for every other type of working, always composing the colors of the same hue according to the type of work—as in fresco, using "dry white" <term>bianco secco: a white pigment made from lime, used in fresco</term> instead of white lead used for oil. Nor will I dwell on treating the quantity that must go into the one and the other color being mixed; for that is nothing but confusion, as it can be known by the likeness of the mixtures taken from any thing when mixing them together. Practice immediately teaches this appearance, along with the quantity that must be added of each. However, it will be enough to only remind you which ones are used to make any color in the likeness of any natural thing.

And to begin, it is found that white lead <term>biacca: a primary white pigment made of lead carbonate</term> mixed with clay <note>original: "crea," likely referring to an earthy clay or light ochre</note> makes a faded color which is similar to straw; and when helped by giallolino <term>giallolino: a bright lead-based yellow pigment</term>, it makes the highlight of a blonde color, similar to buff <note>the color of undyed, sanded leather</note>. Mixed with blues, it makes a celestial color; and likewise with smalts <term>smalti: a blue pigment made from powdered cobalt glass</term>, though these are not entirely so similar. Mixed with verdigris <term>verde rame: a green pigment made from copper acetate</term>, it makes all the colors of plant leaves, such as Willow, olive, and similar dull shades; these can be made softer and more varied by adding a little bit of verdetto <term>verdetto: a secondary green pigment, usually a copper-based green or a mixture</term>.

The same white lead mixed with verdetto makes a yellow color, almost similar to giallolino, and in fresco it creates a very beautiful effect when mixed with "dry white"—which was an invention of Perino del Vaga <note>Perino del Vaga (1501–1547) was a prominent Italian Renaissance painter and a key member of Raphael's workshop</note>. In addition to this, white lead with iron violet <term>morel di ferro: a purplish-red pigment made from iron oxide</term> makes a color like agate. With indigo, it makes a sky-blue color, and also colors like sapphires, hyacinths, and turquoise, though not very vivid. With cinnabar <term>cinabrio: a bright red pigment made from mercury sulfide</term>, it makes the color of under-ripe strawberries; or with flesh-tone, like some roses. Mixed with *falzalo* <note>a specific type of dark earth pigment or umber</note> and other umber earths called "earth-color," it makes the color of tree bark, trunks, wood, stones, hair, and the like. And with black, it makes the color gray <note>original: "bigio"</note>, and smoke-color in the second degree.

The yellows <note>giallolini</note> mixed with blues and smalts make certain green colors which are used much in the distances of landscapes, and also in clothing. With indigo, they also make a green color, but not as vivid as with the blues, though it remains a more vivid green if...

Mixed with indigo is orpiment <term>oropimento: a bright yellow mineral pigment made of arsenic trisulfide</term>. These same *giallolini* <term>giallolino: a lead-tin yellow common in Renaissance painting</term> mixed with cinnabar <term>cinabro: a bright red pigment (mercuric sulfide), also known as vermilion</term> make the color of flame and of splendor. Blues and smalts <term>smalti: a blue pigment made of ground cobalt glass</term> mixed with *verdetto* <term>verdetto: a green pigment, likely a copper-based "green earth" or a mixture</term> make dark green; with lake <term>lacca: a transparent red pigment made from organic dyes</term> they make peacock-color <note>original: "pauonazzo," a deep purplish-blue</note>, or dark murrey <note>original: "morello," the color of a mulberry</note>; with *falzalo* <term>falzalo: likely "falsalo," a dull mixture used for shadows or underpainting</term> they are lost; and with blacks they darken and disappear. Verdigris <term>verderame: a green pigment made by exposing copper to vinegar vapors</term> with *verdetto* makes a more vivid green color that tends toward yellow; with indigo it makes a dark, faded color <note>original: "perso," a term for a very dark purple or bluish-black</note>, and with *falzalo* it is lost; with black it darkens. Indigo mixed with lake makes dark peacock-color; with black and lake it makes the color of iron, silver, mirrors, crystals, tin, and the like, especially if it is mixed with "balla black" <note>original: "nero di balla," likely a high-quality lampblack or charcoal</note>. And these blues produce the same effect as indigo. Cinnabar and lake make the color of ripe strawberries, roses, colored lips, blood-red rubies, and scarlet. And these same ones mixed with white make the color of the cheeks of a beautiful flesh tone, and also of light roses. Cinnabar also with black makes the color of burnt ochre. Lake and red lead <term>minio: a bright orange-red pigment made of lead tetroxide</term> make almost the color of cinnabar, and they sharpen the *falzalo* in the shadows of the flesh; and mixed with blue and white lead <term>biacca: the primary white pigment used in oil painting</term> they make the color of a dried rose, that is, purple. Blues or smalts, and also indigo mixed with lake and black, make the colors of black velvet; but mixed with a light color <note>original: "co'l chiaro," likely meaning white or a pale tint</note> they make the highlights of ash-gray velvet <note>original: "beretino," a bluish-gray color</note>; and thus they can make satins. Ochre with lake, cinnabar, and black make tan <note>original: "taneto," a brownish-orange or tawny hue</note>; but with a little white it is highlighted. And by putting *falzalo* in place of black, and burnt ochre in place of cinnabar and black, it is likewise highlighted; but without the *falzalo* it turns out more vivid and crimson. *Gialdolino* and cinnabar make an orange color, just as red lead does. Majolica ochre <note>original: "ocrea maiolica," a refined earth pigment</note> and black make the color of *falzalo*; and all these compositions are highlighted and pulled into different appearances while they are mixed more or less with white lead. From this we see that in various mixtures made for distant landscapes, such as mountains and trees, white lead is mixed with *verdetto* and combined with blues. Lake mixed with blues makes the color of violets and pansies <note>original: "perfetti amori"</note>, and it also makes dark murrey, especially in the minute folds of satins; this is also achieved with lake mixed with indigo. Verdigris mixed with *verdetto* represents green plains and emeralds, as well as cloths of similar colors; and mixed with dark colors it highlights and makes diamonds, mirrors, arms, and the like shine. Similarly, it highlights all bodies of whatever color desired according to their degree of light. Mixed with black, *falzalo*, lake, and indigo, it makes light ash-gray; with *falzalo* and black it makes a brownish-grey <note>original: "fariccio"</note>; with ochre and majolica it makes the peaks of mountains...

## On the harmony that exists between light and dark colors.
### Chapter VII.

**I**t is a necessary thing for the painter to understand and have perfect knowledge of the harmony <note>original: "conuenienza," referring to how colors suit or correspond to one another</note> that all colors have among themselves in creating light and shadow for one another. This is so that if he makes a cloth of whatever color he wishes, all the colors—both light and dark—have a single harmony and concordance, without seeing red shadows in yellow cloth, or purple <note>original: "morelle," the color of a mulberry</note> or red shadows in white ones, or other colors which do not correspond to them in any part. It has therefore been observed with good reason that white has no concordance with any color other than black; nor can it be shaded by anything else, as they are both extremes of colors. *Gialdolino* cannot be shaded more suitably than by ochre <term>ocrea: an earthy pigment ranging from yellow to reddish-brown</term>, and the same for orpiment <term>oropimento: a bright yellow mineral pigment made of arsenic trisulfide</term>. But the yellow of Germany <note>likely "German yellow," a variant of lead-tin yellow or a synthetic yellow</note>, being more faded than it is, must be shaded with a more faded ochre. Blues and smalts <term>smalti: a blue pigment made of ground cobalt glass</term> shade that cerulean and sky-blue color caused by them and white together. Verdigris <term>verderame: a green pigment made by exposing copper to vinegar vapors</term> also shades that mixture made of itself and white. *Verdetto* <term>verdetto: a green pigment, likely a copper-based earth</term>, "iron murrey" <term>morello di ferro: a deep purple or brownish-red pigment made from iron oxide</term>, and "salt murrey" <note>likely a chemically produced dark purple pigment</note>, and indigo also shade their own mixtures; and so do cinnabar and *maiolica* <term>maiolica: here referring to a specific red pigment or glaze color, not ceramic pottery</term>. Lake <term>lacca: a transparent red pigment made from organic dyes</term> shades red lead <term>minio: a bright orange-red lead pigment</term> when mixed with *maiolica*; it also shades its own mixture with white. *Maiolica* shades burnt orpiment; and the other colors and mixtures mentioned in the preceding chapter are shaded by the colors from which they are created. But in the second degree, true ochre, which shades light yellow, can also be shaded by burnt ochre and by "foul" lake <note>original: "lacca brutta," likely a lower quality, darker, or more opaque batch of red lake used for deep shadows</note>. Burnt and faded ochre is shaded by *salsalo* <term>salsalo: a dull, dark mixture used for deep shadows; spelled "falzalo" on the previous page</term> mixed with burnt ochre, or *maiolica*, or lake. Blues and smalts are shaded by indigo, and also by black and lake together. Verdigris by black, and also by indigo. *Verdetto* by *salsalo*; iron and salt murrey by black; cinnabar by lake, and also by burnt ochre, or by itself mixed with black. In the third degree, black and lake shade true yellow; because the faded yellow is shaded by black,

## On transparent colors, and how they are used. Chapter IX.

**B**ecause there are some transparent colors, such as red lake, verdigris <term>verderame: a green pigment made from acetic acid on copper</term>, and *verdetto* <term>verdetto: a bright green pigment, often a variety of copper green</term>, which are the colors most lacking in "body" <note>original: "priui di corpo," meaning they lack opacity and are translucent</note> that can be used; it is required here that the method of using them be discussed. Now, when working in oil, these colors are used to represent—as if they were real—all clear transparent bodies, such as carbuncles <note>original: "carbonchi," a term for deep red gemstones like garnets or rubies</note>, rubies, and the like. For these, after they are sketched out with imitation mixtures so they look like solid bodies without the shine of transparency and its liveliness, pure, clean, and beautiful red lake is applied over them. This comes to represent in them, most naturally, the highlights and also the darkness without obscuring them in any part, so that they appear covered by a shiny, fiery glass just like real and natural ones. And this cannot be done when working in fresco, although one might give the light or shadow of transparency through the power of drawing. In the same way, verdigris and *verdetto* enliven and represent the temperament of emeralds and similar transparent materials. These same colors are also used to give luster and vividness to satin and *ormesino* <term>ormesino: a thin, lightweight silk fabric, often with a wavy or shot appearance</term> altered from their natural colors over the underpaintings. This practice has advanced so far that, without any regard for the precepts of art and attending only to "prettiness" <note>original: "vaghezza," referring to a pleasing, often decorative visual quality</note>, it is used not only in the fabrics named above but even in cloths of contrasting folds which do not require that transparency or the vividness of silk. And nowadays one cannot represent any cloth of a pure mixture—similar to wool or linen—without wanting to veil it with transparent colors to give it luster. Hence, one can say that the art of painting, as far as coloring is concerned, is corrupted; especially because this "prettiness" in figures is esteemed so much that no painting, however good it may be, can be seen to please without it. And therefore, it is greatly observed by many, so...

...as fathers of the beauty of colors, of whom I named the most famous and excellent at the end of the first book; and not without honor in this book I speak of the Flemish <note>original: "Fiamenghi"</note>, of whose work I have seen certain oil paintings made recently in the house of the noble antiquarian Giulio Calistano. In these, one sees how much they avoid these beauties of transparency; one does not see in all those figures anything but pure mixtures <note>The author is referring to opaque pigments mixed on the palette rather than translucent glazes</note> that represent the truth. And in truth, they are wonderful to see; and those painters who made them deserve no small praise: Gillis Mostaert, Pieter Bruegel, Jacob Grimmer, Frans Floris, and Maerten van Heemskerck.

But leaving this aside, one should still take an example from nature, and see if in nature there are these varieties and superstitions of affected beauty <note>original: "vaghezza," referring here to an over-reliance on pleasing but unrealistic color effects</note>, which is seen in many excellent works by those who have followed it with every study—though sometimes they also omitted it so as not to confuse the drawing with it. This is clearly seen in the coloring of the aforementioned painters, the true fathers of painting, who were great enemies of this "corruption" of the art. It is truly a corruption because, besides the fact that the strength of the art is not shown, a very great error is also committed in using it many times against all decorum: for it has been used not only for the Saints, but for Christ himself and the Queen of Heaven, representing in them highlights and lasciviousness of dress and clothing that were never used by them.

But to return to the subject: there are also other transparent colors, which are used over the underpainting <note>original: "abbozzature"</note> to give luster to those things that require it. For this, one uses asphalt <term>asphalto: a brownish-black bitumen used as a transparent glaze for deep shadows or hair</term> to give shine to blonde and chestnut hair; and likewise the finest *falzalo* <term>falzalo: a mixed pigment often used for shading or transition tones</term> mixed with lake pigment. All these things were commonly used by Leonardo, Raphael, Cesare da Sesto, Andrea del Sarto, and many others who were delicate and of a sweet and suave manner; as were also Antonio da Correggio, Titian, Gaudenzio, and Boccaccino, who was truly a very great colorist and sharp in drawing, as seen in his works made in Cremona, his homeland, and in other places—especially in velvet, brocade, and damask, blending different colors as they pleased.

...on purpose, but only so that they are used in the place where they are required, such as in the bright clothes given to the nymphs of the meadows, of the springs, and the like; and also to certain angels whose clothes reflect light no differently than the bow of Iris <note>Referring to the rainbow</note>. Now this is the greatest delight and pleasure that can be offered to viewers with colors; and it is called the way of making <term>cangianti</term>—that is, a single silk cloth that has one color in the highlights and another in the shadows. Through this diversity, one gives the supreme and ultimate charm and grace to the painting. Because a certain order is required to achieve this and bring it to perfect delight, I will provide some general rules from which all the methods of making them can be derived, based on three grades. Now, in the first of these, white alone is introduced for the highlights; in the second, <term>giallolini</term> <note>Lead-tin yellows or other light yellow pigments</note> and mixtures particularly of white with all colors of that brightness are used; and in the third, all colors that are shaded by the second-to-last dark, and even by black, create the highlight. Therefore, in the first grade, the following order will be kept. First, the white can be shaded with pale blue, yellowish, cerulean, pale green, light mixed green, light agate color, light celestial blue <note>original: "Cilestro"</note>, flesh-tone, violet color, light purple, light <term>taneto</term> <note>A brownish-red or tawny color</note>, gray, flame color, and light <term>beretino</term> <note>An ash-gray or grayish-blue</note>.

In the second grade, these light colors and light mixtures are shaded in this way when one wishes to give them charm. This will serve as the second shadow for the <term>cangianti</term> raised with white, accompanying the first shadow: for the pale blue, the shadow is made by <term>ocrea</term> <note>Ocher</note>, agate color, celestial blue, purple, dark gray, <term>taneto</term>, dark rose color, violet, azure, <term>smalto</term> <note>Smalt, a blue pigment made from cobalt glass</note>, green, mixed green, <term>beretino</term>, <term>cinnabar</term> <note>A bright red mineral pigment</note>, <term>Maiolica</term> <note>A color likely resembling the tin-glaze of pottery</note>, and <term>minium</term> <note>Red lead</note>. And so they also provide shadow to all the other colors that follow in the second order.

In the third grade, these pure colors and mixtures are shaded as follows: for the agate color, one uses burnt ocher, <term>perso</term> <note>A very dark color, often described as a mix of purple and black</note>, <term>pauonazzo</term> <note>A deep violet or peacock-purple</note>, <term>taneto</term>, iron-dark <note>original: "morello di ferro"</note>, and salt-dark <note>original: "morello di sale"</note>, indigo, <term>lacca</term> <note>Lake pigment, usually a translucent red derived from insects or plants</note>, <term>falſalo</term> <note>An obscure pigment term, likely a dark earthy mixture</note>, celestial blue, and so follow all the others one by one in every way. Similarly, black shades all of these, just as white highlights them all—especially those that have a conformity with it—in the same way that black likewise shadows those that have an agreement with it. Furthermore, we can understand that of the <term>cangianti</term> varied by these orders raised with white, and of those shaded by black, about three thousand five hundred eighty-four types can be made in the first grade; and from the first mixtures, half that many are derived, that is, one thousand seven...
