...one hundred and ninety-two, which belong to the second grade; and of the highlights of pure but light colors and mixtures of the same darkness, there are one hundred and twenty-eight types that belong to the third grade. These are followed by those eight dark colors, and after them, black. These are only the most common ones, because, as I have said, others can still be made; such as taking the light mixture—or <term>gialdolino</term> <note>A light lead-tin yellow</note>—beneath the white, and using those mixtures with some of the eight dark colors to create a shadow from which a very great variety would result. This would involve partially leaving aside the light middle colors, such as azure, light green, and <term>cinaprio</term> <note>Cinnabar or vermilion</note>. Even with these pure colors, mixing them with black would generate a very great variety, albeit a melancholy one; this would introduce certain blends into the transitions that one could not even imagine—just as some of those other <term>cangianti</term> <note>Iridescent or "shot" colors where the highlight and shadow are different hues</note> shifting from color to color would amount to more than one hundred thousand variations, drawn from six or four between one and the other.

And these are the ways by which the vain world—entirely intent on appearance and seeking the delight of colors through the eyes—leaves behind the true substance of art. This substance has nothing to do with these mixtures and confusion of colors; nonetheless, many have taken delight in them and earned honor for themselves by knowing how to apply them to <term>disegno</term> <note>Design or drawing; the structural foundation of art</note>. They did this in such a way that one color did not compete with another except in its primary charm or vividness—such as green against red, or yellow against <term>turchino</term> <note>A deep turquoise or dark blue</note>—but always accompanied by different mixtures and intermediaries in the manner that can be learned from what I have said above.

However, it has been seen that the <term>cangianti</term> of the second and third orders, being grave and full of majesty, were used by **Raphael**, who shaded dark pink with <term>morello</term> <note>A dark mulberry or violet color</note>; in short, he used all colors with those that have familiarity and suitability with them, according to the method of the more serious iridescent effects. From this rule, held by such a wise and judicious painter, those who do not know how to harmonize the colors of drapery may recognize their error—not without shame. Such painters leap from one extreme to another, such as from the first to the third grade, mixing and confusing them without any intermediary that might accord and couple them together with grace and charm. 

Now, whoever desires, with these given tips, to become expert in the knowledge of <term>cangianti</term>, should look at all the works of **Gaudenzio** <note>Gaudenzio Ferrari, a prolific Northern Italian Renaissance painter</note>, the leader of all painters in this regard; specifically the angels painted under the <term>tiburio</term> <note>The crossing tower or dome structure</note> of **Santa Maria di Saronno**, and here in Milan in **Santa Maria delle Grazie** in the **Chapel of the Holy Crown**; where angels are seen...

## On the effects caused by colors. Chapter 11.

**B**ecause all colors have a certain quality that differs among them, they cause different effects in whoever looks at them; this is generated by an internal enmity between them, according to the doctrine of **Aristotle**. Of this I shall make some mention, which will serve as a basis for what is to be said further on; for it will make us know the reason why one color does not suit another, yet will sit well with a different one, and other such details that will be touched upon later. Now, to begin, we find that black, shiny, earthy, leaden, and dark colors generate in the soul through the eyes a quality that is nothing other than sadness, slowness, pensiveness, melancholy, and the like. Blackish, green, sapphire-colored, somewhat red or dark colors, and the color of gold mixed with silver—that is, <term>flavo</term> <note>A golden-yellow or blonde color.</note>—yield sweetness and joy. Red, burning, fiery, or flame-like colors, violets, purples, and the color of glowing iron and of blood cause spirit, sharpness in looking, and almost induce ferocity and boldness, awakening the mind through the eye no differently than fire. The colors of gold, yellows, and light, more shiny purples make a man intent in his looking, and render grace and sweetness. Rose-colored, light green, and somewhat yellow colors render pleasantness, happiness, delight, and sweetness. The color white generates a certain simple attention, almost more melancholy than otherwise. Finally, all the colors mixed and diverse among themselves give charm—

## On the color black. Chapter XII.

**T**he Athenians were accustomed, whenever some misfortune befell them, to dress in a dark color, and the Romans represented their sorrow and their sadness with similar garments, so much so that one reads that even for the death of a fish that he kept as a pet, Crassus <note>Marcus Licinius Crassus (c. 115–53 BCE), a Roman general and politician famously said to have wept for a pet moray eel.</note> once dressed in mourning brown. Wherefore, as Marcus Tullius [Cicero] relates in the letters written to Atticus, those who wished to go to cheerful banquets in such mourning attire were severely rebuked. Plato writes in the *Timaeus* that the women of Dannia <note>Possibly a reference to the Danaids of mythology or a contemporary misunderstanding of a geographical group.</note> continually dressed in black, and people called them infamous. The Lycians likewise wore a woman’s garment of black during their times of trouble, so that they might put it aside as soon as possible out of shame, as Valerius writes <note>Valerius Maximus, a Roman author of historical anecdotes.</note>; and that attire was not very different from that which is still used in our times by some when their relatives die, which is commonly called <term>gramaglia</term> <note>A traditional term for heavy black mourning clothes or "widow’s weeds."</note>. In many places in the Holy Bible, black demonstrates and is a symbol of unhappiness. Aristobulus said that all the Egyptians appeared mad because he saw them dressed in black; and therefore some wish for black to be a sign of fury and of madness; because, as the Physicians <note>Natural philosophers or doctors of the time who followed the theory of the four humors.</note> affirm, the mad and furious are moved and overcome by black bile <note>original: "cholera nera," the humor associated with melancholy and, in excess, madness.</note>. Virgil writes in the third book of the *Aeneid* that black lambs were sacrificed to storms as bringers of sadness and death. Terence says that the black dog is an omen of the worst kind. Black victims were sacrificed to the infernal Gods. The Persians dressed their jesters and madmen in black so that they would be avoided. After the destruction of their homeland, the women of the Cimbri were all found dressed in black. Pythagoras used to say that black belongs to the nature of evil; and Ovid holds it so in his curses, as do Horace, Marcus Tullius, and Apuleius in his writings on magic. Alecto <note>One of the Furies (Erinyes) of Greek and Roman mythology.</note> and the other infernal Furies were represented as black, according to Virgil in the

## On the color white. Chapter XIII.

**W**hite color, because it is easy to receive every mixture, signifies simplicity, purity, and even high status <note>original: "altezza," implying nobility or elevated spiritual standing.</note> as some say. Writing about this in the Sixth <note>Referring to Book VI of the *Aeneid*.</note>, Virgil dresses chaste priests, good poets, men of talent, and defenders of the fatherland in it. Therefore Persius says that the "white man" is interpreted as good and pure. Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome, known for his piety.</note>, who was born with a white beard, and Titus Tarquinius were good Kings. Among the twelve royal insignias of the ancient Romans, the chair, being pure, was of white and polished ivory. Aristander <note>Aristander of Telmessos, Alexander the Great's most influential seer.</note>, as was well-suited to a pure and chaste priest, dressed in a white mantle to offer prayers to the Gods during that greatest preparation that Alexander made against Darius.

Wishing to show their purity and brightness toward their husbands, Greek widows—as Plutarch attests, citing Isocrates—used to dress in washed white cloths. Likewise, ancient Roman matrons would place a white band on their heads to similarly denote their simplicity. The ancient Egyptians used to wrap their dead (as some others also used to do, according to what Suetonius writes of Nero) in white mantles, showing thereby that the body was reduced to the end of life, being deprived of the soul; and this custom was common with many other peoples, as is gathered in many places from Servius, Virgil, and Ovid. And everyone knows that the Hebrews used to bury the dead in this way, since one also reads in the Holy Scriptures that Christ was buried thus. In the sacrifices of Ceres <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture; white symbolized the purity of the grain and the goddess.</note>, the priests dressed in white habits. And in garments white as snow, the angels appeared over the tomb of Christ as a demonstration of joy, and Saint Luke, dressed in white, appeared to Saint Mary of Tripoli. Faith, because it is pure—as Horace, among others, gracefully says in one of his songs written to Fortune—is called white-veiled and shining. The crowns of the ancients...

There are also some who say that white denotes blame, because the Jews dressed Christ in this color to cause Him greater blame and scorn; and it is customary to put a white staff in the hands of fools and those who are disgraced, which is why those same Jews gave the white reed into the hand of Christ. And from this, Livy, in his ninth book, mentions an army of Samnites <note>An ancient italic people who fought several wars against the early Roman Republic.</note> which was decorated with a white line to show that it was an army of new soldiers, that is, without any glory. For the same reason, the slaves who were sold by the ancient Italians came into public with white feet as a sign that they were not their own masters. Others have maintained that white is a sign of joy; because the Athenians, during the solemnities of the five-event contests <note>term: "quinquertio" (pentathlon), the five classical athletic events: discus, javelin, jump, running, and wrestling.</note>, as Lucian writes in his philosophical praises, all dressed in pure white, nor could anyone be present at the spectacles in any other color. Thus our Catholic Church, after the Resurrection of Christ, dresses entirely in white in triumph; and the Angels, first after the Resurrection, showed themselves in very white garments as a sign of joy. Christ Himself, likewise, when He wished to show and give a sign of bliss...

Among certain peoples of the ancients, white was held to be a most somber color—vile and of no esteem. Because of this, as Vegetius <note>Publius Flavius Vegetius Renatus, a writer of the later Roman Empire known for his treatise on military matters.</note> writes, new and inexperienced soldiers dressed in white, which is why they were called candidates <note>original: "candidati"; from the Latin "candidus" (bright white), referring to the unblemished state of a novice’s record or shield.</note>; this was a sign that they had not yet honorably stained their hands with the blood of the enemy. ### On the color red. Cap. XIV.

**R**ed, which denotes vengeance, was also used among the ancients to cover the biers in which those who had fought bravely were placed, as one reads in Homer and Virgil. Following this example, we painters use red to dress—or at least provide a mantle to—those who died for the faith of Christ, as a sign of their martyrdom and shed blood. In the Campus Martius in Rome, those who sought <margin>I</margin> magisterial offices <note>The "magistrati" or high-ranking government officials of the Roman Republic.</note> dressed themselves in transparent red veils to demonstrate their undaunted spirit in the actions of war for the fatherland, so that their wounds could be seen more easily. Thus, through such demonstrations of courage, they obtained the dignities and honors they sought. The ancient Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note> dressed their **Recruits** <note>original: "Tironi," meaning novice soldiers or trainees.</note> in this color, as Plutarch relates, when they sent them into the field; this was so they would not lose heart upon seeing their own shed blood <note>The red clothing would mask the blood of their wounds, preventing panic.</note>. The Trojans used to wear red surcoats and garments. Homer, in the third book of the *Iliad*, has Paris wear red plumes upon his helmet; a custom which the Romans also followed to appear more horrible and terrifying to their enemies. But the captains wore a garment of velvet or crimson satin over their armor, and likewise, the standard that was carried when the Emperor was personally present in the field was of a purple color with gold fringes—this purple being a color little different from red. Triumphant captains were dressed in this same color when they went to the Capitoline Hill, as Plutarch writes in the *Life of Paulus Aemilius* <note>Lucius Aemilius Paullus, the Roman general who conquered Macedon.</note>.

### On the Peacock-blue Color. Cap. XV.

**T**he dark-purple <term>morello</term> <note>A color ranging from dark violet to mulberry.</note> or peacock-blue <term>pauonazzo</term> <note>While literally "peacock-colored," in Renaissance color theory and ecclesiastical use, this refers to a deep violet or purple.</note>—which truly signifies what has been said elsewhere—according to some others denotes contempt for death for the sake of love. They say it shows a certain mad spiritedness because of the lake-red color <note>A crimson pigment made from organic dyes, often associated with blood.</note> of blood mixed with the color blue. From these is composed a middle color between Jupiter and Saturn; the first of these, through Mars, shows spiritedness and madness, and the other, through its dark mixture, a certain kind of consideration, though an obstinate one, in which by remaining madly, one is eventually led to the end. But if this were true, without doubt the Bishops and other prelates would not dress in it at certain times as a sign of the greatest love they bear for the holy Church, and of the desire they hold to serve and expand it; nor would the Cardinals and the Popes themselves use peacock-purple mantles at certain determined times, as they do. Thus one clearly understands that the meaning attributed by these people to this color is false and absurd.

## On the color yellow. Chapter XVI.

Because yellow denotes the certain hope of enjoyment, it has caused some to assign it the meaning of desire and joy. It was held by the ancients as an omen of the highest order, as is shown by the woodpecker bird <note>original: "pico vcello"</note> mentioned by *Martial*, which has most of its feathers of this color; from this, people used to draw greater hope than from all other things. Because of this color, the *Athenians* called the dawn "hope." Because *Charon* <note>The ferryman of the underworld in Greek mythology.</note> renews himself from day to day despite being old, he was assigned sails of yellow and the color of gold, as *Homer* says. Newly married Roman women used a veil as an ornament for their heads called the *flammeum* <note>original: "Flamineo"; a bright saffron-yellow veil worn by Roman brides to signify the endurance of marriage.</note>, as one reads in the first book of *Virgil*, which was of this color to show the hope they had of bearing children. Among some, yellow also signifies lordship or sovereignty, because of the primary place that gold holds—being of this color—among all other metals. Hence the robes, scepters, and crowns of Emperors and kings are adorned with this color or metal; and likewise the mitres, pastoral thrones, hangings, light-colored vestments, copes, and similar items of the *Most Holy Father* <note>The Pope.</note> are adorned and embroidered with gold. Finally, the Church Militant <note>The Christian Church on earth, viewed as struggling against sin and evil.</note>, the bride of our Savior, clothes herself in a garment of fine and precious gold, as taken from *David* in the *Psalms* where he says that the *Queen* stood at the right hand in garments of gold <note>original: "Regina... in veſtimenta d'oro"; a reference to Psalm 45:9.</note>; and as a sign of Justice, the thrones and chairs of Popes and Emperors are made of gold, by which it is given to be understood that they must sit and govern justly.

## On the color green. Chapter XVII.

I do not wish to omit the reasons why some, on the contrary, hold that green—which denotes hope—also signifies the end of things. For in any case, even if this were not true, the painter will nevertheless derive no small utility from such reasons, which contain many things pertaining to the knowledge of ancient rites and religions. Now, considering first the ancient custom of the Priests to offer upon the altar of God lighted torches fixed into green wood; once these were entirely burned, finally nothing remained but that green wood in which they were fixed. This custom has passed in part down to our own days, since wax tapers <note>original: "doppieri di cera"</note> are often decorated at the bottom with the color green. *Virgil*

in confirmation of this opinion, over the tomb of **Polydorus** <note>In Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Polydorus was a Trojan prince whose grave was marked by miraculous plants.</note> he places green veils; and bringing **Andromache** to sacrifice to the shade of **Hector** her husband, he has her cover the tomb with green bushes; and in another place he says that **Juturna**, having foreseen the death of her brother **Turnus**, wrapped her head in a green headband. The ancients, as a sign that time brings an end to every created thing, bound their heads with a green band; and it is found written that the graves of the ancients were adorned with green **celery** <note>original: "appio"; this refers to smallage or wild celery, which was used in ancient Greek funeral garlands and the Nemean Games.</note>, and with this the winning poets were crowned when singing in competition over the dead. **Vitruvius** also demonstrates that the invention of the **Corinthian capital** came into use from decorating the dead with green herbs and flowers. It is also found that in the tomb of **Tullia**, the daughter of **Cicero**, an emerald was recovered which is said to have once been in the hands of **Isabella Gonzaga d'Este**, Marchioness of Mantua; which gives us an argument that it is true that the ancient Persians also used emeralds at the death of their wives; and that they betrothed them with these, and with these placed them in the tomb. **Pliny**, in the fifth chapter of the twenty-seventh book <note>The author likely refers to Book 37 of Pliny’s *Natural History*, where emeralds and the tomb of King Hermias are discussed.</note>, also reasons about this custom of burying and adorning graves with the color green, and of placing emeralds there, in the passage where he speaks of the tomb of **King Hermias**. And finally, according to **Servius**, the ancient chaste matrons covered their carriages with the color green. But to these reasons, many more could be brought to the contrary, and prove that properly green signifies nothing other than hope; but as this is such a subtle investigation into the meanings of colors and little pertaining to our purpose, we shall leave it aside.

### On the color turquoise. Chapter XVIII.

**T**urquoise, or let us say azure, besides its other significations, denotes elevation of mind, and also faith and zeal, as the French say. It was used by the **Virgin Mary** in her garments even until the very Passion and death of her son. Much of the **Apostles** used it likewise. And **Christ** himself is painted with a mantle of this color. Thus is **God the Father** represented, because azure is the most conforming to the heavens of all other colors. **Saint Gregory** wished and ordered that the Priests called **Crutched Friars** <note>original: "Frati Crosachieri"; a mendicant order also known as the *Crociferi*, who were associated with the symbol of the cross and, according to this text, blue vestments.</note> should clothe themselves in garments of such a color. And **Isis**, the most ancient Goddess among the Egyptians, as **Plato** writes, had her Priests wear turquoise garments and ornaments; so that when the people looked upon them, they might raise their minds to Heaven, awakened by this color.

### *Of some other colors. Cap. XIX.* ###

**I**t was the custom of the ancient Kings of Troy to dress themselves in the colors of the days as they passed; and the principal barons of the kingdom and knights of war used, on the first day of January, to adorn their shields with the color of that day on which they were to come to battle. Therefore, on the day of the Sun <note>Sunday</note> they dressed in the color of gold; on the day of the Moon <note>Monday</note> in the color of silver; that of Mars <note>Tuesday</note> in the color red; that of Mercury <note>Wednesday</note> in the color blue; that of Jupiter <note>Thursday</note> in the color green; that of Venus <note>Friday</note> in the color purple; and that of Saturn <note>Saturday</note> in the color black. These same ancients, in the solemn festivals of each month, had distinct garments and ornaments of specific colors based on the ceremonies they performed in them. In the month of January, they dressed in white; in February, in ash-gray <note>original: "bertino"</note>; in March, in tawny <note>original: "taneto," a brownish-orange</note>; in April, dark green; in May, light green; in June, flesh-colored <note>original: "incarnato"</note>. In July, red. In August, yellow. In September, blue. In October, violet. In November, purple. And in December, black. The Agagri of Syria have the custom of dyeing their faces various colors; and among them, those who have best designed the colors of both their hair and their flesh are held as most noble. # BOOK FOUR
## ON LIGHTS,
### BY GIOVANNI PAOLO LOMAZZO
#### MILANESE PAINTER.

-> On the power of light. Chapter I. <-

**L**ights in painting possess such force and virtue that I judge that in them consists all grace when they are well understood; and, on the contrary, disgrace when they are not understood. We see a clear experience of this in a well-drawn body, which, even without lights, succeeds very well in its existence and demonstrates its excellence. If it then happens that it is lit <note>original: "allumato," referring here to the technical application of light and shadow</note> without reason and art, such that shadows are placed confusedly where lights are required; and conversely, lights are placed where the middle-tones of shadows should go, and also in the concavities and high surfaces without order and imitation of nature, it is reduced to such a state that it would be better if it were neither drawn nor lit. 

Where, however, when it is well lit, not only is perfection added to the drawing, but it makes the figure stand out from the plane or ground, no differently than if it were a <term>relief</term> <note>original: "rilievo," the sculptural effect of three-dimensionality on a flat surface</note>. In this force and virtue consists principally the supreme excellence of the painter; for it is his own specific role to make fictional figures appear as raised through the impact of lights as those of the sculptor are raised in reality because of their material, which (as we all know) has top and bottom, right and left, front and back. For this reason, we are accustomed to say that within the marble is that thing which the sculptor imagines making, and then goes about carving and forming, whether well or poorly. 

Now, returning to the subject of lights, I say further that although they have the power I have already mentioned to take away the virtue from a drawing <note>i.e., bad lighting can ruin good drawing</note>, their own virtue cannot be taken from them by the drawing. Thus, we see that when perfect and proportionate lights are spread over a body, even one that is poorly drawn and without muscles, it provides greater delight to the viewers, exciting in them a certain desire to see also in that body the muscles and its other necessary parts; as in the paintings of Bernardo <note>Likely referring to Bernardo Luini (c. 1480–1532), a North Italian painter known for his Leonardo-inspired use of soft light and shadow</note>

<summary>This page introduces Book Four, arguing that light is the most critical element in painting for creating the illusion of three-dimensional relief. Lomazzo asserts that while bad lighting can ruin a good drawing, masterful lighting can make even a poorly drawn figure pleasing to the eye.</summary>

[Ber]nardino Zenale of Treviglio <note>Bernardino Zenale (c. 1460–1526) was a prominent Milanese painter and architect who worked at the same time as Leonardo da Vinci.</note>, such as the beautiful *Resurrection of Christ* painted in the convent of the Church of [Santa Maria delle] Grazie in Milan above a door, and many other of his colored narrative scenes and <term>chiaroscuro</term> <note>The use of strong contrasts between light and dark to give the illusion of volume.</note> works in the same place. In these, one sees figures which, to represent their swiftness, are made without emphasis on muscles and are not overly detailed, as they should be; yet they are well-placed and artfully arranged with lights on the outer surfaces so that they appear in <term>relief</term>; such force and vigor do they possess in themselves. Thus, one observes marvelous <term>foreshortenings</term> <note>original: "scorzi," the technique of depicting an object or figure in a picture in depth.</note> there, all of which are the effect of the regulated arrangement of light, without which those drawings would lose much and remain largely without grace, even if they were well-positioned. 

Thus, we also see that many painters, though entirely lacking the art of drawing, are considered talented simply through a certain practical skill in placing lights in their proper places. This praise, however, should not reasonably be granted to them because they possess neither the art of perspective—through which colors or actions might be seen in their works, rather than just pigments and certain primary lights—nor do they truly represent the nature of light.

Now, as an example of the true art of excellently arranging light, we may use—instead of all others—that panel by Leonardo [da] Vinci (besides many other of his highlighted drawings) which is in San Francesco in Milan where the *Conception of the Madonna* <note>The "Virgin of the Rocks," commissioned for the Church of San Francesco Grande in Milan.</note> is painted. In this regard—not to mention his other excellences—it is most wonderful and truly singular. 

Regarding the excellence of light, no less marvelous are two paintings by the hand of Antonio da Correggio, which are found in this city in the possession of the Knight Leone Aretino <note>Leone Leoni (c. 1509–1590), a famous sculptor and collector based in Milan.</note>. In one of these is painted the beautiful Io with Jupiter upon a cloud, and in the other Danae, with Jupiter raining into her lap in the form of golden rain, accompanied by Cupid and other cupids <note>original: "amori," small winged figures associated with the god of love.</note>. In these, the lights are so well understood that I hold for certain that no other painter in coloring and highlighting <note>original: "allumare," the technical application of light to create form.</note> can equal him. These were sent from Spain by Pompeo, his [Leoni's] son, a sculptor. 

In the matter of light, Michelangelo and Raphael—the fathers and masters of painting—were likewise excellent and divine; in whose school one can well say that nearly all the excellent painters of Italy have become talented and famous. 

Since, therefore, light is of such virtue and value, one must attend to it with every study and industry to gain perfect knowledge and art of it, and accompany it with drawing in the manner I have described. For the art of proportion, placement, and foreshortening can serve little and bring little praise to the painter without the knowledge of these same lights, discovered through reason and art, and not merely derived by...

### Of the Necessity of Light. Chapter II.

**U**ntil now, the entire work has been drawn, given motion, and colored without lights; it is like a body without light, which cannot be understood to be round or square except through the intellect—that is, through the internal knowledge one has of it. But it cannot be understood externally, as the external light is hidden from it. This external light, corresponding to the internal, makes the diversity of bodies known by means of the rays of the eyes and visible to the intellect—acting like two suns—based on how those bodies receive the light according to their nature. 

Therefore, I will proceed by discussing these lights; I do not say shadows, though they are treated together. For shadows follow as a necessary consequence of lights, being caused by the withdrawal <note>original: "sfugimenti," referring to the areas where light fails to reach.</note> of those lights. They take on more strength the more the light strikes a body. From this arises that great <term>relief</term> <note>The illusion of three-dimensional volume on a flat surface.</note> and elevation from the natural plane in the body that receives light according to its nature. 

And from this, it will also be understood how, as bodies are different, different lights, reflections, and the refraction of these lights are generated by their nature, diversifying them in the manner that will be described. In this, one will come to see almost the ultimate goal of art. For without this, neither order, nor forms, nor proportions, nor motions, nor compositions—and finally, figures—cannot reach their perfection. They would be like a body without a place to stand, or without spirit; or like stars made of glass, without the light of the sun which, according to their quality, makes them shine and appear to our eyes. 

But to begin what I have promised, I will first discuss what light is; and afterward, with the help of <term>physiology</term> <note>In the Renaissance context, this refers to the study of natural philosophy and the physical properties of the world.</note> and <term>optics</term> <note>The first part of perspective, dealing with the geometry of how light travels.</note>—the first part of perspective—I will treat primary and secondary lights in general, as well as direct and reflected light; and how, by <term>mathematical reasons</term> <note>original: "ragioni mathematice"</note>, many lights are seen...

### What Light Is. Chapter III.

**T**his word "light" <note>original: "lume"</note> is used in diverse ways and meanings. First, and principally, it signifies the image of the divine mind, which is the Son of God and His unique splendor—whom the <term>Platonists</term> <note>Followers of the philosophy of Plato, who often emphasized the spiritual and symbolic nature of light.</note> called the image of the divine mind. It also signifies the fervor of the Holy Spirit. It is taken as a divine power diffused among creatures: in rational beings, it is His divine grace; and in all creatures together, it is the preserving and defending power, such as that which—according to <term>Dionysius</term> <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher who wrote extensively on the celestial hierarchy and the nature of God as light.</note>—belongs to the <term>Seraphim</term> <note>The highest order of angels, whose name is associated with burning heat or light.</note>. In the Angels, it specifically becomes intelligence and a certain joy exceeding all our thought, though received differently according to the nature of the intellect that receives it; and within that intellect, as <term>Marsilio Ficino</term> <note>An influential Italian scholar and priest (1433–1499) who led the revival of Neoplatonism in the Renaissance.</note> says in his commentary on Plato, it is reflected. 

Descending then to celestial things, where it becomes an abundance of life, it is an effective propagation; and in fire, it is a visible splendor, a certain vigor, and an <term>accident</term> <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that a thing has, but which is not essential to its basic nature (e.g., a rose is still a rose whether it is in the light or the dark).</note> arising from its nature. Finally, in men, it is taken for the light of the <term>active intellect</term> <note>In Aristotelian thought, the part of the mind that actively processes sensory information to form abstract concepts.</note>, which illuminates the passive or potential intellect; and in short, for a clear discourse of reason and a knowledge of divine things. 

Lastly, it is taken as a quality emitted by the Sun or by fire which reveals color. And this light is—as the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, often focusing on physical and empirical explanations of the world.</note> maintain—the cause or formal reason by which colored things are seen. Its <term>species</term> <note>The visual "likenesses" or "forms" of objects that travel through the air to the eye.</note>, or images, pass to the imagination and specifically illuminate the eyes, in which an image is formed that first passes to the <term>common sense</term> <note>The internal faculty that gathers data from all five senses.</note>, then to the imagination, and finally to the intellect. This same light diffuses and extends over the bodies it encounters, in which color is revealed along with a radiant beauty—as the Platonists say of opaque bodies—caused by this light together with a certain beneficial and generative power. 

But where the rays do not reach and are scattered—while the rays contract in the eyes—there remains a misty, dark color <note>original: "color caliginoso"</note> which afflicts and torments the soul. Thus, all things according to their capacity feel the vigor of light, which, joining to itself all created things with its life-giving heat and penetrating everywhere, carries their qualities and virtues through all things. For this reason, those skilled in the art <note>Lomazzo refers here to painters and theorists who understand the "science" of light.</note> use a single method to give light to everything; for it is further seen that the

<summary>Lomazzo defines light through a hierarchical ladder, ranging from the "Divine Mind" and the Holy Spirit down to physical sunlight and the cognitive processes of the human eye. This synthesis explains light as both a spiritual force of grace and a physical mechanism that reveals color and form.</summary>

...that the Sun, when it is risen above our horizon and hemisphere, illuminates the whole in an instant without time. And the reason is because light has no contrary that can impede it with its action. Therefore, it performs its operation in a moment within the air. To this purpose belongs what the philosophers say of the darkness of night: that it is not caused by any black or dusky color that tints the air, but only by the hiding <note>original: "occultatione"</note> of the Sun, which—with its clarity and presence, and without resistance—illuminates with equal light all the air of our hemisphere. It would also illuminate the whole earth in the same way, and all bodies composed of earth, if the earth and all those bodies were lucid and transparent like the air. 

But when bodies are opaque, thick, and corporeal, they do not receive light with all its clarity, except in that part which is directly opposite the sun. And therefore, in this hemisphere of ours, when the Sun does not pass perpendicularly and directly over the <term>Zenith</term> <note>The point in the sky directly above an observer's head.</note> of our head, the earth can never remain illuminated without there being a shadow on some side. This does not happen in the land situated beneath the <term>equinoctial line</term> <note>The Equator.</note>, where at midday the Sun illuminates the earth and its inhabitants in such a way that it illustrates the entire circumference of round bodies, and no shadow is seen, even at the feet. 

Wherefore, among those knowledgeable in this art <note>The art of painting.</note>, it is forbidden to give light to all bodies in the same manner. But beyond this reason, which is considered in respect to the illuminating light, the earth, and the illuminated terrestrial bodies, there is another more powerful one drawn from the inner depths of Mathematics, namely from the visual lines of <term>perspective</term> together with the eye. 

<margin>I</margin>
For the understanding of this, it must be noted that in order for one to see, three things must concur: the visual lines, the colored body, and the visible power that resides in the eye. The illuminated visual lines, which are the proper subject matter of perspective, come to our eye in a **pyramidal figure** <note>Also known as the "cone of vision"; a fundamental concept in Renaissance art where the eye acts as the point of a pyramid and the object being viewed acts as the base.</note>. The base of this pyramid resides in the thing that is to be seen, and the cone or angle of the pyramid is that which comes to our eye, becoming more obtuse and large. And for this reason, we see the visible thing more clearly and more distinctly. 

But if the visible thing is distant and far away, the cone or angle of the pyramid comes to our eye more acute and small; thus the eye cannot see the thing as clearly as it otherwise would. Secondly, it must be observed that visible things and the objects themselves do not enter our eye, but rather the <term>visible species</term> <note>In Renaissance science, "species" were the formal images or likenesses of objects that were thought to be transmitted through a medium (like air) to the sense of sight.</note> spread themselves through the clarity as far as...

And if the visible object or colored body stands near, this image comes to our eye in the same quantity and size as the angle of the <term>pyramid</term> <note>The "visual pyramid" or "cone" was a standard concept in Euclidean optics, where the eye is the point (apex) and the object is the base.</note>. But when the colored body and object stand far away, that image comes to the eye in the same quantity as the cone or angle of the pyramid, which is too <term>acute</term> <note>An angle less than 90 degrees; here meaning "narrow."</note> and small. Therefore, it does not fill the eye and wavers, and cannot be seen clearly and distinctly. Regarding the third point, I have nothing else to say except that the <term>visible power</term> <note>The faculty of sight.</note> is brought from <term>potentiality to actuality</term> <note>A concept from Aristotelian philosophy: the eye has the *potential* to see, but it only *actually* sees when light and an image "inform" it.</note>, and is <term>informed</term> <note>The process of the eye receiving the "form" of the object.</note> when the other two requirements we mentioned occur together—namely, the visual or illuminated lines (which are the reason without which the eye cannot see) and the image of the colored body that informs the eye and brings it from potentiality to actuality. With a large image, it informs more and performs its operation better, and the visible object is seen more clearly and distinctly; but with the small image of an object that is too distant, the eye cannot be so well informed, and for this reason, it cannot see the visible object clearly and distinctly. 

From all this doctrine thus declared, two reasons are derived why the same body being painted cannot be <term>illuminated</term> <note>original: "allumare"; to provide with light or highlights.</note> equally in all its parts. The first is because light does not illuminate with all its clarity and strength except for the part that faces it and is opposite to it; but it cannot illuminate the others so perfectly because of the nature of the <term>opaque</term> body—earthy and thick—which blocks the rays so they cannot penetrate inside and produce their effect perfectly. 

The second reason is taken from the perspective of our eye. Because just as the first part of the body being seen—standing closest to the eye—comes to it with a more obtuse and large angle, so it is seen more clearly and distinctly, also being more illuminated. But the second part of the body, because it is further away and recedes, comes to the eye with a smaller angle. It is less illuminated, and therefore cannot be seen as clearly as the first; and for the same reason, the third part remains darker, and the fourth even more than the third, and so on proportionately until the eye can see no more. And if you ask me, when the painter wants to paint two or...

...three or four men, one of whom stands behind the other, and all are illuminated with equal brightness—how should one proceed? I respond, following the doctrine given above, that even though they are equally illuminated, it is nonetheless necessary to paint the second one, who stands further from the eye, more <term>dimmed</term> <note>original: "abbarbagliato"; in this context, it refers to the loss of clarity and sharpness due to atmospheric perspective and the narrowing of the visual angle.</note> in its brightness, and the third more than that, and the fourth much more so, until the last one where nothing more can be seen. The reason is because the second, by standing further away, comes to the eye with a more <term>acute</term> <note>narrow</note> angle, and therefore cannot be seen as clearly as the first; the same reasoning applies to the third and so on to infinity. This same principle is understood even when viewed from the side. And for this reason, all the painters who have observed this doctrine have become excellent and reached the summit of this art, such as **Leonardo da Vinci**, and many others named above in various places, along with **Jacopo Tintoretto**, **Marco da Siena**, **Federico Barocci of Urbino**, **Paolo Caliari** of **Verona** <note>Better known today as Paolo Veronese.</note>, **Luca Cambiaso**, the **Bassani**, and **Ambrogio Figino**. And all this doctrine that I have gathered in the present chapter is drawn for the most part from **Aristotle**, from **Alhazen** <note>An influential 11th-century Arab mathematician and physicist known as the "father of modern optics."</note>, from **Witelo** <note>A 13th-century Polish friar and philosopher whose work on optics was a standard text.</note>, and from **St. Thomas Aquinas**; and to conclude, from the most excellent Philosophers and Theologians. Their opinion still pleases me, even though I may have said something else in another place; but I said it there while reporting the opinions of others.

### Division of Light. Chapter IV.

**L**ight, then, is a quality without a body <note>An incorporeal quality; light was often debated as being neither purely material nor purely spiritual.</note>; for as **Marsilio Ficino** <note>A famous Neoplatonist philosopher of the Italian Renaissance.</note> says, in an instant it fills half the world from east to west and penetrates every part of the body of the air without <term>offense</term> <note>original: "offensione"; meaning resistance or obstruction.</note>, and that of the water with little offense and resistance. Furthermore, when spreading itself over putrid things, it is not stained—conditions which do not suit the nature of a physical body. For a body moves not in an instant, but through time; and one body does not penetrate another without the dissipation of one or the other, or both; and two bodies capable of being mixed together corrupt each other with mutual contagion. This light is divided mainly into primary and secondary. <term>Primary light</term> is understood as that which strikes that part of the colored body standing opposite the luminous body, touching it with straight lines. The <term>luminous body</term> is the name for that which possesses light and brightness, such as the **Sun**, **fire**, and the like. That which then arises around this primary light is called <term>secondary light</term>. But light is also divided in another way of great importance, drawn from physiology...

...the first part of general perspective; and this is the principal branch of **optics** <note>In the Renaissance, "optics" (or *perspectiva communis*) was the scientific study of how light travels and how the eye perceives it, distinct from "linear perspective."</note> among the various types of perspective. Its general effect consists of investigating the principles, causes, and elements of all visibility, along with its parts, types, and essential differences, always considered in a general sense. Because of this, it is divided into three parts based on how it considers visibility. This is because light itself is secondarily divided into three parts: **direct**, **reflected**, and **refracted** <note>original: "ritratto"; in this context of optics, it refers to light that is "bent" or refracted when passing through different mediums like water or glass.</note>. Since these will be treated individually in their proper place, it will suffice for now to have said this much concerning the first and second divisions.

### **On Primary Light. Chap. V.**

**P**rimary light is that which strikes and is received on the part of a colored body that is opposite the luminous body <note>The "luminous body" is the source of light, such as the sun or a candle.</note>. It touches gently and moves across bodies in a natural order—that is, without any obstruction or extreme contrast, as other types of light do. This is observed in "histories" <note>Narrative or historical paintings.</note> that are depicted in the open air, where the light introduces itself without any hindrance and is made to appear as it does on building facades facing the East. This light, when traveling into rooms and other places, touches the upper parts of all the bodies within the space where it enters; and there the light ends. For this reason, it will sometimes happen that a body will be struck by this light from the middle downward, or a little more or less; and also from above, depending on how the light enters differently in relation to the shape or position of the balcony, round window, or standard window. 

From this, one must be careful when depicting open balconies or doors to ensure in the paintings that the light travels inside. This was done previously by <term>Francesco Mazzolino</term> <note>Better known today as **Parmigianino** (1503–1540), a famous Italian Mannerist painter known for his elongated forms and sophisticated lighting.</note> in a small painting of the Madonna. In it, he created two light sources: one that illuminated the Madonna and the Child directly, and the other for a <term>Carthusian monk</term> <note>A member of a cloistered religious order founded by St. Bruno.</note> whom he had painted above a door, which entered through that very door; so that the lights were opposite one another. This example can suffice for everything that can be said regarding this light.

**T**he second primary light is understood to be that which is produced not by the clear air or the Sun, but equally by day and by night by various apparitions of Angels and the like; as in the divine...

## Of the third primary light. Chap. VII.

**T**his third light is that which is born from fires, lamps, torches, furnaces, and the like, showing a certain quantity of light to people according to the strength of the fire. This is just as **Titian** <note>Tiziano Vecelli (c. 1488–1576), the leading painter of the Venetian school.</note> showed it around the grate where **Saint Lawrence** was burning <note>Refers to Titian’s "Martyrdom of Saint Lawrence," famous for its complex lighting effects from fires and the heavens.</note>. However, this light cannot be as powerful as the second light, which is called divine. This light distributes its rays and expansions according to its own strength, now more on one side, now on another, depending on how the flame flares up and swirls, as one sees in fires. It also depends on the matter that burns; just as the fuel can be diverse, so too will the flame be diverse, and consequently, the light will appear stronger or weaker to the eye. For we clearly see that from a small wick, the same light cannot emerge as that which comes from a very large torch. 

And although these lights by day cause a certain color in bodies that conforms to them, they do not, however, take away the first <term>primary light</term> <note>The author uses "primary light" to describe a direct source of illumination, in this case, the sun or daylight.</note>; because of this, one sometimes ends up creating two lights on a single figure: one of which verges toward the celestial <note>Daylight or sky-light.</note>, and the other toward the fire. All these lights strike bodies forcefully, in such a way that they hardly let anything else be discerned except for that part which is directly illuminated, or illuminated by the strength of reflections opposite the light. This occurs in metals and other lustrous and clear bodies. 

Therefore, one must be very careful in showing these lights, whether it is by day or by night, because of the aforementioned effects; and also to represent at night, in all colors, a certain shadow that is almost uniform. Where a certain "rebirth" of color occurs, it should be in the same manner that the **Sun** acts by day everywhere it touches, although at its setting it renders things somewhat red—something that also happens with these artificial lights, where redness appears more frequently. Therefore, in order to know how to dispense this light, everyone will need to read history to know if the fires occur by day or by night, their quantity, and if they are under the open sky or inside dwellings or wherever they may be. For it is found that fires were used differently by **Abel** in the first sacrifices, and afterward by **Noah** when he had come out of the ark to sacrifice lambs, just as **Jacob** also did on his journey with his people; and likewise, fire was used in another manner by **Aaron** upon the altar...

...before the golden calf, and similarly that which he did afterwards for God upon the altar constructed with such art; upon which Nadab and Abihu, placing profane fire in their censers, were burned by that very fire <note>In the Book of Leviticus, Nadab and Abihu were sons of Aaron who offered "unauthorized fire" before God and were consumed by fire from the heavens.</note>. And likewise, in the various mysteries of **Christ**, this primary light should be represented as a night scene—such as when He is captured and brought before **Herod, Annas, and Pilate**; and when He is scourged, crowned with thorns, and mocked. In these scenes, however, almost everyone tends to place the lights as if it were day. Among the pagans, we see this in the fire where **Hercules** dies, the house of **Lycaon** that burns, the fire of the daughters of **Hymen**, the brand of **Meleager** <note>Meleager’s life was tied to a piece of wood (a brand); when his mother burned it, he died.</note>, and finally the fires of **Memnon**, **Prometheus**, and **Troy**. 

These examples, I believe, are sufficient to demonstrate with what care one must apply lights—whether by night or by day—to all things according to their effects. One must always look to <margin>I</margin> the <term>narrative</term> <note>Italian: *historia*; the subject matter or story being depicted.</note>, which places before our eyes how the entire painting must be, and informs us of how things actually were. For this reason, it would not be fitting to represent **Scipio Africanus** (who routed the Carthaginian army by setting fire to their camp) with lit fire as if it were day; nor similarly the defeat the great **Patriarch** <note>Abraham, who rescued his nephew Lot by a night attack on the four kings.</note> dealt to the kings who led **Lot** away prisoner. For these are all events that occurred at night.

## *On Secondary Light. Chapter VIII.*

**F**rom the first, second, and third light <note>The author refers to the three primary sources of light discussed earlier: divine, natural (the sun), and artificial (fire).</note>, in every way secondary light is born. This is understood, first of all, as that light which is caused not by direct rays but by reflected ones. It arises all around from the primary light that enters, for example, into a room, a gallery, a portico, or a similar place. For we see that when the primary light enters therein and strikes one part, it spreads another light all around. This is precisely what we call secondary light, which always follows the primary light. It can never be as clear as the primary light from which it derives and proceeds; therefore, it continues illuminating the more distant parts, eventually ending in the extreme shadows, especially at night.

## *On Direct Light. Chapter IX.*

**I**t is concluded with physiological reasons <term>physiological reasons</term> <note>In the context of the Renaissance and Early Modern periods, "physiology" referred to the study of the laws of nature and the physical world, rather than just the human body.</note> suited to the natural world, that the first direct light—the first of the three types placed in the second division of lights—is nothing other than that which extends and spreads with primary power directly upon any body, in such a way that it finishes by terminating there. This light never extends sideways or in similar ways, but always travels in a straight line. It appears all the more lucid the denser the bodies it finds, as will be discussed elsewhere. It cannot strike any but the surfaces opposite to it, and it illuminates the most prominent parts best, as they are closest <term>proximate</term> to it. But what the power of this light may be will be stated elsewhere.

## *On Reflected Light. Chapter X.*

**R**eflected light is that which arises from the termination of direct light. It becomes more lucid the denser the body is where the direct light touches; it does not pass further through, nor does it return toward the direct source. It illuminates all the bodies it strikes, and especially the rear parts of those already illuminated from the front by the direct light—those parts which are facing it. That is to say, it faces the body where the direct light ends and the reflected light begins; this constitutes the entire boundary where reflected lights extend.

### *On Refracted Light. Chapter XI.*

The final light of the second division is determined by natural philosophers <term>physiologicals</term> <note>The author uses the term "physiologists" to refer to those who study the physical laws of nature.</note> to be that which is generated from direct light when it strikes mirrors, crystals, water, weapons, and other similar shining things that are suited to generate this light. It is that multitude of rays that these objects scatter around upon being touched by direct light—especially if it is sunlight during the day, although the same occurs at night when generated by the Moon, or by some lighted torch or large candle. Nor is it necessary for me to dwell longer upon this; for in short, the whole matter reduces to this: that refraction <term>refraction</term> <note>original: "rifrattione". In this period, "refraction" was often used broadly to describe any "breaking" or bending of light, including what we now distinguish as reflection from a mirror.</note> is nothing other than that breaking of itself which direct light performs within these bodies, scattering light all around, as is seen in clear and limpid water toward the bottom, and also on its surface toward our eyes.

### *In what way all bodies receive light, whether a little or a lot. Chapter XII.*

Since we have so far discussed what light is, how many species it is divided into, and have treated each of them in both the first and second divisions, it follows that we should more minutely investigate its effects on bodies according to their composition and disposition. First, in this place, let us consider in what manner all bodies receive this light, whether a little or a lot. From this arise the diversities seen on the surfaces of bodies, which sometimes seem to go against the rules of art. As the principal elements are the foundation of all corporeal things and of all "elemented" things <note>Things made of the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note> in this lower world, they are composed not by mere gathering or joining together, but by transmutation and union. These elements are transmutable into one another and are mixed together to a greater or lesser degree, rather than being simple or pure. Therefore, starting with them, it is a clear and observed thing that wherever they are found to be more subtle <note>In Renaissance science, "subtle" means thin, rare, or refined, as opposed to "gross" or "dense."</note>, the light that strikes them is seen to be less apparent and more purified; conversely, the light is clearer and larger where the elements are more gross and opaque. And therefore, as the elements are found in all things of each of the three orders, it is seen that in these lower things they are gross and drossy; in the celestial things they are more pure and clean; but in the supra-celestial <note>The "supra-celestial" realm refers to the highest spiritual or divine heavens beyond the physical stars.</note>...

...they are, as the **Platonists** <note>Followers of Plato who believed that physical objects are imperfect copies of ideal, celestial forms.</note> say, full of life, and totally perfect and blessed; whereas in this lower world forms are gross and very large and material, in Heaven they exist according to their own qualities, in a celestial manner, and are more excellent than those found below the Moon in the third order. For there, one finds the celestial firmness of the **earth** without the heaviness of water, and the agility of the **air** without its restless movements. There is the heat of **fire** which does not burn, but rather shines and vivifies everything with its warmth. 

Because of this, among the stars, **Mars** and the **Sun** possess the symbol of and correspond to the element of fire, as the light in them is more powerful and resplendent. **Jupiter** and **Venus** correspond to the air, as their light is somewhat less intense—that is, tending less toward yellow. **Saturn**, who is held by many to have a similarity to **water**, is symbolized by the **earth** by those who live beneath his circle, as his light lacks that solar radiance and tends toward a faded and dark yellow. **Mercury** and the **Moon**, which are held by some to have sympathy with the earth, are of the nature of **water**, because in them the light becomes clear, but dull, and verging toward white. 

The same consideration and theory applied to the lights and celestial bodies is also applied to the <term>triplicities</term> <note>In astrology, a triplicity is a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element.</note> of the celestial signs. And thus the beginning of **fire** is given to **Aries**, the middle to **Leo**, and the end to **Sagittarius**. **Taurus** obtains the beginning of the **earth**, **Virgo** the middle, and **Capricorn** the end. The beginning of the **Air** is ruled by **Gemini**, the middle by **Libra**, and the end by **Aquarius**. The beginning of **water** is assigned to the **Crab** <note>Cancer</note>, the middle to **Scorpio**, and the end to the **Fish** <note>Pisces</note>. From this mixture and sympathy of planets, signs, and elements, all bodies are composed. 

In Heaven, the light of the sun is rare and resplendent; whereby we see the stars, in the manner of a mirror, receive the light of the placed sun; therefore in the midst of them it is like the light and spirit of all the planets. But here among us, it is not as clear and pure as in Heaven, nor as gross and burning as in **Hell**. 

Then, in the **intellectual world**, the elements of the first order—among the **Angels** and blessed intelligences—are considered in this form: that is, that essential stability and power correspond to the **earth**, since they are the firm seat and fortitude of **God**. Clemency and piety correspond to **water**, because of the power they have for purification and cleansing. And thus the **Psalmist** called them, where speaking of Heaven he says, "You who rule the waters and the things superior to them" <note>original: "Tu che reggi le acque e le coſe ſuperiori à loro." ...where the Psalmist says, *You who make your Angels spirits, and your ministers a burning fire.* <note>original: "Tu che fai i tuoi Angeli spiriti, e i tuoi ministri fuoco ardēte" — a reference to Psalm 104:4.</note> From this, theologians—having regard for the offices and the natures of the angels—have determined that the **Seraphim**, the **Virtues**, and the **Powers**, being as they are inflamed by supernatural fire, correspond to **fire**; the **Cherubim** and the **Angels** correspond to the **earth**; the **Thrones** and **Archangels** to **water**; and the **Dominions** and **Principalities** to the **air**. <note>The author is categorizing the nine choirs of angels according to the four classical elements to help artists understand their "material" nature.</note>

Therefore, in giving light to those **glories** <note>In art, a "glory" is the representation of heavenly light, often appearing as a luminous cloud or halo surrounding divine figures.</note> that we painters often create, it is necessary to show the light as almost transparent, penetrating their forms; this is because they reflect the light by which they are illuminated within that divine glory. 

However, because many painters are accustomed to not wanting to paint **God the Father** except when veiled by certain transparent lights—so that His form remains dazzled and obscured—I would say instead that He ought to be made, as our exemplar and like a mirror, with perfect, clear colors. This shows that the perfection of all things exists within Him, as He is their first cause. And so, it seems required to make His light as brilliant as possible, but in such a way that it does not appear to be taken from anything other than Himself. His light, from its own splendor and beauty, first illuminates and shares itself with **Heaven**; and finally, it shines in these lower realms, reflecting as if in three mirrors, according to what the **Platonists** <note>Followers of Plato who taught that light and beauty emanate from a single source (The One) and are reflected down through different levels of reality.</note> say. 

This also conforms with the **Holy Scriptures**, which one must imitate and observe regarding such paintings; for paintings are read by the eyes in a certain way, just as the scriptures are heard through words. Hence, one reads of God in the sacred pages: *the earth shall open and bring forth a Savior*; <note>Isaiah 45:8.</note> and of Him as a **Fountain of living water** that purifies all things; and elsewhere as the **Spirit** who breathes the breath of life; and **Moses** and **Paul** both testify that He is a *consuming fire*. <note>Deuteronomy 4:24 and Hebrews 12:29.</note> 

Thus, in such works, this order shall be observed: 
1. Give the **first light** to God, 
2. The **second** to the Angels, 
3. The **third** to the Heavens, 
4. The **fourth** to us, 
5. And the **fifth** to Hell. 

In all these, consider the bodies that are fit to receive light more or less; thus one will see that in **God** is the source of light; in the **Angels**, reflections; in the **Heaven**, splendor; among **us**, radiance; and in **Hell**, something like the matter and dregs of light, to which all the thickness and dross of things are relegated. And this is the entire foundation of the art concerning this faculty of light, regarding the matter of both imagined and visible bodies.

## *On the effects that light produces in bodies in general.*
### Chapter XIII.

**S**ince it is clear from what has just been said that all bodies naturally possess light and radiance according to their own quality and location—just as the angels do in the **Empyrean Heaven** <note>The highest heaven, believed in ancient and medieval cosmology to be the dwelling place of God and the angels.</note> near God; the stars in the **eighth Heaven** <note>The Sphere of the Fixed Stars in the Ptolemaic system, located above the planetary spheres.</note> near the Sun; humans near the solar rays and the rays of fire; and finally in hell, near the true and proper flame which is a coarse matter of light, deprived of its **charity** <note>In this context, "charity" refers to the divine love or grace usually associated with light; the fire of hell was often described by theologians as a "dark fire" that burns but provides no spiritual illumination.</note>—it is fitting that we treat the effects that light produces when it strikes any body in its being. For it is seen through the senses that light appears so much more resplendent and clear to us (speaking always by way of example) the more it finds, as I said above, denser bodies to receive it. Therefore, we shall go on to discuss in detail the effects that this light produces in each body, starting with those that tend toward the nature of the heavy and opaque earth among the other elements.

## *On the effects that light produces in terrestrial bodies.*
### Chapter XIV.

**F**irstly, then, because the earth does not generate stone—as **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on natural philosophy and medicine were foundational in the West.</note> writes—on account of its dryness, since it lacks the moisture of water that condenses and hardens it together, that part which is pure (such as dust, sand, and dead earth) receives light in such a way that it cannot be very clear or sharp compared to the light that strikes stones. Thus, we see that while light generates reflections when it strikes the earth, it generates them to a much greater degree in stones, according to their greater hardness and density. This is accompanied by a reflection in the extreme parts <note>The edges or boundaries of the object.</note> caused by the reflection of the part struck by the light; for light returns to all things more intensely the less "earthy" the object is. Therefore, we shall say that if one places a piece of marble or another bright object struck by light opposite a part of the earth that appears dull and produces little reflection, that marble will make the earth appear bright in a uniform way—taking almost as much brightness from behind via reflection as it takes from the front from the light source itself. This can be achieved in all other things when they are aided by a body more ready to receive clear and shining light, such as silver is compared to lead,

...and to their copper. This is the certain rule of the effects caused by light through the nature and composition of the bodies that receive it. And to show that this is true, I wish to give the clearest example of it, and the most appropriate and fitting that can be imagined in the whole art of painting; through which one will come to know a certain corruption in painting, which truly, being an enemy to the truth, must be avoided. It has been avoided by <term>Leonardo da Vinci</term> <note>The famous High Renaissance polymath (1452–1519) known for his soft "sfumato" lighting.</note>, <term>Raphael</term>, and the other good painters; even though <term>Vincenzo Foppa</term>, <term>Bramante</term>, and many others were excellent in it—their works bear witness to this.

Now, because of the diversity between flesh and plaster, we clearly see different lights and reflections being received in them. Because flesh is soft, when it is struck by light, it creates a soft and sweet shadow within itself without much reflection, and it is accompanied in such a way that it is not jarring. Thus, when standing a little distance away, one sees that flesh as round and soft without harsh shadow; this is especially true when the flesh is softer, as in youths and children. Conversely, the light and shadow remain cruder when it is less soft—that is, when it tends toward the old and the rough. 

But even so, it will not be as much as in a body of plaster or marble, even if shaped like flesh. Plaster, being the opposite of flesh, has a luster and whiteness; receiving the light into itself, it remains sharper, with certain reflections so crude and apparent that they do not allow the object to appear round like flesh. Instead, as one limb clashes with another because of the lights, they create a visual discordance <note>original: "strepito," literally "noise" or "uproar," here referring to a lack of visual harmony</note>, and all the more so the whiter the body is. 

Many painters, not considering such differences, have portrayed youths alongside such figures of plaster and marble. Using those crude, fierce, and sharp lights, they have maintained such a manner of lighting; which truly, as it is caused by such bodies, should only be expected when imitating such bodies. But these painters, extending this even further without consideration for figures meant to be flesh, use that same quality of light. Because of this, they cannot represent them as life-like, even though <gloss>even though</gloss> they may be very well understood in their <term>disegno</term> <note>A fundamental Italian art concept meaning both the physical drawing and the intellectual design or "concept" behind a work.</note>. ### Concerning the effects that light produces in watery bodies. Chapter XV.

**S**ince the material of precious and fine stones is transparent, or more or less so—like those which we are commonly accustomed to call gems—it is necessary that they receive the sharpest light, in such a way that it has the power to pass through them and carry its virtue with it. This is seen in the Sun, which, striking the stone called the <term>iris</term> <note>original: "iride"; a type of crystal or quartz, named after the goddess of the rainbow, known for its prismatic effects.</note>, has the power to make us see the celestial arc [the rainbow] through it; so that in every way the light, passing through the stones, carries with it the same color that the stone holds, in the same way that the color of wine or water does in a glass vessel upon the surface where it rests. This proceeds from no other cause than this: namely, because light in itself has no color at all, because it proceeds from the Sun, which if it had color would be <term>corruptible</term> <note>In Renaissance natural philosophy, pure light was considered a perfect, celestial substance; "color" was viewed as a modification or "corruption" of that purity caused by material objects.</note>. But even though light has no color, it nevertheless has this property and virtue that it reveals and demonstrates colors where they are. And thus when the light passes through green glass it discovers the green color and demonstrates it to the eye, making it seem as if the light and the rays are green. And so continuing, one can bring as an example when the light passes through a carafe full of red wine. But returning to where we left off, light in such <term>diaphanous</term> <note>transparent or translucent</note> and transparent bodies sparkles and appears all the more the more it finds the body itself constricted and condensed. Therefore we see it sharper and clearer in the diamond than in crystal, and in the latter more than in glass, and more than in ice. And what has been said of the diamond as an example must be understood generally of all other stones. In metals as well, because they are of hard material, one must consider how much force the light can have according to their responsiveness. And we must know that they have three colors, more or less intense according to their purity; the first is common and splendid in flashing like a light that was incorporeal...

Therefore, the shining and flashing in metals commonly occurs from the subtle watery element and from the dry and hard terrestrial element condensed within them. Consequently, of every metal, that which holds the subtlest watery part mixed with the pure and dense earthy part will be the cleanest, most splendid, and polished. For, on the contrary, one sees that in an unpolished metal one part casts a shadow over another, hindering the splendor to some degree. For this reason, gold shines more than any other metal; after it, silver; and iron likewise, when it is polished, is as resplendent as a mirror.

The cause of this splendor, in which images are received according to the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle, who sought to explain physical phenomena through his philosophical framework.</note>, is the terminated and polished surface. But all these images and counter-lights or reflections must be of less clarity than the primary light that the armor has taken from the Sun, or from another primary brilliance; for representing them otherwise is the mark of a common painter, ignorant of the true order and path of <term>perspective</term>. But returning to where I first made a digression, the light that strikes the water, the more purified it is...

### On the effects that light produces in aerial bodies.

->Chapter XVI.<-

**I** do not doubt at all that when the air is naturally purified and clean, one cannot see in it any quality of <term>striking light</term> <note>original: "percussioni del lume"; the physical impact of light rays hitting a medium.</note> except for a flat and continuous light, according to its nature; but I judge that the more it thickens with vapors, such as those of water or fire, it can for that reason receive light. This appears in that matter which comes out of the blowholes on the forehead of certain Northern sea monsters called <term>Physeters</term> <note>original: "Phifiterise"; likely referring to the sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus) or other large whales known for their spout.</note>, and many others more clearly in the field of the air itself within the clouds, which now more and now less appear to us lit up like <term>cotton wool</term> <note>original: "bambagia"; raw cotton. A common Renaissance metaphor for the texture of clouds.</note>. So much so that one can discern within them various forms of animals, shown in relief with their appropriate highlights, according to how much they expand or contract—a thing that is seen in nature. Thus, then, air condensed by moisture receives light less the further it is from that moisture; and we see that when moisture superabounds in the air, no light is discerned, even though the light passes through and puts its natural virtue into action according to the contrast. And this happens when there is so much moisture that no sunbeam can be discerned in the air. This is entirely the opposite of what happens when the Sun strikes the shadows nearest to it at its setting, and also at its rising. For it strikes them so vigorously that it almost makes them appear of its own color, that is, yellow, and toward evening in the most intense red, which tends toward condensed fire on the opposite side from the dry air, in a way that it re-

### *On the effects that light produces in fiery bodies. Chapter XVII.*

**I**n fire as well, there is a certain <term>striking of light</term> <note>original: "percussione di lume"; the physical impact of light rays upon a substance.</note>, and especially when the fire is thicker; as is seen in a fire lit in charcoal, wood, iron, or any other material. This receives light from the nearby <term>rare fire</term> <note>original: "fuoco raro"; refers to a thin, clear flame or pure heat as opposed to the "thick" fuel of glowing coals.</note> which turns into flame. Even within the flame itself, we see that the thicker part takes the light sharply from the thinner and rarer part, as if from a more perfect fire that is less corrupted by mixtures, and also because the light is not restricted within it. This is as it is in the body of <term>Mars</term> <note>The planet Mars, often associated with fire and heat in Renaissance cosmology.</note>, which, having within itself a fire restricted by the great, takes its light from the Sun, as if from a fire excellently dilated through which it passes and shines, making the stars resplendent. And just as this is seen in the fires we light, so—and even more greatly—it is perceived when the fire loses its color and liveliness, as would happen if it were spread under the Sun, because the Sun's splendor is of a <term>second order</term> <note>A higher degree of purity or a more refined category of light in the hierarchical chain of being.</note>, more purified and clear. The same would happen to anyone who could penetrate or see the rays of the Sun itself compared to those of the angels, and these angels' rays compared to the rays of the <term>First Sun</term> <note>original: "primo Sole"; a common philosophical metaphor for God or the Divine Intellect as the ultimate source of all light.</note>; I speak
