...is found in our light. From this, it happens that light striking the color red produces a certain dense yet powerful and sharp radiance. Continuing by degrees through "sanguine" <note>Originally "carni sanguine"—referring to a ruddy, healthy, or blood-rich complexion according to the Four Humors theory.</note> and colorful flesh, such as in red faces, we see that the highlights are sharp and lustrous; as seen on the cheeks <note>original: "meloni"—literally "melons," used here to describe the rounded, prominent parts of the cheeks.</note> and on the tip of the nose and the forehead. We do not see this in pale and sallow faces, such as those of a phlegmatic <note>A person dominated by the "phlegm" humor, characterized by being pale, cool, and calm.</note> color applied to its opposite; in these, the light is scattered and spread out in a thin clarity, as if without any vigor, finding no correspondence to its own nature.

Furthermore, when light strikes dark and black surfaces, it does not provide any sharpness at all, except in cases where that dark material is of an excellent quality, more purified of earth or dross—as would be the case with black silk compared to black wool. Thus, we see more luster in satin and ormesino <note>A lightweight, ribbed silk fabric originally from Ormus.</note> than in cloth; and among these, ink, ebony, and black stone possess more luster due to their greater moisture.

In addition, light on yellow causes a certain clear radiance and a flashing, as it is a color similar to light itself; from this, it generates all those reflections that can possibly be created in order, especially in the most perfect colors that are devoid of paleness. On green-blue <note>original: "verde azurro"—likely referring to a teal or malachite-like pigment.</note>, it causes a certain mediocrity <note>In this context, a "middle state" or moderate intensity.</note> that comforts the visual power rather than sharpening it. Thus, when our sight is weary, we are accustomed to looking at green-blue to comfort it; just as the eyes are comforted by looking into mirrors because of the crystalline moisture which conforms to the eye. These are effects that the extreme colors, such as red or yellow, could not produce.

On white, the light is too continuous because of its clarity, which is why it has much correspondence with black, from which it takes its shadow when struck by light; this is because white is associated with the Moon, and black with Saturn <note>In Renaissance art theory, colors were often linked to the seven planets to denote their "temperament" or symbolic weight.</note>. This does not happen with yellow, whose shadow tends more toward red than any other color, due to the conformity of the fiery nature that the Sun and Mars share between them—though one is dilated [the Sun] and the other is aggregated [Mars].

Because the colors between these boundaries are accompanied by the air—which couples them together by nature more or less according to the power that prevails in one over the other—even though the light is "combust" <note>A technical term from optics or alchemy referring to light that has been altered or "consumed" by the density of the medium it passes through.</note>, it cannot have a fixed boundary of light or dark. Instead, it possesses certain "middle-states," as seen in the influence of Jupiter, in the light greens, and in sapphire, rosy, and straw colors (a color mixed of yellow and white), and also partly in those that tend toward flesh-tone. This is due to the affinity they hold with Mars and with Mercury; the latter being by their nature good with the good, and with the wicked, they are most wicked; even more so in those...

## *On the effects that light produces on any surface.*
### Chapter XIX.

**S**ince we have spoken until now about the effects that light generates in each body, according to its quality in general; it remains now that we say something about surfaces also in general, that is, about the effects that light produces on them as it runs across them. And to do this, I will guide myself by the example of the human body, moving through all the seven ages <note>The "Seven Ages of Man" was a common medieval and Renaissance concept linking stages of life to the seven wandering planets: Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>. For by knowing then how to apply each like thing to its like, the human body will come to have a correspondence with all surfaces. And here it will be seen how much light will generate an effect in bodies according to whether the surfaces are prominent, or low, or narrow, or dilated; from which will result that harshness and sweetness of bodies according to the said quality of the surfaces. 

Now starting from lunar infancy <note>The first stage of life (ages 0–4), governed by the Moon, associated with moisture and growth.</note>, we see in the infant, according to the surfaces, the highlights [lumi] spread out and not sharp, through which there is impressed upon the viewer nothing but a certain spreading of fatty and simple matter without any sharpness. 

This sharpness then begins to be seen in the childhood [pueritia] of Mercury <note>The second age (ages 5–14), governed by Mercury, the planet of intelligence and movement.</note>. For in children the highlights begin to appear sharper, as the surfaces draw closer together; but with all this, they have something of the unstable; and they seem to waver, matching their gestures. This arises from the spirit, which begins to operate in the child, making him discern good from evil, and look towards everything that is to be of his life. 

In the adolescence of Venus <note>The third age (ages 15–22), governed by Venus, the planet of beauty and desire.</note>, which brings ease in attaining and learning the good arts, the surfaces lengthening and narrowing make the body beautiful, as it ought to be forever; and nonetheless soft and delicate, so that it can be called neither thin nor fat, from which it comes that nature is stirred and gives itself over to lust. In this age, the light accordingly generates a very great sweetness, well-corresponding and pleasing to the eye, depriving itself entirely of the spreading of the highlights, but being entirely harmonious within itself. It generates soft and steady shadows; and thus we see the eyes gently shaded, and the nose raised up showing likewise a soft shadow; and thus the legs, the arms, and all the rest of the limbs; no differently than if they were the ancient Venuses of marble <note>The author compares the ideal adolescent form to classical Greek and Roman sculpture.</note>.

Therefore, the man at this time is entirely content and carries himself with reasoned gravity and majesty.

All these things correspond to sadness and melancholy and are unpleasant to look upon.

*How bodies ought to have one principal light above the others.*

## Chapter XX.

**W**e must understand that all surfaces will receive more light the closer they are to the source; whether from above or below, front or back, to the right or to the left. It is necessary that one single "greater light" <note>The primary light source in a composition.</note> be received, and that the others follow it in degrees—whether from below or above, right or left, front or back—serving that first light as their superior. This primary light provides strength and liveliness to all the others. We see that Michelangelo observed this by only placing a principal light on the surfaces closest to that source, and on the others, he diminished it proportionately. Leonardo da Vinci, Raphael of Urbino, Gaudenzio <note>Gaudenzio Ferrari (c. 1471–1546), a prominent Northern Italian painter.</note>, and Cesare da Sesto <note>A pupil of Leonardo da Vinci.</note> observed the same in their figures, though with deeper shadows. Because of this, their figures possess a wonderful <term>relief</term> <note>The illusion of three-dimensionality (rilievo), making a flat painting look like a solid object.</note>, appearing as if they are emerging out of the frame. Bernardino Luini <note>Bernardino da Luino (c. 1480–1532), a painter known for his delicate style influenced by Leonardo.</note> and many others followed this as well, though in a more coarse manner. 

Therefore, to give strength and relief to all figures, one must proceed with order under a single light that is greater than all the rest; the other lights then fade away according to their distance and remoteness. Follow this rule, just as the aforementioned painters and others have done—those who were deemed worthy of the name "painter" because they were so sparing in their use of <term>highlights</term> <note>The Italian "chiaro" refers to the bright or clear areas of a painting.</note>. They distributed light across their figures no differently than if they were handling a precious gem. Consequently, their works achieved such sweetness and relief, and were so full of skill and deliberation—consistent with the nature of the thing depicted and the arrangement of the surfaces—that nature itself could show no more. The truth of everything I have said thus far can be clearly recognized by looking at the opposite: the works of those who held a different manner and style, making their figures all lit in the same way, so that almost no relief can be perceived <margin>is perceived</margin> in them.

### *How highlights are applied to bodies. Chap. XXI.*

**A**s a general rule, all highlights are applied to bodies according to the place where they pass and strike the wall or the painted panel; which must receive it as gently as if it were receiving it naturally by being in relief. Likewise, wearing a hat on the head would cast a shadow over the entire face; in short, all the shadows would be equal all around. ### On Sciography. Chapter XXII.

**S**ciographic science is a most principal science, and it is the second part of perspective, which considers with the same principles the shadows of bodies, just as is done in *grammica* <note>grammica: the art of linear drawing or perspective, focusing on the lines that define shapes.</note> for the lines seen—high, low, and middle—weighing their causes, principles, elements, differences, types, parts, and essential qualities. Throughout, it renders the causes for the observed variety of the images of things by means of distances, remoteness, proximity, and positions—above, below, and in the middle. This, therefore, is that which will teach the logic of shadows; about which there would be much to treat, were it not that in treating light, everything that shadows can be and cause has consequently also been touched upon. But so as not to fail to give it momentum by rendering the principal reasons according to the three real and true views of *grammica* in bodies, I will dispatch with it as quickly as possible, not with lengthy words, but with clarity.

### On the Shadows of Bodies, According to the Anoptic View. Chapter XXIII.

**I** shall not stay in this place to dispute what a shadow is, because we know that all bodies without light are of one and the same darkness to our eyes, so that they can never be perceived or seen by them; but when light is then spread over them, they appear more luminous the more they are opaque and dense. And bodies also show their colors through the light. Hence we see that the shadow partakes of the color of the body that is struck by the light, and not otherwise; so that where the light is lost, the shadow is also [lost], where...

# FOURTH BOOK

...where the light is sharp, the shadow is likewise sharp; where the light is spread out, the shadow is also spread out; and finally, where the bodies are separated, the light tends toward that same point, and the shadow follows the color. From this arises the fact that for as many varieties of bodies as are found, just as many types of lights and an equal number of shadows are found. But to come to the shadows as they appear to our eye—that is, in the <term>anoptic</term> <note>anoptic: from the Greek *ano* (up), referring here to a "sotto in su" or worm's-eye view where the viewer looks up at an object.</note> view—I say that the more the figures are seen to <term>foreshorten</term> <note>original: "scortare," the artistic technique of depicting an object as having less depth or distance than it actually does to create the illusion of three-dimensionality.</note>, and the inner parts are seen to rise, and those parts seen to lower where the lights and shadows follow the lines, the less one will be able to see toward the upper parts of the light. Conversely, much shadow will be seen, because since that body is being seen from the lower parts, those parts must necessarily appear shadowed, and in great quantity. Anyone who did otherwise would err greatly, because this logic of shadows serves no other purpose than the governance of the lines; and therefore, according to how the lines turn, are situated, or vanish, the shadow follows, increasing and decreasing accordingly. This applies to the lower parts and to one side as the light fades above, and to the other side; this is understood to be above the eye in every way according to the quadrant line. But let us pass to the other shadow of the second view.

->*On the Shadows of Bodies, according to the Optical View.*<-
->Chapter XXIV.<-

**I**n order not to lose or greatly foreshorten the lines when they are straight, or slightly above or slightly below the <term>optical line</term> <note>optical line: the horizontal line at the level of the viewer's eye.</note>, it results that the shadows appear softly—except for what can be gained from above by the lines that enter into the body. At the very least, because the frontal parts are lowered when seen from below, less shadow is seen. Thus, in a body according to this view, little shadow is required, except beneath the limbs and the rear part. The light comes to render the rear parts illuminated by the <term>reflections</term> <note>original: "reflexi," or reflected light bouncing off nearby surfaces into the shadowed areas of an object.</note> of the primary light that strikes a nearby area. But shadows and lights are seen much more clearly in the <term>anoptic</term> view; for because of the turning of the limbs seen from below on the side opposite the light, a very great reflection is generated as that part begins to withdraw toward the upper light. This is not unlike the rays spread by the sun before it rises above the sea. Because these rules and observations of radiation are too difficult and troublesome to be explained clearly in writing, I shall proceed to treat the final "real view."

# BOOK V

### Concerning the shadows of bodies, according to the catoptic view.
### Chapter XXXV.

**N**o manner or state of bodies displays fewer shadows than that which is seen under this view. Because, as the body is seen from the upper parts so that the lines behind it appear to rise, it is necessary that since much light is visible, the shadows decrease. The most that can be seen of them is upon the ground plane, which they occupy extensively, and on the side opposite to the light—serving the light in this state as in all others. To speak of these views in minute detail would be too long, and since light has been treated so extensively, one might have remained silent regarding shadows. Nevertheless, I did not want to omit this small mention at the end of the treatise, for shadows are like the "tail" of the lights; they can be nothing but the posterior and lower parts, possessing a nature so melancholy and sad that even the King of Shadows <note>A reference to Pluto or Hades, the mythological ruler of the underworld situated at the center of the earth.</note> down in the center is filled with disdain and wrath toward them. Therefore, let us reason of them at length no further; let us only strive in our works to make them appear not as mere "shadows," but as the very substance of the object being illuminated.

Because by observing this, we will show bodies that are clean, pure, and delightful to the eye due to their naturalness, fleeing the darkness of contrary colors. This is unlike the habit of many who shade a scarlet with black, a yellow with a dull <term>taneto</term> <note>original: "taneto," a tawny, reddish-brown, or "tan" color.</note>, a turquoise with a dark <term>bigio</term> <note>original: "bigio," a dull brownish-gray or ashen color.</note>, or a white with a color that it cannot in any way receive as a shadow—for white cannot receive any color as shadow except for black, which is its only true shadow when mixed with said white. For this reason, one is in a certain way no less melancholy than the other; for if black resembles the earth and the darkness, this other [the mixture of white and black] resembles the color we see men turn when they die. <note>The author is likely referring to the leaden, ashen pallor of a corpse.</note>

## ON PERSPECTIVE,

->Preface. Chapter I.<-

**I**t is a well-worn proposition of Aristotle <note>Lomazzo refers to the Aristotelian principle that the nature of the means is determined by the end they serve, a cornerstone of Scholastic philosophy.</note> that as the goal is, so must be the means that lead to it; that is, they must be suitable and proportionate to obtaining that end which each person proposes for himself. Just as if I wished to climb onto a roof, it would be necessary that I take a proportionate ladder, or some other similar instrument adapted for climbing there. And it is not enough for the means to have just any proportion, but it must be an absolute proportion; otherwise, it could in no way serve as a means to lead to that end. Furthermore, it is also necessary that for a means to be perfect, it must have not only this absolute proportion, but also another which philosophers call <term>for the sake of better being</term> <note>original: "ad melius esse." In Scholastic philosophy, "esse" refers to basic existence, while "ad melius esse" refers to things that make that existence better, more perfect, or more efficient.</note>. Thus, the perfect means must have two qualities: the first, that it can guide us to that end we have proposed for ourselves; the second, that it possesses such goodness and perfection that the end could be achieved better by no other means.

This doctrine, approved and common among all philosophers, shall be the first foundation of everything I have to say in this preface. The second foundation is that all prudent and excellent artisans—finding themselves with two means, one that has only absolute perfection, and the other which has joined with absolute perfection the quality of <term>better being</term> <note>original: "ad melius esse"</note>—should always choose the means that has both perfections united together. For example, if I need to go to Rome and I have two horses—one that will indeed carry me there, but with great labor and discomfort to me, and another that will not only carry me there but also so comfortably that I will feel no unease or fatigue throughout the entire journey—I must, if I wish to be judged prudent, choose that horse which most conveniently... <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page.</note>

...will lead me to the end of the journey I undertake to make. Having established these two foundations, I say that the immediate goal of painting and sculpture, from its very first institution, is to make images represent to human eyes the true proportion along with the other perfections of natural and artificial things, and especially of men. Now, such being the immediate goal of this art, it follows conclusively that the images are the means, and the goal is the eye—consistent with the first foundation and that of the other philosophers mentioned above; and consequently from Aristotle, this means—that is, the images—must be proportionate to the eye, which is its immediate goal.

And if you tell me that images do not represent natural and artificial things to the eye, but to the intellect and the memory, I respond and concede that it is true: the ultimate goal of images is the intellect, but the immediate goal is the eye. Because, as the same Aristotle says, **nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the senses** <note>original: "niuna cosa è nell'intelletto che non fia stata prima nel senso." And if perhaps you reply to me that, although the immediate goal of images is to represent proportion and other properties of things to the eye, the painter nevertheless does this by observing and following the same proportion of the things themselves. For since natural and artificial things are the rule and measure of painting and sculpture, there is no reason to depart from the rule, measure, and proportion found in the things themselves; especially since the goal of this art is to follow nature. This cannot be done otherwise than by making images represent all things with the greatest likeness that the artist can achieve; and it is certain that they are represented with the greatest possible likeness when the artist follows the same proportion found in the things.

For example, if a painter wants to represent to the eye a Julius Caesar who by chance happened to be ten faces in height <note>In Renaissance art theory, the "face" (faccia) was a standard unit of measurement. To do so would be an intolerable error, and would not represent the proportion of Julius Caesar, but rather of someone else with a height of eleven or nine. [...to observe] in their works the natural and proper proportion of things; but both <note>Refers to the painter and the sculptor mentioned in the preceding text.</note> must follow **visual proportion**. Because, in short, the eye together with the human intellect, regulated by the art of <term>perspective</term> <note>Lomazzo uses "prospettiua" here not just as a technique for depth, but as a scientific rule for how vision functions.</note>, must be the rule, the measure, and in a word, the judge of painting and sculpture. For if the painter were to paint only to satisfy and please himself, and did not wish for his works to be seen by others, then he could make the figures according to his own whim and manner. 

But since he seeks two things from painting—namely, **utility** and **honor**—it is necessary for him to create the work in such a way that everyone judges it to be well-made and well-proportioned. And this judgment cannot be made if the eye does not perceive the work and the intellect does not judge its proportion. Therefore, it is necessary to conform to the eye, and this cannot be done in any way by following natural proportion; rather, it is entirely necessary to observe the proportion relative to the visual eye. In this way, he will achieve his goals: honor and utility. 

Let no one say that the judgment of the eye, being fallacious, should not be followed. For besides the fact that such a person is even more mistaken in persuading himself that everyone else is deceived while he alone perceives and knows the truth, it is an easy thing to prove that the eye in seeing proportion, and the intellect in judging it, do not fail. Thus, the eye together with the intellect are upright and just judges. 

So, in every way, painters and sculptors, by holding to this judgment in their works, must follow not the natural and proper perfection of things, but that which returns to the sight. Now, since all our knowledge has its beginning and strength from the senses, as **Aristotle** notes, it is a most certain thing that the human intellect judges the proportion of figures and other things in the way the eye sees them. Thus, when the eye sees the quantity of a figure, the intellect judges that it is nine, or ten, or fewer, or more "faces" <note>A standard unit of measurement in Renaissance art theory, where the length of a human face was used to determine the overall height and proportions of the body.</note>. 

But when figures are distant and far off, the eye cannot demonstrate to the intellect the same natural quantity that they actually possess. From this, it follows that the intellect cannot judge that same [natural] proportion. And that it is true that when figures are far away, the eye cannot see the same quantity, is proven precisely by two very strong reasons. The first is that figures do not present to the eye their <term>species</term> <note>original: "spetie." [...and] the quantity is shorter; the more the air is distant from things, so that if we suppose an image is twenty <term>braccia</term> <note>A 'braccio' (plural 'braccia') was a traditional Italian unit of measurement, roughly equivalent to 23 inches, though it varied by city.</note> or a <term>stadium</term> <note>An ancient Greek unit of length, approximately 600 feet.</note> away from us, that first part of the air which is closest to the image and joined with it receives its **species**, and represents them to the second part of the air. This second part then represents the species of that same image to the third part, but smaller; in such a way that as the species always diminish step by step, they eventually end and proceed no further through the air. This is because they arrive at the eye in a **pyramidal shape** <note>Lomazzo refers to the "visual pyramid" or cone, a fundamental concept in Renaissance perspective where the object forms the base and the eye forms the apex.</note>. 

Thus, even if there were no eye at all in the world, this would still be the nature of all things: their <term>species</term> <note>In the context of Renaissance optics, 'species' (spetie) refers to the visual form, likeness, or "intentional species" that objects cast into the air to be perceived.</note> would travel through the air between two lines that are not parallel. Therefore, necessarily according to the doctrine of all **mathematicians**, these lines come to concur and meet together; and so, at the point of intersection, that which travels behind these two lines ends and terminates.

And if what I have said until now were not true, this much would still be true: that if the species of things were represented in all parts of the air in the same quantity as the things themselves—almost as if between two parallel lines—as for example if the species of a man ten faces tall were represented in every part of the air in that same quantity of ten, a very great inconvenience would follow: that in a finite thing, an **infinite power** would be found. Because if one wanted it this way, so that the species never diminished but were always shown in the same quantity in all parts of the air; then, assuming the case that the air were infinite and no impediment were found in the middle, those species (according to this opinion) would be seen in every part of this infinite air. Consequently, the species of a single man would extend infinitely through that infinite air, such that a finite thing would have infinite power. This is the greatest impropriety and absurdity that can be imagined in **philosophy**, in **mathematics**, and in **theology**. 

And it would truly be a marvelous thing in the world if an **Angel** had his power finite and limited—such that while operating in one place, he cannot at the same time operate elsewhere outside his **actuality** <term>actuality</term> <note>original: "attuità"</note>—and yet a man could extend his species to infinity. And it is of no relevance to say that this is a **passive power**; for no creature can possess even an infinite passive power.

[...that] if the eye were very far from a thing, it would nonetheless see it in the same way as it would see it when being closer to it. Since the same **visual power** <term>potenza visiua</term> <note>The Renaissance concept of the eye's active capacity or faculty to perceive light and form.</note> of the eye is informed by the same **species** <term>spetie</term> <note>From the Latin 'species,' meaning the visual form or likeness that an object radiates through the air to the eye.</note> in the same quantity, it seems almost impossible that it should not see it in the same way, wherever it might be located, whether near or far. However, experience—the true teacher and judge of all things—demonstrates the direct opposite: that we do not see the same thing indistinctly in the same way. Rather, the further we are from it, the less we see it. Therefore, it is necessary that the species do not proceed from things in the same quantity, but that they go on diminishing. 

If we take a very large mirror and use it to experiment with what I am saying, we will see a clear demonstration and the sensible truth of it: that the species of things diminish the further they move away from our eyes. For if we approach the mirror, the entire quantity of the opposite thing will be represented to us, and the species and image of that same quantity will be seen there; but as we move further away, they appear smaller to us, and they will appear smaller and smaller the further we distance ourselves from the mirror, until finally they are not seen at all. 

This is an evident and manifest sign that the species issue forth from things between two lines that are not parallel, but in a **pyramidal shape**; and thus the thing cannot be seen in the same quantity in every place. From this consideration of the way figures **recede** in a mirror, I have derived the rule and the art of making figures **foreshorten** and **recede** in **perspective**, as we shall treat later in the practical section following this book. Because the visual power, when informed by a larger species, judges the thing to be large, and when formed by a smaller species, judges it to be small. 

Therefore, the eye does not fail in seeing, nor the intellect in judging the proportion of things; but the painter and the sculptor fail when they create their works to be seen by the eye and judged by the intellect, and they strive for them to be considered proportionate by whoever looks at them, yet they still make them contrary to the art of perspective and prudence. For if they make an image, for example, of ten **faces** <note>In Renaissance art theory, the 'face' (faccia) was a standard unit of measurement for determining the proportions of the human body.</note> that is to be placed in a location distant from the eye, and therefore must lose one face in the recession of sight, why should they not form it of eleven faces? Therefore, it is necessary that the craftsman always have before his mind's eye this principle of Aristotle, and of all philosophers: to first consider the **end** <note>The final purpose or intended result of a work.</note>, and in accordance with that end, to procure the proportioned and opportune means. Thus, in making the image to be seen and judged as well-proportioned, he fashions it proportioned *to the eye*. This he will do by forming the image larger by as much as it stands to lose due to its distance from the eye; and so he will first note what proportion he wants the image to be judged as having. 

Next, he will note the location where he wants to place it; and if the distance causes it to lose one face, he will add a little proportionally to each of the faces of the image. In this way, if the image is meant to be ten faces high, it should be made eleven, increasing it by one face, and thus the eye will judge it to have ten faces. And if the distance of the location causes it to lose two faces, he will make the image twelve faces high, and it will similarly appear to the eye to be ten faces. 

Thus, if the craftsman makes a **colossus** <term>colosso</term> <note>An exceptionally large statue.</note> of twenty **cubits** <term>braccia</term> <note>Literally "arms," an Italian unit of measurement (braccio) roughly equal to 23 inches, though it varied by city.</note>, and the head of this colossus—being too far from the eye—loses a third of a head, he must make it larger by a third of a head, and so it will appear well-proportioned to the eye. 

The general rule is this: when the entire image diminishes, everything that is lost must be distributed throughout the whole image. But when the head, for example <note>original Latin: "verbigratia"</note>, loses size and recedes, the head must be made larger. He shall make a similar judgment regarding specific arts, and by as much as things diminish, by that much larger they shall be made. This is the true art and the true proportion that the ancients, who were most wise, observed in all their works. 

For this reason, the figures on **Trajan's Column** <note>The famous Roman triumphal column featuring a spiral relief frieze; the artist increased the height of the figures as the frieze wound upward so they would appear uniform from the ground.</note> in Rome that are at the highest point are larger, and thus they all appear to be of the same size. Because that most skillful craftsman made them larger by as much as they were to lose due to the distance and remoteness from the eye. ...natural proportion, and in this way they appear most well-proportioned. To which I respond that even though the image might be near the eye, one must not entirely maintain natural proportion; rather, it is necessary to preserve the **grace** <term>gratia</term> <note>In Renaissance art theory, *grazia* (grace) refers to a sense of effortless elegance and beauty that goes beyond mere technical correctness or rigid proportions.</note> of the figure. And that proportion which will be most beautiful to the eye is the one that should be followed, as **Raphael** <note>Raphael Sanzio (1483–1520), the celebrated High Renaissance painter known for the harmony and "grace" of his figures.</note> and all the talented masters have done, in whose works one sees the feet of the figures a little smaller, and the legs a little longer than in nature. Finally, one can notice other details in their works that give great grace and beauty to the figures. Because the eye delights in seeing that certain parts of the body are slender, others are fleshy and soft, and some that maintain natural proportion; but art cannot give rules for every individual part, as that would be an infinite task. Still, if the reader considers well, he will find in this work of mine so many precepts, so many rules, and so many observations, that if he follows them all, I am confident he will succeed as a master in this profession.

## On the Power of Perspective. Chapter II.

**P**erspective, as all experts know, produces this result: that by following nature, it causes a person to see wrongly and deceives them, showing a small quantity in such a way that it seems large to him. And this proceeds from nothing else than because the eye is never offended by seeing a natural body in any place—be it high, low, or wherever one wishes—because it is accustomed to it; by imitating nature through the correct path of perspective, it follows that by representing a small quantity as something larger, the eye is not offended. So great is the importance of this power <term>virtù</term> <note>The "virtue" or inherent power and efficacy of the artistic technique.</note>, that not only do those works that are perfectly understood achieve their effect, but even those that do not possess a great deal of skill. I have experienced this myself, approving two foreshortened figures <term>scorti di figure</term> <note>Foreshortening: the technique of depicting an object or figure in a picture in depth, making it appear shorter than it actually is to create an illusion of space.</note> made in a way that could have been executed and grounded through the skill of masters,

But the greatest and principal virtue of this art, finally, is that it shows the way by which one can make figures perfect and secure in every manner; and it separates itself from sculpture without imitating or seeing them in relief. Thinking on this, sculptors used to go about proudly, saying that painters could not do without models to see how the light falls to arrange drapery <term>panni</term>, and to make foreshortenings and similar things. They were looking only at certain idiot painters who want to make use of these models; from which it arises that they cannot complete a single figure in a year, and consequently, while they use sculpture in this way with little judgment, they die of hunger—a just and deserved penalty for their ignorance.

Talented painters have not used them [models]. For even if they were to use models, these are nonetheless works of the plastic arts <term>plastica</term> <note>Modeling in three dimensions, as with clay or wax, rather than painting on a flat surface.</note> and not their own. In short, the good painter makes use of the method we mentioned above, through which painting is noble above all others. With such rags, one never represents true drapery as it should be. Thus have arisen so many different styles of drapery that are all far removed from the truth.

From this, one can clearly understand how much such practices should be avoided—not only because they make us waste time, but because they never lead works toward the truth. Furthermore, from these habits follow those stings, passions, and gnawings of the heart and soul in the practitioners, which we must strive in every way to cast out. To work well and to investigate subtly, one requires clarity and serenity of soul, which brings with it ease of execution and the security of art. Thus, without being oppressed by curses and stings, but instead considering all things with the eye of reason, works are brought to their perfect end in the best and most certain ways.

It is true that these things can only take root in the souls of those who know and understand all the first elements of art and all the effects they can produce in every work. This fact exhorts us to attend to the study of the good arts, which are like roads leading us to the desired goal. Nevertheless, we must pray to the Lord; for prayers directed to Him are of such value that in a single moment they make concepts <term>concetti</term> <note>The internal mental idea or "spark" of a work before it is executed.</note> flourish and reveal easy and expeditious paths, which nothing other than the goodness of God can do. In His name, I shall begin to treat perspective <term>prospettiva</term>...

### *Definition of Perspective. Chapter III.*

**P**erspective—a subordinate branch, descendant, and daughter of Geometry—is defined as the science of visible lines. Thus, its subject is the visible line, for which it investigates the causes, principles, and the first universal elements in and of themselves and immediately. It considers its genus, its species, and its essential and accidental differences. Speaking of this science, Geminus <note>Geminus of Rhodes (1st century BC), a Greek astronomer and mathematician whose works categorized the branches of mathematics.</note>, a noble and ancient writer on mathematical matters, divides it into three species: optics (that is, perspective), sciography <term>sciografica</term> <note>The study of how shadows are cast by objects, essential for creating a sense of volume on a flat surface.</note>, and specularia <term>specularia</term> <note>The study of reflections in mirrors or polished surfaces.</note>.

Optics is divided into two species: physiological and grammatical. Physiological optics investigates the universal principles, causes, and elements of all visibility and its parts, species, and essential differences—though always in a general sense—which are principally three. For one is called direct visibility, which deals with direct rays; the second is reflected visibility; and the third is refracted <note>original: "ritratta"</note> visibility, which occurs in water, glass, or similar materials. Grammatical optics <term>grammica</term> <note>From the Greek 'gramma' (line). Here it refers to the mathematical art of drawing lines to represent objects.</note>—that is, the art of drawing—which is more necessary to painting than the other species, is divided into four parts. 

For those who draw must primarily consider either true and real views, or feigned and artificial views of three sorts called anoptical, optical, and catoptical. Anoptical perspective is that which extends upwards and rises at its base above the Horizon. Optical perspective extends straight forward—that is, through the middle level with the Horizon. Catoptical perspective extends downwards below the Horizon, appearing to approach closer to the eye from below. 

But the excellence of the craftsman lies in demonstrating feigned and artificial views as if they were real and true. Achieving this completely is granted to few, as it is entirely occupied with foreshortenings <term>scorti</term> <note>The technique of depicting an object in a picture to produce an illusion of projection or extension in space.</note>, abbreviations, cut-offs, reductions, and shadings. And these four parts serve the art of design—namely linear painting, sculpture, architecture, and engraving <term>celatura</term>—that is, bas-relief, of which the species are: anaglyphic <note>high relief or embossed work</note>, diaglyphic <note>intaglio or sunken relief</note>, encolaptic <note>engraved or incised work</note>, toreutic <note>metalworking, specifically the art of chasing and embossing</note>, encaustic (that is, enameling), plastic (that is, modeling in clay or wax), as well as tonic and paradigmatic <note>terms referring to the creation of models or prototypes in the plastic arts</note>. 

The second species, called sciography, deals thoroughly with shadows, their causes, principles, elements, differences, species, parts, and essential properties; it provides the reasons for the varied appearances of the images of things by means of distances, remoteness, and the proximity of locations—above, below, or in the middle. All these principles, as far as they concern linear drawing, are governed by grammatical optics, which—using the same distances, proximities, and locations—distributes the lines of surfaces in such a way

This **sciography** <term>sciografica</term> <note>The study of how shadows are cast by objects to create the illusion of three-dimensional depth.</note>, using the same principles, then considers the shadows that bodies can produce depending on whether they have a high, low, or wide projecting surface. It is indeed true that many understand this to be the same thing that **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman architect whose "Ten Books on Architecture" was the foundational text for Renaissance building and perspective.</note> calls **scenography** <term>scenografica</term> <note>The art of representing the front and sides of a building in perspective, typically used in stage design.</note>—that is, the front and the sides of a building, and also of any other thing, surface, or body. They make it consist—as if within it lies the power of **linear art** <term>grammica</term> <note>From the Greek 'gramma' (line); the mathematical foundation of drawing lines.</note>—of three principal lines: the plane line, the line going to the point <note>The vanishing point.</note>, and the distance line. They say that **Agatharchus**, **Democritus**, and **Anaxagoras** <note>Ancient Greek thinkers who, according to Vitruvius, developed the first theories of perspective for theatrical scenery.</note> once wrote about this. Furthermore, as if it contained the entire art of **foreshortening** <term>scorti</term> <note>The technique of depicting an object or figure in a picture in depth.</note> and other difficulties, some insist that painters must understand it in every way as a necessity. But let everyone understand it as they wish; I will follow the stated order and the true, ancient definition and division of perspective.

The final species of perspective, which is called **specularia** <term>specularia</term> <note>The study of light as reflected by mirrors; today known as catoptrics.</note>, considers the reflection of rays and assists in the craftsmanship of mirrors, showing all the properties and deceptions of those things that are seen differently according to their various forms: concave, convex, flat, columnar, pyramidal, ordered, crooked, round, angular, inverted, everted, regular, irregular, solid, and clear. **Pythagoras**, **Plato**, and a certain **Hostius** <note>Hostius Quadra, a Roman notorious for his use of distorting mirrors.</note> in the time of **Augustus** (as **Caelius** <note>Lodovico Celio Rodigino, a 16th-century humanist scholar.</note> relates) delighted much in this sort of perspective. **Apollonius** and **Witelo** <note>Witelo (Vitellio), a 13th-century natural philosopher whose work on optics was a standard university text.</note> wrote extensively about it, as it shows—so to speak—mirrors that perform miracles. For instance, we read of a mirror among the spoils of the East brought by **Pompey the Great**, in which an entire army could be seen, and of certain others that can be made in such a way that they demonstrate all those capabilities mentioned above. 

Regarding the necessary linear part of perspective, and regarding **linear art** <term>grammica</term> for its real and feigned views and their arrangements, it is primarily required that we discuss what seeing is, how it is understood, and how it is used. Afterwards, we will proceed to treat the rays of distance and the object; and finally, the three ways of seeing and their lines. In these matters, among other painters, sculptors, and architects, **Clariccio**, **Meda**, and **Bassi** <note>Girolamo Clariccio, Giuseppe Meda, and Martino Bassi were prominent Milanese artists and architects of the late 16th century.</note> are now very proficient. I declare that I will proceed not as a mathematician, but freely, speaking according to the practice held by painters, and as I have observed it and demonstrated it in the figures—both of human bodies in every position, as well as anything else that can be shown through art.

### On the logic of sight in general. Chapter IV.

**F**rom what I recall having read regarding the principles of sight <term>ragione del vedere</term> <note>The underlying physical and philosophical explanation for how vision functions.</note> among excellent theorists <term>speculari</term>, the opinions and views on this matter are diverse and varied. **Plato** believes that sight occurs through clarity—that is, the clarity that comes from the eyes, as light flows out into the external air, meeting the light reflected from physical bodies. However, that light which exists in the air between the eye and the object has a form that spreads out and returns to the power of sight. **Galen** held this same view, as did all the **Platonists** in their commentaries; following their master, they say that the eye sees nothing but the light of the sun. They argue that the shapes and colors of bodies are never seen unless they are illuminated by light, and they do not reach the eye in their actual physical matter. They maintain, therefore, that sunlight—"painted" with the colors and shapes of all the bodies it strikes—presents itself to the eyes; then the eyes, aided by a certain natural ray of their own, capture this "painted" sunlight. Once they have captured it, they see that light and all the "paintings" <note>Images or visual representations.</note> within it. For this reason, the entire order of this visible world—as the great interpreter of Plato <note>Likely referring to Marsilio Ficino, the influential Renaissance translator and commentator on Plato.</note> says—is received by the eyes not in the way it exists in the physical matter of bodies, but in the way it exists in the light, which is infused within the eyes. These are the arguments of the Platonists.

But **Hipparchus** says that rays extended from the eyes, touching objects with a kind of vibration <note>original: "palpitazione"; referring to the "extramission theory" where the eye sends out feelers or rays to 'touch' what it sees.</note>, return what they capture to the sight. The **Epicureans** affirm that the likenesses <note>The *eidola* or *simulacra*—thin films of atoms shed by objects.</note> of the things that appear enter the eyes of their own accord. **Aristotle** is of the opinion that likenesses reach the sight not as physical bodies, but as qualities transmitted through the alteration of the air that surrounds visible things. **Porphyry**, however, says that neither rays, nor likenesses, nor any other thing is the cause of seeing; rather, it is the soul itself, which recognizes itself as visible and knows itself in all things that exist. The **geometers** and **perspective artists** <term>prospettivi</term> <note>Scholars of optics (perspectiva), which was considered a branch of geometry.</note>, approaching the method of Hipparchus in a certain way, describe certain cones formed by the meeting of rays that are sent out from the eyes; thus, the sight encompasses many visible things at once, but most certainly those where the rays converge. **Al-Kindi** <note>A 9th-century Arab philosopher and "Father of Islamic Philosophy," whose work *De Aspectibus* influenced Western optics.</note> says something else regarding aspects. **Saint Augustine** holds that the power of the soul performs an action within the eye. I shall join this view with the others in the following chapters, particularly according to which ones appear closest and most in conformity with the

## *On the logic of sight in particular. Chapter V.*

**A**lthough, following **Aristotle** in one place and **Plato** in another, I have (as can be understood from the first book) treated the logic of sight, the medium, and the object; and although I have already mentioned various other opinions above, I nevertheless wish—for the sake of greater clarity and to align myself with the **Platonic Euclid**, as the Prince and father of this discipline—not to refrain from discussing this more broadly and offering my own opinion. 

First, the eye, the instrument of sight, has several layers <note>original: "sfoglie," referring to the tunics or membranes of the eye.</note>, and in the center is the sight itself. This sight emerges through a passage called the **optic [nerve]** <term>ottico</term> <note>The author describes the visual path from the brain to the eye.</note> which reaches to the edge of the pupil and comes from the brain. Through this passage comes the visual power <term>virtù visiua</term>; as it reaches the outside, the rays dilate, because they emerge with the greatest force and density. For when a very great force and power passes through a narrow place, once it has exited, it spreads out here and there, up and down, with the greatest impetus and speed; thus, it sees by its own direct power, and not by some sharp, forced power. And here, **Euclid** says in his *Perspective* <note>Referring to Euclid’s "Optica."</note> that all things falling under our sight are not seen all at once. He means that we only see where the direct ray is formed; the ray cannot extend itself through others, for that is impossible. Since this is one of the roots of perspective, he set it down as the first proposition. 

But returning to the point, one must know that all the senses proceed from a single power <term>virtù</term>, and this power is present in every part. Indeed, if it were divided into infinite parts, the whole power would be in each one, just as it is in all the other parts together. For example, we see in water and fire that even the smallest part possesses the same nature and power as the whole regarding wetting, cooling, heating, or burning. Therefore, although the soul <term>anima</term>, passing through different places, appears to produce different effects—such as seeing, walking, and the like—these powers are in the soul by its own nature, but they emerge from the center of the body. Because the body is constructed in various ways, as the soul passes...

but through such variety, it works variably together as the body does; just as a musical organ does, which, although it sounds by means of a single spirit—that is, by a single wind or air introduced into it—nevertheless, even though it is only one spirit, it produces a varied voice according to the different bodies <note>In the context of an organ, "corpi" refers to the various pipes of different sizes and shapes that modify the air's sound.</note> it finds. And thus all the many voices and sounds in the world are made like a single air; not because the air contains within itself such a variety of voices and effects, but because it has the power to enable others to have them. 

In the same way, our soul does not possess these various effects within itself, but it is sufficient to allow others <note>Meaning the various organs and limbs of the human body.</note> to have them in things ordered toward it, such as seeing, walking, and the like. And the air does not see the soul, and it has no effect in the way the soul does with the body—with which it produces these effects—but the soul produces them by itself, and more easily, because it is unburdened <note>original: "disciolta," meaning loosened or free from the weight of the flesh.</note>; and being unburdened, it is extremely light, and a light thing moves more easily than a heavy one. 

Therefore, the soul is faster outside the body: just as one sees, for example, the wind and thunder, because spirit is faster. Everything that can contain anything within itself is the spirit, which contains all of Heaven and earth; but the body, within its own body, cannot contain another body because of its physical nature; whereas the spirit does not have a body within itself, and therefore can receive both corporeal and incorporeal things. It receives corporeal things because the spirit does not occupy space <note>original: "loco," the physical place or volume occupied by matter.</note>, while they do; therefore, they can exist in the place of the spirit—though they cannot exist in a place already occupied by another body. 

It receives spiritual and incorporeal things because it is not occupied by the physical; and outside the physical, everything is spirit. Spirit, within spirit, can see the whole of the spirit; because, not being occupied by the physical, it sees all things—that is, corporeal things—since it passes out through the physical part. And because spirit does not abandon spirit, it returns to the spirit and brings all those things it has seen back to itself; when it arrives and finds the body—that is, the eye—it fixes them upon it. Because it has seen corporeal things, it represents them to the corporeal organ, namely the eye, through which it receives them; and by that eye it judges, because they are similar to it—that is to say, corporeal. 

And because they are two things in one, they have two parts within them: namely, body and spirit. And because they are together, they work together: spirit through spirit, and body through body; and spirit for the body, and body for the spirit. The spirit works for the body because it carries corporeal things. And they are carried more by the spirit, for the body without the spirit cannot draw anything to itself; if it wishes to draw something, it must do so through the spirit—or better said, through the void <note>original: "voto," likely referring to the vacuum or the immaterial medium created by the spirit that allows physical movement to occur.</note> of the spirit, which is to say, spiritually.

Because the spirit cannot draw a body to itself physically, but spiritually. And this is the role the spirit performs in the body: nor does the spirit work upon the body to keep the spirit for itself, but rather to know things similar to itself and to make them understood by the spirit. And here one recognizes the thickness of shapes through distance, which are then intersected <note>original: "tagliano al traverso," referring to the intersection of the visual pyramid by the picture plane.</note>, because the eye is positioned relative to those transverse lines, and each one cuts within itself; and through those same lines that go toward the sight, it brings the image back to itself, and within those lines, capturing something of that object. Where those lines then intersect, the object appears smaller or larger, according to how many *species* <term>species: in Renaissance optics, these are the formal images or "likenesses" emitted by objects that travel through the air to the eye</term> it captures in the crossing; but whether near or far from the eye, things seen within the rays are always intersected upon their straight path; because the eye is straight, and transverse, and crooked—in all ways it traverses its rays, and through spiritual things, it sees the spiritual. For nothing occupies the spiritual, since the spirit has no part that can be occupied; and therefore, as soon as it has emerged from physical things, it sees all incorporeal things, as physical things are no longer before it; but because the physical part is not its own, it is occupied by it, and through it, it maintains sight within the eye. And it is necessary that that thing which can contain things within itself <note>The spirit/mind.</note> offers all things to that which cannot contain them <note>The physical matter of the eye or the painting.</note>. But because we must treat the rays and the eye in detail, I will conclude the discussion on the rationale of seeing.

## On the Rays of Sight. Chapter VI.

**T**he rays of sight are those that, departing from the eye, go out to capture all the details of the objects that one wishes to paint—such as the floor plans, the angles, the elevations, the depths, the widths, the intervals, the heights, the thicknesses, and generally every other part that must be represented upon any wall or panel. In the act of painting, these rays reach their limit; the interior rays are distinguished from the exterior or superficial ones of the object's view, and then they return directly to the eye from whence they departed. In this manner, the exterior rays, having captured the object's surface all around, join together in that form—along with its depth and height—at the eye (that is, at the point) with the interior rays, forming an angle there. This angle—as Euclid says in the final part where he speaks of perspective <note>Referring to Euclid's *Optics*, which was the foundational text for mathematical perspective.</note>—is such that according as objects appear larger, they form a larger angle in the eye, and those that appear smaller, [smaller]...

### On the Eye as the Instrument for Seeing Rays. Chapter VII.

**S**ince the eye is the entire foundation of perspective—for without it, perspective could not exist—it is therefore called by those who study perspective the center, the sign, the point, the boundary <note>original: "termine," used here to mean the fixed reference point or limit</note>, and the apex of the pyramid <term>visual pyramid: the cone of light rays with its base at the object and its point at the eye</term>, which, as we have said, is usually formed according to the shape and base of the object during the act of seeing. To begin with the first point: it is called the foundation of perspective because through it two types of seeing occur—the natural and the rational. It is natural insofar as the appearances of things seen simply come to it through the rays, and it receives them; it is rational because, furthermore, it considers the reason and the effect of seeing, from which perspective is derived—that is, the art of knowing how to see—and upon it are formed the first elements of the art. It is called the center because all the lines from the bases and circumferences of objects converge toward it, not otherwise than those lines from a circle to its center point. And from this, it is also called the sign, because it is a fixed location from which the entire logic of the elevation of bodies, their prominences <term>eminenze: the parts of a three-dimensional object that project forward toward the viewer</term>, depths, and receding parts <note>original: "perdite," referring to the "loss" of detail or scale as things move away</note> result by means of those things that depend upon it. It is called the boundary because all things in painting are determined by it, and all those things that are made without the organization of this boundary cannot be good or correct; for they are not arranged to be seen unless they are disposed according to the sight through its rays, which extend from the eye outward in every direction. Therefore, those who work without establishing a fixed boundary—that is, an eye to which all figures and their members must relate—are certainly not worthy of the name of "painter," but rather "plasterers," destroyers of colors, a sickness to the eyes, and a source of confusion for the world. And that this is a necessity, and must be held as the principal and substantial object of the art, is clearly seen; for just as all things that are seen relate to the eye according to their colors and shapes, so too everything intended to be shown must demonstrate the same effect. Otherwise, it is impossible for any body to be seen, regardless of its gesture or placement. Now, these are the credible <note>original: "probabili," meaning visually plausible or convincing to the viewer</note> paintings, and consequently, those that lack this logic are less credible; but those that are entirely deprived of it cannot even be called paintings, but only confusion and a mess made by chance, to waste time and materials—

## On Distances. Chapter VIII.

**W**anting then to paint anything, I say that it cannot be seen without distance, that is, without space between the eye and the thing one wishes to see. For if the thing touched the eye, it could not be seen, as there would be no air in between. And again, if the thing were too far away, it could not be seen; because if one wants to fit a large thing into a small space, it is necessary to make it become small. If, then, the air is to make a large thing visible to the eye, or if the eye truly wants to see it, it must pull the object to itself by means of the air and the rays of the eye. Because to see it, the corporeal eye and the spiritual eye <note>spiritual eye: the intellectual faculty of the mind that perceives proportions and beauty beyond mere physical light</note> must concur with the thing seen, which is the object. 

Indeed, I say that just as in short and obtuse distances things seem to tumble and fall upon us, producing unseemly effects, conversely, those that are too far and at too sharp an angle to the sight do not give strength to the works and steal away the vision too much, appearing too rigid. For these two reasons above all, one must choose a suitable distance, which will ensure that the person viewing stands away three times as much, as...

## Chapter IX. On the Object.

**T**he Object—which is nothing other than the thing that presents itself before us, and is seen at whatever size one wishes, provided it is not so small that it cannot be seen—can never in a painting be closer to us than the space occupied by the distance established in the previous chapter. And if anyone imagines another object there, he errs greatly, because it cannot stand there; for it is necessary in painting that the first thing one wishes to represent on the wall or panel be arranged with a fitting size, so that all other things, following its rule, may have their due and corresponding measure. And this first thing is called **natural** <note>In this context, "natural" refers to the life-size scale or the primary reference point of the painting's proportions.</note>, and it is established in such a way that it represents being drawn exactly at the boundary where the chosen distance ends. From there onward—that is, moving inward according to the extension of the lines or rays—all other things must diminish.

For regarding the object, or natural thing, it is necessary above all else that it diminish as it recedes; and from that point forward [toward the viewer] it cannot do anything. If one wished to place something closer, it would be necessary to break the initial distance, the logic, and the primary object of the larger ones, such that the thing that was principal would be made to diminish—that is, to appear smaller. This is because as a thing moves from its place toward us or away from us, it always increases or diminishes. Therefore, by making something in front of the natural object and the end of the distance, it would be necessary, as I have said, to make it larger than life-size. But this is not based in truth, and not being in truth, it would be false. But by placing the "truth" <note>The "truth" refers to the established plane of reality within the painting's perspective system.</note> closer, those things already made large (like the natural size) lose their status and become smaller than natural; they may seem larger because they are closer to us, but they do not actually seem larger than what they are. And if they are even closer, they will seem even larger than the others, but they will never seem larger than they truly are.

Now, all these things can be done because the distance can be made greater or smaller as much as one wishes; and this is because from the eye to the thing seen, within that boundary, the object exists throughout. Wherever that space is cut or traversed, the thing becomes larger or smaller according to one's wish. However, the true distance must be that which is introduced as I have stated; and this makes the work incorruptible, so that the object arranged with its proper order does not have to be moved here or there like a wanderer <note>original: "uagabondo," implying a lack of fixed placement or stability in the composition</note>. Such things must be very well examined from the beginning, before

### On Anoptics: The First View, or the Royal and Superior Line.
### Chapter X.

**H**aving discussed the first things necessary for <term>lineal perspective</term> <note>Original: *grammica prospettiua*. "Grammica" refers to the use of lines or drawing to define shape and space.</note> which belongs to us painters, it follows in this place that we treat its first "view": that which rises above the Horizon, or the middle, or the straight line. Its duty consists mainly in considering all the parts of the object placed above the Horizon; it works so that, with its rays, it leads those parts to the "cut" (the line of the cut or foreshortening). Then, according to the placement of the body, it makes the deep and posterior parts fall downward, while the most prominent parts sometimes remain above the heights. From this are generated the losses, the gains, the falls, and the "rebounds" of the members of the body being introduced. This **Anoptic** <note>From the Greek *ano* (upward) and *optikos* (pertaining to sight); the study of things seen from below looking upward.</note> line begins at the center—that is, at the start of the distance, or the eye, or the "point" as you wish to call it—and it returns to that point through all its rays or lines that have joined all the boundaries of the complete body. Thus, it can be cut wherever one wants, but the true cut is above the perpendicular line, where the distance from the eye begins or ends.

## *On Catoptics: The Third View, or the Royal and Low Line. Chapter XII.*

**T**he third view is that which reaches with its rays all the parts from the bottom of the object introduced for painting, and leads them to the "cut" <note>The "cut" or intersection is the two-dimensional surface of the painting where the 3D rays are intercepted.</note>. Thus, it shows us if an object is below—that is, beneath the eye—causing the rear parts to rise and the front parts to lower. Conversely, when <term>optics</term> <note>Here referring to the standard eye-level perspective.</note> reaches a body from above, it renders the subsequent depths as flat, both in front and behind. Then, for the higher parts, it begins (like the supreme view) to make the rear parts descend and the front parts rise, with certain prominences overcoming the heights. 

In this way, its rays join with the higher ones of the central or middle view, which then joins with the upper one. Thus we can understand that these three "real views" are understood in all ways depending on whether objects are high or low; according to their assigned parts, they are actually carried to the "cut" at the degree where they are found, and extend no further. As for the rest of the bundle of rays, we leave that to the <term>feigned views</term> <note>Original: *viste mentite o finte*. These are perspectives that simulate a view from an artificial or impossible angle to create specific visual illusions, such as those used in ceiling painting.</note>. Although in truth there is only one such view, they can be called supreme, perpendicular, superior in the vertical plane, middle, and low, as well as by their wonderful effect "on the forehead" <note>Referring to the frontal plane of the viewer's gaze.</note>, due to the variety of foreshortening and expansion <note>Original: *scortare & dicortare*. These refer to the compression and stretching of forms to maintain correct proportions in perspective.</note> they produce.

The vertical projection plane.</note> for the upper parts. ## *On the Second Feigned Oblique View. Chapter XIV.*

This view, or logic of lines, departing from the end of such lines, allows us to see <term>oblique foreshortenings</term> in their proper places—that is, those that can be made on the vaults of chapels, not on flat squares, but in semicircles and the like, such as <term>tiburios</term> or ruins. And from there, despite the curvature of the vaults, it makes the figures and other bodies appear correctly upright, as if the vault were not truly there. Thus, while showing the vault, it does not break it in any way to make the chapel appear open to the living sky, or with other introduced fictions as is customary. This way of foreshortening is the most difficult there is, because one must not only work with the rays [of sight], but one must not err by even a single point, as will be said in the following book. For things made high up cannot sit more than a <term>palmo</term> <note>A traditional Italian unit of measurement, roughly a "palm's" width (approx. 22-25 cm).</note> lower. But because there would be too much to say about this, and even then it might never be perfectly understood, it will suffice to provide some examples of this feigned view for greater clarity. One of these is seen in Milan at Santa Maria del Carmine, in a chapel of the Life of the Magdalene by the hand of **Zenale** <note>Bernardo Zenale (c. 1460–1526), a Milanese painter and architect.</note>. The vault of this chapel is made in this manner and has many Saints seated upon the large cornices, which are by the hand of **Agostino Milanese**. Another is in Parma by the hand of **Antonio da Correggio** <note>Correggio (1489–1534), a master of the High Renaissance known for his revolutionary ceiling frescoes.</note>, showing an Assumption of the Virgin with terrifying figures around her, which are foreshortened in the same manner.

## On the Third Feigned Superior View. Chapter XV.

**T**hrough this view, all the figures or bodies that are placed above the eye level show their lower parts, either more or less, depending on how high they are positioned on the wall relative to the horizon. Because of this, the back parts appear to recede downward, and the front parts appear to rise upward, with one limb often overlapping another. From this, one sees the marvel of vast spaces, arms stretching outward, the "loss" of legs <note>Refers to extreme foreshortening where limbs seem to disappear into the depth of the painting.</note>, and similar effects. Ultimately, in this style of figure, the top parts are not seen unless they lean forward significantly.

Anyone who wishes to see figures in this manner should look in Milan, on the Street of Maravigli <note>Today the Via Meravigli.</note> near the Castle, at a fairly large facade of certain Roman histories. It was painted by the hand of **Troso da Monza** <note>An Italian painter of the late 15th century known for his work in Lombardy.</note>, and it is almost impossible that anyone could ever add anything more to it. It is truly most miraculous, both for the figures and for the architecture and <term>perspective</term> <note>Original: *prospettiua*. The art of representing three-dimensional objects on a two-dimensional surface.</note>, which is astounding. 

One should also see the work of **Bramantino** <note>Bartolomeo Suardi (c. 1465–1530), a Milanese painter and architect.</note> in Milan on the Lattuada facade while walking toward the Beatrice Gate, and another by his hand at the Eastern Gate; also in Santa Maria di Bari, above the organ shutters and at the head of the church. Furthermore, see in Mantua, at the Duke's palace, the *Triumph of Caesar* by the hand of **Andrea Mantegna** <note>One of the foremost artists of the 15th century, famous for his mastery of perspective and foreshortening.</note>. All these works are executed with order and intelligence. One may also see examples in Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, in the convent at the ends of the cloisters, in many "Histories" placed above eye level by the hand of **Bernardo Zenale** <note>An Italian painter and architect (c. 1460–1526) who worked with Leonardo da Vinci.</note>; and by the same artist, the organ shutters where an Annunciation is painted in San Simpliciano in Milan.

## On the Fourth Feigned Middle View. Chapter XVI.

**B**y the "middle view" or "middle line," we mean that which renders a body in such a way that the depths of the lower parts are seen rising from behind, and the upper parts are seen lowering from behind. For this reason, the viewer's direct gaze must relate to a specific part of the body, such as the middle. This is the least <term>foreshortened</term> <note>Original: *scurzata*. Depicting an object with less depth distortion because it is level with the viewer.</note> view of all; nevertheless, it involves all the difficulties considered in the others. In this style, the Chapel of Saint Peter and Saint Paul in San Francesco in Milan is painted by the hand of **Bernardo Zenale**; and by the same artist, along with **Bernardo Buttinone** <note>Bernardino Butinone (c. 1450–1510), a collaborator of Zenale known for his detailed, expressive style.</note> of Milan—who was highly intelligent in these matters—a chapel of the life of Saint Ambrose in the Temple of San Pietro Gessato in the same city.

...by **Bramantino** <note>Bartolomeo Suardi (c. 1465–1530), an influential Milanese painter and architect known for his mastery of perspective.</note> a *Christ Taken Down from the Cross*, likewise here in Milan, above the door of the Church of the Sepulcher; and above all by **Raphael** in Rome. ## *On the Fifth Feigned Inferior View. Chapter XVII.*

All the figures seen from above—whether a little or a lot—on a surface that is below the Horizon are formed by this view. It provides the logic for why they are made in such a way. It causes their back parts to rise high and recede, and their front parts to grow and lower. From below, it reveals what the superior view conversely shows from above. In other respects, it follows the order of the others and shares the same logic, even though the visual effects are different. Within this view are the three narrative scenes by **Michelangelo** painted in the Vatican in Rome: namely, the *Judgment of Christ* <note>The Last Judgment in the Sistine Chapel.</note> and *Saint Peter being pulled onto the Cross* <note>The Crucifixion of St. Peter in the Pauline Chapel.</note>, both of which are in the Pauline Chapel <note>While the Last Judgment is in the Sistine Chapel, the Crucifixion of St. Peter and the Conversion of Saul are in the adjacent Pauline Chapel. The author may be grouping these Vatican works together.</note>.

## *On the Sixth Feigned Deep or "Entering" View.*
## *Chapter XVIII.*

Across all facades, this view shows us bodies stretched out on the ground in <term>foreshortening</term> <note>Original: *scorto*. The technique of depicting an object or figure in a picture in depth.</note>, with the head facing toward the viewer and the feet facing away. These are the figures that seem to totally "enter" into the wall. This occurs in the same way—for example, directly at eye level—as a figure introduced by the first view does on perpendicular vaults. In this manner, we understand those figures that follow the ground plane so that they cannot be seen from above, but only from the front or from below. This applies to those looking at the heads of people standing on the plane, or indeed to those on mountains or towers looking down below. Thus, all these things are derived through such views—or, let us say, lines—which make them visible to us. They provide the reasoning for this through the same method they establish by means of flexions, elevations, turns, reflections, profiles, and the like. It would be a long and tedious task to discuss these further, as they are very obscure matters to treat. To avoid wearying the readers, it will suffice to show them clearly in practice in the following book.
