### On Inflections. Chapter XIX.

**I** call **inflections** <term>flexions</term> <note>Original: *flessioni*. This refers to the rotation and turning of limbs in space, and how the movement of one part affects the proportion of the whole.</note> those virtues that bodies provide through the specific characteristics of their limbs, proportioned to other bodies so that one quantity shows through another, as **Albrecht Dürer** partly teaches in the third book of his *Symmetry* <note>Referring to Dürer's "Four Books on Human Proportion" (1528), specifically the sections on the rotation and bending of the human figure.</note>. And from these, using the art of **diminutions** <note>The reduction in size of objects as they recede into the distance.</note>—which was partially discussed above—one derives perfect **foreshortenings**. How many ways these inflections may be made can be considered from the actions of the human body. For these show themselves to our sight standing, upright, from the front, from the side, from the back, and obliquely—that is, showing one eye and a half <note>A "three-quarter" view where the head is turned so that one eye is fully visible and the other only partially.</note>; and also stretched out from the parts above and those below.

Furthermore, they can be shown standing and curved: from the front, in face, in profile, obliquely, and from the back; and curved from behind in all these same positions; and also to the right, left, front, and back. Finally, all actions are named inflections; for there is no limb that does not require the inflection of another to be formed with proportional logic. And through these, all bodies are made in whatever action one desires—I do not mean in **foreshortening**, where the limbs lose and gain length, but I speak of their **proportion**. 

This is as Albrecht has shown in various heads and figures, where he clearly demonstrates with such order how to carry one quantity into another, and to form faces looking upward, others downward, obliquely, and others from the front, based on the logic of the bases of the limbs and similar principles. Thus, one sees that no one should think of making a proportioned figure without foreshortening if they do not also use inflection—that "virtue" or power of what one wants to do in profile by deriving it from the front or the back, and the others from the profile. In this, one limb is never placed above or below the other. In oblique views, they are likewise derived from other oblique views, but most certainly from the bases. And although there are many other reasons and ways regarding these natural inflections—especially for transferring them into perspective, which requires a deep intellect—nonetheless, I resolve to remain silent about them for now. This is because they belong more to the art of drawing than to writing, and it will be better to pass on to the **elevation** <note>Original: *levatione*. Likely referring to the geometric projection of a figure's height or the next stage of perspective construction.</note>.

<summary>This chapter defines "inflections" as the proportional rotation of the human body, distinguishing it from simple foreshortening and citing Albrecht Dürer's theories on human symmetry.</summary>

### On the elevation of bodies above the ground line. Chapter XX.

**N**o elevation <term>elevation</term> <note>Original: *leuatione*. This is the process of projecting a three-dimensional form upward from a two-dimensional ground plan.</note> of bodies can be performed unless it is arranged in profile and shown in the most convenient manner possible upon that line which I call the ground line <term>ground line</term> <note>Original: *linea piana*. This is the base line of the picture plane where the figures' feet are placed.</note>—that is, the line that remains after the cut <note>Original: *taglio*. In perspective theory, this refers to the intersection of the viewer's cone of vision with the surface of the painting.</note> from below or from above. And although it can be done in other ways, this one shall be followed. Now, this line is the one containing the bases of all the bodies that are to be elevated; and according to how well it is arranged, so shall the work be. Thus, one must pay very close attention to all the profiles on it, so that they show themselves perfectly. For this is the entire root and the foundation of the bodies—that is, of their ground plan—and it is what prevents one body from occupying the space of another in narrative paintings <note>Original: *historie*. These are complex scenes depicting historical, biblical, or mythological events.</note>, or a thing being placed where it cannot stand. It prevents one from being made larger than it ought to be, and ensures that bodies do not appear suspended in the air, or stuck underground in pits. It also prevents one from stretching the legs or taking a wider step than can be made, nor does it allow for similar inconveniences. But with the method and rule of this line, perfect works are made, so that all things recede through their proper degrees, and each body has its due losses and gains <note>Refers to the mathematical "loss" of size as objects recede and the "gain" in perceived volume through shading and positioning.</note>. In these elevations, one sees the distances of buildings in profile, very large in respect to the men, and their sizes and smallness according to the proportions of all the bodies. Because of this, when they are elevated and aided by other views, as is required by the act of seeing, they show themselves perfect without a single worry or fear of error—and if not perfect in other ways, at least in this part, in which consists the primary strength of the art. In this, **Andrea Mantegna** and **Bernardo Zenale** <note>Mantegna (c. 1431–1506) was famous for his radical use of perspective and foreshortening; Zenale (c. 1460–1526) was a Milanese architect and painter who wrote a treatise on perspective.</note> were excellent. And let this be said of elevations, under which all the remainder belonging to it can be considered. Now, bringing an end to perspective—that is, the way of seeing and placing things according to reason—I will say a few things about the other manner of bastard perspective <term>bastard perspective</term> <note>Original: *prospettiua bastarda*. This refers to practical or "shorthand" perspective methods used by painters that did not strictly follow the rigorous mathematical rules of central projection.</note>, so that nothing taught by our ancestors and used in their works remains untouched.

But returning to the beginning, Bramantino writes that Perspective is something that counterfeits nature, and that this is done in three ways: one with reason <note>Meaning mathematical or logical principles.</note>, the other without reason but solely through practice <note>Meaning through experience and visual estimation rather than geometry.</note>, and the third by a mixture of practice and reason. Regarding the first way, which is done with reason—since the matter was concluded by Bramantino in so few words that I judge it could not be said better <margin>I.</margin> as it contains all the art from beginning to end—I will report his own words exactly.

**T**he first perspective creates things from a point <note>Refers to the vanishing point.</note>, the second never does, and the third is closer. Therefore, the first is called perspective—that is, "reason"—which produces the effect of the eye, making things increase and decrease according to the eye's effects. <margin>I.</margin> This increasing and decreasing does not proceed from the object itself, which cannot increase or decrease in itself simply by being far or near; rather, it proceeds from the effects of the eyes. These are small, and therefore, wishing to see such a large thing, they must send out their visual virtue <term>visual virtue</term> <note>Original: *virtù visiua*. Therefore, by cutting <note>This refers to the "section" or "intersection" of the visual pyramid—the flat plane (like a canvas) that cuts through the rays of light traveling from the object to the eye.</note> it in different places, it appears larger or smaller, according to the cut that is made; even though, if one does not move from the eye's position while looking at it in its place, it will always appear the same way. Because the eye captures less of that which is further away, and by this means many beautiful things can be seen and made. And let it be known that this perspective, which is done by reason, measure, and order, is practiced with the compass and the ruler, and with the rule of the said perspective—that is, <term>braccia</term> <note>A common Italian unit of measurement, literally "arms," roughly equivalent to 23 inches depending on the region.</note>, ounces, minutes, poles, and miles. ## *Second way of perspective of Bramantino. Chap. XXIII.*

**T**he other second part is done without any measurement—that is, by drawing or imitating nature, or by working from the imagination. Of this sort, one finds more painters than any other, and they are held as talented because they take pains to imitate reality minutely and create fantasies according to it; but nonetheless, in their works, one sees great errors which are not committed by those who are intelligent in the "reason of seeing" <note>The theoretical principles of optics and geometry.</note> and of working as I have described.

And that which strikes the veil is then outlined or profiled upon the veil, while everything remains still. Because if one of the parts were to move, everything that had been done would then become false, unless it were returned to its original place. # BOOK SIX
## ON PRACTICE,
### OF PAINTING,
### BY GIOVAN PAOLO LOMAZZO,
### *Milanese Painter.*

->*On the virtue of practice. Chapter I.*<-

**T**here is no doubt that all things which are well-composed and fitting among themselves—that is, those which have their parts corresponding to one another in the manner that I will demonstrate through practice <term>practice (prattica)|The physical execution and hands-on application of artistic rules, distinct from abstract theory.</term> in this book, where it is taught precisely how to join this practice with the theory <term>theory (theorica)|The underlying principles, rules, and mathematical foundations of art.</term> of the matters treated above in the previous books—bring the greatest delight. Furthermore, they fully demonstrate the intent of the one who composed them. On the contrary, those things which are discordant and disordered, being repugnant to natural sweetness and intellectual clarity, bring with them the greatest displeasure, equally offending the eyes of the ignorant through their natural senses and the eyes of the learned through their understanding. 

Thus, we must consider that just as composition <term>composition (compositione)|The art of arranging figures, objects, and colors within a work to create a harmonious whole.</term> is one of the most important parts of painting—since it is through composition that painting is known and practically demonstrated to our eyes—so too is the entire connection and embrace of all things contained within it. For it is composition alone which, by joining all the other parts together, brings the entire body of art <note>Original: *tutto il fascio dell’arte*. Literally "the whole bundle of art," referring to the totality of artistic principles.</note> almost by itself to the knowledge of mortals. Because through the union and coupling of fitting things—both natural things learned through imitation and experience, and mathematical things learned through speculation and philosophical foundations—each body is rendered perfect according to its composed nature. This allows the inventions and subjects that have been composed to be seen with great decorum, with vast abundance, and with admirable judgment, in those proper manners, as if they were natural, with ingenious skills and a thousand ornaments. These render those narrative scenes <note>Original: *historie*. In Renaissance theory, this refers to complex paintings that tell a story, usually from history, mythology, or the Bible, considered the highest form of painting.</note> before our eyes as bright and beautiful as is the Sun

...sun at midday near the shadows. But how much help, and at the same time how much satisfaction, does this happy and ingenious faculty bring us? For all the <term>caprices (capricci)|Artistic whims or imaginative inventions that go beyond literal representation.</term>, fantasies, and <term>quirks (gheribizzi)|Playful or eccentric creative ideas.</term> that spring from the mind are shown with such ornament in the works and such enhancement of ordinary paintings. It provides us with so many lovely instruments that adorn both sacred temples and the illustrious palaces of kings; and likewise, within the <term>histories (historie)|Narrative or history paintings depicting significant events from the Bible, mythology, or history.</term> themselves, it provides many ornaments, labors, caprices, whims, and so many other details. These elements, for us painters, enlarge and embellish the subjects of our paintings, in no different a way than Homer and Virgil, with their lovely poetic inventions, raised so far above the truth and embellished the wars of the Greeks and Trojans, and the wanderings and adventures of Aeneas, which were certainly not as great as they have been sung by them. 

What shall we say then of the simple meanings through which this faculty teaches and shows in figure its entire nature? It teaches us how to compose any imagined thing, from which spring so many beauties of the soul and contentments of the imagination through the composition that can be made of emblems, arms, fables, and the like. This suggests that it also falls to the painter to demonstrate in figures the <note>The author argues that painting is a moral and educational tool, not just decorative.</note> instructions of human actions through natural things, ordered to signify according to their nature by means of the histories they paint. In this way, they are not only understood, but enjoyed and seen almost in the same manner in which they occurred. 

These are things, however, that may be called part of ordinary painting. But these other demonstrations—most subtle in their knowledge, most profound in their sense, delightful in their example, and admirable for the splendor they provide to wise and truly virtuous souls—cannot be called so "ordinary." For in them, there must shine the vividness of celestial splendors, of natural furies, of intellectual studies, of bodily diligences, and of the <note>Original: *purgationi de’ colori*. This is so that they are not considered coarse paintings, but excellent and rare ones, painted for no other reason than to continually show through the eyes to the soul the true path that must be taken to live well and pass these unhappy days of ours—which are made of <term>light and shadow (chiaro & scuro)|While a technical term for light and shade in art, Lomazzo uses it here metaphorically to describe the joys and sorrows of human life.</term>—with the fear and love of that Lord whose goodness wished to form us in the likeness of His own most divine image. Thus composed, as those who might understand all things—intelligible, celestial, and elementary—we might dispose of them in the proper manner and compose them with their rightful circumstances. We do this so that within this <note>A common Neoplatonic metaphor of the era, viewing the physical body as a "dark prison" from which the soul seeks to perceive divine truth through art and intellect.</note> dark and gloomy prison of our body, these things would not make a clamor, as they do at every hour, discordantly...

### *On the Necessity of Practice.* Chapter 2.

**S**ince we have finally finished with the theoretical principles of this art, it remains for me in this book to discuss composition, so that we may proceed in an orderly fashion. I will show how the concepts discussed in the previous books work together and how they should be reasonably combined. This, in short, will be the subject of this entire book, where we will discuss nothing but how to put into <term>practice (prattica)|The application of theoretical rules to create a finished work of art.</term> everything a painter is expected to do and may need to represent—as I already mentioned in the first book regarding this genre and its types. For this "practice" is nothing more than the logic by which the various parts are organized in works of painting. It is of such importance and necessity in this art that if anyone tries to work without its logic and assistance, it is impossible for them to create anything praiseworthy or well-executed. 

The principles of practice are founded first on the knowledge of the topics covered in the previous books; that is why I discussed them first as a foundation. Now I follow with the study of practice, which teaches us how to combine all those elements with reason and judgment. Thus we see that a painter, in composing his works, must necessarily understand the subject and the nature of the things he wishes to combine, as discussed above. 

However, in composition, one must always be careful to avoid an overabundance of parts, as well as "poverty" (a lack of detail). Excess leads to confusion and <term>affectation (affettatione)|An artificial or forced style that lacks naturalness.</term>, which must be avoided above all things; while a lack of detail results in dryness and nakedness in the work. Therefore, the latter must be avoided as much as the former by sticking to the "middle path" with beauty, grace, and majesty. One should always be guided by the spirit of the <term>narrative (iſtoria)|The story or subject matter being depicted.</term>. From this arises good composition—a part of painting so essential that it is considered serious and good only in proportion to how closely it resembles the truth in all its parts. 

If one wishes to vary the truth in any part, one must pay attention to appropriateness and the enhancement of the emotional effect, imitating the poets. In many ways, painters are like poets; both in painting and in poetry, there flows the <term>divine frenzy of Apollo (furor di Apolline)|The classical idea that the artist or poet is inspired by a god (Apollo) to create beyond human capability.</term>, and both take as their subject the illustrious deeds and the praises of heroes...

<summary>Lomazzo introduces Chapter 2, shifting focus from theory to 'practice'—the practical logic of composition. He argues that a painter must find a balance between excess and simplicity, comparing the painter's divine inspiration to that of a poet.</summary>

One also reads of other great <term>gymnosophist (gimnosofisti)|Originally an ancient term for Indian "naked philosophers," Lomazzo uses it here to describe painters who are also profound thinkers or philosopher-artists.</term> painters, such as Michelangelo Buonarroti, Gaudenzio Ferrari, Bernardino Luini, and the <term>Bernesque (bernesco)|A style of humorous or satirical poetry named after Francesco Berni; Lomazzo is noting that the painter Bronzino also wrote in this literary style.</term> Bronzino. And from this general conformity that we say is found between painters and poets, there also follows a particular one: that a painter naturally possesses a genius more in harmony with one poet than another; and in his work, he has followed that poet, as is easy for anyone to observe among modern painters.

For it is seen that Leonardo da Vinci expressed the motions and decorum of Homer; Polidoro da Caravaggio the grandeur and fury of Virgil; Michelangelo Buonarroti the profound <term>obscurity (oscurezza)|In a Renaissance context, this refers to intellectual depth, complexity, and the use of difficult metaphors that require deep contemplation.</term> of Dante; Raphael the pure majesty of Petrarch; Andrea Mantegna the sharp wisdom of Sannazaro; Titian the variety of Ariosto; and Gaudenzio Ferrari the devotion found expressed in the books of the Saints. 

Now, returning to the discourse previously set aside, beyond the aforementioned warnings for good practice, it is primarily necessary to take heed of the **point** from which all lines derive, which go from their places on the circumference; just as in the triangle, the square, the circle, and all other forms. And the point is properly the principal figure that is placed in the middle of the aforementioned shapes. Therefore, it should be represented as a single figure that is self-contained. And in a line that has two points at its ends, the figures placed upon them should look toward one another, ending in the point that is in the middle. In a triangle, which has three parts, the figures placed above each of these parts must likewise look toward the point; so too in a square, which has four corners; and finally in a circle, however many figures one wishes to place around it, all must look toward the point, as if toward the primary cause and principal subject from which all other parts derive. 

Therefore, the principal figures should be placed in the middle, and all other parts should be placed around them. Of this natural wisdom, testimony is given by the first <term>histories (historie)|Narrative paintings depicting significant religious, mythological, or historical events.</term> made by the rarest painters our age has had. Such as Raphael in the <note>original: "loggie Papali." Lomazzo is likely referring to the frescoes in the Vatican Stanze, specifically the Stanza della Segnatura.</note> Papal Logge in a large painting, where theology is reconciled with philosophy, and in the middle is the **Sacred Host** <note>This describes the fresco known as the *Disputation of the Holy Sacrament*.</note> above the altar with the Doctors of the Church around it, and behind them other people who dispute over these things. There is also another history where he depicts Saint Paul in Athens preaching to the philosophers. And furthermore, he has depicted Mount Parnassus with the Muses, the poets, and Apollo in the middle as the regulator of the whole. Testimony is also given by the painting...

...of Michelangelo Buonarroti, in the Papal Chapel <note>The Sistine Chapel in the Vatican.</note>, where he has represented Christ, who judges the good and the guilty in the middle, as the principal subject. In short, so many admirable works and panels seen throughout the world are all made in this manner by prudent craftsmen; who, also in palaces, in wars, and triumphs, must place the prince in the middle of the skirmish as the main subject, and likewise the victorious Captain in a triumph. 

In lascivious subjects, one must avoid all those parts that might offend the eyes of the continent <note>Lomazzo uses "continent" to mean virtuous or self-restrained viewers.</note>; rather they should be expressed in a way that nothing shameful is seen, but is covered with dexterity and grace. For even though many sharp and prudent painters maintain that nothing can be created unless these masteries and lascivious acts are interspersed—as Raphael, Cesare da Sesto, Michelangelo, Leonardo, Giulio Romano, Parmigianino, Perino del Vaga, and all the other excellent artists have done—nonetheless, in religious places, the facades and panels must be arranged in a way that conforms to the nobility of the eyes. This is to say that the hindquarters of horses and other animals should not be seen from the front, but from behind, as a part unworthy of being seen; instead, they should be made to show the front, and those parts that can offend the eyes should be left in the back. 

In short, all these things must be arranged with <term>prudence (prudenza)|In Renaissance art theory, this refers to the artist's practical wisdom and judgment in making choices that balance beauty, decorum, and technical necessity.</term>; because it is prudence that gives style and grace to all things. Hence, wanting to make, for example, a painting that was of <term>sesquialtera proportion (proportione sesquialtera)|A ratio of 3:2.</term> in height, one should make the figure of <term>sesquiquarta proportion (proportione sesquiquarta)|A ratio of 5:4.</term> in height; and if in larger <term>histories (istorie)|Narrative paintings depicting grand scenes from the Bible, mythology, or history, considered the highest form of art.</term> one increases the size, one must acutely make the figures grow a little more than the natural beauty of the sight, for the suitability it has with them, even if the histories are in double, triple, and quadruple proportion. 

This method, however, is intended for nearby facades; because for those seen from a distance, one must use <term>perspective prudence (prudenza prospettica)|The use of visual judgment to correct distortions that occur when a painting is viewed from far away or at an angle.</term> even more. These should be designed and sketched with a long rod, so that the eye can master them well and look at the whole; and having mastered the parts, the artist will go closer, arranging the limbs with a shorter rod, so that the history turns out expressed with true prudence. Now, having said enough about this necessity of practice, I will continue to speak of the rules of proportion, and then the others as you will understand by reading.

### **_Rules of proportion concerning the human body. Chap. III._**

**T**he limbs must be <term>symmetrical|From the Greek 'symmetria,' meaning a balanced agreement of parts based on a common measure.</term> among themselves, measured, and harmonically proportioned; so that one does not see in any figure a large head, a small chest, a wide hand, one leg longer than the other, and similar flaws. To avoid such errors in proportion, it will be a most useful rule to keep in the mind and memory the quantity and measure of the principal bones in every proportion. If one does not do this, it is at least necessary to have in the mind the proportion that the principal bones have to one another; because according to the doctrine of *Aristotle*, that which remains fixed and varies or moves little, measures—or at least provides the rule for the measure of—that which moves, namely the flesh. <note>Lomazzo is applying Aristotle's physical principles to anatomy: the rigid skeleton serves as the "fixed" ruler for the "moving" muscles and skin.</note> Because bones never bend, they always occupy their proper space. Therefore, having their proportion in the memory, one will not make any significant error in the proportion of the whole body, even though the flesh, the specific muscles, and the skin may bend or move. And whoever knows the proportion of the bones together with the proportion of the muscles would be a master of the art. 

To create a clothed figure that is well-proportioned, it is appropriate to first draw it naked with its true proportions; in this way, it will still turn out symmetrical when it is later clothed. But because many rules will be taught in various places throughout this book and in others concerning Theory, I will state as a general rule that—to ensure any errors in proportion remain bearable—it is wise to make the hands and fingers long rather than short, and the head small rather than thick. This was the practice of *Lysippus* <note>A famous Greek sculptor of the 4th century BCE known for changing the traditional proportions of the human head to make his statues appear taller and more graceful.</note> (even though *Zeuxis* <note>An ancient Greek painter famous for his realism; some critics of the time felt his figures were too bulky.</note> always made heads large, for which he was criticized). One should also make the chest wide rather than narrow, the feet small rather than large, and the legs with long shins rather than short ones. Such proportions are tolerated in many talented men because they add beauty to beauty, as will be understood even more clearly in the Chapter on the practical application of light. 

Another rule of proportion is that it has its foundation not only in quantity—both continuous and discrete—but also in quality. <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "continuous quantity" refers to geometry and lines, while "discrete quantity" refers to arithmetic and numbers. "Quality" refers to the character or "decorum" of the subject.</note> Therefore, it is necessary to observe this as well; for example, do not give *Eve* in *Paradise* the hands of an old woman; nor give to *Nestor* or *Job* <note>Biblical and classical figures associated with extreme old age and suffering.</note> the neck and chest of *Ganymede* <note>The beautiful youth abducted by Zeus to be cupbearer to the gods.</note>; nor give to *Narcissus* the robust legs of *Milo of Croton* <note>A legendary ancient Greek wrestler famed for his immense strength.</note>; and do not, as many are accustomed to do, give smooth and beautiful flesh to someone who has a snowy white beard and eyebrows. It is fitting

# BOOK II

One must therefore proportion the whole in such a way that no part is devoid of its own proper and fitting function; so that the limbs of the dead belong to the dead, down to the last fingernail, and those of the living are suited to other similar harmonies, which must be shown in every <term>history|In Renaissance art theory, a 'history' (storia) refers to a narrative or storytelling painting, usually depicting a significant biblical, classical, or historical event.</term>. And one must take care not to act like certain painters who steal a hand from *Michelangelo’s* *Moses*, a piece of drapery from a print, a foot from the *Apollo*, or a head from *Venus*—things that it is impossible to fit together harmoniously. For it is a certain rule that it is impossible for a figure created in one place for one specific purpose to ever be used again in another place for a different purpose. 

Also contrary to this precept is the painting of buildings while Adam sins in Paradise—as *Raphael* did, according to a print of his engraved by *Marcantonio* <note>original: "Marco Antonio," referring to Marcantonio Raimondi, the famous engraver who popularized Raphael’s designs.</note>—or the painting of cities while Cain kills Abel, and the like. <note>Lomazzo is criticizing anachronisms, such as placing modern architecture in prehistoric biblical scenes.</note> Therefore, one must pay even more attention to the observation of these proportions, because even the wisest artists stumble; one should especially avoid making figures that do not serve the true proportion, an error into which one of the "two greats" <note>Lomazzo likely refers to Raphael and Michelangelo as the "two greats."</note> fell. 

That proportion maintained by *Raphael* in the painting for Saint Dominic in Naples <note>Likely referring to the 'Madonna del Pesce,' which was originally in the church of San Domenico in Naples.</note> is contrary to the rules of art; for he makes *Raphael the Archangel* of a goodly height, while *Tobias* is shown as a small child who, in that tender and immature age, could not realistically have made such a long journey and walked so many miles as the Scripture describes. <note>The Book of Tobit describes Tobias as a young man capable of a long journey, rather than a small child.</note> 

In histories and compositions of many figures, it is required that the painter be varied in proportion, because a consonant variety delights through the harmony that resonates within it. To this end, in my book on proportion, I have described various manners of proportions for men, women, and children, as well as for other things. This precept is general for these parts of painting—namely, for movement and for coloring—because in every history, the more the painter varies the proportion, age, movement, and <term>decorum|The suitability of a figure's appearance, gestures, and clothing to their social status and the specific context of the scene.</term> of the figures, and the more charming he is in his coloring, the more delightful he makes the history. This has been done excellently, above all others, by *Raphael*, *Polidoro*, and *Gaudenzio*, and among the Germans, *Albrecht Dürer*, *Lucas of Holland* <note>Lucas van Leyden.</note>, and *Jan Mabuse*. 

The proportion of the human body consisting of ten faces is the most beautiful of all; for this reason, the wise ancient sculptors made their god *Jupiter*, who was the prince of all, with this proportion. Hence, if a painter wishes to depict a man of the most beautiful symmetry, he will make him with this proportion, which truly is the one that befits Emperors, Kings, and Monarchs. And it was with this proportion that the ancient painters formed their figures, as the haughty *Parrhasius* used for the great...

# BOOK SIX

<note>original: "S E S T O" refers to the sixth book of Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo's treatise on painting.</note>

...the great **relief** <term>relief|In painting, 'relief' (rilievo) refers to the illusion of three-dimensional depth and volume created through light and shadow.</term> that he gave to them; **Apelles** <note>The most famous painter of ancient Greece, known for his grace and beauty.</note> for his **loveliness**, and **Protogenes** <note>A Greek painter and rival of Apelles, famed for his meticulous finish.</note> for his **extreme diligence**. And among the moderns, this is seen for **majesty** and **beauty** in **Raphael**; for **fury** and **grandeur** in **Rosso** <note>Rosso Fiorentino (1494–1540), a leading Mannerist painter known for expressive, sometimes frantic figures.</note>; for **care** and **industry** in **Perino** <note>Perino del Vaga (1501–1547), a pupil of Raphael.</note>; for **grace** and **lightness** in **Mazzolino** <note>Francesco Mazzola, known as Parmigianino (1503–1540), famous for his elegant, elongated proportions.</note>; and for **fierceness** in **Polidoro** <note>Polidoro da Caravaggio (c. 1499–1543), known for his dynamic facade paintings in Rome.</note>. 

After this, the ancients—considering that the human proportion of **nine heads** holds the second place in beauty—made certain of their Gods, such as **Apollo** and **Bacchus**, of this stature. Among us, this same proportion can be used to paint **Saint George**, **Saint Michael**, **Saint Sebastian**, and similar figures. But while Apollo and Bacchus require limbs and muscles that are soft and gentle, accompanied by a graceful slenderness and a pleasant, soft delicacy, **Bacchus** must also exceed this a bit more, as one who spends his life in delights and luxury in the company of the **Muses** all day long. **Apollo**, meanwhile, must be represented as a bit more fierce in his muscles due to the exercise of archery; in all other respects, both must always be young and beautiful.

The proportion of **eight heads** holds the third rank in beauty, and of this the ancients made their **Neptune**, as he is less delicate than that of **Jove** <note>Jupiter, the king of the gods.</note>. With such a proportion, Neptune and the men who are painted in this degree of beauty require limbs composed with a bit of rawness and relief, so that the muscles appear deeper and more fierce than in Jove; and in this manner, ordinary men are to be painted.

The proportion of **seven heads** is suited for making **robust men**, with broad shoulders and prominent limbs, such as soldiers and other strong and sturdy men. To these belong thick limbs and prominent, strong muscles that demonstrate a sense of **terribleness** <note>In Renaissance art, 'terribilità' refers to an awe-inspiring, emotional power or fearful intensity, most famously associated with Michelangelo.</note>, standing tall without sagging at all as weak bodies do. This involves a binding of the whole torso with all the principal muscles, while largely avoiding the small ones, because these [the large muscles] alone make the body very strong and fearsome to behold. A miraculous example of this is seen in Rome, in the **Campo de' Fiori** at the **Farnese Palace**, in that **Hercules** <note>The Farnese Hercules, a famous ancient statue discovered in 1546.</note> made by the hand of the excellent Greek sculptor called **Glycon** <note>original: "Glaucone." Glycon of Athens was the sculptor who signed the Farnese Hercules.</note>.

The proportion of the man-at-arms, the **choleric** <term>choleric|One of the four humors (temperaments) in pre-modern medicine, associated with yellow bile, fire, and a quick-tempered, ambitious nature.</term> and martial man, requires limbs composed with great rawness: distinct, lean, and pulled upwards. This means, for example, the calves of the legs should be very high and far from the heels, and the shoulders pulled upwards so that they seem to have a certain thickness, no different from Hercules; because of this, they seem to have a bit of a hunch. In addition to this, they should be somewhat long and twisted, as should the fingers of the hand and the feet.

...the feet must be very thick at the joints and thin in the spaces between, even if they are long and free. And in this manner were the figures of **Apelles** <note>The most celebrated painter of ancient Greece, known for his refinement.</note> said to be, of whom it is said that he made them more lean and thin than all others. And so **Pluto** <note>God of the Underworld.</note> was painted with limbs and muscles more rustic and strong than **Neptune**, and consequently more **raised** <term>raised|In Italian 'rilevato,' referring here to muscles that stand out prominently from the body, creating high relief.</term>, visible, strong, and well-squared, so that seeing them they conveyed a certain daring and strength, not otherwise than robust, well-made bodies which, through labor, have highly defined muscles, such as those of peasants, galley slaves, and the like. 

This manner was followed by **Michelangelo**, who was truly born to paint strong, robust, and fierce men, and not soft, sweet, and gentle **Adonises** <note>Adonis was the mortal lover of Aphrodite, the epitome of youthful male beauty.</note>. And for this reason, perhaps, he did not wish to carve the missing hand for the **Adonis of Campo di Fiore** in Rome, in the house of the **Bishop of Norcia** <note>An ancient statue of a youth found in Rome; Michelangelo reportedly declined to restore it because its delicate style did not suit his own "terribilità" or fierce manner.</note>. For a beautiful body, such as that of **Jove** <note>Jupiter, king of the gods.</note> or of **Adonis**, the painter will not make rustic or irregular limbs, such as those prominent limbs of **Hercules**; but rather he will look to a harmonic sweetness of the most beautiful and delicate limbs without any harshness. 

The same shall be observed in **Christ**, though not with limbs so sweet and delicate that they cannot demonstrate proper virility in the best and most beautiful way possible. This same rule shall be held in the painting of **Hercules**—that is, one shall not mix in the sweetest and most delicate limbs of Adonis. Thus, that ancient painting was of the greatest excellence in which the dead **Meleager** <note>A Greek hero; the scene of his body being carried was a famous model for depicting the "dead weight" of a corpse.</note> was depicted, where those who carried him appeared to struggle and strain with all their limbs; and in the dead man, no limb was seen that did not perform its office of being dead, since they all hung down and were abandoned.

The proportion of **ten faces** <note>A measurement system where the total body height is ten times the length of the face from the chin to the hairline.</note>, which in the book of proportion we have attributed to **Venus**, is suitable for all the most beautiful women. Here it is necessary to have great consideration: that in the painting of **Venus**, for example, or of any beautiful woman, the limbs should be extremely soft, in such a way that no harshness is seen nor even suggested; and that they do not sag, but are well-attached so that they do not spread, and in short, no greater tenderness could be desired. This is something I greatly observe in the works of **Nicias** <note>An Athenian painter of the 4th century BCE.</note>, the ancient painter, and also **Zeuxis**, and more than these, **Apelles**, who showed to our eyes the so-celebrated Venus, in which he surpassed the songs of **Homer**. And among the sculptors, it was happily observed by whoever made the **Venus** that is seen in Rome at the vineyard of **Pope Julius**, and that other craftsman who made the **Venus of the Belvedere**, and **Francesco Mo-**

-> # SIXTH BOOK <-

**Schino** <note>Francesco Moschino (c. 1523–1578), a prominent Italian sculptor.</note>, an exceptional sculptor who created the <term>Venus</term> larger than life-size which is found in the possession of the **Duke of Savoy**; and likewise, on par with the ancients themselves, **Raphael**, **Perino**, **Rosso**, **Mazzolino**, and **Correggio** have known how to observe this, especially in drawing and coloring young women with those proportions and that **softness** <term>softness|The Italian 'morbidezza,' a technical term in Renaissance art referring to a lifelike, tender, and subtle rendering of flesh and transitions between light and shadow.</term> that befit them. And along this same path, **Andrea del Sarto**, **Gaudenzio**, and **Pordenone** were equally ready in depicting children. The same softness, as expressed by **Leonardo da Vinci**, is also required in the Christ child and in other infants who require limbs that are round, gentle, and full of sweetness, without raw or harsh muscles. 

But this proportion of ten heads for the female is extraordinary; and from this, one may create the nymphs of the mountains, flowers, meadows, and springs. In short, it is suited to women who are extravagant or dedicated to such pursuits. The ancients made the statue of **Juno** with a proportion of nine faces; considering that **Juno** was not as "heavy" <note>In the sense of being somber or matronly.</note> as the Goddess **Vesta**. And because she is also not as slender nor as perfectly beautiful as **Venus**, they did not make her less than ten faces. 

From this proportion <note>The nine-face canon.</note>, one can create all women of moderate beauty and authority, such as Queens, Duchesses, and the like. For these women, when they pass out of the age of "Venereal" youth <note>The age of youthful beauty associated with Venus.</note>, the limbs must be composed together in such a way that they begin to sag somewhat, such as the breasts, the fleshy parts, and similar areas; and the belly and the waist should thicken, since they are losing their youthful freshness and are spreading out somewhat, becoming soft and languid. Of all these precepts, one sees admirable examples in the ancient statues, both in Rome and in other places. 

Regarding the proportion of nine heads, it is understood from the remains left by antiquity that those most skilled ancient sculptors attributed it to **Minerva**, **Diana**, and **Flora**; because this scale of bodies is entirely slender and full of elegance and grace. Therefore, it will suit virgins of moderate beauty very well. For the ten-face proportion holds the first place, that of nine the second, and this one the third. This third proportion is also suitable for women who possess agility, quickness, and speed, such as certain virgins, nymphs, and Muses; and in particular for <term>Minerva</term>, <note>original: "Miuerua"; the text contains a typo for the goddess of wisdom and war.</note> there are required the most beautiful composed limbs, with a certain liveliness and fierce spirit that is fit to show her as one practiced in war; and yet with a certain sharpness and measure without any heaviness or impediment, so that she may likewise be recognized as excellent in wisdom. Hence, one shall give her limbs drawn upwards, which do not sag at all, well-attached, and always beautiful...

...without excessive **softness** <term>softness|The Italian 'morbidezza,' referring to a tender, lifelike rendering of flesh.</term>, but tightened, thin, and small-boned, with sharp eyes sparkling from beneath the helmet like two stars. The muscles should be barely apparent, indicated at the joints <note>original: "chiaui," literally 'keys,' a technical term for the anatomical points where limbs connect or pivot.</note> of the limbs with subtle drawing; the nose should be slender and sharp, and likewise the eyes. The breasts should be small, and only slightly more raised than those of a male, and the lips thin; in this manner the ancient **Assyrian** warriors and **Amazons** are also painted.

The proportion of the female of eight, and even seven heads, is suitable for very grave matrons full of majesty; hence the ancient sculptors made the Goddess **Vesta** <note>Vesta was the Roman goddess of the hearth; she was traditionally depicted as a fully draped, somber, and dignified woman.</note> of such proportion, and we can do the same for the **Virgin Mother** [Mary] from the time of the Passion of Christ onwards. From this [canon], one can create the **Sibyls**, and **Miriam** the sister of **Moses**, and similar prophetesses, and matrons of great authority, as well as other old, large, and fat matrons who are better suited to the proportion of seven [heads]. The limbs and muscles of mother **Vesta**, who is matched by old and heavy matrons, must have few muscles and be sagging—such as the belly, the breasts, the buttocks, the cheeks, the calves, and similar places where fat abounds along with the flesh.

Then, children who are beginning to walk and support themselves require limbs where the muscles are a bit more pronounced and less soft, as in a **Saint John** next to **Christ**; in him, the limbs will be made thinner and somewhat more muscular, yet still so tenderly that vigor and slenderness are seen. Regarding the length of the body, the general rule is that a child of six heads—that is, at three years of age—reaches half the height he is meant to be; a child of five [heads] reaches the mid-thigh of the father; and one of four heads—that is, at six months—reaches only to the knee. 

Beyond these rules, the painter must consider the quality of each limb; that is, whether it is soft, or from a fat or thin person. Likewise, when the figure is seated upon some stone or other hard object, the buttocks must be seen to widen and overflow outward due to the thickness and quantity of the flesh. A similar effect is seen in the **Magdalene** belonging to the **King of Spain** <note>This likely refers to one of the versions of the 'Penitent Magdalene' by Titian sent to Philip II of Spain.</note>, whose right breast is pressed by her own right hand, and therefore gently swollen. Following this example and many other works by talented men, such as **Titian** and others, we can regulate the representation of all other parts; for instance, when someone tilts their face to one side, make the hanging part of the cheek swell, while the other side pulls back and lengthens. ...rest on something, and the feet, as they rest, should spread out; and likewise the calf of a leg placed over a knee—which, being hard, causes little movement where the flesh widens. And even though the **Satyr** and the **Centaur** have different limbs, it is nonetheless necessary that the **Satyr** and similar monsters have their own proportions in such a way that their middle is exactly in the same place where a man's is; and from there downwards, the goat-like legs (or whatever other limbs of other monsters) should correspond to one another. The painter should also take care that, in order to show himself skilled in the art of **Anatomy**, he does not express every single muscle in every body that the anatomist finds when practicing his art on natural bodies—as **Michelangelo** <note>Michelangelo Buonarroti was often criticized by contemporary theorists for his "terribilità" and his tendency to over-emphasize musculature, making even his female figures look like "bags of walnuts."</note> did—but rather, imitating the most prudent **Raphael** in this, follow nature. Nature shows almost all muscles as raised in a **Hercules** or a **Martial** <note>A soldier-like or warrior type.</note> man; but in a youth or a beautiful woman, she covers and hides certain muscles, while others she reveals softly, showing them covered gently by flesh and skin with a certain harmonic **softness** <term>softness|morbidezza: a technical term for the tender, lifelike rendering of flesh and the subtle transitions between light and shadow.</term>. The limbs must be well-attached, so that they do not sag, or dilate, or twist out of place, although sometimes reason dictates they should dilate and twist in accordance with the motion or violence of the natural body. 

The surface—especially in the human body—is the greatest part of beauty, such that a face where the surfaces are joined together in such a way, and with such art, that the lights glide softly, generating gentle shadows without any harshness of angles, will deservedly be said to possess a principal part of beauty. On the contrary, that face which has some large surfaces and others small, pushed outward in one part and too hidden or recessed in another—as seen in the elderly—will truly be very ugly to see. And what is said of the face is understood for the whole body. 

In short, superficial beauty consists in this: that the form or body has neither too much of the concave nor too much of the spherical, but maintains a middle ground; because that small amount of concavity makes it appear masculine, whereas without it, it would appear too much like a child. And if it held too much of the concave and the thin, it would appear too much like an old man. To the beauty of figures, that which the talented ancient sculptors used to do adds much—that is, a certain tuft of hair on the forehead, which certainly brings a "know-not-what" <note>original: "non sò che," a phrase meaning an indefinable quality of grace or charm.</note> of beauty and grace, leaving the forehead lower by a third. Because of this effect, the ancients also used to represent...

...represent beautiful women in this manner: that is, with a small head; with a forehead neither too wide nor too high; with arched eyebrows; with large eyes; with a moderately long neck; with narrow shoulders; and with the upper arms thick and round, tapering down toward the hands; with long, soft hands and long nails, which at the tips are slightly upturned, yet narrow and thin; with a broad and raised chest and some space between one breast and the other; with a narrow waist; with a raised and prominent belly and a deep navel; with wide hips and thick, round thighs; long from the hip to the knee, and from the knee down somewhat shorter than in a man; and finally, with small feet. 

Ultimately, it is also necessary in figures—and especially in **histories** <term>histories|historie: large-scale narrative paintings depicting significant events from the Bible, mythology, or history, considered the highest form of art.</term>—to maintain the proper proportions of weapons, clothing, habits, and, in short, all other things. For the Italian arms and dresses himself in one fashion, the German in another, the Turk in another, and the ancient Roman in yet another. Many sin against this precept, who in certain battle scenes depict people armed in the Roman fashion as Germans, or barbarians and moderns as ancients, or Spaniards armed as Romans, and Frenchmen dressed in the Spanish style.

## *Rules for the motion of the human body. Chapter IV.*

**H**aving discussed for the most part the movements that can be caused in a body by the various **affects of the soul** <note>The "affetti dell'animo" refer to the internal emotions or passions that manifest as physical gestures.</note>, it is right that we also speak of the movements proper to the body itself. This is so that when making it move in every possible way, one does not end up crippling it or making it stretch its limbs in a manner that is neither possible nor natural. These movements arise from the logic of the lengths, widths, and proportions of the limbs; from their pressing against one another, their rotation, and their coming together with logic and possibility; and further from their twisting, turning, and stretching as far as is possible, according to their **linkages** <note>original: "incatenature" — referring to the way joints are "chained" or hinged together</note> and their **pivots** <note>original: "chiaui" (keys) — a metaphorical term for the mechanical points of rotation in the joints.</note>. 

And these are of such importance that I certainly hold that in them consists the entire importance of the art, and all the praise of the figures—and, conversely, all the shame. For it is from the neglect of these rules that so many works fail, and one sees so many disjointed bodies, so many soldiers in battles who look ridiculous and deformed, so many figures in the air that seem to be resting on something, and others on the ground who cannot stand on their feet, along with similar blunders involving twisted or crippled limbs that perform impossible actions through the turning of the head, the wrenching of the arms and body, or the raising of the legs.

<header>-> BOOK SIX <-</header>

legs; the movement of feet, and the bending of knees. And to provide a certain rule for proceeding with reason when representing these movements, I say they arise from eight modes that the body has of moving, which are: upward, downward, to the right, and to the left; stretching outward, coming forward, turning in a circle, and standing still.

And therefore, wishing to demonstrate a figure, I say that whenever a man stands with his whole body supported by one foot, that foot—acting like the base of a column—is always placed perpendicularly under the **hollow of the throat** <term>hollow of the throat|fontanella della gola: the indentation at the base of the neck between the collarbones, used by artists as a central point for balancing the body's weight.</term>. By this, I mean the instep of the foot. The ancient **Polyclitus** <note>Polyclitus (active c. 450–420 BCE) was a renowned Greek sculptor who developed a mathematical "Canon" for the ideal proportions of the human body and pioneered the *contrapposto* (weight-shifted) stance.</note> was the first discoverer of this posture, following the paths of nature. Consequently, all the ancients observed this rule: to ensure that the face of the person resting in this way turns toward the direction where the foot is pointed.

Furthermore, through such investigations, it has been found that the motions of the head are such that a man hardly ever turns in any direction without some parts of the rest of the body being positioned beneath him to support such a heavy member; otherwise, he must extend some limb on the opposite side, like a **balance scale** <term>balance scale|bilancia: an instrument for weighing; used here as a metaphor for anatomical equilibrium.</term>, to correspond to the weight. For the same effect is seen when someone with an outstretched hand supports a weight: with the other foot fixed as the foundation of the balance, the entire rest of the body is positioned to equalize the weight.

Here, one must take great care to avoid making figures that cannot, in any way, stand on their feet because no limb is placed under the head; or figures that, by throwing themselves totally forward, cannot be supported by the legs; and the same for those leaning backward or to the sides. Furthermore, when a man is standing upright, the head cannot turn further upward than the point where the eyes look in a straight line toward the middle of the Heavens <note>In this context, "the middle of the Heavens" refers to the zenith or the point directly overhead.</note>. Nor can it turn further to the side than the point where the chin is directly above the shoulder. Nor, while standing upright, can it be lowered so much that the chin is not still lower than the forehead, nor can it pass the top of the chest; nor can it protrude so far forward that the chin does not remain somewhat further out than the forehead.

Additionally, the body cannot twist at the waist so much that the shoulder ever comes perpendicularly over the navel; nor can it ever turn so far backward with the arms that the hollow of the throat does not remain directly above the feet. Nor can one lean so far to the sides with the whole head that one shoulder does not remain perpendicular to the foot that supports the side toward which the body leans, while the other leg acts as a **counterweight** <term>counterweight|contrapeso: the principle of balance where one part of the body compensates for the weight of another to maintain stability.</term> for the head and the leaning body. Moreover, one cannot rest, nor can one lean so far forward with the body and the head...

And the head, bending forward, cannot go lower than the knees. The arms, furthermore, cannot be opened so far by throwing them back while open that the **wrists** <term>wrists|bracciali: literally "bracelets," here referring to the wrist joint or the lower part of the forearm</term> of the hands can be further back than the edge of the back; nor can they be raised so high that the **elbow** <term>elbow|gombito: an archaic spelling of "gomito"</term> goes above the top of the head, and that above the head the hands can cross lower than the wrist toward the elbow; and also, while standing straight and extending one arm behind the other to the side, the following arm can pass with the tips of the fingers the hollow of the other arm; nor, if one wishes to cross the arms in front, can the elbow pass the alignment of the **hollow of the throat** <term>hollow of the throat|fontanella: the indentation at the base of the neck</term>, or can they touch each other higher up than the elbow. 

Straight arms with hands joined together, when raised high, cannot have the hands pass the middle of the head toward the back; nor can an arm ever be twisted so much that the palm of the hand can show forward more than the shoulder, nor can the elbow be seen from the front. The hands, joined behind the back, cannot go higher than the end of the **loins** <term>loins|lumbi: the lower back or lumbar region</term> except by force; nor can one firmly touch with the wrist under the armpit of its own arm, nor in such an act can the fingers show higher than the shoulder, nor the elbow higher than the head. 

The hand, furthermore, turning it either forward or backward toward the elbow, cannot turn so much that it makes an angle at the wrist or at the **carpus** <term>carpus|rascetta: the anatomical lines of the inner wrist or the carpal bones</term> except an obtuse one, or at most a right angle; nor can the tips of the fingers pass higher than the carpus toward the fold of the arm [the elbow]; nor, by turning the fingers so far back that their tips pass the beginning of the **metacarpus** <term>metacarpus|pettine: literally "the comb," referring to the bones of the hand between the wrist and fingers</term> at the wrist; nor, by throwing an arm around the neck from the front, does the hand pass the middle of the **nape** <term>nape|copa: the back of the neck or occiput</term> with the fingers, or touch the ear on its own side. 

If one hand is raised high, all the other parts on that side down to the foot follow that upward motion, so that the **heel** <term>heel|calcagno: the heel bone</term> of that foot also rises from the ground by the motion of the same arm. One limb never extends on one side without the others following it, nor conversely is it compressed or drawn in without the others following, almost like lines moving toward a center. 

Beyond this, among all the motions of the legs, the principal ones are these: first, raising one leg forward as far as possible, the tip of the foot goes no higher than the waist, nor does it even reach it. For its limit is to go level with the **hip joint** <term>hip joint|chiaue del galone: literally the "key of the flank," referring to the greater trochanter or the pivot point of the hip</term>, that is, the beginning of the leg. ...that with the rest of the body thrown back, they are not vertically aligned <note>original: "à cateto" — a geometric term referring to a plumb line or the vertical leg of a right triangle</note> under the summit or **hip joint** <term>hip joint|chiaue delle coscie: literally the "key of the thighs," referring to the ball-and-socket joint of the hip</term>. The **heel** <term>heel|calcagno</term>, while standing, can barely touch beneath the buttocks if one knee is kept close to the other; nor can both heels, while sitting or kneeling, or even by raising **one leg** <term>one leg|vna gamba</term> behind, reach above the shoulder with the heel, although on the other side, the head and body may be lowered as much as desired while supporting oneself on one leg, which is precisely like the support of a **balance scale** <term>balance scale|bilancia: a metaphor for the body's center of gravity and equilibrium, essential for the artistic pose known as contrapposto</term>. 

And here, the instep of the foot is exactly perpendicular to the joint of the hip or **thigh** <term>thigh|coscia</term> <note>original: "galone" — an archaic term for the hip or flank</note>. By raising the knee upward and bending the head toward it, in all such actions, one can just reach the mouth or, at most, the nose. The foot cannot be pulled upward in any way so as to reach the navel. Crossed legs cannot create more space between one foot and the other than the length of **one leg** <term>one leg|vna gamba</term>; nor, when spreading them in profile, can they show as much space as the length of the figure; nor, from the front, can the weight-bearing leg pass with its knee the leg that is thrown across, either in front or behind; nor can the foot in such a movement be further from the weight-bearing one than the distance from below the knee to the instep. 

But when taking a step forward with **one leg** <term>one leg|vna gamba</term> in front and the other behind, the space reaches the length of one leg, provided the body is bent down, where the knee in a straight line from behind does not pass more than half a knee's width beyond the one in front on the outer side. The **instep** <term>instep|pettine del piede: literally the "comb of the foot," referring to the metatarsal region</term> cannot turn so far upward toward the leg that it forms an acute angle at the ankle; at most, it forms a right angle. Nor can the instep and toes be turned so far downward that they form a straight line with the front of the leg, because a **small** <term>small|vn poco</term> obtuse angle always remains at the ankle. 

Neither leg nor foot can turn more than what the profile shows from the front, such that one kneecap touches the other, or the heels touch at the back. Nor, while standing on **one leg** <term>one leg|vna gamba</term>, can the other throw the foot forward as far as the length of **one foot** <term>one foot|vn piede</term>, but it reaches its limit at the sides and behind by about a foot and a half, and no more. Nor can the upper part of the knee [of the free leg] go lower than the lower part of the knee of the weight-bearing leg. 

These, then, are the movements which are so important in the poses of all of life, concerning the single leg and the **balance** <term>balance|bilancia</term>, and everything that it is appropriate for a **human body** <term>human body|corpo humano</term> to do to be expressed by the **painter** <term>painter|pittore</term>. And because the principal movements are those of the legs, body, arms, and head, the others that could have been mentioned have been left out as being of little importance. # BOOK SIX

...that these movements vary somewhat among themselves, according to the quality of those bodies; given that it is necessary that in a figure standing upright on one foot, the members on the side where it rests are higher than on the other side. Furthermore, all the aforementioned movements, along with any others that can be made, should always be represented in such a way that the body has something of the **serpentine** <term>serpentine|serpentinato: a twisting, S-shaped pose that suggests movement and grace, central to Mannerist art</term>, a quality to which nature is easily disposed. Moreover, it has always been used by the ancients and by the best moderns—that is, in all the actions a figure can perform, one should always see the twisting of the bodies done in such a way that from the right side the arm always juts forward, or in whatever attitude you choose to place it, and the other part of the body is lost <note>original: "si perda" — meaning the limb recedes into the background or is obscured to create depth</note>, and the left arm serves that right one, and thus the left leg comes forward, and the other is lost. You must observe the same if you wish, on the contrary, to make the left arm jut further out, and thus the right leg, because the right arm must serve the left, and the other part of the body must retreat. 

And this proceeds in all the actions that can be done, whether resting, running, flying, fighting, or lying prostrate, or kneeling; in short, in all the effects a body can produce, which will never succeed in being graceful if it does not have this **serpentine form** <term>serpentine form|forma serpentinata</term>, as **Michelangelo** used to call it, and ensuring that the face is always turned according to its effect, or toward the work of the hands. In addition to this, in a fat and heavy body, it is not possible for the limbs to reach extreme motions except in so far as it approaches the thinness and proportion of a well-proportioned and beautiful body. And therefore, due to its heaviness, it will remain behind; just as, by contrast, a disproportionately thin body with long limbs will make a greater effort in some motions, even surpassing those mentioned. Vigorous motions, then, are suited to soldiers and wrestlers; humble ones to **Virgins and Saints**; slow and lazy ones—which snake less <note>original: "serpenteggiano"</note>—to the elderly; and obstructed and short ones to those who are excessively corpulent, heavy, and fat, always avoiding straight lines and acute angles therein—a rule which should be observed as much as possible, as given by **Buonarroti** <note>Michelangelo Buonarroti</note>.

It does not seem out of place to treat the movements of the horse's limbs here—since its proportions have been discussed elsewhere—as these observations serve as a guide for all other **quadrupeds**. Thus, we read of two ancient sculptors who, having each been commissioned separately to create whatever they deemed most excellent in their art, chose **man** as the primary subject and the **horse** as the second. Both did this without the other knowing, resulting in the two colossi which are now in Rome at **Monte Cavallo** <note>The Quirinal Hill in Rome, named "Monte Cavallo" due to the two colossal ancient statues of the Dioscuri (Castor and Pollux) taming horses.</note>; this was to demonstrate that both recognized that the beauty of the world, after man, is found in the horse.

Regarding this subject, I say that when a horse rears up as high as it can, it will never move in a straight line with the mane over the rump (*groppa*), and in such an action, the head will not extend further out than the hock (*garetto*), nor will the feet remain close together. When kicking out with its feet and raising its entire hindquarters, the rump cannot go higher than the neck, even if the horse lowers it; though in such an act, I have never seen a horse lower its head between its legs. Likewise, the feet cannot rise above the level of the rump, no matter how much they are raised. In this action, the **forelegs** <term>forelegs|mani: literally "hands," a term used historically to refer to the front limbs of a horse</term> remain equally close; for if it were to do otherwise, it could not support itself at that moment.

Furthermore, when the horse turns its head to the side with its neck as far as it can, it cannot touch or reach near its ribs; nor can it raise its head so high that it does not form a significant, though obtuse, angle under the jaws and the start of the throat. When standing straight and pulling its head toward its throat, the tip of the **muzzle** <term>muzzle|mostaccio: refers to the snout or nose area of the horse</term> will never pass below the **pit of the throat** <term>pit of the throat|fontanella: the suprasternal notch or the hollow at the base of the neck</term>. Nor can the head turn so far to the sides that the **curb-chain area** <term>curb-chain area|barbozzale: the chin groove where the curb chain of a bridle sits</term> touches the sides of the neck. When standing still, it cannot raise its head and neck so far back that the mane falls directly over the middle of the back. Nor, when viewed from the front or the back, can the full profile of the head be seen, no matter how much it turns; unless it bows the top of its head toward the ground, which would help it turn further.

When raising a leg, the sole of the foot cannot rise higher than the joint of the hock (*garetto*) of the leg that is planted; and likewise, the hock does not go higher than the end of the flank. When one foreleg is planted and the other is raised, the knee cannot go higher than the lower parts of the chest; nor does the "hand" (hoof) go higher than the top of the knee. When the horse is standing straight, it cannot extend a foreleg upward further than the knee, unless it forms an angle above the knee. Likewise, the horse cannot lower itself so far on its hind legs that...

...the belly reaches the level of the hocks; nor can it rise so high in the front that it can extend its **forearms** <term>forearms|braccia: literally "arms," referring here to the upper part of the front legs</term> high off the ground, but from the knee down they will incline inward. Besides this, a horse cannot, by spreading its legs, leave as much space from one foot to the other as the length of a leg; but standing on one foot, it will leave as much as the distance from the **point of the hock** <term>hock|garetto: the joint in the hind leg of a horse, analogous to the human ankle</term> to the sole of the foot, and the same applies to the forelegs. It cannot turn its joints so far back—whether the front or hind feet—that the tips of the shoes touch the **pastern** <term>pastern|pastorello: the part of the horse's leg between the fetlock and the hoof</term>; nor can it tuck its head completely between its forelegs. Furthermore, the point of the hock always faces its counterpart more from the inside than the outside, where the inner parts of the feet always turn backward, just as the forelegs do at the knee. 

The leg—whether the horse is stretched out or standing—will never be found as straight as the forearm, for it will always form an angle with the hock; and the front foot can hardly touch the beginning of its rear leg when the horse happens to be stretched out or lying down, however it may be; but when standing, it cannot get close to it because its strength weakens. Likewise, when grazing, the head cannot move the **muzzle** <term>muzzle|mostaccio: the nose and mouth area of an animal</term> further from the forelegs than the distance from the knee to the foot; and it cannot turn to the sides, but with great effort it will turn it back so far that the muzzle will be level with the rump. 

When stretching the neck straight forward, it cannot extend so far that it does not leave an angle at the base of the neck; and in no movement, unless the head is on the ground or the flank, can it show its mouth open directly to the sky. Nor can it, while walking, throw the foot so far forward that it passes the vertical line of the beginning of the back or the ends of the mane; nor likewise can it throw the knee as far forward as the line of the head. The sole of the front foot, when pulled back, passes the rear start of the forearm; nor does the tip of the hoof of the leg placed behind go further forward than the start of the inner hock, which remains slightly behind the torso. 

Finally, even when the horse is running as fast as it can, the belly and the legs cannot be in a straight line; because there will always remain an angle between the belly and the point of the **flank** <term>flank|galone: the side of the animal between the ribs and the hip</term>, no matter how much it stretches; nor will the end of the stride remain in line with the torso, and the point of the hock will be as far from the line of the torso as it is from the ground; and similarly the pastern will be as far as the distance from the point of the hock to the sole of the hoof. And while the horse is running, the front part of the belly will be higher than the rear part where the **sheath** <term>sheath|membro: refers to the male reproductive anatomy</term> is located; and observing this, one finds the horse running at full force, where the knees also remain at the height of the end of the—

## On the rule of coloring. Chapter VI.

**T**he natural desire I have to expand this art of painting—in which I was raised and grew from my childhood until the age of thirty-two, at which time I lost my sight, and since then until this age contemplating it—has awakened the eyes of my intellect. It has sharpened my mind in such a way that I could investigate such matters which I hope shall not be displeasing, if not to everyone, at least to the students of this profession of mine, for they have never been declared before by anyone in this manner, especially regarding the art and practice of **coloring** <term>coloring|colorare: in Renaissance theory, this refers not just to hue, but the entire application of paint, including light and shadow</term>, which is one of the most principal parts of painting. For the sake of greater clarity, I will first establish some foundations.

One is that I am not of the opinion of those **Peripatetic philosophers** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy. They generally argued that color was a property of light rather than the object itself.</note> who say there is no color when there is no light and brightness to illuminate the colors. Rather, I say freely that the rays or light of the Sun, or of any other light, do not generate or produce colors; because before the light intervenes, they are already actually produced within the subject. It is indeed true that light causes this effect: it makes the color seen in actuality, which before the arrival of the light was only potentially visible. Although the colors reside equally in the subjects—for example, in a red cloth the red color exists equally in all parts of the cloth—nonetheless, because this color cannot be seen without light, and light causes a different effect in the cloth according to the amount of light received by that subject; therefore, the painter must never paint the color all alone. Instead, he must always paint it **illuminated** <term>illuminated|allumato: meaning the color as it appears when struck by light, showing highlights and variations</term>; that is, with the various effects caused by light not being received equally across the colored objects. The third foundation is that the painter must take the greatest consideration in

...to paint and represent color together with light; for example, to represent light on a light red cloth, and to represent shadow, do not make it so that if it is dark red, it becomes a red darker than it really is. And with the same caution, the painter will proceed in all light and dark colors. This will be successfully achieved by following this rule: to fix and establish very well in the **mind** <note>original: "idea". In Mannerist theory, the 'Idea' is the internal mental concept or divine spark the artist forms before beginning work.</note>, before beginning to paint, the color of that thing which one wishes to paint—whether it is light, medium, or dark. For having well-conceived the color in the mind, when one later wishes to represent light or shadow, one will not change the color they wish to represent.

But the most general and certain precept will be that the painter should study to be a good imitator of nature herself, observing the effects she makes; for thus he will become an excellent **craftsman** <term>craftsman|artefice: an artist or skilled maker</term>. For even if the Sun, with all its light, were to illuminate a dark red cloth, it would never make it become light red; and similarly, shadow will never make that same red become even darker. Rather, light produces this effect in every colored object: it demonstrates and reveals the color just as it is, such that the diversity and multitude or rarity of light never changes the color of the object. By acting in this way, the painter can be called a true imitator of nature and eminent in his art; otherwise, he will deserve to be called a destroyer of nature.

And because I greatly desire to illustrate this part of painting, I want to demonstrate the manner in which some things must be colored, leaving the others to the judgment of the prudent craftsman, which must be colored proportionally. 

Now to begin here, I say first that the painter at one time cannot paint more than one view of a figure; second, that this view of the figure being painted is partly illuminated by the rays of the Sun or another light, and partly in shadow. Because as light strikes an opaque and thick body and cannot penetrate it, that same body creates shadow where the rays and light cannot penetrate. Third, I say that the illuminated part of this view of the figure must be divided into three parts and colored with three colors. And the shadowed part likewise must be divided into another three parts and colored with three other colors. 

We shall therefore treat first of how to make the flesh of a **choleric** man, second of painting the flesh of a **sanguine** man, in the third place the flesh of a **phlegmatic** man, and in the fourth of the **melancholic** <note>These four categories refer to the "Four Humors," a historical medical theory that suggested human personality and physical appearance were determined by the balance of bodily fluids (yellow bile, blood, phlegm, and black bile).</note>. Now, to represent the first most illu[minated]...
