...[illumi]nated parts of the flesh of the **choleric** <note>In the theory of the four humors, a choleric person was thought to be ambitious and energetic, with a yellowish or "heated" complexion.</note> person, one will use two parts of red color, one of yellow, and three of light color; and to represent the second part, which is slightly less illuminated, one must take the same quantity of red and yellow color, and two parts of light color. The third part of the flesh, even less illuminated than the second, will be made with the same quantity of red and yellow with only one part of light color.

But the darkest part will be made with two parts of <term>burnt ochre|ocrea arsa: a natural earth pigment that turns deep red-brown when heated</term>, one of <term>umber|terra d'ombra: a natural brown pigment containing iron and manganese</term>, and another of the third illuminated flesh mixture labeled A. And so, by dividing into six parts this view of the choleric body that can be painted all at once, with the cited proportion of colors, the flesh of the choleric will be represented most naturally.

To express the first illuminated part of the flesh of the **sanguine** <note>The sanguine temperament was associated with blood, resulting in a cheerful, healthy, and ruddy complexion.</note> person, one will mix together one part of red and two of light color, and then blend into this composition three parts of light color; in this way, the flesh will be represented to the life where the light strikes most strongly. To demonstrate the second flesh, a little less illuminated than the first, you will take two parts of rosy color and two of light; and to paint the third part, yet less illuminated than the two mentioned above, you will take three parts of rosy and one of light.

For the darkest and most shadowed part, you will blend one part of burnt ochre and two of <term>bell metal earth|terra di campana: a pigment made from the debris of molds used to cast bells, typically providing a gritty, grey-brown tone</term>; of this mixture you will take three parts, and one part of the third less-illuminated flesh which for now we shall call letter B. You will mix everything together, and thus the least dark flesh will be made. If you then take two parts of the darkest composition already made, and two parts of the mixture in letter B, the second less-dark flesh will result. But the third, even less dark than these two, will be made by taking one part of the darkest composition and three parts of the mixture made in letter B.

# QUESTION 1.

...who have average complexions and qualities. But with all this, let the painter know that in this matter all the art in the world is not enough if the one who works and puts into practice what art teaches does not have **prudence**. For art instructs with general precepts, and to apply this generality to a particular thing, there is a need for great **prudence**, which is 그 virtue that teaches how a man must govern himself in particular circumstances; and thus the painter, guided by this, will very well understand how the precepts of art are to be understood and put into action. 

Therefore, when in the aforementioned rules we have noted that the painter cannot make and paint in one figure more than one **view** <note>The term "veduta" refers to a single aspect or side of a figure visible from one perspective.</note>, as is very true; and that this view is divided into six parts and painted with six compositions of colors, no one should be so imprudent as to take a compass and divide that view into six geometrically equal parts; for this would be a great oversight and a notable lack of judgment. Because it is clear that the part of the round body where the rays of the Sun strike with the greatest force is smaller than the sixth part of that view; for at that very moment, the rays diffuse and scatter. And even though they illuminate the other parts where they strike with light, they do not illuminate them with such brightness and sharpness; but as I said from the beginning, all this must be left in large part to the **discretion** of the painter. 

Furthermore, in mixing the colors with a proportionate quantity of one and the other, one must not be so rigorous; because sometimes one color is finer than another; therefore, here too, the painter’s prudence has its place. Nevertheless, the rule will always be that the color with which one paints the third flesh, which is less illuminated than the other two of which we have spoken in the letters <term>A. B. C. and D.</term>, must be the same color as the flesh; because the third light has no other effect than to uncover and declare the actual color of the flesh. In such a way, this light is tempered with the same color of the flesh; but the first and second light give the flesh a certain radiance greater than that which the flesh naturally possesses. 

And although the light, as we have said, does not change the color of the colored body, it nonetheless gives it this radiance, and the greater light makes that part it illuminates more visible and makes it stand out more; and shadow produces the opposite effect. It should also be noted that, although we have ordered six mixtures of different colors to paint a single view of a single human body, the painter must not for this reason cease to perform his office, which is to **soften** and **blend** together...

[in] such a way and with such art, [mix] these diverse colors so they appear as one color with the flesh; so much so that neither the lighter nor the darker color produces more of an effect in the flesh than light and shadow do in living, natural flesh. Always be mindful that light is received according to the shape of the limb: that is, if the limb or the nude figure is semicircular and round in shape, the primary light should be received upon it directly, like a point at the highest part of such a limb, or like a line. But if the nude figure is round and long, the primary light is always received like a line. Finally, if the limb is flat, the primary light is received in the form of a surface.

Therefore, when one must depict **choler**, **blood**, **phlegm**, and **melancholy** <note>These are the four "humors" of Renaissance medicine—yellow bile, blood, phlegm, and black bile—which were believed to determine a person's temperament and complexion.</note> all inflamed with anger, they shall be made by mixing with the colors mentioned in their place a little glowing red and <term>morello</term> <note>A dark purple or mulberry-colored pigment.</note>. And choleric fear and terror—whether in the phlegmatic, the sanguine, or the melancholic—shall be expressed by mixing with the colors mentioned above <term>biglio</term> <note>A grayish or leaden tone.</note>, yellow earth, and green earth.

Furthermore, the painter should consider that certain parts of the human body must be colored differently from the rest of the flesh, such as with red; I will treat these further below when I discuss the colors of "movements" <note>Referring to the "movements of the soul," or emotions and physical gestures.</note>. There are also certain other parts that must be colored differently: namely, certain <term>bisagioni</term> <note>Likely a technical term for grayish or transitional tones used to bridge light and shadow, derived from "bigio" (gray).</note> in the shadows of the hair above the forehead, in the hollow of the chin, and certain reflections under the <term>bollini</term> <note>Technical term for the rounded, protruding parts of the anatomy, such as knuckles, elbows, or the "bosses" of muscles.</note>; and in the upper and thicker part of the arm, in certain lower parts of the arm, in the curve of the belly, in the <term>varchi</term> <note>The hollows or spaces between muscles or joints.</note>, and in the calves of the legs. These <term>bisagioni</term> must be expressed with great art, just as **Giorgione da Castelfranco**, **Antonio da Correggio**, and **Titian** have known how to demonstrate.

But it is time to move on to speak of highlighted red cloths. Now, the first part of the most highlighted red garment must be represented by making a composition of one part red and three parts white; and the third highlighted part of the two [others], and the second with two parts red and two parts white, with three parts red and one part white. <note>The author provides specific mixing ratios for "allumare" (highlighting), creating a gradient of three stages of light.</note> The darkest part will be painted with two parts of black and an equal amount of burnt ochre; and the second less-dark part will be made with one part of pure black and two of burnt ochre; and the third part, even less dark than the [other] two, will be made with three parts of ochre and one of red.

### How colors are distributed in narrative paintings. Chapter VII.

**W**e must consider that in narrative paintings <note>The author uses the term *historie*, referring to complex scenes depicting historical, biblical, or mythological events.</note> where countless clothed figures are introduced, in distributing the colors one must represent a certain sweet harmony to the eyes, so that no dissonance is perceived; which would result (for example) if one saw a vivid green, so soft, next to a flaming red, all sharp and fierce. Therefore, to accompany and divide all these colors, it would be necessary to consider their principles and causes, from which the aforementioned qualities arise, as everyone can experience in the appearance of each of them. But it would be a long, wandering discourse, and almost beside the point, to discuss all the qualities of the elements and their combinations, as the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of the philosophy of Aristotle, who often met in the "peripatos" or covered walkways of the Lyceum in Athens.</note> say. It should suffice that everything I say can be seen in reality through experience; besides, something has already been said about their quality in the theoretical section.

Now I say that according to the doctrine already given, when I discussed what color was, these colors—as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher whose color theories, based on the mixing of light and dark, remained influential through the Renaissance.</note> says—are no more than seven: two extremes, which are white and black, and five intermediate ones, in the middle of which is red, composed of equal power of white and black. Between red and white, there is yellow, which tends toward red, and pale <note>Italian: *pallido*, referring here to a desaturated, light yellowish or cream tone.</note>, which tends toward white; between red and black, there is purple, which tends toward red, and green, which tends toward black. So it is seen that red is an enemy to the pale, being distant from it by way of white, and to the green, being likewise distant from it by way of black; and it is a friend to yellow and purple. Similarly, white and black, as extremes, cannot stand near each other, for one is too light and the other too dark. And this is their first root and compatibility, which—by always following and fleeing the extremes—results in that beauty sought in paintings. But one must also pay attention not only to the compatibility and repugnance of simple colors but also to that of compound colors; for all those composed of either of the two extremes with red, likewise [will] accompa-

they accompany one another, and they discord, just as those extremes which are their originals do. And therefore, in the nature of yellow are the rosy, flesh-toned, flaming, golden, and orange <note>original: *ranzati*—a deep, burnt orange color</note> colors; in the nature of the pale <note>likely meaning a pale yellow or cream</note> are the greens, faded colors, turquoises, light tones, and light violets; in the nature of purple are the peacock-purples <note>original: *pauonazzi*—a deep violet or purple color named after the peacock's feathers</note>, vivid tans <note>original: *taneti*—a reddish-brown or tawny color</note>, and sky blues; and in that of green are the turquoise and azure. 

So it follows that the purple, peacock-purple, sky-blue, turquoise, green, and azure colors—being close by way of their composition of red and black—will render an ordered beauty <note>original: *vaghezza*—a term implying charm, grace, and visual delight</note> among themselves, without causing confusion to the eyes. By the composition of red and white, the yellows, flesh-tones, rosy, golden, orange, flaming, pale, green, faded, and light turquoise colors have a tempered beauty among themselves. 

With flaming red alone, only the purple, peacock-purple, tan, and sky-blue colors find charm <note>original: *vagheggiano*</note> on the side toward black; and on the side toward white, the yellows, flesh-tones, rosy, golden, flaming, and orange. Because of the proximity they hold with red, the yellows, purples, peacock-purples, tans, and sky blues are beautiful among themselves; and each of these likewise with flesh-tones, rosy, golden, and flaming colors. 

The extremes—namely black and white—being friends by composition (since black can have light from nowhere else but white, and the latter can have shadow from nowhere else but black), cause the colors that participate in them to generate beauty, as they are far from the flame of red, their accompanying middle. And therefore they agree by way of union with the pale colors, greens, faded colors, light turquoises, greens, turquoises, and azures. 

On the other hand, red is most contrary to all these. And let this be proof: if it is too close to them, it enlivens them by its sharpness, as they are the softest among the others. Friends of black, and agreeing with it, are the tans, sky blues, peacock-purples, and similar colors, provided they are dark. Also agreeing are ash-gray <term>berretino</term> <note>A dull, grayish-blue or charcoal color common in Renaissance clothing.</note> and dark gray <note>original: *bigio*</note>. From these onwards, all others are its enemies. 

Friends of white are the greens, turquoises, azures, the pale, and other faded colors of every sort, except pure red when it is not mixed with it (as rosy is). And this is the whole foundation of the proper beauty <note>original: *vaghezza*</note> that colors distributed through paintings ought to have; which, whenever it is understood and observed, will result in works that are fitting, beautiful, and delightful to the eyes. 

Among others, **Raphael** always observed these fitting beauties; for which reason he never wanted—or at least only rarely—to place a particular color of those mentioned above next to another where too much beauty could arise for the eyes and take away some part of the judgment from the beholder...

...ly. And this was also used by the jovial philosopher and painter Gaudenzio <note>Gaudenzio Ferrari (c. 1471–1546), a prominent Northern Italian painter known for his expressive and colorful style</note>, in whose works all this art is visible. It was likewise used by Parmigianino <note>Francesco Mazzola (1503–1540), known for the refined elegance and elongated forms of Mannerism</note>, and many others who always placed **purples** next to **yellows**, avoiding turquoise as being too vivid; and between **flesh tones** and **turquoises**, they placed various dark violet-purples <note>original: *moreletti*—a dark, mulberry-like color used for transitions</note> for tempering. They did the same with all the other middle colors, placing them between the extremes—or let us say, the "sharp" <note>original: *acuti*—meaning high-saturation or high-value colors that can be harsh if not balanced</note> colors—to temper them.

Another very important consideration we must always keep before our eyes, which is never separated from this matter of tempering, is to always place the most vivid colors in the principal figures, as they are larger and more visible. In the secondary figures, as they are further away, one should diminish the colors somewhat due to the softening of the light <note>original: *abbagliamento del lume*—referring to how light and atmosphere blur the clarity of distant objects</note>. Proceed in this way step-by-step until the outlines are completely lost and the light is lost; when things can no longer be seen, they cannot be colored. In this way, works are produced so that the figures do not seem painted, but detached from the surface and in relief <note>original: *di rilieuo*</note>, so great is the power of the tempering of colors among themselves and in the receding elements <term>sfuggimenti: the technique of making objects appear to recede into the distance</term>. 

But this method, as far as can be seen in our times, is understood by few and poorly observed. Thus, in many narrative paintings <note>original: *historie*—large-scale compositions depicting historical, biblical, or mythological scenes</note>, one sees distant figures colored just as vividly as those nearby, and even though they are ten times further away, they result in nothing but a pure, plastered flatness and a rainbow <note>original: *arco di colori*</note> without relief or strength. 

This error appears all the more because there are some who, convincing themselves they are wiser and more knowledgeable than others, say that the figures in the back should be darker than those in front. Therefore, if they paint a battle or other story in the open air, they brighten the first figures with light and weigh down the others with dark colors and shadows, even down to the smallest figures, so that they seem smoked and stained with soot <note>original: *caligine*</note>. In this, they err greatly; for the perfect recession <note>sfuggire</note> and the softening of the vividness and thickness of shadows consists in considering the distance of the figure from the eye. One must soften the figure that is meant to be closer less, and soften more the one meant to be further away and distant. 

Since the eye cannot see the color of lines and surfaces except confusedly at a great distance, one must not by any means tint them even darker, for that would be called an "inverse recession" <note>original: *fuggitiva inuersa*</note>. Nor is the error smaller among those who make the figures in the background larger than those in the front, which is called "inverse perspective" <note>original: *prospettiua inuersa*</note>. And I am persuaded that this may suffice regarding this part of coloring, in which—as I have already noted—consists the principal strength and excellence of this art.

## To which sorts of people colors particularly suit. Ch. VIII.

**T**HOSE who set out to express a certain effect through the use of an instrument, yet do not understand or discern the qualities and properties of that instrument with which they wish to represent that effect, may, in my opinion, be called blind. Just as those who do not know for certain where the ground is good and solid for placing their feet often stumble and mistakenly step into a hole, falling down; so it happens to those who, although they may imitate drapery well in their figures, nevertheless do not consider the status of the figures to whom they assign them. They often produce a certain incongruity that they surely would not create if they knew the cause of what they were doing and establishing with the brush and colors. For colors must have a correspondence to the quality of the figure, just as the figure seeks its own likeness, for "like desires like."

Therefore, to avoid these improprieties and to know the reasons for distributing colors according to the rank of the figures being represented, we must know in general that colors tending toward the dark—and those deprived of bright liveliness—belong to the elderly, philosophers, the poor, the melancholic, and grave persons. If one were to give these people beautiful and cheerful garments of varied colors, it would not be fitting. Whites, <term>pauonazzi</term> <note>A deep reddish-purple or violet color, often associated with the robes of high-ranking clergy; original: "pauonazzi"</note>, reds, and the like belong to Popes, Monarchs, and Cardinals. The color of gold along with yellow, and royal purples, suit Emperors, Kings, Dukes, and great personages. Rosy colors, light greens, somewhat yellowish tones, light turquoises, and other such colors belong to nymphs, youths, prostitutes <note>original: "meretrici"</note>, and the like. Mixed colors likewise suit nymphs; but those tending toward brightness and extreme multi-colored patterns <note>original: "diuisati estremi"</note> belong to drummers, buffoons, trumpeters, pages, and jugglers. 

And so the other colors are dispensed and assigned according to the gravity or the cheerfulness that can be discerned from the things mentioned. Bright golden and shining colors belong to Angels, as well as those tending toward light and white—which is also very fitting for virgins, priests, and saints. For we read that St. Bartholomew used to wear a white mantle and an undergarment of purple, and many other saints did the same. And generally, in this area, one must exercise a certain discretion and judgment. For example, it would not be fitting to give <term>shot color</term> <note>A fabric woven with two different colored threads so that it appears to change color when viewed from different angles; original: "color cangiante"</note> to Our Lady at any time, as many do, even attributing it to Christ and God the Father; and yet there is no one who warns them of it. And because many things regarding colors, such as from whom—

## *On the colors of the four humors, and how from them the flesh tones in the human body of every sort are composed.* Ch. IX.

**A**lthough from several places in the preceding books where we have treated of flesh tones, enough knowledge could be gained to know how to compose them with their proper colors, I will nonetheless not fail to treat them here more particularly for greater clarity, reducing everything under the four colors of our <term>humors</term> <note>In ancient and Renaissance medicine, the "four humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) were bodily fluids thought to determine a person's health and temperament</note>, which represent the four elements. Since all bodies are composed of these, it is a necessity that they hold to their nature, and particularly show their color—most especially and apparently the color of that humor which superabounds within them. By these colors, by which physicians also judge the <term>complexion</term> <note>The "complexion" referred to the balance of humors which manifested in a person's skin tone and personality</note> and property of the nature of each person, we first have the color of earth. This is caused by coldness and dryness, and being dusky and black, it denotes the black bile, which is called <term>melancholy</term>. The color of water, a cerulean that tends toward green, demonstrates <term>phlegm</term>; for coldness is the mother of whiteness, and heat the mother of blackness. The color of the air is somewhat red and denotes blood; but the color of fire, or of a burning flame, denotes <term>choler</term> <note>Yellow bile; original: "colera"</note>. Choler, being easily mixable with all humors due to its subtlety, causes various colors. Thus, if it is mixed with blood, and the blood dominates, it makes the color red; if the choler dominates, it makes the color somewhat red; if they are equal together, it makes it <term>tawny</term> <note>original: "fulvo"</note>. But if "adust" or burnt choler is mixed with the blood, it makes the color of hemp. If the blood dominates, it renders the color red, or somewhat rubicund if the choler dominates. But if it is mixed with the melancholic humor, it tinges the body black; if it is tempered with melancholy and phlegm in equal proportion, it makes the color of <term>canvas</term> <note>A pale, dull beige or off-white; original: "canevaccio"</note>; if the phlegm superabounds, it makes a <term>luteous</term> color <note>A muddy or saffron yellow; original: "luteo"</note>; if the melancholy wins, it makes the color white. But if it is then mixed with phlegm in equal proportion, it makes a <term>citrine</term> color <note>A pale, greenish-yellow like a lemon; original: "citrino"</note>; and if one of these predominates,

And so as not to leave out anything that pertains to a perfect knowledge of this matter, we ought to know that <term>Saturnine</term> <note>Bodies or temperaments influenced by the planet Saturn, traditionally associated with gloom and slowness</note> bodies—in which one finds timidity, sterility, malice, melancholy, old age, avarice, envy, and laziness—are of a color between black and pale. <term>Jovial</term> <note>Influenced by Jupiter; associated with a cheerful and healthy disposition</note> bodies, in which temperance, joy, eloquence, abundance, honesty, faith, and religion reign, are of a white color mixed temperately with red. <term>Martial</term> <note>Influenced by Mars, the god of war</note> bodies, in which cruelty, pride, anger, rashness, impetus, fury, revenge, audacity, and finally war predominate, are of a dark red color, with eyes shining with yellow. <term>Lunar</term> <note>Influenced by the Moon</note> bodies, characterized by purity, simplicity, virginity and the like, are of a very white color with a little red; and the intermediate types among these four representing the four humors are like the <term>Solar</term> <note>Influenced by the Sun</note> bodies, to which belong magnificence, honor, justice, fortitude, and the like, and these have a dusky color between yellow and black, but scattered with red. <term>Venereal</term> <note>Influenced by Venus, the goddess of love and beauty</note> bodies, to which belong grace, courtesy, beauty, and the other qualities mentioned elsewhere, have a white color that tends somewhat toward black, but scattered with red. Finally, <term>Mercurial</term> <note>Influenced by Mercury; associated with intelligence and agility</note> bodies, which belong to the astute, prudent, modest, and quiet, have an intermediate color that is neither white nor black, but is conveniently composed of everything.

In dispensing these colors, one must pay attention not only to the particular constitutions of the bodies, but also to their ages. For the <term>phlegmatic</term> color is suited first to infants, and then to children; the <term>sanguine</term> first to adolescents, and then to youths; the <term>choleric</term> first to men, and then to the elderly; and the <term>melancholic</term> begins in the old, and then becomes perfect in decrepit bodies. And these must also be observed for each age in accidental cases in their proper order. For herein lies all the importance: it being clear that the more the body tends toward red, the more it is brought to life; and conversely, when the body is depicted deprived of that red, it is necessary that it appear dead, because red represents the <term>vital spirit</term> <note>The "spiritus vitalis," thought to be a subtle substance in the blood that sustained life</note>. But because we have spoken of the flesh, we must now turn our attention to the mixtures of shadows corresponding to them, because this matters greatly.

through the qualities of the aforementioned elements with their mixtures; to create <term>melancholic</term> <note>Associated with black bile and an earth-like, somber temperament</note> flesh, colors such as <term>umber</term> <note>A dark brown earth pigment</note> and similar tones are used. For <term>phlegmatic</term> <note>Associated with phlegm, suggesting a pale or sluggish disposition</note> complexions, white is used, accompanied as necessary by green and blue. For <term>sanguine</term> <note>Associated with blood, suggesting a healthy, reddish glow</note> types, a mixture of white and red is used, resulting in a rose color. For <term>choleric</term> <note>Associated with yellow bile and a fiery, irritable temperament</note> types, an extreme red is used, such as <term>lake</term> <note>A translucent red pigment made from organic dyes</note> and <term>cinnabar</term> <note>A bright scarlet pigment derived from mercury ore</note>; however, it should be spread with much white so that it results in a pale color that imitates the color of an extinguished flame. Because just as such an extinguished fire is dark and yet burning, appearing to contain something of black, so we see that the more <term>choler</term> <note>Yellow bile, believed to cause heat and irritability</note> people have, the more they participate in blackness and darkness. Now, all these colors, according to how they are blended together, serve to create the mixtures for whatever flesh tone one desires.

Because of this, we must consider that the color of the shadow must correspond to the color of the flesh. Since the shadow of the flesh is nothing other than the same flesh not illuminated, and the illuminated part is nothing other than the same flesh struck by light, it follows that if the flesh is very red and not very bright, there must be much red and little black in the shadow. If, on the other hand, it has very little red and much white—which verges on a pale or faded tone—there must be much black and little red in the shadow. This is because black naturally overshadows white; therefore, the more white the colors contain, the more the shadows will seem to contain black, and the more the flesh tends toward red, the more red is appropriate in the shadows.

If the red tends toward yellow, the shadow must be of a red tending toward yellow; and if the flesh tends toward white with a little vermilion, as in a mix of phlegm and blood, the shadow must contain more black than red. All these flesh tones and shadows are formed primarily from equal colors, first making the dark flesh tone, into which white is then mixed to express the <term>reliefs</term> <note>The highlights or raised portions of a figure that create a three-dimensional effect</note> in their proper places, and the dark and black shadows. These, when mixed with the said dark flesh, become more or less dark, so that between these three extremes—that is, the flesh, the white, and the darkest shadow—perfect mixtures of flesh must inevitably result, which have been so well expressed by excellent artists.

...pass any further; nevertheless, it seemed appropriate to me to discuss it somewhat more extensively in this chapter, and to investigate which colors are produced by the internal **motions of the soul** <term>moti dell’animo</term> <note>A Renaissance term for emotions or psychological states that "move" the spirit and manifest in the body</note>. And first, it is necessary to mix together, as has been said, the colors according to their suitability, increasing the specific color of the motion all the more, the more that motion conforms to the natural temperament of the figure being represented; as would be adding much more **inflammation** <term>escandescenza</term> <note>A heightened, burning redness</note> to an impetuous motion in one who is of a **choleric** and **Martial** nature <note>Influenced by the planet Mars, suggesting a person prone to anger and war-like aggression</note>. Now all motions, whatever they may be, just as they are different from one another, so they have their particular colors, which nonetheless always follow the rule of the **four principal elemental colors**; these colors have as much power over the surface of the skin as the motion itself dictates. Because in man, slow and **melancholic** motions—resembling the earth—are colored with a tone deprived of the vigor of fire, whereby they remain dark and pale; fearful, lazy motions, full of worthlessness—belonging to **water**—must be expressed as pale, clear, and faint, like those who fear; cheerful, prompt, and courteous motions attributed to the **air** must be colored with a temperate mix of white and red; and finally, impetuous, sharp, and **choleric** motions given to **fire** are colored with a red that tends toward fire for greater terror. And thus, looking with this order at nature, one can easily color all motions of whatever sort. Because one will see an inflamed anger with eyes of glowing coal, and by contrast, a dull patience of an earthy color; and so all other motions in their respective colors. 

One must always take care, however, to color the parts of the body that are continually exposed with more red, because of the color of the **Sun** that spreads over them; as seen in the hands, feet, chest, shoulders, face, and knees of peasants, porters, and other hardworking men. One must also observe in the joints of women and delicate persons to always spread red over the parts that are most exercised and have motion; such as the joints of the legs, the arms, and the knuckles of the hands; and likewise color more vividly the fingers of the hands and the toes of the feet—and much more their joints—the soles, the heels, the knees, the elbows, the chin, the ears, the cheeks, the nostrils, the lips, the navel, and the **peaks of the breasts** <note>The nipples</note>; and besides these, the **collarbones** <term>chiaui delle spalle</term> <note>Literally "keys of the shoulders"</note>, the waist, the hips, the flanks, the **genitals** <term>la natura</term>, and the buttocks, because of the continual rising and sitting of man. And these same things are to be observed in all other bodies as well, always using their appropriate colors. In coloring the hair, one must have regard for the flesh; because white flesh scattered with a little red...

## On the rules of light. Chap. XII.

**L**ight must necessarily be the same throughout the whole **narrative scene** <term>historia</term> <note>In Renaissance art theory, a 'historia' is a complex narrative painting depicting a specific event, requiring internal consistency</note> that is painted, in such a way that within the field of the painting one imagines six parts: namely, front, back, right, left, top, and bottom; and consequently, the painter should feign that the light or rays strike the figures from one side of the place at a time, and in no way should he feign another light from the back or any other side in the same scene. Because it is not possible for the **Sun** to be in the East and the West at the same time. The same must be understood for a single figure in perfectly spherical and round bodies: that the light or rays strike the part or angle opposite to them, and in the other parts they become blurred. And this is seen in the **eye**, where the rays cause a sort of tiny star in the corner opposite to them <note>A reference to the "catchlight" or specular reflection in the pupil</note>; but in round and long bodies, such as a staff or the human body, the rays strike the part nearest to them with more force. This effect the painter will express with a narrow **strip or band** <term>fascia ò cintola</term> of color that represents the greatest light. And if anyone says to me that the entire half of a round body is illuminated equally by the Sun when the body is placed against it, I respond—leaving aside a more subtle dispute on this—that the painter considers not only the way the Sun illuminates, but also has respect and consideration for

From this it is necessarily concluded, in my opinion, that the painter has to express this, and no other effect with the brush. And if he observes this, he will see how he will push back the figures and make them appear rounded <term>tondeggiare</term> <note>The technique of using light and shadow to create the illusion of three-dimensional volume</note>. It is indeed true that that band or belt of light has to be broader; because the eye sees more on a plane than on a round or spherical surface. 

And if the painter wants to be expert in this precept, let him make observations and reflections on polished and smooth bodies, such as in a mirror, in a lustrous column, or in a carafe, and apply that proportionally to other bodies. It is also necessary to declare and demonstrate the effect made by the **primary light** <term>luce prima</term> <note>Known today as a "highlight," the brightest point where light reflects directly off a surface</note>, that is, the clearest light in the hair, in the eyes, in the lips, and in the nails. This is a certain particular brilliance, as everyone can see in nature. Furthermore, one must consider that there are certain parts of a man which, because they have the skin more tightly pulled and stretched over them, naturally receive more light than others; and these are the forehead, the nose, and the breast. Lastly, there are other parts that, because they are oily, likewise receive greater light than others; such as those parts around the eyes. All these things the painter will diligently notice and seek to express.

## *Rules of perspective. Chap. XIII.*

**J**ust as the ancient perspective painters drew all natural proportions from the **pyramid** <note>The "visual pyramid" is a fundamental concept in Renaissance perspective where the eye is the apex and the object is the base</note>, they also wished to portray the beauty of bodies in the best way and order possible, as if in a mirror. This is because optics, which comes from the eye of judgment, never goes up or down, but reaches the facade <note>The picture plane or the front surface of an object</note> directly. Within this, the high line and the low line, being equal to each other, form a cone for the eye, with the upper line indicating the Heavens and the lower one the ground; thus its center remains within the optical field as its beginning and end. With such art the famous painters used to show—as if in a pure mirror—the sacred paintings of the Egyptians <note>Renaissance theorists often believed ancient Egyptian art contained hidden, divine mathematical harmonies</note>.

Egyptians. And likewise the Greeks, to show such art to be true and exemplary, painted the loves, the deeds, the wars, and the councils of their ancestors, as if in a mirror reflecting nature; showing us that the eye should judiciously follow the work to its center, demonstrating a true and singular masterpiece. Thus, the excellent modern painters have followed this same path, such as Petrucci, Raphael, Leonardo, Gaudenzio <note>Gaudenzio Ferrari (c. 1471–1546), a prominent Northern Italian painter</note>, Parmigiano, and many others; and they have followed it as a royal road in <term>prospettiva</term> <note>perspective</note>, as any mediocre painter can easily observe in their works. 

And to return to the ancients, we find that in the time of Augustus the use of painting upon the facades of walls was discovered, which previously was not known out of honor for this art; whereas now it has gone so far that it is shamefully introduced even into stables and into <term>luochi de gli agiamenti</term> <note>literally "places of ease," a common Renaissance euphemism for latrines or privies</note>. 

Now I say that facades are painted in many ways, such as creating an inward depth by forcing the facade with the power of lines, and making porticos with colonnades and loggias. Upon these, nothing should be placed other than histories <note>narrative scenes, often from the Bible or mythology</note> situated in those places, ensuring, however, that the <term>punto</term> <note>the vanishing point</note> corresponds to the height of the visual judgment <note>the viewer’s eye level</note>. For it has been observed that many painters skilled in perspective have never wanted to break the rules of optics either too high or too low, as it is optics that reaches the extreme of human judgment; this is to always show the work as pure and exemplary according to our eye, which is the highest sense, and consequently judges how proportionately the proportions correspond to it. 

In this regard, one can consider as an example the shutters of an organ that is in Milan at Saint Francis <note>The church of San Francesco Grande, now demolished; it was the original home of Leonardo’s Virgin of the Rocks</note> on the left hand side, painted by our Bramantino <note>Bartolomeo Suardi (c. 1465–1530), an influential Milanese painter and architect known for his radical perspective</note>. On the exterior part of these, he has feigned the columns of the same organ with the soffit above; and he has made it so that the figures beneath them recede step by step to the said imagined point according to the structure of the organ. And the background of the figures high up by the soffit, and the last two columns, are made of air <note>painted to appear as if seen against the open sky</note>. And the true masters of perspective have held to this way, not making "Conversions of Paul" or "Nativities of **CHRIST**" <note>original: "CHRISTO"</note> upon those facades where the eye must be raised too high to compare and judge them perfectly. 

On facades, one also paints figures in <term>rilievo</term> <note>relief; painting that mimics three-dimensional sculpture</note>, such as Emperors, prisoners, and the like, feigning them within niches, or above cornices and brackets projecting outward. ...openings, the loggias, and the corridors. To address this, many masters who are rare in this art have discovered the technique of painting upon tapestries and hanging them high up to demonstrate the truth of the <term>historie</term> <note>narrative scenes, usually of a historical, religious, or mythological nature</note>. In these, one must likewise place the <term>punto</term> <note>the vanishing point</note> in the center, as has been observed by many rare masters of perspective—most notably the master Zenale <note>Bernardo Zenale (c. 1460–1526), a Milanese painter and architect known for his mastery of perspective</note> and Vincenzo Civerchio, nicknamed "the Elder," in certain narrative scenes of the miracles of Saint Peter Martyr in [the church of] Saint Eustorgio in Milan, in the chapel of that Saint. In these works, there are four men above the eye level, where one sees the planes recede and the heights descend most gently. 

Polidoro <note>Polidoro da Caravaggio (c. 1499–1543), famous for his monochromatic paintings on the facades of Roman palaces</note> also observed this; upon many facades in Rome where he painted battles, triumphs, and sacrifices of the Romans high up, he showed the ground plane below almost as if in a steady mirror. This represented the truth of the narrative, which the eye must judge from a high vantage point. This is also perceived in Trajan’s Column, in whose narratives the ground planes are visible all the way to the top; thus, they demonstrate the truth of the work to the wisdom of the intellect without being limited by the view from the eye below. Therefore, paintings can be made and placed like a mirror of nature in whatever part one wishes: high, low, or in the middle. 

Finally, for this art, the five modes of seeing are determined by straight lines. Of these lines, three are primary: one is above the eye, falling perpendicularly over it like a <term>Zenith</term> <note>the highest point directly above the observer</note>; the second falls below the eye; and the third is the middle line <note>the horizon line or eye level</note>. If a cube is placed at the end of each of these, only one face can be seen. The other two lines are diagonals which come from the eye itself, one going upward and the other downward, and they serve the three aforementioned lines. If a cube is placed at the end of these diagonals, it is necessary that both above and below, two faces are seen in <term>scorto</term> <note>foreshortening</note> for each, which serve the other three. In this way, the true eye comes to be the center of the true narrative—or, we might say, the mirror—just as the ancient and modern masters of perspective assert. This is especially true of the Lombards, for whom this specialty is their own, just as design is peculiar to the Romans, coloring to the Venetians, and bizarre inventions to the Germans.

...that these proportions are linked one with the other in a circle, just as they are made; beginning at the top of the ear and circling around, it touches the eyebrows; and the end of the ear, circling, touches the tip of the nose. Likewise, descending downwards, all the aforementioned proportions go in a circle, such as the chest, the navel, the elbows, and the knees. And the closer they are to the **frame** <note>original: *telaro*; a perspective frame or "Dürer's window" used to map 3D objects onto a 2D plane</note>, the larger they will appear, and the further away, the smaller, according to the vision of the eye. And this is what pertains to the perfect form. 

Coming then to the frame and its transfers, one shall proceed thus: first, one shall take an iron bar six **inches** <note>original: *onze*; a unit of length</note> high with an opening at the top, and place it in front of the frame at a distance of ten or eight inches, standing upright according to my judgment. And it shall be placed as if it were the man who looks at the face of the frame, and it shall be made either higher or lower according to the sweetness of seeing the figures as perfect as they are, drawn to his eye. Then, using paste, you shall attach a paper to the upright edges of the front of the frame, upon which are the numbers that I now add. You shall begin at the bottom of the frame, as much on one side as the other, and divide it into spaces of half an inch each, and within [each space] ten **minutes** <note>original: *minuti*; small subdivisions of the inch for high precision</note>; and thus you shall continue to the top of the frame, increasing the numbers according to the minutes as well. 

Then you shall take a **small ruler** <note>original: *righetta*</note> that fits exactly from one side of the frame to the other, and upon this you shall mark the minutes and the exact numbers just as they are marked on the frame. Now you shall move the ruler up and down as seems correct; and into the hole of the aforementioned iron, which is to be the eye of the man, you may also pass a thread to which you will hang a small **plumb bob** <note>original: *piombino*</note>. And behind the iron, with the rest of the thread, you shall go about diligently touching the proportions or points already described on the forehead and every other part that you wish. 

Then you shall place the small ruler, which exactly crosses the frame, under the thread that is the limit of the face [of the frame], and there you shall consider the minutes and its numbers, both on the ruler and on the frame. In addition to this, by making another frame exactly like the first, covered with a sheet of paper on an **easel** <note>original: *cavalletto*</note>, you shall transfer the numbers and minutes of the thread onto the paper frame using the said ruler. Following this method, you shall form whatever part is in the figure; and proceeding in a circle, for those parts that recede between one point and another, you shall make a cross. Once a figure is immediately made with its points and crosses, you shall take away the "eye"—that is, the thread—and in its place you shall put your own eye; and upon the paper frame, you shall minutely outline its points and small crosses while still viewing the model from that same eye. Having done this, you shall return the thread and iron to its place; and thus you can make the angles of bricks, tables, and bases from below and above, making them come out correctly to the view; and if the eye is lower, you will look at the figures...

With these proportions and such a **frame** <note>original: *telaro*; a device used to map three-dimensional objects onto a two-dimensional surface</note>, you can make very large figures by enlarging its **numbers** and **minutes** <note>these refer to the coordinate system marked on the frame’s edges</note>, in such a way that you can create whatever comes to mind outside of the small frame. I can say frankly that I did not learn this method from anyone, but rather imagined it myself for the benefit of the professors of this, our art. 

Now, as for "squared" figures <note>this refers to the method of "cubing" or blocking out the human form into geometric volumes to handle foreshortening</note>, **Vincenzo Foppa** <note>an influential early Renaissance painter from the Lombard school</note> drew many of them; he perhaps must have read of those that **Lysippus** <note>a famous Greek sculptor of the 4th century BCE</note>, the ancient sculptor, squared in such a way, with that **symmetry** <note>original: *simmetria*; referring to the mathematical relationship between parts of the body</note> that has no specific name in Latin. Following him, **Bramante** <note>Donato Bramante, the famous architect and painter</note> later drew a book on them, from which **Raphael**, **Polidoro**, and **Gaudenzio** <note>Gaudenzio Ferrari</note> derived great benefit; and according to what is said, it later came into the hands of **Luca Cambiaso of Pozzolo** <note>original: *Luca Cangiaſo Pozzeueraſco*; a Genoese painter known for his "cubist" drawing style</note>, who because of this succeeded in being most rare in the world for his inventions and whimsy. 

Besides this, human bodies can be grown from ground plans in other ways, such as by the power of numbers with the **veil** of **Leon Battista Alberti**, with the frame and the **grid** <note>original: *graticola*; a lattice used for copying or scaling drawings</note> of **Albrecht Dürer**, and of **Jan van Fris of Groningen** <note>original: *Giouanni di Friſia di Graminge*; likely referring to Jan Vredeman de Vries, a specialist in perspective</note>; which instruments I have seen together with many other figures drawn by many using the perspective of **Hans Lencker** <note>original: *Gio. Lenclaer*; a Nuremberg goldsmith and theorist on perspective</note>. 

But returning to the construction of the aforementioned instrument, you shall take two rulers three fingers wide and a quarter-inch thick, and you shall make a small step in the thickness of both, which will follow its minutes and numbers, so as to be able to drive the small narrow ruler inside from above; this is so that its numbers and minutes can be found more clearly. The ruler should be narrow at the bottom and sharp at the top to be able to touch the limbs more minutely, and then pull it forward and backward for the eye. And this can also be done with the string and the **plumb line** mentioned above. To the two main rulers of the frame, you shall nail another ruler at the top crosswise, and at the bottom, you shall drive the two rulers equally into a **block** <note>original: *zocco*; a base or pedestal</note>, leaving them standing upright next to a table or whatever else you wish. You can also make the frame from iron rulers, as will be sufficiently explained when treating the theory of said frame. Regarding the straight and correct plane, which begins at the end of the **optics** <note>the science of vision and light</note> that terminates in the facade or "line of the cut" <note>the picture plane where the 3D view is "cut" into a 2D image</note>; where all the correct proportions go to border and intersect on the facade at the primary eye; you shall place the square obliquely and crosswise, and you shall touch with the string that extends from the eye all the outer circumferences, and thus you shall draw...

And know for certain that oblique and twisted figures can be made in this way, even though it is a very difficult and tedious task. Therefore, it is better to make them using the aforementioned method, which is more certain—that is, using figures made of wood, clay, or wax, with their **cloth** <note>original: *panni*; referring to drapery studies on mannequins</note> and their lighting. Rest assured that by using this method of **proportion** <note>original: *proportione*; here referring to the mathematical relationship between parts</note>, you will immediately find any error that anyone commits in **perspective** <term>prospettiua: the art of representing three-dimensional objects on a two-dimensional surface</term>. There is, furthermore, another kind of curved instrument for **vaults** and **projections** <note>original: *sporti*; parts of a building that jut out from the main wall</note>, which is made arched and is placed upon the work according to the minutes written on paper. With a similarly arched ruler, you can do the same over the drawing you wish to make from the sides, using a ruler in the middle that visits the parts of the figures in **foreshortening** <note>original: *scorto*; the technique of depicting an object as having less depth or distance than it actually has</note>, or whatever else is required.

## The logic of the aforementioned frame. Chapter XV.

**Y**ou shall then draw a vertical line, which shall be called the line of the **facade** <note>original: *facciata*; also known as the picture plane</note> or the cut; at the bottom of this, you shall draw another line at **level** <note>original: *liuello*; the ground line</note>. On the right side, it will create the order of natural proportion from both top and bottom. Now, on the level line behind the foot of the facade, you shall mark four equal spaces, naming them one by one: A, B, C, and D. Then, you shall make four others on the left part of the facade on the level line, calling them "the viewing" and "the eye," marking them 1, 2, 3, and 4. Next, you will place three men crosswise at a distance from the facade on the left side upon the level line, and this shall be the **eye of the distance** <note>a Renaissance method for establishing the viewer's distance from the scene</note>. From this eye, draw an **optical line** <note>original: *linea optica*; a line representing the path of sight</note> that reaches the facade; there, you shall mark a point calling it the **end of the sight** <term>fine della vista: what we now call the vanishing point, where all parallel lines appear to converge</term>, at which all proportions of viewing meet. And so, from the first point marked 1, you shall draw a line to this end of the sight, and likewise from the second marked 2, from the third marked 3, and from the fourth marked 4. Then, from the first eye, you shall draw a line to A, intersecting it at the facade, and likewise to B, to C, and to D, always intersecting them at the

->SIXTH<-

Furthermore, to hang a figure straight down <note>original: *à squadro*; perpendicular or at a right angle</note>, which will be the figure of **proportion**, you must draw its limbs toward the **primary eye** <term>primo occhio: the principal viewpoint or vanishing point in a perspective construction</term>. Where these lines intersect the **level** <note>original: *liuello*; the flat plane of the picture surface</note>, there shall be the limit of the viewer's sight. And at the bottom of said figure, if you wish to create the ground plane, you will draw the spaces marked toward the primary eye; where they intersect on the level, that will be the limit of the sight. In this, the primary eye acts like that of a preacher looking down from a pulpit, and drawing the sight lines to the intersections follows what was said regarding the facade.

This same method must be followed when looking upwards from the primary eye; the end of the sight-line will be found by drawing a line to the level above. Perpendicular to this, you shall create the standing figure, drawing its limbs toward the primary eye. Where it intersects the level, there will be the limit of sight, whether it be far, near, or above. From said level, you will draw those limbs perpendicularly, marked with their numbers in the same manner as they are drawn in a perfect body, whether from the front or in profile.

Afterward, beneath the line of the foot, you shall draw a front-facing figure at a right angle, corresponding to the one transferred in profile. You will draw this front-facing figure with the aforementioned numbers to the previously described foot-line, marking it also with those numbers. These you will draw to the limit of the sight-line, where the head will be at the highest part. According to the transfer to the eye, the body in profile will appear narrower due to its **foreshortening** <note>original: *sfuggir*; the visual contraction of an object as it extends into space</note>. In this way, step by step, the other limbs will appear wider at the feet because they are closer to the eye. Thus, with these widths, you can proceed to the end of the sight-line so that the figure beneath the feet will be seen in a correct and perfect **zenith** <term>Zenith: a perspective view looking straight up or straight down, often called "sotto in su" in Italian art</term> form.

You shall observe the same for the level below, making the head appear thicker because it is closer to the eye, and the feet—being lower—will recede in perspective just like equal planes. Regarding the view of **vaults** and the circles of **chapels**, you shall draw the proportioned figure, drawing the limbs toward the primary eye; where the lines touch the curve or the vault, that shall be the limit of the sight and the point for deepening the vaults. I have demonstrated this in my paintings at **San Marco in Milan** <note>Referring to the Church of San Marco; the author is likely Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo, who decorated the Foppa Chapel there starting in 1570</note> in the figures of the **Prophets**, the **Sibyls**, the **Hierarchies of Angels**, the **Evangelists**, and in all the other narrative scenes, such as those of **Saint Peter and Paul** and the **Virgin**. This also applies to the facades represented in that chapel, which I completed in the year 1570. Thus, we can be certain that by drawing all figures proportionately, no matter how far they are from the primary eye, the distance will be judged correctly. This stands to the confusion of those who consider themselves wise but place figures atop mountains that cannot possibly be seen.

## **Geometric Proportions to be transferred to the view. Cap. XVI.**

**I**n the logic of the instrument, we have spoken of the line of the **facade** <term>facciata: the picture plane or the surface on which the drawing is made</term>, or the "line of the cut," to which the **proportionate level** is placed below on the right side, and on the left is the level line for viewing the object. Now, from the right where **A** is marked, you shall geometrically create a perfect square beneath the proportionate level, so that the line of the facade descends far enough to form one side of the square, which shall be called the **line of sight**. Within this same square, you shall draw two diagonal lines from one corner to the other, intersecting one another. Where they intersect, that shall be the point and center of the square, through which you shall draw the two diameters of the square—upward and across—so that there will be nine points in the square. This is the "rectified and straight square" <note>a perfectly balanced grid</note>, because we will speak of slanted and twisted ones later. 

You shall then begin at the right angle near the facade on the right part of the level to mark **A**, then at the second part of the diameter on the same level mark **B**, and **C** at the other right angle. Next, beneath **A** on the line of sight at the head of the second diameter, you will mark another **A**, then at the center **B**, and at the end **C**. Finally, at the end of the line of sight and the square, you will mark **A**, **B**, and **C** at the other two points. 

Now, coming to the **eye** <note>the viewer's station point</note> mentioned above in the logic of the instrument, you will draw a line to the first **A** that forms the corner of the facade; from the level, this remains a single point because it sits upon it. Then, from that same eye, coming to **B** with a straight line, wherever it intersects the facade, there you shall place **B**. Returning to the eye and drawing to **C**, where the line intersects the facade, there you shall place **C** as the limit of the **diminished proportion** <term>proportione digradata: the way objects appear smaller as they recede in perspective</term>. 

Then, returning to the other line of sight (since it is through this that all things are seen) marked with three **A**s, you will transfer it exactly, ensuring that those marks noted on the inside of the square—as must be done in all other proportions—are continually turned upward and carried to the level line for viewing the object. Therefore, on this line of sight, three **A**s will be marked as the beginning of the perfect square. When these are drawn to the "end of sight" point <note>the vanishing point</note> located on the facade (as was already mentioned in the other Chapter), the intersection of **C** shall be carried perpendicular to the facade up to the line of the last **A**, and the other to the end of sight, and it shall again be marked **C**. You shall do this consequently until the intersection of **B**, marking them in such a way that you will see the perfect square in perspective.

Returning now to the beginning of the **geometric square**, you may create another square crosswise enclosed within those four lines, and likewise draw its diagonal lines and its diameters. Mark them all with their corresponding numbers, and draw them perpendicularly above the **level** <term>liuello: the ground line or horizontal base of the perspective construction</term>, marking them with their numbers. Once you have transported these to the **eye** <note>the vanishing point or the viewer's point of perspective</note>, you shall mark those same numbers at the intersections upon the **facade** <term>facciata: the picture plane or surface upon which the drawing is made</term>.

And returning again to the geometric square, you shall again draw those numbers across—or rather, at the level—to the **line of sight**, which you shall likewise carry over to the **line of seeing** <note>original: "linea del vedere"</note>, so that all are drawn to the **endpoint of sight** <note>the vanishing point</note>. Then, following the square of the facade, you shall bring the first intersection with its numbers, and you shall do the same for all the others. Now, within the said geometric square, a circle can be made, and another that comes exactly to the endpoint of sight on the facade. There you may mark the **fluting** <note>the vertical grooves</note> of the column; once these are drawn to the eye, where they intersect on the facade, that shall be the limit of its visibility. And here also is the proportion of **convex mirrors**, and likewise of **historiated columns** <note>columns decorated with narrative carvings or scenes</note>.

But returning to the first circle: you shall divide it into three to make the triangle and the **pyramid**, as well as a circle—though pointed at the top like the one in the square. Coming to the triangle, by dividing those parts in two, they come to form six angles in the circle. When these are drawn upward to the level line with their numbers marked and carried to the eye, they form their intersections on the facade. When they are carried again to the line of sight at a square or level—and that carried to the view—it is joined part by part in detail, as was already said.

The same shall be done for the aforementioned triangle. However, I will not pause to touch upon the **celestial proportions** of which the ancients already wrote, deriving all the principal geometric proportions regularly from the human figure standing upright. Among the moderns, this was done by **Friar Luca del Borgo** <note>Luca Pacioli (c. 1447–1517), the influential mathematician who wrote "De divina proportione"</note>, who furthermore had all his contours and perfect and imperfect angles drawn by the hand of **Leonardo da Vinci**.

You shall carry these to the eye, intersecting them on the line of the facade and marking their aforementioned numbers. This concludes what pertains to the **straight staircase**. # SECTION

...that with the instrument I have built, I intend to make this understood to all who wish to know it in detail, leaving more subtle thinkers to explore deeper ideas beyond my own reach. 

Now, to transfer figures from profile, you must construct a corresponding frontal figure directly opposite it. All the limbs of the profile figure must be truly transferred and mapped with straight lines. These are the "transportations" of proportion from a profile figure to a frontal one, using the method of transferring one proportion into the other with lines that are parallel—whether horizontal or vertical. 

But to draw figures in <term>foreshortening</term> <note>Italian: *scorto*; the artistic technique of depicting an object as having less depth or distance than it actually has to create an illusion of space</note> for the viewer, the main methods are as follows: figures placed in profile or head-on (on which <term>Albrecht Dürer</term> <note>1471–1528, the German Renaissance master famous for his mathematical treatises on art</note> has treated excellently in his work on proportion), or lying down, or standing before the eye—whether high, low, or directly level. These are the three views of the same eye. Once you have mapped the figures via the "rays of the eye" onto the <term>facade</term> <note>the "picture plane" or the flat surface of the drawing where the perspective is first calculated</note>, you will immediately project them into the perspective view at a right angle to the facade, below the level of the projected figure. 

For if the first proportioned figure near the facade is in profile, it will immediately produce a frontal figure in the perspective view, shown in foreshortening. Thus, below the level of vision, you shall create the frontal figure, proportioned according to the perspective view. Directly in front of the viewer, you will draw all its limbs straight up to the level of vision. There, you will note its measurements and its <term>diminishing proportions</term> <note>Italian: *proportioni digradate*; how sizes appear smaller as they recede into the distance</note>. From here, you will again draw these measurements and proportions straight upwards to the figure that is to be extended. 

And because on the facade—to put it simply—a profile figure of a face (which represents a value of ten) <note>In classical systems of proportion, the human body was often measured as being ten "faces" high</note> is transferred into the frontal view, it will become the size of a foot (which represents a sixth part) <note>Similarly, the body was often measured as being six "feet" high</note>. Therefore, you shall place the <term>navel</term> <note>Italian: *vmbelico*</note> level with the center of the frontal figure in the view. In this same way, you will project all the other proportions to the facade. Where they meet the lines of the level of vision at a right angle, that shall be their endpoint. 

Know also that when transferring proportions between frontal and profile figures, you must always keep this in mind: if the right breast is higher than the left in the frontal view, it must be the same in the profile. In this manner, all other limbs are carried over from one to the other. This process can be seen with much greater ease using the aforementioned <term>instrument</term> <note>likely a perspective machine or drafting grid used by the author to automate these geometric projections</note>.

...depth of its members, which must be marked on the same diameters. Then, from the second, somewhat thicker [measurement], those who have to create figures that are somewhat more <term>terrible</term> <note>Italian: *terribili*; in Renaissance art theory, this refers to a style of powerful, awe-inspiring, or heroic grandeur, famously associated with the works of Michelangelo</note> will take their example from these widths and depths marked on the same diameters. Finally, that of Hercules—the thickest and strongest—extends to the very top of the diameters, while the <term>armature</term> <note>Italian: *anima*; literally "soul," referring here to the central internal axis or structural core of the figure</note> remains straight in the middle of these diameters. One could also make a metal template that precisely follows the contour of the foundations of the members and its floor plan around the same diameters; in this way, you can introduce all the other proportions of any object. This is one of the principal rules that has ever been established in the world, as useful for painting as it is for statuary and sculpture, from which all desired forms may be derived. 

But to come to this same rule, which is swifter than the others that could be made, and likewise to treat its movements in a regulated manner, you shall proceed as follows. First, you will form a flat, square base, and then ensure that each of the four lines surrounding the base on the plane is divided into exactly fifty parts, so that from one side to the other they are all drawn at right angles—those across as well as those lengthwise—marking each part with its numbers, all equal, on one side as on the other, and here as well as there. 

Next, you will make another base exactly like the first, which you will raise upright at a right angle to the first base, calling it the "limit" and the height of the figure you wish to make. You will mark it exactly like the base that it is, as the plan of the figure, with its numbers and squared lines. Now, coming to the figure that is to be placed upon the base in the center, you will take a copper wire as high as the limit, which you will call the <term>armature</term> of the statue. You will then make the diameters of the limbs in a cross on its front and profile; these two diameters, which create four points, you could for greater clarity even make into four, which would result in eight points. 

But for the sake of brevity, let us stick to two diameters. You shall then ensure that the top point of the armature is exactly above the head; then, descending downward, you will make two diameters in a cross. You will first take the measurement of the forehead, then the eyes, the nose, the chin, the neck, the <term>pit of the throat</term> <note>Italian: *fontanella*; the depression at the base of the neck</note>, the chest, the navel, the bottom of the torso, the top of the <term>hip joints</term> <note>Italian: *chiaui de' galoni*; literally the "keys of the flanks," referring to the pelvic crests or hip bones</note>, the knees, the ankles, and the feet. And at the height, marking in that <term>vertical post</term> <note>Italian: *termine*; here referring to a vertical measuring rod or rule set at a right angle to the base</note> perpendicularly as you did at the bottom, you will place the heights of the points of the diameters and their midpoints, which is the <term>armature</term> <note>Italian: *anima*; literally "soul," the central structural axis of the figure</note>. 

To give an example of this, you will take the diameter of the width of the navel, which might be high on one side and low on the other, and you will draw it perpendicularly on the base. Then you will draw the highest part of the navel perpendicularly to its height on the vertical post, and the lowest part in the same way. Thus, from the low point to the high point, you will find in the middle the armature of the statue which passes through the center by way of the numbers of the parts drawn perpendicularly. You will also find its depth, which passes through the navel below a specific point of height on the vertical post. 

And on the base, its floor plan will be drawn perpendicularly, noting with points and marks the limbs of the figure, and on the vertical post their heights and names—that is, in the <term>gridded</term> <note>Italian: *graticulate*; the practice of using a grid (squaring) to transfer or scale a design</note> sections, just as painters do; always considering the numbers. And this is the true path for making models. And if you wish to make a life-sized marble figure from the form of a small model, you will make the base as large as the figure you want to create, and the vertical post likewise. 

But coming to **low relief**, which conforms to the perspective of the eye, you will proceed in the manner described in the past chapters, placing the eye in its location, distant from the facade three times the width, and at its center. Then, in the flat proportion of the facade, you will arrange the figures or whatever else you wish to represent in low relief, and according to those, you will do exactly as I said above with the base and its gridded vertical posts, which you will place in their positions within the <term>narrative scene</term> <note>Italian: *historia*; a term used in art theory to describe a complex narrative composition involving multiple figures</note>. 

Then, from the farthest corner of the proportion, you will draw a line to the eye that touches the facade, and perpendicularly to it within the proportion, you will find the thickness of the marble or metal into which you wish to introduce the low relief. Then, according to the thickness of the marble on said line, you will draw a diagonal line from the foot of the facade and the start of the proportion, which does not pass the aforementioned line, either higher or lower. To this diagonal line—which is the actual plane of the low relief—you will draw with the eye the lines of the bases and vertical posts, so that the figures closer to the facade will remain larger than the others on this diagonal plane of the low relief. You must ensure, however, that the eye performs its part—that is, contouring correctly over the vertical posts drawn by lines to see all its members as the eye would see them, without expressing the other parts. relief should follow the correct path of the lines carried to the eye from the primary base and the first <term>marker</term> <note>Italian: *termine*; the vertical measuring rod mentioned previously</note> to this second one of the <term>low relief</term> <note>Italian: *basso rilievo*; sculpture where the figures project only slightly from the background</note>, as well as its height. This height, following the straight line of the marker, shall be expressed squarely, making the limbs <term>foershorten</term> <note>Italian: *scortare*; the visual effect of an object appearing shorter than it is when viewed at an angle</note>. And so you shall proceed step by step, ensuring always that the proportion further away is shorter on the floor plan. 

But take heed that in low relief the limbs should not simply foreshorten but should attach themselves to the drapery and other elements (and <term>Michelangelo</term> <note>Italian: *il Buonarotto*</note> also observed this precaution in his reliefs). The more the work is pulled close to the front surface, the more it corresponds with painting; and the more it descends toward the bottom, the more it conforms with sculpture, becoming thicker and making the most raised limbs project outward. 

Thus, this art of low relief is true and certain in the parts that are seen; but as for the back parts, they are never found, as they follow the order of diagonal planes, according to which it is clear they cannot be found—unless they are separated from one another. For this reason, in ancient <term>sarcophagi</term> <note>Italian: *pili*; literally "basins" or "pillars," but here referring to ancient Roman funerary monuments</note> and their low reliefs, one finds legs and other rounded parts, just as the excellent modern artists have also imitated, such as Donatello, Caradosso Foppa, and Benedetto Pavese. 

From this, one sees the great differences between sculpture and painting: the former considers geometric proportion, while the latter not only considers it but draws it with a <term>perspective eye</term>. Sculpture does not create the material but the proportion, whereas painting creates both. Finally, sculpture receives natural light, but painting not only receives it but introduces it through its various parts, giving it moreover its losses and gains <note>Refers to highlights and shadows that create the illusion of depth</note>. This is seen in a mirror, in which one perceives everything on a flat surface that is perspectively possible to see through geometry, which is also seen under the term of perspective. However, more has been said extensively about these arts in the <term>disputes</term> <note>Refers to the *Paragone*, a Renaissance debate over the superior art form</note> between their craftsmen written by the Florentine Benedetto Varchi.
