...in his garden, one is as high as the metal one made by <term>Zenodorus</term> <note>A Greek sculptor of the 1st century AD, famous for the colossal bronze statue of Nero in Rome.</note>. Regarding this subject, I will not keep silent about what the divine <term>Buonarroti</term> <note>Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475–1564), the celebrated Renaissance master.</note> used to say concerning the art of making them: namely, that the ancients possessed the true science of knowing how to view statues from both near and far. Because of this, once when he was in Rome at <term>Monte Cavallo</term> <note>The Quirinal Hill in Rome, named "Horse Mountain" because of the two ancient colossal statues of the "Horse Tamers" (Dioscuri) located there.</note>, he had occasion to say these or similar words: that modern painters and sculptors ought to have their proportions and measurements in their eyes so they can put them into execution. He meant to suggest that this science was lost among the moderns compared to those marvelous statues of the ancients, such as those by <term>Phidias</term> and <term>Praxiteles</term> <note>The most famous sculptors of ancient Greece; the statues at Monte Cavallo were attributed to them in the Renaissance.</note> located there in Rome.

To begin, therefore, we must know that since the height of a colossus is nine <term>braccia</term> <note>Italian: *braccia*; a measurement of length based on the arm, roughly 23 inches.</note>, the person who is to see it perfectly must stand three times as far away as the colossus is high—that is, the limit of the human eye. Thus, from the said eye, through a straight <term>optical line</term> to the colossus (which is the same facade where the colossus is to be represented), as if from the optical point, you will take an open compass. Keeping one point of the compass fixed at the eye, you will turn the other around so that it reaches the measure of nine *braccia*, so that you may view it perfectly.

And at the circle, you shall place the measurement of a model, or a copper plate divided into ten <term>faces</term> <note>The "face" or "head" was a standard proportional unit; a figure ten "faces" high was considered heroic or colossal.</note>, which should be of the aforementioned height. This model must have its diameters made in a copper cross according to the widths, depths, and prominences of its limbs; and you shall place it according to the circle in that attitude which the colossus or the model is to take. Then you will carry the points and the centers of these diameters of the limbs from the eye that sees them, using precise strings to the facade; and there you will mark its points. 

Afterward, according to those points, you will outline them accurately; and if by chance you have any doubt regarding the figures in profile, you shall consult the <term>symmetry</term> <note>Refers to *Four Books on Human Proportion* (1528).</note> of <term>Albrecht Dürer</term>, in which you will find the correct parallels of the limbs which intersect the "soul" or core of the figures; just as the widths of their limbs are also placed there in equal measure. 

And so, with this method, you will be able to make all the colossi you wish, always keeping this before your eyes: that if the colossus is ten times taller in proportion than a man, the man must stand thirty times as far away to see it perfectly. For we know for certain that the eye, at the center of the circles, sees the parts marked therein proportionally; and when these are carried from the eye with strings to the facade and marked there, they turn out just as accurately on the facade near the eye as they are in the turn or circumference. # BOOK SIX

->SIXTH<-

And because in such colossi one requires great attention in making them perfectly pleasing to our sight, one must always keep in mind that the center of the diameters—such as those of the <term>fontanella: the hollow at the base of the throat</term> and the shoulders—should be raised with material of clay or wax while they are upright. Then, one must not add much of said material over the four points of the diameters, so that they may successfully meet the heights of their centers. And this is the rarest and most graceful part, through which the high limbs of the colossus can please our eyes, just as I said before regarding those in painting. One could also place the aforementioned colossus in proportion after the frame <note>original: *telaro*; a grid or physical frame used for scaling</note> with the numbers mentioned above; and thus draw all its parts to the eye, and in such a way put them into a drawing and express them in painting, even though the points of the diameters that come outward rise higher, so as not to have their crossing—which so delights the sight, as I said above. And in this art of making colossi in painting and sculpture, one needs a steady promptness in making them. Because, to tell the truth, it requires greater strength of drawing to make its members stand out than is required in natural-sized figures; and whoever tries it can know this. And this way of making them serves as well as the first, even though it is somewhat less certain, even if it is easier. Finally, in the aforementioned circle of the eye <note>a geometric construction used to calculate how objects diminish or distort in the visual field</note> one can transfer the heights of all conforming letters, both in painting and in sculpture, as well as shields and obelisks, provided they are all marked equally in the circle with their divisions. In the same circle, if the five columns of the size of the lowest <term>Tuscan: the simplest and stoutest of the classical architectural orders</term> are marked according to optics, and are carried from the eye to the facade, one will see on that facade the Tuscan column lower than the others; and so, step by step, they will all go on increasing, so that the highest will be the longest. In this, architects, painters, and sculptors must always have this awareness: that all the orders should appear equal to the eyes, like the circle. And let this suffice to have been said regarding this part, even for the spaces of narrow and wide streets according to the convenience of distances, and especially of architecture, which is that which, possessing the whole, also governs it with due prudence.

### Method of making inverse perspective that appears true, being viewed through a single hole. Chapter XIX.

**Y**ou will take, under a portico, following the cross-section of the facade, a canvas or paper fifteen <term>braccia: an Italian unit of measure, literally "arms," approximately 23 inches</term> long across, or more or less as you wish, and one cubit high; and place it on the said wall. Then you will arrange at one corner of the facade a well-made Horse, or a head of a CHRIST, or whatever else you wish.

...you wish to make it upon a frame, and you will <term>graticulerai: mark with a grid</term> it both vertically and horizontally. Let the frame be as high as the paper, and on one side let it be positioned against the wall together with the paper on one side of that same frame. Once this is done, you will pull back so far that the paper attached to the wall meets the frame that is standing away from the wall; and there you will ensure that your eye is placed at a very great distance, exactly in the middle of the frame—that is, that its <term>ottica: line of sight</term> is exactly at the center of it. And at the eye, or whatever device you use, you shall place a stretched string with which you will carry all the proportional grid lines into the frame of that "eye," marking them upon the paper. Thus, in that part which is closest to the corner of the frame with the paper, the lines will be long, and the others even longer, which you will then drop down as <note>original: *piombino*; using a lead weight or plumb line to ensure verticality</note> plumb lines upon the paper. After this, you will transfer the heights of the frame onto the paper exactly by the grid lines from the frame that is near it, and those grid lines you will transfer to the other end of the exact paper; and thus in those parallels of the <term>anello: ring</term>—or eye—one sees the grid of the frame correctly.

Taking away the frame, and keeping it nearby, you will go behind it to draw the lines using a very large rod with a charcoal point tied to the tip, contouring the figure from one side according to the grid lines you have in the frame nearby. And so, from that same ring, even though it is closer to the paper because of the optics, you will be able to see with your eye everything that is on the paper attached to the wall. I have seen such a work by the hand of <note>Gaudenzio Ferrari (c. 1471–1546), a prominent Northern Italian painter</note> **Gaudenzio** of a **CHRIST** in profile, where the hair seemed like waves of the sea, but then, having arrived at the viewing hole where the frame had been placed with the paper, it revealed a most beautiful face of **CHRIST**.

Using this same method, **Francesco Melzo** <note>Francesco Melzi, Leonardo da Vinci’s beloved pupil and heir</note> recounted that **Leonardo** made a Dragon fighting a Lion, a very marvelous thing to see, and likewise the horses he made to give to **Francis Valois, King of France**; which art was well understood by **Girolamo Ficino** <note>Girolamo Figino, a Milanese painter who studied the works of Leonardo</note> in the rendering of horses.

# BOOK SIX

->SIXTH<-

<margin>1.</margin> ...the position of the part upon which it stays and rests, the muscles should be shown as more prominent and visible; in the other part, they should be softer and gentler, as it is a part that does not support the weight of the body. And when drawing from life, the weaknesses of nature must be aided by the strength of art; as among the <term>quadrature: the geometric squaring of forms</term> of the limbs drawn to the eye in <term>perspective</term>, one should first sketch the bones in the middle, and afterward add the muscles as art requires, but always pulling back toward the likeness of the natural. Then it must be noted that after the <note>original: *inuentione*; the composition or creative concept</note> invention is made and established—whether bold or soft—above all, no outline should be left in the parts or around them, for these were introduced only as a rule and standard for the form and the order that must be maintained in the figure. And this can be seen clearly in nature, where nothing is perceived except the division of one body from another, and light and shadow that surround it according to its parts. 

Beyond this, principal care must be taken in the exercise of this art so that the lights are dispensed with prudence alongside the shadows, and the darks are placed in their bold and intense spots as the order of the design requires. The other parts should immediately recede and lose themselves in such a way that there arises that miraculous recession and eminent <term>relief</term>—the high and low of the limbs. This makes it so that those who see them, while observing such <term>separation</term> and relief, seem to become painters through their eyes, even if they are not by practice—much like <term>Masaccio</term> <note>Tommaso di Ser Giovanni di Simone (1401–1428), a pivotal Early Renaissance painter known for his realistic use of light and shadow</note>, who only lit and shadowed his figures without outlines. 

Nor should anyone say that to give strength and relief to paintings, it is impossible to make the lights so well-accompanied by the rest; for prudent artists do this by considering the distance of viewing. They usually add even greater lights to those lights, complicating the first diligent work with greater lights, darks, and half-tones, so that from a distance the paintings respond to the eye as if they were in relief. And the further away the paintings are, the more they must be lit and pushed back with dark. This rule must be observed not only in panel paintings but more vigorously upon walls, for which—the <term>lime</term> <note>original: *calze*, likely a misspelling of *calce*, the lime plaster used for fresco</note> being almost dry—one wants to give this greater light, and especially to those in <term>chiaroscuro</term> <note>original: *chiaro, & scuro*; the use of strong contrasts between light and dark</note>, as <term>Polidoro</term> <note>Polidoro da Caravaggio (c. 1499–1543), famous for his monochromatic facade paintings in Rome</note> used to do. There, the air that is between the eye and the painting causes the reliefs to be accompanied by the rest, as I already mentioned in the first and second [chapters] of the first book, and in many other places. There is also another rule to be observed in making the <term>reflections</term> of the lights more practically, which must be understood by everyone who wishes to be...

Then, ascending higher on the said facade toward the darkness where the protruding loggia casts its shadow, the paintings there should be reflected upward from the lower parts. The more the members <note>the parts of the body or architectural elements</note> protrude, the more they must be reflected near the descending light, and the other parts that recede must be lost and annihilated even more. And the ceiling of the loggia toward the facade must be more reflected than toward the part where the principal light of the Sun descends. Furthermore, when descending upon a figure that casts a shadow on another figure, that second figure must be reflected in the manner I have already described; however, some parts should still be touched by the primary light, which will give great strength to the work. In these reflections, **Antonio da Correggio** was the preeminent master.

Another particular caution should not be overlooked—namely, to place figures with rule and art. If the painter has a massive facade full of figures, so that they appear equal to the eye that sees them, the lowest one should be smaller than the others, and the one above should increase somewhat, adding to them proportionately step by step so that they all appear equal to the viewer. For if they were all of one size and scale on the facade, there is no doubt that the high ones would appear too small compared to those placed below, so that the facade would seem to vanish at the top. Following this rule, **Michelangelo** created his wonderful [Last] Judgment, and all others who have understood this art of placement have always done so, following the architectural order used in placing columns, which was discussed above. Now let us come to the placement of works.

Rather, they should have melancholy gestures and be devoid of laughter, as well suits their duties. Yet, despite this...

### What paintings are required in bright temples, consistories, and in privileged places of dignity. Chapter XXII. ###

In bright temples <note>i.e., churches</note> raised above the ground, there is a requirement for joyful histories <note>narrative scenes</note> full of majesty and wonder, such as the miracles of saints and their greatest deeds. For example: St. John preaching, St. Paul converting, Christ judging, the Apocalypse, the Last Supper, the woman taken in adultery, and other such glorious deeds of Christ and the saints. All of these possess a quality of wonder and greatness, and have nothing of the sorrowful or lugubrious about them. However, one should always attribute to each chapel and altar the specific miracle of the saint to whom it is dedicated, and to the high altar—which represents the entire temple—Christ with glories and thrones of angels in the chapel. It is indeed true that sometimes Christ can be accompanied by the saint in some of his deeds to which the temple is consecrated; indeed, it is necessary, especially in the <term>altarpiece</term> <note>original: "tauola"</note>. Furthermore, in a temple of the Old Testament, the great and wonderful deeds of those most holy men are fitting, such as those of Abel, Noah, Abraham, Melchizedek, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Aaron, Joshua, Mary <note>original: "Maria," referring here to Miriam, the sister of Moses</note>, David, Samson, Hezekiah, Daniel, and other Prophets, Sibyls, and holy men; provided that all possess decency and majesty. However, one reads of lewd deeds among some of these figures, all of which should be avoided. And not only these, but even the simple good ones that have some appearance of lewdness: such as Adam and Eve while they were naked in Paradise, Noah drunk on the road, Lot with his daughters, Judah with his daughter-in-law, Susanna seen by the elders, and others similar to these which are read in the sacred histories. In <term>consistories</term> <note>meeting halls for councils</note> and places where public councils are held, the walls require ornamentation of histories, maxims, studies, counsels, and similar things suitable to the place; in the manner seen in the hall of **Raphael of Urbino** <note>The Stanza della Segnatura in the Vatican</note>, where the wise men accord...

Instead, with the strongest severity, they should always judge according to reason, showing themselves terrible and frightening to the guilty, but to the innocent, appearing with majesty and reason. ### Which paintings should be placed in locations of fire and at places of execution. Chapter 23.

**S**ince among the places where fire is used, which are adorned with historical scenes, the **Fireplace** <note>Italian: *Camino*; here referring to the grand, monumental mantels found in the great halls of palaces</note> in the most spacious chambers and halls is of the greatest consideration; I shall speak only of the manner of decorating this, according to which all others should then be adorned. In fireplaces, therefore, one should not see painted any histories, fables, or symbols other than those where fires appear, along with meanings burning with **Love** and desires. From this, ingenious painters can create many compositions of their own. As for fables and histories, one could represent the fire descending upon the son of **Ocrisia** <note>Referring to the legend of the young Servius Tullius, a Roman king, whose head was seen surrounded by flames while he slept</note>; **Prometheus** when he steals the divine fire of the spirit; **Hercules** when he burns <note>On his funeral pyre on Mount Oeta</note>; **Ascanius** with the flame around his head after the destruction of **Troy**; and, if sacred histories are more pleasing, the **Three Youths in the Furnace**; **Nadab** and **Abihu** burning in their profane fire before the altar; **God** in the form of fire in the bush upon **Mount Horeb** before **Moses**; the **Glory** <note>The *Shekhinah* or divine presence</note> over the **Ark of the Old Testament**; the **Column of Fire** that went before them by night as a guide for the people of **Israel** who fled from **Egypt**; and those same people while they worked at the furnaces in **Egypt**. 

However, it seems that the fables and histories of the heathens are somehow more pleasing, as if they possess a greater beauty of invention. Therefore, it is appropriate to have a good store of fables, such as **Vulcan** when he fashions lightning bolts for **Jove**; **Phaethon** when he sets the earth ablaze; **Dido** when she throws herself into the fire with her treasure; **Althaea** when she places the sacred **Brand** <note>The wooden log linked to the life of her son Meleager</note> upon the fire; **Perillus** thrown into the **Bronze Bull** which he himself had built as a new and unheard-of torture; **Mucius Scaevola** when he burns his hand in the fire prepared for sacrifices in the presence of **Porsena**, King of the Tuscans; **Curtius** who leaps into the fire <note>Traditionally a chasm, here associated with the sacrificial fire</note>; **Medea** who performs the bizarre enchantment to rejuvenate **Aeson**; and **Ceres** who goes searching for her daughter with a burning torch in her hand. ### Which paintings are suited to royal palaces, the houses of princes, and other noble spaces. Chapter 24.

**I**n palaces and other principal places built for the residence and habitation of Kings and Princes, it is most fitting to paint the most worthy and honored deeds of great Princes and famous Captains. These include triumphs, victories, military councils, and bloody battles, in which, by looking upon them, it seems that our souls are raised to thoughts and desires of honor and greatness. Therefore, one could represent **Scipio** against **Hannibal**, **Aeneas** against **Turnus**, **Caesar** in **Thessaly** <note>The Battle of Pharsalus, where Caesar defeated Pompey</note> against **Pompey**, **Xerxes** against the **Spartans**, **Alexander** against the **Persians** and the **Indians**, the **Greeks** against the **Trojans**, and other similar celebrated deeds involving the most famous men who have ever lived. From these, Princes can find examples and lessons in the art of war, such as from the ancients **Dionysius**, **Miltiades**, **Theseus**, **Epaminondas**, **Pompey**, and **Sulla**; and from the moderns, **Arthur of England**, **Charlemagne**, **Charles VIII**, **Francis Valois** <note>King Francis I of France</note>, and **Charles V**, whose sublime deeds and glorious enterprises have consecrated...

This must also be observed in the placement of portraits; for it would not be right to place the portrait of a merchant near that of a Prince, nor that of a Pope near that of a Preacher, nor ***Virgil*** or ***Homer*** near ***Gonella*** <note>Pietro Gonella (c. 1390–1441) was a famous jester at the court of Ferrara; the author uses him here as the social and intellectual opposite of the venerable epic poets</note>, nor the portrait of a coarse and rustic man near ***Saint Ambrose***, ***Saint Peter***, or ***Saint Paul*** (of whom portraits are found), nor even near any other great Christian theologian. 

Regarding the placement of paintings, I judge it to be of no small importance to know how to apply them according to the suitability of the locations, and to divide them among themselves according to their different natures and states of being, following reason. For just as a good painting cannot be made without reason, so too can it not be situated in its proper and fitting place without it; and even a very good painting possesses little grace if it is not accommodated to its appropriate location. To do this, one must always distinguish between Monarchs, Popes, Emperors, and, step by step, all the ranks of people, in Religion as well as in arms and letters. In theaters, one should represent family histories, as did ***Sulla***, ***Caesar***, and many others; and on arches, the triumphs, victories, trophies, spoils, and everything required to completely represent a victory obtained; which also, as I have said, can be suitably represented in palaces along with triumphs and spoils.

In Genoa, and in many other places, and as one reads in the writings of the ancients regarding many people—such as the wonderful and ingenious palace of **Lucullus** <note>Lucius Licinius Lucullus (c. 118–57 BC), a Roman politician famous for his immense wealth and the "Lucullan" luxury of his gardens and villas</note>, a Roman citizen, and many others—we must principally know that whatever narrative is placed there, whether in sculpture or painting, it must be fitting and corresponding to the location. 

Such are the fables of the loves and the various transformations of the Goddesses and the Nymphs, where water, trees, and similar cheerful and delightful things appear. Examples include **Diana** when she bathes with her Nymphs in the **Gargaphian spring** in **Boeotia**; the winged horse <note>Pegasus</note> when he makes the **Castalian spring** gush forth with his hoof; the **Graces**, daughters of **Jupiter**, while they bathe in the **Acidalian spring** of **Orchomenus** sacred to **Venus**; **Narcissus** when he gazes at himself in the **Liriope spring**; **Salmacis** who is transformed into a spring of her own name in **Caria**, where likewise **Hermes** was transformed into **Hermaphroditus**; and other similar mythological events of **Byblis**, **Arethusa**, and amorous games occurring around fountains, such as those of **Egeria**, **Aonia**, **Libethra**, and others. 

These subjects also serve for cups, vases, and similar instruments <note>household objects or vessels</note> which, for ornament, may be engraved with the loves of the Sea Gods and the rivers, as was the practice of **Giuliano Taverna**, **Francesco Tortorino**, the great **Jacopo da Trezzo**, and **Annibal Fontana** <note>These were famous 16th-century Milanese artists specializing in gemstone engraving and goldsmithing</note>, a most great sculptor, along with other compositions and fictions of such a nature that they involve water.

For the satisfaction of certain spiritual persons, one could also paint around fountains our **Lord** when he appeared upon the sea to the disciples troubled by the storm, and when he called **Saint Peter**, **Saint Andrew**, and the two sons of **Zebedee** from their fishing, and also when he made wine from water, and when he found the **Samaritan woman** at the well, and many other similar Gospel examples. 

Around gardens, upon the walls, and likewise upon the open porticos that look toward them like sentinels, stories of joy and cheerfulness are similarly required, which have no shadow of melancholy at all. These would include **Mercury**, who with sweet sound lulls **Argus** to sleep; the **Heliades** who change into trees; **Perseus** who frees **Andromeda** from the Sea monster; **Marsyas** who competes in playing music with **Apollo**; the hunt of **Meleager**; the race of **Hippomenes** and **Atalanta**; the excellence of **Orpheus** in playing; and so many other fables told by the poets. 

And for those who do not wish to represent such things, they could instead paint the times, the seasons, the months, and the years, and besides these, their triumphs, chariots, and effects; and nearby, the tables of the Gods, the banquets, the feasts, the dances, and the jests which the nymphs of **Ceres** were accustomed to perform, either upon or around the oak tree, which was later cut down by **Erisich-** <gloss>Erisichthon</gloss>

[...perfec]tion, with other similar paintings that have a cheerful quality and are appropriate to the location; such as the jests of the **Satyrs**, the dances of the **Nymphs** of the rivers through green meadows, and the leaps of the **Fauns**. The ornaments should likewise follow the flow of the narratives, as will be discussed later when speaking of them. In place of fables, various **perspective views** <note>In the Renaissance, "prospettive" referred to architectural paintings designed to create an illusion of depth</note> can be arranged with no less beauty, which serve to lengthen the porticos and the garden walls. Beyond the columns in the intervals, one might place landscapes so well-matched that they appear to follow nature itself, depicting some of the aforementioned stories that suit such places—for example, **Apollo**, who behind the waves of **Thessaly** follows the beloved **laurel** <note>original: "alloro"; a reference to the nymph Daphne who was transformed into a laurel tree to escape Apollo</note>, or **Cephalus**, who by going out early makes **Aurora** <note>The Goddess of the Dawn</note> fall in love with him. I intend for this same order to be maintained in the private chambers or secluded loggias used by some princes. 

But above all, one must avoid pairing **old age with youth**, such as **Charon** <note>The elderly ferryman of the underworld</note> with the **Night** adorned with stars, or **Pluto** with the beautiful **Proserpina**; for this would provide no delight. Instead, one should always couple youth with youth, even if the man is slightly older, such as **Mars** with **Venus**, **Jupiter** with **Leda**, or **Boreas** <note>The North Wind</note> with **Orithyia**, **Zephyr** <note>The West Wind</note> with **Flora**, and **Pygmalion** <note>original: "Pimaleone"</note> with his **statue**, maintaining the **decency** <note>original: "honestà"; referring to the artistic propriety expected in noble settings</note> that is customary in the palaces of Princes. Though I do not praise lewd representations, I would sooner place there the **Creation of the World**, of the trees, the landscapes, the birds, and of man, or some other similar history. 

Furthermore, because **musical instruments** also require paintings and ornaments of their own quality, I judge that primarily for the **organs of temples**, the **shutters** <note>original: "coperte, ò tauole di tela"; the painted panels or canvases that fold over the organ pipes</note> should not be painted with any subject other than that which relates to what is being done. Since the shutters or covers are made to close the organ, which is built for music—and not, conversely, the organ for the shutters—it follows that since the organ is made for music, it requires that the covers correspond to it, containing nothing but musical subjects. One should not paint there what is most commonly the custom: the **prayers of Esther**, **conversions of Saint Paul**, battles, sacrifices, miracles, annunciations, and other similar subjects that have nothing to do with music. The true paintings that belong there should be on the inner side, which is seen while the organ is fully open and the melody and the voices of the pipes are heard. These should be such that they add sweetness to the sight, appropriate to the music, such as **Angels** in diverse poses and various manners...

In other musical instruments that are not used in temples, one may—without so much restraint—more freely paint all sorts of subjects, such as **Amphion, Arion, Zethus, Sappho, Orpheus, Mercury, Apollo**, and the **Muses**. It would also be a beautiful and imaginative thing to represent the **nine choirs of music** in groups of three, with their instruments and with portraits of men who were excellent in each of them. ### *Which paintings are suitable for schools and gymnasiums, and which are suitable for inns and similar places.* Cap. XXVI.

**B**ecause the school is a place of instruction and discipline, according to the diversity of the sciences and arts, it is required that one sees there only things fit to incite and hold the minds of those who gather there in continuous meditation on the science they delight in; so that they may take examples in various ways to reach those levels of knowledge to which they aspire. Therefore, such paintings must be as different from each other as the schools themselves are different. For in a music school, it would not be right to see homicides, massacres, insults, beatings, and similar spectacles, which are better suited to a **gladiatorial school** to further awaken those who practice bravery and boldness there. Instead, there is a place for famous men playing various instruments—such as the one of whom it is written that, with a certain sound, he kept **Clytemnestra** <note>The wife of Agamemnon; according to Homer, a bard was left to guard her virtue through song</note> chaste and faithful to her husband for a long time, or that other who incited **Alexander** <note>likely Timotheus of Miletus, whose music was said to stir Alexander the Great to battle</note> to war, and others who sing in choirs with various gestures, which are of no small consideration. In a school or gymnasium of the sciences, **Philosophers** are appropriate, with illustrious maxims and books held in their hands with beautiful poses. It will be a supreme ornament, in imitation of the ancients, to display that statue they called **Hermathena** <note>original: "Hermatena"; a composite statue combining the heads of Hermes (Mercury) and Athena (Minerva), symbolizing the union of eloquence and wisdom</note>, where **Pallas** and **Mercury** were joined together; this the ancient philosophers dedicated and placed in their gymnasiums, as **Marcus Tullius** <note>The Roman orator and statesman Cicero</note> mentions in several places, saying it was the ornament of his academy. And they understood by Pallas...

...parts of this art. So did Carlo da Crema <note>A minor artist, likely known for genre or still-life scenes in the Lombard region.</note>, who depicted a kitchen with all its instruments; and so one could compose the Carnival with birds and animals, and Lent with fish and its other foods. Likely referring to a Flemish tradition of composite portraits or perhaps Rogier van der Weyden, though the description matches the style later popularized by Arcimboldo.</note> was singular. In short, all the figures of the sciences and arts can be turned about with their instruments used in place of limbs. Many other similar whims <note>original: "bizarrie"</note> can be made, even of fantastical and terrifying hellish demonstrations, just as **Federico Zuccaro** once drew many sheets, imitating Dante in his *Inferno*; and before him the "Astonished One," **Hieronymus Bosch** the Fleming <note>original: "Girolamo Boschi Fiamengo." Bosch was famously called "the astonished" (L'Attonito) due to his dreamlike and surreal depictions of the afterlife.</note>, who was singular and truly divine in representing strange appearances and terrifying and horrid dreams. 

Besides these inventions, one can paint with no less grace in the said intervals trophies, foliage, **grotesques** <term>grotteſche: a style of Roman-inspired decorative art involving whimsical, interconnected figures and foliage</term>, and similar whims that partake of the nature of the whole, just as Mercury participates in the nature of all the other planets with which he is associated. So, in such places, one must take great care, since in them consists the grace and enrichment of the work; wherefore I would judge that it would not be out of place to apply to them that **Attic Column** which we call the most ornate and whimsical of all the others.

### Which paintings are suitable for facades. Chapter XXVII.

**T**he public streets are considered places of the **Moon** <note>In the astrological system used by the author, different locations are governed by planets; the Moon governs public, changing, and watery spaces.</note>; and therefore, according to the various and different caprices of the painters, all those histories, fantasies, inventions, and whims that come to the heart can be painted there in the open, which will suit them very well—discreetly, however, and with reason, according to the social rank of the people; and above all observing decorum and honesty, which is generally required in everything. And since all other Lunar places, such as rivers, marshes, and others, are locations where paintings cannot be made (even though the ancients used to paint and carve ships with things suitable to them, among whom **Heraclides** <note>Heraclides of Macedon, an ancient Greek painter known for decorating ships.</note> was very clever), I will not speak of them, only reminding the reader of this: that he who creates certain panels in such places will be able to represent Lunar events in them, such as the activities of aquatic animals, sea monsters, river nymphs, hunts, whirligigs <note>original: "girandole" — can refer to fireworks, spinning ornaments, or flights of fancy</note>, simple jests, and nymph-like games, such as running, and similar things.

...similar things. And because street paintings must necessarily stretch across facades, this way of working was considered little noble by the ancients. Wherefore some have left written that when working in fresco <note>painting on freshly laid, wet lime plaster</note> was introduced, the dignity and nobility of painting was cast to the ground; since paintings were no longer held in that reverence as the first ones were, which were made only upon wooden panels. The first who brought about this ruin, Pliny writes, was in the time of the Divine Augustus <note>original: "Diuo Augusto"</note>, speaking of Marcus Ludius <note>A Roman painter mentioned by Pliny the Elder as the first to paint landscapes on walls</note>, the "Helot" painter of the temple at Ardea. Nor will I extend myself longer regarding the placement of histories or fictions; it is enough that everything that can be done with the brush can be placed following the principal rules given in these chapters. These rules, if well observed and understood, will serve us as well as if I had gone about collecting every minute detail, which would have been an infinite and tedious task.

### Compositions of Wars and Battles, Chapter XXVIII.

**T**he first consideration that the practical painter must have in the description and painting of a battle should be the place where the two armies and the military camps are to be positioned. This place should primarily be level, so that in the middle there are no painted trees, nor rivers, nor anything else that could impede the fighting. Because prudent Captain Generals ordinarily choose such places to fight. Nor should one army be painted on the mountain and the other on the plain. And I mean this when the painter paints from his own whim <note>original: "capriccio"</note>; because when he paints a past war, he must represent it in the same manner as history recounts it. Where, however, if there is a disproportion of the place, he will see that the general of the army on the plain will always try to make the enemy also descend to the plain. The painter will act prudently by painting the army near a mountain, or woods, or a city, because captains choose such places to take refuge and save themselves in case they are overcome. He shall also paint some convenient springs near both the army camps. And because it is the ordinary custom of Captains to camp where there is plenty of water, he will add some river passing by the side of the two military camps. The second consideration is the form of the armies; because the Spaniards observe a square form, the Turks arrange their soldiers in a semicircular and half-moon form, and the Romans used a wedge-shaped square form...

...and many others, as one reads in <term>Vegetius</term> <note>Publius Flavius Vegetius Renatus, a 4th-century Roman author whose treatise on warfare remained the standard military manual for over a millennium</note>, *On Military Matters* <note>original: "de re militari"</note>. The third consideration is regarding the clothing and dress of the soldiers. For the <term>Turk</term> <note>referring to Ottoman soldiers, a frequent subject for 16th-century artists depicting contemporary or biblical wars</note> wears garments long to the feet and turbans on his head; <term>Italians</term> and <term>Spaniards</term> wear short garments, and other nations use various other styles of dress. In this, one must observe the custom and the ritual of each people. The fourth point of notice concerns the weapons used by the nations; because the <term>Turk</term> uses the bow, arrows, quiver, the long arquebus <note>an early muzzle-loading firearm</note>, the scimitar <note>original: "la storta," a curved blade</note>, and the short spear; <term>Italians</term> use crossbows, the short arquebus, long swords, pikes, and similarly long polearms, so that the painter must not err in any of these things, for he would be noted for his imprudence. He shall likewise paint defensive armor in the form in which it is used, and not otherwise; since the <term>Turk</term> does not use any defensive armor except a shield in the shape of a crescent moon, while the <term>Italians</term> use the round shield, the target <note>a large infantry shield</note>, the buckler, jacks <note>padded defensive tunics</note>, mail sleeves, and every fashion of strong armor. The fifth consideration is the manner of riding; because the <term>Turks</term> ride "short" so that the heel is near the buttocks; <term>Italians</term> ride with a long stirrup; and the <term>Romans</term> anciently used neither saddle nor stirrups; thus the painter shall observe the custom of the nations he paints. The sixth is regarding the fortifications required in both camps, such as trenches, for so do prudent Captains. The seventh is that he should paint the artillery in front of the two armies, and a band of soldiers guarding the artillery. The eighth is that he should paint the cavalry at the side of the infantry, positioned against the enemy's cavalry. All these and other considerations the painter must have regarding the first part of painting—that is, the proportion to be observed in painting battles. But the principal proportion to be observed must be in the bodies of the best soldiers, who should be seven or eight heads tall, with broad and ample shoulders, and with prominent limbs and muscles, having thick and muscular arms and legs; so that no softness or sweetness is seen in their bodies, but they should be fierce, strong, and terrible men, in the same manner that <term>Michelangelo</term> <note>original: "Buonarroto"</note> once painted in his *Judgment* <note>the Last Judgment fresco in the Sistine Chapel</note> in the <term>Pope’s Chapel</term>; where certainly he did not observe the <term>decorum</term> <note>the artistic theory of appropriateness; critics often argued Michelangelo’s saints looked too much like muscular laborers or soldiers</note> that was fitting for the bodies of glorified Saints, but rather for the aforementioned strong and robust bodies. And I mean this generally for military men; for reason then shows that the Captain-Generals of armies, Emperors, and many other lords who serve in the military should not be painted in this manner, but with reasonable proportions that represent them as graceful and refined...

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on military decorum, specifically completing the "fifth consideration" regarding the fierce yet majestic character required for depicting war, before moving into the technical categories of motion and color.</meta>

<page-num>353</page-num>

-> # QUESTION <-

...not without a certain fierceness, however, but entirely noble and full of majesty.
After the painter has considered the proportion of all things, he shall come to the second part of painting, which is <term>motion</term> <note>original: "moto"; in Renaissance theory, this refers both to physical movement and the "movements of the soul" or emotions</note>. And the first thing he shall paint will be the slaughter that the artillery has caused in both armies, showing in the air heads, arms, legs, and half-bodies being carried upward by the violence of the artillery; and on the ground, he shall make soldiers scattered everywhere, pieces of torn bodies, shredded banners, and bloody weapons. He shall in no way fail to express the smoke of the artillery as a sign that all have been fired, and an end has been put to the horrendous storm of the <term>arquebuses</term> <note>early portable long guns</note>. He shall not make the soldiers fight bravely on both sides; but on one side he shall paint them being put to flight and in chaos, and on the other the victors who press upon them. In this, the painter who does not demonstrate fierce and terrible motions in each of them will turn out very "cold" <note>uninspired or lacking emotional impact</note>. It will be good to feign that part of the cavalry breaks through the midst of the infantry and soldiers, scattering them and putting them into the greatest disorder with horrendous slaughter and killing. Here the painter will have a wide field to show his art and excellence in expressing the horror and fierceness of the actions.

In <term>coloring</term> <note>original: "colorare," the third traditional part of painting after design and motion</note>, which is the third part of painting, this consideration shall be held: that the flesh of the soldiers be such as we have said above, which befits men of a <term>choleric constitution</term> <note>According to the theory of the Four Humors, a choleric temperament was associated with fire, yellow bile, and a reddish or tanned complexion, signifying a courageous and irritable nature</note>. But these colors shall nevertheless be varied, because not all possess choler in the same degree. The captains and generals of the armies shall be made with jovial faces when they fight, mixing in a certain amount of red to demonstrate their magnificence and valor. In those who flee, the color shall be expressed which befits one who fears <note>likely a pale or ashen gray</note>, and in those who die, the <term>mortal color</term> <note>the pallor of death</note>. 

In painting the cloths and garments, I wished to observe this rule: to make those of the Emperors purple and red; after these should follow the turquoise or blues—whatever we wish to call them—along with the colors composed from them; in the third rank, the habits should be made green, and in the other, yellow. However, the painter will still govern himself in this part according to the customs of the nations in dress, which is easily learned by reading histories. From these we also have to derive knowledge of the arms, emblems, and shields 

<margin>¶</margin>that the ancient peoples used to carry in wars and battles, since for modern peoples one simply depicts what they carry; because this is a very necessary part. the <term>lily</term> <note>the fleur-de-lis</note> to the ancient Florentines (who now carry it in red), the marten to the Alans, the Lion to the old French and the ancient Saxons, the toad to the Franks, the war horse to the more recent Saxons, the Bull to the old Cimbri and to the three famous sons of the great Osiris. These ensigns are a beautiful sight to see in their proper places, fluttering in the wind to give grandeur and to signal the various peoples gathered there. 

In applying the light, the painter must also consider that he should not make the light strike into the eyes of any of the armies; for when the light flashes before the eyes of an army, it can be said to be half-defeated—and for this reason, wise Captains always take heed of it. Thus, it is necessary to ensure that both armies share a single light source, which comes from the side of each of them, whether from the right or the left; one should not place the light directly behind or directly in front, as it is against military art. 

As for <term>perspective</term> <note>the mathematical technique for creating the illusion of depth</note>, I have nothing to advise except that one must observe the art declared in the book of perspective, ensuring that the modern artillery, the castles laden with archers atop the elephants of the ancient Carthaginians, the carts full of combatants used by the Trojans, and also the <term>testudos</term> <note>original: "testudini"; mobile shelters or the "tortoise" shield formation</note>, rams, catapults, and other similar engines and machines of war can launch their balls, arrows, spears, swords, and other weapons so that they reach their desired destination in perspective. 

The first inventors of this were Leonardo, Raphael, Polidoro, Titian, Rosso, and Zenale; and among sculptors, Benedetto Pavese was singular, who sculpted the battles of Monsieur de Lautrec <note>likely referring to the tomb of Gaston de Foix, who led the French forces; Lautrec was his successor</note> for his burial in <term>bas-relief</term> in Santa Marta in Milan, assisted by Agostino Busti <note>original: "Agosto Cerebaglio"; a reference to the sculptor known as Il Bambaja</note>, depicting both land and naval wars. In the latter, Luca Cambiaso <note>original: "Luca Cangiaso"</note> was very inventive.

### ***Compositions of naval battles. Chap. XXIX.***

**B**ecause battles are also often engaged at sea upon ships, one must first consider the style of the vessels, as well as their richness and form—such as those of Cleopatra, Mark Antony, and the Greeks—and, beyond the ornaments of the ships, their various military apparatuses. In this genre of battles, some should be seen...

...jans <note>Continuing from "Trojans" on the previous page</note> throwing grappling hooks as enemy ships approach, others holding them back and binding them with the strongest chains; meanwhile, others set them on fire; others leap from one ship to another with naked blades in hand and shields on their arms; others with one foot on one ship and the other on the next, fighting and defending themselves valiantly, wounding and killing the enemies; and others, having boarded the enemy vessel, hack to pieces as many as they find. There, one must show in the defeated humility and pleas, as they pray to the victors for their lives with arms crossed <note>original: "braccia in croce"; a gesture of submission and prayer</note>, surrendering themselves as prisoners with their weapons at their feet; others who, out of fear, throw themselves into the sea; and others who, finding no mercy, are hacked to pieces and, cruelly wounded, are cast into the water; others whose bodies remain draped across the gunwales; others running now to one side, now to the other; others tightly embracing one another, striving to throw each other off the ship; and others who, in despair, cast themselves into the sea, forcibly dragging those of the enemy party down with them. 

One should also see those who attend to clearing the boats of the dead, throwing them into the water, along with the severed limbs of bodies; those who ransack and strip the dead of jewels and valuable arms with great fury and cruelty, accompanied by a wonderful swiftness. Furthermore, let the reinforcements and aid coming from the land be expressed, who, leaping into the ships with no less cruelty, hack, kill, and drag away whoever encounters them and seeks to defend himself; not without the throwing of darts, the shooting of arrows, the slinging of stones, and the thunder of artillery and <term>arquebuses</term> <note>original: "archibugi"; an early type of portable long gun that predated the musket</note> in modern battles. 

And let some ships be imagined fleeing across the sea and others swiftly pursuing them, and some of the soldiers holding them back by force with ropes and chains attached to rings and grappling hooks, and even with their very hands, as it is read that <term>Cynegirus</term> <note>An Athenian hero of the Battle of Marathon (490 BCE) who, according to legend, seized a fleeing Persian ship with his hand; when his hand was cut off, he seized it with the other, and then with his teeth</note> once did to a ship of the Persians. In short, various and diverse orders and methods are to be followed in composing these naval wars; as a certain Giovanni Battista Mantovano <note>Giovanni Battista Scultori (1503–1575), a prominent Italian sculptor and engraver from Mantua who worked in the circle of Giulio Romano</note> knew how to express very well in a drawing, in one print of which, among others, one sees a wonderful fury and intelligence in such compositions.

Concerning battles between land and sea, one must not omit representing some who, having reached the shore, wish to disembark from the ships, and the land soldiers who oppose them with their strength and weapons—as the <term>Trojans</term> <note>In Homer's Iliad, the Trojans famously fought to burn the Greek ships on the beach</note> once did against the Greek fleet, and many others—where marvelous feats of men are seen leaping from the land into the boats, and from the ships onto the land; and thus these clashing with those, and those with these, in diverse manners.

### *Composition of Abductions.* <note>original: "rapimenti"; refers to the classical art theme of "Rapes" or forceful abductions common in Renaissance painting</note> Cap. XXX.

**I**n the histories of abductions, one must principally show in the abductors force and insolence accompanied by a certain amorous desire for the thing being snatched, and also by a certain fury and impetus; for this reason, they should appear terrible in the face and ready for the snatching. But in those who are abducted, one must express weeping, fear, pain, terror, the act of defense, and prayers to mitigate the insolent attacker; therefore, in such histories, it is necessary to labor with every study to show such effects, and accompany them with their proper movements. One should not do as some who, in depicting the Sabine women <note>A legendary episode from Roman history where the first Romans abducted wives from the neighboring Sabine tribe</note> abducted by the shepherds, have depicted them holding tightly to the shepherds as if they were going off in agreement with them, without any act demonstrating the force or violence suddenly done to them; even making one of them sit on the horse's rump behind one of the men as if they were going out for recreation with their husbands, not showing any gesture of fleeing though they could. They must instead be in the act of defending themselves, melancholy and grieving, and therefore striking the captors <note>original: "rapiti"; the author likely meant the "rapitori" (abductors) here</note> with their fists, making acts of breaking free, thrashing their legs, and wanting to take flight; besides this, biting, grabbing at beards, shouting, weeping, and praying humbly for their liberty; and the abductors holding them tight in their arms in various ways. This cannot be achieved without showing naked legs, torn clothing, the baring of arms and breasts, and gestures and acts of force, from which also follow the swelling of breasts <note>from heavy breathing or exertion</note>, the twisting of necks, the spreading of arms, sweat, bites, scratches, punches, and blows; which gestures, joined together, make a delightful display of robustness and violence. With these instructions, one may proceed in all abductions, such as that of Paris and Helen the Greek, of Pluto and Proserpina... <note>Paris’s abduction of Helen triggered the Trojan War; Pluto’s abduction of Proserpina (Persephone) explained the seasons</note>

...women, of which <term>Gaudenzio Ferrari</term> <note>A prolific Italian painter of the Renaissance (c. 1471–1546)</note> once made a painting that was sent to <term>Francis I, King of France</term>. In it, one could see <term>Pluto</term> <note>God of the Underworld</note> all inflamed with lust, furiously carrying <term>Proserpina</term> away in his arms, having his right hand under her right armpit and with the other hand squeezing her left thigh. The Goddess, spreading her arms, cries out weeping and exerts force with her right leg, entangling it with the left leg of <term>Pluto</term>, and from her lap she lets fall the flowers she had been gathering. He did this, perhaps, in imitation of the work painted by <term>Nicomachus</term>, an ancient painter. Similar actions must likewise be expressed in <term>Nessus</term> the centaur when he steals <term>Deianira</term>, and in <term>Boreas</term> <note>The North Wind</note> when he abducts <term>Orithyia</term>, and in countless others mentioned by historians and poets. 

But because abductions are not always of women, or of males—as with <term>Ganymede</term> when he was carried away in flight by the bird of <term>Jove</term> <note>Jupiter's eagle</note>—but quite often also of treasures and goods, as <term>Heliodorus</term> <note>A minister of the Seleucid Empire who attempted to loot the Temple treasury</note> did in the temple of <term>Solomon</term>, one must consider the history very carefully. One must make the bystanders terrified, just as it is appropriate to do in the abductions of women—such as the companions of <term>Europa</term> when <term>Jove</term> abducted her in the manner recounted by <term>Achilles Tatius</term> <note>A 2nd-century Greek novelist</note>—and also like the poor husbands of the <term>Sabine women</term>, some of whom must put up a defense and others must pray, just as the priest did in the temple of <term>Solomon</term>. 

And in such melees, there must be people of every sort; for it is likely that in such tumults where things are turned upside down, both nobles and commoners, rich and poor, young and old, and children all converge in various actions. Some are watching, others are in wonder, and others are defending the treasure and resisting the thieves, with dogs barking. Therefore, no one should be placed there talking to another as if uncaring of the event, or laughing or sleeping without concern, failing to perform a duty appropriate to the effect being shown. Likewise, those who are doing the abducting should not appear slow or lacking industry in carrying out the enterprise. Rather, they must be shown with eyes wide open and appearing to look everywhere, just as the others must look at them, but with menacing and terrible gestures. Some should stand with weapons in hand, laden with prey; others should take vessels; others should struggle; others should stand guard and lie in wait; and finally, they should perform various acts as are well required in such events. This has a place not only in the plundering of temples, but also of cities when they are sacked by soldiers or by bandits when they assault a place unexpectedly.

### Compositions of Various Types of Love. Chapter XXXI.

**L**a composition of love is divided into many manners according to the species of loves. For if the minds are of concordant will, one seeks only to provide delight; if, otherwise, violence and force intervene, one must act differently. In those cases, the lover must express such actions as <term>Achilles Tatius</term> <note>A 2nd-century Greek writer known for the novel *Leucippe and Clitophon*; his vivid descriptions were often used as models for Renaissance painters.</note> recounts in the fable of <term>Tereus</term> <note>A mythical Thracian king who raped his sister-in-law, Philomela.</note> and his sister-in-law. In this scene, one could see the hair all disheveled, the belt loosened, the garment torn, the breast half-naked, and the right hand clutching at Tereus’s face, while the left hand gathered a part of the torn dress around the breasts. On the other side was Tereus, holding <term>Philomela</term> in his arms and pulling her toward him as much as he could with the tightest embraces.

Besides this, the artist must also express in the lover the actions of pressing, of clinching the back with the arms, and of playing with the legs by inserting one between those of the forced young woman; or, if unable to do so, embracing her tightly and placing one hand at her throat, or from behind. By passing the arms under the <term>armpits</term> <note>original: "lesene," an architectural term for pilasters, here used metaphorically for the structures of the torso</note>, he should place his hands with force upon the <term>nape of the neck</term> <note>original: "Coppa"</note>, and thus come to his end. All the actions in such a representation should tend toward nothing else but removing the strength and defense from every limb of the woman. Next, one must demonstrate the weeping, the shouting, the biting, the scratching, the squirming, the pulling back, the defending with the arms, the thrusting of the lover far from oneself, the keeping of the private parts covered with clothes, the entwining of the legs, the pushing back with the knees and feet, the bumping with the thighs and flanks, and the turning of the shoulders. Throughout, there should be a wriggling motion, without letting the figure be fixed in any one pose, with a swift turning and moving of the limbs, and also with a quick fleeing—as the young <term>Joseph</term> <note>Referring to the biblical Joseph fleeing from Potiphar's wife.</note> did from the Queen of Egypt, and <term>Hippolytus</term> <note>A figure from Greek mythology who fled the advances of his stepmother, Phaedra.</note> from Phaedra.

But in those scenes where the will is consensual, one must consider the location where the event occurs (just as one does with the forced ones): whether it was in woods, in beds, in caves, or in other various places. One should always seek to have the shameful parts covered in various ways, such as with other limbs or cloth. One must feign that they are kissing and embracing, or playing, and similar acts, so as not to represent them dishonestly. It is such a fine art to show a delicate gesture either before or after the deed, just as it is to represent the deed itself—and even more so—for in this, modesty is observed, always leaving something new to be desired, upon which delight depends. Thus, one should not express

For all these help to give grace, especially if the event occurred in a chamber. This enrichment of cupids and playfulness was also done by the Attic <term>Parrhasius</term> <note>An ancient Greek painter renowned for his skill in depicting character and emotion.</note>, and after him the prudent <term>Raphael</term> <note>The famous High Renaissance master Raphael Sanzio.</note> used to employ it often, following the manner of the ancients, as I have said above. He placed some of them around the youth, and distributed others throughout the chamber, of whom one carried Alexander's shield, another put the helmet on his head, and another, having put on the breastplate, was stretched out on the ground due to the excessive weight; nearby he placed <term>Hymen</term> <note>The Greek god of marriage ceremonies.</note>, the God of weddings, with a lit torch in hand, and other similar ornaments. This great painter, no differently than a poet, composed all his amorous histories, to whose example everyone ought to adhere.

## The Composition of Joy and Laughter. Chapter XXXII.

**A**mong all the components required for the proper composition of a <term>narrative</term> <note>original: "historia," referring to a narrative painting or scene.</note> depicting joyous things and laughter, the most important is that one see the cause for which the joy, laughter, and clamor are introduced. This would be, for example, in a story of love: jesting, teasing, and other similar amorous charms; and in a ridiculous story: certain things naturally suited to move anyone who looks at them to laughter. Secondly, it is necessary that such causes be introduced appropriately; for if one were to see someone celebrating and laughing without cause, it would certainly be a madness deserving of a beating. Therefore, one must primarily establish the causes of the laughter and express them in such a way that the viewers are moved to laugh by looking at it, even if—through the artist's negligence—no one was seen laughing in the painting, as often happens. 

If this is expressed well, it should lead to the extreme of laughter, showing those carefree faces, some turned upward, some to the side, and others in different ways as they look at one another and laugh. They should be shown dislocating their jaws, revealing their teeth, opening their mouths indecently in new and diverse acts of laughing, widening their nostrils, and hiding their eyes within their heads <note>A description of squinting while laughing heartily.</note>, so that they appear red, unsteady, fleeting, thoughtless, and haphazard, as happens in such circumstances. Furthermore, they should be clapping their hands together, raising and lowering them in various ways, letting themselves lean to the side, toppling backward, and leaning forward facing one another with their hands placed reciprocally upon each other's shoulders, and the like. 

One should also see others; either departing, or arriving, or standing a little way off, who laugh in different ways, some more and some less, remaining attentive to the sight of the cause of the laughter—whether it be a piece of buffoonery being performed, or a ridiculous tale being told about some mockery made of someone ragged and ill-favored, with some bizarre face like <term>Aesop</term> <note>The famous Greek fabulist, who was traditionally described in the Renaissance as being physically deformed and grotesque, yet witty.</note>, who could not be seen without laughter. 

**Michelino** <note>Michelino da Besozzo (c. 1370–1455), a major figure in the International Gothic style in Milan.</note>, a very old Milanese painter who lived a hundred and fifty years ago and was the foremost of those times in Italy (as his works bear witness, along with his animals of every kind in which he was most stupendous), once created a laughing "oddity" in a painting which still circulates in copies; truly, for its beauty, it is worthy of being recounted. He imagined four peasants laughing together, two males and two females. He depicted the oldest one completely clean-shaven, who stands looking all around and laughing as if he enjoys himself beyond measure, such that no man is found so melancholy or sad that he is not moved to laughter upon looking at him;

I wanted to explain this <term>invention</term> <note>In Renaissance art theory, "invention" (invenzione) refers to the original conceptual design and storytelling of a work.</note> at length, so that from it one may learn the ways in which all those who laugh must, in a certain way, take their movement from one another; and thus, as the laughter increases from one to the other, bring it to its peak, and make even the dead laugh if it were possible, for therein lies the power of painting, as **Leonardo** used to say. 

For this reason, he took great delight in drawing old men and deformed male and female peasants laughing; these are still seen in various places, among which **Aurelio Luini** <note>Aurelio Luini (c. 1530–1593) was a Milanese painter and son of Bernardino Luini; he was a contemporary of the author and a known collector of Leonardo’s drawings.</note> keeps about fifty of them drawn by his hand in a small book. Understanding then that laughter must always have harmony across all its effects, it must therefore be represented sometimes more and sometimes less, according to the delight the subject provides. 

I would say that in such paintings one should never express anything apt to show melancholy, such as foolish or weak gestures, drooling old men, those with cloudy eyes, the infirm, offensive animals, philosophers, or other people hostile to laughter and joy; because they disturb and disconcert the whole. And to express joy more minutely, one should paint ostentatious clothing in vivid and cheerful colors; and sometimes children fit well, lightheartedly playing with puppies, or making birds fly while tied to strings, or running with their little banners and playing together, as is seen at major festivals, and in the pleasures of banquets and dances, where nothing is spoken of but fun.

## ***Compositions of Banquets. Chapter XXXIII.***

**I**t is certainly a thing worthy of wonder that among so many painted tables seen daily—depicted full of food with guests all around—one sees in so very few of them anyone in the act of eating or drinking freely. Instead, everyone stands there with various gestures, looking at one another as if they were a spectacle for some other purpose. In my judgment, this seems a very great fault in painting; for art is destined to show all the <term>effects</term> <note>original: "effetti," referring to the convincing representation of physical actions and the underlying emotions or "passions of the soul."</note> as if they were real. To achieve this, it is necessary for painters—who are obliged to represent everything that belongs to these effects—to first consider the location where the banquets are held and decorate them with their proper circumstances. These primarily consist of the following: one should see the **steward** <note>original: "credenziere," the official in charge of the *credenza* or sideboard where silver and gold plate was displayed and drinks were prepared.</note> who arranges everything regarding the entry and exit of the people, prepares the table, and sets out the sideboards with vessels, cups, basins, and flasks of gold and silver. One should see the **cellarmen** who guard the bottled stores, adorned with cups and glasses of silver and crystal. There should be the **seneschal** <note>original: "sescalcho," the high-ranking official who oversaw the serving of the feast and the arrangement of dishes.</note> who announces the meal and places it on the table; and likewise the **carvers** who present the food to this or that guest; and also the **cupbearers** who offer drink with reverence. Finally, servants and pages should stand attentively around, who, with bare heads, serve the guests with reverence and readiness for everything they see is needed. However, there should not be a great tumult of people, so as not to confuse the minds of the guests or those who view the painting. And regarding the food, it must be prepared according to the seasons; for the clarification of which I will provide some examples of the most solemn banquets mentioned in history as having been celebrated in the world. Most solemn was that of **Semiramis** <note>A legendary Queen of Babylon.</note> atop the gardens raised upon columns in the air for that greatest city of Babylon and Nineveh, where Pliny recounts that it was the custom to wear garlands of flowers and leaves on the head, and likewise to crown the cups and vessels with them, drinking with other such indulgences as one reads of them. Memorable was the feast held by **Belshazzar**, King of Babylon. This should be represented with chairs of gold and ivory, and with everything else superb and sumptuous, with an infinite number of servants, depicting the moment when—half drunk—he planned to drink from the gold vessels from the Temple of Solomon. Since there are only Kings, Queens, and similar personages present, one must make the extreme effort of art to show the height of majesty and luxury in every part. Along with these goes the banquet of Lucullus, the citizen

...the Roman banquet in the Apollo room where Pompey and Cicero were; and that of Cleopatra, Queen of Egypt, which she prepared for Mark Antony; those of Sardanapalus, Octavius, Nero, Caligula, Elagabalus, <note>Sardanapalus was a legendary Assyrian king synonymous with decadence; the others listed are Roman emperors famous for their extreme extravagance.</note> and countless others written to have been proud and profuse beyond measure in hosting banquets.

Conversely, the banquets of those early Romans—such as Fabricius, Torquatus, Camillus, and others—must be expressed differently; <note>These figures from the early Roman Republic were celebrated as models of "sturdy" Roman virtue, simplicity, and frugality.</note> that is, as sober and frugal, for in this the artist's skill is also shown. This applies also to the Last Supper that Christ shared with his disciples, which should not be depicted as being as abundant as some are accustomed to painting it.

One must have the greatest regard for the guests, for just as nations are diverse, so too are their manners and ways different. For the **German** eats in an undisciplined manner; the **Frenchman** soils himself with the food; the **Turk** sits on the ground; the **Spaniard** eats delicately; the **Italian** is a composite of all of these; and the **peasants** eat sometimes standing up, sometimes stretched out crosswise on the ground, and in other positions.

One must have regard for their status, so that the most worthy guest is placed in the primary seat, and then the others on the right, degree by degree, according to who is more worthy than the other. On the left, the women should be placed, they too according to their condition and status. The masters of the palaces and the illustrious pages should stand with reverence and in beautiful poses, gracefully doing whatever the guests desire. Musicians and players are appropriate here, filling everything with sweetness with their harmonious concerts. 

In moderate banquets, there is no need to give them the primary roles, but it is enough to scale them down a bit as is fitting among persons of lesser authority, choosing servants and pages instead of great Lords. Then follow the banquets of counts, lords, merchants, and step by step, of people of little value, and even those who eat at taverns, and the poor, and the wretched, and even the gypsies—where in each one, the artist must maintain the proper suitability and decorum. When representing the banquets of Lords, one adds grace by introducing dances, where different actions will be expressed according to the various customs of nations, as I already mentioned in the second book regarding the art of dancing.

### ***Composition of Sadness. Chapter XXXIV.***

->...the one in which he surpassed Timanthes,<- <note>The OCR reads "Collocrotico," likely a corruption of the name Timanthes, a famous Greek painter known for the sacrifice of Iphigenia.</note> where, having made **Calchas** mournful at the sacrifice of **Iphigenia**, and **Ulysses** much more so, and having exhausted all his art and genius on **Menelaus** who was struck down by grief; and having spent all the <term>emotions</term> <note>original: "affetti"; in Renaissance art theory, this refers to the outward expression of internal feelings.</note> and not finding a way he could worthily represent the face of the most sorrowful Father, he covered his face with cloths. This left the greatness of his grief more to be contemplated in the mind of the onlookers than he could have ever expressed with a brush. 

From this, painters shall take an example for distributing this sadness and weeping when painting the **Crucifixion of Christ**: expressing the highest grief in his **Mother**, greater than in all the others standing around the Cross; then in **John** much more than in the **Marys**, as he was closer to Christ in holiness and kinship; then in the **Magdalene**; behind her in **Martha** and in the others according to their qualities, some more and some less. 

And in these compositions, the artist who shows someone in the act of looking at you while weeping will always be extremely praised, as if they wish to tell you the cause of their sorrow and move you to participate in their pain; while the others look at the thing for which they weep and grieve, in gestures that are all mournful and appropriate to their duty. 

Therefore, cheerful things must be far from these spectacles, such as children playing and men laughing; and those who do not share in the weeping should nonetheless show a certain trembling and wonder at the event, standing therefore restrained from laughter—even if they are otherwise content to see those pains and tribulations. This would be the case, for example, with the **Jews** while they have Christ nailed and raised on the Cross, and with those other soldiers who kill the innocent children <note>A reference to the Massacre of the Innocents.</note> while they see the poor mothers weeping, struggling, and tearing their clothes, their hair, and their wretched flesh through excess of grief. 

For one must consider that a person seeing such tragic spectacles, even if they do not participate in those afflictions and sorrows, nevertheless stands stunned with a sad and melancholy countenance—and even in a certain way frightened—rather than being able to laugh. Such an <term>affect</term> <note>A psychological state or emotional response.</note> is generated in our souls by such events, as each of us proves when we see someone die, or even the killing of an enemy. 

Therefore, all these things must be subtly investigated at all hours using the example of **nature** and the ornament of **art**. Nevertheless, some people are still appropriate in such histories who, moved by piety, stand watching the mournful in various ways: some appearing to gesture while speaking with someone else with a grieving and tearful look, others making an effort to push themselves forward to see better...

...and others standing at a distance watching the event, leaning on something, such as a rock, a staff, a bar, or the like; others who are leaving, and others who are arriving anew. These are the mournful compositions, which serve for all subjects, according to the locations, the multitude of people, and the nature of the sadness. 

For in one way shall sinners be made to grieve and weep for their sins—like our first parents <note>Adam and Eve</note> when they were cast out of Paradise, or like **Peter** repenting for having denied the Master, or like **Julian** <note>Saint Julian the Hospitaller, who according to legend killed his parents by mistake.</note> grieving for having killed his parents; and in another way a son who mourns his dead father, as the twelve tribes mourned the father **Jacob** while he predicted for them the things to come; and in another way one who grieves and laments for love, like **Venus** for **Adonis**; and also differently from these, one who becomes desperate for the death of a lover, like the same **Venus** for the shepherd, and **Thisbe** for **Pyramus**; and thus continuing, in another manner the weary lament and grieve—like the **People of Israel** in servitude—the hungry, and those who must die or are led to a violent death and other similar subjects, who differently display gestures of grief: that is to say, the loss of love, or desire, or fear, or deep thought, or torment, or pain, or robbery, or any other <term>emotion</term> <note>original: "affetto"; in Renaissance art theory, this refers to the external physical manifestation of an internal mental or emotional state.</note> one might wish to show. Hence, whoever expresses them well is deemed miraculous, and yet these things, to those who understand them well, are as easy as the rest of the craft.
