All virtuous qualities must be represented. For this reason, in my judgment, many stories from the Holy Scriptures should be avoided, as they cannot be expressed without some degree of lewdness and lack of modesty. Such examples include **Susanna** at the fountain, entirely naked and watched by the three elders; since she is depicted as beautiful and alluring in her nakedness, anyone can imagine what kind of devotion <note>The author is concerned that such images provoke lust rather than religious contemplation.</note> this would excite in the mind. The same applies to **Lot** made drunk by his daughters, and the others I mentioned above when discussing temples: **Adam** and **Eve**, naked and beautiful as the work of God's hand in Paradise when the serpent induced them to sin; **Bathsheba** <note>original: "Bersabe"</note> loosened and uncovered from her clothes when she was seen by **David** from the palace; the wife of Pharaoh <note>The author likely refers to Potiphar's wife, who attempted to seduce Joseph; she is often conflated with "Pharaoh's" household in older commentaries.</note> in a lewd pose in a chamber upon the bed with her limbs partly naked, holding the cloak of the fleeing **Joseph**; and other similar spectacles that cannot be purely represented with modesty and devotion, despite the fact that many of these are nonetheless seen painted in various churches.

And if someone were to tell me that **Michelangelo Buonarroti** <note>original: "il Buonarotto"</note> therefore erred in making such immodest figures with their limbs entirely uncovered in his *Last Judgment*, especially in such a place where the whole world congregates; I respond that this great painter erred in such a subject more through an excess of observation of truth than through indecency. For he did not err in painting the blessed and the damned naked—because that is how they must be depicted <note>At the Resurrection of the Flesh, souls were traditionally believed to rise naked as they were created.</note>—but he erred in displaying the shameful and indecent parts of many of them, a thing he could have easily avoided. For truly, while there should be no clothing there, he nevertheless could have used it to show a measure of modesty.

Now, returning to our purpose and leaving aside the disputes over the opinions of those who say this does not matter (citing the ancients who did this in their temples, placing paintings and statues of their gods mostly naked), I say this is not at all appropriate for our religion, which is entirely modest, devout, and holy. I say that in virtuous stories, and especially in churches, one must avoid as much as possible all shameful and lewd parts, not to mention indecent ones—such as kisses, jokes, laughter, and, in the case of female martyrs, breasts completely uncovered. This includes **Saint Catherine** on the wheels, **Saint Margaret**, **Saint Cecilia** in the oil, **Mary Magdalene** naked in the desert, and likewise other most beautiful virgins and saints who must be represented naked. One must use art to remove appearances that are ugly, lascivious, or hateful to see; always matching everything to the decency of the location, so that by working securely according to what order and craftsmanship require, one may prudently show the truth of the histories. In this way, the artist appears not only as a good painter but as a subtle investigator of the truth.

### Composition of Assaults. Chap. XXXVI.

**I**n composing an assault, many things must be considered because of the various elements involved, according to how different the victims of the assault may be. For if it is an assault on the walls of a city being taken by force by an enemy army, there follow effects very different from those that occur in other situations. To begin with these, one must first take notice of the customs of combat, the weapons, and the defenses held by the citizens, and likewise the methods and the instruments with which the enemies assault the walls. Because, according to custom, one must see the attackers armed, carrying ladders and trying to climb the walls with them, covering their heads with shields, with naked swords in hand, and with darts. Others throw bridges over the ditch; others fill the moats with earth and wood; others dig deep channels with hoes; others with wheels and machines, by force of arms and with ropes, remove the water from the moat; others...

## BOOK 2

...as was the custom of the Romans: some approaching the walls with <term>testudos<note>A military formation where soldiers held their shields over their heads and sides to create a protective shell, resembling a tortoise shell.</note></term>; others battering the walls with blunt rams pushed outward by force; and others with catapults launching darts and arrows with great power against those atop the walls. One should also see others in various places lighting fires, and others having reached the top by sheer force, seizing the wall and throwing the defenders down into the ditch with weapons, shoving, striking, and killing—grabbing them by the hair, the neck, and the arms, in the manner of **Rodomonte in Paris** <note>A reference to Ludovico Ariosto’s epic poem *Orlando Furioso*, where the Saracen king Rodomonte leaps over the walls of Paris and single-handedly wreaks havoc on the defenders.</note>, and making legs, arms, heads, and pieces of shields and armor fly here and there. And in those places where the enemies take the most ground, the others must follow. In these skirmishes, it will be a striking thing to see some ladders break under the weight of the many soldiers, and the soldiers plunging headlong down into the mire; of these, some then struggle to pick themselves up, while others, all filthy, crawl out even as enemy weapons continue to rain down upon them. One should see them throwing ropes and grappling hooks, helping one another, cutting the chains of bridges, and some descending furiously to enter within—not without many falling down into the mud, being wounded, or having their limbs mangled. And if any other attitude can be imagined, it must be expressed to show the richness and the fury of the **history** <note>In art theory, an "istoria" or history is a complex narrative scene that tells a significant story through action and expression.</note> as it happened, not failing to fulfill its requirements. For the painter is as much bound to this as are the poets. 

But continuing our canvas, it is no less appropriate to show the strength of the besieged in their defenses, so that one sees the ruin of those who attack and seek to take the fortress. The defenders atop the walls should hurl arrows, stones, and darts in such abundance against those climbing the ladders that the entire air seems crowded with them. Furthermore, all the defenders should be most ready and swift to throw fire down in various ways—with lit brooms, pitch, bundles of wood, torches, and balls prepared in such a way that they burst, flare up, and burn. This should be done just as those of **Cirta** <note>The author likely refers to the siege of Jotapata (which the author calls Cirta) described by the historian Josephus in *The Jewish War*, where boiling oil was used against the Romans.</note> did, as **Josephus the Jew** describes in the wars of **Jerusalem**, as a final remedy against the Romans who were climbing the walls: they poured down vessels of boiling oil and fat, which, seeping through the armor into the flesh and scorching it, caused them to tumble into the ditch from the pain, without any way to protect themselves. One should see people throwing stones, rolling barrels, and buckets of hot and scalding water, and keeping the enemies at a distance with very long pikes and hollowed spears as they try to climb, filling the ditches with them. Where some are seen to have forcibly mounted the walls, there one must see the clash of arms, grappling, straining, and various actions...

different people throwing themselves down from the walls. One must represent **hoists** <term>baltresche<note>Temporary wooden scaffolds or defensive galleries projecting from the top of a wall, used by both attackers and defenders during a siege.</note></term> raised level with the walls; from which rope ladders and grappling hooks are thrown to cross over the ditch from above, as was formerly the custom; and because of this, many should be seen falling. Avoid showing any figure that appears idle or thoughtless, as that would be most unbecoming; instead, let only banners and standards be seen raised in the air, with soldiers fighting and, at times, being mangled. And if the deaths of captains or illustrious men occurred in such skirmishes, it is well to show it—as beneath the highest tower of *Thebes*, where *Abimelech* <note>A biblical figure from the Book of Judges who was struck by a millstone thrown by a woman during the siege of Thebez.</note> was killed by a piece of a millstone thrown onto his head by a woman—and others that one reads about in histories. And whatever sort of assault one happens to paint, one must vary only the instruments of war, making the soldiers act according to them—just as the *Greeks* did at *Troy* with the horse filled with armed men. In such conflicts and ruins, it will add much grace to show the walls being cast to the ground, women with their arms spread wide going about crying out, others fleeing, some being bound, others killed, and others stripped; furthermore, as at *Troy* and *Carthage*, one should show the lighting of fires and the ruining of houses and palaces—as has already happened so many times to poor *Rome* at the hands of *Barbarians*, and to many other cities of *Italy*. Some, overwhelmed by fear, should be seen fleeing—just as when *Troy* burned, the son of *Venus* <note>Aeneas, the legendary hero who escaped Troy.</note> fled with his old father *Anchises* upon his shoulders and his little son by the hand. Others should be seen handing children down from balconies, others lowering themselves by ropes, others jumping down, and similar scenes of ruin and desperation, which would be infinite to enumerate. 

Beyond the general assaults made in open war, there are ambushes, in which one must represent sudden attacks with disordered and lost ranks <note>original: "fusi intricati & perduti"; likely referring to scattered or broken military formations in the chaos of a surprise attack.</note>, where the attackers are furious and terrible. There, you should express the neighing of horses that show their fury at the sound of the trumpets, some of them wounded and half-dead, with the men here and there all disheveled and as if buried in the dust that swirls through the air. No less in these assaults than in those others, one must see noise, clamor, blows, cries, dismay, slaughter, blood, flight, cruelty, killings, wonders, and the like, without any sign of laziness or stupidity—as if a man did not notice or care for the danger (which, as I warned shortly before, would be ridiculous as well as unbecoming). Instead, let everyone be represented either in the act of attacking with fury or defending themselves vigorously, according to what the *painter* can imagine or what history truly prescribes to us; as, for example, in the assault of *Theseus* against the *Centaurs*.

at the wedding of *Pirithous* <note>original: "Pirithoo"; a mythological King of the Lapiths whose wedding devolved into a famous battle against the Centaurs.</note> when they sought to kidnap the bride, where, with the slaughter and killing of the guests, the tables were turned upside down amidst armed men; or when *Phineus* <note>original: "Fineo"; the rival of Perseus who disrupted his wedding feast to Andromeda.</note> disturbed the wedding of *Perseus*, where likewise the guests, the vessels, and the food were thrown into turmoil; or when *Pluto* suddenly stole the daughter of *Ceres* <note>Referring to the abduction of Proserpina.</note> who, out of fear of him, began to scream and weep in various poses alongside the *Loves* <note>Cupids or Erotes.</note>, which the painter can always represent in such places; or when *Amnon* <note>original: "Ammone"; the son of King David.</note>, for the incest committed with his sister *Tamar*, was killed by servants at a feast by the commission of *Absalom*. In these assaults, one must principally consider the time, whether it was by night or by day; for it is quite a different thing to see, by the light of the city's flames, the fleeing people departing, some dressed, some naked with cloaks and rags over their shoulders, and with bundles of their most precious belongings under their arms, and thus going away with their weeping children. And this must also be observed in specific assaults, such as that of *Abraham* against the five Kings; or that of the servants who, when the torches were lit, killed their masters and Kings in bed with daggers; or of *Joab* when he had *Zechariah* the Prophet killed with stones <note>The author likely conflates King Joash, who ordered the stoning of Zechariah, with the general Joab.</note>. Above all, one must show the movements of the fierce attackers and of the swift and agile victims as they seek to defend themselves with hesitant and uncertain steps—no differently than *Caesar* when he was attacked by *Brutus* and *Cassius*, or *Joab* at the altar, or *Sennacherib* by his own sons before the idols. And to conclude, in such assaults, if there are animals, they should be shown as fierce, such that they leap, bark, and bite out of the horror of the spectacle; and likewise, around the walls, the horses which, at the sound of trumpets and drums, kick, neigh, leap, and buck <note>original: "s’arruotino giocando di schena"; literally grinding or pivoting while working their backs.</note>; showing the greatest possible cruelty and fury that can be expressed, because all these things help to give force to the history. As for the air, in one part it shall be represented as turbulent and crowded with dark clouds, and in the other serene and clear, so that all things show fury and impetus, even to the point that the wind blowing makes the clothes swell, the trees bend, and the banners flutter, as if they too were struggling against the enemies; and likewise, let the flames, the smoke, the clouds, the waves of the water, the flight of arrows, the brandishing of spears, and the trembling of plumes, hair, friezes, ornaments, and belts be seen expressed; the dust raised in the air, and the grass on the ground trampled and suppressed. Such are the compositions of public and private assaults.

There are, besides these, assaults and destructions that are carried out for the pleasure of the destroyer, as when the proud *Nero* stood in the palace...

### Compositions of Terrors. Chapter XXXVII.

**A**ll compositions of terrors should be such that, in those terrified, the cause of the terror can be discerned from their actions and countenances. For when *Moses* <note>original: "Mosè"</note> converted the waters of *Egypt* into blood, taking away the water from all Egypt, the Egyptians must be represented astonished and full of fear, in such a way that they show they are certain of having to die of thirst; and therefore some must weep, others struggle, and others remain like motionless statues. And *Pharaoh* <note>original: "Faraone"</note> and all his people, while frogs leaped upon them in great abundance over their food, must be seen in such an act that they seem unable to quiet themselves or rest because of the great nuisance of the frogs sent to them as a scourge in various ways; so that they show themselves like the "walking dead" <note>original: "morti in piedi"; literally "dead on their feet," describing a state of shock or paralysis.</note>, hesitant and suspended as to what they should do or say. The same applies when they are imagined looking into the air filled with lice that drove themselves even into their eyes, or when flies rained upon them, leaving no place where they did not torment them. For this reason, they should be shown wrapped in cloths running here and there, bowing down, believing they might thereby shield themselves and flee the terrifying plague; in doing so, it would be a foolish thing for the painter to let their faces be seen, for the reason just mentioned <note>Because they would be covering their faces to protect themselves from the insects.</note>. And in another manner they should be shown while they see all the animals die of the plague by divine judgment, with sorrowful and afflicted gestures for the grief of losing their wealth <note>original: "facoltà"; meaning property, livestock, or means of living.</note>, whereby they must die of hunger; so that there one must perceive weeping, pain, struggling, and lamenting. And likewise, while boils <note>original: "vesicche"; referring to the plague of sores or blisters.</note> fell upon them in such abundance, because of the great stench they will be seen grieving, fleeing, and tossing about, [covering themselves...] <meta>catchword: coprirsi (to cover oneself)</meta>

The <term>movements of the soul</term><note>original: "moti"; a central Renaissance art theory concept regarding how outward physical gestures reveal internal emotions.</note> must be expressed with even greater skill when the hail fell impetuously from heaven, along with storms accompanied by lightning and horrible thunder; for here one must show the people as desperate and maddened, with bodies hunched, covered in the act of taking refuge under roofs, seeing all the air full of horror and fright. In other gestures, they should be seen when they were miserably tormented by the locusts and poisonous wasps, which drove themselves into their nostrils, eyes, and ears, swelling their lips and every other part they touched. No less frightened should they be shown in the darkness, when all of Egypt remained so obscured for three days and three nights that the darkness in the air could be felt. But the truly tearful and miserable gestures of scratching oneself, flailing about, tearing one’s clothes, killing oneself in despair, or fainting over the bodies, are required for when the Angel comes at midnight and kills all the firstborn of Egypt; at which point [Pharaoh] was forced to let the people of Israel depart.

And leaving the Egyptians, a different kind of terror was that felt in Samaria by the Assyrians, when they were attacked and killed from all sides by rabid lions. Because they must be depicted fleeing, screaming from the pain of being bitten and torn apart, turning their eyes upward, spreading their arms, kicking, twisting their bodies, turning their heads and arms, and lamenting. Otherwise, terror must be shown in the army of King Sennacherib while it is struck at night by the Angel who killed eighty-five thousand <note>The biblical account in 2 Kings 19:35 usually cites 185,000; the author here records 85,000.</note> of them; because the soldiers must flee hunched over with shields gripped over their heads, and in various ways show the fear of being killed, with others falling dead here and there, according to the circumstance.

The same Gaudenzio had previously made an altar-piece <note>original: "tavola"; literally a wooden panel or table, referring to a panel painting.</note> of it in another style in *Sant’Angelo in Milan*, and I myself have strived to express in the terrifying miracle

## SIXTH BOOK

...of Simon Magus <note>A sorcerer mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles; later legends describe him attempting to fly to prove his divinity, only to fall when Saint Peter prayed.</note> when, in the presence of Nero, the sorcerers, and all the Roman people, he fell from the air at the command of Saint Peter and Saint Paul while they were at prayer. They should be represented in acts of terror, some in one way and some in another, with open arms looking up at the falling Simon; a story which I have painted in San Marco in the said city of Milan. 

Francesco Salviati <note>A prominent Florentine Mannerist painter (1510–1563) famous for his complex, elegant compositions.</note> expressed this similarly in those who were with Paul when, due to the voice heard from heaven, he fell blind from his horse. He showed the fright in them through the brilliance he imagined there, using similar gestures—not only in the men who, dazzled by the excessive light, thrust their hands over their eyes while fleeing, but also in the horses themselves, depicting these effects in them. 

In this same manner must the gestures of the Jews who guarded the tomb of Christ be expressed during his Resurrection, when they fell to the ground terrified by the sudden brilliance in various ways with their weapons, as Albrecht Dürer <note>original: "Alberto Durero"</note> well expressed in his *Passion*, and again in his *Apocalypse* concerning the tremendous Day of Judgment, with the terrifying appearances of the Angels over all the world. 

There are other types of terrors from which various other gestures arise: for example, in the Queen because of the serpent killed by Saint George, and likewise in the saint’s horse itself; or in those who were the reason Daniel was placed in the lions' den, while they themselves are given to be devoured by those lions; and in those others who burned in the fire where they had placed the three youths <note>A reference to the biblical story of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who survived being thrown into a furnace.</note>; and in other terrors and miracles, of which both sacred and profane <note>In this context, "profane" refers to classical mythology or secular history.</note> writings are full, whether of fire, death, or similar things. 

In all of these, one must observe the proper <term>decorum</term><note>A central principle in Renaissance art requiring that the style, gestures, and emotions of a figure be appropriate to their status and the specific situation being depicted.</note>. Just as in the sudden lightning bolts that descend from Heaven, and in the arrows that—shot by the Sun <note>Apollo.</note> and Diana due to the pride of Niobe <note>A Greek mythological figure whose children were killed by the gods after she boasted that she was superior to the goddess Leto.</note>—pierce her children, various gestures of terror and torment must be expressed as they fall and die miserably with arrows fixed in their limbs. And also when Jupiter, with all the other gods, strikes the giants with lightning as they forcefully tried to scale the Heavens. 

Perino del Vaga <note>A pupil of Raphael who became the leading artist in Genoa; his work in the Villa del Principe is a masterpiece of the late Renaissance.</note> expressed this story with great excellence in one of the two halls of the Palace of Prince Doria in Genoa, where one sees Jupiter striking with lightning along with all the other gods and various <term>amoretti</term><note>Little cupids or winged infants, often called putti.</note> with lightning bolts in their hands above the clouds, and the giants below struck in various places. Likewise, in the other hall, he has very charmingly painted a terrifying sea storm, where one sees an angry Neptune upon his chariot, ships tossed by the waves, and the air filled with horrible and very dark clouds driven here and there by the blasts of raging winds.

### Compositions of shipwrecks at sea. Chapter XXXVIII.

**I**n the misfortunes of the sea, or what we might call shipwrecks, which often assault the vessels of unlucky mariners, there are infinite acts of terror and danger to be shown. Primarily, one should see bodies embracing one another, appearing just as they would by moonlight, revealed by the flashes of fire <note>The author suggests using the sudden light of lightning to reveal figures in the darkness, similar to how moonlight creates high-contrast silhouettes.</note>. And next, one should see the Heaven bellowing with the shape of lightning that appears to manifest in the night air, all set ablaze with fire and agitated by winds, as Ariosto <note>Ludovico Ariosto (1474–1533), an influential Italian poet famous for the epic *Orlando Furioso*.</note> says in these verses:

> *From the rage of the wind, which is split*
> *In the rigging come horrible sounds*
> *With frequent lightning, the air is rekindled.* <note>original: "Della rabbia del vento, che ſi fende / Nelle ritorte eſcono horribil ſuoni / Di ſpeſſi lampi, l’aria ſi raccende."</note>

In contrast, one should see the battle of the waters below, which seems in a certain way to respond with its noise to the air; and between the Heaven and the sea, various winds blowing impetuously shriek, and the air seems to resound like a trumpet, as the same Ariosto expressed:

> *Behold, shrieking, the horrible storm*
> *Which the sudden fury of Boreas <term>Boreas: the personification of the North Wind</term> pushes*
> *Flails the sail against the mast.* <note>original: "Ecco ſtridendo l’horribile procella / Che’l repentin furor di Borea ſpinge / La vela contra l’arbore flagella."</note>

Then, one must see the lightning bolts <note>original: "faette," literally "arrows," often used for thunderbolts.</note> falling around the sail, and through the continuous striking, wasting away the people upon the ships, as happened to Aeneas <note>The author attributes the story of Ceyx to Virgil's Aeneas; however, the tragic shipwreck of Ceyx is most famously told by Ovid in the *Metamorphoses*. Virgil describes Aeneas’s shipwreck in the *Aeneid*.</note> in Ceyx while sailing to go to the oracle of Apollo, according to what Virgil writes. One must show the fear there: that with the timbers of the ships broken or the nails wrenched out, the bottom of the ship gradually begins to leak. The entire deck must be hidden by the heavy rain that floods it, under which everyone seeks to enter, staying hidden there as if in a cave, trembling and fearing the storm, seeing themselves without any hope of safety as enormous waves come upon them from every side like mountains, without cries or gestures being of any use. These waves battle one against the other, now from the prow <term>prow: the front of the ship</term> and now from the stern <term>stern: the back of the ship</term>. The ship must always be shown lifted high toward the swollen part of the sea, and toward the flat and low part it should appear as if submerged, also imitating what the same poet feigns, saying:

> *The oars are broken; of cruel fortune*
> *So much does the impetuous rage press*
> *That the prow turns, and toward the wave...* <note>original: "Frangonſi i remi, di fortuna fella / Tanto la rabbia impetuoſa ſtringe / Che la proda ſi volta, e verſo l’onda"</note>

### SIXTH BOOK.

Leave behind the defenseless shore;
Some of the waves should appear like mountains, as the same poet <note>Referring to Ariosto, whose poetry was frequently used by Renaissance artists as a "verbal manual" for painting dramatic scenes.</note> adds:
> *The sea rises and almost reaches the Heaven.* <note>original: "Il mar si leua e quasi al Cielo attinge."</note>
And certain others must resemble the deepest abysses, similar to those described by the same author in Canto forty-one where he says:
> *They see at times the sea rise so high,*
> *That it seems to reach the highest Heaven;*
> *Other times they make such a leap atop the waves*
> *That looking down, it seems to them they see Hell.* <note>original: "Veggon tal volta il mar venir tant'alto, / Che par ch'arriui infino al Ciel superno; / Tal hor fan sopra l'onde in sù tal salto / Ch'à mirar giù par lor veder l'inferno."</note>
Beyond this, the waves should be represented as coming from opposite directions to cause greater terror to the sailors: for it follows that as the water enters the ship, it makes it roll across the deck and fills it entirely, such that, as the poet says:
> *The vessel, defeated, gives way in many parts*
> *And within it the enemy wave passes.* <note>original: "Il legno vinto in più parti si lassa / E dentro l'inimica onda vi passa."</note>
Then everyone there must be seen toiling to empty the ship with the greatest haste they can; because (as the saying goes) while some empty the water, the sea returns into the ship: and next, one must show that ship, as the verse says:
> *Entirely underwater on the right side,* <note>original: "Tutta sott'acqua da la destra banda,"</note>
One should see the waves rising up, and almost touching the clouds in the distance, and coming toward the ship in the manner of very high mountains, as if they want to swallow it and submerge it in the extreme depths of the sea. The men, seeing the battle of the winds and the threatening waves, will be seen astonished and motionless; and others, unable to stay still anywhere due to the impetuous movement of the ship, will shout together in a crowd. And if there are women present, they will weep and let out shrieks and laments. The sailors should be seen encouraging one another, yet all full of terror; and others throwing their belongings into the sea, disregarding weapons, vessels, treasures, or other precious things; and finally the master <note>The "padrone" or captain of the vessel.</note>, who abandons the helm, and leaves the ship at the mercy of the waves, and prepares the lifeboat <note>The "battello" or small skiff used for escape.</note> into which everyone tries to scramble, either with ladders or by other means: and others try to cut the rope that keeps it tied to the ship, leading to a conflict, where they fight with weapons, with spears, with swords, and with oars; and some who have entered the lifeboat by force kill others without regard or respect for persons—the boat itself, because of the multitude and excessive weight, is also in danger of sinking. The ship meanwhile, without steering, spins around, toss— <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "do," likely completing the word "faltando" (failing) or "saltando" (tossing/jumping).</note>

These misfortunes and shipwrecks ought to be interspersed within historical paintings where sea voyages are featured. No less important are the depictions of the turbulent waves and the terrifying, threatening backlash of the waters around the army of Pharaoh, as they are drowned in the Red Sea while pursuing the people of Israel; or the great Deluge <note>The biblical flood of Noah.</note> that submerged the entire human race. ### Composition of Wonders. Chapter XXXIX.

**H**istorical paintings of wonders <term>merauiglia; a sense of awe or astonishment produced by a miracle or extraordinary event</term> require, as much as any other, the greatest consideration. Above all, everyone in the scene should be focused on seeing the miracle or sign that moves them to wonder: some should strive to push forward to see, others should depart stunned, marvelling, and astonished; and many should stand with their arms open, their mouths closed, their eyebrows arched, and similar acts of wonder. In these scenes, it is not appropriate for anyone to laugh, or jump, or for some to joke among themselves. Indeed, such actions are entirely contrary to wonder, as seen among the Egyptians when, in the presence of Pharaoh, the staff of Moses, turned into a snake, devoured those of the Magi which had also been converted into similar animals by magical art; or when they themselves, stupefied and admiring, beyond the other signs, saw the Nile tinted the color of blood. And likewise in many other events where wonders occurred according to what historians write: such as in Rome, when the earth opened in a massive chasm, into which Quintus Curtius <note>The author likely refers to the legend of Marcus Curtius, a Roman hero who sacrificed himself by leaping into a pit in the Forum to save the city. Quintus Curtius was the name of a later Roman historian.</note>, armed and on horseback, jumped for the safety of the fatherland; or when Ocrisia <note>original: "Ocratia." Ocrisia was a woman of the royal household of Tarquinius Priscus.</note>, wife of Tarquinius Priscus, saw the flame surrounding the head of Servius Tullius, which predicted his kingship; and similarly after the fall of Troy, when Aeneas, Anchises, Creusa, and the other Trojans saw the flame surrounding the head of Ascanius. Furthermore (as Pliny relates), among the Romans when Marcus Attilius and Caius Portius were Consuls, they saw it rain milk and blood; and in the Lucanian <note>original: "Lucini."</note> fields the year before Marcus Crassus went to the Parthian war, they saw it rain iron almost like sponges; or when Lucius Paulus and Claudius Marcellus were Consuls, they saw wool raining near the Corisano fortress; and during the Cimbrian wars, when they heard the sky resound with the clatter of arms and the sound of trumpets; and according to what Livy recounts in the Macedonian war among those peoples, in the year that Hannibal departed, they saw it rain blood for the space of two days; (and as the same author tells in the second book of the wars...

## Composition of Games. Cap. XXXX.

**H**aving spoken in general and in particular about the compositions of the principal histories, it remains for us to say something of the other less principal parts, such as the members <note>the individual elements or sub-categories of a scene</note>, so that we may approach the end in an orderly fashion. And beginning with the games, it is clear that they are composed in many ways, according to their diverse qualities. For one reads among the ancient Greeks of the games or Olympic contests, which were held for Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> on Mount Olympus, near Elis, a city of Arcadia, of which Hercules was the inventor and from which he once carried away the victory. This game was performed by running and wrestling, of which Herodotus writes saying it was a gymnic <term>gymnic; from "gymnastic," referring to athletic contests performed without clothing</term> game, and there was a prize offered of a Crown of Olive, with which the victors were adorned; and it was celebrated every five years <note>The Greeks counted inclusively, so the four-year Olympiad was often called a five-year cycle</note>. There were also the Pythian games which were held in memory of the death of the serpent Python, as Ovid says in the first book of the *Metamorphoses*.

The Isthmian games were so called from the Isthmus, a part of Achaia, and were founded by Theseus. They were celebrated by the Greeks in honor of Neptune <note>The Roman name for the Greek sea god Poseidon</note>, and also in praise of Sciron, as Plutarch says. But to Neptune, the Corinthians were accustomed to celebrate them enclosed on all sides, as they likewise did in some other games which they called by the same name "Isthmian," which they celebrated at night in honor of Melicerta <note>The mortal boy Melicerta was transformed into the sea god Palaemon; his funeral games were said to be the origin of the Isthmian festival</note>. The victor brought back a crown of Pine. The fourth principal game, which they called Nemean, was derived from the Nemean forest, and was held by the Argives in honor of Hercules, who slew the Nemean Lion. 

The <term>Pyrrhic Dance: a famous ancient Greek war dance performed in armor to the sound of a flute</term> was instituted by Pyrrhus to exercise the youth in the military art in Candia <note>The historical name for the island of Crete</note>, as Pliny writes, in which Curete <note>One of the Curetes, legendary protectors of the infant Zeus on Crete</note> introduced the dancing of armed men; with which Dionysius agrees, writing that the Pyrrhic dance was led by armed men; and it was found by Minerva, and called *Tranquillo* <note>original: "Tranquillo," perhaps suggesting a measured or steady pace</note>. The game called Troy was practiced by children in a squad, and Suetonius called it the game of boys on horseback <note>Known as the *Lusus Troiae*, a Roman equestrian event for noble youth</note>. The gymnastic games were those performed by naked men, of which Lycaon was the inventor. 

Funeral games were also used, found by Acastus, as Pliny says, and after him they were used by Theseus at the Isthmus. The <term>Palestra: an ancient wrestling school or the sport of wrestling itself</term>, which Mercury found according to Diodorus, was used by strong young men, striving in every way—coming to grips to overcome each other and throw one another to the ground—which we call the game of wrestling; and those who played were accustomed to anoint themselves with olive oil. 

Besides this, the ancient Greeks, like the Aenianian people <note>An ancient tribe of southern Thessaly</note>, honored people of Thessaly, used funeral games with jumping in honor of Neoptolemus on the day he was killed before the altar of Pythian Apollo by Orestes, son of Agamemnon, around the altar, accompanied by cries and weeping; and there were fifty men on horses, twenty-five per side, of whom the Captain of all was one alone crowned with laurel, who moved three times. They also used various other games of jumping and dancing, like the Corybantes in Phrygia, and the Curetes in

Among the Romans there were many other games, as Sebastian Hers. <note>Possibly a reference to a 16th-century humanist scholar</note> says (leaving to the Greeks the game of chess, ball games, dice, and others of little importance), among which was the Lupercal game <note>The Lupercalia, an ancient Roman pastoral festival</note>. This was performed with a sacrifice, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus says, beneath the Palatine Hill in a cave dedicated to the God Pan Lycaeus <note>An epithet for the god Pan, whom the Romans identified with Lupercus</note>, with a dog or a wolf, according to some. There, naked young men ran lasciviously, carrying certain whips in their hands, and women spontaneously offered themselves to be struck by them, believing that they would thus become fertile. According to Ovid, this game was brought by Evander from Arcadia to Italy; it was in this game (as Appian reports) that the naked Mark Antony placed the crown upon Caesar's head.

Besides this, there were the Circensian games, so named from the "turning of swords" <note>The author suggests an etymology connecting "Circus" to the Latin *circum* (around) and *ensis* (sword)</note>; because according to Servius <note>A 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note>, since the ancients had not yet built suitable places for these games, they celebrated them among swords and weapons, not unlike the modern tilting-grounds or lists. From this, the Circus—that is, a place surrounded by walls—was built and named "Circensian" by them, where the games were held. And it was constructed as that which Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian</note> calls the *Maximus* <note>The Circus Maximus, Rome’s largest chariot-racing stadium</note>, in the shape of a long space; at the top were the places from which the horses, joined to the chariot, began their run, and having returned to the top, they turned until they reached the first mark again. The combatants also exercised in the middle, with prizes offered to them (as Virgil says in the fifth book <note>Referring to the funeral games described in the *Aeneid*</note>) that were put on display in the circus. And these games were greatly used by the Romans.

There were also the Saturnalia games, invented by the Pelasgians <note>Mythical ancestors of the Greeks</note> or by the Athenians, which were celebrated in the month of December with magnificent preparation by everyone; and they were full of every joy. ...they would send *Apophoreta* <note>original: "Apoforeti" — gifts given to guests at the end of a festival, particularly the Saturnalia, to be carried home</note>. And because in these games, while they were being celebrated, all things were held in common (as Justin <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a Roman historian</note> writes), all the servants, without any distinction from their masters, sat at the table eating and presenting themselves. Other games were called gladiatorial, in which men killed one another for the sport of the people; and he was most esteemed in these games who not only killed and wounded, but demonstrated the art of doing so. From this, the cruel bystanders derived not only delight but an example of how to shed blood with various techniques of the sword and other weapons. And some of these gladiators can be found in ancient Roman marbles, depicted with rapiers and cloaks. These were celebrated when the Romans were about to go to war, so that they might become accustomed to the conflict of battle and to seeing wounds and blood mingled together; thus, while fighting, they would not fear armed men in the cruel spectacle of wounds and blood. 

There were many other kinds of games in which (according to Cicero) the Roman youth practiced in the Campus Martius <note>The "Field of Mars," a public area in ancient Rome used for military exercises</note> to be more ready for war. There were others called *Equitij* <note>Equestrian games or exercises</note> where the youth on horseback, with swords in hand and shields on their arms, fought against one another; sometimes some on horseback fought against many others on foot. A military prize was offered, such as a shield, a sword, or something similar, hanging from a tree. This was also offered to those who performed a certain other game, in which there were two or three youths tied together by a single cloak at the shoulder; they held a very large club in their right hand and a very large shield on their left arm. There were then as many lions tied by their shoulders to a very sturdy tree, and the youths, passing between the lions and holding their shields with speed, struck them from behind with the clubs, unable to be harmed by the beasts except through their own negligence. 

Another game was likewise played by the youth to exercise with the *cestus* <note>original: "ceſte" — ancient boxing gloves, often weighted with lead or iron</note>, in which (as seen on the ancient monuments <note>original: "pile" — refers to the relief carvings on stone pillars or pedestals</note> of Rome) they wore certain heavy gloves made of wood in the shape of baskets over their hands and up to the middle of the arm, like a gauntlet, and with these they struck one another. They wore nothing else but a shirt bound with cloth and wrapped around the arm. 

There were also naval games, in which ships were seen being brought into the theaters via water conduits, and in those ships, spectacles of naval battles were performed; the Roman people sat all around upon the tiers to watch. They also gathered for games involving animals and men. This was still in use in recent years under the name of the Festival of Testaccio <note>A famous Roman festival held in the Testaccio district, involving bullfights and cart races down the hillside</note>, where they made them run...

There were theatrical games <note>original: "giochi Scenici"</note> that were celebrated by lewd youths and courtesans, where they appeared with new forms of licentiousness, crowned with flowers, in the costumes of nymphs, perfumed and adorned to appear more beautiful; and the young men also made themselves seen in ornate and suggestive clothing. For a time they were held in honor of the Goddess Flora, later considered the Goddess of flowers, and afterwards in honor of Priapus, the God of gardens and generation <note>the god of fertility and procreation</note>; where all the women, both noble and common, to make themselves fertile, went with flowers on their heads around his statue, dancing, jumping, and crowning the statue with garlands of flowers. The children did the same, jumping in a circle around him. 

Next, they had funeral games, with which they accompanied the sacrificial ceremonies in various ways, according to how they were observed on certain days—whether an illustrious man had died whom they worshipped as a deity, or the City had been ruined, or for other such commemorations, as one reads of many that the Romans held in the works of Pliny. In these games, the shields, the spoils, and the portraits of the deceased were carried; and in all those games, there were always crowns as prizes. These were first made of tree branches, and then were mixed with flowers, and they were even woven from plates of gold and silver; some were made round, others pointed, some small in the manner of coronets, some slanted, some sewn, and others tied. Crassus was the first of all to give those woven very thinly of gold and silver, called circles or wreaths <note>original: "cerchi o corolle"</note>, to the victors in his games. And all these crowns—whether they were of copper or olive that were offered to the winners, or of pine, or medlar, or myrtle, or other trees—were preserved in the sacred temples in memory of having been worn on the heads of the victors during their triumphs. 

Therefore, because the games are in a certain way connected with sacrifices, especially these funeral ones and the comedies, it will not be out of place to say something here of the valiant ancients...

Therefore, strong men were formerly small in stature and broad in the shoulders, such as Tritannus <note>original: "Tritano" — a famous Samnite gladiator mentioned by Pliny the Elder for his immense strength</note> among the gladiators, and Sammitius <note>original: "Sammitio"</note> in arms, and his son, of whom it is written that he had straight and transverse sinews throughout his whole body like a grating <note>original: "graticola" — suggesting a grid-like or "lattice" appearance of his musculature</note>; hence, once challenged by someone, he overcame him with just two fingers of his right hand, and finally, having captured him, dragged him into his own camp; he was a soldier of Pompey the Great. One also reads of Ascenius, a very valiant soldier, who was accustomed to supporting wagons while they were being loaded and holding back a cart pulled by horses with his hands, besides many other marvelous things. There was another called Hercules Rusticello who carried his own mule, and one Fusius Salvius <note>original: "Fusio Saluio"</note>, who carried two hundred pounds <note>original: "libre"</note> with his feet and as many with his hands, and two hundred on each shoulder up the stairs. It is written of one Athanatus <note>original: "Atenato"</note> that he dressed himself with fifty lead breastplates <note>original: "cinquanta corazze di piombo"</note> and with leggings of five hundred pounds and thus walked across the stage. Milo of Croton <note>original: "Milone Crotoniate"</note>, the celebrated wrestler, when he stood still on his feet, could not be moved by anyone, and when he held an apple, it was not possible for anyone to move even one of his fingers.

As for speed, it is told of Philippides that in two days he ran 1160 stadia <note>A stadium was an ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 185 meters or 600 feet</note>; of Anystis <note>original: "Anista"</note>, the courier of the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, and of Philonides, the courier of Alexander the Great, who in one day walked 1220 stadia; of a nine-year-old boy who in one day ran 75 miles; and of Tiberius Nero who with three carts made a very long journey of two hundred miles. Among the moderns, the elder Pusterla <note>original: "Pusterla" — likely Pietro Pusterla, a Milanese nobleman and soldier</note> was famous, being very valiant in arms at the time of the Great Trivulzio <note>original: "Triulci" — referring to Gian Giacomo Trivulzio, a prominent Italian aristocrat and military commander</note>; when he was on horseback, three men would go to place the heavy, measured lance in his hand over his thigh, which he then handled as if it were a light rod; moreover, no one could resist his blows, and for this reason, he was banned from jousts and tournaments. Besides him, it is told of Luigi Gonzaga <note>original: "Aluigi Gonzaga" — likely Luigi "Rodomonte" Gonzaga, famous for his physical power</note>, of whom more will be said together with the others in the chapter on Heroes, who broke horseshoes and restrained steeds; just as Antonio Melone and Girolamo Sala <note>original: "Gieronimo Sala"</note> also did, the latter of whom with one hand took by the foot a chair where an armed man was seated and raised it into the air; he raised seven halberds placed one atop the other, and ran with such speed that he could well take the prize from that ancient woman who acquired the golden apples through the race <note>A reference to the mythological Atalanta, who challenged suitors to a footrace for her hand in marriage</note>. It is also told of another who jumped thirty arm-lengths <note>original: "braccia" — a measurement of roughly 23 inches</note> away, and of Pompeo Diabone who before Henry, King of France, besides the grace of his dancing, while jumping would reach high with his foot...

In dexterity and speed, Ambrogio Vespolato and L’Arcuato <note>literally "The Arched One"</note> were celebrated, and for this reason they were singular in the game of the **large ball** <note>original: "palla grossa" — an early form of Italian ball game played with a large, air-filled leather ball</note>. There, the same artist also painted a "freak of nature," namely **Heraclitus** who was weeping and **Democritus** who was laughing, above a doorway. 

But returning to the masters of arms, excellent among those named was Gentile dei Borri, for whom **Leonardo da Vinci** drew all the men on horseback, showing how they could defend themselves against one another and against those on foot, and also how those on foot could defend and attack one another according to their various weapons. It is truly a great loss that this work was never published for the adornment of this most stupendous art. Equal to him are his brother Ottaviano, Giacobo Cavallo, and Francesco Tappa, all from Milan. 

I could go on discussing many other games that can be represented in the manner of the ancients, just as **Polidoro** and **Maturino** <note>Polidoro da Caravaggio and Maturino da Firenze, famous for decorating Roman building facades with monochrome paintings</note> have done on the facades of Rome, together with sacrifices both in painting and in sculpture—which remains more eternal than painting, just as painting in the first degree precedes sculpture as the **spirit** precedes the **body** <note>This reflects the Renaissance "Paragone," a formal debate over whether painting or sculpture was the superior art form</note>. These various games, along with their authors, are divinely represented by **Luca Cambiaso** <note>original: "Luca Cangiasso" — a Genoese painter famous for his "cubic" style of drawing figures</note>—who is most excellent in this and all other parts—with his fortunate hand. Through various actions corresponding to truth, with the correct squaring of limbs and proportioned outlines, he makes visible to our eyes everything that can be demonstrated with this art; for however difficult and impossible to express the actions may be, to him they are easy and light.

->### BOOK SIX<-

...there were three types of sacrifices. One was called the **Holocaust** <note>From the Greek *holokaustos*, meaning "burnt whole"; a sacrifice entirely consumed by fire.</note> and it occurred when the most noble offered two lambs or another male animal of one year; here the priest would wet the rim of the altar with the blood of the victim, and then cut the victim into pieces and burn it upon the altar. The other was the **plebeian** sacrifice which was performed to give thanks to God, in which they sacrificed animals younger than one year, likewise sprinkling the altar with blood; they placed the kidneys, the fat, and the small caul <note>original: "radicella" — likely referring to the lobe or membrane of the liver mentioned in Levitical law</note> into the fire, and gave the breast and the right legs to the priest, and the remainder was eaten within two days by those who had sacrificed. The poor offered two doves or two turtledoves, one of which was offered, and the other the priests took by lot. The third sacrifice, more perfect than any other and common to all men, was called the **sacrifice of praise**, as in **Psalm 112** <note>In the modern numbering this is Psalm 116:16-17; the author uses the Latin Vulgate numbering.</note> where it says, *“You have broken my bonds, and I will sacrifice to you the sacrifice of praise,”* <note>original: "tu hai rotto i miei legami, & io ti sacrificarò sacrificio di laude"</note> that is, the fruit of our mouth that confesses the name of God. To mourn for sins, if someone had unwittingly committed an error, he offered a lamb or a kid of one year; and if the sin was hidden, a ram. In all sacrifices, the purest flour was mixed in, pouring oil into the sacrifice. On the Sabbath they sacrificed two victims; at the beginning of the month, two oxen, one ram, one kid, and seven lambs of one year. For sins, they offered in the seventh month at the beginning a bull, a ram, seven lambs, and a kid. They also added two kids, one of which they sent out into the wilderness <note>The "scapegoat" ritual described in Leviticus 16.</note> to purge the people, and of the other they burned the skin in the outskirts. The High Priest in this sacrifice offered a bull and a ram. And leaving aside the other sacrifices that were offered on solemn days beyond these numbers (as the same **Josephus** <note>Titus Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian whose works were primary sources for Renaissance scholars.</note> says), one must note that in these sacrifices—one in a hundred—(as one reads in **Leviticus**) it must be ensured that the fire burns upon the altar, and that a priest nourishes it; because without that fire, no sacrifice could be performed. And in all sacrifices, one must express humble gestures, such as repenting for one's errors, or praising God, or thanking Him, or praying to Him; as one reads of **Noah** immediately after leaving the ark with his family, and before him of **Adam**, and after him of **Jacob** on the road with his sons going into Egypt, of **Joseph** among the people of Israel escaped from Egypt, and of **Aaron**, **Moses**, and their followers around the sacred altar ordained for this. Now, leaving these compositions of the sacrifices of the Hebrews, and also our own observed in the **Holy Church**, which is the true sacrifice,

->### BOOK SIX<-

...since it contains our Savior, true man and true God, we shall now treat of those of the ancient gentiles <note>The author uses "gentiles" to refer to all non-Christian/non-Hebrew polytheistic cultures of antiquity.</note>. There is no doubt, to begin here, that sacrifices among the gentiles were celebrated with the greatest reverence and ceremony in honor of their Gods and Deities; and therefore, here too, it is fitting that one sees the greatest acts of humility and devotion. Furthermore, with the most religious solemnity, the prince who was sacrificing stood in a devout posture, having first made a prayer to the God that he might grant the grace for which he wished to sacrifice. Next to him, one must always place the **Augur** <note>A Roman religious official who observed natural signs, especially the behavior of birds, to interpret the will of the gods.</note> in his proper attire, and the Priest, who sometimes stood with a rod in his hand, curved slightly at the top and pointed, so that they might take the augury from the acts, the gestures, the color, the skin, and the intestines of the animal being sacrificed.

And that sacrifices were always performed by princes, we read that the Ethiopians outside of Meroë <note>An ancient city on the east bank of the Nile.</note> used to have their King sacrifice to the Sun, and the Queen to the Moon; and among the Romans, we read that Caesar, dressed in purple and seated upon a golden chair, sacrificed; and likewise Caesar Marius in Utica, and near Laurentum with Posthumius the **Haruspex** <note>original: "Aruspice" — a priest trained to practice divination by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals.</note>, who for that reason predicted his victory; and following him, Lucius Petilius, Gaius Claudius, and in short, countless other men of consular rank. 

Now it is necessary to know in what manner one should sacrifice, which animals, and to which Gods among all the gentile nations, so that the **composition** <note>The arrangement of figures and elements in a painting or relief.</note> can be made as is fitting. We read, then, that the Rhodians sacrificed a man to Saturn, and the people of the island of Salamis did the same in honor of Aglauros <note>original: "Agrauale"</note>, daughter of Cecrops, in the temple of Pallas <note>Athena</note>, where the youths led him three times around the altar and then the priest struck him with a spear and burned him. Teucer in Cyprus also sacrificed a human victim to Jupiter, and left such a rite to his descendants. Among the Tauri—a cruel and ferocious people—there was a law that foreigners should be sacrificed to Diana, and the same was observed by the Cerastae in Cyprus, sacrificing travelers to Jupiter, as Ovid writes. The ancient French <note>The Gauls.</note> likewise appeased Esus and Teutates with human victims; whence Lucan says, *Teutates and Esus were appeased, cruel with human blood, and of men slaughtered and burned.* <note>original: "Placavasi Teutate & Heso, crudo d'humano sangue, e d'huomo scannato & arso." A reference to Lucan's Pharsalia, Book I.</note> Those of the island of Chios also sacrificed a man to Dionysus, called the **Omadius** <note>original: "Omaldo" — from the Greek 'Omadios', meaning 'eater of raw flesh'.</note>, after they had cruelly torn him apart; and the Egyptians, the people of the Sun, chose three pure and young men every day and sacrificed them. Apollodorus writes that the Spartans also sacrificed a man to Mars, and the Phoenicians, when they were troubled by war or pestilence, immolated their own friends to Saturn...

...to Saturn. Histo <note>Likely referring to Istros the Callimachean, an ancient Greek historian who wrote about the rites of Crete.</note>, writing of the deeds of Candia <note>Candia is the historical name for the island of Crete.</note>, says that the Curetes <note>Mythological protectors of the infant Zeus on Crete.</note> in ancient times sacrificed children to Saturn. In Laodicea of Syria, a virgin was offered in sacrifice to Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom and war.</note>. Among the Arabs, it was the custom to sacrifice a young boy every year, whom they then buried beneath the altar. And likewise the Thracians, the Scythians, the Carthaginians, and almost all the Greeks, when wishing to go to war, were accustomed to kill some human body in sacrifice. Caesar and Tranquillus <note>Suetonius, whose full name was Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, a Roman historian.</note> write that the Germans at certain times sacrificed with human victims, and that the Romans offered the heads of men to Dis <note>Dis Pater, a Roman god of the underworld, often equated with Pluto or Hades.</note>, and also to Saturn; however, they did not kill them before the altar, but threw them down from the Milvian Bridge and drowned them <note>This refers to the ritual of the Argei, where rush effigies were thrown into the Tiber; the author interprets these as substitutes for earlier human sacrifices.</note>. These sacrifices were called Saturnalia and were later changed by Hercules when he returned through Italy with the herds of Geryon; for he persuaded posterity to change these unhappy human sacrifices, offering to Dis not human heads, but masks fashioned in human form, and to Saturn not murdered men but lit torches, as Ovid says in the *Fasti* <note>Ovid’s poetic calendar of Roman religious festivals.</note>. Philo tells in the history of the Phoenicians that the Prince was accustomed, in the gravest dangers, to sacrifice his most beloved son to his God. In Alexandria there was a rite where, in honoring Saturn, they sent by order of the priest the most beautiful matrons to the temple; there, at night, after the torches were extinguished, they were violated by the priest in the guise of Saturn, and he was called the "Tyrant," <note>original: "Tirano"</note> as Rufinus writes <note>Rufinus of Aquileia, a Church historian who documented the destruction of the Serapeum and pagan scandals in Alexandria.</note>. And the Nasamones <note>A nomadic tribe of ancient Libya.</note> had the custom that on the first night, the bride should lie with all the wedding guests to satisfy Venus. 

But passing to various ways of sacrificing, one reads that at a certain time the Romans sacrificed a hind to Diana, hanging the horns in her temple; for this animal was dedicated to her by the ancients, because she made one appear in place of the virgin Iphigenia, whom the Greeks wished to sacrifice to her to obtain a favorable voyage; just as another time the same people sacrificed the unhappy Polyxena <note>A princess of Troy, sacrificed on the tomb of Achilles by his son Neoptolemus.</note> to appease the soul of Achilles. Herodotus writes that in Egypt, in the sacrifices of Isis, certain cymbals were used, and while making a feast with them, the men played upon pipes <note>original: "tibie" — ancient flute-like instruments often made from bone.</note>. Beyond this, the Scythians sacrificed the horse, as did the Heliopolitans and the Assyrians; the goat and the donkey were sacrificed to Bacchus. Indeed, according to Catullus, the Tamariti <note>Likely referring to the Tamyritae or a similar tribal group mentioned in classical geography.</note>—peoples neighboring the Hyrcanians—and those of Naxos and Thebes also sacrificed horns to him. The Sicilians sacrificed a sow to Ceres, a hind to Diana, and also dogs under the name of the Moon, and to Vulcan. The donkey was the victim of Priapus, the goose of Isis, the rooster of the night (and especially the cockerel), the goat alone of Faunus, the bull of Neptune, the goat of Minerva, the bull of Hercules, a boy of Saturn, a sow

...a pregnant sow to Maia <note>Maia was an ancient Roman goddess often associated with growth and the spring; the month of May is named after her.</note>, which was sacrificed to her once a year by the Romans, and the rooster was dedicated to Aesculapius <note>The god of medicine and healing.</note>. To the Gnidian Hercules they sacrificed with insults and abuse; and to Mars with vigorous and bold gestures, offering either a wolf or a horse. In all sacrifices, of whatever kind they might be, the priest always participated, as did the Prince <note>Referring to the sovereign or chief leader of the state.</note> as I have stated; but the priests differed one from another. For there were priests known as Flamens, Arch-flamens, Philadi, Salii, Hierophants, Fetials, Vestal Virgins, and Priestesses—such as those of Diana in Thessaly—as well as Pontifices Maximi, *Pater Patrati* <term>Pater Patrati: The "Father Spokesman," a chief member of the Fetial priests who handled international treaties and declarations of war</term>, *Rex Sacrificulus* <term>Rex Sacrificulus: Also known as the Rex Sacrorum, a priest who took over the religious duties previously held by the Roman Kings</term>, Augusti, Sodales, Titii, and Arval Brethren, besides many others that would be endless to recount.

The Flamens were instituted by Numa Pompilio <note>The legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing many of its religious institutions.</note> to bind the still-fierce people to the performance of sacrifices. According to their needs, he divided the year into twelve months. One of these priests he dedicated to Jupiter and adorned him with a mantle and curule chairs; one he established for Mars, and another for Quirinus <note>A Roman god of the state or the Roman people, often identified with the deified Romulus.</note>. They were called Flamens from the insignia they wore on their heads, and were almost called *Filamini* <note>Possibly a folk etymology relating the word to "filum," the woolen thread on their caps</note>, while others named them for the pyramidal shape of their hair; indeed, the miter they wore on their heads was called a *flamina*.

The Vestal Virgins were taken from the same order to guard the fire continuously in the temple of Vesta from the age of six up to ten <note>Recruitment age was between 6 and 10; they typically served for thirty years.</note>; and the most beautiful were chosen. Some of them attended to learning the rituals, and others to performing them. They were carried in a chariot, and the magistrates rose to honor them as they passed; moreover, if they happened to encounter someone being led to death, they would grant him freedom. They went about dressed in long garments that were modest yet ornate.

Of the *Pontifices Maximi* <note>The highest-ranking priests in Roman religion.</note>, the first was Marcius, ordained by Numa himself. He was placed in charge of all sacrifices and taught which victims were to be used, on which days, and in which temples the sacrifices should be performed. The same King ordained twelve Salii for Mars and gave them the embroidered toga as their insignia, and above it, a metal plate over the chest, commanding them to carry the celestial weapons called *ancilia* <note>Twelve sacred shields, one of which was said to have fallen from heaven.</note> and to go through the city singing verses and leaping, from which they took their name <note>The name "Salii" comes from the Latin verb "salire," meaning to leap or dance.</note>. And the *ancilia* were certain small, round shields—as Ovid says—which adorned the temple of Mars all around.

Historians write that after the Kings were expelled, the *Rex Sacrificulus* <note>King of Sacrifices</note> was ordained in their place by the Republic, so that he might perform the sacrifices that were traditionally the duty of the Kings and no others; he was likewise subject to the *Pontifex Maximus*, and never performed a sacrifice unless the Pontiff, the Augur, and the *Triumviri Epuloni* <term>Triumviri Epuloni: A college of priests responsible for organizing the sacred banquets at festivals</term> were present. Three men were also chosen to read the sacred books and the prophecies of the Sibyl, who were called *Sodales* and *Titii*, and they went about in the attire of soldiers. It is said they originated as far back as Romulus, as did the companions called Arval Brethren, as Pliny writes, who performed sacrifices so that the fields would yield fruit...

...the fruits copiously; and their insignia (as **Aulus Gellius** <note>A 2nd-century Roman author known for his collection *Attic Nights*, which preserved many fragments of older Roman law and ritual.</note> says) was a crown of grain ears tied at the back with a ribbon. To these priests belonged the **Lupercalia** <note>A very ancient, possibly pre-Roman, pastoral festival observed to avert evil spirits and purify the city.</note> and **Saturnalia** sacrifices. There were also the **Floralia** sacrifices, which prostitutes celebrated on the last day of April in honor of **Flora** <note>The goddess of flowers and the season of spring.</note> with garlands of flowers and varied clothing, signifying the joyful season and the variety of the blooms. In the sacrifices made on the **Aventine Hill** to the **Bona Dea** <note>The "Good Goddess," a deity of fertility and healing whose rites were strictly forbidden to men.</note>, no men were permitted to enter the temple. The **Bacchanalia** sacrifices were performed (according to **Livy** <note>The Roman historian who famously chronicled the scandal and suppression of these secret rites in 186 BCE.</note>) at night, where both sexes mingled together in a shameful state of nakedness. These were also performed with the horns of calves; for **Pentheus** <note>A legendary King of Thebes who resisted the cult of Bacchus and was subsequently torn to pieces by his own mother and other female followers of the god.</note>, having been torn apart by the **Bacchantes**, was transformed into this animal and sacrificed. The same animal was also sacrificed to his son **Priapus**, the god of the garden. In the sacrifices ordained for **Ceres** <note>Goddess of grain and agriculture.</note>, the priests dressed in white and ran at night with torches; and because this goddess was held to be the Goddess of Chastity, the priests would sit and sacrifice to her without drinking wine, offering three types of *hostia* <term>hostia: a Latin term for a sacrificial victim, usually an animal offered to the gods</term>: namely Bulls, Rams, and Pigs. In the sacrifices made during the solemn festival of **Minerva** on the thirteenth of June, the priests would process around with flutes and various garments, just as they did when the Romans were led back to Rome disguised and intoxicated. The **Augur** <note>A priest and official whose main role was to interpret the will of the gods by observing the flight of birds.</note>, as seen on ancient monuments, wore an outer mantle in the military fashion through Rome, and beneath it a toga reaching to the knees; otherwise, he was entirely covered by a long cloak. Furthermore, it was the custom in sacrifices for a single person to play small flutes, as is still seen on ancient sarcophagi, especially when bulls were sacrificed by two soldiers called **Sodales** and **Titii** <note>Minor priestly colleges in Rome; the Titii were established to preserve certain Sabine rites.</note>. In all sacrifices, garlands were used; therefore, the victims were crowned with ivy, especially in the sacrifices to **Bacchus**, its discoverer. And **Virgil** writes that **Evander**, when sacrificing to **Hercules**, crowned himself with a garland of poplar, which was called *Herculea* as it was dedicated to Hercules. And the gods of **Numa**—namely **Segesta**, the goddess of standing grain, and **Seia**, from the sowing—were garlanded with ears of corn, supplicating them with a salty flatbread <note>original: "schiacciata salsa", likely referring to the *mola salsa*, a mixture of toasted grain and salt prepared by the Vestal Virgins.</note> and, as **Pliny** says, with burnt emmer wheat <note>A primitive type of wheat (far) that was sacred in early Roman ritual.</note>, for it is more health-giving. For this reason, the new grain and wines were not tasted until the first fruits had been sacrificed by the priests. The oxen were all black, with robust necks and sharp, simple, and straight horns; one of which was gilded and the other wreathed with crowns of flowers, and they had the cloth hanging down over their knees. Following these was another multitude of sacrifices, where everyone, for greater ornament, led every kind of animal, preceded by flutes and panpipes <note>Ancient woodwind instruments consisting of pipes of increasing length bound together.</note> as the initiators and heralds of the sacrifice. After the animals and their herdsmen followed the young women of Thessaly <note>A region in northern Greece famous in mythology for its horses and witches.</note>, all richly adorned, with their outer robes ungirded and their hair flowing loose; and they were divided into two groups: those who went before carried baskets full of flowers and fruits, and the others also carried baskets of incense and fragrant spices, with which they filled the whole place with a sweet scent. And so, carrying these baskets on their heads, they proceeded in order in a circle, holding hands, so that as they walked, they danced in a ring and sang together the praises of Peleus <note>The father of Achilles; the procession honors the lineage of the hero Neoptolemus.</note> in the form of a song. Then came a company of young men with their Lord on horseback, fifty in number divided into two groups, having in their midst **Theagenes** <note>The hero of the Greek romance "Aethiopica."</note> with a spear in his hand as the leader in the divine ceremonies. From the temple of **Diana** <note>The goddess of the hunt, known as Artemis in Greek.</note> emerged the priestess, dressed as I will describe below, drawn by two oxen upon a seat placed in a carriage open on all sides; and there they all entered the temple, and after the ceremonies were performed at the altar of **Pythian Apollo** <note>Apollo in his role as the slayer of the Python and the patron of the Delphic Oracle.</note> by **Theagenes** and the song was sung by the virgins, with funeral pomp the monument of **Neoptolemus** <note>The son of Achilles, whose tomb was at Delphi.</note> was surrounded with torches by some. And once the young men had led the horses away for the third time, the women made a heavy lamentation, and the men raised a shout full of joy, and at this moment the oxen, lambs, and kids were killed. Where, having a very large altar laden with a great abundance of wood, they placed upon it all the extreme parts <note>The choice portions or limbs reserved for the gods.</note> of the killed animals; and then the priest **Charicles** offered the sacred drink to **Apollo**; and the prince, having taken the torch from the priestess, set fire to the altar, and while the flames ascended, the priest made prayers and asked about the future deeds of **Theagenes**; and this sacrifice was customary every four years. In general, we should know that white victims were sacrificed to the celestial gods, and black to the terrestrial and infernal ones; but to the terrestrial on altars, and to the infernal in caves. <meta>catchword: caves.</meta>

...ue. To the aerial and aquatic gods, birds were sacrificed, but white ones were given to the aquatic gods and black ones to the aerial. To the terrestrial and infernal <note>Deities of the underworld, such as Pluto.</note> gods, nothing but quadrupeds were sacrificed, and especially to the terrestrial ones. No sacrifice was performed for any God unless it used things appropriate to him and according to the rites of that religion. Thus, in the **Holocaust** <term>Holocaust (original: *Holocausto*); a religious animal sacrifice in which the entire offering was consumed by fire.</term>, the victim was consumed in the fire; in the **immolation**, the blood was spilled for the sake of health; in the **pacific** sacrifice, one sought to obtain peace; in the sacrifice of **praise**, one sought to be freed from evils and attain blessings; in the **gratulatory** sacrifice, thanks were returned; and so on for the others. To **Venus**, no other animals were ever sacrificed but doves or goats, along with wood and garlands of myrtle flowers. And according to what ancient authors have left in writing—especially the Egyptians, the Greeks, and the Romans who have treated the trees, herbs, fruits, and flowers dedicated to the Gods—the following associations were held:

*   To **Pallas** <note>Athena.</note>, the Owl and the Goat were sacrificed.
*   To **Juno**, the Peacock and the sheep.
*   To **Neptune**, the Swan and the horse.
*   To the Goddess **Vesta**, the heron and the Lion.
*   To **Diana**, the Crow and the Doe.
*   To **Mars**, the Woodpecker and the Wolf.
*   To **Vulcan**, the goose and the donkey.
*   To **Ceres**, the sparrow and the sow.

Likewise, concerning trees and plants:
*   Sacrifices to **Venus** used the myrtle.
*   To **Pallas**, the olive.
*   To **Phoebus** <note>Apollo.</note>, the laurel.
*   To **Jupiter**, the oak.
*   To **Juno**, the juniper.
*   To **Ceres**, the apple.
*   To **Vulcan**, the boxwood.
*   To **Mars**, the cornel <note>A type of dogwood tree.</note>.
*   To **Diana**, the Palm.
*   To **Vesta**, the pine.
*   To **Neptune**, the olive.
*   To **Bacchus**, the vine.
*   To **Pluto**, the ivy and the Cypress.
*   To the infernal **Furies**, the narcissus (to whom turtle-doves were also sacrificed).

Regarding altars, some were partially perforated with a flat divider so that fire could be lit on top, and the remains of sacred drinks <note>Libations.</note> could be poured into the opening. Others were entirely flat but had a **patella** <term>A small, flat sacrificial dish.</term> nearby on a stool of copper or gold to hold the fire; some of these were wider, others narrower, and others round, according to the ministries for which they were intended. At times, sacrifices were also made only over vessels containing fire, supported by **tripods** <note>Three-legged stands.</note> fashioned with the legs and feet of various animals, such as snakes, lions, goats, eagles, and dogs. And on many altars, it was customary to place the Idol raised high upon a pedestal. It was the custom of the Romans in their sacrifices—as seen on ancient **stelae** <note>The original *Pili* refers to commemorative pillars or funerary monuments.</note>—to carry standards and images with small hangings beneath them, and those of animals like eagles, and still others crafted like vessels with fire burning on top.
