## Composition of Triumphs. Chapter XLII.

Since it has always pleased painters who are rich and abundant in inventions—and who have hands ready for drawing as experts well-versed in the art—to create compositions of "Triumphs" no less than any other true composition, as seen through various drawings, fragments, and many completed works. These include the **Triumph of Caesar** by <term>Andrea Mantegna</term> <note>A series of nine large paintings (c. 1484–1492) depicting the triumphal procession of Julius Caesar, now at Hampton Court.</note> in Mantua; that of **Furio Camillo** in the <term>Council Hall of Florence</term> <note>The Sala dei Cinquecento in the Palazzo Vecchio.</note> by <term>Salviati</term> <note>Francesco Salviati (1510–1563), a prominent Mannerist painter.</note>; that of **Bacchus** in Rome by <term>Daniello Ricciarelli</term> <note>Better known as Daniele da Volterra, a pupil of Michelangelo.</note>; and another of **Bacchus and Silenus** in Ferrara by <term>Titian</term>; and likewise one by his master <term>Giovanni Bellini</term> (brother of Gentile); and many by <term>Polidoro</term> and <term>Maturino</term> in Rome on various facades. Therefore, I do not wish to fail to prescribe an order for composing them. And to do this more perfectly, it will be necessary to repeat the matter from a slightly higher perspective, explaining the origins of the triumph, for what purpose it was instituted, in what form the triumphs were arranged, and how they should be composed according to historical accounts of spoils, trophies, and conquered nations, both in the triumphs of men and of the Gods.

<term>Diodorus</term>, <term>Pliny</term>, and <term>Solinus</term> write that the custom of triumphing over enemies was ordained by <term>Father Liber</term> <note>Original: *padre Libero*; an ancient Roman deity of fertility and wine, later identified with the Greek Bacchus.</note>, otherwise called **Bacchus**. For, laden with the spoils of various peoples, he triumphed—most notably over the Indians, King Pentheus, and Lycurgus—showing himself atop a most beautiful **Elephant** when he returned victorious from India. There, everyone shouted and could rebuke the vices of the victor, who was crowned with a garland of **ivy**, which he then began to weave for the first time to make a crown. For this reason, <term>Alexander the Great</term>, imitating him, desired that his entire army be crowned with such foliage when he returned victorious from India. 

But because Bacchus triumphed in different ways, one must be particularly careful: for when he is depicted triumphing in feminine attire—as <term>Philostratus</term> says—going to **Ariadne** in a beautiful purple robe crowned with roses, one must place around him bold and ferocious women, charming Nymphs, Sileni, Satyrs, and Silvanei, who (as <term>Strabo</term> writes) were his ministers and followers. This triumph was called the "choir" and the company of Ariadne, who all followed the God with joyful praises, as one reads in <term>Catullus</term>:

> *Some went shaking the green <term>thyrsi</term>,* <note>A *thyrsus* is a staff tipped with a pinecone and entwined with ivy, carried by Bacchus and his followers.</note>
> *And others carried the torn limbs*
> *Of a calf, while another part...*

Among his sacred objects, they carried the <term>sieve</term> <note>The *vannus* or *liknon*, a winnowing basket used in ancient rites to symbolize the purification of the soul.</note> in these types of joyful and peaceful triumphs. <term>Diodorus</term> <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BC.</note> writes that Bacchus was represented with beautiful clothes, soft and delicate, all painted with flowers. His chariot was surrounded and covered with vines, as <term>Statius</term> <note>Publius Papinius Statius, a Roman poet known for his vivid descriptions of mythological scenes.</note> writes, and it was pulled by two tigers sprinkled with wine with bits at their mouths; on one side and the other were panthers, and his <term>Bacchante nymphs</term> <note>Female followers of Bacchus, also known as Maenads.</note> wore the skins of foxes, panthers, and tigers, carrying the <term>thyrsus</term> <note>A ritual staff tipped with a pinecone and entwined with ivy or vine leaves.</note> in their hands, their hair tossing in the wind, sometimes bound with garlands of ivy and sometimes with white poplar. Often they also decorated the chariot, the shield, the spear, and the altars with garlands or branches of fig leaves, with which Bacchus most often crowned himself on the days he triumphed joyfully; he usually appeared in the <term>Bassarea</term> <note>A long, fringed Lydian robe worn by Bacchus (Dionysus) and his followers.</note> garment in the Lydian fashion, as I have mentioned elsewhere.

Such are the ways the triumphs of the joyful and peace-loving Bacchus are to be represented, with the circumstances that may suitably belong to him. But in the triumphs of war and victories, he must lead conquered enemies in triumph, prisoners with their spoils and weapons, and in short, the painter must proceed entirely differently. In all places, however, he must be shown beautiful, slender, and with well-formed limbs, not as many do—especially the <term>Barbarians</term> <note>A common Renaissance term for Northern Europeans (Flemish or German artists), whom the author criticizes for depicting Bacchus as a bloated drunkard rather than a refined classical deity.</note>—making him thick and fat, persuading themselves that he is as drunk as they perhaps are. 

This custom of triumphing after Bacchus's example began to be practiced among many peoples immediately thereafter. Thus, the Carthaginian commanders, having led their armies well, were accustomed to triumph. For this reason, <term>Justin</term> <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a Roman historian.</note> says that <term>Hasdrubal</term>, having been wounded and resigning his command to his brother <term>Hamilcar</term>, had already triumphed four times. Among the Romans, it is well known that this custom of triumphing achieved such high reputation that in this they surpassed all other nations. Because from the beginning <term>Romulus</term>, the founder of Rome, as <term>Dionysius</term> <note>Dionysius of Halicarnassus, a Greek historian who wrote about Roman antiquities.</note> writes, being the first of all to overcome <term>Acron</term>, King of the <term>Caeninenses</term> <note>An ancient people of central Italy who were among the first to be conquered by the Romans.</note>, entered the City, crowned...

### BOOK SIX

...crowned with laurel, pulled by four horses, and consecrated the enemy spoils to **Jupiter Feretrius** <note>The aspect of Jupiter to whom the "spolia opima" (spoils of the enemy commander) were dedicated.</note>. As the custom grew over time, **Livy** and **Plutarch** write that **Furio Camillo** <note>Marcus Furius Camillus, a celebrated Roman general of the 4th century BC, known as the "Second Founder of Rome."</note> triumphed upon a golden chariot pulled by four white horses, and according to **Pliny**, the triumphing general was painted with <term>vermilion</term> <note>original: "minio." In early Rome, the general's face was painted red to resemble the clay statue of Jupiter in the Capitol.</note>; this custom later passed to other triumphators. Speaking of this, **Gellius** <note>Aulus Gellius, a 2nd-century Roman author of the "Attic Nights."</note> writes that the triumphator adorned his head with a golden crown, the prisoners loaded with chains followed the chariot, and preceding the Senate they ascended the **Capitol**, and having sacrificed a white bull in the temple of Jupiter, they returned home.

There was also among the Romans another less solemn way of triumphing, which was properly called an **ovation**, because (as **Plutarch** says in the *Life of Marcellus*) a <term>sheep</term> <note>original: "pecora." The word "ovation" was thought to derive from the Latin "ovis" (sheep), which was the sacrifice offered, rather than the bull used in a full triumph.</note> was sacrificed there. This triumphator over lowly enemies, killer of few, and spiller of little blood, according to **Pliny**, was crowned with **myrtle**; he went on horseback followed by soldiers as far as the Capitol, where the sheep was sacrificed. But the **Lacedaemonians** <note>Spartans.</note>, not to remain silent about this other manner of triumph, as **Plutarch** reports, followed a different custom. Specifically, if they had finished a war through trickery, they sacrificed a bull; but if through arms and true force, a rooster. Now, regarding those who celebrated **ovations**, **Massurio Sabino** (cited by **Gellius**) says that they walked on foot, followed by the soldiers and the entire Senate. **Pliny** writes that the first to enter Rome triumphing in this manner was **Postumio Tuberto**. 

The crowns of the triumphing generals were always of laurel in every age, and those of the **ovation** winners, as I have said, were of myrtle. In triumphs, he who had first scaled the walls or who had first entered the enemy camp while fighting was adorned with a crown called the **Castrense** <note>The "Camp Crown," decorated with the likeness of a palisade or rampart.</note>; he who had first jumped onto the enemy ships brought back a crown called **Naval**; both were made of gold and were given to them by the triumphing Emperor as a sign of the feat they had performed. There was also the **Obsidional Crown** <note>Also called the "Grass Crown" (*Corona Graminea*).</note> which was given to that Captain who had liberated a city or a camp of his people from a siege, and it was made of <term>grass</term> <note>original: "gramigna." This was the highest military honor, made from the grass growing on the very site that had been rescued.</note>. 

The **Civic Crown** belonged to him who had saved a citizen from death in war; it was given to him by the person who had been saved, and it was made of **oak** in sign that he had put his life at risk for him. **Coriolanus** <note>Gaius Marcius Coriolanus, a legendary Roman general of the 5th century BC.</note> received many of these, as one reads in his life, as well as many of the others for his illustrious virtues. This custom of crowning citizens, according to **Valerius** <note>Valerius Maximus, a 1st-century Roman collector of historical anecdotes.</note>, was first introduced by the **Athenians** to further increase and ignite virtue within them. As for the form of the triumphs, I will report as an example for all...

...the others that were celebrated by the Romans, such as that of **Aemilius Paullus** <note>Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus (c. 229–160 BC), the Roman general who ended the Third Macedonian War.</note> as **Plutarch** describes it in his *Life*. The Roman people were all dressed in white clothes and had gathered in the equestrian theaters—called by him <term>scaffolds</term> <note>original: "archi," likely a transcription or translation variation of "palchi," referring to the wooden grandstands erected for spectators.</note>—and in certain other places made of wood for this purpose around the forum, and in many other places in Rome through which **Aemilius** was to pass to see the triumph. All the temples of Rome were full of garlands and sweet scents, and a great multitude of certain ministers who carried rods in their hands cleared the people from the streets, so that the way remained free and clear for the triumph, which was celebrated with such a crowd that a single day was hardly enough for the passing of the military standards, the painted panels, and the marble statues that were carried upon two hundred and fifty carts.

On the second day, the most beautiful and ornate arms of the **Macedonians** were likewise carried on carts; these were of splendid and polished iron and arranged in such a way that the victory seemed to have been won more by fortune than by anything else. There were helmets, shields, breastplates, greaves, and certain other small, round shields such as the **Cretans** used to use, as well as other arms of the **Thracians**, quivers, horse bridles, naked swords, and certain weapons called <term>sarissas</term> <note>original: "sarisse." These were the exceptionally long pikes, often 13 to 20 feet in length, used by the Macedonian phalanx.</note>, so arranged that those who had captured them still looked upon them with fear. After the arms followed three thousand men who carried silver coins in three hundred and fifty vessels, each of which weighed three <term>talents</term> <note>A heavy unit of weight; three talents would be approximately 75–80 kilograms (165–176 lbs).</note> and was carried by four men. Others carried silver vases, cups, bowls, and highly ornate chalices of great weight.

On the third day, at the break of dawn, the trumpeters first appeared, sounding not a sweet or pleasant sound, but a harsh and military one. After them were led one hundred and twenty oxen with gilded horns adorned with boughs and certain garlands, led by young men dressed as if they were about to perform a sacrifice; and other boys carried certain gold and silver <term>patens</term> <note>Shallow plates used in religious or ceremonial contexts.</note> used in sacrifices. Behind these came those who carried the gold coins in three-talent vessels, just like the silver ones we mentioned. These vessels numbered eighty-three, followed by those who carried a golden bowl made by **Aemilius** weighing ten talents, all embroidered with precious stones. And besides these came those who carried the gold vessels of **Perseus**, **Antigonus**, **Seleucus**, and **Therida** <note>Historical Hellenistic rulers whose treasures had been amassed by the Macedonian crown.</note>. Then proceeded the chariot of **Perseus** <note>Perseus of Macedon, the last king of the Antigonid dynasty, defeated by Paullus at the Battle of Pydna.</note> and his arms, and above them his crown; and after a short space, the children of **Perseus** were led, accompanied by a multitude...

...titude of their tutors and masters, who, weeping, stretched out their hands toward the Roman citizens, teaching the children to do the same. These children were three—two boys and one girl—who, because of their tender age, could not understand their misfortune, yet they moved the whole populace to such mercy that many were seen shedding tears. And as they passed by, everything was filled with sorrow and joy alike. **Perseus** followed after these, dressed in black and walking on foot, wearing slippers <note>original: "pianelle." Plutarch specifies these were "crepides," a type of Greek footwear, signifying his humble state as a captive.</note> according to the custom of his homeland; and because of the magnitude of his misfortunes, he walked in fear of everything, his mind greatly troubled. Behind him came the mournful multitude of his servants and friends, looking upon him with great compassion and with loud weeping, such that many Romans were forced by pity to shed tears. Next followed the gold crowns which the cities of **Greece** had given to **Aemilius** as a reward for his virtue, numbering four hundred. 

And after these followed **Aemilius** in a most ornate chariot—a man truly such that, beyond the pomp and glory of that **Macedonian** triumph, the majesty of his presence would have given the highest pleasure to anyone who saw him. He went dressed in purple, embroidered and woven with gold, and carried a laurel palm in his hand; and likewise, his men-at-arms carried laurel branches in their hands. According to the order of the legions, squads, and companies, they walked near **Aemilius’s** chariot, all singing his praises in verse in their own language. 

From the form of this triumph (so as not to be too long-winded here), one can generally derive the method for composing any other triumph, noting only the particular customs of the defeated and the principal things belonging to them, which above all must be represented in the triumph. As in the triumph of the ancient **Tarquin** <note>Lucius Tarquinius Priscus, the fifth King of Rome, credited with celebrating the first triumph in the Roman fashion.</note>, where the spoils acquired from enemies were seen; and in those of **Pompey**, the spoils of the pirates, of **Mithridates**, **Aristobulus**, and **Tigranes** <note>Pompey the Great's triumphs celebrated his victories over Mediterranean pirates, Mithridates VI of Pontus, Aristobulus II of Judea, and Tigranes the Great of Armenia.</note>, with greater splendor and pomp than had ever been celebrated in other triumphs before. For as **Pliny** relates, there were silver statues of **Pharnaces**, King of **Pontus**, and of **Mithridates** his father; gold and silver carts; a gold vase with two very large gems; a gold Moon weighing 30 pounds; three gold beds with precious stones; three gold standards; thirty-three gold crowns likewise set with gems; a square mountain of gold with deer, lions, and fruit of every kind; and tables and game-boards made of precious stones. There were also, according to **Plutarch** in his *Life*, all the provinces, cities, and castles represented in figure <note>Models or paintings representing the captured territories.</note>, which he had...

From this, one can understand how diverse triumphs are from one another, for it is also read that the triumphs of **Caesar**—of which he celebrated four in a single month—were all different from each other, according to how the nations he overcame were diverse and varied; and he always appeared crowned with laurel with a branch of the same in his right hand. Thus, in reading, one will find accounts of the triumphs of **Octavius** <note>The Emperor Augustus.</note> and of all the others. And whoever wishes to know more accurately about these triumphs should look at the triumphal arches and the other antiquities of **Rome**, where they will see the proud form of the open chariots, and likewise on the reverses of ancient medals and the instruments upon which arms and trophies were carried.

This has been observed by **Giulio Romano** the great designer, **Rosso** <note>Rosso Fiorentino.</note>, **Perino del Vaga**, **Il Bologna** <note>Francesco Primaticcio, known as "Il Bologna."</note>, **Luca Cambiaso** <note>Original: "Cangiaio."</note>, and **Carlo Urbino**—all worthy inventors of such martial triumphs. Of these, **Urbino** has designed more than a hundred pieces in a continuous sequence, where one sees all the riches that a painter needs in this regard, including garments, vases, weapons, instruments, and everything else used in triumphing by the ancients, as well as the prisoners and slaves who are represented in such triumphs. I will not fail to mention those, besides the others he painted, by **Lazzaro Calvi** in **Genoa**, upon the facade of **Antonio Doria’s** palace, which are among the best he ever represented.

Having said enough so far regarding the martial triumphs of the **Romans** and other nations as a general rule—by which all others may be composed of whatever sort one wishes—it must be known that if one wishes to show a triumph of any **God** named by antiquity (as will be said in the chapter on animals), one must consider all the things that fall under their domain and accommodate them to the triumph. For example: dressing and adorning the victor in garments, colors, and forms suitable to him—either melancholy or joyful according to his nature—and giving him the crown and the leaves of his own tree, and doing the same for the bystanders and the animals that pull the chariot. One should represent the nature of the people subjected to him for some particular effect, such as the great prisoners before the chariot, who decrease <note>This likely refers to artistic perspective or a hierarchy of importance as the procession recedes.</note> as they go forward, and likewise his seasons, ministers, and instruments—both those for offense and those for use and delight. Following this, one should compose the chariot from the god's own metal or wood, adorn it with his specific stones, and similarly express in the god and the ministers appropriate gestures and acts.

appropriated. With this standard, one can form triumphs not only of the gods of the Gentiles <note>The ancient pagans.</note>, but also of death, life, virtues, vices, and whatever else one desires—even of our own religion. This was done by **Titian** in his *Triumph of Faith*, where he depicted the patriarchs, prophets, and the Sibyls of the Old Testament; in the center, Christ is seated, carried on high by the four Doctors of the Church <note>The influential early Christian theologians: Augustine, Ambrose, Jerome, and Gregory the Great.</note> with a banner in his hand, drawn by the animals of the Evangelists <note>The Tetramorph: the man (Matthew), the lion (Mark), the ox (Luke), and the eagle (John).</note>, and before Him all the other saints of the New Testament.

In the same way, one can create triumphs for famous modern men, as the painter **Albrecht Dürer** did for the **Emperor Maximilian**, grandfather of **Charles V**, where he shows him triumphing through the virtues he possessed and the qualities belonging to a true Emperor. There, Reason guides the chariot with many horses in pairs, held by the virtues assigned to him. Upon the chariot are various women holding the Emperor’s crowns, inscribed with their names; since there is a design of this ten sheets wide, carved in wood by his own hand <note>Dürer’s "Great Triumphal Car," a massive woodcut commission.</note>, I will not dwell on describing it here. Indeed, I myself possessed it, along with all the other prints carved in wood, iron, and copper by the High and Low Germans <note>Referring to artists from Germany and the Netherlands.</note>, as well as those of the Italians—especially the principal ones, which amounted to about four thousand pieces.

But let us come to the "Gate" of **Albrecht Dürer**—that is, the *Triumphal Arch* <note>The "Ehrenpforte," one of the largest prints ever produced, made from 192 woodblocks.</note> in honor of the said Emperor—where he sits upon a throne with all his members destined for the understanding of the animals placed there. This is followed by all his provinces and dominions, and the principal wars he fought, along with all his virtues. And because this print consists of forty imperial sheets, so that every detail is expressed with the utmost minuteness—though it is rarely found complete—I will not expand upon it further.

**Piero di Cosimo**, another Florentine painter, created the *Triumph of Death* drawn by two buffaloes, with various tombs opening upon the chariot; Death stands with a black banner in hand, followed by various gaunt horses with men upon them resembling death itself. **Vasari** discusses this in his *Life* <note>Giorgio Vasari’s "Lives of the Artists."</note>, along with the triumph of **Charles V** by **Francesco Valesio**, that of the Grand Duke **Cosimo**, and many others.

## *Composition of Trophies. Chapter XLIII.*

Trophies—also called <term>spoils</term> <note>From the Italian "spoglie," referring to the arms and equipment taken from a defeated enemy.</note>—are nothing other than victorious prizes brought back from enemies. They are understood to be anything of value and importance, whether by craftsmanship, worth, beauty, or quality that can be imagined. Therefore, in triumphs, according to

## BOOK 2

...their arrangements were distributed and accompanied by the ancients, whose example we must still follow in composing them. We must first consider their quality, given that they are nothing other than signs and express records of things obtained; consequently, they are also demonstrations of these things according to their nature. 

Hence we see that the ancients carried them in triumphs as a sign of the manner and quality of the victory achieved, and afterward offered them to the gods for the favors obtained from them. And we see also that they never offered war trophies to **Diana** or **Venus**, but to **Mars**, **Bellona** <note>The Roman goddess of war.</note>, and to **Jupiter Feretrius** <note>Jupiter Feretrius was the specific aspect of the king of the gods to whom the most prestigious spoils of war—those taken by a general from an enemy commander—were dedicated.</note>, just as **Romulus** offered the <term>greaves</term> <note>Armor designed to protect the shins.</note>, helmets, shields, and swords he gloriously acquired in battle. 

But to **Diana**, as a sign of hunting or of chastity, were presented deer horns, bows, and quivers; to **Venus**, mirrors, vases, and similar items which need not be recounted one by one here, it being sufficient only to note that according to the favors requested in sacrifices to the gods, the spoils appropriate to them were rightfully theirs. 

And since the favors were diverse, the gods were also diverse, whom the superstitious ancients assigned each to some art, according as it seemed to have a particular correspondence with them. And thus, in those arts in which each god was esteemed to have power and dominion, one turned to them to ask for favors; and once obtained, they would hang up as trophies those things which had been acquired or won using the instruments of that god’s art. 

So it follows that for a trophy of a victory obtained in playing a lute, one would not place a sword, but rather another similar instrument, because of the correspondence they both have together in the art through which the requested favor is understood. 

Hence, to **Mars** were dedicated the arms conquered by his favorites along with other arms, hanging them in the temple; and the arms acquired for vengeance were sacred to **Jupiter the Avenger**. Therefore, it is understood that just as the gods, the arts, and the instruments are diverse, consequently the trophies must also be diverse:
*   For **Music**: cymbals, trumpets, drums, lyres, and the like, because through these music and the grace of the **Muses** are spread.
*   For **War**: arms, shields, lances, and swords, without which one could not wage war.
*   For **Astrology**: spheres and quadrants <note>Instruments used for measuring the altitudes of celestial bodies.</note>.
*   For **Geometry**: squares, triangles, pentagons, set squares, compasses, and circles.
*   For **Smithing**: hammers, anvils, fires, and the like, given to the forge of **Vulcan**.
*   For the **Hunt**: nets, snares, arrows, bows, quivers, and other gear attributed to **Diana**.
*   And for **Juno**, Goddess of wealth: vases, gems, gold, and precious things.
*   And to **Pomona** <note>The Roman goddess of fruit trees, gardens, and orchards.</note>: all sorts of fruits.

...were suitable; and thus, by reasoning through the other arts, trophies are formed from their respective instruments. Besides this, they must be used with reason in those places where they are appropriate. In this, many err, for in religious scenes <note>original: "historie religiose"</note> they insert trophies of tankards, pots, spits, shields, and similar things repugnant to the quality of the place. Therefore, in such settings, only those instruments used in religion are suitable, such as chalices, basins, and the like.

Among war ornaments and in the crafting of arms—on helmets, shields, swords, and such—one should see nothing but trophies of bellicose instruments; neither do snakes, lions, harpies, or even (as some do) angel heads and musical instruments belong there. And this logic must be observed everywhere, for it is the true and secure way of composing trophies and arranging them where they belong. 

But regarding their composition together, it is necessary to note that not all can be joined everywhere; for religious instruments cannot be paired with those of war in any way, nor the latter in religious histories. That is to say, for the decoration of <term>chasubles</term> <note>The outermost liturgical vestment worn by clergy for the celebration of the Eucharist.</note>, <term>miters</term> <note>The traditional, pointed headgear of bishops.</note>, altar embroideries, and chapels, one cannot use military instruments; nor for war ornaments can one use religious instruments.

For the rest, musical instruments are paired with religious ones more than all others; but one should not use those of fruits, leaves, and flowers there, as these are <term>Satiric</term> <note>Referring to Satyrs; these were considered "rustic" or "pagan" decorations associated with nature and wild revelry.</note> and cheerful trophies. Hunting instruments are paired with military ones; geometric instruments with those of painters, sculptors, smiths, architects, cosmographers, and the like.

But as for the method of composing them and raising them aloft for panels, friezes, or spaces, it must be done so that—especially in the case of arms—a spear, for example, or a trunk always has the strength to support all the trophies, passing straight through the middle, planted in the ground, or however it best fits the design. 

And to give a beautiful form to the trophy, shaping it in the guise of a man, place at the top of the spear the <term>sallet</term> <note>original: "celata," a light war helmet.</note> with feathers above, and below it the breastplate with the tunic <note>original: "camiscia"</note> reaching down to the knees; across the shoulders place the mantle; and at the military chest, a medal, mask, or knot tied over one shoulder. To the right and left, in place of arms, let the shields and bucklers be attached. Between these, on one side of the head or helmet, let the <term>quiver</term> <note>original: "turcasso," a case for holding arrows.</note> rise up with the arrows inside, and on the other side a long weapon, such as a half-halberd. 

Down at the base of the trophy, one should place the <term>greaves</term> <note>Armor for the shins.</note>, swords, and similar war ornaments. And so that these trophies may be distributed across various trunks, one shall ensure that their parts suit each other in the aforementioned manner. Now, to observe these orderly and beautiful forms of

trophies, it will be necessary to always arrange the principal ones and place them in view as large items, of greater majesty and beauty; and to give them the weight of the other smaller ones, always conforming to the works of the ancients seen throughout Rome, and especially to those called the <term>Trophies of Marius</term> <note>original: "i trofei di Mario"; these are famous marble sculptural reliefs on the Capitoline Hill in Rome, historically attributed to the general Gaius Marius, though now believed to date to the era of Domitian.</note>. Since the ancients have captured all the beauty that could be imagined in this art, just as they have in all others. And if any of the moderns have perfectly understood this after the ancients, they were undoubtedly <term>Polidoro</term> <note>Polidoro da Caravaggio (c. 1499–1543), an artist renowned for his façade paintings in Rome.</note>, <term>Maturino</term> <note>Maturino da Firenze (d. 1528), Polidoro's close collaborator.</note>, and <term>Soncino</term> <note>Girolamo da Treviso (c. 1498–1544), an Italian painter and architect.</note>; it is truly a marvel to see with what skill they have arranged their trophies. 

If one wishes, therefore, as an example, to represent Rome, or Victory upon trophies, she shall be seated upon breastplates, shields, helmets, and the like; then she will be adorned around and enriched with other trophies. And this applies not only to trophies of war, but generally to all others; for in all of them, beauty is equally sought in its own degree, which cannot exist where things are not composed according to the instructions given. Therefore, one must proceed with reason and care, for everything will then result with the greatest ease, tempering the toil of patience with the delight of working prudently. 

Following these, old and modern painters have been accustomed to composing bunches of various fruits, flowers, and leaves, and placing them in ornaments in stead of trophies; it seems to them that these are, in a certain way, trophies of <term>Ceres</term> <note>Goddess of grain.</note>, <term>Flora</term> <note>Goddess of flowers.</note>, <term>Bacchus</term> <note>God of wine.</note>, and <term>Pomona</term> <note>Goddess of fruit trees.</note>. This practice is now so frequent that it is used without distinction, not only for the ornaments of masks, histories, porticoes, and loggias, but even in temples around sacred figures, in the ornaments of chapels (as I said before), and even on pilasters, having children and angels swirl around them, and applying the faces of Cherubim to the angels and their extremities. 

But if the ancients used this sort of vain and <term>lascivious</term> <note>original: "lascivi"; in this context, it refers to playful, decorative, or non-serious motifs that lack religious gravity.</note> trophy, they used it around Satyrs, courtesans, and masks of playful Fauns, and not in the histories and temples of <term>Jupiter</term> <note>original: "Gioue"; king of the gods.</note>, <term>Pallas</term> <note>Pallas Athena, goddess of wisdom.</note>, and <term>Vesta</term> <note>Goddess of the hearth.</note>. Yet in our times, as I was just saying, this use has progressed so far that there is no place that is not smeared with such trophies, much to the shame of the corrupt judgment of our moderns, and to the greater glory of the ancients, who proceeded with as much reason and discernment in every detail as they did in more important matters. From this arose the harmony of design, which, so to speak, delighted more than nature itself; because they arranged both this and that with prudence, and not with confusion.

## *The Composition of Buildings in General. Chapter XLIV.*

**H**aving treated the compositions of the bodies of <term>histories</term> <note>original: "historie"; in Renaissance art theory, a "history" is a narrative painting depicting a significant biblical, mythological, or historical event.</note> in general and in particular, and likewise the things belonging to them, it is a necessary thing that the buildings required for these histories be discussed in any case. For no painting can be well ordered without a knowledge of the building—both regarding the place where the work is to be made, and the building required by the history being depicted, which serves as its foundation and support. 

The composition of buildings, then, is of many kinds, being divided according to various peoples and different nations; from this arose the diversity of the <term>orders of architecture</term> <note>The classical styles of architecture—Tuscan, Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian—each with distinct rules for proportion and decoration.</note>. Thus, the way of building in a rustic and strong manner is called **Tuscan**; and with less rusticity, but no greater ornament, **Doric**; building in a medium way, neither very ornate nor very rustic, is **Ionic**; and building with delights, beauty, and ornament is called **Corinthian**—possessing a lightness, however, so that it should not have to support great weights, such as <term>galleries</term> <note>original: "galiere"; likely referring to galleries, upper loggias, or lighter architectural extensions.</note> and the highest parts of buildings. 

From these orders are composed all the buildings that can be imagined. But it is then fitting to make a choice judiciously, accommodating now one and now another, according to what the state and the condition of the people requires. For we can well recognize that for peasants and similar coarse folk, buildings of neither the ornament nor the Corinthian proportion would be appropriate; nor even for poor and humble people. For them, only plain walls, sturdy pillars, and low windows are suitable. And so, the style increases step by step up to the royal palace of the prince, with all the aforementioned ornaments of the orders, and for sacred temples, yet differently according to their specific qualities. The painter must always have these considerations before his eyes, so that he knows how to judiciously distribute buildings to people according to such orders. But I will not stay here to declare particularly the compositions of each

order, it being sufficient here only to advise how they must be composed among themselves according to the places and statuses of the people. This certainly could not be done without knowledge of the history <note>In this context, "history" refers to the narrative or story being depicted in a painting.</note> that follows; for by it one can know where buildings are required, so as not to err by making a very beautiful building, for example, in the place where **Angelica** entered with the wounded **Medoro**, as it was a small grotto or hut <note>A reference to Ariosto’s *Orlando Furioso*; the author argues that the setting should remain a humble rustic hut as described in the poem, rather than a grand palace.</note>. And so, in the time of the Greeks, one should not imagine the <term>Composite order</term> <note>The most ornate of the classical orders, combining Ionic and Corinthian elements; it was developed by the Romans, so using it in a Greek setting is an anachronism.</note>, as it had not yet been introduced; nor should one represent palaces and temples in the Greek or Roman style in histories read as occurring before the Flood; nor, when describing the war of Caesar and Pompey in Thessaly, imagine the Tower of Babel in the distance; nor in Tartary, where they live upon wagons, introduce in any of their wars pyramids, cities, or castles in the Italian style; nor yet, when painting the capture and ruins of Rome, make houses in the German fashion and similar improprieties, as is found in the architecture of **Albrecht Dürer** <note>Dürer was a master of the Northern Renaissance, but Italian theorists often criticized his "Gothic" architectural style as being inappropriate for classical Roman subjects.</note>, from which **Lambert Lombard** <note>A Flemish Renaissance painter known for introducing Italian classical influences to the North.</note> has partly moved away. 

Instead, in all places, buildings must always be made appropriate to their use and manner. Nor should any of the others be mixed in, but rather they should be represented as composed of their particular members, so that to those who understand their differences, they will be appropriate. Likewise, they will prove appropriate to the rank and status of the people to whom the building is to be attributed, not neglecting the principles of the ancient stage-sets. These being of three kinds, they are prepared differently according to the rank of the characters who are to be represented by the actors: 

**The Comic** where the actions of private individuals like merchants and citizens are represented, is prepared with houses that are likewise private. 

**The Tragic** where the deeds of great men are represented, requires palaces and buildings for kings and great princes. 

In the third scene, called **Satyric**, where satires were represented, there were seen (as **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman architect whose ten-volume work *De architectura* became the foundation for Renaissance architectural theory.</note> says when speaking of them) trees, rocks, hills, mountains, plants, flowers, fountains, huts, and cottages, suitable to the rusticity of the people introduced there. 

From this one can understand with how much reason and consideration the ancients proceeded in their works. If these were diligently observed by the painters of our own time, one would not see in their paintings of the temples where Christ was born broken columns and bases, as if some Roman or Greek palace had been there, it being a manger and a place for beasts; nor, as I have said elsewhere, where Christ holds the Last Supper with the Apostles, a building decorated with columns and other ornaments.

...as if it were a royal palace, even though it was a humble house, just as the house was where the Virgin Mary was announced to by the Angel <note>The Annunciation</note>. Yet, many painters imagine it adorned with many ornaments and columns in the manner of a temple. The same is done for the house where the Holy Spirit descended upon the Virgin and the disciples in tongues of fire <note>The Pentecost</note>. In short, one sees infinite buildings in the paintings of various artists that do not at all suit the **history** <term>history</term> <note>In Renaissance art theory, "history" (historia) refers to the narrative or subject matter of the work.</note> they represent, or believe they represent. 

This narrative truth, however, must of necessity be observed by the painter, leaving aside ornaments and royal palaces, even though they may seem to greatly embellish the painting. I judge that this occurs because many painters depict them so often only to clutter the minds of the viewers, perhaps not knowing how to demonstrate the emotional effect of the story through the figures with true art. And so, out of pride, they gild even humble things, and little by little they distance themselves from good precepts. 

They do this without even noticing that they are erring, as many do, by making buildings such that the man depicted there could not comfortably enter through the doors, as if they were natural; or climb the stairs and move freely through the openings and spaces appropriate to them. Instead, following certain notions of theirs in imitation of the painters of the old style—such as **Cimabue**, **Giotto**, and those of the time of **Petrarch**; **Laodicia**, and **Andrino di Edesia**, and after them until the time of **Michelino** <note>Michelino da Besozzo, a prominent International Gothic painter in Milan.</note>—they still make certain buildings so small that the figure could not fit inside in any way. 

They even depict **Christ** tied to columns so thin that he, in the manner of **Samson**, could easily carry them away and ruin the portico. This is a disorder into which **Israel van Meckenem** <note>Original: "Israel Metro." A German printmaker often criticized by Italians for his Gothic proportions.</note> fell along with many others. Such other follies are better left unmentioned, being entirely devoid of the art of creating a proper view. 

The discoverers of this proper art <note>The art of perspective and architectural proportion.</note> were **Giovanni da Valle**, **Constantino Vaprio**, **Foppa** <note>Vincenzo Foppa, a leading figure in the Early Renaissance of Lombardy.</note>, **Civerchio**, **Ambrogio** and **Filippo Bevilacqua**, and **Carlo**, all Milanese; **Faccio Bembo** from Valdarno, and **Cristoforo Moreto** of Cremona, **Pietro Francesco Pavese**, and **Albertino da Lodi**. These men, besides their various other works, painted those armed barons around the great court of Milan in the times of **Francesco Sforza**, the first Duke of that city.

But leaving these arguments aside, it remains to be noted that just as a building can be made without regard for a figure, so no figure can be made without a building <note>Or a defined space/setting.</note>. This occurs in two ways: the first is that when the circumstances serve the figure in the narrative, the figure can only be placed in two ways, consistent with the natural building—that is, that it suits the place by its nature, and that it accompanies...

->BOOK SIX<-

...match the location and the architectural order. And this is done in two ways: one is when it is to be represented as forced <note>This refers to *quadratura*, or illusionistic painting that appears to be a physical extension of the room's real architecture.</note>, as if it were truly there where it is feigned; it should be harmonized to enter into the building and its nature which surrounds the **history** <term>history</term> <note>In Renaissance art theory, *historia* (history) refers to the narrative or subject matter of the work.</note>. And with this order, nothing is represented except what can exist in that place by reason and order approved by the natural site; and it is not permitted to show stories whose ground plane would have to be suspended high in the air. For they cannot be harmonized up there, nor down below, since by forcing and following the natural order, one can only show what could naturally be there. In this, many perspective painters of the modern time err, who wish to assert that one can do as they do, to their own shame and the ridicule of the world.

The second way is when some story is feigned as if transported, either from high or low, and here the horizons must be raised to the level of the eye of the first figure, or in the middle of the story: because everywhere it represents the man who sees the painting, whether it be small or large, or from high or low (which matters not, as I said in the rules of perspective). Therefore, in these one has full freedom, both to show ground planes and to do as one pleases, high and low: which cannot be done in the others, which are feigned as forced. For in every way they must match the natural building to which they are attached in order to enter inside. And these are not called paintings as paintings, but paintings that demonstrate the truth of the building as perceived by the distance of the eye, and through them one achieves as much perfection as art can promise. This is the general order of composing buildings in paintings, which all talented painters have followed, and especially those who understood the art of optics and architecture. For without these nothing can be done, just as nothing can be done without **drawing** <term>drawing</term> <note>The Italian *disegno* implies both the physical act of drawing and the intellectual concept of design or composition.</note>, proportion, and the manner of expressing with a stylus upon paper. Thus, talented architects, both ancient and modern, understood the order, proportion, and measure that are subject to the painter: and therefore they have the same power to match one member with another, with due proportion and beauty.

[treat]ments of the triumphal arches of Rome depart significantly from standard architecture; as evidenced among others by the **Arch of Titus**, of which only the uppermost cornice, the frieze, and the architrave remain. Here, the cornice is too tall in proportion to the architrave, and it contains too many members—especially the consoles <term>mensole</term> <note>Decorative brackets that support a weight, such as a cornice.</note> and dentils <term>dentelli</term> <note>Small, rectangular blocks used in a row, resembling teeth.</note>, which Vitruvius forbids within a single cornice. Nonetheless, because it is so well-crafted, especially the upper molding <term>cimasa</term>, it is considered a fine example among ancient works. Furthermore, the impost <term>imposta</term> <note>The structural block from which an arch begins to curve upward.</note> of the arch is very different from various other ancient examples; they usually featured one carved member and the next one plain, whereas this arch has them all carved, one under the other. This makes it appear so rich that some consider it excessive, despite the fact that this practice of carving and working all the members was used by other ancients, as seen in various bases, cornices, and other parts.

Near **San Giorgio in Velabro**, one finds a building of the **Composite order** <note>A mixed style of architecture combining elements of the Ionic and Corinthian orders.</note> made in the time of **Septimius Severus**, in which the architect strayed far from the others. This is especially true in the upper cornice where, besides the richness of the carvings on every member <gloss>member</gloss>, he made no division of a ruler or listel <term>listello</term> <note>A small, flat, plain molding used to separate other elements.</note> between the dentil and the egg-and-dart <term>uouolo</term> <note>A rounded molding, often carved with egg-shaped ornaments.</note>; and under that dentil, he placed two moldings, that is, cymatia matching the same carving—a thing seen observed by no one else.

In the triumphal **Arch of Septimius Severus**, one sees a plinth <term>zoccolo</term> under the pedestal <term>dado</term> of the base, which is not seen used by others, and the frieze is worked smaller than the architrave; even though **Vitruvius** says it ought to be a fourth part larger. Furthermore, compared to other members, the cornice is high and its projection is greater than its height—all things contrary to what Vitruvius prescribes. The dripstones <term>gocciolatori</term> <note>The projecting part of a cornice designed to throw off rainwater.</note> are smaller than the cyma recta <term>gola dritta</term> <note>An S-shaped molding, convex at the bottom and concave at the top.</note>, with other similar diversities even in the capitals, as anyone can see.

In the **Arch of Constantine**, one likewise sees—in place of a dripstone in the impost of the smaller arches—two flat surfaces between a small torus <term>tondino</term> under the upper molding, and an egg-and-dart below. The bases and plinths are very high, and the impost of the larger middle arch is greater and has more members than the upper and principal cornice; the dentils and consoles are placed one above the other, all carved.

In addition, to raise the columns in the **Arch of Ancona**, one sees plinths with moldings on the inside under the pedestals of the bases, and the capitals match those of the **Rotunda** <note>The Pantheon in Rome.</note>; that is, they are much taller than what the author [Vitruvius] writes. One also finds in the **Arch of Polla** two plinths under the bases, and the columns project from the main wall. Above, they are fluted, with bases in the **Doric** form, yet the delicate carvings show it to be **Corinthian**, and the capital...

**Bramante** <note>Donato Bramante, the primary architect of High Renaissance Rome.</note> drew many of these variations with his described proportions, as did **Petrucci** <note>Likely referring to Baldassarre Peruzzi, a contemporary of Bramante known for his exquisite architectural drawings.</note> as well. Of the latter, many examples can still be seen, such as two ovolos, two cornices, or two moldings <term>cimatij</term> placed together. 

Regarding carvings, the members also look better when they are not worked in a confused or cluttered manner, but rather where one is carved and the next is not, as this is judged to result in a more beautiful <term>vago</term> effect. This should always harmonize with the nature of the specific order, just as Bramante designed so well by measuring ancient works, and Petrucci, as seen in his **Sebastiano** <note>Likely referring to the published works of Sebastiano Serlio, which were heavily based on Peruzzi’s drawings.</note>; everything depends on this.

There, basins were used to collect the blood from which the sacred drink was made for the God, or even as a symbol of the temple’s title.

...cornucopias, and various knots, of which **Albrecht Dürer** <note>Albrecht Dürer (1471–1528), the celebrated German Renaissance artist. His "Gate of Honor" refers to the *Ehrenpforte*, a massive triumphal arch commissioned by Emperor Maximilian I, composed of 192 woodcut blocks.</note> made many in the **Gate of Honor**, where one sees griffins, lions, horses, storks, and the like, which create a very beautiful sight. Now, as for composing one order with another, one must observe the aforementioned logic of harmony; for a **Composite order** would not look right next to a **Doric** or **Tuscan** one, and also poorly next to the **Ionic**, nor the **Corinthian** next to the **Tuscan** or **Doric**. This is true even though among the ancients one sees the opposite to have been observed, as is seen in the **Portico of Pompey** <note>The *Porticus Pompeiana* in Rome, once part of the Theater of Pompey complex.</note>, which is still called the **House of Marius**, where the **Corinthian columns** with pilasters next to them are supported above the openings of the **Doric order** below; a thing that I do not know how it can be tolerated, neither for beauty nor for strength, even though the architect provided a remedy for this, as is seen. But in the **Colosseum** <note>The Flavian Amphitheater in Rome, famous for its vertical stacking of the Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian orders.</note> one finds the ultimate example of how one must regularly raise one order above another.

Therefore, I shall say no more on this, although it was in use among the ancients to make an entire building or temple in a single order, according to the purpose of the things that were to be done inside with respect to the God of that temple, as I have said many times above. And thus this should suffice regarding the composition of the orders against one another; only advising everyone that in composing such orders and their members together, the whole matter lies in knowing their nature and proceeding according to it, always following the beauty of the object, avoiding extremes, and not coupling things together that are not "friends" to one another.

And because (as I said from the beginning) this is the work of none other than painters and skilled draftsmen <term>designatori</term> <note>From *disegno*, which in the Renaissance meant both the physical act of drawing and the intellectual concept of design.</note>, I judge that others, even if they are engineers profound in mathematics, cannot achieve this faculty. For, not knowing how to demonstrate through drawing, they cannot conceive in their mind the variety and beauty of things that can be imagined; being deprived of that faculty of drawing which **Vitruvius** <note>Vitruvius (c. 80–15 BC), the Roman author of *De architectura*, the foundational text for Renaissance architects.</note> so highly praises at the beginning of *Architecture*, stating that it must be perfectly known. Hence, he does not speak of it as he does of the other sciences necessary to the architect—where he says one must not be ignorant of them, or that one must know of them and hear of them and similar ways of speaking—but he expressly commands that in this art of drawing, first of all, one must be knowledgeable and instructed. Therefore, painters will not fail, when introducing buildings into their narrative paintings <term>historie</term> <note>Large-scale narrative or history paintings, considered the highest form of art in the Renaissance.</note>, to adorn and compose them with the proper logic, just as the greatest draftsmen, skilled in the two arts <note>Likely referring to Sculpture and Architecture, which were considered subordinate to the art of *disegno* (Drawing/Design).</note> subordinate to drawing, have done.

## Composition of Terminal Figures. Chapter XLVI.

**S**ince terminal figures <term>termini</term> <note>original: "termini"; these are statues where the upper body or head emerges from a pillar-like pedestal.</note> are so closely associated with buildings, performing the role of columns in supporting weights or standing as architraves <term>architrave</term> <note>The horizontal beam that rests upon the capitals of columns.</note>, and also being placed in other arrangements that offer great ornament to works—as evidenced, beyond the many painted facades in Italy by various artists, by that of the Ducal Palace in Ferrara <note>Likely referring to the artistic commissions of the Este family; Dosso Dossi (c. 1489–1542) was their primary court painter.</note> painted by **Dosso** and his brother with most beautiful figures, where with wonderful art one sees that the terminal figures support the architrave—I wish to make some mention of them here, discussing the manner of composing them suitably for buildings. 

In ancient times, certain peoples understood "terms" to mean only those figures who were worshipped under the name of the **God Terminus** <note>The Roman deity who presided over boundary markers; his statues were traditionally immovable stones or pillars.</note>, so that they might look after the boundaries and the borders of the fields. These were formed in the style of those found in the garden of **Cardinal Cesis** <note>Cardinal Paolo Emilio Cesi (1481–1537); his Roman garden was a famous "open-air museum" of classical antiquities.</note> in Rome, of which there are many ancient examples. They have only a head at the top and a long, square base, with the male member in its place. The ancients varied these heads, making them sometimes like a **Faun** <note>A mythological half-human, half-goat creature.</note>, sometimes like a **Hermaphrodite**, sometimes like **Jupiter Ammon** <note>A version of the king of the gods depicted with the curling horns of a ram.</note>, or sometimes like **Demosthenes** or another ancient philosopher with somewhat long beards. 

The Greeks worshipped **Mercury** <note>The messenger god, known as Hermes in Greek.</note> in this form under the name **Cyllenius** <note>An epithet for Mercury/Hermes referring to his birth on Mount Cyllene.</note>; for they called those statues "Cilli" where there was no member except the head; and these were placed on the roads and honored with stones. This type of terminal figure, older than the others, is frequently used by modern painters for various ornaments and supports, such as for porticos, windows, loggias, and the like, both in profile and facing forward. They are often adorned with ornaments such as baskets of leaves and festoons <note>Carved garlands of fruit or flowers.</note>, and with bases featuring masks, drapery, and various animal feet. 

Modern artists also add ornaments like baskets to the heads, with the neck below and a portion of the chest, so that part of the breasts appear with various decorations of bands, flowers, and cloth. These heads are mostly female for greater grace; of this kind, **Antonio Vegiu** <note>Antonio da Viggiù, a 16th-century sculptor active in Lombardy.</note> sculpted two large ones under the organ of **Santa Maria presso San Celso** in Milan <note>A significant Renaissance church known for its rich sculptural program.</note>, with beautiful heads and very graceful drapery. Thus, they become dissimilar not only to the ancient examples because of their ornaments, but also to certain others that are nonetheless called terminal figures, which are used along porticos, halls, and similar places. These are full-bodied figures which, though varied, serve as columns, in imitation of those ancient matrons called **Caryatids** <note>Female figures used as architectural supports instead of columns, named after the women of Caryae.</note>,

Within it, they placed the likenesses of the prisoners in their barbarian style of dress, supporting the roof. And from this, they later began to place **Persian statues** to support arches with their ornaments; from which there was the opportunity to increase the variety of styles in these marvelous works, which were also called terms <term>termini</term> <note>Statues where the upper body emerges from a square pillar.</note>, especially by the moderns, as were others concerning the openings and proportions of windows, porticos, and the spaces between columns <term>intercolumniation</term>. 

Now, regarding the method of composing them with reason, according to what the orders bring and require: first, it must be considered that since the orders of composition are those already mentioned and no more, one must always match the pedestal and ornament of that specific order to which the terminal figures are to be applied. And regarding the full-figured terms, taken from the **Caryatids** and the enslaved **Persians**, as I have said: in the **Tuscan order**, they are required to be long, following the proportion of its column, but all thick and well-squared, so that they seem to support weight like a pillar. Therefore, the legs, arms, and the whole body should be formidable <note>original: "terribile"; meaning powerful, robust, or awe-inspiring rather than "scary."</note>, with thick and strong muscles in relief. The arms should not be spread out, but held close, or helping to support the weight around the head. 

And because of the rusticity <note>The "Tuscan" order was considered the most basic, sturdy, and unrefined of the architectural styles.</note> of the order, one can also make the legs in the manner of a single trunk, or even divided, in which the muscles are nonetheless indicated in their proper places, and thus join with the body in a handsome way. Of these sorts of terms—with cloths wrapped around them, with long heads and beards, and with hands tucked inside—one can make them to represent provinces and states subject to Lords, just as **Antonio Ascona** did at the palace of **Leone Aretino** <note>Leone Leoni, the famous sculptor; his house in Milan, the *Casa degli Omenoni*, is famous for its massive stone figures supporting the facade.</note>. However, take care not to use female figures here because of their weakness and delicacy, which is not suitable to this order. In the right hand, or in both, one can place a knotty and thick trunk or similar things that can be appropriately applied, but without ornament. The **Doric order**, which because of its strength...

## Composition of Friezes. Chapter 47.

**I** consider it a most certain truth, recognized by everyone, that he who lacks the true and perfect knowledge of a faculty must struggle much more and endure far greater labor in his works than he who understands it and knows how to proceed with reason. Hence it is that all the studious men of the world, in whatever thing they pursue, are accustomed to undertake such heavy labors in their profession so that they may attain true knowledge of it; from this, they eventually acquire both the taste for and the ease of execution. This is something those who do not direct their studies toward this end and goal can never reach, for it is study that shows us the true path to clarity. Therefore, after the reasons and precepts which have been discussed as clearly and distinctly as possible until now, it is necessary to add in this place that which pertains to the <term>composition of friezes</term> <note>The frieze is the middle part of an entablature, located between the architrave and the cornice, often used for decorative carving.</note>. I am certain this will seem somewhat difficult to some who have observed no law or rule regarding this matter; nevertheless, they should attend to it with patience. By understanding, one always finds it easier to show the truth and the possible through beautiful proportions, rather than the false and impossible through crooked and obscure paths. The former way is entirely clear and safe, leading anyone who sets out upon it to the height of excellence and perfection. Regarding <term>friezes</term>, then—imitating nature and observing the decorum of their composition—I will treat them according to their types, which are as numerous as the manners of <term>narrative scenes</term> <note>Original: "historie." In Renaissance art, this refers to narrative paintings depicting historical, mythological, or biblical events.</note>. For any history or invention whatsoever, and indeed every whim and extravagance, can be displayed within friezes. But first, one must understand what a <term>frieze</term> is, where it derived from, and how it is understood within the orders of <term>Architecture</term>. Now, among certain <term>Phrygian</term> peoples <note>The Phrygians were an ancient people of Anatolia (modern Turkey), famous in antiquity for their intricate embroidery.</note>, a certain kind of band was in use that surrounded carpets, garments, and the like, composed of foliage, flowers, and embroidered knots. From their name—as they were the inventors of these scrolls of foliage, clusters of flowers, and various other whims enclosed within parallel lines—it was called a <term>frieze</term> <note>The Italian "fregio" is etymologically linked here to "Frigi" (Phrygians).</note>; and the

From their work, the gold and silk fringes found around pavilions were also later derived. The <term>Ionic</term> order, which is more delicate, was adorned directly above the columns with candlesticks, vases, and similar items, toward which griffins, lions, and such animals turned—sometimes on all four feet, and sometimes with their hindquarters on the ground, turning their backs to one another. And here the field was adorned with foliage and similar ornaments that descended from the candlesticks, or vases, or floral bosses, whatever they might be; and thus it was adorned with similar whims, always including some animal. In the <term>Corinthian</term> frieze, they expressed above the columns baskets and vases of flowers, and also the beginnings of foliage that gracefully spiraled around; and in the middle, some beautiful display of figures was made in keeping with the order, avoiding offensive and deformed animals. Therefore, one always saw there some maiden or nymph representing Europa atop a Bull, with some cupids tumbling about. Among the foliage and the scrolls of the leaves and rosettes, they placed either graceful youths or pleasant animals, such as rams and the like. 

In the frieze lately composed <note>Referring to the Composite order, the "latest" addition to the classical system</note> without brackets or modillions, they expressed youths, or nymphs, or children—not whole, but from the waist up; and the rest was distributed into foliage that coiled around, filling the spaces with animals such as swans and the like, with tails made of leaves and wings made both naturally and of foliage. One can also place sea monsters within and without, such as Tritons, Sirens, and Nymphs who, beyond their wings, are transformed into fish tails and sea-claws above the waves of the sea, performing their actions according to the <term>fancy</term> <note>original: "grilo", literally a 'cricket', used idiomatically to mean a whim or caprice</note> of the painter. In short, into this frieze no animal figure entered that was whole, but all were diversely composed; and thus one saw Harpies and Sphinxes in the form that Suetonius describes them, and others...

The same is seen in the <term>Composite</term> order, but with an abundance of flowers and buds, with flower vases, jagged rosettes, and the like placed between the modillions. 

Where, following the ancients, in the <term>Doric</term> frieze one wants to place animals and human figures according to the locations; in the <term>Ionic</term>, fierce and terrible animals, but shown whole, with males and more robust females like *Satyrs*, *Pan-gods*, and sylvan *Nymphs*; in the <term>Corinthian</term>, pleasant, beautiful, and delicate animals, figures of *Children*, *Virgins*, *Maidens*, and *Nymphs*; in the <term>Composite</term>, the same things but not as whole figures, as I have said; for these are composed with dogs, lions, and other animals emerging from foliage; and in the <term>Tuscan</term> order, more rustic figures, such as *Herculeses*, *Cacuses* <note>Cacus was a monstrous giant from Roman mythology who lived in a cave and was killed by Hercules</note>, and the like, with fiercer and harder foliage. 

Such is the rule for composing friezes in each order. By observing this rule—as it is the most secure and founded on the authority of the ancients—one will avoid making those friezes so noisy and confused, in which things are entangled that cannot naturally exist. Such errors accuse the painter or sculptor of having little foresight or judgment, and they throw everything into disorder: such as showing a child who embraces or plays with a serpent, or with any other poisonous and harmful animal, which by nature he should flee from in fear; or fierce animals that do not harm each other, or pleasant ones who do not fear those more ferocious than them, and other similar compositions that cannot

### BOOK II

...staying together. Nor should anyone tell me here that in <term>friezes</term> <note>the middle part of an entablature, often decorated with sculpture or painting</note> one can do whatever one wants, since they are "whims" of the painter; for such a person would be in a very great error. Since painting is a demonstration of all things that are made and that can be imagined possible to be made, and since ornaments and works are imagined to increase the beauty of architectural members, it is necessary that this beauty—if it is to appear—accords with our mind in the most delightful and best way possible. This is because things that clash cannot bring taste or delight, as they do not conform to the natural world, from which is born what appears beautiful to our eyes, along with their pleasure and delight.

And that it is necessary to observe this, do we not see that all the ancient architects derived the curves of the foliage, the <term>rosettes</term> <note>rose-shaped ornaments</note>, the carvings of the <term>egg-and-dart</term> <note>a decorative molding consisting of alternating egg-shaped and leaf-shaped or arrow-shaped motifs; original: "uouoli"</note>, the <term>cyma moldings</term> <note>S-shaped decorative moldings; original: "cimasi"</note>, the <term>torus moldings</term> <note>large, convex, semi-circular moldings, often at the base of a column; original: "bastoni"</note>, the <term>dripstones</term> <note>the projecting part of a cornice designed to throw off rainwater; original: "gocciolatorij"</note>, and finally all the other members from the principal geometric forms? These were done so that they would undoubtedly bring beauty and pleasure to the eyes of the viewers. These forms are principally taken from the human being, the perfect example and model of all buildings and works. Hence, we see them using circular, square, and oval shapes, and similar geometric proportions, having banished other forms as less perfect. 

And therefore, if a leaf in a <term>cyma</term> were wider than it was high, it would not be beautiful, as it would lack the logic of the square with which it is made; and if an **egg-and-dart** were either narrower or wider, not observing the oval proportion, it would not be understood. Likewise, in the curves of foliage, those that do not take after the oval or the circle cannot be beautiful or graceful.

Now, if there is logic in these small details, how much more must there be where animals and figures enter. And so, following my purpose, I say that besides the things already noted regarding friezes, we must express in them the gestures appropriate to the bodies of which the friezes are composed. Therefore, where <term>putti</term> <note>figures of young, often winged boys, common in Renaissance art; original: "fanciulli"</note> and such things enter, one seeks cheerful acts, jokes, and jumping over rams or with puppies; furthermore, let them have birds and masks in their hands, and let them climb and play upon the foliage and <term>festoons</term> <note>carved or painted garlands of fruit or flowers</note> that support them, and in short, let all the acts they are capable of doing be shown there. But for wild animals and men, such as <term>satyrs</term> <note>mythological creatures, half-man and half-goat, representing the wilder side of nature</note> and the like, one wants to maintain a different manner that suits their nature. And so for all the others, you can go on reasoning for yourself. Furthermore, the spaces want to be balanced; do not let one place be a great void while another is cramped with foliage and figures. For this reason, one must avoid this with diligent attention, ensuring that as much above, as...

## Composition of Grotesques. Cap. XLVIII.

**A**lthough Monsignor Barbaro <note>Daniele Barbaro (1514–1570), an author and translator of Vitruvius whose commentary was a standard Renaissance text on architecture</note> in his commentary on Vitruvius does not freely admit <term>grotesques</term> <note>a style of decorative art characterized by fanciful, intertwined human, animal, and floral forms; the name comes from "grotte" (caves), referring to the buried Roman ruins where they were rediscovered</note>, regarding them as dreams and chimeras of painting because they are a confused composition of diverse things—and since painting, like every other thing made by men, ought to represent some effect to which the entire composition is directed—nevertheless, following in this the opinion of Baldassare Peruzzi <note>original: "Baldessar Petrucci," a prominent architect and painter</note>, I would say that they should be freely admitted by making them in the [empty] spaces, as he teaches in the works of Serlio <note>Sebastiano Serlio, an influential architect whose "Seven Books of Architecture" helped spread the Renaissance style</note>. Because just as a <term>history</term> <note>a narrative scene or monumental painting</note> cannot be made in the air nor without support, so neither can these, which are a bizarreness and caprice introduced for the ornament of said history. In these grotesques, the painter expresses things and concepts, not with their own forms, but with other figures: as if one wants to represent someone of good fame, he will make Fame in the grotesques cheerful and splendid; if another of ill fame, he will make the same Fame dark and black; and if in places of sacrifice, there will be sacrifices. And because they do not freely demonstrate our concept, I said that they would not look well in a place of primary support, but must be placed in the empty spaces for their ornament and enrichment. 

I have heard many say that Raphael, Polidoro, Rosso, and Perino have removed part of the ancient grotesques so as not to let their own inventions, found through those with supreme artifice, be seen. But I do not know how grotesques can be removed, nor even blamed, seeing many of them made by the ancients in Rome, at Pozzuoli, and at Baiae; from the imitation of which these artists—as they have always done in every other invention of theirs—have brought back that honor which is granted to them by everyone. They also learned the manner of expressing their caprices and discoveries so ingeniously in these sorts of paintings, and taught others never to depart from the tracks and vestiges marked by the ancients in every thing that one undertakes to do. Many others have also been excellent in this regard, such as Polidoro, Maturino, Giovanni da Udine, Rosso, Giulio Romano, Francesco Fattore, and Perino del Vaga, who were the first to introduce into grotesques animals, sacrifices, foliage, festoons, trophies, and other similar bizarreness; taking them from the ancient caves <note>the "grotte" or buried Roman rooms like the Domus Aurea</note> painted by Se-

# S I X T H.

[Se]rapion <note>continuing from the previous page: the ancient painter Serapion</note> and from others, the most beautiful and charming elements that could be taken; with which they have since adorned all of Italy and the other provinces, along with his other followers such as **Aurelio Busso**, **il Pessa**, **il Soncino**, and **Giacobo Rosignolo of Livorno**. These men have worked so marvelously that they truly leave those who claim <term>grotesques</term> <note>a style of ornamental painting using intertwined natural and fantastic forms</note> are merely "dreams" in a state of confusion, forcing them to confess that when such works are made with invention and diligence, they are of the greatest ornament and richness to art. **Troso da Monza** <note>a 15th-century painter from Milan known for his work in the Cathedral of Monza</note> has drawn a book of so many and such varied sorts of these, that I judge no more could be made or even imagined; for he has truly occupied everything that can be done in such a faculty. In sculpture, **Silvio Lucchese** was rare and foremost, as is seen in his works, as was **Giovanni Battista Cerabalia** in ironwork. Therefore, let us leave those certain narrow-minded <note>original: "stitichi" (literally "constipated"), implying people who are stiff, pedantic, or lacking in creative flow</note> critics to croak, who do not wish to admit these works—being people who, lacking the skill of design, do not recognize the beauty and ornament of art, and who are as the verse says:

->*People for whom night falls before evening.*<-
<note>This poetic line suggests people who are willfully blind or whose understanding fails them prematurely.</note>

For truly, through these [grotesques], one can gracefully suggest lewdness in the satyr and the naked woman, the joyful lover in the shepherd and nymph, the baseness of the lover in the beauty of the siren, prudence in the Sphinx, and all other concepts under such appearances, just as in sacred paintings.

Now, to treat this more distinctly, I will not stand to investigate too subtly exactly what grotesques are—for truth itself does not know it any better than the painters do—nor what things they are composed of. But I will say this much before I come to their compositions: it is the opinion of many learned men and experts in letters that these "grotesques" are so named not only from the "grottoes" <note>underground ruins or caves</note> because the ancients sometimes wished to take refuge there secretly for pleasure and delight with some beloved; but because they were appropriately made as nothing other than riddles, or ciphers, or Egyptian figures called <term>hieroglyphics</term>, to signify some concept or thought under other figures, just as we use in <term>emblems</term> <note>a symbolic picture accompanied by a motto and a poem</note> and in <term>impresas</term> <note>a personal device or heraldic-like symbol combining an image and a short motto to express a personal goal or philosophy</note>.

And for my part, I believe this was because there is no way more suited to design or show whatever concept one wishes than through the grotesque. For to the grotesque alone in art are granted sacrifices, trophies, instruments, steps, hollows, convexes, circles, pendants, and reliefs; and besides these, all animals, foliage, trees, figures, birds, rocks, mountains, rivers, fields, skies, storms, lightning bolts, thunder, leaves, flowers, fruits, lamps, lit candlesticks, chimeras, monsters, and in short, everything that can be found or imagined.
