[In]vestigation, which is of such great importance as I proposed just now, I will extend myself only to discourse upon their composition, which is of great significance. For just as <term>grotesques</term> <note>a style of painting featuring intertwined fantastic and natural forms</note> are put into use for the sake of freedom, so too—in order to delight—they must be founded upon the authority of art, since they are nothing other than a demonstration of art and an ornament for certain suitable and secluded places. And that it is true they must possess, above all other things, a proper composition and art, is seen by the example of so many painters who, though excellent in depicting figures, have been unable to achieve any praise or honor in this particular field. This is chiefly because in the invention of grotesques, more than in any other style, there flows a certain <term>fury</term> <note>original: "furore," referring to a state of creative frenzy or inspired artistic passion</note> and a natural <term>bizarreness</term> <note>original: "bizarria," a prized quality of whimsical and inventive ingenuity in Renaissance art</note>. Those who lack these qualities, despite all their technical skill, accomplish nothing; likewise, little more was achieved by those who, although they were bizarre and capricious, did not know how to represent these things with art. For in this matter, both must concur together: natural fury and art.

Their composition, therefore, primarily requires a total natural verisimilitude <note>the appearance of being true or real</note>. For example, in the center there should be columns or trees that support candelabra; in the parts that appear more solid and heavy, there should be temples with <term>statues</term> <note>original: "simolacri," referring to sacred or decorative images</note> and the like; and at the bottom, as a base, there should be bizarre animals, monsters, and such things that act as supports, adorned with <term>mascarons</term> <note>original: "mascheroni," decorative carvings of human or fantastic faces</note>, harpies, ladders, and <term>cartouches</term> <note>original: "cartozzi," scroll-like ornaments often used for inscriptions</note> that convey a sense of stability. But if these elements were made to hang from above by a tiny thread, as many artists do, they would be suitable neither at the top nor at the sides. This is because those things which do not, in some way, agree with nature cannot show grace; even if they possessed internal consistency, they must follow the logic of natural things, as grotesques do.

Furthermore, one must take care that all the branches and small shoots have a certain "root" in the more solid parts—these connecting to the trunks, and the trunks to the stem—no differently than flowers connect to leaves, leaves to trunks, and trunks to the main stem. Beyond this, they must be equally distributed so that there are not more branches in one place than in another. I say the same of the animals, monsters, birds, figures of children, and masks; all must have a symbolic relationship and suitability among themselves. For it would not be a beautiful sight to see more animals on one side than the other, nor all the figures at the top and the animals at the bottom, nor the leaves or branches all in one place, even if they were somewhat mixed together. Thus, all these bizarre elements, when composed together, must occupy the space equally. The size of things must also be appropriate according to the comparison, so that the child appears small...

...small next to the large figure, and this one should appear equally small next to the animals. Everything present must, down to the last detail, serve its purpose and be represented in such a way that it is clear they were not made by chance, but through study, to achieve the effect they produce. For example, a bird in flight should appear to be fleeing from some flame or the sight of a snake, rather than simply flying over it; or perhaps it flies toward something it likes, such as a stalk of millet, a vessel of fruit and flowers, or a fountain. Furthermore, let the figure show that it is supporting something, such as a <term>frieze</term> <note>original: "fregio," a horizontal band of sculpted or painted decoration</note> or some other object placed before it; or let the figure be warming itself, or performing some other action with animals and the like—such as fishing from a small boat, where the water is depicted enclosed by rocks and banks drawn with thin lines. 

Their movements must conform to nature. For in these <term>grotesques</term> <note>original: "grottesche," a style of painting featuring intertwined fantastic and natural forms</note> there is all too much liberty taken to represent whatever one wishes with reason, art, and <term>whimsy</term> <note>original: "bizarria," a prized quality of whimsical and inventive ingenuity</note>, without the need to create—as many often do—haphazard <term>inventions</term> <note>original: "inuentioni," the conceptual design or subject matter of an artwork</note> that are out of place. Such painters represent children larger than men, or make children smaller than certain other figures; they paint birds larger than lions, and lizards and snails larger still. Many other such confusions occur: making children play with snakes or jump laughing into fire, or showing men and animals fleeing through the air without anything to support them and without wings—even fish in the air without water, or hanging massive weights from a very thin thread, and representing temples narrower than a lizard’s hole. 

From this it follows that so few grotesques are seen to be beautiful and well-conceived; it is no wonder that some, who do not look deeper, condemn them. They would not do so if they saw the beautiful ones that only a few have been granted the skill to create. Whoever, therefore, follows natural reason in the <term>composition</term> <note>original: "compositione," the arrangement of elements in a work of art</note> of these grotesques may be certain that everything will turn out most successfully, and he will achieve honor and glory. In this, he will open wide the eyes of his <term>judgment</term> <note>original: "giudicio," the artist's ability to make discerning aesthetic and technical choices</note>. For, in my opinion, it is a much more difficult thing to bring order to something disordered than to follow an ordered thing, which, already possessing order within itself, requires nothing more than to be recognized. In the former, beyond needing to know that order, one must reduce it from its disordered nature to an ordered one. Thus, by converting <term>history</term> <note>original: "historia," a narrative or representational painting of a specific event</note> into <term>fable</term> <note>original: "fauola," a mythological or imaginary story</note>, one adds the expected ornaments, "singing" it in verse and through other figures with a more graceful and charming manner; whereas the other [history] can be composed simply in prose with its own proper figures without further ornament.

<summary>The author argues that even though grotesque art is whimsical, it must follow a "natural reason" and structural logic to be successful. He compares the artist's task of ordering the "disordered" grotesque style to the difference between writing complex poetry (fable) and simple prose (history).</summary>

# Compositions of lamps, candlesticks, fountains, epitaphs, ornaments for <term>stylobates</term> <note>original: "distilo-bate," the continuous base or platform that supports a row of columns</note>, columns, vessels, intervals, figures, foliage, frameworks, monsters, animals, and instruments.

### Chapter 49.

**S**ince the invention of lamps was found among the Egyptians—as **Clement** <note>likely Clement of Alexandria, an early Christian author who discussed Egyptian history</note> writes—their use increased to such an extent that they were not only composed of small ornaments for use in houses and palaces among all peoples (made of stone, gold, silver, and other metals, as some ancient examples can still be seen), but they also began to be manufactured to adorn temples and honor their deities and gods. These were made in the likeness of trees which, spreading their branches all around, supported a vessel at the top containing either a wax torch or a wick in burning oil. Of this sort was the one that **Alexander the Great** took from the temple of **Apollo Palatine** <note>original: "Apolline Palatino." While "Palatine" usually refers to Rome, the author is referencing a famous lampstand taken by Alexander from Thebes and later dedicated at Cyme, as recorded by ancient historians like Pliny</note> when he conquered **Thebes**; he later offered it to the temple of the same god in the city of **Cyme**. 

These lamps, shaped like most magnificent trees cast in gold and other metals, spreading their branches around as has been said, were fashioned partly with foliage and fruits with some buds here and there. They had their roots at the bottom like a tree, though only those branches that supported the torches or wicks appeared outside the trunk. These featured various growth points and endings of long leaves that joined with the stem, which was also ornamented, but more heavily, to give the impression of decorative movement and the "flowering" of those branches. 

Beyond this, the beginning of the trunk was made in the form of vessels, from which branches emerged like rods made with various moldings and carvings, such as those used in tournaments <note>original: "tornei," referring to the decorative turnery or the specialized lances used in knightly games</note>. In these, one could likewise vary the shapes to make triangles, squares, or whatever was desired. The branches that supported the torches were made to sprout with a most beautiful and appropriate distribution, joining at their base with the vessel through moldings suitable to their <term>order</term> <note>the specific style of architecture, such as Doric or Ionic, governing the proportions</note>. This method is still used today in many small candlesticks, handles of instruments, and the like. 

Sometimes they were composed of various animals, placing the most terrifying ones at the bottom as bases to support the whole. Some small lamps were made in the likeness of animals that held the wick out of their mouths; others were composed of simple square frameworks with a few leaves around the handle; others were formed with various carvings, some with masks, and others with different figures and strange monsters, of which, as I have said, some ancient examples can still be seen.

-> SIXTH <-

than in our own times. From this practice of lighting torches and wicks for lamps, **candlesticks** were devised, primarily for the worship of the Gods in sacred temples; their use and magnificence grew so much over time that, having completely abandoned lamps, all the ornaments and riches of gold and precious stones were transferred to them, though in a different form. Therefore, according to the Roman rule, they rise upward almost in the manner of pyramids, being two or three times wider at the bottom than at the top, proportioning their height to their thickness according to the **human proportion** <note>The author refers to the Renaissance architectural principle that the proportions of objects and buildings should relate to the ideal measurements of the human body.</note>. 

They are made in triangular, circular, and square forms, and are composed in six manners: 
1. One is of only animals and figures.
2. Another of only foliage, fruit, and flowers.
3. Another of frameworks and patterns.
4. Another is round, shaped on a lathe and then decorated with various carvings and fluting.
5. Another of the same frameworks, but clothed in foliage from which emerge certain <term>cauliculi</term> <note>original: "caulicoli," small stalks or stems resembling those of a cabbage, commonly seen in the decoration of Corinthian capitals</note> and sprouts of seeds.
6. And the sixth is a mixture of all these things, coupled together with judgment. 

Because just as this final style gathers the sum of all ornaments, one must act with the greatest dexterity and skill to ensure all things correspond with one another in an orderly fashion. One must divide the candlestick into three equal parts: the lowest belongs to the firmest, **strongest**, and most solid parts; the upper to the lightest and most ornate; and the middle to the mediocre <note>In this context, "mediocre" means the middle-ground or moderate style, rather than "poor quality."</note>. 

Each of these three parts is further distributed into another three: in the base, one places the less heavy and solid at the top, the extreme of weight and gravity at the bottom, and the middle is composed of both. Likewise, the superior part should have the lightest and most ornate at the top, the least at the bottom, and in the middle, that part which approaches lightness and beauty should be on top, and that which approaches gravity and lesser ornament on the bottom. The middle section must be tempered no differently; for the heavy parts with little ornament should be thick and low, the light and highly ornate parts should be long, and the slender and moderate parts must hold the middle place. 

Thus, the square proportions remain at the bottom, the <term>sesquialter</term> <note>original: "sesquialtere," a mathematical and musical ratio of 3:2</note> in the middle, and the double <note>A ratio of 2:1</note> at the top. From these are composed and formed the vessels, the frameworks, knots of foliage, and every other thing that might enter therein, observing such proportion that—according to the elevation of the candlestick and the width given to it at the bottom and top—the members are distributed and diminish as they ascend, so that the upper parts do not overwhelm the lower ones, just as less...

Certain bases are also formed supported by sphinxes and various monsters with strange ornaments on the base itself, such as hanging festoons, masks, and **cartouches** <term>cartozzi</term> <note>original: "cartozzi," scroll-like decorative ornaments resembling curled paper or parchment, common in Mannerist design.</note> that encircle the tails of the monsters, which are partly turned into foliage; and some others are arranged in the manner of serpent tails. Here one sees cloths hanging from the mouths of the masks, necklaces, and similar things, taking care not to place festoons there, which, being heavy, must be placed at the bottom. In the upper part above the vases, they rise high with lids rich with **fluting** <term>cannellature</term> <note>Vertical grooves carved into a surface, typically used to give a sense of height and rhythm.</note> and tiny leaves, and sprouting flowers; and from the handles of the vase hang necklaces and jewels. Here, male figures or any other figures are not appropriate; rather, only the tapering of the bottom part is required. It is true that down at the base, to accompany the middle part, one could make some square patterns, some child's mask, or some bird, but nothing else. And in this manner, the candlestick comes to be composed by order, and presents itself as beautiful and strong—rules which some do not observe, as they tend to do everything in reverse. With this same order, the legs of beds, the magnificent columns of pavilions, the **frames** <term>bardinali</term> <note>High-quality ornamental supports or bed-frames intended for princely furniture.</note> for princes, and similar things are to be made; and besides these, certain round columns that **Gaudenzio** <note>Gaudenzio Ferrari (c. 1471–1546), a renowned Northern Italian painter and sculptor known for his expressive, ornate style.</note> and others used extensively, as we see in their works. These same rules serve equally for making those candlesticks for square columns in the **Attic style** <note>Referring to the classical architectural style of ancient Athens, known for its elegant proportions.</note>, where trophies are also used; and likewise for the pillars of chapels or other places. Beyond this, the ancients in their sacrifices made certain small gold jars, made according to these same principles, and also certain small candlesticks and lamps as seen on some **stone basins** <term>pili</term> <note>original: "pili," ancient stone sarcophagi or large vessels often reused as fountains or decorative elements in Rome.</note> in Rome; and one was seen in Milan in times past which was held to be the candlestick of the Temple of Solomon, as **Aeneas Sylvius** <note>Enea Silvio Piccolomini (1405–1464), the humanist scholar who became Pope Pius II.</note> recounts in his histories; or similarly the pastoral staffs of Popes and Archbishops, and finally all the instruments that are needed

For the worship in temples, or for the service and splendor of princes, objects are regulated and ordered in this manner. Thus, one sees tables, chests, fireplaces, and also vessels of various forms—circular or oval—just as Ambrogio Maggiore <note>Ambrogio Maggiore was a celebrated Milanese wood-turner of the late 16th century, famous for his technical virtuosity.</note> crafts them in wood using a lathe, making them so thin both inside and out that it is a source of great wonder to see them. These include long and short vessels, cups, glasses, basins, buckets, chairs, thrones, triumphal carriages, and carts, all decorated and arranged according to such compositions. With similar candlestick-like forms, one can also manufacture in gold or iron the guards for swords and knives, as well as stucco work finished with a file—an art in which Ferrante Bellino of Milan <note>A renowned Milanese metalworker and engraver known for his intricate detail.</note> never had, nor likely will ever have, an equal. Furthermore, from the shape of the aforementioned candlesticks are derived round, oval, and square fountains; at the bottom of these, a basin is made to receive the water that pours out from above through the mouths of masks or other similar features. At the summit, one places some Sea God or Nymph who presides over the waters, adding also scenes of sea gods and their loves, as can be seen observed in so many examples with which the world is filled—and most notably in Messina, where among others is that fountain so celebrated in the life of Brother Angelo <note>Referring to Giovanni Angelo Montorsoli (c. 1507–1563), a Servite friar and sculptor who designed the Fountain of Orion and the Fountain of Neptune in Messina.</note> the sculptor, where it may be read about in the most minute detail.

Epitaphs are likewise made in this fashion using the forms of animal skins and **scroll-work** <term>cartozzi</term> <note>original: "cartozzi"; decorative ornaments resembling curled paper or parchment, typical of the Mannerist style.</note>, which contain the deeds of those for whom the epitaphs serve, as if written on paper. In these, one can also place shields, emblems, histories, landscapes, and other whimsies; they are also called by another name, namely **cartouches** <term>cartelle</term>, which are similarly placed in friezes as we see done even in the halls and rooms of those who are not princes. **Stylobates** <term>stilobati</term> <note>The base or platform supporting a structure.</note> are likewise decorated in the same manner according to the things they support and govern. Therefore, if they support an obelisk, they are decorated heavily; if they support an epitaph, they are adorned with the remains of melancholic, **Saturnine** <note>Associated with the planet Saturn, which in Renaissance astrology governed melancholy, old age, and death.</note>, and nocturnal animals, dressing the figures that appear there according to the rank of the deceased. This is also observed in the massive **catafalques** <term>catafalchi</term> <note>A decorated temporary framework used to support a coffin during a funeral or memorial service.</note> where figures are placed to denote the past power of the one being honored. 

Now, as for these Stylobates, following the ancient Romans and, before them, the Egyptians, as a sign of virtue, one places Angels and divine symbols; as a sign of Empire and valor, triumphant Eagles and the like; as a sign of strength, Lions and Bears; and for humanity, oxen, rams, and other similar animals with their proper attachments and ornaments. They are also decorated according to the things they contain within them; for example, leaving aside the ancients, we Christians use around the...

Throughout all the intervals in these works, one observes the practice of filling the space with various compositions of foliage, always being careful that the thicker and firmer parts are in the center, and the thinner ones at the sides. Thus, for pilasters, facades, triangles, empty spaces, columns, and similar elements, one must always follow the rule of forming <term>candelieri</term> <note>literally "candlesticks"; a style of vertical, symmetrical ornamentation common in the Renaissance, where motifs are stacked like a candelabrum.</note>. They have found a new way of making <term>grotesques</term> <note>fanciful wall decorations inspired by ancient Roman paintings found in "grotte" or excavations.</note>, meaning that all the parts of the grotesque begin and likewise end within the design itself. Because of this, one does not see birds or other things floating in the air; rather, everything is logically supported by something else that can bear it. In this way, the entire aforementioned logic of the "candelieri" is maintained straight through the middle, though with some variety, and all the other elements springing from the sides support one another.

And this is the true and ancient way of making grotesques, though understood by few who, instead of these, should rather make <term>arabesques</term> <note>original: "rebeſche"; decorative patterns of intertwined lines, often more abstract or two-dimensional than grotesques.</note>. These, lacking depth or prominence and being represented in a single color, are formed in circles with forks, sprouts, and flowered foliage, as we see used in embroidery work and in <term>agemina</term> <note>original: "gemina"; the decorative technique of inlaying gold or silver into harder metals like steel, often used on armor.</note> upon weapons. Regarding trees, a beautiful invention was also found by Leonardo <note>Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519).</note> to make all the branches in various bizarre clusters, a style which Bramante <note>Donato Bramante (1444–1514), the influential Renaissance architect.</note> also used, interlacing them all like basket-work. By this same path, finally, are found the measurements and proportions of military instruments, which without doubt are also derived from the true geometric way—both ancient and modern—and, in short, all the engines and instruments of military architecture.

### Composition for Portraiture from Life. Chapter L. ###

**T**he practice of drawing from life—that is, of making images of men that resemble them, so that they are recognized as those very people by anyone who sees them—is, I believe, so ancient that it was born at the same moment as the art of painting itself. Originally, painting was not invented for any other purpose than to make images, namely the portraits of great men, like idols on earth. Hence, in those earliest times, only Princes used it, as Lactantius <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian author.</note> writes, saying that images or portraits—both in relief and in painting—were first made for the memory of Kings who, while living, had governed the people well, so that upon dying they might leave a great longing for themselves among their descendants, awakened by those [portraits]...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the moral and social functions of art, moving from decorative motifs like grotesques to the history and purpose of portraiture and statues of famous men.</meta>

<page-num>431</page-num>

-> B O O K   S I X . <-

paintings or statues often repeated in their memory their illustrious deeds and glorious works, so that they might be inspired to imitate them. Thus one reads of Caesar the dictator <note>Julius Caesar</note> that upon seeing the statue of Alexander the Great in Egypt, he was first lost in thought and then, having regained his courage, always desired to use a seal with the image of Alexander so that he would always have him before his eyes. And likewise, Roman ladies used to wear his image carved into their rings, and all the noble Romans were accustomed to doing so in the games and with the images of their ancestors. 

But returning to our purpose, Eusebius <note>an early Christian historian, often called the "Father of Church History"</note> writes in his *Ecclesiastical History* that it was also the custom of the Gentiles to grant to persons who had been of some benefit to human life—through any invention they had discovered—the right to have their portraits made, or else the Prince or the Republic had them portrayed. This the Athenians did for Socrates after his death, and for Pythagoras; and the Romans did for Aesculapius <note>the god of medicine</note>, for Quirinus <note>an early Roman god of the state</note>, and for infinitely many others. This was done so that posterity might know in what great reverence those were held who had become excellent in virtue and had been beneficial to the world, and so that others might be inspired to imitate them. From this it arose that all wise men kept the images of their wise ancestors as a memorial, so that by seeing them they might remember their works and take example from them. 

No other sort of people, therefore (according to what one reads), could have their portraits made among the ancients except for Princes and the virtuous. For all others it was prohibited, even if they were very rich. And I believe this custom lasted until Constantine transported the empire and the honor of Italy to Byzantium <note>Constantinople</note>. For earlier, if we read among the Assyrians of Belus, Ninus, and Nimrod, we find that their images were made only by order of Semiramis, the Queen of Babylon. And among the Egyptians, one finds no portraits of their kings except for the famous ones like Ozymandias <note>original: "Simandio"; referring to the Pharaoh Ramesses II</note>, Amasis, Arsinoe, and a few others; and even fewer of the virtuous, such as Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurio Trimegiſto"; a legendary figure associated with the origins of wisdom and art</note>, who used to say that when painting was born, religion was also born. 

This is because the study of painters is focused on sacred images; and among the Greeks, there was an edict that only the nobles should practice painting, so far is it from the thought that they would allow common and base men to have their portraits painted from life. Rather, this was absolutely reserved only for Princes and Wise men. Likewise, among the Romans, no other statues are seen than those of courageous Consuls, Emperors, and those similar to Princes, or at least of men who were prized and singular in some regard, such as women or beautiful youths. Thus one sees the statue of Antinous <note>a youth famed for his beauty and the favorite of Emperor Hadrian</note>, the most beautiful youth among all...

...all the others who were loved by Trajan <note>Roman Emperor from 98–117 AD, known for his philanthropic rule and military success</note>, or portraits of strong men like Hercules and Milo of Croton <note>a famous 6th-century BC wrestler known for his incredible strength</note>. From this we understand in what high regard the art of portraying from life was held by all peoples—chiefly because it was practiced only by excellent painters, sculptors, and <term>engravers</term> <note>original: "incauatori," referring to those who carve or incise designs into metal or stone</note>. Yet in our times, it has become so common that almost all its dignity is lost. This is not only because princes and republics allow anyone at all, without any distinction, to seek to preserve their memory as eternal and immortal through portraits, but also because every rough painter who barely knows how to daub on paper wants to try his hand at portraiture. And from these painters come the portraits of <term>swindlers</term> <note>original: "ciurmatori," meaning charlatans or quacks who often used painted banners to sell their wares</note> seen on banners, and of other sordid and infamous men. 

And even if this abuse has not, at least among the knowledgeable, diminished the value of this art in any way or stained its purity, it has nonetheless caused some damage in that judgment has become somewhat confused. It is now difficult to discern what the proper method of portraiture should be, according to the status of the people being depicted and according to what the art itself requires and teaches. For since this abuse has taken hold, if anyone wishes to make a portrait using those principles and parts required by art and by the rank of the person being portrayed, it is permitted to him by only a very few; instead, he is forced to set aside the rules and precepts of art to satisfy the whim of the one being painted. For this reason, the good painter rarely expresses his own <term>concept</term> <note>the intellectual idea or "disegno" behind a work of art</note>, without which it is impossible for any good thing to succeed—and this is even more true for clumsy and material-minded painters. Thus, instead of portraits, one sees what might be called <term>metamorphoses</term> <note>a reference to Ovid’s tales of transformation; the author suggests the portraits look like different, distorted creatures rather than the subjects</note>. Nonetheless, I have still wished to collect here some things necessary for the true composition of portraits, so that those who do not know may partly come to recognize the error they are in, whether they are painting or having themselves painted.

Firstly, then, one must consider the quality and status of the person who is to be portrayed. According to that status, one must give them their particular sign that makes them known. For an Emperor, this would be the laurel crown, as seen in ancient statues and as Titian <note>Tiziano Vecellio, the leading Venetian painter of the 16th century</note> judiciously observed in the "Caesars" <note>a famous series of paintings of the first eleven Roman emperors commissioned by the Duke of Mantua</note> that he painted for the Duke of Mantua, depicting them with laurels nearby and with batons in their hands denoting their dominion. This is also shown by the scepter and by ancient-style armor; but all this should be done with a certain discretion to avoid the ugliness of the costume, so that the portrait always remains beautiful. For this reason, the ancient Emperors desired that in statues and figures they should be...

...represented so armed. Sometimes they were also made naked to signify that the Emperor must be free, and show openly what he is to the people, and thus that he should be revered for his goodness and feared for the justice he administers. Secondly, the Emperor—above all others, just like every King and Prince—requires majesty, and must have an appearance conforming to such a rank, so that it breathes nobility and gravity, even if he were not naturally so. For it is the painter's duty to always increase the grandeur and majesty in the faces, covering the natural defects, just as one sees the ancient painters did. They were always accustomed to disguise and even hide natural imperfections through art; as Zeuxis <note>a famous Greek painter of the 5th century BC</note> and Aurelius did in the portraits of Goddesses; and in the case of Pericles <note>the famous Athenian statesman</note>, whom the artist depicted with a helmet on his head because it was pointed <note>original: "acuta"; Pericles was often mocked by contemporary poets for having an elongated, "sea-onion" shaped head, which he hid with a helmet in many portraits</note>; and we read of Apelles that when portraying Antigonus, he hid his defective eye <note>Antigonus I Monophthalmus was a general under Alexander the Great who had lost an eye in battle; Apelles famously painted him in three-quarter profile to conceal the injury</note>. And these qualities must be observed accurately by those who are knowledgeable. 

For this reason, Alexander the Great commanded by public edict that no one should dare to portray him except Apelles in painting, Pyrgoteles in <term>intaglio</term> <note>original: "di cauo," referring to the art of engraving or carving into a surface, specifically for gems or seals</note>, and Lysippus in sculpture. With such art, one comes to gracefully disguise and cover the imperfections and failings of nature, and to increase and expand the good parts and beauties. These principles were not observed by the ancient painter Demetrius <note>Demetrius of Alopeke, a 4th-century BC sculptor criticized by ancients for being "more fond of likeness than of beauty"</note>, who was more curious about representing likeness than beauty. Thus, the ancients expressed stability in Cato, study in Socrates, penetration in Pythagoras, cruelty and ferocity in Nero, clemency and nobility in Octavian <note>the Emperor Augustus</note>, lust in Heliogabalus, harshness in Marius, Majesty in Caesar, and so in all the others they always used to make shine forth that which nature had granted them as excellent. 

And so we see that many moderns have observed this in certain portraits of poets, as Giotto did, who expressed depth in Dante; Simone of Siena <note>original: "Simon Sanese," referring to the painter Simone Martini</note> in Petrarch, ease; Brother Angelo, prudence in Sannazaro <note>Jacopo Sannazaro, an Italian poet famous for his work "Arcadia"</note>; and Titian, eloquence and ornament in Ariosto, and majesty and accuracy in Bembo <note>Pietro Bembo, an influential cardinal and scholar</note>. Regarding garments, they should be diminished grade by grade according to the status of the people; although I praise the fact that one should only portray virtuous Princes and the most beautiful youths and women. In this part regarding the distribution of garments, whether through ignorance or lack of attention, very great errors are seen; for example, Emperors with <term>caps</term> <note>original: "berrette," referring to the soft, flat caps common to the professional and merchant classes of the 16th century</note> on their heads that make them look more like merchants than Emperors, something which is all the more unseemly and out of place since, given their imperial air, it seems that they should...

Among the modern painters, **Scipione Gaetano** <note>Scipione Pulzone (c. 1544–1598), called "Il Gaetano"</note> is most notable, especially in his portrait of **Gregory XIII** and **Cardinal Granvella**, wherein we see all the greatest beauty of nature—such as the dignity of the face in the former and magnificence in the latter. Likewise, **Giovanni da Monte of Cremona** and **Giuseppe Arcimboldo of Milan** in their portraits of the **Emperor Maximilian**, where imperial majesty is seen to shine forth. So too in the **Catholic King Philip** <note>Philip II of Spain</note>, and in the portrait of the Prince his son <note>likely Prince Diego or the future Philip III</note> by the hand of **Sofonisba Anguissola**, **Antonio Moro**, and **Alonso Sánchez** <note>Alonso Sánchez Coello (c. 1531–1588)</note>, in one shines grandeur and gravity, and in the other highness of soul. Finally, there is the portrait of **Charles Emmanuel, Duke of Savoy**, by **Giorgio Soleri**, **Alessandro Ardente of Lucca**, and **Decio**, where this <term>decorum</term> <note>the artistic principle of suitability, where a subject's depiction matches their social status and character</note> is equally seen to be observed—to say nothing for now of many others who are most worthy of the highest praise in this regard.

Among these, at such a fresh age, **Ambrogio Figino** is second to none, as is seen in the most beautiful and skillful portrait he painted of the most eloquent **Father Panigarola** <note>Francesco Panigarola (1548–1594), a celebrated Franciscan preacher</note>, a Minor Observant of Saint Francis, as well as **Girolamo Ciorcha**—both of whom are Milanese and my own disciples. 

For this reason, no labor should ever seem too heavy for us to learn this art, as it provides such delight and ornament. It expressly allows us to see so many diverse <term>physiognomies</term> <note>the practice of judging character or merit from facial features</note> of men and women, which, by reviving in our souls the memory of the virtues of our great and illustrious ancestors, serves us not only as an example but also as a stimulus to emulate their deeds and enterprises, walking in the footsteps they have left marked and impressed for us.

Hence, we are primarily and greatly obliged to continually offer singular thanks to **Christ our Lord**, who willed Himself to be a painter by imprinting His most sacred likeness upon the **Veil of Saint Veronica**; so that it might remain for posterity as a singular example of Him, inclining those who see it to love and revere Him, as it is seen in Rome. And after Christ, we must revere **Saint Luke the Evangelist**, who left for us, carved by his own hand, the portrait of the **Virgin Mary** with her Son in her arms in Rome; by whom it is believed there are also likenesses of **Saint Peter** and **Saint Paul**, besides many portraits of the most Holy Pontiffs and other saints like **Saint Thomas Aquinas** and infinite others. These, beyond the delight they bring us in seeing them, undoubtedly edify us...

...that such deep relief would be impossible to achieve, and of the sculptors I know plenty. Beyond sacred images, one also sees how much ornament it brings to Emperors, Kings, and Princes to see the statues, medals, and paintings of other famous men, since they create **Museums** of them. Such is the case with the Emperor, the King of France at **Fontainebleau**, the King of Spain, the Duke of Savoy, the Grand Duke of Tuscany, the Duke of Bavaria, **Paolo Giovio**, Bishop of Nocera <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552) was a famous physician and historian whose "Musaeum" at Lake Como housed a massive collection of portraits of famous men, becoming a model for future galleries</note>, and in short, many other Princes and Lords. In these collections, one sees everything that our mind could no longer desire to see; except, perhaps, if one were to see the vast museums and priceless paintings of those ancient Emperors and Princes, who were painters themselves—such as **Nero**, **Valerian**, **Alexander Severus**, and also those of the **Manilii**, **Fabii**, **Turpilii**, and **Emilii** families. Likewise, one might wish to see those of others who not only practiced the art, but took great delight in it, such as **Demetrius of Phalerum**, for whom three hundred and sixty statues were made—some on horseback, some in carts, some in coaches—within the span of four hundred days.

This is to say nothing of the grand statues and paintings of **Sulla**, **Lucullus**, **Octavius**, and of **Semiramis** <note>The legendary Queen of Babylon</note> among the Babylonians. As **Diodorus Siculus** <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BC</note> recounts, when she had the bridge crossing the Euphrates built in Babylon, she had various animals painted in their natural colors along the circuit of one of the two royal courts for a distance of thirty <term>stadia</term> <note>An ancient unit of length; thirty stadia is roughly 3.4 miles</note>. From this, we can argue that painting was then in greater use and esteem than it is now; just as statues were likewise of much greater quality and size than modern ones. This is apparent from a statue that Semiramis herself had carved into a rock seventeen stadia high, depicted with her hair loose on one side and braided on the other.

One could also go on remembering other museums of the most ancient Kings, both before and after those of Egypt, such as in the time of the ancient **Memnon** and of the other famous painters of **hieroglyphs** and sacred paintings. Many of these were designed at the tomb of **Osymandyas** <note>transcribed as "Simandio," referring to the Pharaoh Ramesses II</note>, the great King of Egypt. In addition to these, there were massive figures and portraits of the judges and of all the Gods of Egypt, shown with gifts offered to them according to their nature. In others, all the animals fit for sacrifice were shown ascending toward the burial place of the King’s body. There, one could see painted each day of the year, the rising and setting of the stars, and their significance (according to the doctrine of the Egyptians), specifically in each of the 365 spaces of a cubit...

# S I X T H.

...one [unit] in thickness; the whole of which place was surrounded by a very large circle of solid gold that was later removed by Cambyses, King of Persia. Nor should we remain silent about the great portrait that Dinocrates <note>Dinocrates of Rhodes was an architect and technical advisor to Alexander the Great, famous for planning the city of Alexandria.</note> wished to make of **Alexander the Great** on the immense Mount Athos, in which he intended that he should hold in his left hand a city capable of housing ten thousand people, as Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the 1st-century BC Roman author of the influential treatise 'De architectura'.</note> recounts. 

Though far greater are the intellectual portraits, which are placed into natural forms by the hands of craftsmen to meet the eye, expressing the concept of the mind, or "Idea." For this reason, I have never found that any painter or sculptor, whether ancient or modern, ever kept in their private studies any drawings or reliefs other than those in which they could find contentment and satisfaction for their studies and concepts. 

But leaving aside the ancients and speaking of the moderns, I have never found anyone who, having followed the footprint or example of another, was able to equal them, let alone surpass them. **Michelangelo** bears witness to this; he was never able to match the beauty of the **Torso of Hercules** by Apollonios the Athenian—which is found in the Belvedere in Rome and which he constantly followed—just as Daniele Ricciarelli <note>Daniele da Volterra (c. 1509–1566), a pupil of Michelangelo famously known for painting loincloths over the nudes in the Sistine Chapel.</note>, Perino del Vaga, and others who followed the manner of this same **Michelangelo** were never able to equal him. 

Likewise, the style of **Raphael** was never reached by **Parmigianino**, **Giulio Romano**, and others who followed it; and to that of **Leonardo** [da Vinci], Cesare da Sesto, Salaì, and Boltraffio were never able to attain; nor could those who followed the styles of **Titian** and **Giorgione** match them; nor those who proposed to imitate the manner of **Antonio da Correggio**, such as Federico Barozzi and many others. Similarly, the manner of the great <term>miniaturist (illuminator)</term> Don Giulio Clovio <note>Giorgio Giulio Clovio (1498–1578), considered the greatest illuminator of the Italian Renaissance.</note>—who made it shine as brightly as painting—was never fully equaled by Agostino Decio and his son. 

And returning to the ancient philosophers and painters, it has never been found that they joined together in their wisdom; rather, they separately diversified the same art. Among these were **Socrates**, **Plato**, **Pyrrho**, and **Metrodorus**, among others who were also painters. 

But the whole power of portraying what is imprinted in the mind consists in having a great awareness of oneself and what one’s mind desires, and expressing it in a work with ease and grace—selecting that which is beautiful and good from what one sees in others. This is a very difficult thing, even though it has been easy for some; such as for our Fontana <note>Likely Prospero Fontana (1512–1597), a Bolognese painter of the late Renaissance.</note>, who has chosen the man[ner]...

### *The composition of natural portraits through art. Chapter 51.*

**T**he ancient peoples used to express all their concepts with natural figures, and these were held by them to be sacred paintings, and therefore called Hieroglyphics <term>Hieroglyphics: From the Greek 'hieros' (sacred) and 'glypho' (to carve). Renaissance thinkers viewed them as mystical symbols rather than a phonetic alphabet.</term> by the Egyptians, according to what various ancient authors have left in writing. Among these peoples, it was a very frequent custom to signify everything they wanted with certain pictures. So from this, one can deduce that the art of design existed thousands of years before the characters for writing were found, which God showed to Moses upon the mountain. Now, as for these figures used by the ancients, I will come in this place, for the benefit of painters, to make a collection—not a universal one (because one can always turn to Pierio Valeriano <note>Giovanni Pierio Valeriano Bolzani (1477–1558), author of 'Hieroglyphica', a massive and popular Renaissance encyclopedia of symbols and their meanings.</note>, who has treated them so copiously that nothing more can be desired)—but of portraits of the human body alone. 

And first, a man with a scythe in his right hand and a bow in his left signifies that at one time he labors, and at another, he exercises himself with effort in matters of war; a man who has a dog’s head and extends his right hand into the air, while in the other he holds a staff, means a litigious person; one who shows various things of the world with his right hand and holds the other at his belt signifies a peaceful man; one who has curly hair and holds a sparrowhawk <note>original: "sparuiero"</note> in his right hand and a whip in the other, indicates a man who...

### Composition of the members of the human body. Chapter 52.

**S**ince we have treated natural and artificial portraits sufficiently, it is right that we now speak of their members and how they signify, reserving for later the discussion of how they signify when composed and joined. And first, it must be considered that this manner of composing is properly that through which all intended concepts—both simple and mixed, as we shall say later—are demonstrated. It is precisely that art of making <term>hieroglyphs</term> <note>symbolic pictorial signs believed by Renaissance scholars to hold secret, divine knowledge</note> of every sort that the Egyptians used in sacred images, as much of animals as of human figures, and in their joining and separation of limbs, following the nature of each thing for some particular quality. By this way, the ancient Egyptians represented everything that was possible to imagine and indicate in figure through their hieroglyphs; as <note>original: "Platone"</note> Plato amply testifies, saying that in Egypt all the images that could be painted were placed among sacred things, and that beyond those, no others could be invented anew in any way,

...not as in other places it was permitted to do. And therefore, these **Egyptians** did not allow such pictures to be multiplied further, because they had already occupied the entire field of representation and verification for every kind of created thing, whether of instruments or of gestures. Now, as we must begin the method of composing such significations of every kind, for any thing whether alone or accompanied, I will begin with the pure members of the human body, and then I will proceed to treat the whole body.

It is read, then, that the ancients attributed each of the members to some **Deity** <note>original: "Nume"</note>, such as the **ear** to memory—especially the right one, which **Virgil** also attributes to **Phoebus** <note>Phoebus Apollo, the god of light and prophecy</note>. The **right hand**, which is a sign of fortitude and shows the power of action—because the oath is made with it—was therefore attributed to **Faith** <note>original: "fede"; referring to Fides, the personification of trust and oaths</note> by **Numa Pompilius** <note>the legendary second king of Rome</note>, as **Livy** writes; and we also, wishing to pledge our faith, offer the right hand. The **fingers**, with which works are performed and which therefore denote **mastery** <note>original: "magisterio"; expertise or craftsmanship</note>, are ascribed to **Minerva** <note>goddess of wisdom and handicrafts</note>. The **knees** are given to **Mercy**, which is why those who ask for pardon bend their knees. The **navel**, some give it to **Venus** as if it were the seat of lust, while others, who reduce all the members to a central point, say that it is consecrated to **Jupiter**.

The **right eye**, because it denotes knowledge and because nothing is hidden from it, is dedicated to the **Sun**, which is understood to represent **Justice**. Whence **Apuleius** swears by the eye of the Sun and of Justice together. The **heart** is likewise under the protection of the Sun and demonstrates **sincerity**, **loyalty**, and men who do not hide themselves in any part; and therefore people are accustomed to say that there are no words more pure or loyal than those that come from the heart; and we say the same of **prayers** <note>original: "orationi"; can mean either formal speeches or prayers</note>. The **entire head**, as the principal member, the Egyptians depicted to represent **Justice**. The **left hand**, stretched and open—because it is naturally colder and slower than the right—was therefore a symbol of a man who is not fit to do injury to anyone.

**Lame legs** denote **prayers**, regarding the manner in which one prays, which is not free, just like the gait of the lame <note>this refers to the Homeric "Litai," the personified prayers who are described as wrinkled and lame, following behind Sin to heal the damage it causes</note>. **Shamelessness** was shown, as the **Egyptian Homer** <note>a reference to the belief that Homer's wisdom and symbols were rooted in Egyptian mysteries</note> says, with the bloodshot eyes of the body. The **head**, being placed in the highest part of our body, is a symbol of **Empire** and **lordship**, and therefore its Deity was **Jupiter**; and because it contains within itself all the senses through which all operations are performed, it also denotes **wisdom** and is given to **Minerva**. The **right foot** denotes **reverence** and **need**; for in showing reverence to someone, one always draws it back while bowing: and its deity, as a lower and servile part, is **Saturn**. The **mouth** denotes speaking free- <note>The text continues on the next page: "...freely"</note>

...clearly, and therefore it is given to <term>Mercury</term> <note>The Roman messenger god, associated with eloquence and trade</note> together with the tongue, which, in the manner of a plectrum <note>A small flat tool used to pluck stringed instruments</note>, tempers and generates words. The feet denote our affections <note>original: "affetti"; in this context, the passions, desires, or inclinations of the soul</note>, and especially the heel, which signifies the government of our will. For this reason, one reads that <term>Achilles</term> became invulnerable in all parts of his body—except for his feet—by being immersed as a child in the <term>Stygian waters</term> <note>The River Styx in the underworld; Achilles' mother, Thetis, held him by the heel, leaving that spot untouched by the magical water</note>. This means that such a great man could be constant in all his parts, provided he was not touched in his affections. And in <term>Genesis</term> it is written: "You shall be ambushed by your heel," <note>original: "Sarai insidiato dal tuo calcagno"; a variation of Genesis 3:15</note> that is, by your passions. 

Furthermore, <term>Hercules</term> (signifying the Spirit) could never defeat <term>Antaeus</term> (signifying the body) in a wrestling match as long as he held him high off the ground against his chest—the seat of wisdom and prudence. This was because as long as Antaeus's feet (his passions) did not touch the earth <note>Antaeus drew strength from his mother, Gaia (the Earth), whenever he touched the ground</note>, he could not regain his strength. From this, we also come to know that the chest signifies the seat of prudence and wisdom; for this reason, it is imagined to be under the protection of <term>Mercury</term>, from whom the perfect knowledge of virtues proceeds. 

According to the **Egyptians**, a single finger denotes measure. The left hand signifies the industrious man, because it is the hand that holds the work which the right hand performs, thus serving it; and for this reason, it too is under the protection of <term>Mercury</term>. The male organ signifies the disposition to procreate, and was therefore sacred to <term>Priapus</term> <note>A minor rustic fertility god</note>; without the seminal vessels, it denotes sterility. The belly signifies fruiting or giving birth and is subject to <term>Ceres</term> <note>Goddess of agriculture and motherly relationships</note>. The flanks signify agility and also strength. Consequently, there is no member or joint that does not signify some particular thing according to the ancient gentiles <note>A term used by Renaissance writers to refer to the polytheistic Greeks and Romans</note>, and specifically, they are all attributed to some Deity <note>original: "Nume"</note>.

### *The composition of gestures and acts of the members of the human body.*

#### *Chapter LIII.*

**B**esides the aforementioned things, various meanings—all founded upon reason—are also derived from the gestures of these members when combined. Thus, the hand or the index finger placed straight across the mouth denotes silence, because the hand naturally closing the mouth where speech is formed results in silence. The same right hand raised high denotes peace, and when extended with the arm level, it signifies quiet. Therefore, it is not without purpose that one sees many statues of ancient Princes in such an attitude, holding the right arm extended level, as is evidenced (among others) by the bronze equestrian statue of <term>Marcus Aurelio</term> <note>The famous Roman Emperor; his bronze equestrian statue still stands in Rome</note> in

**Capitoline Hill.** <note>The text likely refers to a specific statue located on the Capitoline Hill in Rome, used here as an iconographic example.</note> Furthermore, a hand held behind the back denotes a lazy, good-for-nothing person; and touching a foot or heel demonstrates **passion** <note>original: "affetto"; in this context, it refers to being governed by base desires or emotions rather than reason</note> and a lack of prudence and virtue. Clasped hands and the covering of the private parts are the figure of a continent, patient, and modest man. With a closed mouth and puffed-out cheeks, and with the face turned toward the feet from behind, one shows a man who applies himself to evil things—but from the front, to good things. The lowering of the head and the curving of the body demonstrates servitude; conversely, doing so toward the back signifies tyranny and fury. Standing straight and composed reveals the "unknown man," for it is through movements that the **passions** of a man are known. The open and free hand denotes that everything is revealed; and the closed hand, making a fist, denotes the secrecy of things.

Intertwined fingers of both hands show a soul averse to labor. Hands disposed to work, but with eyes closed, signify one who does not know what he is doing in that craft; and eyes open, but not looking at the hands, signify one who works out of necessity and not out of study or delight; for where there is delight, all the limbs concur and remain intent on that act from which the pleasure comes. A man with his hands on his hips shows himself to be useless and of little wit; the right hand to the forehead denotes the power of contemplation; and the hand closed straight except for the index finger signifies pointing and denoting; and turned downward, it is a sign of authority or command.

Raised upward in that same gesture, it signifies that there is one God, the creator of all; and three fingers signifies three persons comprised in one essence and unity. From this, blessings are given in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, with three fingers open—namely the thumb, the index, and the middle finger—while the other two remain folded. However, unity is also signaled by the thumb alone being raised, from which we always begin to count and say "one," which signifies the single principle of things. But outside of those things—just as unity is not itself a number but the principle of number—so too is God the principle of all things, and yet He is none of them. <note>This reflects the Aristotelian and Neoplatonic idea that the number "one" is the source of all numbers but distinct from the series itself, much as God is the source of creation but distinct from created matter.</note>

Hands that close the ears denote a person who is forgetful, since the instruments of memory and speech become blocked; and they likewise signify pertinence and obstinacy in one who does not wish to hear reason. ...contempt for something; for there is no greater sign in a man of abhorrence and scorn for a thing than the wrinkling of the nose at an odor. A laughing mouth signifies a **carefree man** <term>carefree man: original "homo spensierato", referring to someone who is light-headed or lacking in serious thought</term> of little wit who is given over to delights. A mouth opened as wide as possible demonstrates terror and loud noise; moderately closed, it shows stability; and when tightly closed, it shows continence. 

A face with eyes raised to Heaven, with open arms, and with all the limbs down to the soles of the feet appearing to lift off the ground, demonstrates hope, faith, and the **elevation of the mind** from mortal and base things to those that are divine and sublime. Conversely, looking and bowing with the body toward the ground with open arms demonstrates despair, infidelity, and a specific inclination toward vices and sins. 

In a straight posture, without raising or lowering the head, one denotes counsel, contentment, and reason. By turning the face to the right, one demonstrates counsel regarding good things, and to the left, the opposite. Looking toward the right side while turning the face there is a sign of **Charity**, clemency, liberality, and the like; but toward the left, it signifies vengeance, anger, fury, and offense. 

For this reason, when giving alms, it is not proper to ever turn the face toward the left side, but rather toward the right; this is because the right hand is the one that acts. On the other hand, when we are continually offending someone or shouting, we turn toward the left; this is because the right hand that offends takes a **great swing** <note>original: "gran tratto"; refers to the physical arc or momentum needed to deliver a powerful blow</note> when threatening with the hand or attacking with a sword or staff, which we could not do if we were turned toward the right side. 

And thus, **Christ** the Judge, having turned His face toward the left side and raising the right arm of **justice** against sinners, will deliver the great stroke of the curse; and, on the contrary, turning His Holy face with kindness toward the right and raising the arm of **blessing** and mercy, He will give to faithful souls the glory of eternal life, into which may it please God that every faithful person might enter. 

Finally, to conclude the entire sum of the **meanings** of the actions of the **limbs**, as they have been naturally impressed one by one, it consists in this small summary: all limbs that pull upward signify good and **elevation** in their nature, and those that, by contrast, bow downward signify evil and dejection in their nature. Movements toward the front demonstrate the power to act; from behind, they show privation. To the right, they signify majesty, strength, and **deliberation** in action; to the left, failure, disgrace, weakness, or the impotence to act. By then intersecting and joining these limbs in various ways as the need arises, one can compose demonstrations not only—

...of Hieroglyphs, but of all human acts and gestures; and to tell the truth, this is that art which the ancient painters and sculptors used so much, in whose works one finds no motions that are not all fitting according to the status of the figure to whom the motion is assigned. And this [lack] comes only through our misfortune, for if these principles were well understood, they would be celebrated and observed in such a way that they would certainly repay the artist for all his study and labor with great advantage, bringing him as a reward such praise and glory that everyone would revere him according to their abilities and status; and all the more so since so few in our age—though excellent in other respects—have been able to penetrate this, or have done so so little that one can say it is nothing. And because of this, we no longer see figures in acts of demonstrating not just mysteries and hidden meanings <note>The author refers to the "hidden meanings" or "hieroglyphics" of the body, where a specific posture signifies a specific moral or philosophical concept.</note>, according to what we have discussed thus far; but not even formed in a way that represents what suits their nature, nor with that motion that expresses the effect that the artist pretends to make them do. ### Composition of figures with one another. Chap. LIV. ###

Beyond the **Calumny** painted by **Apelles** <note>Apelles was a renowned painter of ancient Greece. His "Calumny" was a famous lost painting described in literature and frequently reconstructed by Renaissance artists like Botticelli to show the personification of various vices and virtues.</note>, and many other bodies that cannot exist without one another, there is also **Pleasure** and **Displeasure**: one a most beautiful youth in face, of a lovely and delightful appearance with blond and curled hair; and the other a sad old man of mournful appearance. These are painted together because one is never separated from the other, and with their backs turned to each other because they are totally contrary. They are attached with skill by the armpits from the back to a single body, which joins their bodies from the waist down. And this is done to demonstrate that they have the same foundation; for the foundation and origin of pleasure is labor <note>The original Italian "fatica" implies both physical labor and the hardship or "pain" that precedes a reward.</note> together with displeasure; and conversely, the foundation and root of displeasure are vain and lascivious pleasures. Therefore, one is depicted with a **reed** in his right hand, which is hollow and without fruit—exactly as pleasure is—and to **Displeasure** is placed in the right hand a great quantity of arrowheads to denote the sharp and poisonous stings with which he pricks hearts, having let some of them fall onto the floor upon the—

But in the left hand, pleasure holds a great quantity of shields <note>The Italian *scudi* refers to both shields and a common gold or silver coin; the author likely intends a double meaning of protection and worldly wealth.</note> in front of displeasure, some of which it lets fall to the ground, to demonstrate how displeasure gazes upon these worldly vanities that pleasure holds out; where, in contrast, it holds out before pleasure those stings of arrows without which pleasure cannot be born. Thus, a branch of roses with thorns signifies nothing other than fragile, vain, lost pleasure, and the certainty of present annoyance and the stings of things.

Beyond this, the right leg of this body rests upon a pile of hay; and the other upon a plate of gold, to demonstrate their diversity: and that one foot—that is, the affection for worldly pleasure—is low, weak, and soft; and the other—the affection for displeasure—upon the gold, is certainly firm and resplendent through pain, matching the tips of the arrows. This monster is also depicted in the aforementioned form upon a bedstead, to signify the various dreams of pleasure and displeasure that are presented to us there at night, and the loss of the great part of life that occurs there, consuming much time, and especially that of the morning, when the mind is sober and rested and the body is fit to take up new labors. In short, it represents the many vain pleasures that are taken there with the mind imagining things impossible for oneself, or with the body delighting in things that are often the causes of its death.

There are also formed, for the teaching and instruction of human life, other figures of this kind, such as Evil Thought with Envy or Ingratitude, which is represented as disheveled and ill-suited upon a frog, which represents imperfection. And before it is Evil Thought—that is, the intent of Envy—all thin, drained, dry, pale, and choleric <term>choleric: in the Renaissance, this meant having an excess of yellow bile, leading to a quick-tempered and irritable nature</term>, with an evil face and wicked gesture, shooting an arrow at a target. He is entirely naked to show that he is so intent on offending others (as the shooting of the arrow alludes) that he does not notice he is seen naked and known to be wretched and malignant. 

But Envy, who is behind following her wicked thought, is depicted as old, ugly, and pale, as Apelles <note>Apelles of Kos (4th century BCE) was the most renowned painter of ancient Greece; his lost painting of "Calumny" featured a famous personification of Envy.</note> once made her. A whip is added to her hand, with which she continually strikes the frog that carries her along with her evil thought. And because of this, since she strikes the one who does her service, she can also be called Ingratitude, because the ungrateful person seeks no less to offend...

...to bite and sting <note>original: "saetare" — literally to pierce with arrows, used here to describe verbal or mental attacks</note>, with both thought and words, the one who has done him a favor, just as envy does against the virtuous and the good. They are shown departing from imperfection to denote that the wicked thoughts and the detractions of the ungrateful and envious cannot perfectly obtain victory against goodness and virtue, as they are founded upon that same imperfection. In another way, envy is also demonstrated by a saying which hints that the body will sooner be without a shadow than virtue will be without envy. For as soon as virtue is born, she gives birth to envy against herself. 

Now, virtue is depicted almost in the form of Apollo, such that she partakes of both the male and the female, owing to the delicacy represented in her face and hair, while the rest of her body resembles Minerva; and she is made entirely naked, because true virtue is not covered by any vice or ignorance. She holds only the quiver at her side as a sign of the masculine virtue of Apollo, and she has a crown of olive upon her head. She is formed standing upright, in a most beautiful profile pose, giving birth from her own body to Envy—a thin, ugly, and pale woman. This Envy, having turned against her, seeks with her right hand to take away Virtue's strengths, which are represented by arrows <term>arrows<gloss>symbolic tools used to destroy ignorance and vice</gloss></term>. With these arrows, Virtue destroys ignorance and vice, acquires honors and palms <note>The palm branch was a traditional Roman and Renaissance symbol of victory</note>, and penetrates divine as well as celestial matters. 

Furthermore, Envy is in the act of trying to light and burn Virtue's hair and crown, to strip away the honor and beauty that she offers to the world; and with a poisonous snake’s tongue, she seems to want to poison her face. Indeed, as a sign that Envy is of a cold nature—that is, without love and charity—and entirely poisonous and pestiferous, she is depicted with a twisted scorpion’s tail and flat, tangled hair. On the other side, masculine virtue—which is so called by the wise, as is also Justice—gouges out Envy's eyes with the tip of the trunk of the olive branch held in her right hand (signifying pure victory and peace). With her left hand, she drives an arrow into Envy's right ear, to demonstrate that in the end, virtuous strengths and works blind and deafen the envious within their own selves; although they always have their poisonous tongues and snares ready against the virtuous, and their hands quick to stain their honor and reputation.

# *Composition of the colors and of the customs of the peoples and countries of the world.*

## **Chapter LV.**

**I**t is a significant matter for the painter to have to represent not only the diversity of the flesh of various peoples, but also their customs, and almost their very spirit and voice. This is so that, just as we see in nature, whoever sees themselves painted may be immediately and distinctly recognized by these features as an Indian, a Moor, a German, or from whatever other nation one might desire. This occurs because of our natural understanding, which is instilled in us by the heavens, causing us to see those peoples as different in color, customs, and skills. Therefore, I have judged it necessary to also give some rules and knowledge regarding this part.

Thus, regarding the quality of human bodies, those who live on the Equator <term>Equator<gloss>the original term "Equinottiale" refers to the celestial equator or the equinoctial line</gloss></term> as far as the tropics of Cancer and Capricorn are black, of a twisted stature <note>The author likely means "distorted" or "stooped" according to the racial theories of the time</note>, with curly hair that is thick and short, with wrinkled faces, and fierce customs due to the excessive heat.

And these peoples are—starting from the West at Cape Verde where the Black River <note>original: "fiume Nero" — likely referring to the Senegal or Niger rivers</note> empties—the peoples of the Kingdom of Mali, of Caragola, of Timbuktu, of Guinea, of Bornu, and of Barnagasso where Prester John <note>original: "Preteiani" — a legendary Christian patriarch and king popular in European lore, often associated with Ethiopia</note> lives, who has seventy-two kingdoms under him, diverse in languages, colors, faces, and customs. Then there are those of Calicut, Cannanore, Narsingha, and Bisnagar <note>Narsingha and Bisnagar refer to the Vijayanagara Empire in Southern India</note>, where the body of Saint Thomas the Apostle lies; of Ceylon; of Malacca, where four hundred soldiers always stay in the name of Portugal; of the Molucca Islands; of Taprobane <note>An ancient name used for either Sri Lanka or Sumatra</note>; of Greater and Lesser Java, Borneo, Palawan, the Philippines, Mindanao, and Java <note>The text lists "Chiaua" separately, perhaps referring to a specific region or island in the Indonesian archipelago</note>, where the King never lets himself be seen nor permits any foreigner to disembark in his kingdom.

From there, one passes to New Spain, to the great city of Mexico, where the Spaniards have a monopoly on the merchandise of those countries to bring them to Spain; to the Yucatan peninsula in the Gulf of Mexico, within which is the island of Cuba, Hispaniola, and many others; and finally the island of Deseada <note>original: "Isola desiata" — literally "the desired island," now La Désirade in the Lesser Antilles</note>, first found by Christopher Columbus, the Genoese inventor of the New World; and lastly to the islands of Cape Verde.

The inhabitants of the New Indies, especially of Peru and those of the Great King of China, are without beards with only a single hair in the middle; they go naked, both the men and the women, except that the married women wear a cotton band around their private parts; and in many places they eat one another. And then one passes through unknown lands to the islands of Saint Peter and Saint Mary, between Florida and New France <note>Early French colonies in North America</note>, and to the Terceira Islands of Spain <note>The Azores</note>. The inhabitants of these countries are of a moderate <note>original: "mediocre" — meaning mid-toned or balanced</note> color, like a well-ripened hazelnut; they are of gentle customs and suited to every kind of science; of medium and strong stature.

In the other region, from 46 degrees up to 50, are France, Britain, Normandy, Picardy, Flanders, Switzerland, Lower and Upper Germany, Bavaria, Franconia, Austria, Hungary, Transylvania, and Wallachia.

Of all these named countries, those that are more Eastern are more manly, robust, and firm of spirit, hiding nothing; because the Eastern part is of a solar nature, and therefore that part is called "right." Wherefore we see that in animals the right side is more vigorous and robust; on the contrary, Westerners are effeminate, soft, and dissemblers, because that part, as the "left," is attributed to the Moon, although in parts of the aforementioned countries some of every sort are born. Therefore, here the painter has to express in the "air" <note>the general appearance, demeanor, or "aura"</note> of each of them the differences of the countries, just as happens, for example, in the histories of the Sibyls, who differ in color and air.

### Compositions of draperies and folds. Chapter LVI.

**S**ince it is necessary to clothe and adorn human figures, I will treat in this place the method of composing draperies <note>original: "panni"</note> and folds, which are so necessary in garments that without them a figure, however much it is covered, if the grace of the folds is not present, still seems to be ashamed. This is seen in many paintings in which, the folds not being well-disposed in their proper places on the garments, not only is shame brought upon the figure in a certain way, but it is also left looking maimed, as if they were driving [the folds] through the limbs...

...[it] looks without discretion, or truly, standing so far off from the body that they would need other clothes underneath to cover them. But coming to their composition, three things must be considered to make the drapery <note>original: "panni"; refers to the depiction of clothing or fabrics in art</note> excellent and proportionate to the figure who wears them: the first is that, regarding the folds and pleats <note>original: "falde & pieghe"</note>, they must be of such quality that they suit the person who must wear them; the second is that they must follow all parts of the nude body that lies beneath; and the third is that they should be able to stand on their own merit, following the nude but not too closely.

Regarding the first point, which is of no small importance, I say that the excellent painter must not always make the same kind of drapery with the same folds for every figure, whether they be few or many. For according to the nature and rank <note>original: "grado"</note> of the figures represented, one must apply the drapery and dress them accordingly. Thus, if it is a Philosopher or a Prophet, it is necessary to give them heavy robes; and the fewer folds one gives them, the more appropriate it is. The artist is praised for this, as we see has been observed by many, and especially by Michelangelo <note>original: "Michel Agnolo"</note> in the Prophets and Sibyls on the wall <note>original: "volto"; literally face or vault</note> of his chapel where he painted the *Judgment* <note>The Last Judgment in the Sistine Chapel</note>; by Raphael in many places; and by Polidoro <note>Polidoro da Caravaggio, known for his facade paintings</note> where it was necessary to express them. For if the folds were broken into small pieces, they would not correspond to the gravity of the face and the stature of the figure.

Conversely, for a Nymph or another young woman who represents grace and charm, fluttering and light drapery is fitting—indeed, necessary—with minute folds that show the lightness of the fabric, corresponding to the nature and quality of the Nymph. For this reason, one attributes to them veils and charming, light belts, distinguished by very small folds. This must also be observed in Angels, as we see has been done by Gaudenzio <note>Gaudenzio Ferrari</note>, Leonardo <note>da Vinci</note>, Boccaccino, and Mazzolino, matching the lightness of the drapery to their nature and quality. Therefore, they are likewise given thin veils and very light belts with small and very minute folds, yet wide in certain places according to their turns; in this manner, they are praised.

Drapery with folds that are neither as rare or thick as the first kind, nor as frequent and thin as the second, is suited to perfect men and majestic matrons—such as Jupiter among the Gods, and among us Christians, the robes and mantles of Our Lord, the Virgin, the disciples, and the like. To these belong "perfect" drapery, which should have reasonable and moderate folds, as those that hold the middle ground. In this style, Leonardo, Raphael, and Gaudenzio were most excellent...

who was rare not only in this, but also in making them <note>The fabrics or drapery</note> appear as if they were truly of brocade, silk, wool, linen, or fleece, and in short, of everything that is possible for a painter to show through practice and speed, with his rare turns and intricate twists. One should not place these upon those for whom modesty is appropriate in every thing, such as the saints and the Virgin, upon whose head many imprudently paint jewels and pearls, as Ludovico Mazzolino <note>An Italian Renaissance painter known for detailed, often crowded compositions</note> once did. How contrary this is to religion, truth, and devotion, I could prove with many reasons and authorities, if this were not more a matter for a Theologian than a painter, and if there did not remain so many other more necessary and relevant things to say.

The second consideration that one must have is, as I said, that the <term>drapery</term> <note>original: "panni"</note> follows the <term>nude</term> <note>original: "nudo"; the underlying anatomical form of the body</note>. If the body is well-proportioned and well-built, it remains in the same proportion even with the clothing over it. This style of <term>drapery-work</term> <note>original: "panneggiare"</note> is more artful than natural. To make his own worth known in the rendering of nudes and the interlocking of limbs, Michelangelo <note>original: "Michel Agnolo"</note> used this in the Pauline Chapel in the Vatican, showing at once both the nude and the clothed. Furthermore, this divine man also wanted to show with this how difficult such a style is to achieve, and subsequently to show us how he went about attempting all the ways and manners of draping.
