secure, and better than all other ways of rendering <term>drapery</term> <note>original: "panneggiare"; the art of arranging and painting the folds of clothing</note>. And this is the third part that we said above must be considered; although many other sorts of drapery are found painted, such as by Bramante, Andrea Mantegna, and others, taken from models dressed in paper and glued canvases. From there, upon returning, he used another style of making drapery that appeared, by contrast, too soft and relaxed. There are, besides these, other rough sorts of drapery which must be avoided, and above all a certain confused manner, because it is as far from the design and drapery of Raphael as can be, as is seen in practice; for one sees there neither order, nor beginnings, nor ends of <term>folds</term> <note>original: "falde"</note>, but rather the whole garment is confused in the manner of white <term>ormesini</term> <note>A thin, lightweight silk fabric originally from Ormuz</note>, velvets, and brocades wrapped in tiny, minute folds. I do not say that these extremes are in the drapery of Titian, Giorgione, or Giovanni Bellini, but it is clear that they have not expressed the <term>attitudes</term> <note>The specific poses or "airs" of the figures</note> introduced into drapery by Raphael, by Gaudenzio <note>Gaudenzio Ferrari, a prolific Northern Italian painter</note>, and by others named above.

But leaving aside these observations, I say finally that in composing drapery, one must take care that the clothing not only follows the <term>nude</term> <note>The underlying anatomical structure of the body</note> and everything else it covers, but it also must bend and settle according to the wind or whatever else moves it. For it is necessary that according to the wind, the cloth flutters and inflates, and the folds go to find the nude toward those parts where the wind is imagined to blow. And if a figure sits or is leaning, the clothes must rest and withdraw behind the body, finding the nude; and where they have no body beneath them, they must fall, like the tablecloth around a table. But to see and know more clearly these things I say, I advise and exhort everyone who desires honor to observe and see for once drapery as it is done from life. Because nature, to those who understand it, is the true example, the principle, and the foundation of art and the true Master; just as Eupompus <note>A Greek painter of the 4th century BCE</note> pointed out to the painter and sculptor of Samos <note>Referring to Lysippos, according to historical accounts</note> by stretching his hand toward a multitude of men, intending to tell him that nature was the true demonstrator of art.

<meta>This page transitions from the technical discussion of drapery into the symbolic use of animals in art, specifically in the context of heraldry (shields and emblems) and ancient Egyptian hieroglyphics.</meta>

<page-num>458</page-num>

-> # BOOK # <-

For shields and emblems, as in any other effect, animals are particularly required, which by their natures are very well suited to signify, for example, the same things and express all concepts. Hence the Egyptians, among their sacred images which we call <term>hieroglyphics</term> <note>original: "Ieroglifici"; the ancient Egyptian writing system using pictures to represent words or sounds, which Renaissance thinkers often viewed as purely symbolic or mystical</note>, had about six hundred and some different images of simple animals. These were placed alongside the figures, which in all their acts and gestures had no further action to perform, having completed them all, as Plato writes of them. And so they had alongside them all the significant instruments which, like letters, demonstrated the concept that was hidden beneath to the eyes of those who did not know how to read. 

But returning to where we departed: the ancients, wishing to represent something simply by subtly investigating the natures and qualities of animals, used to paint that animal whose nature was corresponding and conformed to the concept they wished to suggest. And so, to signify audacity and spiritedness, they painted the **Lion**. And because the **Rooster**, being closer to the nature of the Sun due to a certain movement and harmony it shares with it, sings at the end of the night, they painted it with an open mouth to represent the beginning of the day. 

Besides this, for timidity, they painted the **Hare**, which was held as such by Queen Hermodice <note>likely referring to Hermodice of Cyme, associated in antiquity with the invention of coinage and being the wife of King Midas</note>; for rapacity and voracity, the **Wolf**; for astuteness and fraudulence, the **Fox**; for adulation, the **Dog**; for avarice, the **Raven** and the **Crow**; for pride, the **Horse**; for anger, the **Tiger**, the **Bear**, and the **Wild Boar**; for sadness and melancholy, the **Cat**; for lust, the **Sparrow** dedicated to Ceres. 

And wishing to denote one who is alone, of a strong and virile spirit, and an only child, and also to suggest the Sun itself, they painted the <term>scarab beetle</term> <note>original: "scarabeo"</note>, because this creature is alone without females <note>An ancient biological misconception that scarabs were only male and reproduced by rolling balls of dung</note>. With the **Raven** holding its mouth open, they denoted the diviner, because it was the bird of Apollo; and with the **Swan**, song and also the day were shown, for which reason it was dedicated to the Sun. 

To signify one who sees and understands all things, they made a **Sparrowhawk**, because this bird has the sharpest sight, and under this image they worshipped. The sparrowhawk was also an image of speed and swiftness. For vigilance, they again used the **Rooster** and the **Serpent**; for sterility, the **Mule** and also **bullocks**; for nature and foresight, the **Vulture**, because there are no males among these birds, as Aelian says <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author whose natural history works often included moralizing myths about animals</note>. For the increase of human generation, they used the God **Pan** in the form of a **He-goat**, with the member erect, as this animal is always ready for coitus; for earthly riches, the **Peacock**.

# SIXTH [BOOK] .

For faith, they used the white **Dog**; for fidelity, the **Crow**; for concord, the **Stork**, and according to <term>Aelian</term> <note>Claudius Aelianus (c. 175 – c. 235 AD), a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric who wrote "On the Nature of Animals."</note>, the **Hooded Crow** as well. Wishing to show that religious matters must be hidden beneath divine mysteries, they painted the **Sphinx**; for guardianship, the **Griffins**; for wisdom that knows all things, the **Owl**, because it alone sees at night and is the crest of **Minerva**; for victory, the **Eagle**; for frequency and deliberation, the **Woodpecker**, which is under the protection of **Mars**; for the world, a **Serpent** devouring its tail; and for another representation, the **Cynocephalus** <note>original: "Cenocefalo"; a dog-headed baboon or ape associated with the Egyptian god Thoth</note>, which was also a figure of the world. This was because just as the world consists of seventy-two <term>climates</term> <note>latitudinal zones used in ancient geography to divide the known world</note>, so this animal—as <term>Horapollo</term> <note>original: "Oro Apolline"; the supposed author of a 5th-century treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs that was immensely popular during the Renaissance</note> says—dies over as many days, with one part of it dying for each day.

To represent strength, he painted the front parts of the **Lion**, as these are the widest parts it possesses; for vigilance and guardianship, a **Lion’s head**, because when it is awake it keeps its eyes closed, and when it sleeps it keeps them open <note>A common medieval and Renaissance belief about lions, making them symbols of the watchful guardian or the resurrected Christ</note>. For fear, they used the whole **Lion** together, because this animal alone, upon meeting whatever other animal it wishes, enters into fear <note>This likely refers to the "fearful" lion of emblems, which was said to be terrified by the crowing of a white rooster or the sound of wagon wheels</note>. For imperfection, they made a **Frog**, an imperfect animal; for a manifest or clear thing, a **Hare**, because it always keeps its eyes open. For this reason, the first Romans engraved it upon their coins, wanting to say that they must be "manifest" <note>likely a pun or symbolic link between the "open-eyed" hare and the "public/evident" nature of currency</note>; and similarly in **Phrygia**, the <term>Cunei</term> <note>likely referring to the inhabitants of the region or a specific tribal group</note> engraved them upon their coins, denoting that in handling money one must proceed with timidity.

For length of life, and to demonstrate the unity of something, they used a **Phoenix**, as it is unique in the world. For villainy, destruction, and hatred, they painted a **Fish**; this was because it was prohibited in sacrifices, and also because by its nature it destroys whatever it finds, not even sparing its own offspring, as Horapollo says and as is seen by experience. Wishing to show a strong and aged man, they made a **Bull**; for hearing, they painted the ear of that same animal because of the way it senses the lowing of the Cow that calls it to mate. For judgment, they used a **Mouse**, because of how it discerns the best bread among those given to it. For impudence, the **Fly**, because though chased away many times, it returns again. For providence, the **Ant**, because in summer it provides for its living in winter. For gratitude or merit, they painted the **Cucufa** bird <note>original: "uccello Cucufa"; the Hoopoe, which in Renaissance lore was praised for caring for its parents in their old age</note>. For a forgetful person, the **Pelican**; for ingratitude, the **Dove**, because the male, once he has grown strong, drives out the father and mates with the mother. For obedience, the **Bees**; for rapacity and fury, the **Crocodile**, because it is prone to snatching in a fury even against itself; for old age, the **Stag**; for...

...death is represented by the **Barn Owl**, because it assaults chickens and chicks by night, just as death takes us unexpectedly; sleep is represented by the **Marmot**; the **Swallow** serves as a symbol of a very rich inheritance and of memory; a deadly man given over to lust is represented by the **Pig**; nourishment by the **Bat** <note>In Renaissance natural history, bats were unique as "birds" that nursed their young with milk, making them symbols of maternal care or nourishment</note>; secrecy by the **Cicada**; and for love toward one's father and mother, they used a **Stork**. For blindness, they used a **Mole**; for instability, the **Hyena-serpent**, which is now male and now female, whose form is described by many who depict it being ridden by unstable Death; and for gluttony, the **Crocodile** with its mouth open.

To overshadow <note>original: "adombrare"; to represent metaphorically or cast a shadow of a meaning</note> malice, they painted a **Leopard**, because this animal hunts others by stealth; for one who is cautious, prudent, and vigilant, they used the **Crane** with its leg raised <note>The "Crane of Vigilance" was often depicted holding a stone in its raised claw; if it fell asleep, the stone would drop and wake it</note>. Similarly, **Theology** is represented by the **Crane** when it flies, because it flies higher than any other bird can be found, in such a way that it passes above the clouds. For laziness and slowness, they used a **Camel**, because it alone among walking creatures bends its legs so much; for solitude, or for a man who is an enemy to all, the **Eel**, because it lives far from other fish and is never found with any other. For prodigality <note>wastefulness or reckless spending</note>, they used the **Octopus**, which eats greedily and then throws everything away. 

Thus we see that they represented not only virtues with the figures of animals, but also vices. In this way, they signaled cruelty in the **Tiger**, impiety in the **Bear**, bestiality in the **Boar**, ferocity in the **Lion**, obstinacy in the **Ox** and the **Mule**, deceit in the **Fox**, malice in the **Chameleon**, bitterness in the **Dog**, despair in the **Elephant**, revenge in the **Camel**, madness in the **Donkey**, buffoonery in **Apes**, fraudulent flattery in **Sirens**, fury in **Centaurs**, greed in **Harpies**, lust in **Satyrs**, and deity in the **Ox** among the **Egyptians**—as witnessed by the people of **Israel**, who also wished to worship it <note>A reference to the biblical Golden Calf</note>. 

In addition to these animals and infinite others that could be painted to denote every thought of the painter by alluding to their natures and instincts, one also finds certain behaviors of animals through which many concepts can be vividly expressed. This has been observed by all others who have written on this subject. Thus, for envy, one can paint the **Kite** <note>A medium-sized bird of prey</note>, which, seeing its chicks become fat, strikes them with its beak out of the displeasure it feels at their fatness. For temperance, one can use a **Bull**, as the Egyptians did, because once it has bred, it no longer seeks the female. For love, the **Calandra Lark**, because if it is brought to a sick person and they are destined to die, it immediately turns its head away. And for sadness, the **Raven**, which, having once been white, was changed to black by **Apollo**. For cruelty...

...they painted the **Basilisk**, which kills men with its gaze alone; for avarice, the **Toad**, which, living only on earth, always fears it will run out; for fraud, the **Siren**, who deceives listeners with her song; and for madness, the **Buffalo**, because it only leaps, runs, and makes various body movements without purpose. The **Ox**, which is used for tilling the soil, signified agriculture. To teach this to his people, Theseus—and after him Servius, King of the Romans—had this animal carved on their coins so that they would apply themselves to agriculture and not remain idle, as Plutarch and Pliny write. The **Wolf** signaled injustice, as it wishes to seize everything, whether by right or wrong; and the **Mole** represented lies, because it lives while underground but dies as soon as it emerges into the air. 

To demonstrate pride, they used the **Falcon**; for peace, the **Beaver**; for mercy, the **Pelican**, which signifies Christ on the Cross <note>The "Pelican in her Piety" was believed to peck its own breast to feed its young with its blood, a common symbol for Christ’s sacrifice</note>; for humility, the **Lamb**, which likewise represents Christ; for liberality, the **Eagle**; for truth, the **Partridge**; for diligence, the **Spider**, into which Arachne was transformed due to her contest with Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom and weaving, who turned her rival Arachne into a spider</note>; for constancy, the **Phoenix**, which is like a peacock but yellow with purple spots and three crowns on its head, which was gathered in Ethiopia by the Egyptian priests; for temperance, they depicted the **Camel**; for ignorance, the ears and head of the **Donkey**; for chastity, the **Turtledove**; for moderation, the **Ermine**; and for unhappiness, the **Tawny Owl** <note>original: "alocco"</note>. 

The **Tortoise** signified money, from which arose the motto that the Peloponnesians stamped on their coins: *Tortoises conquer virtue and wisdom* <note>original: "le Tartaruche vincono la virtù & la sapienza"</note>, meaning money. Furthermore, just as certain animals are nourished by the elements, they also used them to signify those elements; thus, for fire, they painted the **Salamander**; for earth, the **Mouse**; for air, the **Chameleon**; and for water, the **Beaver**. 

And from the natural qualities of these same animals they signaled many things, such as strength, ascension, spirit, vivacity, daring, sharpness of intellect, and also its destruction and ruin, by the **Salamander**; by the **Chameleon**, things without substance, such as simplicity, foolishness, and abuses—from which it is commonly said that light and vain men feed on air, like chameleons; by the **Beaver**, volatility, uncertainty, and the like, because water never stands still or rests, and waves are always seen to be uncertain; and by the **Mouse**, slowness, stability, firmness, gravity, and similar qualities that belong to the earth. 

The seven mortal sins are also represented by specific animals: for **Lust**, the **Camel**, the **Rooster**, and the **Beech Marten** <note>original: "foino"</note>; for **Wrath**, the **Bear**, the **Basilisk**, and the **Wild Boar**;

But it would be long and infinite to go on discussing all of them. I will only caution that when something is represented with animals, it is necessary to paint them in that posture which signifies the intended meaning; for in this way, many things will be shown through a single animal painted in different acts and effects. And therefore, one must not be thoughtless, for these demonstrations are not as easy as some might perhaps think. ### The Composition of Colors. Chapter LVII.

**B**ecause many writers have written differently about **colors** and their meanings—such as the **Platonists**, the **Aristotelians**, **Lucretius**, **Donatus**, **Marco della Frata**, **Pliny**, **Mario Equicola**, **Virgil**, **Servius**, **Telesio**, **Marcello**, **Falcone**, **Fulvio Morato**, **Artigo**, and others—I, having to write of them, have thought it best to freely follow **natural reason**, by which they are caused according to the **elements** (as we have said), and according to that, accommodate their meanings, choosing the best. And it is not out of place, having sought the meanings of other things, to also seek the meanings of colors, for herein is founded the knowledge of these colors, from which one then learns the judgment of distributing and applying them with...

fittingly for Kings, for Priests, and for eminent persons in their garments, according to the rank of each and the diverse rites of nations. Besides the fact that colors are not only attributed separately to social ranks, but also to the seasons, virtues, vices, senses, temperaments <note>original: "complessioni," referring to the four humors of the body</note>, accidents, passions, and to every other thing that can be imagined. And from this, through the composition of subjects, arise emblems, shields, crests, devices, and finally everything else one might desire. Furthermore, these colors signify the aforementioned things, and everything that we shall say in our discussion, signifying more or less of both good and evil, according to their dignity and baseness.

But because these things—without my touching upon them in particular—will be clearly perceived from what has been said thus far and will be said hereafter, I shall move on to note the meaning of the primary colors, advising that I shall mention only the principal ones, for there would be too much to say, and it would also be beside the point.

The first color, then, is **yellow**, dedicated to the **Sun** to resemble its rays, and to **gold**, the principal metal, which is known to be the heaviest of all. And because the Sun, even if it is more tinted with red at its center, nevertheless has rays that withdraw more toward the dryness of the earth, it signifies nobility, wealth, religion, clarity, gravity, justice, faith, and corruption.

**White** signifies and represents innocence and purity. In man, it is depicted for **phlegm** <note>One of the four bodily humors, associated with a calm or stolid temperament</note>; in the seasons, for **Autumn**; and among the virtues, because it is an immaculate color, it also signifies **justice**. Among the elements, it represents **water**, and among metals, **silver**; and among the Theological virtues, **hope**, which must be pure and clean.

**Red**, which among the elements represents **fire** and among the planets the **Sun** <note>Note that yellow was also linked to the solar rays, while red represents its fiery core</note>, signifies boldness, highness, victory, blood, and martyrdom—especially when inclining toward the darker and murkier red of **Mars**. In man, it shows **choler** <note>The humor of yellow bile, associated with a quick-tempered nature</note>; in the Theological virtues, **charity**, which must be kindled with love and burning; and among the seasons, it represents **summer**.

**Ultramarine blue**, which corresponds to **Jupiter**, signifies the **sanguine** temperament <note>The humor of blood, associated with a cheerful and social disposition</note>. It demonstrates highness, glory, dignity, sincerity, joy, and the like; and among the elements, the **air**.

**Black** signifies melancholy, sadness, grief, gravity, and stability, and its deity is **Saturn**. Of the seasons, it represents **winter**; of the temperaments, **melancholy**; of the virtues, **prudence**; of the elements, the **earth** (which is also shown with yellow because of its dryness); of the ages, **decrepitude**; and of accidents, **death**, which signifies division and separation. And when one wishes to write or draw with a dark color, one goes about dividing the paper by those spaces that are created.

**Green**, which demonstrates **spring**...

...and it corresponds to <term>Venus</term> <note>The planet Venus was traditionally associated with the color green or sometimes blue, representing growth and the element of water</note>, it signifies joy, charm, hope, goodness, cheerfulness, and similar things; in the stages of life, it represents youth; and among the elements, it is likewise given to water. <term>Purple</term> <note>original: "porpora"</note>, a color composed of all those mentioned above—which is nothing other than that color we call <term>dried rose</term> <note>original: "rosa secca," a dusty or muted pinkish-purple</note>, as <term>Sicillo the Herald</term> <note>Jean Courtois (active c. 1430), a famous herald known as "Sicillo," who wrote a definitive treatise on the symbolism of colors</note> says—is given to <term>Mercury</term>. It signifies, because it contains all the other colors within it, triumph, merit, honor, preeminence, and the like. For this reason, the Romans dressed in it during triumphs, as did the Emperors; and Christ Himself wore an undergarment of it, in addition to the royal cloak that was put on Him in mockery. It likewise signifies an abundance of goods, and among the ages of man, youth, and among the virtues, temperance. It also denotes the pure grace of God and of the world, and among the days, <term>Saturday</term> as a holy day. 

These are the principal colors according to the seven planets, from which all others originate and signify according to their mixtures. Hence the color <term>pale yellow</term> <note>original: "giallollino"</note>, which is made of yellow and white, signifies despair and deception; the <term>pale</term> color, which resembles pale yellow but leans a little toward black, signifies treason, suffering, anguish, and the like; therefore, a man shows no good sign when he turns pale and takes on this earthy color in his face. <term>Flesh-color</term> <note>original: "incarnato"</note>, composed of white, cinnabar, and lacquer, signifies health, a short life, high-mindedness, pleasantness, and goodness, and this is similar to the rose; but that which turns more toward white and is faded signifies hidden despair and sorrow, which is why *Ariosto*, speaking of *Bradamante* <note>In the epic poem "Orlando Furioso," Bradamante is a female knight who often expresses her emotional turmoil through her attire</note> when she was prepared to die, depicts her dressed in this color. 

The color <term>violet</term>, composed of blue, red, and white, signifies coldness, friendship, loyalty, sincerity, gratitude, and sweetness. The color <term>morello</term> <note>A dark mulberry or blackish-purple</note>, composed of the same blue, lacquer, and white—according to the ancient Arameans, who call it <term>moal</term>—signifies elevation; and from this the name <term>Morello</term> was given to the highest mountain in Tuscany. ...simple; and the dark shade that leans toward black signifies sorrow, imagination, and sadness mixed with consolation. The violet-tinged <term>beretino</term> <note>original: "beretino" — a grayish or bluish-gray color often associated with the robes of certain religious orders</note> signifies hope for courtly love, toil, patience in friendship, and simple loyalty; that which leans more toward white and is mixed with small points of red signifies hope of soon having happiness and joy, patience in adversity, labor without pain, and little knowledge; and the other which resembles ash signifies troubles and notorious thoughts that tend toward death. Azure that leans toward violet demonstrates loyalty in matters of love, good breeding, and courtesy; and the <term>taneto beretino</term> <note>original: "taneto" — a dark, tawny, or brownish-red color</note> composed of these two colors signifies little hope and consolation from weariness. Finally, all colors that can be composed of others signify according to the meanings of the simple colors from which they are made. But because meanings of virtue have been attributed only to the principal and simple colors, one must note that they can also signify the opposite depending on the places where they are placed; for if they are arranged pleasingly and with grace in worthy things, they will denote virtue, but if clumsily and in unworthy things, they will surely signify the opposite, as if corrupted.

### ***The Composition of the Colors of Precious Stones.*** Chapter 59.

**P**recious stones also have their own proper meanings, both in themselves and in respect to the things where they are painted for ornament, such as on medals, rings, thrones, miters, diadems, crowns, and scepters. And therefore, according to their nature, it is appropriate to ornament particularly the gods of the Gentiles <note>The "Gentiles" here refers to the pagan deities of Greek and Roman mythology</note> that we encounter when representing histories, as well as the Emperors—such as Gaius, Caligula, and Nero, who were the first to wear them—and princes; and not only these and others, but heaven itself, which is crowned with twelve stones, according to the elements. Beyond this, it is also necessary to ornament religious figures and priests, because we read that Aaron <note>The brother of Moses and the first High Priest of the Israelites</note>, the most ancient and principal priest among the Hebrews—leaving aside Melchizedek <note>A mysterious priest-king mentioned in Genesis; the author notes Aaron's vestments are more detailed for his purposes</note>—had upon his <term>breastplate</term> <note>original: "rationale" — the sacred "Breastplate of Judgment" (Hoshen) worn by the High Priest</note> four rows of precious stones, almost in the form of planets. In the first of these were the <term>sard</term> <note>a reddish-brown stone, often called sardius or carnelian</note>, which indicated the tribe of Dan; the topaz, which demonstrated that of Reuben; and the emerald as a sign of the tribe of Judah. In the second row was the <term>carbuncle</term> <note>a glowing red gemstone, typically a garnet or ruby</note> for the tribe of Manasseh; the sapphire for that of Asher; and the jasper for that of Simeon. In the third was the <term>ligure</term> <note>original: "Lincuri" — a legendary yellow or orange stone sometimes identified as tourmaline or amber</note> for the tribe of Issachar; the agate for that of Benjamin; and the amethyst for that of Naphtali. And finally, in the fourth was the <term>chrysolite</term> <note>a yellowish-green stone, likely peridot</note> for the tribe of Gad,

...the <term>onyx</term> <note>original: "onichino"</note> for the tribe of Zebulun, and the <term>beryl</term> for that of Ephraim. Indeed, more so because of their color, transparency, and perfection—not being corruptible like other stones—I judge that there could be nothing more suitable than them to represent the <term>angelic virtues</term>, considering that whatever other virtue one might imagine depends upon them, as does every one of our exterior and interior senses. This is all the more true because we find the virtues of these precious stones to be particularly consistent with those of the angels; therefore, it is with good reason that they can be applied to them and serve to represent them.

Consequently, the <term>sapphire</term> represents the <term>Seraphim</term> because of its transparency and color, the comfort it provides to the heart, and its power to make a person pure. The <term>emerald</term> represents the <term>Cherubim</term> to signify chastity, given its nature to lose its color or even break if someone holds it while engaging with a woman, as happened to that of the King of Hungary <note>The author refers to a popular medieval legend that an emerald would shatter if worn during an act of unchastity; King Bela IV of Hungary was often the subject of this specific anecdote.</note>. The <term>carbuncle</term> <note>original: "carbonchio" — generally referring to a deep red gemstone like a ruby or garnet</note> represents the <term>Thrones</term>, for just as they are the exalted seat of the Most High, so this stone is the most solid and brilliant among others, such that it shines in the darkness. The <term>beryl</term> represents the <term>Dominions</term>, providing help against enemies and wicked people, and making a person invincible, benign, and of good wit. The <term>onyx</term>, that is, <term>chalcedony</term>, represents the <term>Powers</term> <note>original: "podestà"</note> for driving away fantastic and melancholic illusions, for making a person victorious, and for strengthening the faculties of the head. The <term>chrysolite</term> <note>original: "grisolito"</note> represents the <term>Virtues</term> <note>The angelic rank of "Virtues."</note> for its power to grant wisdom to the soul and to repel madness and phantoms. The <term>jasper</term> represents the <term>Principalities</term> for making a person favored, powerful, and secure from fraud and from wicked men. The <term>topaz</term> represents the <term>Archangels</term> for quieting impetuous furies; thus it is said that when thrown into boiling water, it makes the boiling stop. And finally, the <term>sard</term> <note>original: "scardo/sardo"</note> represents the <term>Angels</term> for sharpening the wit and inviting souls to joy and virtue.

Not only can these stones represent the Angels in the manner we have described, but they also signify their virtues, especially the twelve stones and the Angels numbered in the twelve parts of the City of God <note>A reference to the New Jerusalem described in Revelation 21.</note> mentioned by John in the Apocalypse. There, the <term>sapphire</term> demonstrates comfort and purity; the <term>emerald</term>, chastity; the <term>carbuncle</term>, clarity of mind and justice; the <term>beryl</term>, victory, kindness, and wit; the <term>chalcedony</term>, dominion and health; the <term>chrysolite</term>, wisdom; the <term>jasper</term>, grace, wisdom, and sincerity; the <term>topaz</term>, refuge and restraint; and finally, the <term>sard</term>, sharpness, the kindling of joy, and the end. Therefore, in distributing these stones within ornaments, one must always have regard for these meanings of virtue attributed to them, so that there may be that correspondence and proportion from which beauty is born in all things.

## BOOK 2

I could further describe how these same precious stones correspond to our senses in terms of their colors and virtues; but I would be too lengthy. Therefore, it will be better to proceed to explain how they signify the seasons, the months, and the times, following the natural order. 

<term>Martianus</term> <note>Martianus Capella, a 5th-century author whose work on the liberal arts remained influential through the Renaissance.</note> writes, in providing a portrait of the **Sun**, that he wore a crown on his head set with twelve precious stones. Three of these signified **Summer**; they were placed at the front, above his brow, sparkling so intensely that one could not fix their gaze upon them. They were called <term>lyncurium</term> <note>original: "lincuri" — a legendary stone said to be formed from lynx urine; historically associated with amber or tourmaline.</note>, <term>carbuncles</term> <note>original: "carbonculi" — deep red gems like rubies or garnets.</note>, and <term>ceraunia</term> <note>original: "cerauni" — "thunder-stones," believed to fall from the sky during storms.</note>. With great reason these three stones have been chosen as symbols of this season: for the first, being radiant and flaming, represents the month of **June**. The second, redder and more brilliant than the first, represents the great heat of the sun in the month of **July**; and the third, yellow in color, almost like fire and shining, demonstrates the final month of the season, **August**. 

On the left side of the crown, the Sun then had three other stones that represented **Spring**: namely, the <term>emerald</term>, the <term>Scythian stone</term> <note>original: "scithi" — likely a variety of emerald or green jasper from the Scythian region.</note>, and <term>jasper</term>. This is because the first is supremely green and tints the surrounding air with green, just as the earth turns green at the beginning of Spring; therefore, it signifies the month of **March**. The second is likewise green like the first, and perhaps even more so, as it is the most perfect stone of its kind; thus it is placed at the midpoint of Spring, representing flowery **April**. The third is a transparent green, but mixed with diverse colors, especially red, whereby it represents **May**. 

Next, on the right side of the crown, he had three other lovely stones which indicate **Autumn**; these were <term>hyacinth</term> <note>original: "giacinto" — in historical lapidaries, this often refers to a yellow or orange zircon rather than the modern blue flower.</note>, <term>pracondità</term> <note>original: "pracondità" — a rare or perhaps corrupted name for a translucent, water-like stone.</note>, and <term>heliotrope</term> <note>original: "Elitropia" — also known as bloodstone, a green stone with red spots.</note>. The first is yellow, but retains a watery quality—that is, a pale gold—and here Autumn begins, denoting the month of **September**. The second has a translucent whiteness like pure water and is the middle of Autumn, representing the month of **October**. The third is clear and green, marked with red streaks, and represents the month of **November**. 

Lastly, on the back part, he had three others which represented **Winter**, which he names as <term>hieracitis</term> <note>original: "Hieracita" — the "hawk-stone," so named because its patterns resemble hawk feathers.</note>, **diamond**, and **crystal**. The first is of a variegated color and turns black like the feathers of a sparrowhawk; therefore, it represents horrid and melancholy **December**. The second shows a color that tends toward black, by which it signifies dark **January**. But the third is clearer than the diamond, whereby it denotes the month of **February**, which approaches Spring. From the colors of these stones, one can dress the figures of the seasons and months as required. Furthermore, these same stones, which we discussed a short while ago, have several other meanings...

The **Diamond** primarily signifies hardness and stability; the **alabaster**, purity; the **magnet** <note>original: "calamita" — lodestone</note>, power and strength; the **jasper**, quenching <note>original: "ammorzare" — to dampen or extinguish; in lapidaries, jasper was believed to "quench" or stop bleeding and fever.</note>; the **heliotrope** <note>Also known as bloodstone.</note>, blindness; the **topaz**, coldness; the **abeston** <note>original: "abeston" — asbestos, which in medieval and Renaissance lore was considered a "stone" that, once lit, could never be extinguished.</note>, continuation, since once lit it is never again extinguished; the **agate**, fortitude and also persuasion; the **alectorius** <note>original: "alettorio" — a mythical stone supposedly found in the gizzards of capons or roosters, believed to grant invincibility.</note>, lust; the **almandine**, intelligence; the **amethyst**, vigilance and sobriety; the **balas** <note>original: "balaso" — the balas ruby, a variety of spinel.</note>, lodging, because it is the "house" of the carbuncle; the **borax** <note>original: "boraso" — likely the "toadstone," which was sometimes called borax in early mineralogy and was associated with cleansing toxins.</note>, purgation; the **beryl**, love; the **coral**, beginning and end; the **caesite** <note>original: "cesita" — possibly a reference to *gaesates* or another mineral described as changing appearance in the presence of metals.</note>, the harlot—because just as the stone takes on every sort of metal color, so she takes every sort of money, to say no more; and the **pearl**, whiteness. 

And with the colors of these stones, one can "clothe" all the figures that they signify. Now, to express them in historical paintings, one must employ the rarities of the stones, first imitating their color and then their luster—whether using the color of silver or gold, whether light or dark, as we shall see is required. And if other garments go over them, one can create the brilliance on top and shade it with its own shadows, while the underlying garment remains distinct with its own various shadows.

In this art, **Gaudenzio** <note>Gaudenzio Ferrari (c. 1471–1546), a renowned Northern Italian painter and sculptor famous for his lifelike multi-media displays at the Sacro Monte of Varallo.</note> was most exquisite. And in this area, the sculptors lose ground, because they do not extend themselves to this level (as I said in the first book), nor are they able to express in faces the movements and colors in the form that nature grants to painting. Thus, they are far from the target that the Florentine **Varchi** <note>Benedetto Varchi (1503–1565), an influential humanist whose "Paragone" debate compared the merits of painting and sculpture.</note> wrote about regarding these arts.

### The Composition of Various Instruments. Chapter 60.

**A**ll the science that the **Egyptians** possessed in their sacred images <note>A reference to hieroglyphs, which Renaissance scholars viewed as purely symbolic or allegorical images.</note> made of instruments alone—with which we walk, work, and finally do everything we can—was based on nothing other than the effects that these artificial bodies (or those imitated for orderly convenience) produced, of which they always chose the most principal of every kind. Because by choosing one that produced a certain effect, and another that expressed it more than the first, it would certainly carry another particular significance. Since all instruments, just as they perform and achieve all effects, so do they signify all things. 

Hence, as **Horapollo** <note>Horapollo was the purported author of the *Hieroglyphica*, a work rediscovered in the 15th century that offered (often imaginative) symbolic explanations for Egyptian carvings.</note> writes, the Egyptians, wishing to depict a man who is always of one mind <note>original: "d'una voglia" — of one consistent will or desire.</note>, painted a **lyre**, because alone among all instruments it continues...

...which <note>referring to a hunting horn or trumpet from the previous page</note> is used to gather dogs for the hunt, just as God himself gathers the waters, the winds, and the sea gods. The long and curved **trumpet** denotes movement and incitement; because with its sound, soldiers are moved and invited to battle. The **bell** signifies assembly and also a sign. A single painted **arrow** represents the liberal art of **Logic**, and it is also indicated by a **rolled paper** held with it, because logic stings with its words, discerning the false from the true in the manner of an arrow; and it is shown with the paper because one does not know what it wishes to infer unless it explains itself, and no other science is permitted to penetrate it, but it penetrates and discerns the others. 

The figure of the **Cross** signifies faith; the common **column** signifies fortitude; the **base** signifies the beginning; the **capital** <note>the top part of a column</note> signifies the end; and the **beam** signifies support, for it serves no other purpose. A lit **torch** denotes an ambush; the **bit** <note>the part of a horse's harness</note> denotes reason; the **goad** with **spurs** denotes indissolubility; and the **ring** denotes recognition.

And therefore, different crowns signify different principalities; **nets** denote gathering, while **closed nets** denote imprisonment; the **road** signifies freedom; a **rope** and a **knot** signify servitude; an **altar** with its equipment signifies religion; a **castle on a mountain** signifies nobility; a **cithara** <term>cithara: an ancient Greek musical instrument similar to a lyre</term> or **harp** signifies joy; and a **water bird** that bathes signifies instability. 

Two **birds** facing each other with open beaks denote doubt; a painted **tower** denotes strength of action; an **empty chariot** without anything else denotes a man without reason; two **gates** denote hospitality; a **naked, drawn sword** denotes war; the **ball** denotes the world; a **bridge** over water denotes labor without fruit; the **file** denotes robbery <note>original: "rapina", implying something that steadily wears away or snatches</note> that always takes; **white paper** denotes subjection; the **writing pen** denotes knowledge; the **nail** denotes firmness; the **brush** denotes painting; the **chisel** denotes sculpture; the **square** denotes architecture; the **sphere** denotes astrology; the **tile** <note>original: "tessera", often used as a mnemonic token</note> denotes memory; the **alembic** <term>alembic: a tool used in distilling, here representing the art of chemistry or alchemy</term> denotes alchemy; **masks** denote comedy; **playing cards** denote discord; a **line** denotes geometry; **numbers** denote arithmetic; a **blowing wind** denotes fury; a **torn garment** denotes poverty; and a **cap with feathers** denotes light-mindedness.

...hidden prudence; a **urinal** <note>original: *un'orinale*; a glass vessel used for uroscopy, the primary diagnostic tool of the era, here symbolizing medicine</note> represents medicine; and wishing finally to represent the **laws**, they painted the instruments with which wrongdoers are punished by justice. For we read that certain peoples sought out a Greek philosopher to ordain some law for them, by which they might live uprightly; and he had various instruments for punishing wrongdoers manufactured, and having placed them in the square before their eyes, he said: "take heed that this is the law I give you," and then he fell silent. And thus one may compose subjects, emblems, devices, and the reverses of medals, which all move toward a single end: to signify some hidden subject, acting as the soul to the body, in which the intelligence is demonstrated under other forms.

### *Composition of painting and creating diverse landscapes. Chapter LXI.*

**I**t is certainly a most difficult work to represent landscapes with the artifice required of them, regarding both the sight and their **recession** <term>recession: the technique of making objects appear to move back into the distance of the picture plane</term>; which is a particular grace given to painters. This is because landscapes must be distinguished into three parts. The first must be visible from nearby; the second more blurred; and the third should almost lose itself entirely, vanishing into infinity, so that the second is effectively composed in correct perspective with the first. And to express this well, one must have a particular grace and a divine gift, because however eminent one may be in making figures, one cannot acquire this art unless he has a natural grace for demonstrating it. This was the case with the greatest painter among the moderns <note>Likely referring to Michelangelo, who focused on human anatomy and famously disregarded landscape painting</note> and many other excellent men who remained excluded from this skill. 

But those who have possessed excellence and grace in this part, in both private and public places, have found diverse ways of making them. First are the fetid, dark, subterranean, religious, and mournful places, in which are represented cemeteries, tombs, uninhabited houses, terrifying and solitary places, dens, caverns, pools, stagnant ponds, and the like. Then there are privileged places in which are expressed temples, consistories, tribunals, gymnasiums, and schools. There are places of fire and blood, where there are furnaces, mills, slaughterhouses, gallows, and scaffolds <note>original: *patibuli*</note>. Others are clear and of serene air, in which are represented palaces, the houses of princes, pulpits, theaters, thrones, and all magnificent and royal things. Others are delightful, in which are fountains, meadows, gardens, seas, shores, baths, and places where...

...[they are] danced. There is also another kind of **landscapes** <note>original: *paesi*; here referring to scenic backgrounds or landscape paintings</note> in which are depicted workshops, schools, taverns, merchants' squares; others are made as deserts, forests, cliffs, rocks, mountains, woods, ditches, waters, rivers, ships, populous places, and **steam baths** <note>original: *stuffe*; small heated rooms or saunas</note>, or as we might call them, thermal baths. And he who has knowledge of these types of landscapes will be able to successfully bring them together in practice into one scene, or into several, according to what seems orderly to his judgment. 

The first among the ancients who, in making landscapes, expressed lightning bolts, flashes of light, seas, and thunder was **Apelles** <note>The most celebrated painter of ancient Greece (4th century BCE)</note>; and among the modern Italians, it was **Titian**, who in his landscapes expressed everything that is possible to represent with such art. Many other Italians also succeeded in this, among whom was **Raphael**, especially in expressing the dark night, the bright day, and the lovely dawn. **Gaudenzio** <note>Gaudenzio Ferrari, known for his dramatic frescoes and mountain scenes</note> was most successful with rocks, grottos, cliffs, mountains, and caverns, and with small grasses and flowers, investigated in their natural whimsy. 

**Giorgione of Castelfranco** was successful in showing fish beneath clear waters, trees, fruits, and whatever he wished with a most beautiful style. **Dosso Dossi** excelled in the **recession** <term>recession: the illusion of depth or "fleeing" into the distance</term> of woods with rays of the Sun flashing through them, which **Lorenzo Lotto of Bergamo** also did, as did **Barnazano**, who was rare in demonstrating, among other things, fine sand. Together with them were **Girolamo Muziano**, **Paris Bordon**, and **Francesco Vicentino**, who expressed dust in the air in such a way that truly anyone who sees it can consider it nothing other than dust being agitated by the winds, especially over certain figures somewhat distant from the eye. 

All painters must observe this prudence, unless they wish to place figures directly before the eyes without any **recession** <note>original: *sfuggimento*; the way objects appear to diminish and lose clarity in the distance</note> of the sight. **Girolamo Romanino** and **Bassano** excellently expressed animals, and depicted frogs beneath the water and figures from the waist down appearing different from those same parts that are above, showing their **distortion** <note>original: *tortuosità*; likely referring to the refraction of light in water</note>, and likewise all the other parts that belong to landscapes. The son of this same Bassano was also singular, who divinely expressed mountains, the splendor and reflection of the Moon in the waters, and all that was required in landscapes. 

**Aurelio Luini** understood this art very well; it happened once that while visiting Titian and asking his opinion on how to harmonize trees with the background—besides many reasons he heard from him about blurring the leaves with the field—he saw a marvelous landscape of his [Titian's] in the house. Upon seeing it, Aurelio initially judged it to be a **smeared mess** <note>original: *cosa empiastrata*; referring to Titian's thick, late-style brushwork which looks messy up close but resolves at a distance</note>, but then, having retreated to a distance, it seemed to him that the sun shone within it, making the roads recede here and there; so much so that Aurelio had to say that he had never seen...

...the rarest thing in the world for landscapes. And therefore, in these, one must make the principal trees tall, so that the figures placed near them appear in the correct proportions, as they should be. This effect was demonstrated by **Titian** <note>Tiziano Vecelli (c. 1488–1576), the leading painter of the Venetian school</note> himself in the great wood where **St. Peter Martyr** <note>referring to Titian's lost masterpiece, *The Assassination of Saint Peter Martyr*</note> was killed; this landscape is the most beautiful ever painted, and is on a panel in Venice in the church of San Giovanni e Paolo.

Among the Germans, both High and Low <note>referring to Upper Germany and the Low Countries/Netherlands</note>, those who have been excellent in landscapes are **Joachim of Antwerp** <note>Joachim Patinir</note>, and above the others **Herri met de Bles**, called "of the Owl" <note>original: *Henrico Blessio dalla ciuetta*; known for hiding a small owl in his landscapes</note>, **Matthys Cock**, and that other one called **of the Hare**, **Jan of Holland**, **Frans Mostaert**, **Pieter Bruegel**, **Giacomo Grimaldi**, **Lucas of Holland** <note>Lucas van Leyden</note>, **Albrecht Dürer**, **Georg Pencz**, **Hans Sebald Beham**, Giovanni the brother of Herri of Antwerp, **Hubert**, and many others. 

There have also been some who have created various chimeras and monsters with birds and fruits, such as among the Italians: **Piero di Cosimo**, **Perino del Vaga**, **Rosso [Fiorentino]**, **[Giovanni da] Udine**, and **Troso**; and among the foreigners: **Pieter Bruegel**, **Jacob de Backer** <note>original: *Giacomo di Lunghi*</note>, **Pieter of Holland**, **Israhel van Meckenem** <note>original: *Israel Metro*</note>, and the good **Martin [Schongauer]**. 

And in this matter, let painters always be advised that the Germans and others most excellent in this field have always placed the figures against the darkest background, such as in woods, caves, and caverns; so that they stand out better to the eye, making the background so that it is not mixed with red nor green, but of a **tawny** <note>original: *taneto*; a dark brownish-orange or tan color</note> and dark color, as is used by excellent and knowledgeable painters. Also, if one wishes to make a history <note>a narrative or mythological scene</note> where many figures stand, with much air and landscapes, one must always take care to place the brightness of the air away from the figures, so that the tinted air remains behind the figures with dexterity and grace, just as those who had the design and strength for such a part have done successfully. 

And in such recessions of landscapes, **Francesco Pelliccione**, called **Il Basso**, was rare in the art of **damascening** <term>damascening: the art of inlaying different metals into one another, typically gold or silver into steel; original: *gemina*</term>, an art subordinate to painting, leaving behind the other arts likewise subordinate to painting, such as **mosaic**, **marquetry** <note>original: *tarsie*; inlaid wood</note>, **stone inlay** <note>original: *comesso*</note>, **miniatures**, the **weaving of histories** <note>tapestries</note>, **niello** <note>a black metallic alloy used to fill engraved designs</note>, **sgraffito**, **embroidery**, along with the other arts which are named in the fifth book when treating perspective and its definition. In these arts, albeit differently according to their genres and species, all sorts of landscapes suited to the aforementioned painting are arranged.

...color, now of the dawn, now of flowers, now of April, and now of May, which the poets have alluded to no less appropriately than charmingly. Thus in the child, there is nothing more graceful and more lovely than that purity and sincerity which is always seen shining through all the acts of a tender infant. If an ingenious painter or sculptor happens to express this happily and represent it to the life in his works, it is a marvelous thing to say how much ornament and grace it adds to them. Indeed, it seems that without such an ornament, complete loveliness cannot be given to any work, however excellent and perfect it may be in other respects. Therefore, the greatest minds that have flourished in our age have adorned and, so to speak, seasoned the majority of their works with them. 

For in the mysteries of the Passion of our Lord, they have created children who weep for his death, and others who carry through the air the spears, the crowns of thorns, and the other instruments of the Passion. And they have also been accustomed to place children alongside the Prophets and the Sibyls, as is seen in the heavens of the [Last] Judgment by **Buonarroti** <note>Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475–1564); referring to the Sistine Chapel</note> and in the *Peace* of **Raphael** <note>Raffaello Sanzio (1483–1520); likely referring to his fresco of the Sibyls in the church of Santa Maria della Pace in Rome</note>. 

One should, therefore, take these as examples in paintings to represent children who, as a sign of humility, hold a lamb; others with a skull; others around dark tombs with torches—either lit or extinguished—weeping bitterly; others with rays of fire and torches; and others with trophies of the Passion in their hands. In more cheerful histories <note>The term "histories" (istorie) refers to narrative paintings depicting historical, biblical, or mythological events</note>, these infants should be introduced, for example, with the papal keys and the throne, or with miters, bulls <note>Official papal documents</note>, and other similar emblems of dignity and triumph. 

Beyond this, in the heavens above the clouds, there should be **putti** <term>putti: plump, often winged infant figures used in art to represent cherubs or secular spirits</term> with joyful expressions and their characteristic childish manners and acts, but with twists and playful poses <note>original: "rauolgimenti & scherzi"; referring to the complex, spiraling physical movements (contrapposto) typical of Mannerist art</note>. Others still, with crowns in their hands, should be in the act of placing them on the head of the Virgin, or on the heads of some of the saints. Around Christ and his mother, these children are also well-placed with birds in their hands, violets, lutes, and other cheerful things for the delight and pleasure of the Christ Child; and likewise when he and his mother ascend to heaven, representing them in various and diverse attitudes. 

Where beauty, lordships, virtues, and especially **Charity** <note>In Renaissance iconography, the virtue of Charity is almost always personified as a woman nursing or surrounded by several young children</note> are painted, children must not be omitted, for they are appropriate to these subjects not only for beauty but for ornament. Likewise, on candelabra and on coats of arms, there should be children around trophies and victorious spoils, with masks of animals attached—such as rams, lions, goats, monkeys, eagles, the flayed heads of bulls, and wild boars—and with the heads of laughing demigods, such as satyrs, fauns, sileni, and pans, who go...

[they are] crowned with herbs, flowers, and fruits, according to their nature, sometimes even wrapping them in scrollwork <term>scartocci</term> <note>Ornate ornamental frames or cartouches that look like rolled paper, typical of Renaissance and Mannerist decoration</note>. Many times children are also made flying to crown poets with laurel; furthermore, in friezes, following the order of music, they are introduced jumping, shouting, and making their various bundles. Similarly, around the **Moon**, they carry vessels and water jars <term>hydriae</term> that pour water. Finally, around **Chastity**, the loves should be chained, stripped of their quivers, bows, and weapons, and given over as prey to pure and chaste loves. In this part, beyond the other precautions one must take, the principal one must be to represent these children in a believable and appropriate manner, and not to do as some who place a heavy weight in their arms, which it is impossible could be suitable for them. And this shall suffice to outline all that must be observed and noted in this matter.

[The palm] tree <note>The text begins mid-word, continuing from the previous page's "palmi-"</note>, sends out every month at the birth of the Moon a branch, so that the entire year is completed in twelve branches. For this reason, when they wished to represent a single month, they painted a small palm twig. To signify the victory of **Diana** <note>Goddess of the hunt and the moon</note>, they likewise used a branch of this palm or a garland; to signify life, they painted the oak of **Jupiter**; for sadness and for death, the cypress of **Pluto** <note>God of the Underworld</note>; for peace, the olive of **Mercury** and **Minerva**; for victory, they similarly painted the laurel tree dedicated to **Apollo**, and also for liberty. With the pine they represented fraud; with the mulberry <term>celso</term> consecrated to the Goddess **Vesta**, sadness and death; with ivy, lust; and with the poplar, time, attributed to **Hercules** as an indicator of time.

The fig given to **Silvanus** <note>A Roman spirit of the woods and fields</note> was a symbol of memory; the vine consecrated to **Bacchus** <note>God of wine and ecstasy</note> represents ourselves—to what end we are produced in the world and what we are bound to; the myrtle signifies pleasantness, and therefore it was given to **Venus**. The peach was attributed to the God of silence called **Sigaleon** by the Greeks, and by the Egyptians, **Harpocrates**; they paint grass <term>gramigna</term> for firmness and renewal, and it is subject to **Mars**. The pomegranate demonstrates the expectation of fruit from faith; the medlar <term>nespolo</term> signifies lost hope; the hazel <term>nizzuolo</term> a wicked tongue; the elm sacred to **Neptune** is a symbol of obtaining what one desires; and the pear, of dying.

The quince signifies worthlessness; the willow, artifice and the skill of persuasion; and the fir is a sign of sustaining danger. The alder denotes sterility, as does the wild olive; the Turkey oak <term>cerro</term> represents resistance and robustness; the <unclear>idalogo</unclear> <note>Possibly a reference to a plant from Mount Ida, or a corruption of another botanical term</note> signifies sorrow; the juniper sacred to **Juno** represents maintenance and stability; the boxwood <term>busso</term>, which is under the protection of **Vulcan**, represents a union of strength; and myrrh signifies weeping and preservation. The yew <term>nasso</term> or <term>tasso</term> demonstrates a man of bad quality, and the walnut <term>noce</term> one who harms <note>A wordplay on the Italian "noce" (walnut) and "nuoce" (he harms)</note> and is without love. The sessile oak <term>rouere</term> dedicated to **Hercules** demonstrates hardness and strength; the Italian oak <term>escolo</term> abundance and wealth; the linden <term>tiglia</term>, for being incorruptible, signifies health.

And so all the other trees have their natural meanings and are under the protection of a God, such as the apple of **Ceres**, the cornelian cherry of **Mars**, and the coral of **Mercury**. Therefore, in the first rank of flowers is the **red rose**, which represents spring under its Goddess, and signifies tenderness of soul. But the **white** one demonstrates pure love; the **flesh-colored** one signifies lascivious love. The **lily** signifies chastity; the **white violet** the beginning of purity, and the **yellow** the beginning of nobility. **Turquoise** colors denote reality; **purple** denotes majesty; **orange-colored hollyhocks** <note>original: "rosoni"; likely referring to large, rose-like mallows</note> denote love of wealth and nobility; flowers of **violet, turquoise, red, and white** denote a loyal and pure beginning. The **amaranth** demonstrates immortality; the **acanthus** despair; the **sunflower** <note>original: "clitia"; referring to the nymph Clytie who turned into a heliotrope</note> unhappiness; the **narcissus** death; the **poppy** the illness of man <note>likely referring to the sleep-inducing or numbing effects of opium</note>; the **carnation** desire; **jasmine** discarded purity; the **broom** plants nobility without wealth; and those of the **orange** and **citron** fruitful purity. These and all other flowers, fruits, herbs, and trees of whatever sort they may be, can each be composed by themselves and together upon the bodies <note>referring to the allegorical figures or "bodies" of emblems</note> which we have treated above.

Lastly, concerning metals: **gold**, the first and most noble of all, from which crowns are made, signifies loyalty, liberty, empire, rest, contentment, joy, dominion, justice, devotion, and similar virtues; **silver** signifies doubt, timidity, and fear; **copper** signifies lust, flattery, deceits, adulation, and frauds; **iron**, from which crowns are also made, signifies anger, disdain, sorrow, insolence, cruelty, envy, slaughter, and robbery; and finally **lead**...

There are many other compositions, both natural and imagined or invented by capricious painters, which I have not collected in this book. We will treat lastly the composition that must be imprinted upon the imagination of painters; and how and in what manner they should express it following true prudence; and afterwards, we will discuss the various passions <note>original: "affetti"; the emotional and physical expressions of the soul</note> of the human body described by the rarest poets who have ever lived in the world.

### *The Composition of Forms within the Idea.* Chapter LXIV.

**F**rom the deepest and most intimate parts of the minds of those first ancients, the rare and unique forms of composition already sprang forth. These were held in wonder and awe by the world until that most happy and Golden Age, which has never been equaled, which produced the divine and immortal painters and sculptors **Apelles**, **Timanthes**, **Protogenes**, **Lysippus**, **Phidias**, and **Praxiteles**. No one in any other age has ever been able to reach their height and eminence, neither in Greece nor among the Romans. Among the Romans, these two arts declined due to the floods and ruins brought by the barbarians, and they later began to rise again in the time of **Cimabue** <note>Cenni di Pepo (c. 1240–1302), an early pioneer of the Italian Renaissance</note> and reached their peak in the times of **Buonarroti** <note>Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475–1564)</note>, so much so that there is no doubt that from that age onward, they have begun to decline somewhat. This happened for no other reason than that their practitioners have abandoned the aforementioned path of the ancients: conceiving and, so to speak, composing in their mind and **idea** <note>the Neo-Platonic concept of a perfect mental image that precedes the physical work of art</note> what they intend to do, before they take up the brush or chisel and put it into practice. This process must first and continually be done in solitude and silence; without these, it is impossible for anyone to ever speculate <note>contemplate or visualize</note> well, as was done by the most famous and celebrated men in this art whom we have already named in the penultimate chapter of the first book. Elsewhere, in the chapter on the necessity of practice, we have compared them to poets. Besides these men, **Perino del Vaga**, **Antonio da Correggio**, **Rosso** <note>Rosso Fiorentino</note>, **Mazzolino**, **Sarto** <note>Andrea del Sarto</note>, **Luini**, and among the Germans, the singular **Albrecht Dürer** and **Lucas van Leyden**, were accustomed, before all other things, to...

...[no one is able] to conceive in their Idea the form of whatever they proposed to do, and before they set out to draw anything, to see it perfectly well with their imagination. Therefore, in imitation of these [ancients], once the story has been read or the whim <note>original: "capriccio"; refers to a playful or inventive artistic idea</note> of what one wishes to paint has been thought out, it is necessary to have it in the mind, as formed and distinct as if it were seen in reality with the eyes. And then, with one’s talent <note>term: *ingegno* — the innate creative intelligence and spirit of the artist</note>, one should go about considering the space where the thing read or imagined is to be represented; thus it will succeed in execution without any offense to the beholders. And it must be noted that herein consists the principal perfection of the work. For a perfect beginning cannot exist without the knowledge of its middle and its end.

Whoever becomes familiar with this composition within the Idea, let them know for certain that they will not be among the number of the imprudent who wish to make—or as they say, "give motion to"—the forms imagined by others. For even if such forms were imagined by them, but not composed within the Idea, they would nonetheless express them poorly, as if afflicted by that curse which confuses and strips the spirit of its strength. I speak of that great quantity of inventions drawn upon printed papers, recently discovered in Germany by **Israel van Meckenem** <note>original: "Israel Metro"; referring to the prolific 15th-century German engraver</note> and in Italy by **Andrea Mantegna**; these are truly a confusion for our souls. Without doubt, if our souls were deprived of these examples, they would investigate more subtly, and, sparing no effort, would always produce some beautiful invention of their own, according to their nature and genius.

Nor do I believe for any other reason that the works of the ancients were so marvelous and excellent, as we see (leaving aside paintings) in many relics of their sculptures. The skilled painter, therefore, knowing the sentiment of the stories and having composed them in the mind, then knows how to express them easily and without looking at the inventions of others, using the measurements and motions suitable to the nature of things. Therefore, I will always praise him who, before setting himself to the work, first seeks to see in the Idea everything he wishes to do. For the composition of the mind, which is not seen, offends judgment less than the composition of practice, which is seen, which interrupts knowledge through the eyes from which it is seen <note>The author argues that a mental plan is purer than a physical draft; physical "practice" can distract the eye and mind if the concept is not fully realized internally first.</note>.

And it is certain that to those who imagine subtle things, it seems that not seeing and not hearing brings them help, as they do not feel themselves disturbed by the inconveniences that the eyes bring through objects and the ears through sounds. Hence, all skilled painters, as I said at the beginning, have practiced this: forming all things they wished to do first in their Idea. To do this more easily, it is necessary in every way to flee from noise, and especially from opportunities to see [other things]; because there is nothing that more draws a man...

...[moved] out of purpose and does not let it stay collected within itself, [distracted] by objects. Thus we see that those who, amidst noise and din, stand with the stylus and with the pen storming upon the papers, in the end cannot find the <term>invention</term> <note>original: "inuētione"; the creative conceptualization and arrangement of a subject</note> of anything they wish to do, nor even "give motion," as they say, to the imagined figures. It is read for this purpose that Homer, Democritus, and Plato deprived themselves of the light of their eyes <note>A common Renaissance trope suggesting that physical blindness allows for greater spiritual or intellectual vision</note> to better and more subtly investigate the nature of that which they had conceived and imagined in their minds. 

Now returning to our first purpose, I find also that once a thing has been formed in the <term>Idea</term> <note>the perfect mental archetype of a work of art</note>, which one then wishes to draw, it will be more easily drawn on material that is not extreme—such as, for instance, on very white paper—and with an instrument that is not extremely sharp, such as a pen dipped in ink. Instead, one should use a very fine pen dipped only in watercolor, or with German stone <note>likely black chalk or slate</note> and red chalk, and upon tinted paper. In this way, because there is little difference between the color of the drawing and the paper, and without the confusion caused by the object, everything conceived in the mind may be quietly hinted at. Then, without taxing the brain, one proceeds to the <term>practice</term> <note>original: "pratica"; the physical execution of the art</note>, transferring the work onto tinted or white papers, or wherever one wishes, to make them diligent and clear. 

In this manner, I have seen many drawings that Leonardo <note>Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519)</note> made of inventions on tinted papers, and also white ones, but then drawn and barely touched with red or black pencil, so as not to generate confusion in the mind by seeing two extreme colors contending together—as is black ink upon white paper. Upon such paper the profound Buonarroti <note>Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475–1564)</note> used to draw subtly and with great thoughtfulness; he would then use darker ink to deepen those parts that, according to his great Idea, seemed to require it. 

And in this, all the excellent painters have cried out, some in one fashion and some in another, with long and profound speculation. Thus, some—like Raphael, Polidoro <note>Polidoro da Caravaggio</note>, Gaudenzio <note>Gaudenzio Ferrari</note>, and others whom it would take too long to remember—have mostly composed their inventions on tinted papers and reached the pinnacle of excellence, both in drawing and in invention. 

Although neither invention nor drawing has ever been so fully mastered that a thing, however ingenious and well-drawn it may be (a truth that holds in every profession), cannot be improved by considering it and making of it a visible mirror in the Idea; for reason and experience are the mothers of judgment. Therefore, whoever wishes to proceed judiciously in their works should first form the composition in the mind. With the speed of the intellect, what is missing is suddenly supplied, and what is superfluous is taken away; everything is arranged with swiftness, and afterward, through practice, it is expressed in the manner described, for practice [is...]

## BOOK 2

...servant of <term>science</term> <note>original: "scienza"; here meaning the theoretical and mathematical foundations of art</note> and of the <term>Idea</term>. He who does not observe this, but follows only <term>practice</term> <note>original: "prattica"; technical skill or habit without theoretical backing</note>—which, however, cannot be good without science—ultimately produces nothing reasonable nor worthy of praise. 

And finally, I conclude, following natural judgment, that no matter how great or diligent a colorist one may be, if they lack <term>invention</term> and simply lift figures wholesale from the papers and works of others, they should not be called a painter, but rather an imitator—or indeed, a destroyer of the art. Such people are content to merely labor over the inventions of others and abhor the laborious study that must necessarily be undertaken by anyone aspiring to any degree of excellence. I have emphasized this many times in various places in these books, as it is a matter of the utmost importance. 

Therefore, everyone must, by all means, follow the spark of their own inventions and arrange them according to proportionate and natural orders. One should leave behind the inventions and eccentricities of others, or at least imitate them in such a way that they are altered and made to appear as one's own particular style, to the honor and reputation of Painting—which sees and contemplates everything as a prudent imitatress of nature. 

To these warnings I have gathered so far—which have come largely from the most singular men in our profession—some others are added that are of equal importance. Perhaps I have mentioned them scattered in other places, but they can never be remembered enough. 

Among others, I judge that the painter should never take up the brush except when he feels himself excited by a **natural furor** <note>original: "natural furore"; a state of divine or poetic inspiration believed to be necessary for true creativity</note>. There is no doubt that this flows within painters just as it does within poets. Nor should he ever constrain himself to the commands of others, for it is impossible to create any praiseworthy work in defiance of the Muses, who are greatly indignant at being "hired out like carriages" <note>original: "mandare à vettura"; a metaphor meaning to be used for menial, mercenary, or forced labor</note>. 

And for this reason, I would also advise that one should never paint according to the whim and prescription of others unless the painter is absolutely forced to do so. Instead, one should only paint one's own inventions. If our modern painters observed this, I have no doubt that this age could also have its own **Parrhasius** and **Apelles** <note>Famous painters of Ancient Greece, cited here as the pinnacle of artistic achievement</note>. This is especially true if, as I have said elsewhere and must be repeated a thousand times, one always keeps proportion, so to speak, before one's eyes, along with a perfect knowledge of **perspective**. Without these, I have mentioned elsewhere that someone used to say:

-> The painter is in the same condition as a Doctor who does not know Grammar. <- 
<note>This analogy suggests that perspective is the fundamental "language" or syntax of visual art; without it, the artist is illiterate in their own field.</note>

It is also an important warning that when one has to render a figure or anything else that has already been done once, the form and proportion should always be changed. It is never possible, while keeping the same proportion and contour, to make it as good as the first. Furthermore, in depicting movements, one must always avoid acute angles and straight lines, because they do not follow the natural form...
