-># BOOK SIX<-

<term>serpentine line</term> <note>original: "linea serpentinata"; a S-shaped pose characteristic of Mannerist art, suggesting movement and grace</note> represented by the circumference and the twisting of a flame of fire. I further recommend that one should never place an arm or any other limb in front of the figure's face, unless forced to do so by necessity—and especially when the figure is positioned high up, where the face must turn downward. This is because the face is the part of the body that our eyes always look upon first and with the greatest delight. 

And returning to <term>inventions</term> <note>original: "inuentioni"; the creative concept or compositional arrangement of a work</note>, another thing comes to mind that is quite harmful: the self-imposed restriction of painting inventions proposed by others—that is, taking and essentially tracing things already painted by someone else. I would advise that no one ever do this. Besides the manifest risk of being seen as a thief, one suffers much more and completes the work with greater labor. Indeed, even a painter of little understanding and practice will undoubtedly express and complete his own concept with greater speed than a practiced expert will when painting a discovery made by another. 

Nevertheless, he who does his work more accurately, even if it takes more time, is always more worthy of praise than he who works with speed and does it poorly. One must keep many principles before one's eyes that the latter lacks. It is written of <term>Apelles</term> <note>A celebrated painter of ancient Greece</note> that when someone told him they had completed a large painting in a short time, he replied that this was quite obvious from the work itself—just as <term>Michelangelo</term> once joked with his <term>Vasari</term> <note>Giorgio Vasari, the famous biographer and painter, who was known for his speed</note>. 

In this regard, several artists have been principally celebrated: <term>Raphael</term>, <term>Polidoro</term>, <term>Parmigianino</term>, <term>Gaudenzio</term>, and certain Venetians. Some of these, however, used inventions with coloring and natural imitations while leaving behind <term>design</term> <note>original: "disegno"; meaning both drawing and the underlying structural plan</note> and anatomy, which are the proper foundation and base of all inventions. We find many others who create their inventions so superficially, and draw so many of them, that today they are used by <term>apothecaries</term> <note>original: "speciali"; pharmacists or spice merchants who used scrap paper to wrap goods</note> as paper cones for their wares. 

In short, there are few who inwardly penetrate this art. If it were well understood, one would realize that in its inventions, it shows us how much it surpasses—on a flat surface—not only sculpture, but nature itself. It raises things up through <term>foreshortening</term> <note>original: "scorti"</note> by way of <term>perspective</term>, so that every part turns according to the rays of our eyes as they retreat. These <term>foreshortenings</term> are enclosed and restricted within the smallest spaces, yet to our sight they appear as massive as natural objects—especially when given their true lights and shadows. 

Of this, I will give one tiny example among the many to be seen throughout the world: a **Dead Christ** before his mother, with **Saint John** and the **Magdalene** kneeling at the sides. In this work, the seated **Christ** has his legs in <term>foreshortening</term>, crafted with such art that from whatever side they are viewed, they seem to turn precisely toward the eyes of the beholder. ## Of various human affections. Chap. LXV.

Considering the reason why that ancient saying was born—that there is such conformity between Poetry and Painting that, being almost born of the same birth, one was called "speaking painting" and the other "silent poetry"—and because it is rare that a mind suited and inclined toward one of these does not also extend to and take great pleasure in the other in equal measure; I conclude, finally, that this is caused by nothing other than both being studious imitators of the nature of things and their <term>accidents</term> <note>original: "accidenti"; in Renaissance theory, these are the non-essential or transient qualities of a subject, such as light, shadow, or expression, as opposed to its permanent substance</note>, insofar as it is granted to them. 

By doing this with such skill—I speak of the good masters—and such wonder for others, those very things which by their nature usually bring us annoyance, horror, or disgust, do not do so when imitated excellently; instead, they have the habit of bringing us delight and the greatest admiration. And leaving aside for a moment their stupendous representations of almost everything that can fall under the knowledge of the senses, and especially of so many human gestures and actions; do we not see (which is even more difficult) the images of love, hate, pity, anger, fear, boldness, shame, and finally all other human <term>affections</term> <note>original: "affetti"; the internal emotions or passions of the soul, which a painter must express through external physical signs</note> expressed by their divine hands? 

Thus, competing together—one with brushes and the liveliness of colors, and the other with chosen, rhythmic words and charming concepts—they demonstrate these emotions in such a way that, as <term>Petrarch</term> <note>Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), the preeminent Italian poet whose work deeply influenced Renaissance art theory</note> said, they <note>original: "pingon cantando"</note> "paint while singing," so clearly and truly that the verse itself does no more. But what is more? Through singular artistry, they snatch us up with immense wonder and transform us into those same movements and emotions. Now, to cease discussing painters in this place—whose works are for the most part exposed to the eyes of the whole world—and coming to Poets, I am pleased to descend to some more illustrious examples, recounting some small part of them, as I estimate...

...this labor of mine should bring not only a certain utility and beauty to readers; since poetry is like the shadow of painting, and the shadow cannot exist without its body—which is nothing other than painting itself, as <term>Leonardo</term> <note>Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519), who famously argued in his "Paragone" (comparison of the arts) that painting was superior to poetry because it represented the "body" while poetry only represented the "shadow" or words</note> so elegantly described it. ### But let us now see the portraits of its opposite, sorrow.

->Theocritus<-

> *Upon blood-stained cloaks Adonis lies,*

*From the center of the heart, lively kisses, while*
*Through my lips even into the center of the soul,*
*Your sweetest spirit descends into me,*
*From your body that sweet fire, fleeing,*
*I shall drink, and from your breast all my love;*

*In you, my beloved, since you leave me and flee*

*From his white limbs he pours forth*

*With eyes turned livid and a face drained of color.*
<note>This passage describes the death of Adonis and the grief of Venus. The "livid eyes" and "drained color" are specific visual cues for a painter depicting a dying figure and a mourning lover.</note>

*Such seemed the virgin’s beautiful face.*
<note>This famous simile describes Lavinia’s blush in *Aeneid* XII. It is included here as a model for painters on how to depict the "fire" of shame or modesty through color.</note>

-> BOOK <-

### Statius
<note>Publius Papinius Statius was a Roman poet whose epic, the *Thebaid*, was a favorite source for Renaissance artists depicting high drama and tragic grief.</note>

As if out of her mind at the sad news,
The unhappy mother gave swift belief,
So that, casting womanly decorum aside,
She tears her hair and her face, and with bared breast
The extreme sorrow gave to the wretched woman
Force and vigor in her elderly age;
Then her companions lift her up in her affliction
And lead her to her chamber, offering consolation,
Where she sits with her breast torn,
Shunning all comfort and light,
And fixes her eyes to the ground without a word,
Deprived of voice and intellect alike.
<note>The description of the mother sitting in silence and "shunning light" provides a painter with a specific composition for depicting "melancholy" or "stupefying grief."</note>

### Dante
<note>The following lines are adapted from Dante Alighieri's *Divine Comedy*, specifically describing the physical toll of suffering on the human form.</note>

His eyes were toward the ground, and his brows were shorn
Of all boldness, and he said through his sighs:
"Who has denied me the sorrowful homes?"
Through their eyes, their grief burst forth;
From this side and that they helped with their hands,
Sometimes against the vapors and sometimes the hot ground;
In their eyes, each woman was dark and hollow,
Pallid in the face, and so wasted away
That the skin took its shape from the bones.
<note>These lines evoke the imagery of *Purgatorio* XXIII, where Dante describes the souls of the gluttons who are so emaciated that their skin clings to their skeletons—a reference for artists painting famine or extreme asceticism.</note>
When he saw me, he distorted himself entirely,
Blowing into his beard with sighs.

### Statius, continuing after Dante

Here, having fallen together around the body,
By turns they embrace it, and equally
They join their hair, their tears, and their laments.

### The sisters of Eteocles and Polynices
<note>In Greek mythology and Statius's *Thebaid*, the sisters Antigone and Ismene mourn their two brothers, Eteocles and Polynices, who killed each other in a duel for the throne of Thebes.</note>

They press now one limb, then another, and to the face
They give kisses, and hang from the beloved neck.

### Argia, wife of Polynices
<note>Argia is the devoted wife who risked her life to give her husband a proper burial.</note>

Her face runs with horror, and her heart is fierce,
Nor can what she hears or encounters frighten her;
For she who looks upon her can bring back fear,
So much has she become secure through desperation.
At the sound of the cruel rumor, they moved in a tumult,
The bereaved mothers and the unhappy wives,
Like captives wounded in the center of their hearts.

*And in all of them a similar appearance: their hair loosened,*
*Their robes unfastened, and their cheeks blood-red,*
*And their arms swollen from wiping away tears.*
<note>This likely continues the description of the mourning Argive women from Statius's *Thebaid*, providing painters with a template for depicting collective female lamentation.</note>

### Oedipus
<note>These lines describe Oedipus after he has blinded himself in shame and grief, a common subject for "The Terrible" style of painting.</note>

*Having heard of the wicked end, the father*
*Emerging from cruel and dark places,*
*Showed a living death; his horrid hair,*
*Filthy with old blood, and his wicked beard*
*Seemed to shroud his furious head,*
*And those sad places where the light was cut off.*
<note>original: "intercetta luce" — literally "intercepted light," referring to his blindness.</note>

### Bembo
<note>Pietro Bembo was a Venetian cardinal and influential poet whose work defined the refined "Petrarchan" style of the Renaissance.</note>

*Upon his own sacred and honored bust*
*The ancient father fell, a heavy burden to himself,*
*With his chest torn and his face full of death.*

### Ariosto, on Ruggiero
<note>Ludovico Ariosto’s epic *Orlando Furioso* is the source for the following three excerpts. Here, the hero Ruggiero is consumed by the shame of having abandoned his beloved Bradamante.</note>

*Here, thinking of how much injury he had*
*Done to the Lady, and how ungrateful, and how*
*Unthankful he had been to her, he rages;*
*Not only does he mourn, and afflict himself so much*
*That he bites his hands, he bites his lips,*
*And bathes his cheeks in a continuous weeping.*

### On Bradamante
<note>Bradamante, the female warrior and Ruggiero's lover, reacts to the news that he has not returned.</note>

*When she sees the messenger return to her without her lover,*
*After so long a term of waiting,*
*She remains pale and wan and so trembling,*
*That she has no strength to keep herself on her feet.*

### On Orlando
<note>These famous lines describe the moment Orlando loses his mind (the "frenzy") upon discovering the betrayal of his beloved Angelica. This "stony" grief was a favorite theme for sculptors and painters.</note>

*He remained at last with his eyes and with his mind*
*Fixed upon the rock, as indifferent as the rock itself.*
*He was then on the verge of losing all his senses,*
*So completely does he leave himself a prey to sorrow;*
*His chin had fallen upon his chest,*
*His brow was lowered, deprived of all boldness,*
*Nor could he find—so much did the grief occupy him—*
*A voice for his complaints, or moisture for his tears.*
<note>Ariosto emphasizes that Orlando's grief is so profound he can no longer even perform the physical act of crying.</note>

*Orlando strives to hide his pain, and yet*
*It exerts its force, and he can poorly conceal it;*
*Through tears and sighs from mouth and eyes*
*It must, whether he wills it or not, at last break out;*
*Afflicted and weary, he finally falls into the grass.*

The excerpts focus on the physical collapse of the body, the biting of hands in rage, and the "stony" silence of total despair.</summary>

## Virgil on Laocoön
<note>Virgil was the greatest of the Roman poets. This passage is a translation into Italian of his *Aeneid* (Book 2), describing the Trojan priest Laocoön being strangled by sea serpents.</note>

With his hands he strives to loosen the knots,
His sacred headbands spattered all around
With foul blood and dark venom,
And at the same time he sends horrific shrieks to the sky.

## Sadoleto on the same,
<note>Jacopo Sadoleto (1477–1547) was a Cardinal and poet. He wrote a famous Latin poem shortly after the ancient "Laocoön and His Sons" statue group was rediscovered in Rome in 1506. This text provides an Italian translation of his vivid description of the sculpture.</note>

The burning serpents turn in long coils
And encircle the three bodies in thick knots,
Nor can the eyes bear to look upon the punishment
And the horrific event; and behold, one of them, burning and fierce,
Binds Laocoön tight from every side
And pierces his belly with a poisonous bite;
The entangled body recoils,
And you can see the distorted limbs and the curved flank
Shrink back because of the wound.
Driven by profound pain and by the torment,
He shrieks with a great voice, and tries with great force
To loosen his grim teeth, and shields his back
From the serpent with his hand, every nerve strained;
And in vain is the final effort of his power.
He yields to the fury, and groans from the wound.
And the serpent, with frequent turning, returns
Slithering to bind the lower parts,
Where the leg swells, and the vital members
Exceed their normal size because of the struggling pulse,
And the veins are filled with dark blood.
Nor is the horrible force less cruel to the sons,
As the raging chain constricts and tears them,
Their wretched limbs; and already from one
It has torn the bloody chest; to the father
Who asks for help in a faint and mournful voice,
He is imprisoned by various harsh bonds,
While the other son, who still prepares himself,

<note>Theocritus (c. 300 BC) was a Greek poet and the creator of ancient pastoral poetry.</note>

*No sooner did I see him run toward me swiftly*
*Than I became as ice, and from my forehead*
*There flowed a thick moisture like frost;*
*My tongue was halted and my speech fixed,*
*Pale as marble and with eyes cast down.*

->Virgil<-
<note>Virgil (70–19 BC) was the greatest of the Roman poets, author of the Aeneid. This passage describes the chaos and terror during the Fall of Troy.</note>

*Throughout the rooms the women are heard to howl,*
*Scratching themselves in weeping; and in an afflicted sound,*
*The shrieks go up even to the golden stars:*
*The timid, sorrowful, ancient mothers*
*Running through the wide halls, now here, now there,*
*Embrace tightly and give kisses to the doors.*
*Here stood Hecuba, and here run swiftly*
*Her daughters in vain around the sacred altar,*
*Crowded together, like doves.*
*Hastily they go through the dark temples,*
*Embracing the images of the Gods.*
<note>Hecuba was the Queen of Troy. The "doves" metaphor emphasizes the vulnerability of the women seeking sanctuary at the altar as the city falls.</note>

->of Aeneas<-
<note>Aeneas is the hero of Virgil's epic, recounting his flight from the burning city of Troy while carrying his elderly father and leading his son.</note>

*Now through harsh deserts and wild places*
*We go together; and I, whom just before,*
*No throwing of weapons could move*
*Nor Greeks in armed ranks, now at every wind*
*And every little noise I tremble in suspense,*
*Such care I have for my dear companion and my burden.*
<note>The "burden" (original: *peso*) refers to his father, Anchises, whom Aeneas carried on his shoulders out of the city.</note>

->Ovid<-
<note>Ovid (43 BC–17 AD) was a Roman poet famous for the *Metamorphoses*. He is often cited for his ability to describe psychological states.</note>

*To the nurse who heard, a cold fear*
*Ran through her bones and her hair stood on end.*

### On Leucothoe.
<note>Leucothoe was a princess loved by Apollo (Phoebus). When he revealed himself to her, she was overcome by a mixture of terror and wonder.</note>

"I burn for you," Phoebus told her; and she
Let both the distaff and the spindle fall to her feet,
And that fear increased her grace and beauty.

### On Europa.
<note>This describes Europa as she is carried away across the sea by Jupiter, who has disguised himself as a white bull.</note>

Already she was seen looking back at the abandoned land,
And calling out to her companions,
And timidly pulling her feet back from the waves.

### Statius.
<note>Publius Papinius Statius (c. 45–96 AD) was a Roman poet. This passage likely describes the terror within the city of Thebes during the siege described in his epic, the *Thebaid*.</note>

Now the City is full of flight and shrieks,
For they already have before their eyes the fire and the enemy’s breast,
Which fear presents to them; and houses and temples,
Statues and ungrateful altars, are flooded with weeping,
For fear is equal across unequal ages.
If the elderly desire to die, the young
Live suspended between fear and daring,
And feminine laments strike the heavens.
The children weep, though the cause is unknown to them,
Astonished only by the weeping of their mothers.

### Pontano.
<note>Giovanni Pontano (1426–1503) was a leading Italian humanist and poet. Here he provides a more sensual and detailed account of Europa’s fear on the back of the bull.</note>

The golden veil gleamed across the sea,
Which goes skimming her beautiful, white foot,
Which she lifts and timidly draws back into herself.
The breeze meanwhile made a lascivious assault
Upon her lovely breast and her youthful bosom;
And while the wave either rises or falls against the bull,
The unhappy girl turns a thousand colors
And with scattered hair she invokes the Nereids,
<note>The Nereids were sea nymphs in Greek mythology, daughters of Nereus.</note>
Asking that if their divinity has any power,
Or if pity can move them as it usually does,
They might quiet the waves and bring her aid.

### Ariosto on Ferraù.
<note>Ludovico Ariosto (1474–1533) wrote the epic *Orlando Furioso*. This describes the Saracen knight Ferraù when he is confronted by the ghost of Argalia rising from a river.</note>

At the sudden appearance made
By the shadow from the water, every hair stood on end,
And the Saracen’s face turned pale;
The voice that was about to emerge stopped in his throat.
<term>Saracin</term> — Saracen; a term used in medieval and Renaissance literature to refer to Muslim knights and people.

### On Angelica.
<note>Angelica is the princess of Cathay in *Orlando Furioso*, constantly fleeing from various suitors and dangers.</note>

By pulling the bridle he cannot turn him,
More and more that creature always rushes upward,

# S I X T H.

He who could hardly draw breath from his chest,
"Alas, my Lord, alas!" he repeats many times
Before he has begun to say anything else:
"Today the Roman Empire, today it is buried."
<note>In the context of Ariosto's *Orlando Furioso*, the "Roman Empire" refers to the Carolingian Empire of Charlemagne, which the poet frames as the successor to Rome.</note>
Even still, his cowardly and miserable mind
Was sculpted upon his pale face;
Even still, because of the fear they have endured,
They wander about pale, mute, and senseless.

->**Doralice.**<-
<note>Doralice is a primary female character in *Orlando Furioso*, a Saracen princess whose beauty causes conflict between several knights.</note>

Tears, like a flowing river that follows,
Fell like divine snow upon her beautiful breast,
And in her lovely face one could see that at once
She grieved for the misfortune of others and feared for her own.

When the atrocious Saracen became known
By his strange weapons and his scaly skin,
<note>original: "scagliosa pelle." This refers to Rodomonte, the king of Algiers, who wore armor made from the impenetrable skin of a dragon (or sea serpent) inherited from his ancestor Nimrod.</note>
There where the old men and the less fierce folk
Strained their ears for any news,
A cry arose, a shout, a loud voice,
And a beating of hands that reached the stars;
And whoever was able to flee did not remain there,
But locked themselves away in temples and houses.

Ladies and young maidens with pale faces
Stand timidly in the manner of doves;
They stand there, then, to watch the battle
With mournful faces and trembling hearts.

<margin>Follows</margin>He was no sooner upon the ground than he rose again,
Filled far more with shame than with anger,

For he turned his eyes toward Bradamante,
And saw her beautiful, serene face troubled;
At his fall, she remained in uncertainty,
And her very life seemed about to fail.
<note>Bradamante is the female Christian knight and heroine of the epic. This stanza describes the moment she unhorses a powerful opponent, likely Rodomonte or another suitor, and the emotional shock that follows.</note>

->**Alamanni.**<-
<note>Luigi Alamanni (1495–1556) was a Florentine poet and statesman. His inclusion here serves to show a different stylistic approach to the "poetry of fear" compared to Ariosto.</note>

Now, who might see the devout ones all around:
The infirm old men, the weary mothers,
Disheveled and barefoot, walking night and day
Among a thousand pale and graceful faces
Of a young troop neglectedly adorned;
Among brothers, relatives, and righteous fathers,
Of children and maidens with loosened hair,
With tears and sighs and fear upon their faces.

Even though jealousy might be judged by some to be the daughter of Love, as if it were best paired with him, nonetheless, it is in my view born instead of Cerberus and Tisiphone <note>Cerberus is the three-headed hound of the underworld; Tisiphone is one of the Furies, a deity of vengeance who punished crimes of passion.</note>, rather than from a father so sweet and divine. But let us not leave behind disdain, the eternal companion of the former passion.
<note>The author transitionally links the "bitterness" of the previous poem to the broader concept of *sdegno* (disdain or indignant anger), particularly in lovers.</note>

# SIXTH BOOK . I

*Unable to contain it in her swollen and pregnant heart,*
*It escapes through her eyes and her bold tongue.*
<note>This couplet serves as a general introduction to how internal pressure—specifically anger—physically forces its way out through speech and expression.</note>

### Armida.

*Here she fell silent, and it seemed a royal disdain,*
*And noble, kindled her expression.*
*And turning her foot, she made a sign to depart,*
*Fully scornful and sad in her gestures.*
*Her weeping poured forth without restraint*
*As anger usually produces it when mixed with grief,*
*And the newborn tears, to see them,*
*Seemed like crystals and pearls in the sun’s rays.*
<note>Armida is the famous sorceress from Torquato Tasso's epic *Jerusalem Delivered*. This passage illustrates "noble disdain," where the character's anger does not make her ugly but instead transforms her tears into something beautiful like jewelry.</note>

*Then Rinaldo smiled, and with a face*
*In which disdain flashed amidst the laughter.*
*But within the disdain with which his brow is laden,*
*Still a ray of pity shines through,*
*So that others fear him indeed, but do not despair,*
*And desire him more the more haughty he appears.*
<note>Rinaldo, the hero of Tasso's epic, displays a mixture of authority and mercy. His "disdain" is a sign of his power and high status, which makes him more attractive to the observer.</note>

### of Armida.

*She came sublime, seated in a great chariot,*
*Girt in a dress, an archer with a quiver,*
*And the new disdain was mixed in such a way*
*With the native sweetness in that beautiful face*
*That it gives her vigor; and cruel and slightly bitter*
*She seems to threaten, and while threatening, she allures.*
<note>This describes Armida on the battlefield. The poet suggests that her anger ("sdegno") provides her with a new kind of "cruel" beauty that remains seductive even when she is dangerous.</note>

*Armida turned and saw him unexpectedly,*
*For she did not hear him when he first arrived;*
*She raised a cry, and from that beloved face*
*She turned her eyes away in disdain, and fainted.*
<note>A dramatic moment where Armida encounters Rinaldo again. The overwhelming conflict between her love for him and her indignant pride leads to a physical collapse.</note>

### Homer on Achilles.

*Throwing foam around his mouth,*
*His eyes burned horribly fierce,*
*And the clashing of tooth against tooth was heard from afar.*
<note>original: "Gettando spuma..." This is a vernacular translation of a passage from Homer’s *Iliad*, describing the terrifying physiological effects of Achilles’ legendary rage.</note>

### Theocritus.

*He caught fire like one offended, and was troubled in such a way*
*That his lips were dry, his face pale,*
*And not as before of a rosy color;*
*And his eyes, once the seat of love, now squinting and burning,*
*Threaten slaughter and death to whoever looks at them,*
*Armed with cruelty, anger, and disdain.*
<note>Theocritus was an ancient Greek poet. This excerpt focuses on the physical transformation caused by anger: the loss of healthy color and the hardening of the eyes from "the seat of love" into weapons of war.</note>

### Virgil’s description of Hecuba.

*She saw the lifeless body of Polydorus,*
<note>Polydorus was the youngest son of King Priam and Queen Hecuba of Troy. During the Trojan War, he was sent to Thrace for safety but was murdered by King Polymestor for his gold.</note>
*And noticed the deep wounds—oh, horrendous sight!—*
*Inflicted by the wicked Thracian blades.*
*Though the Phrygian women then raised a loud cry,*
<note>original: "Donne frigie". Phrygia was the region where Troy was located; "Phrygian" is often used as a synonym for "Trojan."</note>
*A bitter and cruel sorrow struck her mute,*
*And that grief which she sees and which consumes her within*
*Stripped the voice from her words and the moisture from her tears.*
*Her limbs became like hard stone,*
*And her eyes were now fixed upon the earth, now turned*
*With a sideways glance toward the hostile heavens;*
*Now she gazes at the beautiful face of her dead son,*
*Now at the harsh wounds—or rather, almost always*
*At those alone—and she is kindled with anger and fury*
*To take a bitter vengeance upon that tyrant.*

### Here is the virgin Cassandra, also a daughter

*Of the good King Priam, with her hair disheveled,*
*Dragged from the temple and the sacred places*
*Of Minerva, lifting her eyes in vain—*
<note>Minerva is the Roman name for the Greek goddess Athena. Cassandra had sought sanctuary in her temple during the Sack of Troy.</note>
*Her eyes, inflamed, toward Heaven—for cruel shackles*
*Had bound her tender and pure hands.*

### Coroebus, inflamed with anger and pity,

*Could not endure such a sight, and into the midst*
*Of the enemy ranks he threw himself,*
*Without caring in the least for life or death.*
<note>Coroebus was a suitor of Cassandra who died attempting to rescue her during the fall of Troy.</note>

### But Dido, terrified and driven to ferocity

*By her cruel undertakings, turning around*
*Her bloodshot eyes, and her trembling*
*Cheeks marked by many dark blotches,*
*Already pale at the prospect of the impious death*
*Which she was soon to suffer, she passes quickly,*
*And full of fury she suddenly climbs*
*Upon the high funeral pyre, and draws the Trojan sword*
*From its scabbard, after she saw there*
*Before her the Trojan spoils and the familiar bed.*
<note>This describes the final moments of Dido, Queen of Carthage, who committed suicide after being abandoned by the Trojan hero Aeneas. The "spoils" and "bed" are reminders of their past love.</note>

### Ovid’s description of Juno.

*She seized her by the hair with great rage*
*And thrust her to the ground, dragging and tearing at her;*
*The other raised her tearful and beautiful eyes,*
*And like a suppliant, stretched her arms out toward her.*
<note>This likely refers to Juno’s physical assault on Callisto, a nymph who had been seduced by Juno’s husband, Jupiter. Juno’s "rage" here is the physical manifestation of divine jealousy.</note>

<summary>This page provides classical examples from Virgil and Ovid of how overwhelming passions like grief, vengeful fury, and despair are physically expressed through silence, "stony" features, and violent action.</summary>
<keywords>Hecuba, Polydorus, Cassandra, Coroebus, Dido, Juno, Virgil, Ovid, Trojan War, physical expression of emotion, grief, fury, vengeance</keywords>

# S I X T H .

## Mother of Meleager.
<note>Meleager’s mother was Althaea. According to myth, the Fates decreed Meleager would live only as long as a certain wooden brand remained unburnt. After Meleager killed Althaea's brothers in a dispute, she was torn between maternal love and the duty to avenge her siblings.</note>
*Full four times out of indignation she wished*
*To burn the branch of final laments,* <note>original: "omei". An archaic poetic term for cries of grief or "alases."</note>
*And four times she softened that foolish thought.*
*The mother and the sister struggle within her,*
*And two different names push a tender breast*
*Toward thoughts now good, now wicked;*
*Often, thinking of her error, she grew pale,*
*Often burning anger reddened her eyes,*
*Her face was stained with I know not what cruelty—*
*A face like one who threatens, burning—*
*And now it appeared painted with deep pity;*
*And if her tears were dried by the heat of her mind,*
*They poured forth anew, just like*
*A rock struck now by wind, now by a clashing wave,*
*Wherefore anger alternately flares and falls silent.*

## Statius.
<note>Publius Papinius Statius (c. 45–96 AD) was a Roman poet. This passage describes the death of Tydeus from his epic poem, the *Thebaid*.</note>
*Tydeus rises and comes forward, mad*
*No less with joy than with anger, having*
*Caught sight of that face full of death and the eyes*
*Rolled back, in which he sees himself mirrored;*
*And after he has cut off the enemy's head,* <note>original: "capo hostile". This refers to Melanippus. In the myth, the dying Tydeus committed the ultimate "impious" act by gnawing on the skull of his killer.</note>
*Holding it with his hand while still warm,*
*He looks at it intently and enjoys the sight,*
*Those dark eyes still trembling on the ground;*
*Then, having bitten it unworthily,*
*He tastes, while dying, the sucking of that blood,*

## Of Eteocles & Polynices.
<note>The sons of Oedipus who fought a civil war for the throne of Thebes and eventually killed each other in single combat.</note>
*Like desperate men they do battle,*
*Employing only anger and hatred, without care or defense,*
*And beneath their helmets their burning eyes*
*Search only for the hated face;*
*Already the ground gives way, already they are so close*
*That they come to the mid-sword and to the struggle,*
*Both trembling with rage as if the sound*
*Of a horrendous trumpet kindled them to arms.*

## Of the Mother.
*Where do you turn your menacing face,*
*And why in a single moment does it vanish*
*And then blood spreads across your cheeks?*

### of Armida.
<note>Armida is the famous sorceress from Torquato Tasso’s epic poem *Gerusalemme Liberata* (Jerusalem Delivered). These lines from Canto XVI describe her volatile reaction when the hero Rinaldo abandons her.</note>
> *Her eyes flash and her glances strike like lightning,*
> *Sweet in her anger, as they must be in her laughter,*
> *Showing clearly how much fury she has gathered,*
> *With disheveled hair, a grim gaze, and a flushed face,*
> *While the warrior speaks to her in such a way,*
> *She finds no rest, troubled and restless,*
> *For a good while now, with a scornful brow,*
> *She turns, looks again, and at last breaks out in insults;*
> *Known by many signs, he is watched by her*
> *With eyes of anger and trembling desire;*
> *His face changes just a little,*
> *She turns to ice and then becomes fire,*
<note>original: "Lampeggiar gl'occhi... Ella si fa di giel poi diuien foco." These verses capture the physiological shifts of a "woman scorned"—the alternating heat of rage and the coldness of despair.</note>

### Edward on his slain wife.
<note>This refers to the character Odoardo (Edward) in Tasso’s *Gerusalemme Liberata* (Canto XX), who discovers his wife Gildippe has been killed in battle.</note>
> *What should he do in such a dire case? Anger and pity*
> *Hasten him toward different paths at the same time:*
> *One leads him to support his falling beloved,*
> *The other to take revenge on the striker.*
> *Indifferent Love persuades him*
> *That neither anger nor pity be neglected;*
> *With his left hand he runs to support her,*
> *The other he makes the servant of his design,*
<note>Tasso uses this scene to show the "servant" hand (the right hand) seeking vengeance while the other provides comfort, illustrating the duality of his emotional state.</note>

### Virgil.
<note>This is an Italian translation of the famous description of Charon, the ferryman of the underworld, from Book VI of Virgil's *Aeneid*.</note>
> *Charon stands there, the ferryman guardian of the waters,*
> *Of a vigorous and robust old age,*
> *Squalid and black, from whose chin hangs*
> *A white, ill-kept beard;*
> *Flames came out of his eyes, and a tight knot*
> *Of a stained cloak hung from his shoulders.*
> *He, with a rusty and black skiff,*
> *Pushing with the oar and with the sail,*
> *Carries those empty bodies to the other shore,*
<note>original: "Stà Caronte il nocchier..." The "empty bodies" refer to the shades of the dead who no longer possess physical weight.</note>

### Horace on Regulus.
<note>Marcus Atilius Regulus was a Roman general who, according to legend, insisted on returning to Carthage to face execution rather than accept a peace treaty he deemed dishonorable. This is a translation of Horace’s *Odes* (III.5).</note>
> *The chaste kiss of his modest wife,*
> *And pushing his small children away from him*
> *As if he were frantic, his fierce face and eyes*
> *Regulus never moved from the ground,*
<note>Horace depicts Regulus’s "fierce" or steadfast gaze as he refuses to look at his family, fearing their grief would weaken his resolve to fulfill his duty to Rome.</note>

> *Here the Greek throng could not hold back*
> *The tears that were held by her,*

Despite himself, the priest himself
*Still weeping, alas, with the hard iron*
*Opens and strikes that strong and chaste breast.*
*She always maintains a steady countenance*
*Even unto death, and even while falling she covered*

### Statius.
<note>Statius was a Roman poet of the 1st century AD, famous for his epic the *Thebaid*. This excerpt likely comes from an Italian translation of his work, describing the courage of women during wartime.</note>

*Those in whom love weighs more than their own decorum,*
*Give to their husbands iron, anger, and heart,*
*And running alongside them through the dangers,*
*They remind them of their children and their homes.*

### Dante.

*Do you not see how they gnash their teeth,*
*And with their brows they threaten me with pains,*
*And how they roll their eyes to strike,*
<note>original: "Non vedi tù che digrignan li denti..." These lines evoke the vivid, physical depictions of demons or the damned in Dante Alighieri’s *Divine Comedy*.</note>

### Farinata.

*But that noble, great-souled man, at whose request*
*I had remained, did not change his look,*
*Nor move his neck, nor bend his side.*
<note>original: "Ma quell' alto magnanimo..." This describes Farinata degli Uberti in Canto X of Dante's *Inferno*. Even in the fires of Hell, Farinata maintains a posture of immense pride and aristocratic stoicism, refusing to show pain to his political enemy.</note>

### Ariosto.

*As Alzirdo saw that Count approach,*
*Who had no equal in valor in the world,*
*With such a resemblance and such a proud brow*
*That the God of Arms seemed second to him,*
*He remained stunned by those well-known features,*
*By the fierce gaze and the furious face.*
<note>original: "Come Alzirdo appressar vide quel Conte..." From Ludovico Ariosto’s *Orlando Furioso*. "The Count" refers to the hero Orlando. Alzirdo, a minor king, is paralyzed by the sheer martial presence of Orlando, who looks more like Mars (the God of War) than a mortal man.</note>

### Rodomonte.

*He sighs and rages with such a horrible face*
*That he threatens the elements and all of Heaven.*
<note>Rodomonte is the quintessential "boastful warrior" and antagonist in Ariosto's epic. This describes his cosmic defiance and terrifying physical presence.</note>

### Tasso.

*Argante was dying, and died even as he lived;*
*He threatened while dying and did not languish,*
*Proud, formidable, and ferocious,*
*His last movements were his last words.*
*In such a way he flashes in his armor, and grim and twisted*
*He turns his eyes, drunk with blood and wrath,*
*His fierce acts breathe out the horror of death,*
*His face breathes out the threats of death:*
*He holds his sword naked, raising and shaking it*
*Crying out, and strikes the air and the shadows in vain.*
<note>original: "Moria Argante, e tal moria qual visse..." From Torquato Tasso’s *Gerusalemme Liberata* (Canto XIX). This depicts the death of the Circassian knight Argante. Tasso emphasizes that the warrior's character—his pride and ferocity—remains unchanged even as his life ebbs away.</note>

### Tasso on Dudone.
<note>Torquato Tasso (1544–1595) was a celebrated Italian poet. These lines from his epic *Gerusalemme Liberata* (The Liberation of Jerusalem) describe the death of the knight Dudon of Consanza in Canto 3.</note>

> *He fell, and his eyes, which can barely open,*
> *A heavy stillness presses and an iron sleep.*
> *Three times he raised them, and the sweet rays of heaven*
> *He sought to enjoy, and to rise upon an arm;*
> *And three times he falls back, and a dark veil*
> *Shadowed his eyes which, weary, at last closed,*
> *His limbs dissolve, and the mortal chill*
> *Has made them rigid and scattered them with sweat.*

### on Clorinda.
<note>These stanzas describe one of the most famous scenes in Italian literature: the death of the Saracen warrior Clorinda, who is accidentally killed in a duel by her lover, the Crusader Tancred, who does not recognize her in her armor.</note>

> *In such gentle acts he gazes upon her trembling,*
> *Languishing eyes, and her neck falling upon her back;*
> *The pallor is so lovely, and from her features*
> *A pity so sweet breathes from death:*
> *That it softened the heart which before was marble,*
> *And tears gushed forth in the midst of anger.*
> *Her white face is sprinkled with a beautiful pallor,*
> *As if violets were mixed with lilies;*
> *And with her eyes fixed on Heaven, and the Heaven and the sun*
> *Seem turned toward her out of pity.*
> *And raising her bare and cold hand toward*
> *The Knight in place of words,*
> *She gives him a pledge of peace; in this form*
> *The beautiful lady passes, and it seems she sleeps.*

### Pity or tenderness. Homer.
<note>This is an Italian translation of a scene from Homer’s *Iliad*, likely the famous parting of Hector and Andromache, where Hector places their son Astyanax in his mother's arms.</note>

## Ariosto
<note>Ludovico Ariosto (1474–1533) was the author of the epic *Orlando Furioso*. His style is often noted for its blend of irony, romance, and vivid imagery.</note>

*“Oh my life, do not weep,” Giocondo says to her,*
*and he himself weeps no less than she.* <note>From Canto 28. Giocondo is a character famous for his beauty who discovers his wife's infidelity.</note>
*He would have believed her to be a fashioned statue,*
*of alabaster or other illustrious marbles,*
*if he had not seen the distinct tear,*
*between fresh roses and white privets,* <note>Ligustri: a type of shrub with white flowers, often used to describe fair skin.</note>
*making the small, firm apples* <note>original: "crudette pome" — a poetic metaphor for young breasts.</note> *dewy,*
*and the breeze fluttering her golden locks;* <note>This description is of Angelica, the poem's heroine, when she is found bound to a rock as a sacrifice.</note>
*And as he fixed his eyes upon her beautiful eyes,*

## Tasso.
<note>Torquato Tasso’s *Gerusalemme Liberata* (1581) is a more somber, religious epic compared to Ariosto's work. The following excerpts focus on the pathos of his characters, particularly Sofronia and Clorinda.</note>

*She fell like a flower half-cut,*
*bending her slender neck, he supports her.*
*And with one arm he made a pillar for her lovely side:*
*and meanwhile he loosened the dress at her breast,*
*and the beautiful face and beautiful breast of the wretched girl*
*he bathed with piteous tears;*
*as by a silver and morning rain*
*a faded rose becomes beautiful again.*
*So she, returning to life, raised her bowed*
*face, now tearful with a weeping not her own.* <note>This describes the hero Tancred baptizing Clorinda with his own tears as she dies by his hand.</note>
*Sofronia raises her face and humanely*
*gazes upon him with eyes of pity:*
*“Why do you come here, oh wretched innocent?”* <note>Sofronia speaks to her lover Olindo; both have been condemned to the stake.</note>
*Here the crowd of pagans exalts in weeping,*
*the faithful weep but in voices much lower;*
*something unusual and soft*
*seems to pierce the King's hard breast;* <note>Referring to Aladino, the King of Jerusalem.</note>
*he sensed it, and grew indignant, nor wished*
*to bend, and turned his eyes away and withdrew.*
*You alone do not accompany the common grief,*
*Sofronia, and though wept for by all, you do not weep.*

She began with a faint and weary sound.
<note>This line describes Olimpia, a character from Ariosto’s *Orlando Furioso*, awakening abandoned on a desert island.</note>

->concerning Olimpia.<-

And while she spoke, turning about
She moved in the same manner as Diana is carved
Or painted at the fountain,
Who throws the water in Actaeon’s face,
Who hides her breast and belly as much as she can,
Being more liberal with her flanks and her loins.
<note>In Greek mythology, the hunter Actaeon stumbled upon the goddess Diana bathing; she transformed him into a stag as punishment. Ariosto uses this image to describe Olimpia’s modest attempt to cover herself.</note>

->Tasso, concerning Armida.<-

Or rather, holding her modest eyes cast down,
She adorns and colors herself with virtue.
So that she comes to hide the fresh frosts
Beneath the roses wherewith she makes her beautiful face flower,
Just as in the coolest morning hours,
From its first birth we see the Aurora;
And the redness of disdain comes forth together
With shame, and is confounded and mixed.
<note>From Tasso's *Jerusalem Delivered*. Armida is a sorceress using a facade of modesty—the "roses" of a blush—to deceive the crusaders.</note>

These are the reasons, but not the only ones—
And here she fell silent and was tinged with redness,
And she lowered her eyes, and her final words
She wished to hold back, and did not speak them clearly.

->concerning Sophronia.<-

Fortitude moves the great thought, but it is arrested
By virginal modesty, and she withdraws;
Fortitude conquers, or rather they agree and she makes
Herself bashful, and her bashfulness bold.
<note>Sophronia is a Christian maiden in Tasso's epic who heroically confesses to a "crime" to save her people, balancing her natural modesty with her courage.</note>

She bowed to him reverently and then,
Somewhat shyly, did not speak a word;
But that redness, but those fears of hers,
Reassure the warrior and comfort him.
Then she turned her eyes, and yet even then she feigned
To see those two, and she was all colored with a blush;
And the hair that she had gathered atop her head
In a single knot, she immediately loosened,
Which, falling very long and thick down below,
Enveloped the <term>soft ivories</term> in a golden mantle.
<term>soft ivories</term>: A poetic metaphor common in the Renaissance to describe the smooth, white skin of a woman.
Oh, what a lovely spectacle is taken from them!
But no less lovely was she who took it from them;
Thus, hidden by the waters and by her hair,
She turned to them, joyful and bashful.
<note>Although under the heading of Sophronia, these final stanzas return to Ariosto’s description of Olimpia (*Orlando Furioso*, Canto 11) being rescued. Her hair serves as a natural "golden mantle" to preserve her modesty.</note>

## Apelles' Venus.
<note>Apelles was the most famous painter of ancient Greece. This poem is likely an "ekphrasis"—a poetic description of a work of art—specifically his "Venus Anadyomene" (Venus Rising from the Sea).</note>

> *Over her face and over her shoulders flowed loose*
> *The hair of gold which a light breeze ripples,*
> *Which you, with a sweet hand, gather on your brow;*
> *Sparks come out from eyes haughty and strange,*
> *And the whiteness of the beautiful breast irradiates the sea*
> *And the firm fruits <note>original: "crudi pomi" (cruel or unripe apples). A standard Renaissance metaphor for firm, youthful breasts.</note> go playing in the wave:*

### Catullus.

Septimius, holding his love
Acme in his lap,
Said, "My Acme, if I
Do not love you, and am not ready
To love you eternally
As much as one can possibly love,
May I be the prey of lions."
Whereupon she, turning
Her beautiful neck softly,
And sweetly kissing 
The drunken and amorous eyes
Of the graceful youth
With her rosy lips,
Said, "Thus, my little Septimius,
My life, let us love,
And serve one love alone,
Just as I feel my heart melting
With a greater flame."
<note>This is a translation of Catullus’s Poem 45. The names Septimius and Acme represent a pair of idealized lovers. The "drunken eyes" is a classical metaphor for being intoxicated by passion.</note>

### Horace.

While she turns her neck to dear kisses,
Sometimes she sweetly, wickedly denies them,
And holds these sweet thefts dearer than prayers;
Now it even pleases her to snatch them back first.
<note>original: "Oratio." This excerpt captures a moment of playful flirtation often found in the Odes of Horace, where the beloved teasingly withholds affection to increase the lover's desire.</note>

### Ovid.

At the sight of Jason's extinguished flame,
It shone again and both cheeks became crimson,
And she gazes at him fixedly, as if never seen before,
Nor does she ever turn her intent eyes elsewhere.
<note>original: "Ouidio." This likely refers to Medea seeing Jason again. The "extinguished flame" <note>original: "estinta fiamma"</note> refers to her suppressed passion which is reignited at his sight.</note>

### Valerius Flaccus.

Even though near her parents,
The maiden becomes mute and trembling,
As if alone in her beautiful, sad eyes;
Nor could she keep her clouded face 
Bowed to the ground; rather, she turns her eyes
Toward the path where he goes, who was soon reached;
Alas, upon departing he seemed more charming,
And more graceful to the unhappy lover.
<note>Valerius Flaccus was a Roman poet who wrote the *Argonautica*. This passage describes the internal turmoil of Medea as she watches Jason depart, highlighting the conflict between her duty to her family and her overwhelming love.</note>

# SEVENTH BOOK
## OF THE HISTORY
### OF PAINTING,
## BY GIO. PAOLO LOMAZZO,
->*Milanese Painter.*<-

->*On the virtue and necessity of history, or what we may call the form of painting. Chapter I.*<-

Anyone who examines the history of painters—not only those of these recent times following the decline of the Roman Empire, but also those of those first happy centuries when painting and all other arts flourished—will undoubtedly find many examples, whether by looking at their works or reading what others have judiciously written of them. He will find many who, although they were excellent in certain aspects of this profession, nevertheless remained obscure because they lacked knowledge of <term>form</term> <note>Lomazzo uses "form" (forma) to refer to the essential structure and proportions of an object, rather than just its surface appearance.</note> and <term>delineation</term> <note>Delineamento: the foundational drawing or outline that defines the limits of an object.</note> which is required in both artificial and natural things. Indeed, the fame of their names has barely reached posterity as a faint echo. 

It is certainly impossible for anyone to express any <term>invention</term> <note>Invenzione: the intellectual concept, story, or "historia" that the artist chooses to depict.</note> with the brush—which is the most solid part of painting for reducing obscurity—if they do not understand the external form of what they have conceived. From this it follows that by erring due to ignorance of these principles, many practitioners (as I have mentioned) have ended their works in shame. This is because wise men appreciate that which is seen in a painting less than that which is hidden beneath it—a splendor veiled by beautiful colors. 

This is much like in poems, where we speak of verses with delight more for their concepts and hidden substance than for that harmonious binding of words that the ear hears on the surface. Thus, we see clearly how knowing the external form of every thing is not only useful but necessary in painting. Therefore, in this final book of my entire treatise, so that the painter—whenever he must set his hand to the <term>panel</term> <note>tauola: the wooden panel used as a support for painting before canvas became the standard.</note>...

<summary>In this opening chapter of Book Seven, Lomazzo argues that intellectual "form" and structural "delineation" are more important to a painter's legacy than mere technical skill or color. He compares the underlying structure of a painting to the deep meaning of a poem, which is more valuable than its rhythmic sound.</summary>
<keywords>Giovan Paolo Lomazzo, history of painting, art theory, form vs. color, Mannerism, delineation, invention, Renaissance aesthetics</keywords>

--- Page 563 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the divine or spiritual can be represented through physical forms. Lomazzo is justifying the anthropomorphic representation of God in art by citing numerous biblical examples where God is described as having human body parts or wearing clothing. This provides a theological foundation for "History" painting, which often requires depicting the divine in human-like form.</meta>

# SEVENTH [BOOK].

...as certain ways through which the grace of these members is spread, just as it is clearly suggested to us in various places of the sacred scriptures. Hence we read in the Song of Songs <note>Original: *Cantici*</note> that the head of God is like Carmel, and his hair like the purple of a King. Regarding the eyes, eyelids, and ears, it is said in the Psalms: "The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers," and elsewhere, "his eyes behold the poor, and his eyelids try the children of men." Of the mouth and the <term>throat</term> <note>Original: *gozzo*, meaning the crop or throat, here used to encompass the entire gullet.</note> and of the teeth, we read in Isaiah: "you did not ask my mouth"; and in the Song of Songs: "your throat is like the finest wine, worthy of my beloved, and food for his lips and teeth to chew upon." To Him are also attributed nostrils, with which (as is often found in the Law) He smells the sacrifices as an odor of sweetness. 

And besides these, the shoulders, arms, hands, and fingers, of which we read in Isaiah: "The government is laid upon his shoulders," and "To whom is the arm of the Lord revealed?"; and in the songs of the Royal Prophet <note>King David, traditionally considered the author of the Psalms.</note>: "Your hands, O Lord, have made me and fashioned me," and "I will behold your heavens, the work of your fingers." Of the right and left hand the same is said: "The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand"; and in the Gospel we find that those who will be damned on the last day will be placed on the left. Of the heart, the breast, the back, the hindquarters <note>Original: *parti posteriori*</note>, and the face, we read in the Books of Kings that He found David, a man after his own heart; and in the Gospel, that breast upon which John, while sleeping, conceived divine secrets <note>A reference to John the Apostle leaning against Jesus' chest during the Last Supper.</note>. In the Psalms, his back is described in the paleness of gold; in Jeremiah: "I will show them the back and not the face in the day of their perdition"; and to Moses: "You shall see my back parts." 

Finally, of the feet, the Psalmist sings: "Darkness was under his feet"; which is also suggested in Genesis, where He is said to walk at midday. In the same manner, mention is made in sacred letters of various ornaments and garments of God, as in the Psalmist: "The Lord has reigned, he is clothed with beauty and surrounded with light as with a garment"; and in another place: "you have clothed yourself with praise and beauty, the abyss as its garment and covering"; and in Ezekiel, God speaking: "I have spread my garment over you, and I have covered your shame." One also reads of the rod, staff, sword, and shield: as in the Psalmist: "your rod and your staff have comforted me," and "his truth shall surround you with a shield"; and in Deuteronomy: "the sword of his glory." ## BOOK 2

Because it would be too long to go about collecting every minute detail concerning this subject found throughout the sacred scriptures, what has been said so far must suffice as an example and a norm for what the painter must observe when representing God. For the rest, one must take care never to show Him performing any act that is base or unworthy of such great majesty. Instead, the painter should strive to penetrate so deeply with the intellect that he manages to represent the Deity within the work through the excellence and distinction of form, stature, color, movement, placement, and light—setting Him apart from the other figures placed around Him. This is something so difficult that even **Leonardo** <note>Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519). The author refers to his struggle to complete the face of Christ in *The Last Supper*.</note> himself could not fully achieve it in the Christ he painted in the **Refectory of [Santa Maria] delle Grazie in Milan**. 

But despite this difficulty, no one should give up trying to achieve it with all their study, just as **Raphael**, **Antonio da Correggio**, and **Gaudenzio** <note>Gaudenzio Ferrari (c. 1471–1546), a prominent Northern Italian painter known for his expressive religious works.</note> have expressed it. For if this effort is not made, we will continue to see God represented in temples not only devoid of Majesty, but crippled and expressed worse than the other figures. Thus, instead of moving us to devotion and reverence, such art moves us to mockery and contempt for the craftsman, and consequently, it even diminishes our devotion. Furthermore, because God is not always to be represented in one and the same gesture, but differently according to the story being told, it will be useful to follow the understanding of those ancient Hebrews. They identified many names, functioning like "members" of God, which all signify different things—such as Wrath, Fury, Complacency, Love, Hatred, Delight, Indignation, and the like. 

For example, the name **Elohim Gibor** <note>Hebrew: "Mighty God."</note> signifies a robust God who punishes the sins of the wicked; **Adonai Sabaoth** <note>Hebrew: "Lord of Hosts."</note> means the God of armies, as does **Elohin Sabaoth**—though the latter refers not to war and justice, but to mercy and harmony. **Sadai** <note>Shaddai</note> means the Almighty, who satisfies everyone. Following this, there are ten names in total, which are contained within as many numerations called **Sephiroth** <note>In Jewish Kabbalah, the ten attributes or emanations through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note>. These are mentioned in the *Idea of the Theater* by **Giulio Camillo** <note>Giulio Camillo "Delminio" (c. 1480–1544), famous for his "Memory Theater," a mnemonic system intended to encompass all human knowledge.</note>, where he says that through instruments, or rather garments, or patterns of the model, they flow into all created things from the highest down to the lowest and most base, according to a certain order that is not necessary for us to recount now. It is enough to know that according to whether the story requires God to appear robust, or severe, or full of majesty, He must be represented that way to the sight. Now, to come to our Savior **Jesus Christ**, and to see what form He took in human flesh, this can be fully gathered from that letter written—

Their orders were named <term>Hierarchies</term> <note>From the Greek 'hieros' (sacred) and 'arche' (rule/principality).</note>—that is, sacred principalities—by the most holy <term>Dionysius</term> <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century theologian whose "Celestial Hierarchy" defined the nine orders of angels.</note>, disciple of St. Paul the Apostle. He distinguished them into superior, middle, and inferior levels, such that the superior contains three orders: <term>Seraphim</term>, <term>Cherubim</term>, and <term>Thrones</term>; the middle contains another three: <term>Dominations</term>, <term>Powers</term>, and <term>Virtues</term>; and the inferior level likewise contains three others: <term>Principalities</term>, <term>Archangels</term>, and <term>Angels</term>. And they are also distinguished into nine choirs by <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD).</note>, by St. Gregory in his *Moralia*, and by <term>Proclus</term> <note>Another influential Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD).</note>. Now, having to prescribe the form of any of these nine orders of angels to be able to represent them around God with the rest of His glory—both in temples and elsewhere—in the manner they have sometimes been seen by those chosen by God; although this investigation is more the work of a theologian, I will not hesitate to provide the order for it with some examples. I will keep before my eyes their influence, suggested by the divine names attributed to each of them, and furthermore the particular office through which we come to know the pure principle from which they originate.

The **Seraphim**, therefore, the most noble spirits of the first Hierarchy—whose name in Hebrew means <gloss>burning</gloss> or <gloss>warming</gloss> <note>original: "incensiui ouero riscaldanti"</note> because they contemplate the power of God, who knows in them as truth—are assigned fire, which is nothing other than a shining love. They should be represented as resplendent, in such a way that they scatter rays around them like suns, and with six wings, like the one mentioned by the Prophet and the one that appeared to <term>St. Francis</term> with Christ in the middle of the cross, representing his desire. In these angels flows the name of the divine essence and the first <term>enumeration</term> <note>Referring to the Sephirot in Jewish Kabbalah; the first is Keter (Crown).</note>, interpreted as **Crown** or **Diadem**.

The **Cherubim**, whose name in Hebrew signifies <gloss>multitude of knowledge</gloss> or <gloss>infusion of wisdom</gloss>, contemplate the goodness of God, who loves them with charity. In them, "earth" is nothing other than the very stability and immobility of their essence. Therefore, with great judgment, some represent them with a round child’s face and eight wings around it: two above, two under the chin, and two per ear, denoting the aforementioned parts of stability. The face denotes the purity of the mind, through which God loves and infuses wisdom and the knowledge of things, which are held in no other place but the head. The second name <note>Referring to the second Sephirah or divine name associated with the Cherubim.</note> fashions as many figures as there are ideas contained within it, distinguishing the chaos of creatures through its intelligence. It is indeed true that they are sometimes even depicted with only two wings, and also in the form of whole children with hands and feet in various poses, perhaps for some other secret reason. And of Solomon it is also written that in his temple he had two made standing upright with wings all of gold. But so much license has every painter taken nowadays that, without any certain rule, they depict them in whatever way pleases them most, and most of the time contrary to the truth. 

The **Thrones**, which in Greek signifies an exalted and elevated seat where a judge sits, contemplate the equity of God, who sits in them as equity and through them determines His judgments. The water in them is nothing other than clemency and piety. These in Hebrew are also called <term>Aralim</term> <note>Hebrew: *Erelim*, often interpreted as "the valiant ones" or "heroes," and associated with the order of Thrones.</note>, that is, great, strong, and robust angels; and therefore they should be depicted not as entirely pleasant, nor yet terrible, but full of majesty, and as righteous in an act representing true justice. Among the <term>Platonists</term> <note>Followers of Plato, specifically the Neoplatonists who influenced Renaissance angelology.</note>—who perhaps in this followed the doctrine of the Egyptians—justice is determined to be no more female than male, nor more male than female; this is to show that justice must be administered without any passion. Thus, these angels of whom we speak, as the seat of divine judgment, must partake of both the masculine and the feminine, in the same way that Minerva was represented among the Greeks, and also Justice: with certain ornaments of armor that well suit virility, just as, conversely, it is fitting to accompany them with the rest of the garments that tend toward softness, clemency, and piety, without which virtues justice would not be perfect. 

Through the choir of these angels flows the influence of the third name attributed to the Holy Spirit through its <term>numbering</term> <note>Referring to the *Sephirot* or emanations in Kabbalah; the third is *Binah* (Understanding).</note>, which signifies remission and rest, Jubilee, penitential conversion, the great trumpet, redemption of the world, and the life of the world to come. And these three orders, as supra-celestial angels, are placed in this superior <term>Hierarchy</term> to contemplate the order of divine providence. Hence, by their command, everything is done and executed by the others as inferiors. 

The **Dominations** rule the offices of the angels, and in them God reigns as Majesty; and the air that is in them is nothing other than a most subtle and penetrating spirit. Through them flows the fourth name, whose numbering is <term>Hased</term> <note>Hebrew: *Chesed*, the fourth Sephirah, representing Loving-kindness or Mercy.</note>—that is, clemency or goodness—which signifies grace, mercy, piety, magnificence, scepter, and the right hand. ## SEVENTH BOOK

... [they should be] pleasant and full of majesty, with garments that draw out to a great length in some parts, with a diadem or crown upon the brow, with scepters in hand, with faces that are not heavy but slender and of a sharp appearance, with shining and magnanimous eyes, and likewise with all limbs proportionate, with nimble hands and fingers, and with clothing that is not overly ornate so as not to possess <note>The author distinguishes between divine majesty and the ostentatious "magnificence" of worldly courts.</note> worldly magnificence. In this form, they will properly represent their office, just as the wise painter will be able to understand through their symbolic meanings—always taking care to make the right hand free as a sign of command and dominion.

The **Powers** restrain the power of demons, and God defends them as a savior. Through them flows the fifth name according to its numeration <note>This refers to the Kabbalistic system of the Sephiroth; the fifth Sephirah is Gevurah, representing Strength or Judgment.</note>, which is Power, Strength, Security, and Judgment, which punishes with slaughter and war; they are situated at the tribunal of God, at the belt, sword, and left arm of God Himself. Therefore, they must be represented as severe, in such a way that strength and security shine through their limbs, with thick hair upon their heads, with fierce eyes, with magnanimous gestures, and with a proportion that tends more toward the masculine than the effeminate, and with solid clothing without ornament. I would further judge that they could be represented as armed in a most beautiful manner, both because of the office they hold and because they are placed over the **sphere of Mars**, being attributed to the sword and the belt of God. For this reason, it is not without purpose that they can be depicted with a belt and with palms, as a sign of restraining and binding diabolical forces, and also as a symbol of the victories they obtain—not without our own salvation.

The **Virtues** are those to whom belong all the operations of mortals, and in whom God works as virtue; He influences them through the sixth name of His numeration <note>The sixth Sephirah, Tiferet, which represents Beauty and Balance.</note>, which is Ornament, Beauty, Glory, Pleasure, and signifies the **Tree of Life**. They must be formed differently according to their various operations, for without doubt the clothing is born from the operation: just as the diadem or crown comes from ruling; the scepter from dominion; the toga from gravity; arms from combat; and from the priesthood, a habit different from the secular. Therefore, I would say that since God works in these angels specifically as virtue—which is understood as the flower or scent that comes forth from any thing—all their garments should possess the height of beauty, both in ornaments and in their arrangement and fastenings. Thus, they should appear most beautiful and graceful, providing infinite pleasure to whoever beholds them, with the clothing corresponding to the figure and limbs; yet with such discretion that...

# BOOK 2.

->ob I 1<-

...since they have various virtues within them, they should also be formed with various and distinct manners of ornament and beauty. The **Principalities**, in which God rules as a sovereign, are presidents and overseers over the leaders of Peoples; they have care for public matters such as Princes, Magistrates, Provinces, and Kingdoms. Hence we read in <term>Daniel</term> <note>Daniel 10:13</note> that "the Prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me for twenty-one days," and <term>Jesus son of Sirach</term> <note>Ecclesiasticus 17:17</note> testifies that a Governor Angel is appointed to every nation. This also seems to be suggested by <term>Moses</term> where he says, "When the Most High divided the nations, He set their bounds according to the number of the Angels" <note>Deuteronomy 32:8. Older translations often used "Angels of God" instead of the modern "sons of Israel."</note>. Into these, God flows the seventh name of His numbering, which is Triumph and Victory <note>In the Kabbalistic tree of life, this refers to the Sephirah *Netzach* (Victory), which is the seventh station.</note>; to them is assigned a right-hand column, which signifies the eternity and justice of God the Avenger. 

Their form must correspond to the particular care that each of them holds; since peoples and nations are diverse in nature as well as in dress and color, these angels must also be represented diversely. And so, in this choir, one will perceive at once angels who are swift, slender, grave, graceful, masculine, delicate, ornate, glorious, beautiful, honest, stable, pure, and of every other manner, according to the character of the peoples over whom they are placed. In this, the artist should always transform what is a vice in the people into the nearest neighboring virtue in the angels: such as changing volatility into speed, harshness into gravity, and lightness into grace. 

The **Archangels** are the bringers of greater things; they offer the prayers and sacrifices of men in the presence of God, who <unclear>reveals</unclear> Himself in them as light. He flows into them the name <term>Elohim Sabaoth</term> <note>original: "Elohim Sabaoth", Hebrew for "God of Hosts".</note> through the numbering of <term>Hod</term> <note>The eighth Sephirah, representing Splendor or Majesty.</note>, which is interpreted as Praise, confession, ornament, and celebrity; to them is attributed a left-hand column. 

These angels, primarily acting as ambassadors or messengers, must have a form corresponding to the manner and quality of their embassy, carrying explanatory signs in their hands. For a sign of purity, they hold the Lily; for this reason, it is with great justification painted in the hand of <term>Gabriel</term> when he announced the incarnation of the Son of God to the Virgin <term>Mary</term>, wearing garments of pure color to match the effect he had come to execute. But for a sign of peace, the Olive is appropriate, as seen in the hand of the one who appeared to the Shepherds singing the gracious hymn. Conversely, another sign is given to those who announce war, such as those who appeared to <term>Abraham</term> in the form of pilgrims, announcing the ruin of the five Cities <note>The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah.</note>. Thus, the signs and ornaments will vary according to what best suits the subject of the history that is to be represented.

...to represent. For instance, the Angel who appeared to **Hermes** in the garb of a **Shepherd**, and warned him that Easter should be celebrated on a Sunday, appeared in shepherd’s clothing according to what **Pope Pius** <note>Pope Pius I (reigned c. 140–154 AD) was traditionally associated with the author of "The Shepherd of Hermas."</note> writes. Lastly, the **Angels** are the guardians and teachers of the human generation; they announce future things of lesser importance and lesser gravity than those announced by the **Archangels**. For this reason, we read that the Prophet **Zechariah**, when the Lord wished to free the People from the Babylonian captivity, saw one who learned things from an Archangel, who had likewise learned them from the superior angels. Now, as they are messengers, they must also be represented in clothing and manners that hint in part at what they come to announce—as we just said regarding the Archangels—but with less beauty and excellence than the others, as they are more familiar to us. 

Now, for a general instruction: even though all the angels of any Choir must be formed in this proper way, it must always be observed that each one, according to its nature, looks with its acts and gestures toward God as the "first light"; thus, various acts of devotion come to be discerned. And since they must all be represented with instruments in hand, in the act of continually playing and singing hymns in praise of the Lord, certain instruments must be distributed to each choir conforming to its nature—for everyone understands that, for example, a **Drum** would not be suitable for a humble angel. 

And whoever desires to become an expert and judicious painter in distributing choral instruments and clothing to the Angels should continually contemplate and look upon those primarily painted by <term>Gaudenzio</term> <note>Gaudenzio Ferrari (c. 1475–1546), a renowned Northern Italian painter and sculptor famous for his crowded, musical celestial scenes.</note> around the Christ who crowns the Mother and Virgin in heaven, in <term>Valtellina at Traona</term>; and also in the great **cupola** at <term>Santa Maria di Saronno</term> around the Virgin ascending to Heaven. In these, he has expressed everything that can be imagined or represented in an angel through the whims and folds of cloths, the positioning of heads and hair, and new types of instruments. So gifted was this great man in every kind of invention that he may truly be said to have been sent down by God Himself to enlighten this art of painting. 

These orders described by me in such a sequence are those written by <term>St. Dionysius</term> <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian whose "Celestial Hierarchy" established the nine ranks of angels.</note>, because **St. Gregory** and **St. Bernard** place the **Principalities** in the second Choir of the second Hierarchy, and the **Virtues** in the first of the third. ...number of Angels that can be known. Know that just as it is certain and settled among everyone that there are three hierarchies and nine choirs, it is equally uncertain how many angels are found in each choir. Although the prophet **Daniel**, according to the **Seventy interpreters** <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, says there are a thousand thousands <note>original: "mille Millenarij"</note>, and ten thousand ten-thousands <note>original: "decies mille, diece millenarij"</note>; where, by repeating thousands and thousands—which are two very large numbers—and multiplying them by themselves (since he says a thousand millions, and "myriads," which means ten thousand times ten thousand <note>original: "miriades cioè decies mille, decem mille"</note>), he silently demonstrates that they exist in a truly vast number. Indeed, a circle beginning in itself and ending in itself seems to demonstrate an incomprehensible number. And according to the other translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note>, another number is interpreted, which is also infinite: namely, "thousands of thousands, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand" <note>original: "millia millium decies millies centena milium"</note>.

But **Albert** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a prominent Dominican theologian and philosopher.</note> in his *Compendium of Theology* writes that each choir contains six thousand, six hundred and sixty-six legions; and each legion has as many Angels as there are legions. Thus, each choir comes to have forty-four million, four hundred thirty-five thousand, five hundred and fifty-six Angels. By multiplying this number by the nine choirs, the total comes to three hundred ninety-nine million, ninety-two thousand, and four Angels. If you wish to subtract the number of one choir from this total—because that is the number of those who fell—there remain in the nine choirs three hundred fifty-five million, four hundred eighty-four thousand, four hundred and forty-eight Angels. All of these should be represented with wings as a sign of their elevation and speed; **Dante** writes that these wings are made of gold because of the preciousness of their work <note>A reference to Dante Alighieri's descriptions of angels in the *Divine Comedy*, where gold symbolizes divine grace and purity.</note>. Let this suffice for what has been said regarding this part of the angels according to our theologians, omitting how the **Hebrews** name them and how they contemplate them.

### Of the form of the militia of heaven. Cap. IIII.

Beyond the **Thrones**, **Cherubim**, and **Seraphim**—who, being close to God, praise Him continually with hymns, magnify Him without intermission, and pray to Him for our salvation—**Athanasius** <note>St. Athanasius of Alexandria, to whom various medieval angelological schemes were sometimes attributed.</note> posits seven other orders, which he calls by the single name **Militia of Heaven**. The first order he calls **Doctrinal**, one of whom was the one who spoke to **Daniel**, saying: "Come, so that I may teach you those things which are to happen to your People in the last days." The leader of this order should be represented in long robes, with a crown on his head, olive branches in his hand, and with books and similar objects in his hand,

The second order is called **Protective** or **Tutelary** <term>Tutelary: serving as a guardian or protector.</term>, of whom we also read in the **Book of Daniel**: "Behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, comes to help me"; and in the same place it says: "At that time Michael shall stand up, the Great Prince who stands for the children of your people."
