He returned with **Rachel** <note>original: "Rachel"; the biblical Book of Tobit names the bride Sarah, but the author may be using a variant or misremembering.</note>, his daughter taken as his wife, and with the gall and heart of the fish, with which he healed his father's blindness. Their form must be adapted to the place, time, and persons they take under their guardianship, just as **Raphael** took the form of a companion when he went to protect Tobias, while he was seeking company in the square of **Nineveh** to go to **Rages**, a city in **Media**, to find Gabelus. 

The third order is called **Procuratorial** <term>Procuratorial: acting as an agent or advocate for another.</term>, of which it is written in the **Book of Job**: "If there be an angel speaking for him, the Lord will be entreated, and He shall be favorable unto him." Of this order it is said there are those of whom it is written in **Ecclesiasticus** <note>Also known as the Wisdom of Sirach, a book of the deutero-canonical scriptures.</note>: that in God’s judgment their works have existed from the beginning, and from the creation of mankind, God gave them their assigned parts of those works in an orderly fashion; that their origins are among their own nations; that He adorned His works for eternity; and that they never suffered hunger or fatigue, nor did they ever cease from their works for that reason, nor shall any one of them ever distress his neighbor forever. To these, one may give a scroll <term>original: "breue", a short written document; here likely a scroll of petition or prayer.</term> or some token to remember the prayer they offer to Divine Justice on behalf of sinners. Their garments may be varied, showing legs and arms sometimes bare and sometimes covered, according to the variety of their duties and the written records of the sinners. 

The fourth order is called **Ministerial**, of which **St. Paul** says in the **Epistle to the Hebrews**: "Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to serve those who shall inherit salvation?" The painter shall vary these figures in their clothing, as well as in their proportions and form, according to the nature of their service. For their ministries can be of all kinds, conforming to the nature and merits of those who receive them. For example: one who ministers through charity should appear merciful and pleasant; one through chastity, entirely youthful and sincere; and one through justice, masculine and deep in thought...

The fifth is called **Auxiliary** <term>Auxiliary: an order of angels characterized by providing direct help or military-like intervention.</term>, of whom one reads in **Isaiah**: "The Angel of the Lord went out, and struck in the camp of the Assyrians one hundred and eighty-five thousand." These shall be formed with the appropriate weapons, according to the manner of the help they provide, or according to the offense they strike. The sixth order is named **Receptive of Souls**, of whom we read in **Saint Luke**: "The soul of **Lazarus** was carried by the Angels into the bosom of **Abraham**." In the same place we are taught that we should make friends for ourselves with riches, even if poorly acquired, so that they may receive us into the eternal tabernacles. In addition to a cheerful face, they shall be given very large and rich ornaments around their garments, but varied and distinct; and on their heads, garlands of flowers. This is because the receiver must present himself as joyful and lovely in every way that can delight the one who has been made worthy of his reception. 

The seventh and last is called **Assistant**, of whom we read in **Zechariah**: "These are the two sons of the oil of splendor <note>original: "figliuoli dell'olio di splendore"; usually translated in modern bibles as "the two anointed ones."</note>, who are assistants to the Ruler of the whole earth." Since their form is well enough known by their office, I shall pass over it in silence.

## On the form of the blessed souls. Chapter V.

**U**nder the choirs of the Angels and blessed spirits follows the **animastic** <term>Animastic: pertaining to the soul (from the Latin 'anima').</term> order. This order of blessed souls, in which the happiness of the **Queen of Heaven** is shown in the form of a **white rose** <note>A reference to the "Candida Rosa" in Dante's Paradiso, where the saved souls are seated.</note>, is called the **Holy Militia**—that is, the souls of the blessed who down here have fought and conquered the World, the Flesh, and the Devil by virtue of the seven gifts of beatitude. # SEVENTH

In the center, and on one of the most exalted leaves of the rose, sits **Mary**, around whom shines the greatest light from the **Trinity**. Surrounding her are infinite joyful **Angels**, each distinguished by their own splendor and manner of celebration (because some shine more and some less, according to how much they are capable of receiving divine love). There, divine beauty shines forth, which is the true joy felt by all the other saints, and principally by **Mary**, who is the most beautiful among all other beauties and most resembling **Christ**. In the second tier of the leaves, **Dante** <note>Reference to Dante Alighieri's *Paradiso*, Canto XXXII, where the seating of the blessed is described.</note> places at the feet of **Mary** our ancient mother <note>Eve.</note>; and at her feet in the third tier he places **Rachel**, the wife of **Jacob**. Descending tier by tier, one under the feet of the other, he places **Sarah**, the wife of **Abraham**; **Rebecca**, the wife of **Isaac**; **Judith**, the widow; and **Ruth**, the wife of **Boaz**, who bore **Obed**, the father of **Jesse**. From this seventh degree downward to the flower of the rose—that is, to the **Yellow** <note>Dante refers to the "giallo de la rosa," the golden center of the celestial flower where the light of God is most concentrated.</note>—he places other Hebrew women who believed in the **Christ** to come.

On the other side of the rose, on the highest leaves opposite **Mary**, he places **John the Baptist**. Just as below the bench and seat of **Mary** he places those of **Eve**, **Rachel**, **Sarah**, **Rebecca**, **Judith**, **Ruth**, and the other Hebrew women of the Old Testament one below the other down to the flower of the rose, so on the other side, below the seat of **St. John the Baptist**, he places those of **St. Francis**, **St. Benedict**, **St. Augustine**, and the other contemplatives of the New Testament, one below the other down to the flower. In this way, between the Hebrew women who are under **St. Mary** and the contemplatives who are under **St. John the Baptist**, this rose is divided into two equal parts, almost in the form of a wall, starting from the flower outward—which we have seen is circular in form and made of most splendid light.

To the left of **St. Mary**, he places **Adam**, our first father, and after him **Moses**, the first Prince of the people of God; then the other Fathers, Patriarchs, and prophets: **Abraham**, **Isaac** with his son; but first the twelve <note>The twelve Minor Prophets of the Old Testament.</note>: **Malachi**, **Haggai**, **Zechariah**, **Amos**, **Hosea**, **Micah**, **Jonah**, **Obadiah**, **Zephaniah**, **Nahum**, **Habakkuk**, and **Joel**, along with all those in the Old Testament who believed in the **coming Christ**. On the other side, to the right of **St. John the Baptist**, is **St. Anne**, the mother of **St. Mary**; and then the other Hebrew women who similarly believed in the **coming Christ**. And so, down to the middle of the rose, he states that all the seats are full of Hebrew men and women of the Old Testament. But from the middle down to the flower, it is filled with **little children** <term>pargoletti: young children or infants who died before reaching the age of reason.</term> who, without any personal choice, were previously saved through their innocence and the faith of their parents; and those who were later saved through circumcision. Now, regarding the colors with which the souls in that blessed glory should be represented, this has already been discussed; for if they were not colored, they could not be painted, being invisible in themselves. Thus, the representation of the imagined painting would not exist, though it is necessary that it does; for this [imaginative painting] is of greater excellence in many respects than that of simple imitation, as everyone can easily conclude from the reasons cited elsewhere. And in this manner, such blessed souls—with the aforementioned signs in hand, and with palms and diadems as a sign of their sanctification—must be painted in divine glories and appearances, in ascensions, and in the triumphs of faith and religion, and also in the stories of the **Last Judgment**, just as **Michelangelo** expressed them for the most part in the heaven of his Judgment in the **Vatican**; and similarly in their miracles.

### *On the form of Saturn, the first planet according to the ancients.*
### Chapter VI.

**N**ow, leaving aside the celestial spheres beneath the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest heaven, believed in ancient and medieval cosmology to be the abode of God and the angels.</note> that were imagined by the ancients—and after many ages by more modern astrologers—and that sphere where the Zodiac is imagined, divided into twelve signs and animals, and also the one containing the 48 images of the Heaven <note>The 48 constellations of the Ptolemaic system.</note> with their stars (which **Alessandro Piccolomini** <note>A 16th-century Italian humanist and astronomer known for his popularization of science.</note> collected among others in his book on the sphere), I will come to speak of **Saturn** <term>Saturn</term><note>The furthest of the seven classical planets, associated with time, melancholy, and agriculture.</note>. This is the seventh sphere, which was depicted in many ways by the ancients according to its various meanings. 

Firstly, the Italians and especially the Latins depicted him with the **scythe**, because in the time of **Janus** <note>The Roman god of beginnings; myth says Saturn fled to Italy and was welcomed by Janus.</note> he showed them how to cultivate the fields, calling him **Stercutio** <term>Stercutius</term><note>A Roman deity associated with manuring the fields (from 'stercus', meaning dung).</note>. And because he was held to be the God of Time—wherefore the Greeks called both the planet and Time by the same name, **Chronos** <term>Chronos</term><note>Greek for Time; often conflated with the titan Cronus.</note>—he was figured as an old man with a child in his hand whom he devours, to denote that Time destroys all things. An exception was made for those four children who were feigned to have escaped his hands, signifying the **four elements**: namely, **Jupiter** (Fire), **Juno** (Air), **Neptune** (Water), and **Pluto** (Earth). These cannot be devoured by Time, and therefore Saturn is called *Theue* <note>original: "Theue"; likely a corruption of a Greek term meaning 'devourer'.</note>, that is, "devourer."

(This is also signaled by the scythe they placed in his hand, with which he mows and cuts down everything.) **Martianus Capella** <note>A late-antique author whose work on the liberal arts was a standard textbook in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> paints him as reaching out with his right hand a snake biting its own tail <note>The Ouroboros, an ancient symbol of eternity and the cyclical nature of time.</note>, which is likewise a figure of Time. He adds that Saturn walks with a slow and tardy pace, his head covered by a greening veil, and his hair and beard are entirely white. The green veil shows the beginning of the year, when the whole earth reclothes itself in plants, and the white hair shows the end of the year, when everything is covered in snow and frost. He is feigned with slow steps because of the slow revolution his sphere makes compared to the others. And because dismal effects come from Saturn (as the Arabs hold), he was feigned as a lazy, slow old man, of a pale body color, bent, thin, veiny, with thick lips, thin legs, with his eyes turned toward the ground, and his head wrapped up because of...

<header>-> S E V E N T H <-</header>

...cold, dry, and melancholic nature. Otherwise, according to **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian and bishop who recorded many ancient Phoenician myths in his *Preparation for the Gospel*.</note>, his sister—the Goddess of the Phoenicians called **Astarte** <term>Astarte</term><note>A prominent ancient Near Eastern goddess associated with fertility, sexuality, and war.</note> by the Sidonians—represented him with a crest that had four eyes: two in front and two behind, which closed and slept in turn, so that two were always open. He also had four wings upon his shoulders, of which two were spread as if he were flying, and two were folded and retracted as if he were still. This signifies that even while he sleeps, he still sees, and is simultaneously awake while sleeping; likewise, even while staying still he flies, and while flying he stays still—qualities which all correspond to the nature of **Time**. 

The same Astarte, daughter of Heaven and his wife and sister (as the same author says), placed two wings upon his head, wishing to show the excellence of the mind through one, and the senses through the other, conveying the angelic mover <note>Referring to the "Intellectual Mover" or celestial intelligence believed to guide the motion of the planets.</note> who is later understood through the medium of the senses. **Martianus** <note>Martianus Capella, a 5th-century author whose work *The Marriage of Philology and Mercury* was a fundamental textbook on the liberal arts in the Middle Ages.</note>, in the *Marriage of Mercury and Philology*, when he has her ascend from Heaven to Heaven, says that she reached the sphere of **Saturn** and found him there in a cold place, frozen and covered with frost and snow. He had upon his head as a crest sometimes a serpent, sometimes the head of a lion, and at other times the head of a boar baring its teeth. According to what some write, these represent the effects of time. 

However, the most ancient **Egyptians** represented him in another way to signify Time, placing him near the statue of **Serapis** <note>A Graeco-Egyptian deity whose cult was established in Alexandria. He often represented the sun or the lord of the underworld.</note>—that is, with three heads: one of a dog, another of a lion, and the third of a rapacious wolf, with their necks joined together so that they formed a single body. Around these was wound a serpent in such a way that it hid the whole body, with its head turned toward the right hand of Serapis, whom they worshipped under that name as the **Sun**. And since this planet is the author and master of time, they placed it under his right hand. 

Now, the lion’s head signaled the present time, because it is stronger than the past and the future, just as the lion is among other animals. The dog’s head on the right denoted the future time, which flatters us with new hopes; and the third, the wolf on the left, showed the past time, which snatches and devours all things. Others interpret this Egyptian statue differently, claiming that the staff signified authority, the circle perpetuity, and the three heads the three sons of **Osiris**: namely the lion for **Hercules**, the wolf for **Macedon**, and the dog for **Anubis** <note>Anubis is the jackal-headed god of the dead; Macedon and the Egyptian Hercules were often depicted as sons or companions of Osiris in syncretic myths.</note>. **Macrobius** <note>Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius (5th century AD), a Roman provincial whose *Saturnalia* is a primary source for ancient religious lore.</note> relates that the ancients also depicted him with his feet tied with a woolen thread, and they kept him thus all year long, except that they untied him in December during certain days consecrated to him; wishing in this way to demonstrate that the creature...

In the mother's womb, the child remains bound with tender and soft knots, which are loosened when the time of birth matures in the tenth month <note>In antiquity, pregnancy was often calculated by lunar months or inclusive counting, leading to the "tenth month" as the standard time for birth.</note>. Likewise, for the length of life, he was figured by others as an old man sitting upon a high chair, with his arms raised above his head, and in them a fish, or a scythe, and under his feet a cluster of grapes, with his head covered with a black cloth and his garments likewise black and dark. He was also depicted for the power of growth as an old man leaning on a staff with a curved scythe in his hand and black clothing. But because it would be an infinite task to recall one by one all the images attributed to this God by superstitious antiquity, we shall move on to discuss **Jupiter**.

### *Of the form of Jupiter. Chapter VII.*

**Jupiter**, Lord of all the other Gods and master of the sixth sphere <note>In the traditional Ptolemaic geocentric model, Jupiter resides in the sixth celestial sphere.</note>, was represented by the ancients—as **Suidas**, **Eusebius**, **Porphyry**, and many others relate—seated, to show that the power which rules the world and preserves it is stable and firm, and never changes. His upper parts were made naked and exposed to give us to understand that God manifests Himself to divine intelligences; and the lower parts clothed because we cannot see Him while we dwell in this low world. He held a scepter in his left hand, because just as the principal member, which is the heart, stays in this part of the body—from which come the spirits that are then shared throughout the whole body—so the world has and receives life from God; who, like a King, dispenses and governs it according to His will. With his right hand, he held out an **Eagle**, and sometimes a small image of **Victory**, to show how he is as superior to all the people of Heaven as the Eagle is to all birds. And in this form was his statue in the port of **Piraeus** of the **Athenians**. But wanting (as **Orpheus** did) to depict him in the form of the whole world, which contains all things within itself, the head will be made with golden hair representing the serene Heaven adorned with shining stars, from which issue...

...[he has] two golden horns, which signify one the East and the other the West, with eyes that denote the Sun and the Moon; with a broad chest and spacious shoulders, which suggest the air, with two great wings as a sign of the velocity of the winds, and as proof that God makes himself present swiftly to all things: with an ample belly for the greatness and vastness of the earth surrounded by the waters of the sea: and with feet to demonstrate the lowest part of the world, which is the center of the earth. Another statue was once made by the **Romans** which was entirely naked, except that it had a goat skin around it, and it was—as **Justin** <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a Roman historian who epitomized the works of Pompeius Trogus.</note> recounts—in a Temple at the roots of the **Palatine Hill** called **Jupiter Cicco** <note>original: "Gioue Cicco." This likely refers to an epithet of Jupiter; in some Renaissance mythographies, it is associated with specific local Roman cults or may be a corruption of "Vica Pota" or another archaic title.</note>. The **Greeks** had **Jupiter** the creator just as the **Egyptians** did, whom they made in the form of a man of cerulean <note>A deep sky-blue color, often used to represent the heavens.</note> color, who held a circle in one hand and in the other a royal rod, and on the top of his head a feather, which showed that it is difficult to find the Creator of things who is King, as the scepter <note>The "royal rod" mentioned previously.</note> demonstrates; because it is in his hand to give life to the universe: a thing that he does while, understanding within himself, he revolves; as the circle he holds in his hand clearly shows us. He then sent out of his mouth an egg from which **Vulcan** was born; for the egg signifies the world, and **Vulcan** that virtue <note>In this context, "virtue" (Italian: *virtù*) refers to an inherent power or life-giving energy.</note> which in it gives life to things. In another way they also figured him in **Egypt** as the world, that is, as a man with his feet twisted and knotted together, and with a robe that covered him down to the feet, all varied and of different colors, who supported a great golden ball with his head, to signify that the world is round, nor does it ever change place, and that the stars are varied and distinct: and in another manner with two circles, one above the other, crossed with a serpent that had the head of a hawk. Since the circles are a figure of the greatness and form of the world, and the serpent of the good demon <note>Likely a reference to the *Agathodaemon*, a spirit of good fortune in Greek and Egyptian syncretism.</note> preserver of all, who embraces the universe with his power; and they added the head of a hawk for its great speed and agility. There was once in **Crete**, as **Plutarch** writes, an image of **Jupiter** without ears to warn those who have power over others, and have to govern, that they must not lend ears to what is said to them, nor hear this one rather than that, but stand firm and steady, so that they never bend from the right for the words of others. Conversely, the **Lacedaemonians** <note>The Spartans.</note> made him with four ears, as if **Jupiter** hears everything and understands; which refers to the prudence of one who has power, who has to hear and understand everything that his people do. In **Egypt**, according to **Plutarch**, to overshadow <note>To represent or symbolize figuratively.</note> a King, they depicted **Jupiter** in the form of a scepter with an eye on top, alluding to the power of Kings because the scepter is a sign of the greatness and power they have over others, and the eye refers to the vigilance they must have in their government, showing themselves just in every action: and near it they placed the image of **Justice**, showing that nothing should be done without her. And for this reason, the **Romans** used to give the **oak crown** <note>The *corona civica*, one of the highest military honors.</note> to anyone who had defended a Roman citizen from death in war: as the sign of life was rightly owed to the one who had been the cause of another's survival.

# On the form of Mars. Chap. VIII.

**M**ars (according to the pagans), lord of the fifth sphere, was held by the **Acitani** people of **Spain**, as **Macrobius** <note>Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius (c. 385–430 AD), author of the *Saturnalia*.</note> writes, to be the very heat of the **Sun**. Wherefore they made his image adorned and flashing with rays in the manner of the Sun, worshiping him with the greatest reverence. All the ancients, as the God of war, represented him as fierce and terrible in appearance, fully armed with a spear in hand and with the sphere <note>The "sphere" here likely refers to the celestial orb or a symbol of world power.</note>: sometimes they placed him on horseback, and sometimes upon a chariot (like the **Thracians** among whom he was born), which was (as **Homer** says) pulled by two horses called **Terror** and **Fear**, accompanied by **Impetus**, **Fury**, and **Violence**. In imitating this, **Statius** <note>Publius Papinius Statius (c. 45–96 AD), author of the *Thebaid*, an epic poem about the war between the brothers Eteocles and Polynices.</note>, when he introduces **Jupiter** calling **Mars** to send him to sow the seeds of war between the **Argives** and the **Thebans**...

> *Of those balls: here Mercury watches*

## BOOK 2

->Representing<- <note>The text begins with the conclusion of the word "representing," continued from the previous page.</note> him, the Egyptians and the priests of Memphis <note>original: "Mesi," likely a corruption of Memphis.</note> used to depict this God—for the power of both good and evil, and as a source of awe among the nations—in such a form: an armed man on horseback atop a lion, holding a straight, naked sword in his right hand, and a human head in his left. They represented him in yet another form to symbolize audacity, courage, and luck in war and strife: fashioned in the guise of an armed soldier, wearing a crown, with a sword girded at his side, and grasping a long spear in his right hand. The Romans, believing themselves to be descended from him, built him a temple with a statue, giving him the name of Mars the Avenger <note>Latin: "Mars Ultor." This famous temple was located in the Forum of Augustus in Rome.</note>; and before it they had placed two of those statues that used to support the pavilion of Alexander the Great; and within the temple they hung many iron bowls <note>original: "Schifi." These were likely "scyphi," a type of ancient drinking cup or vessel.</note> as Pliny describes. In the Temple of Concord, they also dedicated a statue of him made by the hand of Pythicritus; and near the Flaminian Circus of Marius, they kept another by Scopas <note>A famous Greek sculptor and architect of the 4th century BCE.</note> in the Temple of Brutus Callaicus, fashioned in the form of a Colossus.

And when they wished to decide upon some war, they would build him an altar of grass <note>original: "Gramigna," referring to sod or turf.</note>, upon which they performed sacrifices with those ceremonies recorded of the Salii priests <note>The "leaping priests" of Mars who carried the sacred shields (ancilia) through the streets of Rome.</note>, who went about leaping in his honor. For this reason, the Romans held no crown more worthy or of greater honor than the grass crown <note>Latin: "Corona graminea," the highest Roman military decoration, awarded only to those who saved an entire army.</note>, as it was dedicated and consecrated to their ancient Father; nor did they give it except to one who, in extreme danger, had saved the entire army or lifted a siege. To this God, by common opinion, the rooster was dedicated to demonstrate the vigilance of soldiers; the vulture, for the natural greed of this bird in following dead bodies while trailing behind armies; and the woodpecker—for this reason sometimes called "Martian"—due to the many ways it conforms to him. Likewise, the wolf, a most rapacious animal, was dedicated for its instinct similar to that of soldiers to always have hands ready for plunder, and also for its sharpness of sight, which is chiefly required in a soldier so that he does not incautiously fall into the ambushes and snares of the enemy.

Finally, temples were erected to Mars and statues consecrated not only by the Romans or by his fellow Thracians (especially on Mount Haemus), but also by the Thermodontines, Scythians, English, Gauls, Germans, Idumeans, and by those who inhabited the hollows of Syria, Commagene, Cappadocia, Metagonitis, Mauritania, and infinite other regions, of which there is no room here to make a catalog; for these facts can easily be gathered by anyone who has read about the customs and religions of the nations.

## On the Form of the Sun. Chapter IX.

**T**he Sun, lord of the fourth sphere <note>In the geocentric Ptolemaic system, the Sun occupies the fourth celestial sphere, positioned between Venus and Mars.</note> and the one who illuminates all the others, has been depicted in many ways by the ancients; although among some of the Assyrians, as one reads in Lucian, he was not painted because he and the moon could be seen from down here. Before I say anything of his forms, being the principal planet, the ancients say that he holds the government and administration of the Heavens and of the bodies that dwell beneath the Heavens. He is the lord of all Elemental power; and the Moon, by his power, is the lady of generation, of increase, and of decrease. Therefore, an ancient Astrologer said that life is infused into all creatures by means of the Sun and the Moon, and Orpheus named them the "vivifying eyes of Heaven." The Sun by himself gives light to everyone and bestows it copiously upon all, not only in the Heaven and in the air, but also upon the earth. Thus, Heraclitus calls him the "source of celestial light," and many of the Platonists have placed the soul of the world in the Sun, as that which fills the entire Globe of the Sun and diffuses its rays like spirits everywhere, distributing life, sense, and motion to the universe.

And therefore the ancient natural philosophers called him the "heart of heaven"; the Chaldeans placed him in the midst of the Planets, and the Egyptians in the center of the world. This planet, among all others, is the true light of both worlds, and by his essence he represents the Father, by his splendor the Son, and by his heat the Holy Spirit. Plato names him the "Son of God"; Iamblichus the "image of divine intelligence"; and Dionysius <note>Likely referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher.</note> the "beautiful statue of God." He sits like a King in the midst of the planets and surpasses the others in light, greatness, and beauty; he illuminates them all, gives them the power to govern lower things, and directs their steps. And because he holds the middle part of the world—just as the heart does in animals for the whole body—he thus helps to vivify and generate the entire world. He is also the measure of time, since from him come day and night, cold and heat, and the other qualities of time. He disposes the body of man, whereof Homer and Aristotle said that our movements are such as the Sun brings to us each day.

Now, the ancients primarily imagined him as a King, and they also designed for him a Royal dwelling, of which Ovid speaks in the second book of his greatest volume <note>Referencing Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*, Book 2.</note> in this manner: The house of the Sun was constructed with very high columns, entirely gilded, and resplendent with the brightness of Pyropus <note>original: "Piropo." A brilliant alloy of gold and bronze, or a gemstone resembling a fiery coal.</note>, of which the walls were built, so that it flashed more than fire. The roof

They gave it only to one who, in some extreme danger, had saved an entire army or lifted a siege.

Finally, temples to Mars were erected and statues consecrated not only by the Romans or by his compatriots the *Thracians* (especially on Mount *Haemus*), but also by the *Thermodonts, Scythians, English, Gauls, Germans, Idumeans*, and by those who inhabited the valleys of *Syria, Commagene, Cappadocia, Meragonitide* <note>Likely a reference to a region in North Africa or the East mentioned in classical geographies.</note>, *Mauritania*, and infinite other regions. It is not the place here to make a catalog of these, as they can easily be gathered from those who have written on the customs and religions of nations.

## On the Form of the Sun. Chapter IX.

**T**HE Sun, lord of the fourth sphere <note>In the geocentric Ptolemaic system, the Sun occupies the fourth orbital sphere, positioned between Venus and Mars.</note> and the light that illuminates all the others, has been depicted in many ways by the ancients. However, among some of the <term>Assyrians</term>, as one reads in <term>Lucian</term> <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125–180 AD), a rhetorician who wrote "On the Syrian Goddess."</note>, he was not painted because he and the moon could be seen from down here. Before I say anything regarding his forms, because he is the principal planet, the ancients say that he holds the government and administration of the Heavens and of the bodies that stand beneath the Heaven. He is the master of all elemental virtue; and the Moon, through his power, is the mistress of generation, of increase, and of decrease. For this reason, an ancient astrologer said that life is infused into all creatures by means of the Sun and the Moon; and <term>Orpheus</term> called them the vivifying eyes of Heaven. 

The Sun by himself gives light to all and bestows it copiously upon everyone, not only in the Heaven and in the air, but also upon the earth. Whence <term>Heraclitus</term> calls him the fountain of celestial light. Many of the <term>Platonists</term> have located the <term>Soul of the World</term> <note>The "Anima Mundi," an intrinsic connection between all living things on the planet, which Neoplatonists often associated with solar energy.</note> in the Sun, as that which fills the entire Globe of the Sun and diffuses its rays like spirits everywhere, distributing life, sense, and motion to the universe. And thus the ancient physicians called him the heart of heaven; the <term>Chaldeans</term> placed him in the midst of the Planets, and the <term>Egyptians</term> in the middle of the world. 

This planet, among all others, is the true light of both worlds <note>Referring to the physical/material world and the spiritual/intellectual world.</note>; in his essence he represents the Father, in his splendor the Son, and in his heat the Holy Spirit. <term>Plato</term> names him the son of God; <term>Iamblichus</term>, the image of divine intelligence; and <term>Dionysius</term>, the beautiful statue of God. He sits like a King in the midst of the planets and surpasses the others in light, greatness, and beauty; he illuminates them all and gives them the virtue to arrange inferior things, and he governs their steps. Because he holds the middle part of the world—just as the heart does in animals for the whole body—so he helps to vivify and generate the entire world. 

He is also the measure of time, since from him come day and night, cold and heat, and the other qualities of time. He disposes the body of man, wherefore <term>Homer</term> and <term>Aristotle</term> said that our movements are such as the Sun brings to us each day. [The palace] was entirely of ivory, and the doors were of burnished silver, all resplendent. The house was carved with figures in relief, such that the workmanship far surpassed the material. <margin>I</margin> For here **Vulcan** <note>The Roman god of fire and blacksmithing, credited with crafting the marvelous dwellings and tools of the gods.</note> had carved the great seas that surround the Earth, and she [the Earth] was seen depicted in her own form. The Heaven was carved there, and all the Marine Gods: **Triton**, the Trumpeter of Neptune; **Proteus** and **Aegaeon** with his great arms; **Doris** half-hidden in the sea waters and half out, with green hair in the Sun. Various fish were sculpted there, each different from the other. And besides this, there were carved the Cities, the Fortresses, the forests, and the wild beasts that dwell upon the earth, and the rivers in which the **Nymphs** live; the gods of the villages; the images of the Heaven and six signs <note>Referring to the first six signs of the Zodiac.</note> on the right side of the door, and the other six on the left. After this, the poet <note>Ovid, in his *Metamorphoses*.</note> also describes the royal majesty and his Barons, saying that there sat the Sun, dressed and veiled in purple upon a throne shining with emeralds; and he had at his right and his left the days, the months, and the years; and there were also the world with the century <note>original: *secolo* — here referring to "the Age" or "Time" personified as *Aion*.</note> and the hours, which showed how time passes within him. In the emerald throne one saw carved **Spring**, with a crown of lovely flowers upon her head; **Summer**, with a garland of grain-ears on her head; **Autumn**, all foul and stained with wine; and cold **Winter** with hair scorched by the frost.

Then he depicts the chariot:

> Of gold also the rim of the wheels, and those
> Had spokes of silver, the workmanship of which
> Contained within itself marvelous and beautiful things.
> Such rich yokes they had upon them
> Scattered like the lovely stars in the heaven
> Among rich pearls and beautiful distinct rubies
> Resplendent chrysolites and hyacinths.

...to the last, a cold old man <note>This completes the description of the Four Seasons, specifically Winter, who is often depicted as an elderly man.</note>; the rest of his body seems to be all flame, and he has wings at his feet adorned with most burning carbuncles. Around him, he wears a cloak woven of gold and purple; in his left hand he holds a most brilliant shield, and with his right he proffers a lit torch. But returning to the chariot, the same **Ovid** added the horses, saying:

> Meanwhile Eous, Pyroeis, and Aethon,
> Winged horses of the Sun, and the fourth, Phlegon,
> With burning neighs beyond the stars,
> Make themselves heard, striking out strongly.
> <note>original: *In tanto Eoo, Piroo, & Etone / Del ſol caualli alati, e il quarto flego / Con annitrir ardente oltre le ſtelle / Si fan ſentire percotendo forte.* These lines are a translation of Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, Book 2.</note>

Now, this carriage, being so bright, denotes his never-interrupted volatility, with the light that never fails as it circles the entire world. The four wheels demonstrate that the four seasons already described are caused by his rotation; likewise, the four horses denote the qualities of the day. **Pyroeis**, who is the first, is painted red because of the rising of the Sun, which is red in the morning; **Eous**, who is the second, is painted white and is called "shining" because, the Sun having already spread out and cleared away the vapors, he is brilliant and clear; the third, called **Aethon**, is depicted as red and inflamed so that he tends toward yellow, since the Sun, being then in the middle of the sky, has a burning and inflamed light; **Phlegon**, who is the last, is painted yellow tending toward black, to demonstrate the declination of the Sun toward the earth.

Others have given them different names, such as **Fulgentius** <note>Fabius Planciades Fulgentius, a Latin writer of the late 5th/early 6th century known for his mythographies.</note>, who names the first **Erythraeus** (red), as the Sun is in the morning; the second **Actaeon**, because he extends his rays toward the earth; the third **Lampros** (splendid), because at midday he shines greatly; and the fourth **Philogeus** (lover of the Earth), because toward the evening, he sinks toward her. **Martial** mentions only two of them, but leaving these subtleties aside, I will speak of the other images of the Sun. **Macrobius** writes that in a certain part of Assyria there was a gilded statue of the Sun without a beard; standing with his arm raised, he held a sphere in his right hand in the manner of a charioteer, and in his left hand a lightning bolt and some ears of grain, which showed that his power and that of **Jupiter** were joined together. Under all the names attributed to him, he was always depicted with a beardless face, as **Tibullus** sang:

> Only Bacchus and Phoebus are eternally
> Young, and both have long and blond hair,
> <note>original: *Sol Bacco e Febo ſono eternamente / Giouani & ambi han chioma longa e bionda*</note>

The blond hair signifies the resplendent rays, and the youth gives us to understand that his power, and that heat which gives life to all created things, is always the same and never grows old, so that...

...becomes weak. He is also given a seven-stringed lyre in his hand to represent the number of the planets, which, moving with the proportion that is most suitable to each of them, create a most sweet harmony. This lyre was placed in the hand of the Sun because, being in the midst of the planets, **Macrobius** <note>Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius (5th century AD), a Roman provincial whose works on mythology and astronomy were widely read in the Renaissance.</note> says that he gives the law to all of them; thus they move quickly or slowly according to whether they receive more or less vigor from him. For this reason, they also made him the leader of the **Muses**, that is, the leader of the harmony of the Heavens. He carries a shield at his side, which represents our hemisphere made in a circle; and he carries arrows because, as **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (3rd century AD) who wrote extensively on allegory.</note>
<margin>H</margin> wrote, just as arrows penetrate with great force when they are shot from a bow, so his rays penetrate with their power even into the bowels of the earth, and to the lowest part of the world. Hence, as **Servius** <note>A 4th-century grammarian known for his commentary on Virgil.</note> affirms, he was called the God of Heaven, Earth, and Hell. The **Lacedaemonians** <note>The Spartans.</note> made a statue of him with four ears and as many hands, because they saw him fighting for them in that form, as some say; according to others, it was to show in this manner the prudence that comes from him, which is slow to speak but stands with ears wide open to listen. The **Persians**, as **Lactantius** says in his commentary on **Statius**, had him in a cave where they worshipped him, with the head of a Lion, dressed in their own clothing with his head adorned in the manner of their women, holding a cow by the horns with both hands by force. They intended to suggest with the Lion's head that he has greater strength in the zodiac sign of **Leo** than in any other sign, and that he is among the stars as the lion is among the animals; and by the figure of the cow, they meant the moon, which he grips by the horns because he often takes away her light <note>An ancient explanation for eclipses or the lunar phases.</note>. The **Assyrians**, to demonstrate his virtue and power, alone among all people used to depict him (as **Lucian** reports) with a long beard pointed at the end, with a certain object in the form of a basket <term>calathos</term> <note>A basket-shaped crown symbolizing divinity and abundance.</note> upon his head, rebuking those who depicted him without a beard. He wore a breastplate on his chest and held a spear in his right hand, which had a small figure of **Victory** at the top; in his left hand he held out a flower, and over his shoulders was a cloth on which was painted the head of **Medusa**, surrounded by serpents. There were eagles at his side that seemed to be flying, and before his feet was an image of a woman, who had two other images of women on either side, whom a great serpent knotted together with swift coils. Regarding this statue, **Macrobius** says that the beard hanging down
<margin>I</margin> over the chest signifies that the Sun spreads his rays from heaven to earth; the golden basket rising high shows the celestial fire of which it is believed he is made; the spear and the breastplate show the forceful...

...the burning heat that he gives to <term>Mars</term>, so that by many he is held to be one and the same thing as <term>Mars</term>; the victory signifies that everything is subject to him; the flower denotes the beauty of things; the woman at his feet is the Earth, which he illuminates from the Heavens with his rays; the other two women signify the matter from which things are made and the nature that makes them; the serpent that binds them shows us the winding path that the <term>Sun</term> takes; The eagles, because they fly swiftly and high, show us the height and speed of the <term>Sun</term>; The cloth with the head of <term>Medusa</term>, the emblem of <term>Minerva</term> <note>The goddess of wisdom; her shield or aegis bore the Gorgon's head.</note>, teaches us that his power, by means of <term>Minerva</term>, enlightens human intellects and infuses prudence into the minds of mortals. Another statue of the <term>Sun</term>, according to <term>Pausanias</term> <note>A 2nd-century AD Greek traveler and geographer.</note>, was once in a certain part of <term>Laconia</term> <note>The region of Greece surrounding Sparta.</note> consecrated to him, made of metal; it had a helmet on its head, a bow in one hand, and a spear in the other. 

<term>The Egyptians</term>, among the other statues they erected to him, had one with a half-shaved head, so that hair remained only on the right side. According to <term>Macrobius</term>, this meant that the <term>Sun</term> is never so hidden from nature that he does not continually provide some benefit with his rays; and the cut hair shows that the <term>Sun</term>, even at the time when we do not see him, has the strength and power to return to us anew, just as cut hair tends to grow back since the roots remain. In addition to this, they made him with feathers of various colors—one dim and dark, and the other bright and lucid, which they called celestial, just as the other was infernal. This is because the <term>Sun</term> is said to be in Heaven when he passes through the six signs of the <term>Zodiac</term> that create the summer season and are called superior; and he is said to descend into hell <note>In this context, 'inferno' refers to the lower hemisphere or the underworld/winter months.</note> when he begins to travel through the other six of Winter, called inferior; and the feathers were a sign of his speed. 

Under the name of <term>Serapis</term> <note>A Graeco-Egyptian deity who combined traits of Osiris, Apis, and Zeus.</note>, they also formed him in the likeness of a man wearing a <term>bushel</term> <note>original: "moggio," a grain-measure worn as a crown (modius), symbolizing fertility and the sun's role in the harvest.</note> on his head, as if to say that in all things one must use proper measure. In <term>Alexandria</term>, in the Temple dedicated to him, there was his statue made of all kinds of metals and woods, so large that by stretching out its hands it touched both sides of the Temple; and there was a small window made with such skill that the <term>Sun</term>, always upon his appearance, entering through it, would illuminate the face of the statue. Seeing this, the people were convinced that the <term>Sun</term> came every morning to visit <term>Serapis</term> and to kiss him. 

<term>Martianus Capella</term> <note>A Latin author of late antiquity known for his encyclopedic work on the liberal arts.</note>, when he introduces <term>Mercury</term> and Virtue coming to <term>Phoebus</term> <note>Another name for Apollo or the Sun.</note> to take counsel on whether he should marry, feigns that they find him sitting upon a high and great Tribunal, with four covered vessels before him, into which he looked, uncovering them...

taking only one at a time: and they were of diverse forms, and of various metals; one of iron, from which issued living flames called the head of **<term>Vulcan</term>** <note>The Roman god of fire and metalworking.</note>; the other of shining silver, full of serenity and temperate air, called the laughter of **<term>Jupiter</term>**; the third of livid lead, named the death of **<term>Saturn</term>**, full of rain, frost, and snow; and the fourth, closest to **<term>Phoebus</term>** <note>A common name for Apollo as the Sun god.</note>, of shining glass, containing within it all the seeds that the air scatters upon the Earth, called the breast of **<term>Juno</term>**. From these vessels, now from one and now from the other, and sometimes from this one and sometimes from that, according as he had need, **<term>Phoebus</term>** took that from which mortals then had life, and sometimes also death. For when he wished to bestow upon the world the sweet aura of the vital spirit, he mixed part of the temperate air from the silver vessel with part of the seed that was in the glass vessel; and when he then threatened plague and death, he added the burning flames of the iron vessel, or truly the horrid cold of the leaden vessel. From which it is clearly seen that the diversity of the weather comes from the hand of the Sun.

<term>The Egyptians</term>, before the use of letters, represented the Sun by a royal scepter, and they placed an eye at the top, which they also called the eye of **<term>Jupiter</term>**, as if he saw all things and governed them with supreme justice; because the scepter shows the government. <term>The Phoenicians</term> made a black stone, round and wide at the base, but which grew narrower toward the top, which—as **<term>Herodotus</term>** <note>A 5th-century BC Greek historian often called the "Father of History."</note> writes—they boasted of having received from Heaven. **<term>Alessandro Napolitano</term>** <note>Also known as Alessandro d'Alessandro, a 15th-century Italian humanist jurist.</note> writes that in a certain place they placed a flattened and round stone at the head of a long rod, and they worshiped that as the image of the Sun.

And **<term>Pausanias</term>** relates that in **<term>Patras</term>**, a city of **<term>Achaia</term>**, in a temple consecrated to him, a metal statue was placed, entirely naked except for its feet, which were covered; one of these feet he held over the head of an ox, because they said oxen were pleasing to him, as **<term>Alcaeus</term>** <note>A Greek lyric poet from Lesbos.</note> sings in a certain hymn he wrote to **<term>Mercury</term>**, and before him, **<term>Homer</term>**. <term>The Trojans</term> depicted him with one foot upon a mouse, for which reason they also called him **<term>Smintheus</term>** <note>An epithet of Apollo; "Smintheus" comes from the Greek word "sminthos," meaning mouse.</note> in memory of the mice killed by him, which destroyed the harvest every year. One reads in **<term>Pliny</term>** of another statue made for him by **<term>Praxiteles</term>** <note>One of the most renowned sculptors of ancient Greece.</note>, which was not very dissimilar in meaning to this one: for he stood with an arrow on his bow as if in ambush to kill a lizard that was a short distance from him. In <term>Naples</term>, a statue was erected to him, which, besides the other insignia and ornaments given to him, had a dove upon the shoulder, with a woman before it who looked at it fixedly in an act of adoration; and she was **<term>Parthenope</term>** <note>In mythology, one of the Sirens and the legendary founder of the city of Naples.</note>;

...Parthenope; because they said that this bird was his guide when he came from Greece to the Neapolitan fields. **<term>Eusebius</term>** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian and scholar.</note> writes that in **<term>Elephantine</term>** <note>An island city in the Nile, southern Egypt.</note>, a city in Egypt, there was a statue of him in the form of a man who had the head of a ram with horns, entirely cerulean <note>A deep sky-blue color.</note> in color; which, as the color of the sea representing the humidity in the universe, is meant to show us that the Sun, when joined with the Moon in **<term>Aries</term>** <note>The sign of the Ram in the zodiac.</note>, is much more humid than at other times.

Some others, wishing to show the invincible and honored man who brought things begun to their conclusion, and drove away novelties and dreams, and who is safe from fevers and illnesses, fashioned him crowned, sitting upon a chair with a **raven** in his lap, a globe under his feet, and dressed in a saffron-colored robe. And wanting to represent a fortunate man, rich and loved by all, they made him in the form of a crowned woman in the act of jumping and laughing, standing upon a chariot pulled by four horses with a mirror in her right hand—or rather a shield—and in the other a staff resting against her chest, and upon her head a flame of fire.

The ancients sacrificed the **wolf** to him because, just as the Sun with its rays draws to itself and consumes the humid exhalations of the earth, so the wolf snatches and devours the flocks. And **<term>Martianus</term>** <note>Martianus Capella, an author of the 5th century who wrote on mythology.</note> says that the raven was given to him as a sign of the prophecy that was believed to come from him; and the **swan** was added to it, to show by their contrary colors that the Sun makes the day similar to the whiteness of the swan when it comes to us, and in departing, it likewise makes the night as black as the raven. 

But **<term>Pausanias</term>** <note>A Greek traveler and geographer of the 2nd century AD.</note> reports that in Greece the **rooster** was revered as the bird of **<term>Apollo</term>** <note>The Greek god of the Sun, music, and prophecy.</note> because by singing it announces the morning and the return of the Sun. **<term>Homer</term>** has the **hawk** consecrated to him, for which reason he calls it the swift messenger of Apollo when he writes that **<term>Telemachus</term>** <note>The son of Odysseus.</note>, having returned home to **<term>Ithaca</term>**, sees a hawk tearing a dove in the air, from which he took a good omen that he would free his house from his mother’s suitors. 

Similarly, in Egypt, under the image of the hawk, they often understood **<term>Osiris</term>** <note>The Egyptian god of the afterlife and regeneration, often solarized in later traditions.</note>, who is the Sun, both because this bird has very sharp sight and because it is very swift in flight. And **<term>Porphyry</term>** <note>Porphyry of Tyre, a Neoplatonic philosopher.</note> recounts that the Egyptians held sacred to him not only the hawk, but also the **beetle** <note>The scarab, a primary symbol of the rising sun in Egypt.</note>, the **ram**, and the **crocodile**; the first because, in early times, a hawk arrived—without anyone knowing from where—and brought to the priests in **<term>Thebes</term>** a book written in red letters, which taught how and with what reverence the gods should be adored; from which it arose that the writers of sacred things there always wore red hair. <note>original: "capello rosso". This likely refers to a specific priestly headdress or ritual hair coloring associated with Egyptian sacred scribes.</note>

...head, with the wing of a **sparrowhawk**. The second symbol was held, as we read in **<term>Eusebius</term>** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian.</note>, as a true image of the Sun: the **scarab beetle**. This was because, according to **<term>Aelian</term>** <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric who wrote "On the Nature of Animals."</note>, all scarab beetles are male; therefore, it was commanded that soldiers should continually wear them carved into their rings to remind them that they must possess a virile, and not an effeminate, spirit. The third symbol was attributed to him because they understood the **crocodile** to represent fresh water, from which the Sun purges and removes every foul quality with his temperate rays. For this reason, the Egyptian theologians used to place the statue of the Sun in a boat, as Eusebius writes, which was carried by several crocodiles. Also dedicated to him—whether because of the myth of **Daphne** <note>The nymph who turned into a laurel tree to escape Apollo's pursuit.</note> or for some other reason—was the **laurel**, and thus garlands were always made for him from it.

Now, he was called **<term>Sole</term>** <note>The Italian word for Sun.</note> because he is the only one <note>original: "solo"</note> who shines; **<term>Phoebus</term>** for his radiance; **<term>Lycius</term>** from the Lycian temple of Delos; **<term>Soconia</term>** <note>Likely a reference to a Syrian epithet for the Sun mentioned in Macrobius's Saturnalia.</note> by the Syrians, as **<term>Macrobius</term>** writes, which is derived from the splendor of the rays called by them the "golden tresses of the silver-bearer," because as he rises through the highest space of the world, a certain white and silver arch is shaped from which rays shoot out like shining arrows. He was called **<term>Horus</term>** as a most great and sublime giant, as we all see him, which name was given to him by the Egyptians. They fashioned him of iron in the temple of **<term>Serapis</term>** <note>A Greco-Egyptian deity.</note> so that he stayed suspended in the air by the **lodestones** <note>original: "calamita"; naturally magnetized pieces of the mineral magnetite.</note> they had placed all around him. He had many other names as well, which Macrobius collected in his *Saturnalia*.

In Lycia and in Delphi, he was held as an oracle, and in Scythia many temples were sacred to him, for those people worshiped him as their only God, sacrificing a **horse** to him. He was likewise worshiped by the Assyrian Heliopolitans, and under the name of **Apollo** by the Rhodians, who erected to him that greatest **Colossus** made by **Chares** the Sculptor <note>Chares of Lindos, the creator of the Colossus of Rhodes.</note>. It was seventy cubits in height and worth three hundred talents, which comes to one hundred and eighty thousand French gold crowns, at a rate of six hundred crowns per talent according to **<term>Budé</term>** <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), a French scholar who wrote extensively on ancient weights and coinage.</note>; from this statue, the people were later called Colossians. He was also worshiped by the Hyperboreans and the Milesians.

Specifically sacred to him were the mountains of **Parnassus**, **Phaselis**, **Cynthus**, and **Soracte**; and the islands of **Tenedos** and **Delos**. In Delos, **Erichthonius** constructed for him that most magnificent temple, where part of the columns and marbles can still be seen, along with his colossus of 18 cubits with Greek letters. Other sacred sites included Clarus, Mallus in Lesbos, Gryneium, Patara, Arephnia, Chusa, Therapna, Cirra, and Delphi, where his oracle was located and to which all of Greece flocked, in a temple painted by **Aristoclides** and **Polygnotus**. The inhabitants of Cyme also built him a temple, to which **Alexander the Great** offered a magnificent lamp...

## *On the Form of Venus. Chapter X.*

**T**he form of **Venus**, lady of the third sphere, is found to be quite varied; but the general form (setting aside **Cupid**, who is represented beside her as her son) is that which we have described by **<term>Apuleius</term>** <note>A 2nd-century Roman author and philosopher.</note>, where he says that she was of a most beautiful aspect, of a sweet and joyful color, and almost entirely naked, showing her perfect beauty. This was because she had nothing around her but a very thin veil, which did not cover her, but only shaded her parts—which are almost always hidden—and the sweet wind blowing lightly would at times lift it a little, swelling it, so that the flower of youth could be seen; at other times it would press it and bring it close to her beautiful limbs,

...so that it almost no longer appeared. The entire body was of a celestial white; and the thin veil was of a cerulean color, being that such is the color of the sea from which she was born. Before her went the charming Loves <note>Small winged figures associated with Cupid, often called *putti* or *erotes*.</note> with burning torches lit in their hands; and on one side she had the **Graces** and on the other, the most beautiful **Hours** <note>The *Horae*, goddesses of the seasons and the natural order of time.</note>, who seemed adorned in various ways with lovely garlands of flowers; on one side the Goddess of Pleasures, who holds **Cupid** in one hand and **Anteros** <note>The god of requited love, who punishes those who scorn love.</note> in the other. Others then, because she was born in the sea from the testicles of **Heaven** <note>original: "Cielo"; referring to the Greek Titan Uranus, who was castrated by Cronus.</note>, depicted her with a sea shell in her hand, as beautiful as possible, and with a garland of roses on her head, because they turn red and prick, just as is the nature of lust. Others imagined her still swimming through the sea, to demonstrate that the lives of unhappy lovers are joined with bitterness, and buffeted by various fortunes, with frequent shipwrecks, whence **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who often interpreted myths allegorically.</note> says:

> *Of Venus in the sea, poor and naked.*

And **Ovid**, while she swims in the sea, induces her to say thus to **Neptune**:

> *And I too have something to do,*
> *Amidst these waves, if it is true that I was*
> *Once dense foam in the sea, from which*
> *I had the name; which today I still keep:*

Because the Greeks call her **Aphrodite** from the foam <note>The name is traditionally derived from the Greek word *aphros*, meaning "foam."</note>, **Virgil** likewise has **Neptune** respond to her when she prays him to finally quiet the sea storm that had assailed her son **Aeneas**:

> *It is right that you trust in my realms,*
> *Because you were once born of these.*

Wanting to show this, the ancients painted her emerging from there, standing in a large sea shell, young and beautiful, as much as was possible, and entirely naked. And they gave her the sea shell because, as **Juba** <note>Juba II, a learned king of Numidia and Mauretania known for his writings on history and natural sciences.</note> says, in joining with the male it opens entirely and reveals itself, to allude to what is done in amorous pleasures. She was made entirely naked because she makes naked those who imitate her, and to show that which she is always prepared for, and also to give to understand that he who goes after lascivious pleasures often remains stripped and deprived of every good, having lost riches, the body weakened, and the soul stained; which has nothing more of beauty; and besides this, to make us know that amorous thefts cannot always remain hidden; wherefore, for this or whatever other cause it might be, **Praxiteles** made for the **Knidians** that so celebrated naked Venus of whitest marble; so beautiful...

...so beautiful that many sailed there just to see her; of whom, as **Lucian** and **Pliny** write, one man became so enamored that he left upon her hip the stain of his desire. <note>This refers to the famous Aphrodite of Knidos by the sculptor Praxiteles; legend says a young man was so overcome by its realism that he hid in the temple at night and left a physical mark of his lust upon the marble.</note> And many hold the opinion that this is the very statue—because of the wonderful beauty found in it—which is now in Rome, and which I too have seen. Many years ago, this statue, along with the other principal statues of the ancients and moderns, was cast by **Knight Leone Aretino** <note>Leone Leoni (c. 1509–1590), a famous sculptor and medalist from Arezzo who built the "Casa degli Omenoni" in Milan.</note> and sent to his most beautiful palace in Milan to adorn it. To her, as to the other Gods, was likewise given a chariot, upon which, besides the sea shell, she traveled for pleasure through both sea and air, wherever it pleased her most; although **Claudian**, when he imagines her going to the wedding of **Honorius and Maria**, depicts her carried upon the hair of a Triton who, with his raised tail, provided her with shade. Chariots were given to the Gods, first for their greater majesty, and then because they serve to demonstrate the rotation of their spheres; and to each were assigned animals of a similar nature to the God to pull them. 

<margin><unclear>Handmaidens</unclear></margin>
Thus, the chariot of Venus is pulled by the whitest doves, because they are exceedingly lascivious; and at other times by swans, as **Horace**, **Ovid**, and **Statius** write, because of the sweetness of their song, by which the delight in amorous pleasures is greatly increased. One reads that among the **Saxons**, this Goddess stood upright upon a chariot drawn by two swans and as many doves; she was nude, with her head wreathed in myrtle, with a burning torch in her breast, with a certain round ball in the shape of the world in her right hand, and in her left, three golden apples; behind her stood all three **Graces** with their arms intertwined. And since from her comes no less the ceasing of love than loving itself, **Marcellus**, after the victory of Sicily, built her a Temple one mile outside of Rome, so that she might take away from the minds of Roman women every lascivious desire; to this Temple young girls would go to offer small figures made of stucco and cloth. 

**Pausanias** is the authority that among the Thebans there were three Venuses to whom **Harmonia**, the wife of **Cadmus**, gave names: the first was the Celestial, who represents pure and sincere love, far removed from the joining of bodies; the second was the Popular, who inspires lascivious and libidinous love; the third was **Apostrophia** <note>original: "Apostrophia"; from the Greek, meaning "The Averter" who turns people away from illicit passion.</note>, whom we may call the Adversary, who was opposed to dishonest desires. For the Popular Venus, **Scopas** once made a statue which, according to what **Alessandro Napolitano** <note>Alessandro d'Alessandro (1461–1523), a Neapolitan jurist and humanist.</note> reports, sat upon a ram and trod upon a tortoise with one foot. And **Phidias** likewise made one for the people of **Elis**, which stood on foot upon a tortoise, to show women that the care of the house belongs to them. <note>The tortoise was a common symbol for domesticity because it carries its house on its back and is silent.</note>

...and it is appropriate to speak as little as possible, as **Plutarch** notes in his instructions <note>Plutarch’s *Conjugal Precepts*</note>, because according to **Pliny**, the tortoise has no tongue. In addition to the Graces and the Cupids, **Plutarch** writes that the ancients used to place the statue of **Mercury** next to that of **Venus**; this was to suggest that pleasant and clever words are the sweetest seasoning for amorous pleasures, as they produce and preserve love between people. For this reason, among the Graces who accompanied that Goddess, they included one called **Pitho** <term>Pitho: The Greek personification of persuasion, known as Suada in Latin, emphasizing the role of gentle speech in love</term>, named after the act of persuasion.

The **Spartans** <note>original: "Lacedemoni"</note> once built a temple to her and placed within it her statue fully armed, as a sign of the victory their women achieved when they marched out of Sparta in armor and destroyed the **Messenians** (as **Lactantius** writes). Regarding this **Armed Venus**, **Ausonius** imagines that a resentful **Pallas** <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom and strategic war</note> challenged her to a contest under the **Judgment of Paris**, and that Venus replied to her: "O rash one, how do you expect to defeat me now that I am armed, if I already overcame you while I was naked?"

The **Romans** fashioned Venus called the **Victress** <note>Venus Victrix</note> in the form of a most beautiful woman in a gown reaching the ground; with her right hand she held out a small image of Victory, and in her left she held something resembling the object worshipped by the people of **Paphos** under the name of Venus—which some believe was a mirror. This is because **Philostratus**, in his description of the painting of the Cupids, writes that the Nymphs erected a statue to Venus as a reward for having made them mothers of such beautiful offspring as the Cupids, and they dedicated a silver mirror to her with ornaments on gilded feet.

In another way, **Venus the Victress** is seen on a medal of **Faustina**; there she holds with her left hand a shield resting on the ground, which has two tiny figures carved in the center, and with her right hand she offers a Victory. **Pausanias** writes that near the **Sicyonians** in Greece, there was a temple dedicated to Venus in which no more than two women could ever enter; of these, the one who served as guardian never went with her husband throughout that entire year, and the other had to be a virgin. All others who went there to pray to the Goddess remained outside. The statue of Venus inside was made entirely of gold and was seated, holding some poppy heads in one hand and an apple in the other, with something atop her head representing a *polos* <note>original: "polo" or "gághero"; a high cylindrical crown worn by ancient goddesses</note>—or let us say a pivot—whereas that other statue made by **Tyndareus**, which was in chains, wore a certain veil that women of those times used as an ornament. Near the Temple of Armed Venus, there was a chapel where she was shown seated, called **Morpho** <note>Morpho: A cult title of Aphrodite/Venus meaning "the shapely" or "of the beautiful form," emphasizing her role in physical beauty and matrimonial bonds</note>, with a certain veil upon her head and with certain bonds or shackles upon her feet; this was to show that women must maintain the firmest loyalty toward those to whom they are joined in the marital knot. The **Romans** had a temple they called that of **Venus Calva** <note>Venus the Bald</note>, and such was her statue, in memory of the fact that by means of the hair of Roman women they had been liberated from the **Gauls** <note>original: "Franceſi"; referring to the siege of the Capitoline Hill by the Gauls in 390 BCE, where women allegedly cut their hair to make bowstrings</note> on the **Capitoline Hill**, even though they knew very well that beautiful hair is appropriate for Venus, as **Claudian** writes:

> *The golden hair, and one of the others*
> *Extends and loosens it with an ivory tooth [comb],*
> *The third binds it with beautiful order,*
> *With a white hand, and gathers it in lovely pins.*

In **Cyprus**, she was worshipped with a beard, as **Alessandro Napolitano** <note>Alessandro d’Alessandro (1461–1523), a Neapolitan jurist who wrote about ancient customs</note> reports; thus her statue had the face and appearance of a man, although she wore the clothing of a woman. Of her, **Suida** <note>The Suda: A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> writes that she was also sculpted by the Romans with a comb in her hand and a beard on her face, for having delivered Roman women from a certain disease that caused their hair to fall out; she was also depicted as male from the waist up and female from the waist down, as she was the cause of the universal generation of all animals. And because of this, the ancients, considering her to be the same entity as the **Moon**, used to sacrifice to her—men in women’s clothing and women in men’s clothing. There was once on **Mount Lebanon** an image of her with a mantle around her that covered her entirely starting from the head, in which she appeared completely desolate and grieving, with one hand wrapped in the mantle supporting her downturned face, so that everyone believed tears were falling. This was in memory of the death of **Adonis**, for which **Plutarch** writes that even in **Athens**, on certain sacred days called the **Adonia** <note>The Adonia was a private festival celebrated by women to mourn the death of Adonis, the lover of Aphrodite</note>, women throughout the city would set out certain images resembling dead bodies. And they would carry these to the burials, weeping as if they were people who had only just died. ### On the form of Mercury. Chapter XI.

**A**s the Pagans used to fashion different images of a God under different names according to the qualities they wished to attribute to him, it followed that for **Mercury**, Prince of the second sphere <note>In the Ptolemaic system, Mercury is the ruler of the second planetary sphere</note>, they gave various forms according as they attributed to him now the care of profit, now of speech, and now of thefts. ...was not one that announced bad things. This form was that of a young man whose beard was just beginning to sprout, with two small wings above his ears on a small hat; he was completely naked, except that from his shoulders a cloth of modest size hung down behind him. In his right hand, he held a purse resting on the head of a goat <note>The Italian "becco" refers to a male goat, often associated with Mercury's role as a protector of flocks</note> that lay at his feet along with a rooster. In his left hand, he held the **Caduceus** <note>Mercury’s herald’s staff, featuring two entwined snakes</note>, with winged sandals on his feet—which were the feathers—as **Homer**, **Virgil**, and many others testify. The Egyptians, who were the first to depict him in this way, fashioned the Caduceus in the form of a straight rod with two snakes around it—one male and the other female—knotted together in the middle so that they formed a sort of arch with the upper parts of their bodies. Their mouths met at the top of the rod, while their tails wound around the bottom of the same rod, from which two small wings emerged. This was a sign of peace, and therefore ambassadors who brought peace used to carry it; for this reason, they were called *Caduceatori* <note>Heralds or peace-bringers</note>. Now, the feathers on his head signify speech, because in speaking, words "fly"; and because by this God were discovered letters, Music, Geometry, and the Wrestling School <term>Palestra: an ancient Greek wrestling school or gymnasium</term>. He was also fashioned in a square shape, and such statues were placed in schools, as the Arcadians did according to what **Pausania** <note>Pausanias, a 2nd-century AD Greek traveler and geographer</note> reports. **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher</note> depicts him as a beautiful youth, made not by artifice but naturally cheerful in appearance with bright eyes, standing upon a square base, showing the steadfastness of virtue to students—a virtue that does not fear the injury of fortune. The Greeks likewise called him Mercury **Cyllenius** <note>Usually referring to his birth on Mt. Cyllene, but the author here interprets it via the Greek "kullos," meaning maimed or without limbs</note>—that is, without limbs except for the head—and they sometimes made him like a die <note>A cube or gaming piece</note> without any other member besides the head, showing by this that the power of speaking has no need for any other part of the body. As the God of merchants—who have a need to know how to speak their reasons well—wings were placed on his feet, which signify (as **Fulgentius** says) the speed of those who trade, who never stay still but are always awake and practiced in their business; and by the rooster, the vigilance required of men of science is indicated. In **Corinth**, there was a statue of him made of bronze, which sat with a lamb at its side. Among the **Tanagrians** (a people of Boeotia), there was one who carried a ram on his shoulders because, by walking around their city in such a manner, he had freed them from the pestilence. Another was brought from Arcadia to be offered at the Temple of **Jupiter Olympus**, which was armed with a helmet on its head and dressed in a short soldier’s tunic, carrying a ram under its arm. When they depicted him to represent reason and that light which guides us to the knowledge of things, they placed a rooster at his side. This signifies the vigilance that ought to be in men who devote themselves to learning; for them, it seems a blameworthy thing to consume the entire night in sleep. This is because reason and light do not wish for us to remain buried in sleep for so long, but rather that, once our spirits are refreshed, we return to our accustomed works and the consideration of things. In a certain part of Achaea <note>A region in the northern Peloponnese of Greece</note>, according to **Pausanias**, there was once an image of **Mercury** above the road in a square shape with a beard and a hat on his head. These square statues, consisting only of a head and an erect phallus, showed that the Sun (who was represented by them) is the head of the world and the sower of all things. ...go often to the underworld to bring messages from Pluto <note>The Roman god of the underworld</note>, as is seen in the works of **Statius** <note>A Roman poet of the 1st century AD</note>, where an angry Pluto sends him to the Gods of Heaven because the light of day had descended into his kingdom when the earth opened to swallow **Amphiaraus** <note>A hero and seer in the war of the Seven against Thebes</note> during the Theban war. **Claudian** <note>A late Latin poet</note> likewise imagines that the same Pluto sends him to Jove <note>Jupiter</note> to ask him for a wife. For this reason, **Macrobius** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist writer</note> wishes for Mercury to be understood as the Sun, since he descends from Heaven into the underworld and rises from the underworld back to Heaven, just as the Sun does. Among all the nations of the world, there were never any who worshipped this God with greater ceremony than the **Gauls** <note>Ancient inhabitants of modern-day France</note>, for whom they erected, besides many other statues in **Auvergne**, that famous Colossus crafted by **Zenodorus**, which surpassed in beauty all other colossi of that time. The inhabitants of **Lysimachia** commissioned **Polykleitos**, the most famous sculptor, to make a beautiful statue of him, which was later brought to Rome and placed in the portico of the Emperor **Titus**. He was also depicted as the one who nursed **Bacchus** in his infancy, as evidenced by that most beautiful bronze statue made by the elder **Cephisodotus**; and **Pisicrates** expressed him in another manner, as did others according to what they intended him to signify. But I shall not stay in this place to mention all the offices, meanings of ornaments, or effects given to him by the ancients, according to which the other statues and images they built for him were extremely diverse. These were made by the inhabitants of **Mount Cyllene** in Arcadia (where he was first worshipped), the **Hermopolitans**, the **Memphites**, the **Cyrenians**, the **Marmaricans**, the **Elamites**, the **Hyrcanians**, the **Armenians**, and the inhabitants of the city of **Tricca** <note>Original: "Treceri"</note>, who worshipped him in a form made of iron, suspended in the middle of the Temple by <term>lodestones</term> <note>Natural magnets; the text describes a statue held aloft by magnetic force</note>, and many others of whom it would be too long to speak. It is enough to say that until the time of **Saint Paul** and **Barnabas**, he was held in reverence among the Lystrians of Lycaonia; for, because of their miraculous works, the people wished to worship them and offer them sacrifices, calling Barnabas "Jove" and Paul "Mercury" as he was prudent and eloquent, as is read in the **Acts of the Apostles**.
