Others gave her a mule, such as **Sextus Pompeius Festus** <note>A 2nd-century Roman grammarian who wrote a treatise on the significance of words</note>, alluding to her sterile nature being like that of the mule, which does not reproduce; others gave her two white stags under the name of **Diana**, as will be mentioned when speaking of the Mountain Nymphs; and others two bullocks, as **Claudian** <note>A 4th-century Latin poet</note> and **Ausonius Gallus** <note>Likely referring to the poet Ausonius</note> say existed in **Aegina**, a city in Greece, in a temple consecrated to her. There she was called **Lucina** <note>The Roman goddess of light and childbirth</note>, as **Horace** also names her, because of her moisture, which softens the woman's womb so that it opens easily during childbirth.

**Pausanias** <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer</note> writes that there was a statue of her covered by a very thin veil, except for the hands, feet, and face which were made of marble; one hand was extended, and with the other she carried a lit torch, to denote that she was the bringer of light to newborn children, offering them help to emerge from the mother's womb. **Marcus Tullius Cicero** <note>The famous Roman orator, in his legal speeches against Verres</note> once described a statue of Diana that he took in Sicily, tall and large, with a robe that covered it entirely down to the feet, with the face of a youth and a virginal appearance. In her right hand, she carried a burning torch, and she held a bow in her left, with arrows hanging from her shoulders. The lit torch signaled that, shining at night, she was a guide to travelers, as the **Arcadians** <note>Inhabitants of the central Peloponnese in Greece</note> believed; as Pausanias writes, they had a metal statue of her that they called "Diana the Guide and Leader." The bow and arrows showed the sharp stings of pain that women feel in childbirth, which is why they nearly always depicted her with them.

The Moon, under the name of Diana, was worshipped as the Goddess of the Hunt; for this reason, they fashioned her in the habit of a nymph, with her tunic tucked up <note>Specifically, "succinta," meaning her skirts were pinned up for mobility</note>, a golden bow in her hand, and a quiver full of arrows at her side; they placed dogs at her side and gave her a company of several hunting nymphs. The Arcadians, as Pausanias reports, made her dressed in a deer skin with a quiver full of arrows hanging from her shoulders, while with one hand she carried a lamp and with the other two snakes; and at her side stood a hunting dog. She was dressed in deer skin because it was dedicated to her; no ancient Temple of the Moon was ever found where deer antlers were not hung. Thus **Claudian** depicts her as the Goddess of the Hunt in these few verses:

> *Much less wild, but more graceful and beautiful*
> *Was Diana, whose eyes and cheeks*
> *Seemed like those of Phoebus; the splendor and the sex* <note>Phoebus is another name for Apollo, Diana's twin brother. original: "Men fera assai, ma più leggiadra, e bella / Diana era ch'in lei gli occhi e le guancie / Parean di Febo, lo splendor, e'l sesso / Sol chi fosse di lor scoperto haurebbe."</note>
> *Only by being uncovered would one know.*
> *The naked arms of celestial whiteness*

In the Temple of Juno, near the chest of **Cypselus** <note>A famous carved cedar chest dedicated at Olympia by the tyrants of Corinth, described in detail by Pausanias</note>, there was, according to **Pausanias**, a golden figure of **Diana** with wings on her shoulders, who held out a dart with her right hand and a lion with her left. Under the name of **Trivia** <note>From the Latin *tri-via*, meaning "three roads"</note> or **Hecate**, she was also regarded as the Goddess who cared for and guarded the crossroads where ways from different places come together. For this reason, the poets fabulized that she had three faces, whence **Ovid** says:

> *Behold how Hecate with three faces looks upon*
> *Three ways that then all lead into one.*
<note>original: "Vedi che con tre faccie Hecate guarda / Tre vie che poi riescon tutte in vna." A translation of Ovid's *Fasti* 1.141-142.</note>

But **Virgil** calls her **Trigemina**, **Trivia**, and **Triformis**; as **Seneca** also calls her, wishing thus to show the varied aspects of the **Moon** that she shows us. Her power is not only active in Heaven, where they call her **Luna**; but on earth, where they call her **Diana**; and even down in hell, where they call her **Hecate** and **Proserpina**. It is believed that she descends into hell during all that time she remains hidden from us <note>Referring to the phase of the New Moon</note>. Thus, they depicted her in three ways: the first was with white and golden garments, with a lit torch in her hand, denoting her when she begins to give light to mortals and thereby brings growth to all things. The second was the basket in which they carried her sacred items, denoting her when she already has half of her light, by which, increasing every day, the fruits that are gathered in baskets are ripened. And the third was with garments that had a dark hue, along with laurel and the poppy, showing her when she has completed her light <note>The Full Moon or the waning phase</note>. The laurel shows the power she takes from the **Sun**, and the poppy represents the multitude of souls which they believed were in her orb—almost as if it were a great city of people. This is because the poppy, having its head shaped at the top like the walls of a city <note>Referring to the "crown" or crenelated top of the poppy seed pod</note> and containing within itself a great number of tiny seeds, represents a great number of people united in a city. **Pausanias** recounts that in **Aegina**, a city of the Corinthians <note>Actually an island in the Saronic Gulf</note>, Hecate was worshipped more than all the other Gods, and that there she had a wooden image made by **Myron** <note>A famous Greek sculptor of the 5th century BC</note> with a single face, and the rest of the body shaped like a trunk, showing that she was not always made with three faces. It is believed that **Alcamenes** <note>A Greek sculptor and contemporary of Phidias</note> was the first of all...

Of the three heads that the statue of **Hecate** possessed, one was that of a horse, another of a dog, and the third, according to some, was that of a rustic man—though according to others it was a wild boar. This latter perhaps better suits what is said of the **Moon**, who, when considered as she scatters her light upon us, is called **Diana** the huntress. This is represented by the boar, as it always dwells in the forests and woods; likewise, the head of the horse, a swift animal, shows us how she rapidly circles the Heavens. The head of the dog represents the same Goddess when she is hidden from us; for this reason, she was believed to be the Goddess of the underworld and called **Proserpina**, as the dog is an animal dedicated to the God of the underworld. 

Another statue of her once existed, as **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian of the early Christian church who often recorded pagan traditions.</note> writes, in **Apollinopolis**, a city of Egypt. This statue showed that she does not possess light of her own but receives it from the **Sun**. It was fashioned in the form of a man, entirely white, with the head of a **sparrowhawk** <note>original: "sparviero". In Egyptian iconography, the hawk or falcon is a solar symbol associated with Horus.</note>. The whiteness signifies that the Moon has no light of herself, but receives it from another—namely the Sun—who also gives her spirit and strength, signified by the hawk’s head, because this bird (as was said above) is consecrated to the Sun. 

In accordance with this, the **Egyptians** depicted **Isis** dressed in black to show that, by herself, she is a dim and dark body. She was none other than the Moon, as was clearly recognized by her statue made with horns, a <term>cymbal</term> <note>Likely the sistrum, a rattling percussion instrument used in the worship of Isis.</note> in her right hand, and a vase in her left. As **Servius** <note>A 4th-century grammarian known for his commentaries on Virgil.</note> says, she was also held by some to be the **Genius** <note>A guardian spirit or personification of a place or quality.</note> of Egypt, the Earth, or the very nature of things subject to the Sun. Thus it happened that they sometimes depicted her full and heavy with breasts <note>This refers to the "Polymastos" or multi-breasted iconography, similar to the Artemis of Ephesus, symbolizing fertility and nature's nourishment.</note>, placing a small boat in her right hand and in the other the herb **southernwood** <note>original: "abrotano". ## Of the form of Vulcan, God of fire. Chap. XIII.

**I**n the second region, called "elementary," which is subject to corruption and continuous variability, the first sphere below the Moon is that of fire, of which the ancients depicted Vulcan to be God, and they willed that the virtue and power of fire proceed from him. Hence, they made for him a statue in human form with a hat on his head of a sky-blue <note>original: "color celeste"</note> color as a sign of the revolving of the Heavens, near which true, pure, and sincere fire is found; this cannot be said of the fire down here, which does not maintain itself but always needs new matter to nourish and sustain it. And from this also arose the fiction that Vulcan was lame, because thus the flame appears: for in burning, it does not ascend straight, but twists and almost struggles, now in one direction and now in another, because it is not as pure and light as it would need to be to ascend to its proper place. They made him, moreover, black in the face, ugly, and smoky over his whole body, just as blacksmiths are; sometimes naked, and sometimes neither naked nor clothed, but only with certain rags around him. Aelian writes that the Egyptians consecrated lions to him, as these animals are of a very hot and fiery nature; hence it is that, because of the heat they have within, they fear greatly when they see fire, and they flee from the rooster because it possesses more heat than they do. Alessandro Napolitano <note>Alessando d'Alessandro, a 15th-century Neapolitan jurist and scholar known for his "Geniales Dies."</note> says that in Rome, in the Temple of Vulcan, there were dogs...

dogs, as guardians and watchmen, who never barked except when someone went there to steal something. And so we also read that near Mount Etna <note>original: "Mongibello," the historical Sicilian name for Mount Etna</note> in Sicily, dogs guarded the Temple of Vulcan and the sacred grove that surrounded it. The Egyptians possessed a statue of this God holding a mouse in his hands, because they say that he once sent a vast multitude of mice among the Arabs, enemies of the Egyptians, who had taken their bows, shields, horse bridles, and other similar things; because of this, the enemies were forced to flee. He was called by another name, namely Mulciber, and was held to be the father of many children. Three smiths were attributed to him, named Brontes, Steropes, and Pyracmon. The first two denote the effects of the thunderbolt, for Brontes signifies "thunder" <note>original: "tuono"</note> which is born from the fracture and violent breaking of the cloud in which the vapor is ignited. Steropes signifies the "lightning flash" <note>original: "baleno"</note> which is nothing other than the flickering of fire that appears in the broken cloud; and Pyracmon refers to the tools of the forge, for it signifies "fire" <note>from Greek *pyr*</note> and "anvil" <note>from Greek *akmōn*</note>. But Hesiod <note>Ancient Greek poet</note>, instead of Pyracmon, calls him Arges <note>OCR reads "Arpesa"</note>, to denote the violence of the thunderbolt, which makes a slaughter and plunder of everything, from the Greek word which means "to seize" <note>original: "rapire"</note>. And whoever desires to see this forge depicted with Vulcan and his smiths and other figures around it should see the print produced by the hand of the man from Bologna <note>Likely referring to the artist Giambologna or Pellegrino Tibaldi</note>, in which one can examine all the art that is possible to show on this subject; and also that of Mazzolino <note>Ludovico Mazzolino, an Italian Renaissance painter</note> where one sees Mars and Venus lying together.

## BOOK 2

called Queen of kingdoms and of riches, and then according to Fulgentius <note>Fabius Planciades Fulgentius, a late antique author known for allegorical interpretations of mythology</note>, she was depicted with a veiled head and with a scepter in her hand. For this reason, they also held that she was the same as the Earth, just as they held that Saturn was the Creator of things, and Ops <note>A Roman goddess of fertility and earth, often identified with Rhea</note> was matter, and consequently Juno was her daughter, in whom everyone knows the kingdoms of the world reside. Therefore, she was adored as the lady of kingdoms, which they indicated with the scepter; and for the same reason as the lady of riches, because just as she holds all metals within her bowels—which is signaled by the veiled head—so on the surface, she has grains, fruits, and herds, in which earthly riches consist. And hence she was also held to be the Goddess of marriages, because they are contracted by means of a dowry.

But leaving aside further search for her names and coming to her form, she is seen on the medals <note>In this period, "medals" usually refers to ancient Roman coins</note> of Faustina <note>Faustina the Elder or her daughter Faustina the Younger, Roman Empresses often depicted with divine attributes</note>, made in the form of a woman of already perfect age, dressed in the habit of a matron, who holds a cup <note>A patera, used for pouring libations</note> in her right hand and a half-spear in her left; for although she was sometimes peaceful, she showed herself terrible, and from quiet to fierce, as when in the Trojan War she had the audacity to go into battle against the Trojans together with Minerva, as Homer recounts. He describes her chariot thus: it had an axle of iron that supports it across, wheels of copper with eight spokes, and the rims around them were of gold encircled above with copper; the body from which the spokes emerge was decorated with silver, and above where the Goddess stood was a seat made with straps of gold and silver, the pole was of silver, the yoke of gold, and the ornaments of the horses—which then served her more than peacocks—were likewise of gold.

Virgil likewise gives her a chariot and arms when he says that she loved Carthage so much that she kept her chariot and arms there. The nymphs who served her were held to be fourteen to allude to as many phenomena <note>The author uses "accidents" to mean physical occurrences or atmospheric changes</note> that are generated in the air for various reasons, such as serenity, the force of the winds, clouds, rain, tempest, dew, thunderbolts, thunder, comets, the rainbow, inflamed vapors, lightning flashes, and storm clouds. However, some add a few others to indicate other things belonging to the earth. Of all, the most familiar attributed to her by the Poets is Iris the messenger, which signifies the rainbow; she was the daughter of Thaumas, which means admiration <note>From the Greek *thauma*, meaning wonder or marvel</note>, because in her appearance she seems marvelous for the colors she shows, just as riches make fools marvel—which pass away as quickly as we see the rainbow disappear. # SEVENTH BOOK

...the commands of Juno; to whom the peacock was afterwards given in protection to make clear the qualities of the rich. For just as the peacock, as **Boccaccio** <note>Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375), the famous Italian author who also wrote "Genealogia Deorum Gentilium," a key source for mythographers</note> says, is a bird that cries out, so the rich man boasts with haughty voices. And just as the peacock lives upon roofs and always climbs upon the highest places of buildings, so the rich man always seeks preeminence, and if it is not given to him, he usurps it. Beyond this, the peacock is adorned with beautiful feathers, delights in praise, and is so drawn to admire itself that it turns its eye-covered tail in a circle, leaving its rear parts bare and full of stench. 

By this, we are shown the purple of the rich, the garments of gold, the vain glory, the proud pomp, and ears inclined to flattery; from which it naturally follows that their filth—which otherwise might perhaps have been hidden—is revealed. Under that splendor appears a wretched heart, tormented by anxious thoughts, shiftlessness, madness, the ineptitude of their habits, the filth of their vices, and many times bodies rotting from foulness. 

But to return to the first point, not only was the peacock given to Juno, but also, as **Aelian** <note>Claudius Aelianus, a 2nd-century Roman author who wrote "On the Nature of Animals"</note> says, a certain kind of sparrow-hawk and vulture, with the feathers of which the Egyptians crowned the statue of **Isis** <note>The Egyptian goddess, often synchronized with Juno/Hera by later scholars</note>. And as a sign of nobility and antiquity of lineage, the wings of this bird, according to **Alexander of Naples** <note>Alessandro d'Alessandro (1461–1523), a humanist scholar known as Alessandro Napolitano</note>, were attached by them to the primary entrances of their houses. 

**Martianus Capella** <note>A late antique author whose "Marriage of Philology and Mercury" describes the gods in elaborate allegories</note>, wishing to represent in the image of Juno the qualities of the air with all that is generated from it, feigns that she has her head covered with a certain shining and white veil, upon which she has a crown adorned with precious gems, such as the green **Scythian stone** <note>Likely an emerald</note>, the fiery **Ceraunian stone** <note>A "thunderstone," traditionally believed to fall from the sky during storms</note>, and the white **Hyacinth** <note>In ancient texts, this could refer to a zircon or a sapphire-colored stone</note>. These were placed there by **Iris** <note>The goddess of the rainbow and Juno's messenger</note>, who has a face that is almost glowing and much resembles her brother <note>Likely referring to the Sun or perhaps a personification of light</note>, except that he is always cheerful and never disturbed, while she changes in countenance and sometimes shows a cloudy face. 

He then gives her an undergarment clear and shining like glass, but the over-mantle is dark and misty, though in such a way that if it is touched by some light, it shines. He girds her knees with a band of diverse colors <note>Representing the rainbow</note> that sometimes shines with wonderful beauty, and sometimes becomes so thin that the variety of colors no longer appears. He makes her shoes of a dark color, and they have soles so black that they represent the darkness of the night; although **Hesiod** and the other poets feign them to be golden. In her right hand he makes her hold a lightning bolt, and a drum in her left. 

**Pausanias** <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer</note> writes that formerly in Corinth there was a great statue of Juno made of gold and ivory by the hand of **Polyclitus** <note>A famous Greek sculptor of the 5th century BCE</note>, which had a crown on its head where, with wonderful craftsmanship, were...

...separated from the Hours and the Graces; and in one hand she held a pomegranate, and in the other a scepter, upon which stood a cuckoo. This is because the poets imagined that Jupiter, having once fallen in love with Juno, changed himself into this bird, and she took it up as a jest; through this trick, he was then able to enjoy her company. In the writings of **Lucian** <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125–180 AD), a Syrian-Greek satirist and rhetorician</note> one reads that although the **Syrian Goddess** <note>Atargatis, a Great Mother goddess of Northern Syria</note>—so revered in Hierapolis, a city of Assyria—was Juno, the statue in her temple nevertheless represented not just one goddess, but many. This was because one could see in it something of **Pallas** <note>Athena</note>, something of **Venus**, of **Diana**, of **Nemesis**, of the **Fates**, and of other goddesses; for she sat upon two lions, holding a scepter in one hand and a **spindle** <note>A tool used for spinning wool, often associated with the Fates who spin the thread of life</note> in the other. Upon her head, she bore rays and several other items attributed to various deities.

From this, **Lucian** concludes that Juno was a divinity worshipped in diverse ways under different names. It is also for this reason that some ancients depicted her with a clean and pure body, in reference to the body of the **Moon** <note>Juno was frequently identified with the air or the moon in "physical theology," where gods represented elements of nature</note>. Following this, **Homer**—where he assigns a particular physical trait to each deity—gives Juno white and beautiful arms. Others dedicated the eyebrow to her, as the preserver of sight or the light that comes from her through the eyes. 

**Apuleius** <note>Author of "The Golden Ass," who describes a theatrical reenactment of the Judgment of Paris</note>, when representing the Judgment of Paris on stage, depicted her in yet another way. He says that a young woman came forth who resembled Juno, possessing an honest face, her head encircled by a white diadem, and a scepter in her hand. She was accompanied by **Castor and Pollux** <note>The Gemini twins, sons of Jupiter and Leda</note>, who wore helmets topped with the crest of a star. Because these twins usually appear in the air to bring fair weather to sailors, and the air is symbolized by Juno, they were rightly placed in her company by **Apuleius**. 

These brothers, as **Aelian** says, were usually depicted as large, beardless men, identical to each other, wearing military cloaks, with swords at their sides and spears in their hands. In place of stars, they were sometimes shown with small flames on their heads, though according to **Festus Pompeius** <note>A 2nd-century Roman grammarian</note>, they wore their hair long. 

Next, Juno was crowned with garlands of lilies, called "Juno’s roses," because they became white after being stained by her milk. This happened once when Jupiter, while Juno was sleeping, placed the infant **Hercules** at her breasts, so that by nourishing him with her divine milk, she would not later hold him in hatred <note>Hercules was the son of Jupiter and a mortal woman, Alcmena; Juno's jealousy of him is a central theme in his myths</note>. But the child sucked so greedily that he woke the Goddess. Recognizing him, she immediately pushed him away so forcefully that her milk was scattered across the sky, creating that white band seen there, which is called the <term>Milky Way</term> <note>original: "via lattea"</note> by astronomers. ## BOOK SEVEN

In Boeotia, there was a temple consecrated to her containing a large statue of her standing upright; there she was called the "Bride," for no other reason than the reconciliation she made there with **Jove** <note>Jupiter, king of the gods</note> when she discovered an oak tree in the place of the new bride she believed Jove had taken. She was held in similar regard on the island of Samos, for having been a virgin there before she married Jove. Thus, in her temple there was a most beautiful statue made in the form of a bride, wearing that colored veil used by brides which covered her face.

**Tertullian** <note>Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (c. 155–220 AD), an early Christian author from Carthage</note> writes that in the Greek city of **Argos**, there was a statue of her encircled with vine branches, which had a lion skin beneath its feet, as if in contempt of **Bacchus** <note>Dionysus, the god of wine, often associated with vines</note> and to the dishonor of **Hercules** <note>Heracles, whose signature attribute was the skin of the Nemean Lion; Juno was his legendary antagonist</note>.

In **Lanuvium**, a city of **Latium**, she was adored under the name of **Hospita** <note>Latin: "The Hostess" or "The Savior"</note>, whom we might call "The Savior" as the principal deity of that place. According to the account of **Livy** <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian</note>, her statue—as **Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and orator</note> writes—wore a goat skin and held a spear and a small shield.

On certain medals of the **Emperor Nerva**, she is found in the form of a matron crowned with rays, seated upon a high throne, with a scepter in her left hand and a pair of **shears** in her right; she was then called the **Fortune of the Roman People**. 

And because they held that she was the inventor of marriage, they depicted her standing, holding poppy heads in her hand and with a **yoke** <note>term: giogo; a wooden beam used to couple oxen, here symbolizing the "bond" of marriage</note> at her feet, alluding to the marital knot with which they believed she joined people in matrimony. For this reason, the Romans built her a temple in a certain place called **Vicus Jugarius** <note>The "Street of the Yoke-makers" or "Street of Marriages" in Rome</note>.

But whoever wished to search precisely for all her forms would not easily find an end to them, especially if they sought those made in marble by **Dionysius** and **Polykleitos** <note>Two of the most famous sculptors of Greek antiquity</note>, one of which was formerly in the temple of this goddess within the **Portico of Octavia**. There were also those in the temple of **Juno Lacinia** near the people of **Agrigento**, where there was also that **panel painting** <note>tauola</note> by **Zeuxis**, which he painted by selecting the most beautiful features of five virgins chosen from among all the most beautiful girls of Agrigento. There was also the bronze statue made by **Bedas** <note>A Greek sculptor, son of Lysippus</note>, so excellent that the Romans placed it in the **Temple of Concord**.

Nor shall I dwell on searching for how many other forms other peoples represented her, such as the **Falisci** <note>An ancient Italic people</note> when they began to be famous, who worshipped her in a robust form upon a chariot, calling her **Quiris** <note>original: "Gurite"; a title of Juno as a protective, spear-bearing goddess</note>, as did the Carthaginians, the Proconnesians, the Argives, the Mycenaeans, and the Heliopolitans.

### On the form of Oceanus, of Neptune, of the Nymphs, and of Sea Monsters. Chapter XV.

**O**ceanus, the source and father of all waters, who surrounds the entire world, took his name from his great speed <note>The author likely refers to a Greek etymology connecting 'Ocean' to the word 'okys' (swift)</note>. For this reason, the pagans gave him a chariot to show us precisely that he travels around the earth; the roundness of the earth is signified by the wheels. They feigned that he was pulled by **Whales**, because they roam through the whole sea just as the waters of the sea flow around the whole earth, and being dispersed within it, they occupy the greater part of it. **Theodontius** <note>A lost medieval author often cited by Boccaccio as a source for Greek myths</note> adds that besides the chariot pulled by whales, **Tritons** went before him with **conch shells** in their hands as trumpeters and heralds. This denotes that the crashing of the waves upon the shore, with a more terrible noise than usual, is a most certain messenger of a storm; for the Triton is nothing other than the striker and disturber of the earth. In addition to this, they made him rich with many **sea oxen** <note>The "sea oxen" of Proteus are seals or monk seals, which have calf-like faces</note>, under the guardianship of **Proteus** who was their shepherd. This was because the Carpathian Sea has a great number of seals, which have front parts similar to calves, and other similar animals, where Proteus was imagined to be the lord. They then added many hosts of **Nymphs** as his servants and companions, attributing to him a vast multitude of children, who denote nothing other than the many properties of waters. The color of his clothing and his flesh was like the color of his waters, which is <term>cerulean</term> <note>A deep, greenish-blue typical of the sea</note>. And at times it is black, as demonstrated by its great depth. **Neptune**, the God of the sea, was depicted in various ways: sometimes tranquil, quiet, and peaceful, and at other times entirely turbulent, as one reads in **Homer** and **Virgil**, for the sea is also seen in such states at different times. And it was imagined that he went traveling across the sea upon a chariot, followed by many, as **Virgil** describes in these verses:

> *To the proud steeds he joins the chariot*
> *And sets the foaming bits; from his hands*
> *He lets the entire reins fall, and he flies*
> *With the dark chariot over the light sea.*
> *The waves stand still, and beneath the heavy weight*
> *The sea likewise spreads out its waters;*
> *The dark clouds flee from the wide sky:*
> *Various forms come in his company,*
> *Enormous whales, and the ancient choirs*
> *Of Glaucus, Ino’s son, and Palaemon, and the swift*
> *Tritons, and then the army of Phorcus* <note>original: "Ai superbi destrieri il carro aggiunge..." – This is an Italian translation of Virgil’s Aeneid, Book I, describing Neptune calming the storm</note>

Others, like **Boccaccio** <note>Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375), who wrote an influential genealogy of the gods</note>, have said that the trident is given to Neptune in place of a scepter to denote the triple property of water: that it is flowing, navigable, and good to drink. **Plato** adds to Neptune’s company a hundred **Nereids** <term>Nereids: sea nymphs, the fifty daughters of Nereus and Doris</term> who sat upon as many dolphins; there he describes the miraculous Temple that was once consecrated to him among the **Atlanteans** <note>A reference to the myth of Atlantis described in Plato's *Critias*</note>, where he says that Neptune stood upon a chariot, holding the reins of winged horses in his hand, and was so large that his head touched the roof of the temple. One also reads that dolphins were very dear to Neptune, wherefore **Hyginus** <note>Gaius Julius Hyginus, a Roman mythographer</note> writes that in all his statues they placed one in his hand, or under a foot; and not without reason, for the dolphin is as primary among fish as the lion is among animals and the eagle among birds. In the *Marriage of Philology*, **Martianus** <note>Martianus Capella, a 5th-century author who wrote an influential encyclopedia of the liberal arts</note>, introducing Neptune, describes him as naked and entirely green, like the water of the sea, with a white crown on his head representing the foam created by the agitated waves. 

**Philostratus** <note>Likely Philostratus the Elder, known for describing ancient paintings</note>, depicting two small islands which shared a single common square—where one island brought what it gathered from cultivated fields, and the other what it went plundering across the sea—says that a statue was erected there to Neptune with a plow and a chariot as a "cultivator of the earth." This was to show that the people of those islands recognized him as the source even of what comes from the land; but so that he did not seem solely a terrestrial god, a ship's prow was added to the plow, so that it appeared as if he were plowing the earth while sailing. In the contest that took place between him and **Pallas** <note>Pallas Athena</note> for the city of **Athens** in the presence of the other Gods, **Ovid** <note>The Roman poet of the *Metamorphoses*</note> writes:

->*He pastures the herds and the scaly sea-calves.*<- <note>Original: *fozzi buoi marini*. This refers to seals, which were poetically described as the "herds" of the sea god.</note>

**Homer** <note>The legendary Greek author of the *Iliad* and *Odyssey*</note> says that when he is forced to answer questions, he changes into various forms to shield himself from answering, which **Virgil** <note>Publius Vergilius Maro (70–19 BC), the Roman poet who describes Proteus in the *Georgics*</note> also demonstrates where he says:

->*Suddenly he becomes a bristly boar*<-
->*Full of scales, and now a tawny lion,*<-
->*And sometimes he turns into liquid waters,*<-
->*A cruel tiger, and a dragon,*<-
->*Now a fire that sends out burning flames*<-
->*That seems as if it had escaped its bonds.*<-

<margin>The marine nymphs</margin>
The marine nymphs—which is a general name for all humidity—were daughters of **Nereus**, the sea god, and of **Doris** his sister. For this reason, some are called **Nereids**, and of them **Homer** in the *Iliad* mentions thirty, of whom he says three came to grieve with **Thetis**, who was afflicted by the death of her son **Achilles**: Glauce, Thalia, Cymodoce, Nesaea, Spio, Thoe, Cymothoe, Actaea, Limnoria, Melite, Iaera, Amphithoe, Agave, Doto, Proto, Pherusa, Dynamene, Dexamene, Amphinome, Callianira, Doris, Panope, Galatea, Nemertes, Apseudes, Callianassa, Clymene, Ianeira, Dianassa, Maera, Orithyia, and Amatheia. 

Furthermore, he maintains that there are many others, which, however, signify nothing else but the properties of sea water or the <term>accidents</term> <note>In this context, "accidents" refers to the changing qualities or characteristics of the water, such as its motion or color.</note> surrounding it, which can easily be understood from the etymology of the name given to each. Regarding their form, **Alessandro** <note>Alessandro d’Alessandro, the Neapolitan humanist mentioned on the previous page.</note> says that a certain **Theodore Gaza** <note>Theodore Gaza (c. 1398–1475), a Greek humanist and translator.</note> claimed to have seen one in the Peloponnese, cast upon the seashore by great misfortune; she had a human face, quite beautiful, and was covered from the neck down with hard scales as far as the thighs, which, joined together, ended in a fish. 

We must not imagine, however, that all are of the same form, but rather of different forms according to their various names. But leaving aside the others, I will speak only of **Galatea**, so named for the whiteness that perhaps the foam of the water represents in her. And therefore, according to **Hesiod** <note>An early Greek poet (c. 700 BC), author of the *Theogony*.</note>, she must have hair—

...white arms and a face like milk. Thus **Polyphemus** <note>The one-eyed Cyclops from Homer’s *Odyssey*</note>, who was in love with her, praises her in the works of **Ovid**, calling her whiter than the whitest **privet** <note>A shrub with small white flowers, used as a standard for whiteness in classical poetry</note>; and **Philostratus**, in a fable he created about the Cyclops, introduces **Galatea** traveling across the calm sea upon a chariot drawn by dolphins. These are guided and directed by certain daughters of **Triton** <note>Sea-gods with the upper bodies of humans and the tails of fish</note> who surround the beautiful Nymph, always ready to serve her. She, raising her lovely arms, stretches a purple cloth to the gentle breeze of **Zephyr** <note>The West Wind</note> to provide a covering for the chariot and shade for herself. Her hair should not be shown scattered in the wind, but should lie flat as if wet, partly over her white face and partly over her white shoulders. A depiction of her was once made upon a seashell with **Polyphemus** and various sea gods who were stealing away her nymphs, shown in various poses by **Raphael** in Rome, in the house of **Chigi** <note>Original: "casa del Ghisi." This refers to the famous fresco *The Triumph of Galatea* by Raphael in the Villa Farnesina, then owned by the banker Agostino Chigi</note>, with several cupids flying through the air shooting arrows around her as she is drawn by dolphins over the sea.

Besides the **Nereids** <term>Nereids: the fifty sea-nymph daughters of Nereus and Doris</term>, there were also other sea nymphs, such as **Eurynome**, whose name is interpreted as "shepherd of the winds" or of the sea's fortune; **Perse**, who was born from the ebbs and flows of the sea; **Pleione**, which is the same as "rain," caused by the moist vapors that rise high from the ocean; **Clymene**, interpreted as "humidity," the daughter of the **Po River** <note>original: "Pō fiume"</note> and of **Melatone**, daughter of **Proteus**, who is interpreted as the whiteness born from the foam of the sea; **Aethra**, daughter of the Ocean; and her sister **Idothea**, which signifies "beautiful goddess" and is therefore understood as the tranquility of the sea. There is also **Scylla**, daughter of **Phorcys** and the nymph **Cratais** <note>original: "Correide"</note>. **Ovid** describes her when he imagines **Glaucus**, in love with her, watching her from a high mountain; he says she was marvelously beautiful with very long hair and a fish's tail hanging between her legs, and so she went through the sea fleeing from **Glaucus**, for which reason she was turned into a sea monster by **Circe** out of spite.

But writers disagree somewhat on what form she took. For **Homer** says that she took refuge in a dark and frightening cave and made the sea resound with terrible barking; she had twelve feet and six necks with as many heads. Each mouth had three rows of teeth, from which it seemed that deadly poison continually dripped. She often poked her terrifying heads out of the cave into the sea, watching to see if any ship might pass, to make them her miserable prey, as she once did with the companions of **Ulysses**. **Virgil**, however, describes her differently:

->There is a cavern that hides Scylla,<-
->Who draws the ships into rocks and hard crags;<-
->She is a woman in appearance, and her breast...<-

And **Ovid** <note>The Roman poet, likely referring to his *Metamorphoses*</note> says otherwise: that as **Scylla** entered the water, as was her custom, and was submerged up to her waist, her hair suddenly transformed into the mouths of dogs, which barked as she tried to flee. Thus her thighs, legs, feet, and groin remained full of dogs' mouths, while from the waist up she remained as she was before. Many other sea monsters could be described, which are mentioned by **Mattioli**, **Salviani**, and **Guillaume Rondelet** <note>These were famous 16th-century naturalists and physicians who wrote extensively on fish and marine life</note>, and especially some of strange forms resembling both birds and quadrupeds, which I shall omit for the sake of brevity. But it seems to me more a matter of curiosity than necessity to mention all the sea monsters, given that in this regard the painter—in the manner of a poet—can invent them himself according to his whim, or else read what the naturalists write of them.

There remain the **Sirens**, daughters of **Achelous** <note>A river god</note> and the muse **Calliope** according to **Fulgentius** and **Servius**; there were three of them: one sang with her voice, the second with the lute, and the third with the flute. But **Leontius** maintains there were four, named **Aglaope**, **Thelxiepeia**, **Pisinoe**, and **Ligeia**, and that they were the daughters of **Achelous** and **Terpsichore**, adding that the fourth sings to the beat of a drum. **Aristotle**, where he treats "Marvelous Things Heard," says that at the tip of Italy where **Pelorus** <note>Cape Peloro in Sicily</note> gives entrance from the **Tyrrhenian Sea** into the **Adriatic**, there are the "Siren-like" islands of the Sirens, where a temple is built and they are worshipped with very solemn sacrifices. ...they call them Thelxiope, Molpe, and Aglaophonos <note>These are traditional names for the Sirens in Greek mythology</note>. But whatever their names may be, their form is this: they have the face and middle body of a maiden, but from the waist down they are fish. Some also give them wings, as does Albericus <note>A medieval mythographer likely referring to the "Third Vatican Mythographer"</note>, and the feet of a hen. **Servius** <note>A 4th-century grammarian known for his commentary on Virgil</note> describes them not as fish, but as birds in that part which is not womanly; and **Ovid** says the same when he recounts that they were companions of **Proserpina**, and after she was abducted by **Pluto**, they were changed into sea monsters who had the faces and breasts of women, and the remainder was that of a bird. 

And because they were—as **Palaephatus** <note>A Greek author who wrote rationalizing interpretations of myths</note> says—prostitutes who, along the river of **Aetolia** held by their father, had prostituted their lives to many, they come to signify lust and the allurements of harlots. Therefore, it is feigned that with their sweet song they lulled sailors to sleep and then killed them, just as happens to poor, maddened men who, overcome by the flatteries of "women of the world" <note>A euphemism for prostitutes</note>, become their prey and are eventually devoured. For this reason, the ancients sometimes painted them in green meadows strewn with the bones of dead men, showing the ruin and death that follows from lewd pleasures, and especially those of prostitutes, who in face and gestures seem like embankments <note>Likely referring to a protective but deceptive appearance</note>; like **Parthenope**, they are well-adorned in appearance, but unchaste like **Leucosia**, and in words they are sweet and flattering like **Ligeia** <note>The text uses "Iligi"; these three names represent the famous Sirens of Neapolitan lore</note>.

### *Of the form of rivers and of their Naiad Nymphs. Chapter XVI.*

**B**ecause rivers were also depicted by the ancients in various manners, and even placed in the Heavens as an ornament—as the **Egyptians** did with the **Po**, depicting it with two horns—I will briefly note here some of the more notable forms attributed to them, and then I shall add something regarding the form of their nymphs. Firstly, then, rivers were for the most part represented in the form and appearance of a man with a beard and long hair; some reclining, and some leaning upon one arm, as **Philostratus** <note>A Greek sophist who described a gallery of paintings</note> says when he depicts **Thessaly** (for rivers never stand upright), and some—or rather most—leaning upon a large urn that pours out water. Hence **Statius**, speaking of **Inachus**, a very great river of **Achaia**, says:

> Inachus, his head adorned with two horns,
> Sitting, leans his left hand upon the urn
> Which, tilted, pours forth waters abundantly.

Of whom **Ovid** also writes, saying that he remained shut up in a vast cave, and by weeping, he increased the waters with his tears.

Beyond this, they were depicted with horns, as <term>Servius</term> <note>Maurus Servius Honoratus, a 4th-century grammarian famous for his line-by-line commentary on Virgil</note> says, either because the murmur of the waves represents the lowing of oxen, or because we often see the banks of rivers curved in the manner of horns. For this reason <term>Virgil</term> <note>The great Roman epic poet, author of the Aeneid</note>, where he calls the <term>Tiber</term> <note>The main river of Rome, referred to here as "Thebro"</note> King of the rivers of Italy, also calls it "horned," and depicts it thus:

> *Amidst the poplar leaves, to show himself*
> *Already old, his shoulders and his chest*
> *Girded with a verdant veil and shaded reed,*
> *He covers and surrounds his sodden hair.*

And <term>Sannazaro</term> <note>Jacopo Sannazaro (1458–1530), a celebrated Neapolitan poet</note>, not without reason calling it "triumphant," crowns it not like the others with willows or reeds, but with the greenest laurels because of the continuous victories of its sons <note>The Roman people</note>. Likewise of the <term>Po</term>—otherwise called the <term>Eridanus</term> <note>A river in Greek mythology often identified by later poets with the Po in Northern Italy</note> because of the fable of the youth <term>Phaethon</term> <note>The son of Helios who fell from the chariot of the Sun into the river</note>—<term>Virgil</term> says in another place that it has the face of a bull, with both horns gilded; and there an interpreter explains that it is imagined with the face of a bull because the sound that arises from its course is similar to the lowing of bulls, and its banks are twisted like horns. <term>Aelian</term> <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric</note> similarly writes that the statues of rivers, which at first were made without any specific form, were later made in the form of an ox. Therefore, if I were to fashion the <term>Po</term> as the King of Rivers—as many poets call it, and especially <term>Petrarch</term> <note>Francesco Petrarca, the famous 14th-century Italian humanist and poet</note> where he says:

> *King of the others, proud and haughty river.*

I would make him a robust old man, of grave and venerable aspect, with thick tufts in his hair and beard, so they would not tend toward the <margin>q</margin> <note>This letter 'q' in the margin is a signature mark used by early printers to help binders assemble the book in the correct order</note> scruffy look that one might give to other lesser streams; I would then make him in an entirely fierce posture with arms and all the limbs of the body well-formed and robust, with the <term>horn of plenty</term> <note>The cornucopia, a symbol of abundance and nourishment</note> in his right hand, denoting the fertility he brings. And under his left arm, upon which I would have him lean, I would add a very large vase with five mouths from which water would impetuously flow, to denote the entry he makes with five mouths into the Adriatic Sea. I would encircle him with a crown made of all the various leaves with which the others are crowned; and quite fittingly one could place a scepter nearby, or perhaps in his right hand next to the horn. And to give place to the fable, so that it might be better expressed, I would place in the surrounding marshes those trees that cast shade, into which the sisters of <term>Phaethon</term> were transformed because of their long weeping <note>According to myth, the Heliades wept so much for their brother Phaethon that they were turned into poplar trees and their tears into amber</note>. But departing now from this river, we should know that all [rivers] were ordinarily crowned with reeds, because these stalks are born and grow much better in watery places than elsewhere; wherefore <term>Virgil</term> covered the head of the Tiber...

[...encum]bered with reeds. And Ovid, recounting the fable of Acis—who was transformed into a river after <term>Polyphemus</term> <note>The cyclops from the Odyssey who crushed his rival Acis out of jealousy.</note> had crushed him with a rock—leads him to speak thus of himself:

> Suddenly above the waters there appeared

> Turns green; and his head is adorned
> By one and another horn, <note>The Italian OCR reads "corpo" (body), but the poetic rhyme with "intorno" (around) and the mythological context of river gods strongly suggest the original text was "corno" (horn).</note>

When afterwards Ovid relates how <term>Achelous</term> <note>The god of the largest river in Greece, who wrestled Hercules for the hand of Deianira.</note> recounts to Theseus the battle he fought with Hercules for Deianira, he stands leaning upon one of his arms with his head encircled by green reeds and a green mantle around him; and not like the others with two horns, but with only one, because the other was broken off by Hercules. Filled with various flowers and fruits, it was given to the Aetolians, who afterwards called it the <term>horn of plenty</term> <note>The cornucopia.</note>.

With this fable, they intended to signify nothing else (according to the account of <term>Diodorus</term> <note>Diodorus Siculus, a historian who sought to explain myths as historical or natural events.</note>) except that Hercules, with the greatest labor, diverted a branch of that river from its original course and turned it elsewhere; this area, because of the water that the river sometimes spread over it through the new branch, became exceedingly fruitful. And while they feigned that in fighting Hercules he took the form of a serpent, they wished to hint at his winding course, like the sliding of a snake; just as by feigning that he then changed into a bull, they signified to us that he turned from that crooked course and split himself into two branches in the manner of two horns. Of these, they feigned that one was broken by Hercules because the river then entered the sea with only one mouth; and they say it was given to the goddess <term>Copia</term> <note>The personification of Abundance.</note> because that branch had served to make the country fertile.

And for this reason, not without purpose, a wise sculptor—not regarding what the ancient poets had said of the form of rivers—made that marble <term>Tiber</term> <note>The original text uses "Thebro." This refers to a famous ancient Roman statue of the river god, often shown with Romulus and Remus.</note> which is now found in Rome, not with horns or the head encircled by reeds, but adorned with diverse leaves and fruits, wishing to show in that way the fertility and abundance that it generates in the country that is watered by its currents. And on the other hand, not wishing to distance himself entirely from the opinion of the poets, he placed a reed in its hand; because it grows in watery places, the reed cannot reasonably be omitted, unless perhaps one is representing a river that does not produce any—in which case the reed would be unbefitting as something not its own. Hence it is necessary to be well-aware—

->BOOK VI<-

...rivers being variously described by poets, sometimes according to the quality of their waters, sometimes according to their course, and at other times according to the nature of the land through which they pass. Hence it is that <term>Pausanias</term> <note>A 2nd-century AD Greek traveler and geographer whose "Description of Greece" is a crucial source for ancient art.</note>, when discussing <term>Arcadia</term>, writes that in a certain part of that country there are several statues of the most noble and celebrated rivers of the ancients, all made of the whitest marble except for the **Nile**, which is made of black stone; adding then that this was reasonably done because, as it runs to the sea, it passes through the land of the **Ethiopians**, a black people. Writing of this also, <term>Lucian</term> <note>A Hellenistic satirist known for his witty descriptions of artworks.</note> says that the Egyptians depicted him sitting upon a <term>river horse</term> <note>A hippopotamus.</note>, which is a certain creature that has a head much like a horse, with several small children around him, all joyful and playing. 

But leaving aside the warnings and rules that could be given in general regarding the manner of painting or sculpting rivers—for they are so many they would bring confusion rather than clarity—and coming to examples: who is there who would not represent the river **Peneus** grieving for the transformation of his daughter into a laurel tree in the <term>Vale of Tempe</term> in Thessaly? There, where he is born at the foot of **Mount Pindus**, he should be shown with a vase arranged under one of his arms, pouring out water copiously, and surrounded by a great number of little laurels, which grow in great abundance in those lands and from which the fable of his daughter <note>Daphne, who was transformed into a laurel tree to escape the pursuit of the god Apollo.</note> originated. 

And furthermore, would one not represent him as a weary, sad old man, full of grief, with drooping lips and sunken eyes, with his head bowed, crowned with laurel, and surrounded by other rivers that comfort him—such as the **Spercheios**, **Giteius**, and **Apidanus**—and the nymphs to whom he is accustomed in that place to give account and assign the duties of the waters? 

And if one had to paint the **Ticino**, a most clear river of Italy so transparent that even from the deepest part one can see the smallest stones, anyone who knew its nature and qualities would undoubtedly fashion him as a robust young man, beautiful and well-made, in a bold posture and with a countenance not like other melancholy rivers, but cheerful, with hair and beard not so drooping, but somewhat curly due to the robustness of the waters. And to denote its clarity, one would have a cloth as transparent as glass play around him, crowning him not only with the willows that grow in great abundance upon its banks, but also with fruits and flowers, alluding to the pleasantness of the places through which it flows. 

Beyond this, due to the abundance of fish that it nourishes, it would be appropriate to place some near him of the kind it produces in greatest quantity, just as the Egyptians did for the Nile; and for the golden sands carried by the slender <term>Panoo</term> <note>Likely a reference to the Po (Padus) or a specific tributary known for gold-washing; the text may contain a printer's error for "Padano."</note>, it would be well to have him strewn with little rods or droplets of gold. The cold **Tanais** river... <margin>The cold Tanais</margin> <note>Now known as the Don River in Russia, anciently considered the boundary between Europe and Asia.</note>

-># IMITATION<-

<page-num>299</page-num>

In the *North*, there is no doubt that one ought to depict him as old, dry, thin, twisted, and shrunken together, with his hair and beard frozen to demonstrate his coldness, as he originates from the *Rhipaean* <note>A legendary mountain range in the far north of Eurasia, often associated with the source of cold winds.</note> mountains. To the *Tigris*, because it is so named for its most rapid and swift course—which in another language means arrow <note>original: "faetta"; likely referring to the Old Persian word "tigra"</note>—one would quite fittingly place a dart in his right hand, representing him otherwise as thin and long, with the vessel from which the water flows following that same swift motion. The *Euphrates*, which means "fertility" <note>original: "fertilità"</note> in Hebrew, so called for the abundance it brings; in any case, he must hold a <term>cornucopia</term> <note>A "horn of plenty," a symbol of abundance and nourishment.</note> and a cup in his hand as if offering a drink, denoting the goodness of the waters. To the *Jordan*, in memory of the baptism of *Christ* our Lord, which brought eternal peace there, I would place an olive branch in his hand, such as the ancient ambassadors of peace were accustomed to carry.

And of these, being the most famous, it will suffice to have reasoned by way of example to serve us in knowing how to form the others. I will remind you only of this: that it is necessary, in rivers as in all other things one wishes to form, to always read and express their principal part and quality. For in this way, the works will turn out successfully, showing that diversity among things from which their principal beauty and excellence result. Examples include the black waves of the *Acheron* <note>One of the rivers of the Greek Underworld, the "river of woe."</note>; the concealment of the *Alpheus* <note>The river Alpheus was said to flow underground beneath the sea to emerge in Sicily.</note>; the fame of the *Amphrysus*; the lack of air and the mist of the *Anaurus*; the sterility of the *Arno*, though otherwise famous; the impetus of the *Asopus*; the <term>river horses</term> <note>Hippopotamuses.</note> and crocodiles of the *Bamboro*, a river of *Ethiopia*; the course of the *Danube* toward the East, contrary to the course of other rivers; the windings and the abundance that the *Meander* brings to the Hirgaleti fields; the gold and the ports of the *Prigeus* in *Hyrcania*; the golden sands of the *Pactolus*, a river of *Lydia*, and likewise of the *Tagus*; the saltiness of the waters and the impetus of the *Timavo*; the seven mouths through which the *Ganges*, a most great and famous river of *India*, enters the Ocean; the oracles of the *Cephissus*, near which there once stood the Temple of *Themis*, Goddess of Prophetic Responses, before there were the oracles of *Apollo* or others. Hence the ancients held those waters to be prophetic, as are the sea reeds that surround the river of *Laurentum*.

In addition to this, one must express certain notable and marvelous qualities that nature has placed in some of them, such as in those two rivers of *Atandria*, one of which makes sheep black and the other white when they taste its waters; in the *Astacus*, a river of *Pontus*, which causes sheep to produce black milk with its waters; and in the *Phiterus* which, according to *Aristotle*, causes black lambs to be generated; in the...

[BOOK IV]

<page-num>596</page-num>

The Silarus <note>original: "Silare"; the modern Sele river in Italy, which Pliny the Elder and other ancient writers claimed could petrify objects.</note> which turns to stone whatever is submerged within it; in a river of Egypt that makes the hair of the head fall out; and in another in Ethiopia that makes people go mad. But to come now to the Nymphs, who were imagined to inhabit the rivers, they can generally be formed in the guise of naked women with a languid and soft expression, with limbs that appear relaxed and their fleshiness in some way spread out <note>This suggests a soft, painterly style that emphasizes the fluidity of the water they represent, rather than rigid or muscular forms.</note> just as one sees in actual women. And just as the Nymphs and the Gods of the sea are mostly depicted as old, so these [river nymphs] should be represented as less old, in proportion to the size of the river as it flows toward the sea; yet they should be charming and beautiful, especially if they are nymphs of a pleasant and delightful river like the Ticino; and they must be placed in a way that shows their greatness. But if one wishes to adorn and clothe them, they shall be fitted with garments conforming to the color of the water and the foam of the river, and ornaments of stones, leaves, and other such things corresponding to the nature and quality of their particular river. Thus, some will show themselves cheerful, others sad, some old, others young, some thin, others fat, some tall, others small, some beautiful, others ugly, some white, others black, some dressed, others naked, some adorned, and others unkempt, always following the established rule for forming the rivers themselves.

## On the form of the Muses. Chap. XVII.

**T**he nine Muses, held as Goddesses of the sciences by the pagans <note>original: "gentili"; referring to the non-Christian peoples of antiquity.</note>, are described by Lucian <note>A 2nd-century Syrian-Greek satirist and rhetorician.</note> with a modest and reverent face, and always intent on study and song. Because of the mutual benevolence that exists between them, they are considered sisters; and because according to Mario Equicola <note>An influential Renaissance humanist and courtier.</note> the sciences are linked together as if in a bond, they are always depicted as companions. For this reason, Plutarch <note>The famous Greek biographer and philosopher.</note> wants them to be called Muses because they are together <note>original: "quasi, ò musæ"; the author is referencing a Greek etymology where "Muses" is derived from *homou ousai*, meaning "being together."</note>. They were formed as winged, young, beautiful, and charming like nymphs, and crowned with various leaves, and especially with palm, with a feather on their head to allude to the victory they had over the magpies <note>original: "piche"; according to myth, the Pierides (daughters of Pierus) challenged the Muses to a contest and were transformed into magpies upon their defeat.</note>, as Ovid tells among others, and over the Sirens according to Pausanias, who at the instigation of Juno provoked them to a contest, and there lost their feathers. And in this form, some ancient statues of them are seen in Rome. They were crowned with Palm because this tree is delightful and always green, difficult to climb, and bears sweet fruit. Pindar attributes black hair to them, which although it can refer to beauty, we must nonetheless understand it to signify the hidden and obscure meanings of the Poets. There is also given to them the lau... <note>original: "lau-"; the catchword "ro" on the next page completes the word "lauro," or laurel, the traditional crown of poets.</note>

...laurel <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion of the laurel tree, sacred to Apollo and the Muses.</note>, because according to Giraldi <note>Lilio Gregorio Giraldi (1479–1552) was an influential Renaissance mythographer.</note> this tree contributes to inspiration, or perhaps because the ancients believed that the faculty of poetry could be acquired solely by the taste of it, as Lycophron <note>A Greek poet of the 3rd century BCE.</note> says; or rather because it remains forever green, just as we say that the verses of good poets likewise remain perpetually green in the mouths of men. Furthermore, they are made to sing while **Apollo** plays the lyre, who for this reason is called **Musagete** <note>original: "Muſagete"; from the Greek *Mousagetes*, meaning "Leader of the Muses."</note>, that is, the leader of the muses. Besides him, **Peitho** <note>original: "Pitho"</note>, the Goddess of Persuasion, is given to them as a companion; she gives some of them to drink from a most limpid liquid drawn from the Orchomenian <note>Orchomenus was a city in Boeotia, ancient Greece, famous for its sanctuary to the Graces.</note> fountain of the **Graces**. Columella <note>A Roman writer on agriculture.</note> gives them the **Sirens** as companions. Some depicted them together with nine **Bacchuses**, varied in name, and others added **Hercules** as well. Hence, Fulvio Orsini <note>A famous Renaissance humanist, historian, and antiquarian.</note> recounts having seen a silver medal of Hercules with the club at his feet, with the lion's skin on his back, and a zither in his hand with the **Hours**, the **Fates**, and the **Graces**; all of whom, as daughters of Jove, constitute the sacred choir of the muses in the number of nine, three by three. They were imagined as presidents of choirs and were honored with those vows and ceremonies with which **Ceres** <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture.</note> was honored. But Virgil speaks of them otherwise and holds that **Clio** was the inventress of history, **Melpomene** of Tragedy, **Thalia** of Comedy, **Euterpe** of the flute or bagpipe, **Terpsichore** of the psaltery, **Erato** of Geometry, **Thalia** of letters, **Urania** of Astrology, and **Polyhymnia** of Rhetoric. John Grammaticus <note>Also known as John Philoponus, a 6th-century philosopher and grammarian.</note> maintains that Poetry was found by **Calliope**, history by **Clio**, the art of planting by **Thalia**, the flutes by **Euterpe**, song by **Melpomene**, dances by **Terpsichore**, and weddings and feasts by **Erato**, cultivation by **Polyhymnia**, and Apology <note>In this context, likely meaning the art of defense or formal justification.</note> by **Urania**. One reads that they once had a contest with the **Pierides** <note>The nine daughters of King Pierus who challenged the Muses to a singing contest and were transformed into magpies upon losing.</note>, which signifies nothing other than the war that the learned sometimes have with the ignorant...

...who in the end reap nothing from their daring and boldness but confusion and shame, just like the **Pierides** <note>The daughters of Pierus who challenged the Muses to a musical contest and, upon losing, were transformed into magpies as punishment for their hubris.</note>, into which the poets feigned they were transformed. Some others have wished for **Polyhymnia** to represent the star of **Saturn** for contemplation, **Terpsichore** that of **Jupiter** for delight, **Clio** that of **Mars** for the fire of glory, **Melpomene** that of the **Sun** for harmony, **Erato** that of **Venus** for love, **Euterpe** that of **Mercury** for pleasure, and **Thalia** that of the **Moon** for the moisture through which the earth grows green.

The birds sacred to them, besides swans, are the **bees**; their fountain is the **Castalian**; and their mountains are **Olympus** and **Helicon**. **Giraldi** <note>Lilio Gregorio Giraldi (1479–1552), a prominent Renaissance scholar and author of *De deis gentium*, a primary source for mythography.</note> recounts having seen **Poetry** depicted holding a globe in one hand, with a tucked-up kirtle and a wide, flowing over-garment, embroidered and painted, with her right foot bare and her left shod in a charming manner, and with various garlands scattered before her of laurel, ivy, myrtle, and other interwoven leaves.

But so that, beyond the rules and precepts given, the painter may also have some example to set before his eyes these same rules and precepts—whereby he may more clearly come to understand them and more easily learn the manner of putting them into practice with true judgment, both regarding their form and colors and, in short, all other circumstances—he may see and minutely consider the **Muses** who are painted in the **Papal loggias** <note>While the author refers to the Loggias, this most famously describes the *Parnassus* fresco in the Stanza della Segnatura in the Vatican.</note> in Rome by the hand of **Raphael**. There they are seen in a beautiful choir surrounding **Apollo**, who, seated in the center with his lyre <note>original: "cetra"; Raphael depicts Apollo playing a contemporary Renaissance instrument, the lira da braccio.</note> in hand, plays with them near the fountain of **Mount Parnassus**. Standing attentively around to listen are the most celebrated poets, ancient and modern, portrayed from life, with some children <note>Often referred to as putti or cherubs in art history.</note> flying through the air in the act of crowning them with laurel garlands, with which the entire mountain is seen to be filled.

One may also observe, especially regarding the coloring, the Muses painted by **Callisto of Lodi** <note>Callisto Piazza (c. 1500–1561), a follower of Titian and Romanino active in Lombardy.</note> in Milan, in the garden of the house that once belonged to **President Sacco** <note>Giovanni Battista Sacco, a high-ranking official in the Duchy of Milan.</note>, near the Church of the **Servants**, where, along with many other figures, one sees the portrait of the President himself and his wife. Of this painting, I can say without a hint of boldness that it is not possible, regarding the beauty of the coloring, to make another more graceful and charming in fresco <note>The technique of painting on wet plaster, highly valued for its permanence and luminosity.</note>.

Regardless of who the author of this invention <note>The "invention" refers to the allegorical personification and mythological origin of Fame.</note> might be, she sees what is done in heaven, in the sea, and on land, and she searches the whole world; but the ancients depicted Fame in the form of a woman, sometimes dressed in a thin cloth <note>Transparent or light fabric was often used in Renaissance art to denote airiness or spirits.</note> and all tucked up <note>Dressed in a short tunic (succincta) to allow for unhindered movement.</note>, showing her running quickly, with a shrill trumpet at her mouth. > *Or upon high and eminent Towers,*
> *Dismaying great Cities: and as much of the false*
> *As of the truth is she a tenacious messenger.*

And because both good and bad news are brought, the ancients held that there were two Fames: one was called the "Good Goddess" <note>original: "buona Dea"</note> who announced good things, and the other "Bad Fame" who brought evil; to her, as a distinction from the other, they attributed black wings. Whence Claudian <note>Claudius Claudianus (c. 370 – 404 CE), a Latin poet associated with the court of the Emperor Honorius.</note>, writing against Alaric <note>Alaric I (c. 370 – 410), king of the Visigoths who famously sacked Rome in 410 CE.</note>, says that Fame spread her black wings; and some attributed bat wings to her. In the company of Good Fame, they depicted **Shouting** <note>original: "il grido"</note> with swollen and inflamed eyes from violent yelling; **Rumor**, swift and noisy in the manner of an idle person; triumphant **Glory**, full of pleasure but pale of face, who like a Queen sits in a high seat, holding the virtues under her feet; **Boasting** <note>original: "il vanto"</note> with hands toward Heaven as if rejoicing; and **Honor** full of majesty, so that everyone seems to show him reverence.

### Of the form of the winds. Cap. XIX.

Because I do not doubt that the Earth stands so firm that I may add her in her proper place, I have thought in the meantime to treat the form of the winds; which, according to Lactantius and Servius, were the sons of Astraeus <note>The OCR reads "Astico," but the author refers to Astraeus, the Titan god of the dusk.</note> the Titan and Aurora <note>The Goddess of the Dawn.</note>. These at first remained quiet and free, but later, having been incited by Juno against Jupiter because of the birth of Epaphus <note>The son of Jupiter and Io; Juno’s jealousy often triggered mythological conflicts.</note>, they were shut up in caves by Jupiter and confined under the command of Aeolus; although others say it was not Juno, but the Furies of Hell, at the prayers of Strife, who incited them to try to drive him from Heaven. Isidore <note>St. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636 AD), a scholar whose "Etymologies" was a primary source for medieval and Renaissance knowledge.</note>, a most Christian man, says in his book of *Origins* that there are twelve winds. The first, which from the beginning of winter tends toward the West, is called *Subsolanus* <note>The East wind, named because it rises "under the sun" (sub solis ortu).</note>, because it is born beneath the appearance of the Sun; to whom he adds two winged companions: namely, *Eurus* on the left, so named because it blows from the West in Summer, and *Vulturnus* on the right, so called because it thunders on high. The fourth, which blows from the south, is called *Auster* <note>The South wind.</note> because it pours out water, and is called *Notus* by the Greeks; to which he places on the right side *Euroauster*, so called for being between Eurus and Auster; and on the left side *Austro-Africus*, because it is between Auster and Africus, and it is also called *Libonoto*, because on one side it has Libya and on the other Notus.

-># BOOK SEVEN <-

the seventh that blows from the West named *Zephyr*, because with its breath it brings life to flowers and herbs; otherwise called by the Latins *Favonius*, because it favors things that are born; on its right side, he places *Africus* or *Libyus*, so named from the country from which it blows; and on the left *Chorus*, so named because it closes the circle of the winds and forms almost a choir <note>The author suggests an etymological link between the name of the wind *Chorus* (the North-West wind) and the word for a musical choir, implying a complete circuit.</note>, even though others also call it *Caurus* and others *Agrestis*. The ninth which breathes from the North retains the same name [Septentrio], because it rises from the circle of the seven stars <note>Referring to the "Seven Oxen" or *Septentriones*, the stars of the Big Dipper that mark the north.</note>. On its right side he places *Circius*, so named from its proximity to *Chorus*, and on the left *Aquilo*, so named because it dissolves the clouds and disperses the waters; or *Boreas* because it seems to come from the *Hyperborean* mountains. But so as not to report here all that *Isidore* <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), a scholar whose "Etymologies" served as a primary encyclopedia for the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> discusses more extensively regarding these twelve winds and some others he adds, I will come to the beautiful invention described by *Vitruvius* <note>The Roman architect Vitruvius, whose work "On Architecture" was the foundational text for Renaissance building and design.</note> in his architecture, found by *Andronicus of Cyrrhus*, to show how there were only eight winds. This man built in *Athens* a *Tower* <note>The "Tower of the Winds," an octagonal clocktower in Athens that still stands today.</note> with eight corners, and on each he had the image of the wind carved to which that face was turned; and finally, having made a marble capital atop the *Tower*, he placed a bronze statue upon it which held a rod in its right hand. This, being turned around by the blowing of the winds, pointed out with that rod which wind was blowing. And thus it was observed that between *Solarius* <note>The East wind, often called Subsolanus.</note> and *Auster* [South], there was *Eurus* [South-East]; between *Auster* and *Favonius* [West], *Africus* [South-West]; between *Favonius* and *Septentrio* [North], *Caurus* or *Chorus* [North-West]; and between *Septentrio* and *Solarius*, *Aquilo* [North-East]. This description, according to *Boccaccio* <note>Giovanni Boccaccio, who in his "Genealogy of the Pagan Gods" compiled extensive mythological lore.</note>, is good and true. And therefore, not discussing any longer the various opinions that exist regarding the number and names of the winds—especially *Vitruvius* who, in his third book, wants there to be twenty-four—I will speak of their forms as far as they are found among the writers. From these, we will easily learn to form the others by considering the nature of the wind we wish to paint. *Notus* or *Auster* is described by *Ovid* <note>The Roman poet Ovid; the following is a vernacular translation of a passage from his *Metamorphoses*, Book I, describing the South wind.</note> in such a manner:

> *And with wet wings Notus flies,*
> *Carrying his horrible face covered*
> *In dark mist, then his beard,*
> *Is all twisted, and water comes out*
> *From his white hair, and on his forehead*
> *He carries the clouds, and all moist is his chest.*

Of *Zephyr* or *Favonius*, *Philostratus* <note>Likely Philostratus the Elder, a Greek writer who described works of art in his "Imagines."</note> makes such a drawing: that he should be a youth with a soft and delicate face, with wings on his shoulders, one

And for this reason, he was imagined to be the husband of <term>Flora</term> <note>The Roman goddess of flowers and the season of spring.</note>, worshipped by the ancients as the goddess of flowers, wearing a garment all painted with flowers of various colors. <term>Aquilo</term> <note>The North wind, known for its cold, clear blasts.</note> or rather <term>Boreas</term>, <term>Pausanias</term> <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler whose descriptions of lost artworks are vital to art history.</note> writes, was sculpted on one side of the chest of <term>Cypselus</term> <note>A famous, intricately carved cedar chest dedicated at Olympia.</note> in the Temple of <term>Juno</term> among the Eleans in Greece, shown kidnapping <term>Orithyia</term> <note>An Athenian princess in mythology who was carried off by the North wind.</note> as the fables imagine; but he does not say how he was depicted, except that instead of feet, he had the tails of serpents, perhaps judging that from his works and powers, anyone could easily represent him. For <term>Subsolanus</term> <note>The East wind.</note>, as <term>Bede</term> <note>The Venerable Bede, an Anglo-Saxon monk whose scientific writings on nature were widely read in the Renaissance.</note> says, is a warm and dry wind, but moderately so; <term>Vulturnus</term> <note>The South-East wind.</note> dries everything out; <term>Eurus</term> <note>The East or South-East wind.</note> constricts and generates clouds; <term>Septentrio</term> <note>The North wind.</note>, because it is born in watery and frozen places and on high mountains, makes the air clear; <term>Eurus</term> or <term>Notus</term> <note>The South wind.</note> is cold and dry; <term>Circius</term> <note>The North-Northwest wind.</note> causes snow and tempests; <term>Africus</term> <note>The South-West wind.</note>, entirely tempestuous, generates lightning and thunder; and <term>Chorus</term> <note>The North-West wind.</note> makes the air cloudy in the East and clear in the West. Concerning their birth and dwelling place—since it sometimes happens that one must represent it, together with <term>Aeolus</term> <note>The mythical keeper or king of the winds.</note> their King—thus writes <term>Ovid</term>.
