## On the form of the Earth. Chapter XX.

**T**HE Earth, daughter and also the seat of <term>Demogorgon</term> <note>A primordial deity often cited in late antiquity and the Renaissance as the ancestor of all gods, representing the mysterious forces of nature.</note>, was worshiped by ancient peoples under various images because of the diversity of names given to her. Therefore, she was sometimes called the wife of <term>Titan</term> <note>Titan here refers to the Sun, who "impregnates" the earth with life-giving warmth.</note>, by which the Sun is understood; because the Sun works upon her as upon matter suitable for producing every kind of thing. And she was called *terra* from "covering" <note>original: "à Terrendo". A classical etymology suggesting the earth is named because it covers or hides what lies beneath its surface.</note>, because it covers that which belongs to the surface alone. According to <term>Macrobius</term> <note>A 5th-century Roman author whose "Saturnalia" is a primary source for ancient religious lore.</note>, she was depicted by the Egyptians among their sacred images in the guise of an ox or cow, for no other reason than the utility derived from this animal. She was sometimes named <term>Tellus</term> <note>The Roman personification of the Earth as a goddess.</note> because we take fruits from her, as <term>Rabanus</term> <note>Rabanus Maurus, a famous medieval encyclopedist and theologian.</note> says; *Tellumene* for that part which is not covered [by water]; *Humus* according to the same author for that part which has much moisture, being near marshes and rivers; *arida* [dry] because it is plowed <note>The author makes a wordplay between "arida" (dry) and "arare" (to plow).</note>; and "Bona" [the Good] according to the testimony of Macrobius in the *Saturnalia* because she is the cause of all the goods necessary for our living. For she nourishes the things that produce herbs and fruits, and provides food for the birds and pastures for the beasts, by which we also are nourished. And in those times she was represented holding some green plants in her hand, as if they had just now sprouted; at other times with a scepter in the left hand, which led people to believe she was equal in power to <term>Juno</term> <note>The Queen of the Gods in Roman mythology.</note>; with a vine branch upon her head and at her side a serpent with a myrtle wand, because of the fable that her Father was in love with her. Furthermore, she was called the "Great Mother" as the creator of everything, as <term>Statius</term> <note>A Roman poet of the 1st century AD.</note> affirms in his *Thebaid*:

> *O eternal mother of men and of Gods,*
> *Who generates the forests and the rivers and all*
> *The seeds of the world, of animals and wild beasts.*

->## SEVENTH. <-

Regarding this <term>Great Mother</term> <note>The goddess Cybele, known to the Romans as *Magna Mater*, personifying the fertile earth.</note>, **Isidore** <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), an influential scholar whose *Etymologies* preserved much classical knowledge for the Middle Ages.</note> writes that she was sometimes depicted with a **key** in her hand to show that the earth is locked up in the winter time, and pulls back into herself the seeds scattered upon her, which then germinate and come forth in the **Springtime**, at which time she is said to open herself. She was crowned with various garlands, sometimes of **oak**, because just as mortals once lived on the acorns produced by oak trees, so today they live on grain and other fruits produced by the earth; and sometimes of **Pine**, because this tree was consecrated to her.

One reads in **Cornelius Tacitus** <note>In his work *Germania*, Tacitus describes the rituals of the Germanic tribes, specifically the goddess Nerthus, whom he identifies with Mother Earth.</note> that some peoples of Germany worshiped Mother Earth, believing that she intervened in all the affairs of men; but because they had neither temples nor idols, they performed their ceremonies in a forest, where there was a **cart** covered entirely with cloths, which no one was permitted to touch except the priest, as if he alone knew that the Goddess was there. For this reason, he followed behind it with great reverence, having it pulled by **two cows**. These were then days of joy and gladness, and no war could be waged, but all iron weapons remained locked away; the country was full of peace, and the places where she went were guarded with great respect. When she was satisfied with her journeying and no longer wished to converse among mortals, the cart was immediately washed in a certain lake along with the cloths that covered her, and she likewise; and the servants who performed this task were swallowed by the lake so that they were seen no more.

In another part of Germany, as the same Cornelius adds, some peoples, having no temples or idols, worshiped her by carrying around the image of a **Wild Boar**, and in this way they considered themselves safe from all dangers and enemies. One sees on an ancient medal <note>In this context, "medal" refers to a Roman imperial coin, likely an *aureus* or *sestertius*.</note> of **Faustina** <note>Empress Faustina the Elder or her daughter Faustina the Younger, both of whom were depicted on coins with the attributes of Cybele.</note> her image as the Great Mother, who has her head encircled by **towers**, and sits with her right arm leaning on the seat, and with her left hand holds a shield resting on her knee, and on each of her sides is a **Lion**.

Nor shall I omit to mention that she was sometimes called **Fauna**; because, as **Macrobius** says, she favors <note>original: "fauorisce", a play on the name Fauna.</note> every use of animals; and **Fatua** from *fando*, which signifies **speaking** <note>An ancient Roman goddess often identified with the "Bona Dea"; her names were linked to her prophetic powers.</note>; and **Cybele**, as **Pompeius Festus** writes, from a certain geometric figure made like a die called a **Cube**, which was also consecrated to her by the ancients, as the **Platonists** write, to show the firmness of the Earth. This is because a thrown die, on whichever side it falls, always remains steady; and under this name she was likewise represented with her head encircled by towers, according to **Lucretius** where he says:

> They encircled her high head, and adorned it
> With a crown of **Myrtle** to show

And she was likewise given a chariot pulled by **lions** to show that there is no wildness so great that it cannot be overcome by **maternal piety** <note>original: *pietà Materna*; the idea that a mother's love can tame even the fiercest beasts</note>, as **Ovid** holds. However, **Diodorus** <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BC.</note> suggests this was because she was nurtured and raised by lions on Mount Cybelus in Phrygia, from which some believe she took her name. **Phurnutus** <note>Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher known for his allegorical interpretations of Greek mythology.</note> suggests that the Earth is also called **Rhea**, as if she were the cause of the rain falling <note>A folk etymology connecting the name Rhea to the Greek word *rheo*, meaning "to flow."</note>; and he says that she was given **drums**, **cymbals**, **torches**, and **lamps** as signs of the thunder, lightning, and flashes that usually precede the rain. Others, however, believe the drums signify that the earth contains all the **Winds** within itself. 

But the most specific name given to her by the ancients is **Ops**, who was imagined to be the wife of **Saturn**, because this word signifies "help" <note>From the Latin *ops*, meaning power, wealth, or assistance.</note>; and there is no one who helps the life of mortals more than the Earth. Hence **Homer** calls her the **Giver of Life**, because she provides us with a place to dwell and offers us the means to nourish ourselves, and in other ways benefits us like a devoted Mother. Thus **Martianus** <note>Martianus Capella, an author from late antiquity whose work on the liberal arts was a standard textbook in the Middle Ages.</note>, describing her, says that she is of great age and has a vast body; and although she gives birth often and has many children around her, she nevertheless wears a garment entirely painted with flowers of diverse colors, and a cloak woven of green herbs. In this cloak, there appear to be all those things most prized by mortals, such as all the **gems and metals**; and one could also see a great abundance of all fruits and a wonderful plenty of all things. In this portrait, everyone can very clearly recognize the **Earth**. 

**Varro**, as reported by **Saint Augustine** in *The City of God*, suggests she was called **Ops** because she becomes better through human work <note>original: *opera*; a play on words between the name Ops and the Latin word for work or labor</note>, and the more she is cultivated, the more fertile she becomes. At other times she was called **Proserpina**, because the crops emerging from the Earth go as if "creeping" <note>original: *serpendo*; the name Proserpina is here linked to the verb *proserpere*, to emerge or creep forth</note>; and **Vesta**, because she "clothes" herself <note>original: *veste*; from *vestire*, to clothe</note> in green herbs. Under the name of Ops, she is described with a **towered crown** on her head, because the circuit of the Earth is entirely filled with Cities, Castles, Villages, and other buildings, like a crown; with a garment woven of green herbs, and surrounded by leafy **wings** <note>original: *Vanni*; likely referring to winnowing fans or wings, here allegorized as vegetation</note> which signify the trees, plants, and grasses that cover the Earth. She holds a **scepter** in her hand, which indicates that all Kingdoms and all human riches, the power of earthly Lords, are found upon the Earth; and she has **drums**, by which is understood the roundness of the Earth.

# SETTIMIO

...divided into two hemispheres, of which one is called the **upper hemisphere** and the other the **lower hemisphere**, with a chariot of four wheels. This is because, even if the Earth stands still and is immobile, the works done upon her are nonetheless varied with a certain order through the **four seasons** of the year, which follow one after another. This chariot is pulled by **tame lions**, to allude to what **farmers** do when sowing grain: they immediately cover it so that greedy birds do not make a prey of it, just as **lions** do when they walk through dusty places, wiping away their footprints with their tails so that hunters cannot track where they have gone. The seats that are imagined around her show that although all other things move, she always remains still. 

The priests called **Corybantes** <note>Ancient priests of the goddess Cybele who performed rhythmic, spear-clashing dances.</note> who surround her, standing upright and armed, are an argument that not only the cultivators of the Earth, but also those who have the government of Cities and Kingdoms, must not sit still nor remain in idleness; rather, everyone must take up their arms—some to cultivate, and others to defend the fatherland, exposing themselves to every danger for its sake. 

Briefly gathering then what I have said: this Goddess, according to **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar and writer.</note>, is to be placed upon a chariot pulled by **lions**, with her head encircled by towers in the manner of a crown, with a scepter in her hand, dressed in a mantle heavily laden with branches, herbs, and flowers, with some empty seats around her, accompanied by castrated priests who, being armed, strike their **drums** <note>original: *timpani*; these were small hand-drums or tambourines used in ecstatic worship.</note> with their hands. 

Beyond this, because the earth is not suited to produce in every place, that part which is fertile—and therefore cultivated—was called **Ceres**. Her statue was made in the form of a **Matron** with garlands of ears of grain on her head and a bunch of **poppies** in her hand, which is a sign of fertility, pulled in a chariot by two fierce **dragons**. Hence **Claudian** <note>Claudius Claudianus, a Roman poet of the late 4th century AD.</note>, when he describes her returning from Sicily where she had hidden her daughter, says:

> She ascends the chariot to her maternal home,
> Directing the flight of the **Dragons**, whose limbs
> She often strikes; and they through the clouds
> Wave in twists, hissing, and the bit
> They placidly lick, which soft
> Renders the foam of the friendly venom.
> These, having their proud foreheads covered,
> Hold high crests, and have their backs
> All scattered with knots and circles,
> And their long scales, shining,
> Seem to cast sparks of gold and fire.

-> # SYMBOL <-

Snakes were given to her to demonstrate the winding furrows that oxen make while they plow the earth, and also because grain does not rise very high, but seems to almost crawl [serpent-like] along the ground. According to **Hesiod** <note>An early Greek poet, author of the *Theogony*.</note>, this was also in memory of that serpent which fled from the island of **Salamis** to save itself and entered the temple of **Ceres** in **Eleusis**, where it then remained forever as a minister and servant. But that Ceres signifies the flat and wide earth, the producer of grain, is shown (as **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian and bishop.</note> says) by her image being crowned with ears of grain, with several poppy plants around her to show fertility. They further gave her torches in her hand because of the story told of her, when she went searching for her daughter **Proserpina** who had been abducted by **Pluto**; as **Praxiteles** <note>One of the most renowned Greek sculptors of the 4th century BCE.</note> once made a statue of her. In **Arcadia**, there was another statue where she sat holding a torch in her right hand and reached out with her left toward another statue of a certain other Goddess called **Hera**. 

In Arcadia, near a cave consecrated to her, she was called "the Black One" because she was dressed in black, partly due to grief for her stolen daughter and partly due to the indignation she felt at the violence done to her by **Neptune** in the form of a horse. While she was hidden in that cave, no longer wishing to see the light of Heaven, the earth no longer produced any fruit; from this followed a great famine <note>original: "pestilenza" - while often meaning plague, in this context it refers to the disastrous crop failure and subsequent mortality.</note> that persisted until she was found by chance by **Pan**. He then reported her to **Jupiter**, and out of pity for the world, the **Fates** <note>The three goddesses who preside over human destiny.</note> were sent to plead with her. Therefore, having set aside all sadness, she emerged appeased from the cave, and the famine immediately ceased, and the earth produced its usual fruits. So that the memory of this event should remain, the people of that country consecrated that cave to her with a wooden statue sitting upon a rock, in the figure of a woman except that she had the head of a horse with its mane, around which serpents and other wild beasts played; she wore a garment that covered her entirely to her feet, and held a dolphin in one hand and a dove in the other. 

She was also, as I said above, called **Vesta**, but not the one who was the Goddess of fire—that is, of that living heat spread through the bowels of the Earth, which gives life to all things born from her—but rather the one who denotes the roundness of the earth and its "clothing." The ancients represented her as a woman of virginal appearance, as **Pliny** says the excellent sculptor **Scopas** made her, with a <term>timpano: a hand drum or tambourine associated with the rhythmic worship of Earth goddesses</term> in her hand. **Phurnutus** <note>Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher known for his allegorical interpretations of myths.</note> further says that she used to be made almost entirely round—so narrow were her shoulders made—and with a crown of white flowers, because the Earth is round and entirely surrounded by the whitest element there is, which is the air. Beyond this, from the magnitude <note>original: "magnitudine", likely a pun on 'Maia' and 'Major' (greater).</note> of the Earth, she was called **Maia**, from whom the month of **May**...

### **Of the form of Pan, of Echo, of the Satyrs, Fauns, and Silvans.**
### ->*Cap. XXI.*<-

**T**he Satyrs, or **Onosceli** <note>literally "donkey-legged" beings.</note>, Fauns, Silvans, Incubi, and Pans, were held—as **Theodontius** <note>An author cited by Boccaccio in his genealogy of the gods.</note> writes—to be the sons of **Faunus**, and by others, such as **Leontius**, to be sons of **Saturn**; but the Fauns and Satyrs were considered Gods of the Woods, who, as **Rabanus** <note>Rabanus Maurus, a prominent Carolingian scholar and archbishop.</note> says, predicted future things with their voices. The Pans were held to be Gods of the fields, and the Silvans Gods of the forests. **Pomponius Mela** <note>A Roman geographer of the 1st century AD.</note> says that beyond Mount Atlas in Mauritania, lights have often been seen at night and the clatter of cymbals and pipes heard, while by day nothing is found; for this reason, it is firmly believed that these are the Fauns and Satyrs. And **Rabanus** says that the Fauns, or "little men," have hooked noses, horns on their foreheads, and the feet of a goat, and that one of these was once seen by the **Blessed Anthony** in the solitudes of the **Thebaid** <note>A desert region in Egypt.</note> while he was traveling to visit **Saint Paul the First Hermit**. And likewise, **Saint Augustine** writes of having seen many by experience, and that they are by nature very lustful and lovers of women. All these are imagined in nearly the same form, as shall be understood in order. **Pan**, the leader of the pans, is the God of Shepherds, who was thus worshipped on Mount Lycaeus and Maenalus in Arcadia, and on the Aventine in Rome by **Evander**. He had horns and goat's ears, a small tail, temples wreathed with Pine, a long beard, and a pastoral staff in his hand curved at the top, a red and fiery face, and around him a leopard skin, or sometimes a panther skin, with a panpipe of seven reeds in his hand, out of love for **Syrinx** or **Echo**, according to **Macrobius** <note>A Roman provincial of the early 5th century, author of the *Saturnalia*.</note>. Of her form, **Ausonius Gallus** <note>Decimus Magnus Ausonius, a Roman poet and rhetorician.</note> sang thus in an epigram:

> To what end do you seek, oh foolish painter,
> To create a picture of me, who am such...

Not much different from them and from the *Siluani* <note>Spirits of the woods in Roman mythology.</note> are the *Fauns*, who are likewise woodland Gods; and they may all be crowned, as the ancients used to do, with lilies, poplar, fennel, and the reed into which *Syrinx* was transformed while being loved by *Pan*, just as *Ovid* sings in the *Metamorphoses*.

### Of the form of the Nymphs. Chap. XXII.

**T**he nymphs have had various names from the poets according to the various places where they imagined they lived. [Anatomy], the cartilages, and the small bones similar to sesame seeds (which are found in the hands as well as the feet, numbering at most forty-eight), which according to some consist of two hundred and twenty-four bones, and according to others, two hundred and fifteen. Although it is not strictly necessary for a painter to have an exact [medical] knowledge of these—as that belongs more properly to the anatomist—it cannot be denied that it is nevertheless beneficial for him, as it is for the sculptor, to know their number in detail, as well as the art with which they are composed and joined together. For in this part of the study, which I judge to be the very core of this art, one must know whom to take as a model to imitate. These masters have known how to demonstrate this art and make it visible to our eyes, competing with the ancient Greeks. 

To demonstrate their prowess in this field, the Greeks usually depicted nude figures, as did the most ancient Arabs, Indians, Babylonians, and Egyptians. After them, the Romans began to make clothed figures, perhaps because they could not achieve this art with that same ease and felicity with which those ancients achieved it. And chief—indeed unique—among all, by common judgment, has been the divine **Michelangelo**. Since the time of the ancients, there has not been, nor will there be, anyone who has expressed nudes more vividly or placed the entire art of anatomy so clearly before our eyes. After him, **Leonardo da Vinci** was excellent; various drawings of his are found in many hands, and principally in the house of **Francesco Melzi**, a Milanese gentleman and his disciple, besides...

### On the shape of the bones in the human body. Chapter XXIV.

**A**MONG all the parts of the human body, there is no one who does not know that the bones are the principal part. This is because they are the proper support and boundaries of the limbs, and their true and solid chain. It is therefore necessary that we see in what manner they are composed among themselves.

<meta>This page transitions from the list of artists who mastered anatomy to a practical lesson on the skeletal system. ->### BOOK 3<-

...so that, knowing the foundation of the body, the other parts can be easily added to it, according to that precept which **Leonardo** <note>Leonardo da Vinci, whose anatomical notebooks were famous among artists even before their formal publication.</note> once left written in his anatomy of the human body. There, speaking of the bones and their linkages <term>incatenatura (articulation)</term>, he says it is impossible for a painter to reasonably create a body without knowing how the bones lie beneath. This is because they are the true measure of the length of the limbs and their proper boundaries. Thus, it can easily happen that a figure is "crippled" if one does not realize, for example, that a bone cannot twist, nor break, nor be raised or turned in the joints beyond a certain point. It follows that many figures are seen to perform forced and broken actions in their limbs. Above all others, **Michelangelo** always carefully observed this, as can clearly be seen in his works. 

But as I must speak here of such things as briefly and clearly as possible, I will run through the field of anatomy, seeking only what pertains to our art regarding the bones of the human body. Beginning with the head—that part covered by hair—it is protected by a bone called the **cranium** <note>the skull</note>, which is composed of eight bones. The first occupies the forehead and takes its name from it <note>the frontal bone</note>; the second and third form the crown <note>the parietal bones</note>; the fourth and fifth occupy the temples, where the ear-holes are located; the sixth takes the nape and half of the base of the skull <note>the occipital bone</note>; the seventh is encased in the middle of the base of the skull like a wedge, and thus takes its name <note>the sphenoid bone; from the Latin 'cuneus' meaning wedge</note>, and forms the center of the hollow of the eyes. The eighth and last fills the entire hole at the bottom of the forehead bone which corresponds to the nasal passages <note>the ethmoid bone</note>. 

The joints <term>commissure (sutures)</term> of the skull, when joined together, form an **H**. There are three: one is the **coronal**, another the **Lambdoid**, and the third is called the **sagittal**. From the eyebrows to the mouth, the upper jaw is formed, which has twelve bones—six on each side—of which it is not necessary to say how they are composed or how they make their nine joints. The lower jaw and the entire chin, the jaw teeth, and the jawbones are made of two bones that join at the point of the chin. From there, it narrows on each side until the points of the jaws, and there it widens again, but more thinly, rising toward the ears and ending in two "horns." The first of these ends under the **jugal bone** <note>the cheekbone or zygomatic bone</note>, and the other at the angle between this and the ear. There are thirty-two teeth, sixteen per jaw: the four in front are called **incisors** <note>original: "Tomis", from the Greek for cutting</note>; after which follow two **canines**, one on each side; then five on each side called **molars**; and finally two with three roots, which with...

->SEVENTH.<-

they are encased in the sockets of those jaws. Now, leaving aside the <term>Hyoid</term> <note>a U-shaped bone at the base of the tongue</note>, or <term>Ypsiloid</term> <note>named after the Greek letter upsilon (υ)</note>, which is at the root of the tongue and composed of eleven little bones; I will come to the <term>backbone</term> <note>the spinal column</note> which, in the manner of an aqueduct with many channels, descends from the brain down to the <term>tailbone</term>, and is composed of thirty bones called <term>nodes</term> <note>vertebrae</note>. All of these are wide at the front part, except for the first, which is almost round and is perforated without a fixed order, where branches of veins and arteries enter to nourish these bones. 

In the other parts, every node has many <term>processes</term> <note>bony outgrowths</note> around it, like thorns, which are all together called the <term>spine</term>; some go upward, some downward, others from the sides, and others toward the back, with an intervention of <term>cartilages</term> of which it is not necessary to make a more exact mention. It is enough to know that the <term>spine</term> is divided into four parts: the <term>neck</term>, the <term>shoulders</term>, the <term>loins</term> <note>the lumbar region</note>, and the <term>great bone</term> <note>the sacrum</note>. 

The <term>neck</term> is named from the end of the <term>nape</term> <note>original: "collottola"</note> to the <term>shoulders</term> <note>original: "omeri"</note>, and it has seven <term>nodes</term>. The first two of these are joined to each other on every side, while the rest are attached only at the front part, called the <term>body of the node</term>. All have the <term>processes</term> at the back bifurcated <note>split into two</note> except for the first. To these are joined the <term>nodes of the shoulders</term> <note>thoracic vertebrae</note> which are twelve—smaller above and larger below—which have a hollow on both sides into which the heads of the <term>ribs</term> are inserted. They have their seven processes: two high, two low, two at the sides, and one at the back, connected in the manner shown by <term>Vesalius</term> <note>Andreas Vesalius, the pioneering 16th-century anatomist</note> regarding the <term>loins</term>. 

The <term>nodes of the loins</term> <note>lumbar vertebrae</note> are five, and they have the same seven processes as the others, arranged so that none mount upward, except those of the last one, to avoid the <term>hip bones</term> <note>original: "ossa de' galoni"</note>. The <term>posterior processes</term> of these bones are strong, thick, and short, and they end in a very rough part. The <term>sacrum</term> <note>original: "osso sacro"</note>, which is the largest part of the <term>spine</term>, is hunched at the back and concave at the front; it has six <term>nodes</term>, of which the upper ones are larger and the lower ones smaller. The <term>tailbone</term> <note>original: "codione" or coccyx</note> consists of four <term>nodes</term>; the first has a small hollow on top into which the last <term>node of the sacrum or great bone</term> (whichever you wish to call it) is encased. Thus, the second comes to be joined to the first, and then the others, which I will omit. 

The <term>chest</term> <note>original: "petto"</note>, which is 그 part at the front stretching from the <term>clavicles</term> <note>collarbones</note> to the <term>pit of the stomach</term>, has a <term>wide bone</term> <note>the sternum</note> in the middle that occupies the space from the <term>hollow of the throat</term> between the two clavicles down to the <term>cartilage of the stomach</term> <note>original: "forcella dello stomaco"</note>. And because the chest is oval-shaped, the upper and lower ribs are smaller, and those in the middle are larger. The <term>shoulder blades</term> <note>original: "palette delle spalle"</note> are those bones in which the arms are set; they are located between the first and fifth ribs. Each of them is bound on its side to the bone of the nape, to the nodes of the spine <note>the vertebrae</note>, and to the ribs by means of certain muscles. 

Furthermore, each shoulder blade is distinct; for besides having many <term>processes</term> <note>bony projections</note>, cavities, joints, and <term>protuberances</term> <note>original: "grommi"</note>, it is of an unequal triangular shape. Thus, the back side with the thick edge extends along the length of the shoulders, being somewhat hollowed in the middle; the front side runs obliquely from the end of this toward the front; and the top side drops somewhat forward until it ends in a small socket near the neck of the shoulder blade, approaching the front side. 

The <term>clavicles</term> <note>collarbones</note> are then set into the highest socket of the process of these shoulder blades called the <term>point of the shoulder</term> <note>the acromion</note>; and into those two sockets made in the highest part of the sides of the first bone of the chest <note>the sternum</note>. Their heads are similar to these sockets—that is, arched—and they go from the front side toward the back, where they are less wide but more raised. 

The bone of the <term>humerus</term> <note>the upper arm</note>, which is what extends from the shoulder blade to the elbow, has a large joint at its highest part where it joins the shoulder blades. This joint forms a large head, which is slightly divided; the inner part, which is larger and shaped like a half-sphere, is set into the socket of the shoulder blade, while the outer part, being somewhat unequal, projects outward and is divided into two heads. The lower part of this bone, which joins the two <term>spindles</term> <note>original: "fuselli," referring to the radius and ulna</note> of the arm at its lower part, has a socket and two protuberances that form the shape of a <term>pulley</term> <note>original: "girella," the trochlea</note>; it has the back head more raised than the outer one. Above the pulley are two sockets, made such that the one in back is larger; and within them play the processes of the larger spindle of the arm. 

The spindles <note>forearm bones</note> extend from the elbow to the <term>wrist</term> <note>original: "bracciale"</note> and are two in number: one larger, which creates the movement of the elbow, and the other smaller. The larger one, called the <term>ulna</term>, which is set into the pulley toward the wrist, becomes thin and ends in a head, at the end of which is a round joint. The smaller one, called the <term>radius</term>, joins with the larger one below; twisting above, it does so in such a way that in the middle it does not touch the other bone anywhere. Below, near the wrist, where it thickens, it ends in a joint on the inner side; and above, it is somewhat round and hunched. The wrist, to which the spindles join...

# BOOK SEVEN

The **wrist** <note>original: "bracciale"</note> is that upon which the hand plays, and it has eight bones, which, all encased together on the inner side, form a hollowed-out "O" shape. The **first** is humped on the outside and depressed on the inside; it joins with the **lesser forearm bone** <term>radius</term> <note>original: "minore fustello"</note>, and to the second, fifth, sixth, and seventh bones of the wrist. The **second** is somewhat round everywhere, except underneath, and joins to the first, seventh, and third by an <term>arthrodia</term> <note>a gliding joint</note> connection, and to the lesser forearm bone. The **third**, somewhat round except on top, joins at the sides to the second and fourth; and below, it is set into a cavity of the eighth. The **fourth** joins to the third. The **fifth** is in a certain way square, and has a cavity on top in which a head of the first is encased, and on the outer part it has another cavity in which it receives a head of the sixth, and below another in which a small head of the first bone of the **thumb** <note>original: "pollice"</note> is set. The **sixth**, which is almost triangular, joins on the inside to the fifth, on the outside to the seventh, and below to the fifth, besides the part where the second bone of the **palm** <note>metacarpal</note> and the first that supports the index finger are encased. The **seventh** joins to the first, second, sixth, and eighth, and to the bone of the palm that supports the middle finger. The **eighth** and last enters like a wedge between the seventh and the third; it joins to the bone of the palm that supports the ring finger and the little finger.

The **palm** <note>original: "palma"</note> is that space from the wrist to the first joints of the fingers, which is called the **comb** <term>metacarpus</term> <note>original: "pettine"</note>, and it is composed of four almost round bones. The longest of these supports the middle finger and is attached together with the other three bones that support the other three fingers, along with the thumb, which is not numbered in the "comb." Each finger of the hand, by means of the joints, is composed of three bones, and each is wider at the beginning than at the end; and they follow this pattern, their size being recognized by this. The heads are thicker than in the middle; on the outside they are round, and on the inside they are hollowed, which is not the case in the thumb. Furthermore, the first bone is attached to the palm; the second joins with the first, and the third with the second.

The **hips** <note>the pelvis</note>, which join to the processes of the **great bone** <term>sacrum</term> <note>original: "osso grande"</note>, are composed of three bones. The first makes up the highest part that corresponds to the flank, called the **point of the hip** <term>ilium</term> <note>original: "punta del galone ouero anca"</note>. The second makes up the part below where the head of the thigh bone is encased, called the **hip bone** <term>ischium</term> <note>original: "anca"</note>. And the third makes up the front part and is called the **pubic bone** <term>pubis</term> <note>original: "osso del pettignone"</note>.

The **thigh bone** <term>femur</term> <note>original: "osso della coscia"</note> is the longest of all others in the body, and has at its ends a joint: on the upper side it joins to the hip bone, and below to the **greater shin bone** <term>tibia</term>. The **shins** are those two bones from the knee to the ankle <note>original: "collo del piede," literally neck of the foot</note>; one is called the **tibia**, which is larger and sits on the inner side of the legs, and is more...

...is thicker than the other **lesser shin bone** <term>fibula</term> <note>original: "stinco minore"</note>, which sits on the outside and is called by some the **Scirà** <note>An archaic term for the fibula or shank.</note>. Both have their joints at the top as well as at the bottom; but the upper part of the **larger shin bone** <term>tibia</term> <note>original: "maggiore [stinco]"</note> is wider and thicker than the other, and at its highest point it has two hollows into which the two heads of the **thigh bone** <term>femur</term> <note>original: "osso della coscia"</note> are encased. The lesser bone does not rise high enough to join with this thigh bone; but below the larger one, at the front of the knee, there is a round bone, somewhat flat at the back and front <term>patella</term> <note>original: "osso tondo," referring to the kneecap</note>. In the middle, it has a ridge that fits into the hollow formed between the two heads of the thigh bone; furthermore, at its lower part, it has a point that corresponds to the upper part of the larger shin bone.

The **foot** is divided into the ankle bone, heel, navicular bone, instep, comb of the foot, sole, and toes. The **ankle bone** <term>talus</term> <note>original: "talone"</note> is double; the first is that into whose highest part the two shin bones of the leg are encased, which for this reason is round in that area and raised at the sides. On the outer side it is deeper and square, and there the process of the lesser shin bone is encased, which sits lower than the second larger one. The **heel bone** <term>calcaneus</term> <note>original: "calcagno"</note>, which is the second bone of the foot, is round on the inside from the bottom, hollow in the middle, and raised. The third bone, called **navicular** <note>original: "navicolare"</note> because it resembles a small boat, has a head and a long hollow on the inside, into which the head of the ankle bone is encased; on the front part it has three sides, into which the three bones of the **instep** <term>tarsus</term> <note>original: "collo del piede"</note> are encased. And on the upper part it is somewhat round, and underneath it helps to form the arch of the foot, being hollowed out. 

The instep of the foot has four bones, three of which join to the navicular, and the fourth is similar to a **die** <term>cuboid bone</term> <note>original: "dado"</note>. The **comb of the foot** <term>metatarsus</term> <note>original: "pettine del piede"</note> is the name of the upper part between the instep, the toes, and the lower part of the sole. It has five bones, similar to those four of the hand, which join to those of the instep in order with small heads that are almost flat. The one that supports the **big toe** <note>original: "pollice"</note> is encased in the first bone of the instep; the second, which supports the index toe, into the second; the third, which supports the middle toe, into the third; and the last two are encased in the bone similar to a die mentioned before. The **toes** are each made of three bones, like those of the hand, except for the big toe which has only two; the first of these forms the first bone of the "comb," and in the rest they are similar to those of the hand. 

This is what I have wished to collect here, as briefly as I could, regarding the composition of the bones; for I have reasoned enough elsewhere concerning the muscles, their **functions** <note>original: "officij"</note>, and other matters. But to speak freely of what I feel: to understand them perfectly, it is in any case necessary to see them from life, just as good **painters** and **sculptors** have done a thousand times.

->SEVENTH<-

### On the form of Heroes, Saints, & Philosophers, both ancient and modern. Chap. XXV.

**I**t would certainly be a most significant oversight if, after having spent so much time investigating the form of Satyrs, Nymphs, and other mythical peoples, and having recently treated the form of the human body, I did not touch upon the form of Heroes and other famous men and women. I have gathered what I could observe from sacred and profane histories, including those of the Hebrews, Greeks, Assyrians, Romans, and other ancient nations. Most authors mention these figures, and they are cited in the first and second **handbook of ancient and modern medals** <term>prontuario delle medaglie</term> <note>These "prontuari" were popular 16th-century books that provided woodcut portraits of historical figures based on ancient coins and medals to serve as visual references for artists.</note>, alongside their lives, as well as the lives of Saints, Philosophers, and Emperors—both Barbarian and Italian—and also their Generals. This is so that the painter may be well-informed in all his works, representing histories with **reason** <term>ragione</term> <note>Meaning historical accuracy and logical consistency.</note>, and not showing, as many do, one thing for another. One should not paint a **Nero** <note>The Roman Emperor known for his cruelty.</note> who resembles **Charlemagne** <note>The medieval King of the Franks and first Holy Roman Emperor.</note>, or an old Saint Paul for the young man falling from his horse, or a cruel man in place of a merciful one; such paintings can have no value, even if they were made by **Apelles** <note>The most celebrated painter of ancient Greece.</note> himself.

Because a painter is required to represent not only the form and arrangement of bodies but also the qualities of the soul within those figures, which are quite clearly demonstrated by the ancient figures of both Princes and Sages, and the Gods of the City of Rome. These were meticulously collected along with the locations where they are found in the book called **Lucio Mauro** <note>A reference to "Le antichità della città di Roma" (1556) by Lucio Mauro, a standard guidebook for the ruins and statues of Rome in the Renaissance.</note>, where one can see the greatness and wonders of the Greeks, and later the Romans, in this faculty. I will proceed by noting in this place everything I have been able to observe through reading, regarding the form and disposition of the body as well as the quality of the soul and certain peculiar bearings of the most signal men who have lived from the beginning of the world until our own days, whom painters often have occasion to represent in histories. This, in my judgment, will be a most useful thing, from which many warnings may be drawn to work with judgment and prudence. 

And beginning with **Adam and Eve**, I have no doubt that the form of both was most beautiful, and graceful above all others, because they were the handiwork of God’s own hand. It is known that He created all things in the most beautiful and perfect way possible, as was demonstrated with the greatest excellence a mortal man can achieve by the divine **Raphael** <note>Raphael Sanzio, the Renaissance master, famous for his "Stanze" in the Vatican which included depictions of Adam and Eve.</note>, who then was followed by...

# BOOK II

I judge that it could be better done or understood by no one other than the master himself. **Saint Cecilia** was beautiful, of a generous and unconquered spirit, as were many other virgins and martyrs of whom it is not precisely known how they looked, though they are painted in various ways, as is also done with many saints and hermits. **Saint Lawrence** was as beautiful as an Angel; thus once the Devil, to drive his father and mother to despair, appeared to them in his place in a most hideous form. **Saint Christopher** was larger than all others of his time, for he was twelve cubits tall <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger; twelve cubits would be approximately 18 feet or 5.5 meters.</note>. **Saint Roch** used to dress in the humblest clothes, with a hat on his head, a small pouch at his side, and a pilgrim's staff <note>original: "bordone"</note> on his shoulder. In this attire he came from Montpellier <note>original: "monte Pesulano"</note> to Italy, just as **Cesare da Sesto** <note>Cesare da Sesto (1477–1523) was an influential Italian painter and a pupil of Leonardo da Vinci.</note> painted him on a panel in the church of Saint Roch in Milan, with a humble gesture, signifying his devotion to the Angel. 

Now passing to the Assyrians: **Nimrod** <note>original: "Nembroth"</note>, son of Cush, who had the **Tower of Babel** built, was of a stature similar to the giants, as one reads, and was strong beyond measure, proud, and splendid. **Semiramis**, Queen of the Assyrians, who surrounded Babylon with walls, went with her head uncovered, dressed publicly as a male. **Sardanapalus**, the last King of that nation, was soft of face and effeminate of spirit; thus he was found by Arbaces <note>original: "Arface"</note>—who transferred the monarchy to the Medes—in the midst of harlots, dressed in purple, with a necklace around his neck, in the habit of a woman with a distaff and a spindle <note>Tools used for spinning wool, symbols here of his supposed lack of masculinity.</note>. 

Among the Persians, **Artaxerxes**, seventh King of Persia, was of a most beautiful body and had arms so long that with his hands he almost touched his knees, for which reason he was called **Longimanus** <note>Latin for "Long-handed."</note>. **Esther** was so beautiful of body that she was taken as a wife by Artaxerxes, otherwise called Memnon, and sometimes Ahasuerus. **Zopyrus**, a famous man in the times of King Darius, was entirely deformed, because he had self-mutilated by cutting off his own nose, lips, and ears to flee, and in this way he waged war for Darius <note>According to Herodotus, Zopyrus mutilated himself to trick the Babylonians into trusting him, allowing him to betray the city to Darius.</note>. 

Among the Greeks—leaving aside Heaven, Saturn, Jove, and the other Gods, of whom we have sufficiently reasoned—**Hercules** was broad in the shoulders, with thick and prominent limbs, short and thick of neck, and with a sparse beard, just as he was principally expressed in a statue by Euthycrates, son of Lysippus; he constantly wore the lion’s skin and carried a club, a bow, and arrows. This man, although the Greeks held him to be the son of Jove, was nevertheless truly the son of Osiris <note>original: "Ofiri"</note>, King of Egypt, just as the first Heroes were sons and descendants of Noah; for this reason, Ninus is called the "Jove of the Babylonians." **Bacchus** was of a delicate body, such that he was accepted among the Muses; he had blond hair, and despite all this, he traversed the whole world three times, destroying tyrants.

For which reason **Alexander the Great** later ordered his captains to have the Macedonians cut their beards, as **Plutarch** reports in the *Life of Theseus*; where he also says that he <note>Theseus</note> was so named because of this shearing <note>original: "tensura"; This refers to the tradition of "the shearing of Theseus" at Delphi.</note>. **Zetes** and **Calais** had wings, with which flying they drove the **Harpies** from Arcadia, and went to **Colchis** with **Jason** and the other **Argonauts** to acquire the **Golden Fleece**. **Erichthonius** <note>A legendary early king of Athens.</note> had the feet of a serpent, and for this reason was the first inventor of the chariot, as **Virgil** says. **Priam**, the most famous King of Troy, was very handsome, except that he had squinting eyes; he was tall, with a long beard, and was robust and strong. **Helen**, abducted by **Paris**, was as is known to everyone an example of beauty, but she had a somewhat long neck, as **Lucian** says. **Hector** the Trojan was handsome, with well-proportioned limbs, tall, strong, and prudent. **Achilles** was haughty in appearance, walked with his head held high, wore his hair cut over his forehead like Theseus, had a nose that denoted a fierce spirit, nostrils that exhaled breath in great abundance, eyes of a color that leaned more toward sky-blue than black, and a proud but not unpleasant look. Whence **Homer** says that he fought on the banks of the **Scamander** with a grave and honorable aspect, as was his custom, so that he was a marvelous sight to all. **Aeneas** was very beautiful and tall, so that he stood above others from the shoulders up. **Pallas**, son of **Evander**, was found entirely intact near Rome at the time of Emperor **Henry III** by a peasant who was digging the earth; he surpassed the walls of Rome in size and height, and one could still see in him the wound made by the spear of **Turnus**, which was four feet long <note>This refers to a popular medieval legend regarding the discovery of a giant's corpse believed to be the Virgilian hero.</note>. **Agamemnon** had hair, a face, and a beard similar to those of **Jupiter**, as **Achilles Tatius** <note>A 2nd-century Greek novelist.</note> says; so beautiful was he and full of majesty. **Oedipus**, King of Thebes, had pierced feet, and having become king, he plucked out his eyes. **Medusa**, before she united with **Neptune** in the Temple of **Minerva**, had hair like gold and was otherwise very beautiful, but afterward it turned into snakes. **Otus** and **Ephialtes**, the feigned sons of Neptune who captured **Mars**, King of Thrace, and chained him, were not yet nine years old when they were of

He wore his hair in long curls, and his beauty was nonetheless fierce and full of majesty, such that he inspired both terror and love in whoever looked upon him; for this reason, one reads that **Cassander**, his captain, used to be frightened merely by contemplating his statue. Furthermore, his soul would become so inflamed that no one dared stay near him; indeed, one reads that once, when he was oppressed by great danger in **India**, he became so incensed that it seemed to those barbarians that he cast light all around the place where he slept, even though there was nothing but his sword under the pillow beside the bed. **Antigonus**, his successor as portrayed by **Apelles** <note>The most renowned painter of ancient Greece.</note>, had but one eye. **Lysimachus** was of such immeasurable strength that he killed the lion that was meant to devour him by the command of **Alexander** in his presence. **Agesilaus, King of the Lacedaemonians** <note>Spartans</note>—who is seen with horns on the ancient medals called **Lysimache**—was modest in appearance as he was in soul, temperate, and kind, even though he was very ugly of face; for which reason he did not wish for any sculptor or painter to portray him. Among the philosophers and other wise men, one reads that **Homer**, the most ancient of all poets, was so named because he was blind, having been named **Melesigenes**. **Pythagoras** was of a very beautiful body and a graceful appearance. **Hippocrates** was small of body, but handsome; he had a large head and a steady gait, and when he stood still, he looked at the ground. **Theon the Stoic** was of a very small body. **Cleobulus of Caria** was handsome and strong. **Socrates**, the father of all moral philosophy, was very ugly; for he had a snub nose and a bald head; a hairy neck and shoulders; unkempt hair; crooked legs and feet; and short arms. So that he could better attend to his meditations, **Diogenes** <note>Diogenes the Cynic, known for his extreme asceticism.</note> went about in winter wrapped tightly in a single cloth, barefoot, and carried a scrip <note>A small bag or satchel used by travelers or beggars.</note> and a staff; he was always barefoot, and his facial expression never changed. **Plato** was robust of body and broad in the chest; for this reason, he was named "Plato" <note>From the Greek 'platýs', meaning broad.</note> by **Ariston**. In his old age, he plucked out his eyes so that his spirit would not be troubled <note>A common, though likely apocryphal, anecdote in Renaissance texts suggesting that physical sight distracts from intellectual "vision."</note>. **Alcibiades**, the Duke of Athens, was most beautiful and expert in all things. **Xenophon**, called the "Muse," was also beautiful beyond measure, but he was freckled; he was well-mannered, gracious, and an expert in arms. **Demosthenes** had a terrible look in his eyes, as **Aeschines** says; he had a venerable face and a grave and modest gait. **Elico** <note>The author likely refers to Aeschylus, the "inventor" of tragic drama.</note>, the inventor of Tragedies, had a completely bald head; this was the cause of his death because an eagle, thinking his head was a stone, dropped a tortoise on it and crushed it. **Aristotle** had a handsome face and a long beard, and his eyes had certain small rings <note>The original "lunette" may refer to circles around the pupils or a specific shape of the eyelids.</note>; inside <note>Meaning his physical build.</note> he was small of body, hunchbacked, malformed, and a stutterer. **Aesop**, the writer of fables, was deformed and scrawny beyond all other men, for he had a long head shaped like a pumpkin, divided almost into sections like a melon; he had a wide, flat nose, a short and twisted neck, and thick, protruding, hanging lips. He was black in color—from which he was named Aesop <note>The name was traditionally (though incorrectly) linked to "Aethiop" or Ethiopian.</note>—he had a large belly, and legs so crooked and distorted that his calves were where his shins should be; finally, he was a hunchback and of monstrously small stature. **Sappho**, who was the inventor of lyric verse, was very beautiful. **Virgil** was large of body with an aquiline nose, and a rustic, thin face because he was of poor health. Of the modern poets, such as **Alberto** <note>Possibly Leon Battista Alberti or Albertus Magnus.</note>, **Dante**, **Petrarch**, **Ariosto**, and the others, I will say nothing, because their forms are well enough known through the many medals that are continually engraved of them.

Of the **Sibyls** <note>Ancient prophetesses believed to have foreseen the coming of Christ.</note>, the **Phrygian** wore her hair loose over her shoulders and dressed in red; the **Libyan** wore a green garland; the **Persian** wore garments of gold and covered herself with a white veil. So too did the **European** Sibyl, of whom one reads that she had a very beautiful face. Of the others, no mention is found, except that many of them are seen painted—principally by **Raphael** in the Church of the Peace <note>Santa Maria della Pace in Rome.</note> in Rome, and by **Michelangelo** in the Chapel of his *Judgment* <note>The Sistine Chapel.</note>. Among the most ancient Italians, **Eryx**, King of the Sicilians, was a very great giant and carried in his hand a staff like a tree filled with lead. **Senta** <note>Commonly known as Fauna or Bona Dea.</note>, wife of **Faunus**, the second King of Italy, was never seen in the face, so modest was she. As for **Turnus**, King of the Rutulians, a clear argument for how great and strong he was is the wound four feet long with which he killed **Pallas** <note>A character from Virgil's Aeneid.</note> in the forehead. Among the ancient barbarians, beginning with **Antaeus**, King of the furthest parts of Mauritania—where **Pomponius Mela** says his shield of immeasurable size was made of elephant bone—he was a giant, broad in the shoulders, well-squared, strong and fierce, such that he wrestled with **Hercules**. He was of a horrible face, wherefore he took pleasure in frightening others with his look, so much so that he would stand before a mirror investigating which kind of look was the fiercest; he had very sunken eyes and temples, a broad forehead, a pale complexion, and in that part of the head where he had hair, it was very light, while the rest of his body was hairy beyond measure. **Claudius** was tall of body, of medium build, very beautiful of face, and always showed in himself a certain gravity and authority; he had white hair and was weak in the legs, and when he became angry, tears came to his eyes. **Nero** was of mediocre stature, neither large nor small; he had a face more beautiful and graceful than honest, blue eyes that were somewhat large but of uncertain sight <note>Historical sources suggest Nero was near-sighted and used an emerald to view gladiator matches.</note>, blond hair, a thick neck, a belly...

...strong, with a large and round head, with a red beard, but somewhat flaxen <note>pale yellowish-brown</note>, and with small, blue eyes. **Genseric**, King of the Vandals, **Fritigern** <note>original: "Frindegino"</note>, and **Theodoric**, King of the Goths—of whose father it is read that he threw sparks from his entire body—were proud, fierce, and cruel, but most of all **Huneric**, son of Genseric. **Attila**, surnamed the **Scourge of God**, King of the Huns, was small of body, broad in the chest, large-headed, with small eyes, little beard, gray-haired on his head, and of a fierce complexion. Among the Lombard Kings, **Pasone II** <note>likely a reference to a specific Lombard ruler, perhaps a variant of Alboin or a local regional naming</note> was robust and warlike, but cruel. **Agilulf** was of a most beautiful body, for which he deserved to be taken as husband by Queen **Theodelinda**, who was endowed with every beauty of soul and body, and who had the church of Saint John in **Monza** built. **Grimoald** was of medium stature, prudent, and expert, as the historian **Paul** <note>Paul the Deacon, author of the History of the Lombards</note> says. **Perctarit** <note>original: "Partharo"</note>, **Clemens**, and **Cunipert** <note>original: "Iuniperto"</note> were very strong warriors and pious; but there was never anyone who equaled **Liutprand** in strength, who was of almost giant-like stature, as no one ever dared to fight with him. 

Of our ancient **Visconti**, **Eliprando**, Lord of Milan, emulating the virtues of his grandfather, the Count of Angera, was a very strong Captain, such that with his unconquered valor he liberated his homeland from the Emperor **Conrad**. **Ottone** was likewise very strong, whereby in the enterprise of Jerusalem he acquired the heraldic device of the **serpent** <term>biscio: the "Biscione" or man-eating serpent, the heraldic symbol of the House of Visconti</term>, with the child in its mouth. **Azzo** had prudence joined together with strength. **Luchino** was humane and kind. **Giovanni**, the Archbishop, was gracious, merciful, and liberal. **Gian Galeazzo** was beautiful of body and of a gracious appearance. **Filippo Maria**, the last, was very large of person and of a terrible face. 

**Francesco Sforza**, the first, was very strong, had a high forehead, and used to wear his hair long <term>zazzera: a long, flowing hairstyle popular in the Renaissance</term> and go clean-shaven. **Galeazzo Maria** was very large and broad in the shoulders; he similarly wore long hair and went clean-shaven. **Gian Galeazzo**, his son, was of a very beautiful facial profile and a no less beautiful body, and had blond hair, as shown by his portrait by the hand of **Foppa** <note>Vincenzo Foppa, an influential Renaissance painter in Milan</note>, engraved on a medal along with those of his father and his uncle **Ludovico**, who was of a dark color, and therefore had the nickname **"The Moor"** <note>il Moro</note>, and wore his hair long, so that it almost covered his eyebrows, as shown by his portrait by the hand of **da Vinci** <note>Leonardo da Vinci</note>, in the refectory of the **Gratie** <note>The church of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, home to the Last Supper</note>, where one also sees the portrait of **Beatrice**, his wife, both kneeling with their children before them, and a Christ on the Cross on the other side. **Massimiliano** had a simple countenance, and **Francesco II**, the last, was hunchbacked, but of a venerable face, with white skin and a black beard, as shown by his portrait painted by **Vecelio** <note>Tiziano Vecellio, known in English as Titian</note>.

# BOOK [634]

And to make a transition to the Barbarians of the East, **Michael Palaiologos** <note>Michael VIII Palaiologos, the Byzantine Emperor who recovered Constantinople</note> the Greek was a most cruel Emperor along with all his descendants, and in particular his son. **Osman**, Emperor of the Turks, and **Orhan** <note>Osman I and Orhan, the first two rulers of the Ottoman Empire</note> were terrible in appearance, and likewise **Murad**; but the latter was even more horrible, so much so that he terrified anyone who dared to look him in the face. **Mehmed the Great**, eighth <note>Mehmed II, the Conqueror of Constantinople; the author's numbering of "eighth" likely includes the disputed rulers of the Ottoman Interregnum</note> Emperor of the Turks and Lord of almost all the Orient, possessed a human face but a most rough appearance; he had squinted eyes that turned back in the corners, especially when he looked at others; he had a high forehead and a prominent back of the head, a nose swollen in the middle and somewhat hooked and <term>aquiline</term> <note>shaped like an eagle's beak</note> over the lip, a thin face and most pale between hollowed cheeks, a robust body that exceeded common size, and besides this, he was much inclined toward hard labors. 

**Selim**, son of Bayezid, was large of body and fierce in look; he had <term>roan</term> <note>original: "rouani"; likely referring to a reddish or speckled hazel color</note> eyes, an aquiline nose, a small mouth, thick lips, a thin chin, a thick nape, and a similarly thick body, yet well-disposed and strong, and he used to go clean-shaven. Finally, **Suleiman**, King of the Turks, was of a large but rough body, of magnanimous appearance, and he used to wear his mustaches long, reaching over his shoulders, but he kept his cheeks and chin shaved. 

Among the Tartars, **Tamerlane** <note>Timur the Lame</note> was large of body and strong beyond measure, a person rough and harsh; some say that he was similar in presence to **Hannibal** of Carthage, and that he had burning eyes full of fury; for which reason he was also most cruel. Among the Armenians, **Uzun Hasan** <note>original: "Viumcaſſano"; leader of the Aq Qoyunlu (White Sheep Turcomans)</note> was terrible, strong, and frightening to all beyond measure, for which reason he was called the "Father of Victories." **Gregory of Serbia**, even though he was of a most wicked nature, nevertheless had great majesty in his appearance, such that he was revered by everyone. 

**John the Great Voivode** <note>John Hunyadi, the Hungarian military leader</note> was large of body and excellent in arms, the worthy father of the famous **Matthias**, King of the Hungarians, who was similar in all his actions to **Julius Caesar** and **Alexander**. Finally, among the modern barbarians, **Hayreddin Barbarossa**, King of Algiers—to set aside other more barbarian nations like the Scythians, Moors, Persians, and Phrygians—had a large belly, sharp, dark, and terrible eyes, very thin eyebrows, brown skin but red and inflamed, a short and gray beard; he had a body of virile proportion and was strong beyond measure, but of rustic customs, and was most expert in the maritime arts.

# SEVENTH.

...[Geoffrey] <note>Likely Geoffrey de Lusignan, known as "Geoffroy à la Grande Dent"</note> of the Great Tooth, so named for a tooth that protruded very far from his mouth; he was the son of Melusina <note>A legendary figure of European folklore, depicted as a woman who is a serpent or fish from the waist down</note>, Lord of Melle, who was half-serpent. He was exceptionally strong and followed Godfrey of Bouillon <note>A leader of the First Crusade and the first ruler of the Kingdom of Jerusalem</note> to Jerusalem. **Mastino della Scala** <note>Also known as Mastino I or II of the Scaliger family of Verona</note>, son of Cane, Lord of Verona, was so valiant and invincible in arms that he brought terror to all of Italy, and especially to the Emperor Louis <note>Louis IV, Holy Roman Emperor</note>. **Antonio de Leyva** and **Gonzalo Fernández** <note>Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba, known as "The Great Captain"</note>, both Generals of Charles V, were portrayed by Titian. **Philibert Octave**, Duke of Savoy, was most religious, good, magnanimous, and possessed excellent physical beauty; his face was so handsome and his expression so cheerful that it seemed a certain splendor flashed from his eyes. 

**Gian Giacomo Trivulzio** "the Great" of Milan was small of body but well-made; he had a broad forehead, a prominent nose, and wore his hair in a long <term>zazzara</term> <note>a thick, bobbed hairstyle popular in the Renaissance</note>, though he went clean-shaven, as seen on a medal by the hand of Caradosso Foppa and in a portrait of him painted by Leonardo [da Vinci]; he possessed singular valor in arms. **Bartolomeo Colleoni** of Bergamo was well-built in body but tall, possessing a graceful yet grave beauty. Throughout his life, he was accustomed to going clean-shaven. He was of the greatest strength and of such speed in running that he surpassed horses, so much so that he was considered another Asahel the Hebrew <note>original: "Afael Hebreo"; a biblical figure described in 2 Samuel 2:18 as being "as fleet of foot as a wild gazelle"</note>. We see his likeness in the bronze equestrian statue in Venice in the Square of San Giovanni e Paolo, made by Andrea Verrocchio, larger than life-size. 

**Niccolò Fortebraccio**, called "Piccinino" <note>Historically, Niccolò Fortebraccio and Niccolò Piccinino were two distinct rival captains; the author here appears to conflate them or use the nickname for Fortebraccio</note>, was small of body and lame, but so valiant that he almost always overcame the enemy. **Galeazzo Gonzaga** was likewise small of body, but of such strength and muscle that he overcame the Frenchman Boucicaut <note>Jean II Le Maingre, a famous French marshal</note> in hand-to-hand combat, even though the latter was of giant-like stature and immeasurable strength. **Charles**, brother of Ludovico Gonzaga, the second Duke of Mantua, had the form of a giant and was of extreme vigor. 

And all these men were equaled in physical strength as well as in valor and virtue by **Luigi Gonzaga**, nicknamed "Rodomonte" <note>named after the fierce character in "Orlando Furioso"</note>, who was supernatural in his insuperable strength. Furthermore, he was endowed with such physical beauty that he had no superior in his time. But the envious Fates <note>The Parcae of Roman mythology who spin and cut the thread of life</note> took his life before his time, although the fame of his virtues will live eternally despite them. 

But surely, I believed from the start—as the poet says—that I could count the stars one by one and enclose all the waters in a small glass when I thought to collect in this chapter all the famous Italian Captains. There have been so many families, some of which flourish more than ever even now, from which infinite illustrious men have emerged: such as the **Aragonese** of Naples, the **Medici** of Florence, the **Este** of Ferrara, the **Manfredi** of Faenza, and the **Bentivoglio** of Bologna...

And Francesco Ferrante, Marquis of Pescara, a son worthy of such a father and grandson of such a grandfather in every heroic virtue; in beauty of body, arrangement of limbs, and gracefulness, he far exceeded his father. I have portrayed him in armor, and Fontana <note>Annibale Fontana, a Milanese sculptor and medalist</note> engraved him on a medal with a reverse showing Hercules stealing the golden apples in the Garden of the Hesperides.

## On the form of monstrous men. Chap. XXVI.

**S**ince it is not possible to assign a certain rule or law for the formation of monsters—in which Nature herself observes no law or rule—I see nothing else that can be said on this subject, unless we gather some examples with which a painter might conform himself, should the need arise either for historical necessity or for the embellishment of a scene. In the time of the Emperor Maurice, in the year 583, it is recorded that a monster was born without arms; from the waist up it had a human form but no eyes, and from the waist down it was like the tail of a fish. In Gascony in the year 945, another monster was born that was perfect from the navel down, like a young girl, but from there upward it was divided...

In the year 1127, during the reign of Emperor Lothair III of Germany, there was born in Spain the perfect body of a boy, but attached to his back was an entire dog, standing upright. In the time of Pope Gelasius <note>Pope Gelasius II, who reigned 1118–1119</note> in the year 1118, a story is told of another who was entirely a pig, except for the face, which was human. In 1495, two creatures were born in Germany who were attached to one another by their foreheads. 

In Rome in the year 1496, it is told that a monster was born with the head of a donkey, while the belly, the breasts, the genitals <term>la natura</term> <note>original: "la natura"; in Renaissance Italian, this term was a common euphemism for the sexual organs</note>, the hand, the right arm, the neck, and the legs had a natural shape; but for the rest, it was covered in scales, with the right foot of an eagle and the other of an ox, and in place of buttocks it had a human face, with a tail beneath in the shape of a serpent’s neck with a snake’s head at the tip, and the left arm in the manner of a stump. 

In Florence in the year 1507, a child was born without arms, with the face of a lion and a horn in the middle of his forehead, with a human body and right leg—except that in the middle of the knee there was an eye—and he had two bat wings, the breasts of a woman, a twisted penis <term>verga</term> <note>original: "verga"; literally "rod," a period term for the male organ</note> that was sharp at the tip, a left leg covered in eagle feathers, and a foot almost like that of a goose.

In Cracow in the year 1543, it is said that a child was born who spoke immediately and lived no longer than three hours; he had the trunk of an elephant, the ears of a donkey, two monkey heads in place of breasts, and two dog heads at the bends of the arms, the hands and feet of a goose, and two other dog heads at the knees, with a very long forked tail. 

And although many other monsters could be remembered and depicted—among them all those that **Leonardo da Vinci** <note>The author refers to Leonardo's famous "grotesque" drawings and anatomical studies conducted in Milan</note> portrayed in Milan, one of which was a very beautiful boy with a penis on his forehead and no nose, and with another face on the back of his head, with a penis under the chin and the ears attached to the testicles (both of which heads had the ears of a faun); the other monster had a penis on the tip of his nose and eyes on the sides of the nose, while for the rest he was likewise a very beautiful boy. Both of these are found in drawings by his own hand, held by the sculptor Francesco Borella.

Regarding the <term>Phanesii</term>—whom <term>Pomponius Mela</term> <note>An early Roman geographer</note> calls the <term>Sarmatians</term> of the Northern Ocean—it is rumored that they have ears so long and wide that they cover their entire bodies. In the innermost part of the East, <term>Pliny</term> writes that there are men without noses and with flat faces; others without an upper lip, and others without ears.

...the aforementioned Thibii, who have two pupils in one eye and an image of a horse in the other; and others in India who are five cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of measurement based on the length of the forearm, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note> in height. But far more numerous and more deformed are the monsters that ingenious Nature is accustomed to produce in the other parts of Africa, to show men what she knows and what she can do. And Saint Augustine says in *The City of God* <note>Original: "città d'Iddio"</note> that although God knew from which parts, with similarity and diversity, He composed the beauty of the universe, He nevertheless also wished to produce many monstrous men in the world. I will not dwell any longer on this subject, because to discuss the diversity of all peoples in detail would be a work not only long but superfluous; given that it is easy to know that the Ethiopians are black and have coarse, curly hair because of the excessive heat; and that the northern peoples are white and have blonde hair; and that in the latter, the humors <note>In pre-modern medicine, bodily fluids like blood or bile that were thought to determine physical traits and health</note> move downward, and in the former, they are pulled upward, so that they [the Ethiopians] remain narrower at the foot and more robust and wide in the hips and shoulders; and finally, that the peoples who inhabit the middle between these are more temperate, even though every kind of man can be found in each nation.

->[continued from previous page]<- ...their private parts with leaves out of shame; and men continued in this way until they began to sacrifice sheep, and then they covered their flesh with the skins of those sheep and other animals. This occurred before Cain killed his brother. And for this reason, with all due respect to Raphael <note>The famous Renaissance painter Raphael Sanzio (1483–1520), known for his biblical frescoes.</note>, those who depict them in cloth or linen garments are in error. It is certain that after Cain fled to India—where he built a city for his daughter Naamah <note>Original: "Neoma." In some traditions, Naamah is the daughter of Lamech, but here associated with the lineage of Cain and credited with the invention of spinning.</note>—she, finding the foliage that produced wool <note>Likely a reference to cotton, which ancient writers often described as "tree wool."</note>, was the first in the world who began to spin it; and at that time, they also began to wear pearls and other jewels, of which India is abundant.

And although this is the truth, others do not hesitate to say that Pallas <note>Pallas Athena or Minerva, the goddess of wisdom and crafts.</note> was the first inventor of spinning and weaving, and that Arachne <note>A mortal weaver who challenged Athena and was transformed into a spider.</note> was the inventor of nets, having provoked the goddess after learning the art. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of "Natural History."</note> also writes that the Egyptians were the first to weave; and Servius <note>A 4th-century grammarian and commentator on Virgil.</note> maintains that the tapestries with which halls are decorated were first seen in the royal hall of Attalus, King of Asia. Thus, Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian.</note> holds that the use of garments was discovered by Minerva, as if he meant to imply that Uranus <note>Original: "Cielo."</note>, Saturn, and the other first gods went naked, which is not true.

It is quite believable that the Chaldeans, the Egyptians, and other peoples of those parts took the example of dressing themselves in garments of skin, which were used not only by the sons of the first father [Adam], but by Adam himself. After the Deluge <note>The Great Flood.</note>, the Egyptian Hercules—son of Osiris and born of Ham, according to Diodorus—used these; he wore a lion's skin as armor and carried a club in his hand, whereas the Greek Hercules dressed in iron [armor]. And therefore, one must be careful how these different versions of Hercules are painted and dressed, so that one is not mistaken for the other, as has been done by some.

Regarding the people of the Balearic Islands, there is no doubt that they were the discoverers of that garment called the <term>laticlavius</term> <note>A tunic with a broad purple stripe worn by Roman senators.</note>, which Julius Caesar (according to Tranquillus <note>Suetonius, whose full name was Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, author of "The Twelve Caesars."</note>) wore with a fringe reaching down to his hands. Of the making of brocade—that is, weaving with gold—Pliny writes that King Attalus was the author; because before him, no king is found to have used garments of gold. Similarly, before the Phrygians, embroidery was not in use by anyone, nor any other manner of foliage and decorative borders; this having been their invention, which is why they were called <term>fregioni</term> <note>The author links the Italian "fregio" (frieze/border) to the "Phrygians."</note>. 

That garment which we commonly call a tunic was discovered by Tanaquil <note>The wife of Tarquinius Priscus, the fifth king of Rome, traditionally associated with feminine virtues and weaving.</note>. The military cloak of the Greeks, and that mantle which covers the waist such as the one worn by Joseph and the other Hebrews, was an invention of those same Hebrews. The weaving of garments of various colors, such as iridescent <note>Original: "cangianti."</note> fabrics and the like, originated with the Babylonians. The use of silk was discovered by the Seres <note>The "Seres" was the ancient Greek and Roman name for the people of northwestern China, known for silk production.</note>; and the garment called the *Bassarea* which, according to some, extends down to the knee—
