# SEVENTH #

->...[wreath] of Bacchus.<- But since there are infinite manners of clothing, which multiply more and more every day—not so much for utility as for pleasure and pomp—I will pass over them in silence. I will mention only that in costumes, as in weapons, one must exercise the most diligent care in the histories <note>In this context, "histories" refers to narrative paintings depicting historical, biblical, or mythological scenes.</note> that are represented. For it is these things that distinguish the Turk from the Indian, and the German from the Italian. In this matter, even excellent painters have sometimes erred, disagreeing among themselves in this part of representing the same subject, solely because they lacked knowledge of history. 

This was a mistake never committed by the ancients, who always expressed things truthfully and according to history; thus, in their works, one saw figures who, though varied with different ornaments and whims, were always consistent in their weapons and bearing. Witnesses to this are their statues of Hercules, Minerva, Jupiter, the Amazons, Venus, and other famous figures, which—because of this consistency of costume and weaponry—were immediately recognized one from another, even if the artistic style differed, and were therefore held in such high esteem. This is further proven by many ancient relics, and especially regarding costumes, by Trajan’s Column <note>A Roman triumphal column in Rome that depicts the emperor Trajan's victory in the Dacian Wars; it is a primary source for Roman military dress.</note> and many triumphal arches. 

But in our times, it is indeed true that in a battle one will sometimes see soldiers armed in the Roman fashion standing in for Germans, and Barbarians or modern men standing in for ancients, with similar such metamorphoses of men and nations. To avoid stumbling into such improprieties, one must be careful to note not only what people are to be painted—giving them their appropriate costume—but also at what time the history or fable one wishes to represent occurred. For the world has always been changing, and customs and manners continue to change; it is certain that the ancient Romans went about in different dress than that used by moderns, and the Spaniards of our time differ from those ancients who, clothed in bark <note>Original: "scorze," referring to tree bark or rough skins used as primitive clothing.</note>, lay upon the stones, eating roots to the murmur of the waters. 

Furthermore, one must have regard for the variety of status, rank, and the religions of each nation. For if the priests of a single nation differ among themselves in habit, how much more differently should one represent the Hebrew Aaron from the <term>Gymnosophists</term> <note>Gymnosophists: Meaning "naked philosophers," these were ancient Indian ascetics known for their wisdom and lack of clothing.</note> of Meroe <note>An ancient city on the Nile in modern-day Sudan.</note>, or from the <term>Salian Priests</term> <note>Salian Priests: The "leaping priests" of Mars in Rome, who performed ritual dances in armor.</note> who, fully armed, leaped around the Goddess Rhea, or from the Pope today? Likewise, the modern Imperial habit is not like the ancient one, nor is that of Germany <note>Original: "Lamagna," an archaic Italian term for "Allemagna" or Germany.</note> like that of Constantinople. 

Therefore, I have wished to note here some things regarding the form of costumes and weapons, beginning with the Romans, and first with the <term>velites</term> <note>Velites: A class of light infantry in the Roman army who typically fought in the vanguard.</note>, under which name were understood the <term>Javelin-throwers</term> <note>Original: "Iaculatori."</note> and the <term>Archers</term>, who at every slight movement would carry out raids and skir-

According to **Polybius**, these men for the most part had their heads protected by a strapped <term>large helmet</term> <note>original: "celatone", a type of open-faced helmet or sallet</note>, and on the left arm to cover and defend themselves, a wide <term>round shield</term> <note>original: "rotella"</note> along with a weapon called a <term>javelin</term> <note>original: "pilo", referring to the Roman pilum</note> three and a half feet long, similar to a leopard <note>original: "pardo". This is likely a printer's error for "dardo" (dart/javelin), as comparing a javelin to a leopard is atypical for this context</note>, and on the right side a <term>dagger</term> <note>original: "daga"</note> one arm’s length long. But in the time of **Trajan**, **Hadrian**, and **Antoninus Pius**, some were armed with simple <term>breastplates</term> <note>original: "corsaletti"</note>, some of which were made of <term>scales</term> <note>original: "scaglie"</note> similar to those of the archers; and some, namely the <term>slingers</term> <note>original: "fonditori"</note>, were simply covered by their own garments with cloaks over them, in which they carried the stones they hurled at the enemy. The foot archers wore the same <term>helmet</term> <note>original: "celata"</note>, with the <term>quiver</term> <note>original: "faretra"</note> hanging behind from a belt that went from the left shoulder under the right arm, and a <term>scaled breastplate</term>, at the bottom of which they had a simple mantle reaching the knees, with the bow and arrow in hand. Those who followed the archers were, by age, the most robust and were covered in heavy armor: the head with a <term>large helmet</term> that covered them in front down to the eyes and in back down to the shoulders; the chest with a long <term>cuirass</term> <note>original: "corazzina"</note> that hung down to the knees with its skirts; the arms with <term>vambraces</term> <note>original: "bracciali"</note>, and the legs with <term>short boots</term> <note>original: "stiualetti"</note>, with a shield four feet high and half as wide, or a little more, rimmed with iron. Furthermore, they had a sword belted at the left hip and a dagger on the right, and in their hands they held darts and <term>spears</term> <note>original: "spiedi"</note> with two wings <note>referring to cross-guards or lugs on the spearhead</note> about five feet long, all tipped with iron. What the legionary looked like can be seen in **Mainz** on an ancient marble, and in another found in **Narbonne**, as portrayed by **Guillaume du Choul** <note>A 16th-century French antiquarian whose works on Roman military and religious life were highly influential for artists</note>. The **Standard-bearers** <note>original: "Alfieri"</note> carried different insignias, for some had the image of the Prince portrayed there, and these were called <term>image-bearers</term> <note>original: "imaginiferi"</note> by the **Latins**; others a staff with a hand at the top as a sign of concord; others a silver eagle atop another staff, who were called <term>eagle-bearers</term> <note>original: "Aquiliferi"</note>; and others a dragon with a silver head, who were similarly called <term>dragon-bearers</term> <note>original: "Dragoniferi" or "Dragonarij"</note>, and all the rest of the standard was made of <term>sendal</term> <note>original: "zendale", a thin, light silk fabric</note>. The <term>imperial standard</term> <note>original: "labro", a variation of "labaro" or "labarum"</note> that was carried when the Emperor was in the field was an insignia of purple color, adorned all around with gold fringe and precious stones. The men-at-arms on horseback were armed with a <term>great lance</term> in the right hand and a large shield in the left, and covered with a shirt of mail down to the knees with <term>vambraces</term>, iron gauntlets, <term>greaves</term> <note>original: "schinieri"</note>, and strapped <term>helmets</term> with a large plume. The horses were armed with plates of iron joined together or with mail, like the cuirasses and jacks of times past. ...[cinched] below the breasts which reached down to the feet, and then they covered the chest with another cloth cinched at the neck, which fell down to the navel. Nor did the Greeks lack their own particular manners and fashions of dress and arms. For as can be gathered from countless passages of Homer’s *Iliad*, the soldiers used to arm themselves with <term>breastplates</term> <note>original: "corazze"</note>, with <term>greaves</term> <note>original: "schinieri", armor for the shins</note>, with swords, with shields, and with the <term>large helmet</term> <note>original: "celatone"</note> adorned with massive plumes, and with spears. And this style of red and black plumes—and others atop the helmets a foot and a half high—was also used by the ancient Romans; for they made the soldier look larger, more honorable in appearance, and more terrifying to the enemy. Besides this, some have written that the Greeks, and especially the Macedonians, carried <term>pavises</term> <note>original: "paluesi", large shields used to create a defensive wall</note> in their phalanxes, which were certain large, semi-circular shields later used by the Romans to carry their baggage when they were crossing a river by wading; and furthermore, they carried certain long spears eighteen feet in length. The <term>men-at-arms</term> <note>heavy cavalry</note> on horseback did not use breastplates, but fought in a <term>tunic</term> <note>original: "saglio", a military overgarment</note>, with spears, darts, and shields made of ox-hide. Dio, in his *Life of Caracalla*, writes that in the times of Alexander the Great the phalanx consisted of sixteen thousand men who used helmets of raw ox-hide, small <term>linen breastplates</term> <note>original: "corazzine... di lino", likely referring to the linothorax</note> made of three layers, brass shields, long pikes, the <term>javelin</term> <note>original: "chiauerina"</note>, and the short sword. <insert>Heliodorus</insert> <note>Heliodorus of Emesa, author of the ancient Greek novel "Aethiopica"</note>, in depicting the companions of Theagenes of Thessaly, described them thus: with shoes tied with small purple straps and laced above the heels, wearing a white <term>surcoat</term> cinched at the chest with a gold belt decorated at the edges with a black band; and on the horses he placed <term>bards</term> <note>horse armor</note>, the headpiece, and other ornaments of silver and gold in <term>livery</term> <note>uniform colors</note> with the riders, who likewise had their garments patterned in the same way. And in depicting Theagenes, he represents him on horseback well-armed, brandishing an ash spear, with a purple surcoat and a belt where Pallas Athena could be seen, who had made a shield for her chest from the head of Medusa. Shortly thereafter, the same Heliodorus describes <insert>Charicleia</insert> <note>The text reads "Carithia," likely a transcription error for Charicleia, the heroine of Heliodorus's novel</note>, a priestess of Diana, who was upon a seat open on all sides placed atop a white wagon drawn by two oxen, dressed in a purple robe that extended to her feet, all decorated with gold stripes, with a belt made in the form of two serpents whose tails were entwined, and whose heads came up under her breasts, tied together with a coiled lace; they hung in such a way that the excess of the binding dangled from both sides. These were made entirely of gold but covered with a dark sky-blue color up to the head, so that against the yellow of the gold they might show the roughness and shifting appearance of their scales.

The braids, he says, were neither entirely gathered nor entirely loose; but the greater part, that is, what hangs behind at the nape of the neck, went wandering over the ears and the shoulders, while that which hangs toward the forehead was encircled with tender laurel branches. Regarding the dress of the Persians, the same Heliodorus <note>Heliodorus of Emesa, author of the ancient Greek novel "Aethiopica" or "The Ethiopian Story," often cited for his vivid descriptions.</note>, after he has described the court and the Magi, depicts Queen Arsace seated on a high throne, adorned in a garment of purple and gold. She had a haughty and proud look because of the rich necklaces that encircled her neck, and because of the value of the most sumptuous headdress that covered her head, which could be removed without any difficulty—contrary to what the wives of the Persian Emperors use now <note>The author compares the ancient Persian styles to the "modern" Safavid Persian fashions of his own era.</note>, who, burdened with rolls of fabric and gems and a thousand windings of hair, cannot take them off their heads without unwinding them. I am quite pleased, in these modern Persian women, by that first garment which encircles their bare limbs with beautiful grace, so charmingly adorned with jewels and precious stones.

But returning to the ancients, Quintus Curtius <note>A Roman historian known for his biography of Alexander the Great.</note> relates that the <term>men-at-arms</term> <note>original: "huomini d’arme", referring here to heavy cavalry</note> of Persia had horses armored with plates of iron. And in the *Ethiopian Histories* one reads that each of them put on a <term>helmet</term> <note>original: "celata"</note> made of a single stone, shaped so that it resembled a human face; and with this, he covered everything from the top of the head down to the nape of the neck, except for the eyes. In his right hand he then carried a great spear, holding the reins with the other, and a sword at his side. For the rest, he was armed with a <term>breastplate</term> <note>original: "corazza"</note>, protecting not only the shoulders but indeed the entire body. The breastplate was constructed in this manner: some plates of copper or iron were drawn out into a square shape, a palm's width in every direction, and placed one beside the other down to the ends of the ribs. They were arranged so that the one above overlapped the one below with its bottom edge and side, and so on progressively. Where the joints met, some small hooks like blades were sewn around, with which a garment covered in <term>fish-like scales</term> <note>original: "scaglie di pesce"</note> was attached, encircling and girding the whole body. This garment had sleeves, and from the nape of the neck it stopped above the knees, necessarily open at the thighs toward that part which rested upon the shoulders of the horse.

## BOOK 2

<page-num>646</page-num>

**Greaves** pulled from the tops of the feet up to the knees were joined with the **breastplate**, and with those they bound **iron shoes**. In a similar manner, they also armored the horse, covering its head entirely with an **iron headpiece** <note>Also known as a chanfron</note>, and attaching a cover of **woven iron** from the shoulders to the belly on both sides. The most ancient **Egyptians** used certain breastplates made of **linen cords** as armor, like one that is still shown in Rhodes in the temple of Minerva, which belonged to the very ancient **King Amasis** <note>Amasis II was a pharaoh of the 26th Dynasty; Herodotus also mentions his famous linen corselets</note>. 

The **Ethiopians**, experts in the art of archery and stone-throwing, were accustomed to wearing certain wraps twisted around their heads in their battles, and they would stick arrows into them so that the sharp points poked out like so many rays; from there, as if from a quiver, they easily drew them out while jumping in a **satiric manner** <note>original: "maniera Satirica" — referring to the wild, energetic dancing associated with Satyrs in mythology</note>, crowned with arrows and with their bodies naked against the enemy. Their arrows were made from the **backbones of dragons** <note>In the 16th century, "dragons" often referred to large reptiles or serpents, whose vertebrae or ribs could be sharpened</note>, made sharp at one end. 

And these methods were also used by the **Troglodytes**, the **Blemmyes**, the **Eseri**, and in short, almost all of **Scythia**. Hence we read that the **Amazons** practiced nothing other than the shooting of **crossbows** and bows, and the throwing of darts and stones; but they dressed in thin robes, leaving the right breast exposed; and in battle they used **leather breastplates**, and also certain covers made of **fish scales**; nor is it found that they ever used a sword or spear. 

The **Parthians** wore leggings full of folds down to the tops of the feet, and there they tightened them like a purse with shoes laced in various ways along and across the instep. They then wore a **long tunic** <note>original: "saione"</note> down to the knees, and over it a military garment with various fringes tied at the loins over the right or left shoulder with a lace or a medal; and they went about with their bodies and legs cinched below the knees, with a small hood on their heads. The dress of the **Armenians**, and especially their Kings, was not dissimilar to these. 

The ancient **Goths**, instead of breastplates and corselets, armed themselves with quilted cotton and wool garments that they called <term>taiacomache</term> <note>A corruption of "thoracomachus," a padded garment worn under armor or as light armor itself</note>, which the Romans likewise used after the loss of the Empire, as did all the Italians, accompanied by very large iron crossbows, until the **harquebus** <note>A heavy portable matchlock gun, the invention of which revolutionized warfare and rendered such quilted armor obsolete</note> was found. 

The **Huns**, at the time of **Attila**—who bore the eagle and also the crowned goshawk as his ensign—armed themselves with corselets and breastplates, bows and quivers; others carried a shield, spear, and scimitar; others covered themselves in leather, and others in iron, girding themselves with a long sword and a dagger. Furthermore, they dressed in skins and wore long beards and hair, which increased the ferocity and horror of their appearance, so that with...

...with that alone they struck terror into their enemies. As a particular insignia they had the **crowned Eagle**. The **Suebi**, men of very large stature, wore no other clothes than certain skins so small that they revealed a good part of their naked bodies. The ancient **Germans**, a few years after Christ, used the sword little in battle, but made much use of certain somewhat long spears called <term>frameae</term> <note>original: "framee"; a Germanic spear described by Tacitus as having a short, narrow iron head</note> with a small iron point. The soldier on horseback was armed with a **shield**, and the infantryman threw **darts**, of which each carried a great number with him; he fought naked or covered by a brief jacket. Their shields were distinguished by colors they chose according to their own fashion, and few used breastplates, and hardly one or two a helmet or a visor.

Among the ancient **Gauls**, at the time when Mercury was worshipped, the common folk dressed in **skirts**; and instead of a tunic, they wore a short garment which barely covered half their buttocks, made of coarse wool but with long hair, from which they wove shaggy **white mantles**. These peoples had long, white bodies, and they all armed themselves in the same fashion, carrying at their side a long sword, and a shield equally long, and a spear. They also used bows, and sometimes slings and **maces**, and when returning from war, they were accustomed to hang the heads of the slain from the necks of their horses.

The old **Scots** did not differ in dress from the **Irish**; for both wore a **white cloak** on top, and a **skirt** below, both dyed in a **saffron color**. They went with naked legs up to the knees, using no other weapons than the bow and arrows, a fairly long and wide sword, and a dagger that had a cutting edge on only one side. The **Turks**, both women and men, wear wide clothes, long down to the feet, so that in no movement they might need to make do they reveal their private parts.

But whoever desires to fully know the clothing and the styles of arms of other peoples—such as the **Cimbri**, the **Goths**, the **Alans**, and similar barbarian nations—should read the book titled <note>original: "de gentium aliquot Migrationibus"</note> *On the Migrations of Certain Peoples* <note>A famous 1555 work by Wolfgang Lazius detailing the movements and customs of European tribes</note>, in which they will see their bizarre weapons and clothing illustrated; and let them consult the histories, where they will be fully satisfied.

I will not extend myself further on this subject except to describe the **priestly habit of Aaron** made by **Bezalel** <note>The master craftsman appointed by God to build the Tabernacle and its furnishings in the Book of Exodus</note>, which, being a most notable thing, it seems to me should not be omitted in any way. Now, the first garment of such a habit was primarily all of turquoise color, purple, and **twisted fine linen** <note>original: "bisso ritorto"; *byssus* was a rare, costly fabric often called "sea silk"</note>. The <term>ephod</term> <note>original: "superumerale"; a vestment worn over the shoulders by Jewish high priests</note> was similar in form to the **cope** <note>original: "piuiale"; a long liturgical mantle worn by Catholic clergy</note> of the Popes, woven of gold, turquoise, purple, crimson, and twisted fine linen in embroidery work, with gold foliage; and from the...

## *On the form of temples, & other buildings. Chapter XXVIII.*

**S**ince the painter must represent the histories of all parts of the world, and of all ages; who does not see that he must proceed with infinite care, to represent them appropriately, with the circumstances that suit them regarding the manners and customs of 그country, and of 그age, in which the history he represents occurred; and so that he does not fall, as many have done, into such errors as imagining buildings in times when they were not yet built, or Roman-style buildings in barbarian places, and similar improprieties. Therefore, I have thought to briefly outline a sketch of the manner of buildings, which will open our understanding so that we may guard against such errors. In which, to begin from a bit further back, we must recall to memory that in the earliest times the houses inhabited by men were those of nature, namely: caves, ravines, dens, and woods. And afterwards, as <term>Vitruvius</term> <note>original: "Vittruuio"; Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman architect whose ten-volume work became the foundational text for Renaissance architecture</note> says, finding the comfort of life in fire, they began to chase away the cold by making coverings of leaves, digging under mountains, and making dens by hand, as did the <term>Troglodytes</term> <note>literally "hole-dwellers"; ancient peoples reported by Greek historians to live in caves</note>, and some peoples of <term>Libya</term> near the <term>Ethiopians</term>, as <term>Strabo</term> <note>ancient Greek geographer</note> relates. Shortly thereafter, they began with woven wicker and mud to make roofs and houses, of which <term>Pliny</term> and <term>Gellius</term> <note>Aulus Gellius, a Roman author</note> make <term>Toxius</term> <note>original: "Toſio"; a mythological figure credited by Pliny the Elder with inventing mud-brick construction</note>, the ninth son of Heaven, the author; taking the example from the swallows in the making of their nests. Then followed the making of walls with forked posts, mud, and rods interspersed with roofs of reeds and branches, to defend themselves from rain and heat. And of this manner of dwellings, and others like them, were those of the people before the <term>flood</term> <note>original: "diluuio"; the Biblical Great Flood</note>, speaking generally. After the flood, the first <term>Gauls</term> before <term>Marcomir</term> <note>a legendary early king of the Franks</note> inhabited that country, and likewise the <term>Portuguese</term>, the <term>Phrygians</term>, and the first <term>Germans</term> also retained the same way of building. It is still retained by many of them, especially by the common <term>Swabians</term> and <term>Saxons</term>, although the houses of the nobles are built of boards and bricks with crossbeams of timber. This style is much used in <term>Paris</term>, and was used in <term>Milan</term> in the old days, indeed throughout all <term>Lombardy</term> and the rest of Italy, such usage having come from the <term>Goths</term> and other Barbarians after architecture departed from Italy along with the Empire. Wherefore it happened at those times that all the churches and houses were seen made without Greek or Roman design, and without any architectural order described by Vitruvius and observed by the ancients. But by the singular favor of God afterward, who wished to embellish the world, and adorn—

...to adorn his temples, the fog that had not allowed the light of the **good arts** to be seen was cleared from the eyes of mortals in the times of our grandfathers; and **Bramante** <note>Donato Bramante (1444–1514), a key architect of the High Renaissance who designed the initial plans for St. Peter's Basilica</note> was born, who with his admirable intellect revived architecture, encouraged also by the magnificence and liberality of **Francesco Sforza**, first Duke of Milan. And successively many other painters, and particularly **Michelangelo**, have expanded and simplified it hand by hand, in such a way that by now even stone-cutters make themselves architects: although the praise of invention and the beauty of the **capricci** <note>artistic "whims" or imaginative, playful inventions that depart from strict rules</note> remains nevertheless with the painters and sculptors; these [stone-cutter] people being without skills in <term>disegno</term> <note>a term encompassing both drawing and the intellectual concept behind a work of art</note>, and so ignorant that they do not see a painting unless they look at a brick. 

Now returning to the subject, I say that besides the nations already named, many others still use those primitive houses, especially in villages. Indeed, there are also people who wander in the open without houses in wagons, like the **Scythians**, the **Normans**, the **Saracens** in Africa who are called **Savages** <note>original: "Saluatici"</note>, and the **Tartars**, who are seen all day wandering through the countryside upon wagons arranged like tents and pavilions, to protect themselves from the cold and the sun. 

Thus, growing from time to time and varying the custom of building, architecture was born and had its beginning among the ancients, which teaches us the way to build with order; as can be clearly seen in the "Tree of Architecture," which will be discussed further below. This art, according to some among whom is **Diodorus** <note>Diodorus Siculus, a 1st-century BCE Greek historian</note>, was first discovered by **Pallas** <note>Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom and crafts</note>, but **Josephus** <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> maintains—and it is certainly more likely—that it was **Cain**, the first son of **Adam**, who, instructed in all the arts and sciences of the world by his father, before all others built the city of **Enoch** <note>original: "Enochia"</note> in India; after whom **Tubal**, together with his brother, sons of **Lamech**, made the columns on which they wrote the prophecies they had heard and the observations of the stars. 

Nor is it to be said that such buildings were not constructed with art and architecture. For Adam, being perfectly endowed by God with all the sciences, taught them to his sons, and they showed them to others: and it is rather to be concluded that the ancients understood this art better than those who came after, being <note>as the latter are</note> further removed from those first masters who were instructed and filled with every science. Successively **Nimrod** built the first tower in **Babylon**, which was later surrounded by very high and thick walls by **Semiramis**, with gates of metal; although regarding the length of the circuit of these walls there is no certain or determined opinion, as the **Sicilian** <note>Diodorus Siculus</note>, **Pliny**, **Paulus Orosius**, and other writers have spoken of it differently; and after him **Sostratos** the architect built another in

### SEVENTH BOOK ###

-> **SEVENTH** <-

Egypt, on the Island of Pharos, from which the Kings of Egypt used to be called Pharaohs. **Jabal** <note>original: "Joboal"; the biblical figure described in Genesis as the father of those who live in tents</note> taught how to make tents; **Solomon** afterwards among the Hebrews had the first temple constructed, which surpassed the most ancient ones, and all those yet to be made, in beauty, magnificence, and expense. Among other peoples, **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman author of 'De architectura'</note> writes that **Pythius** was the first to build a temple to Minerva in **Priene** <note>original: "Pirene"; an ancient Greek city in Ionia</note>. The first wells were dug in Argos by the daughters of **Danaus**. Later, labyrinths were invented with uncertain and deceptive paths, through which a man, once entered, immediately became lost. There were four primary ones: one in Egypt, which **Tithoes** <note>likely referring to Amenemhat III</note> built before the others according to **Pliny**; another was made by **Daedalus** in Crete; the third was built by **Phimilo** in Rhodes and **Theodorus** in Lemnos; and the fourth was constructed in Italy by **Porsenna**, King of the Tuscans, with dressed stones for his own tomb.

**Cheops** <note>original: "Chemi"</note>, King of Egypt, was the inventor of pyramids for use as tombs; he had one built between Memphis and Heliopolis <note>original: "Delfo"</note> of such immeasurable size that 360,000 men could not bring it to completion in less than twenty years. After this, his brother **Khafre** <note>original: "Cabreo"</note> made another, and the third was made by **Menkaure** <note>original: "Micerino"</note>. From this arose the custom of making tombs, among which was the much-celebrated one in Caria for **Mausolus**, commissioned by his wife. It was built upon 36 columns by four principal sculptors, each of whom completed one part, named **Scopas**, **Bryaxis**, **Timotheus**, and **Leochares**; and by a fifth named **Pythius**, a pyramid was made for him with a chariot and four horses on top. Among the Romans, there is the superb **Mole of Hadrian** on the Tiber, which is now called **Castel Sant'Angelo**.

It is indeed true that this custom of tombs was not universal among all peoples. For one reads that the **Massagetae** ate their dead, and the **Tibarini** hanged them, and others burned them and placed the ashes in urns, which they located sometimes high up—as are the ashes of **Caesar**, atop the **Vatican Obelisk** <note>original: "Guglia di Santo Pietro"; in the author's time, the bronze sphere atop the obelisk was believed to contain the ashes of Julius Caesar</note>—and sometimes underground.

But to come to the parts of architecture—so that what I have touched upon scattered in many places throughout this work may be more easily understood—it must be considered that the ancients derived this art from two things: from **practice** <note>original: "fabrica"; the manual act of building</note> and from **theory** <note>original: "discorso"; the intellectual reasoning or ratiocination</note>. These two they drew from eleven sciences: letters, drawing, geometry, perspective, arithmetic, history, philosophy, music, medicine, law, and astrology, of which Vitruvius speaks amply. Then I shall divide it into two parts, namely, into accidental and substantial parts. The accidental ones are six, some of which spread into other parts, as is clearly seen in the [genealogical] tree. The substantial parts are three: namely, <term>gnomonica</term> <note>the art of making sundials and measuring time by shadows</note>, <term>machinatione</term> <note>the invention and use of machines for construction and war</note>, and <term>edificatione</term> <note>the actual practice of constructing buildings</note>.

...distinction: In the first is contained the art of making **clocks** <note>original: "horologi"</note> and similar things, which **Janello Torriano** of Cremona possessed perfectly, as he well demonstrated in the stupendous clock that he gave to the Emperor **Charles V**. In the second is contained **lifting** <term>levatoria: machines for raising heavy weights</term>, **hauling** <term>trattoria: machines for pulling or transporting loads</term>, **pneumatics** <term>spiritale: machines powered by air or steam</term>, and all the machines used both for raising water and for offense and defense. Among the ancients, the greatest in these fields were **Archimedes**, **Philon**, **Dinocrates**, and **Polybius**. Among the moderns are the aforementioned **Janello**, **Galeazzo Alessi**, **Pellegrino Tibaldi** <note>original: "Pelegrino de' Pelegrini"</note>, **Giovan Battista Clariccio**, and **Giovan Domenico Lonati**; and among writers, **Leonardo da Vinci**, **Cardano**, **Agricola**, and **Orlandi**.

The third part contains **organs**, **hydraulic machines**, machines moved by **fire**, fountains, pneumatic organs, and machines driven by the force of air—such as those of **Ctesibius** <note>original: "Tesibio"; an ancient Greek inventor in Alexandria</note>—and others without air, such as **water screws** <note>original: "coclee"</note> and pumps. Finally, it includes military instruments: among the ancients, **catapults**, **scorpions**, **tortoises**, **rams**, **ballistae**, and the like; and among the moderns, **artillery** and **muskets**.

The third substantial branch, called **building** <note>original: "edificatione"</note>, is divided into **private** and **public**. Private building is of two types: **urban**, which includes, for example, rooms, libraries, and bedchambers; and **rustic**, which includes presses, mangers, mills, and similar structures. **Leonardo da Vinci** drew thirty pages of these in light and shadow, which have come into the hands of **Ambrogio Figino** <note>Giovan Ambrogio Figino, a Milanese painter who owned several of Leonardo's notebooks</note>. In these drawings, one sees various mills that grind with water and others without, all different from one another. Besides Leonardo, **Civerchio** and **Butinone** also drew them, and their works were given by **Gaudenzio** to **Cesare Cesariano**, the commentator on **Vitruvius**.

Public building consists of three types: **defense**, **utility**, and **religion**. The first teaches us to make towers, walls, fortresses, **cavaliers** <term>cavalieri: raised platforms within a fortification for positioning cannons</term>, and similar structures. In this field, those worthy of memory are **Albrecht Dürer**, **Giovan Maria Olgiato**, Captain **Jacopo Fusti** (called **il Scarioto**), **San Martino**, **Baldassarre Lanci**, **Vitelli da Città di Castello**, **Cavalier Paciotto**, **Rocco Guerrini**, **il Fratino da Morcò**, **Soldati**, and **Gabrio Busca**. 

The second type <note>utility</note> contains **plazas**, **porticos**, and **baths** <note>original: "therme"</note>. Many of these in Rome were named after those who had them built, such as the baths of **Agrippa**, **Domitian**, **Antoninus**, **Alexander**, **Gordian**, **Septimius**, **Diocletian**, **Aurelian**, **Constantine**, and **Novatian**, along with those of **Titus Vespasian**. Additionally, it includes sea ports, forums, **xysti** <term>xisti: covered walkways or garden galleries used by the ancients for exercise</term>, gymnasiums, senates, treasuries, basilicas, prisons, and **stage scenery** <note>original: "scene"</note> for comedy, tragedy, and satire. It also covers **theaters** and **amphitheaters**, such as the one in Verona called the **Arena**, built in rustic masonry; and that other one in the middle of Rome <note>The Colosseum</note> begun by **Vespasian** and finished by his son **Titus**.

...son <note>original: "figliuolo"; likely a metaphorical reference to a smaller or derivative structure</note> which was called the **Colosseum**, and that which is in **Pula**, a city of **Dalmatia**. Finally, for the third and last part, he has taught architecture—and teaches the whole world—how to make temples sacred to the Gods. The designs <note>original: "aspetti"</note> of these were named by the ancients, as **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman author of "De Architectura," the foundational text for Renaissance building</note> says, partly by their columns and partly by their **intercolumniation** <term>intercolumniation: the specific distance or spacing between two adjacent columns</term>. 

Those which were named by their columns are seven: 
1. The first is called **In antis** <note>original: "Antis"</note>, which is formed within the pilasters, such as the Temple of the Three Fortunes, one of which was near the **Colline Gate**. 
2. The second is called **Prostyle**, which was observed on the **Tiber Island** in the Temple of **Jupiter** and of **Faunus**. 
3. The third is called **Amphiprostyle**. 
4. The fourth is **Peripteral**, of which the ancients gave an example in the portico of Metellus for **Jupiter Stator**, and the **Marian** Temple of Honor and Virtue. 
5. The fifth is named **Pseudodipteral** <term>Pseudodipteral: a temple that appears to have a double row of columns, but the inner row is omitted to create a wider porch</term>, as was the Temple of **Diana** at **Magnesia**, built by **Hermogenes of Alabanda**, and the Temple of **Apollo** built by **Mnestrus**. 
6. The sixth is called **Dipteral**, which **Theosiphontes** <note>original: "Tesifonte"; likely referring to Chersiphron, the architect of the Temple of Artemis</note> followed in the **Ionic** Temple of **Diana at Ephesus**, and the Romans in the **Doric** Temple of **Quirinus**. 
7. The seventh is called **Hypaethral** <note>original: "Hipetros"; a temple open to the sky</note>, which was observed in **Athens** in the Temple of **Olympian Zeus**. 

The designs, or manners as we might call them, named by the spacing of the columns are five, as **Vitruvius** recites in the third book: **Pycnostyle**, **Systyle**, **Diastyle**, **Araeostyle**, and **Eustyle** <note>These terms range from "Pycnostyle" (very tight spacing) to "Eustyle" (the spacing Vitruvius considered most beautiful and functional)</note>. 
- Of the first manner was the Temple of the **Divine Julius**, and the Temple of **Venus** in the **Forum of Caesar**. 
- Of the second, the Temple of **Equestrian Fortune**. 
- Of the third, the Temple of **Apollo** and of **Diana**. 
- Of the fourth, the Temple of **Ceres** and of **Hercules** in the **Circus Maximus**, and the **Pompeian Capitol**. 
- And of the fifth, the Temple of **Father Bacchus** in **Teos** in Asia; **Hermogenes** was the inventor of this manner (which is more reasonable than the others) and of the **Pseudodipteral** design.

Now, all these types of temples are made each with their proper **orders**, by which generally all approved buildings and palaces are constructed with reason; and these are five, named **Tuscan**, **Doric**, **Ionic**, **Corinthian**, and **Composite**. Each of them consists particularly of a **pedestal**, **base**, **columns**, **capitals**, **architraves**, **friezes**, and **cornices**, with various diversities of members and ornaments, as was said in the book on proportion. While I have mentioned only some who have been excellent in modern times in this final part of architecture regarding construction, it is not because there have not been many others worthy of being celebrated by a louder trumpet than mine. But because it is not my purpose to go on discussing illustrious craftsmen and singing their praises, I have passed over them in silence; all the more so since this has already been done successfully by **Giorgio** <insert>Vasari</insert>...

<page-num>654</page-num>
<header>BOOK</header>

**Vasari**, in his *Lives of the Painters, Sculptors, and Architects*, will satisfy curious readers more fully in my place regarding this matter. One must know that these **orders** were derived from the measurements of the human body, as **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman authority on architecture</note> states in the first chapter of the third book. Hence we read that **Dorus**, son of **Hellen** and **Orseis** <note>original: "Optice"; likely a variant of Orseis, the mythical nymph</note>, who reigned in **Achaia** and the **Peloponnese**, built the **Temple of Juno** in **Argos** using the first order, which he named **Doric** after himself. Much later, in imitation of that, the **Ionians** built the **Temple of Panionian Apollo**. 

But when they came to the columns, they found no established symmetry in those made by **Dorus**. Seeking a method by which they could make them strong enough to bear the weight and beautiful to look at, they measured the footprint of a man. Taking that thickness—which they used for the base of the lower shaft—they raised the column to a height six times that measure, including the capital. Thus, the **Doric column** and its proportions began among the **Greeks**, modeled after the human body. 

However, although many hold this view, the use of this order was found long before the **Greeks**. **Leon Battista Alberti** <note>A foundational Renaissance architect and theorist</note> writes in the seventh book of his *On Architecture* that the capitals later called **Doric** by the **Greeks** had been in use among the ancients for a long time; he adds that these same people were the inventors of statues. 

Similarly, the **Ionians**, building a temple to **Diana**, drew a new form and manner of column from the same principles, but with a feminine slenderness. They made its thickness one-eighth of its height and adorned it with many qualities suited to a woman. This was called the **Ionic** order after them by those who, much later and with greater refinement, set the height of the **Doric** at seven diameters and the **Ionic** at eight and a half. 

The final order found by the **Greeks**, called **Corinthian**, was formed in imitation of maidenly slenderness, as well as her grace and elegance. Regarding the invention of its **capital**, it is told that after a maiden of **Corinth** died, her nurse gathered the vases the girl had enjoyed, placed them in a basket, and set it on top of her burial place with a tile <note>original: "regola"; here referring to a flat stone or cover</note> over it. It happened that the basket was placed over an **acanthus** root. In the spring, due to the weight, the root sent out twisted stalks; growing along the sides of the basket and at the corners of the tile, they were forced by the weight to bend at the ends into **volutes** <term>volutes: the spiral, scroll-like ornaments found on the corners of a capital</term>. 

Then **Callimachus**, a most refined architect, seeing that basket with the tender leaves growing around it and being delighted by the style and novelty of the form, created the columns for the **Corinthians** in that likeness, with their proper measurements. But the [Tuscan] order...

<meta>The text cuts off as it begins to describe the Tuscan order, the fourth architectural style.</meta>

<page-num>655</page-num>
<header>SEVENTH</header>

The **Tuscan** order, known through many very ancient works, was considered an invention and discovery of the Tuscans, from whom it took its name. The square column called <term>Attic</term> <note>A square pillar or pilaster used in ancient Greek architecture</note> was devised by the Athenians. Much later, the Romans—realizing they could not add to or surpass the Greek invention of those first three orders—devised a new one composed of the <term>Ionic</term> and the <term>Corinthian</term>, placing the <term>Ionic volute</term> <note>The spiral, scroll-like ornament on a column's top</note> along with the <term>echinus</term> <note>original: "uouolo"; the rounded, egg-like molding below the top of a capital</note> upon the <term>Corinthian</term> capital. They used this order for triumphal arches, wanting to show that they were masters over the nations that had invented those three orders; they did this by placing one order above the other, as seen in the <term>Colosseum</term>, with the <term>Composite</term> <note>The Roman "composed" order</note> above the Corinthian, serving as their crown and lord. 

The form of temples was likewise drawn from the movements of the human body—the round as well as the square, the cross-shaped as well as all others. Similarly, from the arrangement of human limbs, they took the ornaments, the foliage, the moldings, and the other details of the orders. Furthermore, we read in the first book of <term>Vitruvius</term> <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman authority on architecture</note> that the ancients used to place figures in the form of slaves instead of columns, such as the <term>Caryatids</term> <note>Draped female figures used as pillars</note> among the Greeks and the <term>Persians</term> <note>Male figures used as pillars, often representing defeated enemies</note>; and before these, they used <term>Trophies</term> <note>Memorials of victory, originally comprised of the captured armor of a defeated enemy</note>. This practice was later changed into <term>terms</term> <note>original: "termini"; boundary markers or pillars topped with a bust or torso</note>, which are figures from the waist up, and from the waist down are blocks, columns, trunks, or similar forms. In those times, they also used natural heads as capitals, decorated according to the style of the column, more or less; for they did everything with the greatest proportion. 

For this reason, they assigned the <term>Tuscan</term> order to fortresses and, among the gods, to <term>Hercules</term>, mixing it with other orders as the strongest and most rugged of all. The <term>Doric</term> order was assigned to <term>Mars</term> and also to <term>Hercules</term>; the most slender <note>original: "suelto"; literally "loose" or "graceful"</note> to <term>Jupiter</term>; the <term>Ionic</term> to <term>Apollo</term>, <term>Diana</term>, and <term>Bacchus</term>; and the <term>Corinthian</term> to the <term>Goddess Vesta</term> and to <term>Venus</term>. 

But even though the rules of <term>Architecture</term> are thus limited and prescribed, they are not understood by everyone in the same way. For the Germans practice it in one way, as seen in their buildings and temples derived from the Lombard style, by <term>Giacomo da Bergamo</term> and other architects, and in the books already published by <term>Albrecht Dürer</term> <note>The famous German Renaissance artist and theorist</note>. In these, it clearly appears how far their rules are from those we Italians have used from the time of <term>Bramante</term> <note>Donato Bramante, who pioneered the High Renaissance style in Rome</note> until now. The French, the Spanish, and other nations understand it in yet another way. The painter must carefully note this so that in his narrative paintings, one sees that correspondence and harmony of things which is required.

## On the form of some Gods imagined by the ancients. Chapter XXVIIII.

**So** that nothing may be lacking for the complete knowledge of this art, I have wished to add in this place something concerning the form of certain Gods, as the ancients imagined them to be, or as they reasonably ought to have been. And first, they shaped **Providence** as a mother who takes care of the universe—an old woman in the habit of a grave matron, with her arms somewhat open. They depicted **Demogorgon** <note>A primordial deity often associated with the underworld or the origin of the gods in late Roman and Renaissance mythology</note> as the father of all human and lowly thoughts: pale, surrounded by the darkest mist, and covered in a certain woolly moisture, inhabiting the center of the earth. **Eternity**, who contains all ages within herself, was shown standing upright in the form of a woman, dressed in green, with a sphere in her right hand and a wide veil stretched over her head, covering her from one shoulder to the other—though **Claudian** <note>Claudius Claudianus, a late Roman poet</note> forms her in another way, as can also be seen in the translation made of him by **Cartari** <note>Vincenzo Cartari, author of a famous 16th-century handbook on the iconography of the gods</note>; and from this they formed another figure dressed in green because she never grows old. They painted **Chaos** almost as a mass without form or likeness, as **Hesiod** says, with **Discord**—the first daughter of Demogorgon—on horseback behind the confused things; for this reason, she was considered by philosophers to be the preserver of the world. **Fraud**, who was painted by **Apelles** <note>The most famous painter of ancient Greece</note> alongside Calumny in the form of a woman, is depicted by **Dante** in the form of a monster with the face of a good and just man, where he says:

> And that filthy image of Fraud
> Came forward and landed its head and its torso,
> But did not pull its tail onto the bank.
> Its face was the face of a just man,
> So kind was its skin outwardly,
> And the rest of its body was that of a serpent.
> It had two paws, hairy up to the armpits;
> Its back, its chest, and both its sides
> Were painted with knots and small circles.
> With more colors, inlaid and overlaid;
> Never were there Tartar or Turkish cloths
> Nor were such webs ever set by **Arachne** <note>original: "Aragne"; the mythological weaver turned into a spider</note>.

The young **Apollo** was represented dressed in sky-blue, with a sphere in his hand and a vessel full of coals, with many sparks scattered around. They painted **Python** <note>The monstrous serpent of Delphi, here personified</note> all in yellow with a fiery mass in his hand; **Obstinacy** all in black with branches of clinging ivy. **Ignorance** with a leaden die upon her head. **Complaint** <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "covered"</note>

# BOOK SEVEN

...covered with a tan-colored cloth, and with a solitary sparrow that had made its nest in the styling of her hair. They formed the **Hydra** and the **Sphinx**, daughters of **Tartarus**, entirely naked and stripped, with a garland of cloth on their heads and their mouths hanging open. **License** <note>representing unbridled liberty or lack of restraint</note> was dressed in clothes of various colors, in which a veil of gauze was wrapped. **Thought** <note>here meaning "Care" or "Worry"</note> was depicted as having an old face, dressed in black, with an extravagant head-dressing of hazelnuts; beneath his garments, which occasionally blew open in the wind, his chest and his entire person were revealed to be scratched and pierced by a thousand sharp thorns.

The god **Momus**—the god of blame and slander, according to them—was figured in the form of a stooping, talkative old man. The boy **Tages**, son of the <term>Genius</term> <note>a guardian spirit in Roman religion</note>, was shown all resplendent; because he was the first inventor of the art of <term>haruspicy</term> <note>the practice of foretelling the future by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals</note>, he was depicted with a lamb hung around his neck, displaying a good portion of its intestines. The giant **Antaeus** was adorned in barbarian dress with a dart in his right hand, with which it seemed he wished to give manifest signs of his ferocity that day. **Day** was formed as a resplendent and joyful youth, adorned and crowned entirely in white cloths.

They painted **Labor** <note>or "Toil"</note> dressed in the skin of a donkey, with his head and legs likewise covered by the same skin. **The Oath** was shown in the guise of a terrified old priest. Among the Egyptians, **The Year** took the form of a serpent biting its own tail <note>the Ouroboros, symbolizing cyclicality</note>; among the Romans, following the authority of **Numa Pompilius** <note>the legendary second king of Rome</note>, it took the form of **Janus** with two faces, with the fingers of his hands arranged to show as many days as there are in the year. **Prayers** <note>referring to the 'Litai' mentioned in Homer's Iliad</note> were depicted as women, lame, with sorrowful faces and squinted eyes. The Phoenicians represented the **World** as a serpent turning back on itself and biting its tail.

The four seasons of the year are briefly described by **Ovid** in these verses:

> *Spring crowned with flowers,*
> *Naked Summer with hair bound by stalks of grain,*
> *Autumn with his feet stained by pressed grapes,*
> *And Winter, frozen, horrid, and somber.*
> <note>original Italian translation of Ovid: "Coronata di fior la Primauera, / La nuda Eſtà cinta di ſpiche il crine, / L'Autunno tinto i piè d'vue ſpremute, / E l'Inuerno agghiaccicciato borrido, e triſto."</note>

**Orpheus**, in another manner, represents **Summer** in the form of a matron with garlands of grain on her head and a bouquet of poppies in her hand as a sign of fertility, riding upon a chariot pulled by two dragons. With each season, it is customary to paint the God attributed to it by the ancients: for **Spring**, **Venus**; for **Summer**, **Ceres**; for **Autumn**, **Bacchus**; and for **Winter**, **Vulcan**, or **Aeolus** with the winds. **Spring** is also accompanied by **Flora**, the wife of **Zephyr**, who is crowned with flowers and wears a gown painted all over with flowers of diverse colors.

# BOOK 8

**Youth**, whose goddess was **Hebe**, was represented as a most beautiful young woman, wearing a dress of many colors and a garland of flowers on her head; the god **Bacchus** was also usually painted in this manner, if we are to believe **Tibullus** <note>Albius Tibullus, a Roman poet often referenced for his descriptions of Bacchus's youthful appearance</note>.

For **Success** <note>specifically "Good Outcome" or "Bonus Eventus"</note>, they depicted a man in the clothing of a poor person, holding a cup or a mirror in his right hand, and a stalk of grain in his left, just as **Praxiteles** once carved a most beautiful statue that was placed on the **Capitoline**. For the **Father of Health** <note>Asclepius, the god of medicine</note>, they fashioned a man with a long beard, wearing a garment like a shirt with another short, belted cloak over it. In his left hand, he held various fruits wrapped in the hem of his robe, and in his right, two roosters, with a serpent nearby—this was particularly common in **Epidaurus**. However, the people of **Phlius** <note>an ancient Greek city-state</note> placed a knotted staff with a serpent in his hand and called him **Aesculapius**.

For **Health** <note>Salus/Hygieia</note>, they formed a woman seated upon a high throne with a cup in her hand, near an altar upon which rested a coiled serpent raising its head. For the first reddening of the Sun in the East, **Homer** imagined **Aurora** <note>the Dawn</note> with blonde and golden hair upon a golden throne, wearing a dress of the same color. Others placed a lit torch in her hand, upon a chariot pulled by the winged horse **Pegasus**, and others gave her two shining horses, showing that at her appearance she, being all colorful, scatters yellow and crimson flowers and roses through the air.

Among the **Egyptians**, the **World** was figured as a man with his feet twisted and knotted together, and with a robe wrapped around him that covered him entirely, made of many different colors, while he supported a golden globe with his head. These same people used to represent the **Universe** with two circles, one above the other, crossed by a serpent that had the head of a hawk.

Those who administer **Justice** were depicted by the **Thebans** without hands; they also represented Justice as both male and female. They made **Fortitude** male and **Temperance** female. They figured **Marriage** with its neck in a yoke and its feet in shackles. The god of weddings, called **Hymen**, was made as a youth crowned with flowers and green <term>marjoram</term> <note>original: "Perſa" (Origanum majorana), traditionally used in wedding wreaths</note>, with a torch in his right hand and in the other that red or yellow veil <note>the *flammeum*</note> with which they covered the faces of brides, and wearing two yellow <term>slippers</term> <note>original: "ſocchi," referring to the *soccus* or soft shoe worn in antiquity</note> on his feet, just as **Catullus** describes him, saying:

->Adorned with lovely flowers,<-
->With green marjoram in your hair,<-
->Lovely Hymen, and with the beautiful veil in hand,<-
->Return to us joyful,<-
->Make him approach us.<-

A happy deity of yours, because in vain / of gold of lead on the head. <note>These final lines appear to be a fragmented continuation or a variation of the poetic text.</note>

**Pomona**, the Goddess of fruits and flowers, they dressed in a garment painted with fruits and flowers, with a crown on her head woven likewise of flowers and fruits, and especially of apples <note>original: *pomi*</note>. **Vertumnus**, who was imagined as her lover because he took diverse forms according to the various seasons of the year, and was believed to provide the opportunity <note>the "right moment" or *kairos*</note> for men to do anything according to the season, is described by **Propertius** with a crown of grapes and ears of grain on his head, and otherwise in various forms, according to the opportunities he offers us; wherefore he leads him to say: "I shall be a man if the toga is given to me <note>Referring to the *toga virilis*, marking the transition to manhood</note>, and a youth if I am in feminine dress, and a reaper if I have the scythe and my brow is adorned with hay." # SEVENTH

## S E V E N T H

...with other figures in the Ducal Sacristy of Florence <note>The New Sacristy of San Lorenzo, designed by Michelangelo to house the Medici tombs</note>. **Wisdom**, in both war and peace, was made with an almost masculine face and a very stern appearance, with sky-blue eyes. She was armed, according to **Homer**, with a long spear in her hand, a crystal shield on her arm, and a helmet on her head, sometimes crowned with olive. According to **Apuleius**, she wore a crest of a serpent with somewhat long hair, accompanied by Terror and Fear. This figure was formerly made under the name of **Minerva** in Athens by **Phidias**, out of gold and ivory at a height of twenty-six cubits <term>cubit: an ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18 inches</term>; her form is clearly described in the *Natural History* by **Pliny the Second** <note>Pliny the Elder</note>. **Silius Italicus** alone speaks of the Goddess of war called **Bellona**:

> *She shakes the lit torch, and her golden hair*
> *Is scattered with much blood, as she goes running,*
> *The great Bellona, through the armed ranks.*

Others made her similar in both dress and arms to **Minerva**, but fiercer, with a shield of iron and armor that was more polished and menacing, adding **Mars** as her charioteer. For the **Terror** that frightens and forces men to do what is desired, a terrible man was depicted with the head of a lion; such was the one carved into the shield of **Agamemnon**. But the Corinthians dedicated one to the sons of **Medea** with the dress and face of a woman, in a frightening and horrible gesture. **Truth** was made as a beautiful and tall woman, honestly adorned, entirely bright and resplendent, with eyes as clear as two stars. **Opinion** was made as a woman neither beautiful nor ugly, but entirely bold and ready for everything that presents itself to her. **Virtue** was described as ancient and modern. The **Ancient** was worshipped before the Temple of Honor; she had wings and sat like a matrona <note>a dignified married woman</note> upon a square stone, leaning with her left arm against a column and holding a serpent with her right. The **Modern** was depicted as a thin woman, sad and pained, dressed in a few rags and beaten by **Fortune**. **Will** was made as a beautiful young girl, entirely lascivious and charming because of the artificial ornaments she wore about her. **Honor** was represented as a boy dressed in purple cloth with a laurel wreath on his head, to whom the God **Cupid** gave his hand to lead him to Virtue, according to **Alciati** <note>Andrea Alciati, author of the famous 16th-century *Book of Emblems*</note>. The Goddess of pleasures called **Voluptas** <note>Pleasure</note> was represented in the form of a woman with a pale face who sat like a Queen upon a high throne and held the virtues under her feet. The Goddess of silence called **Angerona** was made, as **Solinus** says, with her mouth bound and sealed. The **Silence** called **Harpocrates** by the Greeks and **Sigaleon** by the Egyptians was figured in the form of a young man...

...who held a finger to his mouth, and was also depicted without a face, wearing a small cap on his head and wrapped in a wolf skin covered in eyes and ears <note>This figure represents Secrecy or Silence, often associated with the Egyptian deity Harpocrates</note>. **Fury** was painted with a terrible expression on his face in the act of gnashing his teeth; he was placed sitting upon breastplates, helmets, shields, swords, and other armor, with his hands tied behind his back with chains. **Virgil** depicted him in this form in the Temple of Janus <note>A reference to the *Aeneid*, Book 1</note>. **Aristides** <note>Aelius Aristides, a Greek orator</note> describes **Discord** with her head held high, with livid and deathly pale lips, and with eyes askew, damaged, and full of tears that continually furrow her pale cheeks; she never keeps her hands to herself but is always ready to move them, with thin and twisted legs and feet, and with a knife thrust into her breast. **Virgil**, speaking of her, says:

> *She knots and binds the mad Discord’s*
> *Viper-like hair with a bloody headband.*
> <note>original: "Annoda, e stringe alla discordia pazza / Il crin vipereo sanguinosa benda." This is a poetic paraphrase of Virgil’s description of the Fury Allecto or Discord in the Aeneid.</note>

**Pausanias** says she was a woman with a most hideous face, and she was represented as such by **Calliphon of Samos** in the temple of **Diana of Ephesus**. **Slander**, whom **Apelles** painted according to the account by **Lucian**, was shown as a man sitting in the manner of a judge with long ears similar to those of a donkey; two women, one on each side, appeared to be whispering something softly into them. One of these was **Ignorance**, the other **Suspicion**. She <note>Suspicion</note> reached out her hand to **Slander**, who came toward him in the form of a beautiful and adorned woman, but whose expression showed her to be full of rage and indignation; in her left hand she held a lit torch, and with her right she dragged a naked youth by the hair, who lamented miserably, raising his joined hands toward heaven. Before her went **Malice**—that is, **Envy**—who was a thin, pale old man, as if he had been sick for a long time; and behind her came two women who seemed to flatter her, celebrating her beauty and adorning her as much as they could; one was called **Fraud** and the name of the other was **Deceit**. Following behind these was another woman called **Repentance**, with a few rags around her that were all torn and shredded; weeping profusely, she afflicted herself beyond measure and seemed to want to die of shame because she saw **Truth** approaching. Anyone who wishes to see a similar figure should look at the print by the modern **Federico Zuccaro**, expressed with the greatest wit and diligence <note>Zuccaro’s "Calumny of Apelles" (1572) is a famous complex engraving based on this Lucianic description</note>. **Victory** was made in the form of a beautiful winged maiden, who with one hand offered a laurel crown and in the other held a palm branch. For **Drunkenness**, they made a bald old man, completely shaven, fat and naked, encircled with garlands of grapes and vines, with two small horns sprouting from his temples. Others made him as a youth, entirely...

->joyful and naked like Bacchus.<- The God of banquets <note>This refers to Comus, the personification of revelry and festive mirth</note> was depicted as a beautiful young man, standing as if he were asleep, with his cheek falling upon his breast, and his left hand resting upon a spear <note>original: "asta"</note> which supported him; he held a burning torch in his right hand, which, as it hung down, seemed as though it would burn his leg. He wore a garland of flowers on his head, with many other flowers scattered beneath his feet. **Priapus**, the God of gardens, was made as the God of generation in the form of a man with a ruffled beard and hair, entirely naked, holding a curved sickle in his right hand, and with an erect member like a boy beside him with his right hand. The guardians of places, such as the **Penates** <note>Household gods of the Romans</note>, were fashioned in the guise of young men in military dress and ornament, seated with a javelin <note>original: "pilo"</note> in hand. **Good Fortune**, who bestows goods and happiness, was represented in the dress of a matron with the Horn of Plenty <note>original: "corno della Douitia"</note> in her hand. According to **Pausanias**—who asserts that among ancient figures none is more prominent than the statue made by the architect and sculptor **Bupalus** for the people of **Smyrna**—she was in the form of a woman who had a celestial pole <note>original: "polo"</note> upon her head and held the horn of plenty in one of her hands. This was to show the office of Fortune, which is to give and take away riches (represented by the horn of plenty), which revolve continually just as the heavens revolve around the two poles. And **Lactantius** writes that she held the horn of plenty, and a ship’s rudder was placed beside her. In ancient marbles, she is seen sitting as a modestly dressed woman in the habit of a sad and disconsolate matron, before whom stands a beautiful young woman of charming appearance who gives her her right hand; behind them is a young girl with one hand leaning on the seat of the matron. This matron represents past fortune, and therefore remains sad. The young woman giving her hand is the present fortune, and the girl behind her is that which is to come. The ancients also depicted her as bald at the back of her head <note>This imagery is often shared with Occasio or Opportunity: "seize fortune by the forelock"</note> with very long hair in front, and very swift in running, as **Callistratus** sculpted her. Others made her without feet, others of glass, and others with two horns of plenty turned toward each other around the caduceus of **Mercury**, with two wings above and a hat on top, to make us aware that good fortune never comes to us except by means of wisdom and learning. **Bad Fortune**, who brings misfortunes and labors, is made as a thoughtless youth with hair scattered in the wind, standing upon a round ball in the act of not knowing which way to turn, with a rudder in hand. But others gave her a sail, upon a wheel among the waves of the sea, and others wrapped her in a thin cloth, in which she had gathered all—

The Greeks called Opportunity by the name "opportune time," and thus he was named **Caerus** <note>original: "Cero," the personification of the "right moment"</note>, who was fashioned as a youth in his most flourishing age, handsome and graceful with his hair scattered in the wind, and his hands and arms in the act of seizing hold. **Favor** was fashioned as a youth with wings but blind, and with his feet upon a wheel. **Happiness** was represented by the Romans in the guise of a woman upon a beautiful throne with a caduceus <note>a herald's staff</note> in her right hand and a great horn of plenty <note>original: "corno di diuitia"</note> in her left. For the forgetting of past love, they made the **God of Love** scattering water from the river **Lethe** <note>the river of forgetfulness in the underworld</note> upon glowing coals; and for various types of love, they made naked winged cherubs <note>original: "puttini"</note>, some of whom held arrows in their hands, others snares, and others torches. The **Hours**—who stand at the gate of heaven with **Janus**, and remove the bridles from the horses of the sun, staying there to honor **Jove** and the **Fates**—rather than recounting how the poets described them, **Philostratus** <note>likely Philostratus the Elder, an ancient Greek writer known for describing artworks</note> says that having descended to earth, they go about turning the year (which is in the form of a certain round object) with their hands. From this turning, it follows that the earth then produces from year to year everything that is born; they are blonde, dressed in very thin veils, and they walk upon the dry stalks of grain so lightly that they do not break or bend even one. They are of a sweet and cheerful appearance; they sing most sweetly, and in turning that orb, ball, or circle, whatever it may be, they seem to offer wonderful delight to those watching; and they move as if almost always leaping, often raising their beautiful arms high. They have blonde hair scattered over their shoulders and flushed cheeks, like someone who feels heated from a great race,

# SEVENTH.

...warmed, with shining eyes, and quick to move. And because these are held to be the same thing as the **Graces**, I say that some made them four to represent the four seasons of the year—as there were also that many **Hours**—crowning them with garlands: one of flowers, another of ears of grain, the third of grapes and vine leaves, and the last of olive. They imagined that **Apollo** held them in his right hand, because the changing of the seasons comes from the sun. Other ancients wished for the Graces to be two, and others three, in which opinion almost everyone concurs, especially **Hesiod**, who makes the three Graces the companions of **Venus**—as if they were her daughters—and of **Bacchus**. He names them **Euphrosyne**, **Aglaia**, and **Thalia**, signifying by the first "joy and gladness," by the second "majesty and beauty," and by the third "pleasantness." These were first represented clothed, and later as naked young maidens, happy and laughing, with their hands joined together; this was to show that where a service begins, it is proper that it should return. For it is imagined that one of them performs the service, the other receives it, and the third returns the favor. Such figures were once seen larger than life in the portico of Athens, sculpted by the hand of one of the two **Socrates**—either the sculptor and painter, or the sculptor <note>The author refers to a tradition that the philosopher Socrates was originally a sculptor who carved a famous group of the Graces</note>. It is enough to say that these did not yield in beauty to any others placed in that location; they can still be seen in Rome in ancient marble. They are also seen painted in Rome by the hand of **Raphael** together with other Gods, and from that painting there are printed designs with the **Seven Virtues** engraved by **Marcantonio**; all of these are excellently made. From **Rosso** <note>Rosso Fiorentino</note> there are also about twenty diligently formed Gods in print.

I could bring here the descriptions of many other forms, such as **Seia Idea**, so called from sowing <note>original: "seminare"</note>, of **Segesta** <note>Goddess of the standing crops</note>, of **Pandora** and her jar, of the Goddess **Carma**, of **Libitina**—Goddess of the dead—of the **Twilight** <note>original: "crepuscolo"</note> sculpted by **Michelangelo** in Florence along with **Day** and **Nature**, and of many other things that can be studied for the most part through the authors cited in the *Genealogy of the Gods of the Ancients* and in the exposition of their images made by **Vincenzo Cartari**. These I will omit for the sake of brevity, as it would be too long an undertaking, since the studious painter can easily find them for himself through the examples cited, and by observing and imagining the ancient figures already sculpted in Rome as described by **Mauro**, as well as in other places. For this reason, I will also omit reporting the forms of the twelve months—four of which represent the seasons—and their instruments and clothing, which can nonetheless be seen in prints designed by Flemish and Italian artists. And since we must color them, we shall make use of the composition of colors, which are...

### *On the form of certain infernal monsters, and of Minos, Aeacus, and Rhadamanthus. Chapter XXX.*

**N**ear the mouths of Lake <term>Avernus</term> <note>A volcanic crater lake near Naples, which ancient Romans believed was the entrance to the Underworld</note>, where according to **Dante**—who in this followed the fabulous inventions of the ancient poets—one enters a swampy forest by descending into the depths. This place is full of putrid and black waters, entangled by many trees laden with thorns, where there is no light other than that which reflects from the waters like a mirror, and from the eyes of many foul animals that lie there hidden in the mud. Some of these are called <term>striges</term> <note>original: "strigi"; mythical screech-owls or vampires believed to prey on children</note> which according to **Ovid** were born from the **Harpies**, and were certain large, frightening birds that feed on human blood, which he describes thus:

> They have a large head, and the eyes protrude
> Far beyond the common sort, large and prominent,
> Filled with a foul and cruel horror;
> The claws are curved and intent on prey,
> The beak is hooked, and of a hoary <note>Grayish-white or aged in appearance</note> color
> Are the feathers, and it seems that everyone fears them.

Some others are imagined there who eat living flesh, who are said to be born in <term>Acheron</term> <note>One of the rivers of the Greek Underworld, often used to refer to the Underworld itself</note> and conceived by the infernal furies, with the face of a woman; speaking of these, **Statius** says:

> Cruel monster, who in the deep Acheron
> Was conceived among the furies and born.
> And she has the breast, neck, and brow of a woman,
> Separated from a hissing serpent,
> Which seems to rise and mount from the crown
> Of the head, and toward the face is bent;
> This plague wanders by night, and feeds
> Upon the children she finds in the cradle and in swaddling clothes.

There are others called <term>Lamiae</term> according to **Dio**, which have the face and breast of a very beautiful woman, and the rest of the body covered in very hard scales; because of this, she changes into a serpent and ends in a frightening head of such an animal. The **Sphinges** are described by **Pliny** as having breasts thick with hair, with two teats and a monstrous face; and some others have the face and breast of a woman with wings, and the rest of a lion according to **Ausonius**. The Egyptians used to place the image of these beneath the arm of the **Nile**; and **Julius Caesar**...

*And only skin clothes the bones:*
*And from the bones joined in various ways*
*Appear various forms and various knots.*

*The knot of the knees extends outward,*
*And through the dry thighs seems swollen:*
*The breast, which hangs suspended from the ribs,*
*Resembles a wind-ball without breath:*
*No belly is contained within its belly,*
*But the place where the belly once seemed to be,*
*Resembles, in short, the famished rage*
*Of a skeletal <term>anatomy</term> <note>original: "notomia"; a term used for a skeleton or a flayed body used for medical study</note> that still possesses a soul.*

But before him <note>The author likely refers to Virgil, whose description of Charon was common in this period</note>, Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – AD 65), the Roman Stoic philosopher and playwright; this description comes from his tragedy *Hercules Furens*</note> describes him in the form of a horrific old man, with a dark countenance, hollow and squalid cheeks, a tangled beard, eyes like two flames, and a cloth gathered around him by a crude knot that partially covers his limbs. He holds a long pole, with which he steers the small boat that carries souls into the valley of the abyss, which is entirely shrouded in the darkest clouds. In its depths, in a vast place, are set those who never worshipped God, along with those who did not know Him. The punishment of these souls is to weep continually, to bite, and to beat themselves. From here rises a great castle surrounded seven times by high walls, around which runs a small river with a bottom of fine sand; this is crossed by a bridge that leads to a meadow beyond the walls covered in greenery called the **Field of Truth**. Through this field wander people of authority, and it splits into two paths: one leads to Pluto <note>The king of the Underworld in Roman mythology</note>, and the other to the Isles of the Blessed.

Going toward Pluto, one reaches a place where, at the entrance, stands **Minos** behind **Aeacus** and **Rhadamanthus**, who are judges in the Field of Truth—one for the dead of Europe and the other for those of Asia <note>In Greek mythology, these three were mortal kings famous for their justice, appointed after death to judge the souls of the deceased</note>. Minos then determines where they must go, recognizing the actions of each soul as soon as he sees them, for their deeds are marked upon them. Aeacus and Rhadamanthus hold a rod in their hands while judging, but Minos sits apart from them alone and holds a golden scepter in his hand. However, Dante <note>Dante Alighieri (1265–1321); this quote is from Canto V of the *Inferno*</note> depicts him otherwise, insisting he has the form of a beast, where he says:

> *There stands Minos, horribly, and snarls,*
> *He examines the crimes at the entrance,*
> *He judges, and sends according to how he entwines himself.*
> *I say that when the ill-born soul*
> *Comes before him, it confesses all,*
> *And that connoisseur of sins*
> *Sees which place in Hell belongs to it;*
> *He girds himself with his tail as many times*
> *As the levels he wants it to be cast down.*

In this form, he was painted by Buonarroti <note>Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475–1564); the author is referring to the figure of Minos in *The Last Judgment* in the Sistine Chapel, where the judge is depicted with donkey ears and a serpent/tail wrapped around him</note> in his *Judgment* in the Vatican.
