> *With three throats barks like a dog*
> *Over the people who are submerged here.*
> *His eyes are red, his beard greasy and black,*
> *His belly wide, and his hands hooked;*
> *He claws the spirits, flays them, and rends them.*

And such forms can be seen excellently represented in the *Labors of Hercules*, which are published in prints by the hand of the miraculous **Rosso Fiorentino** <note>Giovanni Battista di Jacopo (1494–1540), an Italian Mannerist painter</note> and of **Aldo Grave the German** <note>Likely Heinrich Aldegrever (1502–1561), a German painter and engraver known for his "Small Masters" style</note>. From here, one passes over a bridge where sits **Pluto**, King (according to the pagans) of the earth, of hell, and of the dead, with many devils around him, and at his side **Proserpina**, the three **Fates**, and **Night** who serve him. He sits, as Seneca says, as a King, with an appearance that clearly shows him to be the brother of **Jupiter** and **Neptune**, upon a high throne all carved with terrifying monsters, appearing entirely horrific with his head encircled by a dark mist, and according to **Claudian** <note>Claudius Claudianus (c. 370 – 404 AD), a Latin poet</note>, with a rusty scepter in his hand. But **Martianus** <note>Martianus Capella (5th century AD), author of an influential encyclopedia on the liberal arts</note> maintains that he is of a dark color and has upon his head a crown of black ebony tinted with the darkness of night, and holds in his hand a small black scepter, or according to **Pindar** <note>Pindar (c. 518 – 438 BC), the ancient Greek lyric poet</note>, a rod. And because he never allows anyone to return who once sets foot in his kingdom, the same poet gives into his hand the keys...

...ue. Some others have at times crowned him <note>Referring to Pluto, the king of the Underworld</note> with woven garlands, sometimes made of the cypress (a funerary tree), and sometimes of maidenhair fern and narcissus, which are pleasing to the dead. But everyone depicts him as horrible and fierce in appearance, with a certain gravity, yet disagreeable and hateful; and they give him a chariot drawn by four very fierce black horses that breathe fire, named Orphnaeus, Alastor, Aethon, and Morpheus <note>original: "orneo, alastro, ethone, & morfeo"; these are the classical names for the steeds of Pluto's chariot</note>; and according to Boccaccio <note>Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375), the famous Italian author who also wrote on classical mythology</note> by three only, whom he calls Amatheus, Astraeus, and Nycteus; where he also claims the chariot has only three wheels. Proserpina, his wife, is imagined with a helmet on her head and with Cerberus at her feet according to Fulgentius; but certainly, as he is a most voracious animal, he is more reasonably placed by others among the gluttons, just as Dante places him in his *Inferno*. Regarding the three Fates <note>The Parcae, who controlled the metaphorical thread of life</note> who are always imagined together ruling the threads of our life: the first, who is the youngest, holds the <term>distaff</term> <note>A tool used in spinning to hold the unspun fibers</note> and pulls the thread; the second, of greater age, winds it around the <term>spindle</term>; and the third, already old, cuts it. All three, according to Catullus, have a white robe decorated with purple fringes (as some would have it), with which they cover their trembling limbs, and they have their heads encircled by a white band; and according to Plato, they are crowned with a garland of narcissus. Homer describes them with wings and with their heads sprinkled with very white flour <note>Likely referring to the dust or powder of the ages or the gray hair of old age</note>. Some make them daughters of Erebus <note>The personification of darkness</note> and of Night, and call the first Clotho, the second Lachesis, and the third Atropos. And others have wanted them to be the daughters of Demogorgon, and have called them Nona, Decima, and Morta <note>These are the Roman names for the Fates, associated with the months of pregnancy and death</note>. And these were painted and released in prints at the beginning of the great history of *Cupid and Psyche* by the blessed hand of Raphael <note>The famous Renaissance painter Raphael Sanzio; he designed the frescoes of the Story of Cupid and Psyche in the Villa Farnesina in Rome</note>. In the third place, that of **Avarice**, the tyrants and usurers are confined, suffering various punishments and torments. The tyrants are shot at by fire and by infinite centaurs while standing in the middle of a lake of boiling blood, enclosed all around by freezing ice; and the greedy are condemned to forever move massive weights, which always fall back down from high to low; and some lie on their backs, and afterwards are turned into trees. Among these, the most well-known are Aglauros, who is turned to stone; Eriphyle, wife of Amphiaraus, who casts herself down; Marcus Crassus <note>A Roman general famous for his great wealth and greed</note> lying on his back; and Tantalus, father of Pelops, immersed in crystal-clear water up to his lower lip with various fruits hanging above him reaching his other lip; and when he bows down to drink, the waters recede, and when he reaches up to eat of the fruits, they are pulled away. Above them fly and make their nests the Harpies, daughters of Thaumas, who according to Virgil inhabit the Strophades Islands; whose form Ariosto <note>Ludovico Ariosto, author of *Orlando Furioso*</note> describes in this manner:

<margin>And Dante, imitating Virgil, speaks of them thus in his Inferno</margin>

> Who drove the Trojans from the Strophades
> With a grim announcement of future woes;
> They have wide wings, human necks and faces,
> Feet with claws, and a great feathered belly;
> They make their laments upon the strange trees;
<note>These lines are from Dante's "Inferno," Canto XIII, describing the Wood of the Suicides where Harpies dwell.</note>

Descending further, one finds a gate with a large square before it, where the slothful <note>The "accidiosi," those guilty of the sin of sloth or spiritual apathy</note> and the heretics are confined. The souls of these heretics have certain lids over them that cast out flames, by which they are all set ablaze. From there, a path ends at the edge of a very high cliff, entirely broken and steep, from which stones roll down to the bottom as they break away; and there a great stench is smelled, which sickens many other heretics who burn there among those rocks. At the bottom of the cliff, many branches of sloth are seen scattered on the ground, tossed about by the wind, with some <term>Minotaurs</term> <note>Mythological creatures with the head of a bull and the body of a man</note> around them, whose leader is the son of <term>Pasiphae</term> <note>In Greek mythology, Pasiphae was the Queen of Crete who gave birth to the Minotaur</note>. There passes the river <term>Phlegethon</term> <note>original: "Flagetonte"</note>, which signifies heat and fire, and is born from <term>Cocytus</term> <note>original: "Cocito"; usually the frozen lake at the bottom of the Inferno, though here described as the source</note>. Here also, arrows, lightning bolts, and glowing embers of fire rain down upon a plain, striking those who rebelled against God. They all lie there naked on the ground, with <term>Capaneus</term> <note>One of the Seven against Thebes, known for his defiance of the gods</note> in their midst, a scorner of <term>Jove</term> <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>, who bellows horribly. Not far off is the giant <term>Tityus</term> <note>original: "Ticio"</note>, stretched out and bound to the earth with a raven tearing at his liver and intestines, which always grow back after being devoured. Along with these, <term>Dante</term> also places <term>Tages</term> <note>An Etruscan prophet child</note>, <term>Alcmaeon</term> <note>original: "Almeon"</note>, <term>Aruns the Tuscan</term>, <term>Astyages</term> <note>original: "Astriande"</note> King of the Medes, the son of <term>Oileus</term> <note>original: "Olideo"; likely referring to Ajax the Lesser</note>, <term>Asdente</term> <note>A cobbler from Parma whom Dante identifies as a soothsayer</note>, <term>Calchas</term>, <term>Tiresias of Thebes</term>, and other diviners. Beyond this, around the same river, other slothful souls are seen being broken in all their bones, tossed about from head to foot like a wheel. But the <term>Phlegethon</term> falls with a terrifying roar down into a certain depth of a cliff where the fraudulent dwell with <term>Geryon</term> <note>In Dante, the personification of Fraud</note> in the form of a monstrous figure; for he has a human face, but the rest of his body is that of a serpent.

Above the marsh is a very large arch, after which one arrives at a very high tower, which at the summit burns and blazes with flames; and at the foot it has a body of water, through which the souls are carried in a boat to the City of Dis <note>Dite: the lower part of Hell in Dante's cosmology, named after the Roman god of the underworld</note>, which has infinite devils of strange forms above the gate (which is entirely sunken around it), all with the wings of bats and serpents. It is surrounded by very high towers and seems girded by a putrid marsh; and here stay the three Furies, daughters of Charon and Night.

<header>BOOK SEVEN</header>
<sig>Yv 3</sig>

...of which he then made another that is now found in Florence. There remain the Blessed Isles, which were also placed in the center of the earth; however, because they are entirely a matter of fable, we shall leave them to be enjoyed by the pagans who were their inventors. I will also refrain from speaking of the spirits of Satan who have been depicted by various painters in ways suited to their evil effects; they are rendered with powerful draftsmanship in diverse forms with the heads, wings, and joints of satyrs, dragons, lions, wild boars, and the like. They are shown with large ears, with the breasts and legs of satyrs, donkeys, lions, eagles, and griffins, and with terrifying tails and wings. Similarly, they appear in the air with the tails of monsters and harpies, with horns twisted in various ways, and with limbs formed partly of scales, partly of coils, plates, ridges, lumps, small wheels, slats, and such things. Their hair is rough, harsh, filthy, shaggy, and ruffled, which clearly demonstrates to our eyes how ready and bold they are in terrifying the suffering and, with their bites and snares, poisoning and deceiving the world.

The aforementioned <term>Martin Schongauer</term> <note>original: "Buon Martino." Schongauer (c. 1445–1491) was a famous German engraver whose prints were highly influential in Italy.</note> expressed many such bizarre and fantastic monsters in a print, showing them tearing the clothes of Saint Anthony while in the air. <term>Albrecht Dürer</term> <note>original: "Alberto Durero."</note> did the same in his print of the <term>armed figure</term> <note>original: "senso armato." This refers to Dürer’s famous engraving "Knight, Death and the Devil" (1513).</note> on horseback with his dogs, with Death likewise on horseback nearby holding an hourglass in his hand and showing it to him. In that work, as a diabolical tempter behind the knight's shoulders, he placed a figure with the face of a pig and twisted horns in a bizarre pose; the rest of it is so fantastic that it is impossible to see anything better. 

And when <term>Christ</term> goes to Limbo to free the Holy Fathers, one can imagine various such terrifying monsters with trumpets and horns in their mouths, sounding them noisily, as seen in a print by the hand of <term>Andrea Mantegna</term>. Likewise, they can be represented in the fearsome Judgment of Christ, as <term>Michelangelo Buonarroti</term> <note>original: "il Buonaroto."</note> very carefully observed in his own work through various other gestures and forms. He created their bodies according to their actions, giving them disdainful and fierce faces—many of which can be imagined with one face behind the shoulders and another in front, or others on the knees. He rendered them in the color of ebony and with moth-like wings; others have horns and teeth protruding from their mouths, and with claws extended from their feet and hands, made in the diverse forms of animals and in various colors like iron-grey, yellow, red, ashen-grey, and similar mixtures, all of them discordant with one another. 

To achieve this, the limbs of the aforementioned monsters at the entrance of Hell will be very useful, as will other terrible, fierce, predatory, melancholic, and aquatic animals, because they will better serve to demonstrate their wicked and perverse effects through such forms.

...can be made into the most cruel monster that tempts Christ, as has been shown by <term>Lucas van Leyden</term> <note>original: "Luca d'Olanda." A leading Dutch engraver and painter of the early 16th century.</note> and <term>Hans Sebald Beham</term> <note>original: "Hisibil Peum." A German printmaker known for his small, masterful engravings.</note>, and that other one who scourges Job, which is seen drawn in the book of Damiano Marassio and in many paintings. But those who were the principal painters of these bizarneries were mentioned above in the chapter on the landscapes of monsters and chimeras. And this ancient serpent with seven faces of diverse crowned animals and as many necks joined to its monstrous body to demonstrate its wicked and pestilential natures, was represented—as seen in the print of the *Apocalypse* of Saint John—by <term>Albrecht Dürer</term> <note>original: "Alberto Durero."</note>. This is enough to surpass the bizarre forms of the Hydra of Hercules, and the immense, ugly beast represented in the <term>Stregozzo</term> <note>original: "stregozzo." A famous and mysterious engraving often called "The Witch’s Procession."</note> after <term>Michelangelo</term> <note>original: "Buonarotto."</note>, which print was released as an engraving cut by <term>Marcantonio Raimondi</term> <note>original: "Marco Antonio Bolognese."</note> and others. There are also other monsters described by the ancients and by the moderns <term>Boiardo</term> and <term>Ariosto</term> <note>Authors of the epic poems *Orlando Innamorato* and *Orlando Furioso*, which are filled with fantastical creatures.</note>, and others, who in this regard have gathered the best that could be imagined concerning such monsters and serpents.

### Conclusion. Chapter XXXIII and Last.

**F**inally, by the grace of God, we have, according to the order proposed at the beginning of this treatise, discussed all those parts in which, in my judgment, consists this most noble art of painting—an art equal to any other <term>liberal art</term> <note>An art involving intellectual discipline rather than just manual labor.</note>. Although I have done so with much weaker powers of intellect and art than such a high undertaking required, I have nevertheless worked with such industry, diligence, and labor that I believe I have in some part compensated for my lack of natural talent. For as much as concerns those parts that are not so specific to painting that they are not also shared by other arts—such as <term>perspective</term> and history—I have turned and returned to them. I have also employed a good part of the time that I would have otherwise spent in the practice of painting (to my great personal profit) in studying all those books from which I hoped to gather anything that could illustrate this art. Regarding the other parts, I have not spared myself the inconvenience or expense of going to see many parts of Italy—and especially illustrious Rome and Florence, which are rich in such ornaments above all others—to study all the works, both of painting and sculpture, by the most famous and excellent craftsmen, both ancient and modern. From these, as if from so many <term>Canons of Polycleitus</term> <note>Polycleitus was an ancient Greek sculptor who wrote a "Canon" (now lost) defining the ideal mathematical proportions of the human figure.</note>, I have observed what is the true norm and rule of painting (as much as I could achieve with my weak judgment). This is what I have forced myself to explain in these books with the greatest possible ease and clarity possible in a subject so <margin>ria così <note>Catchword for the next page: "subject so [complex...]"</note></margin>

# BOOK SEVEN

<margin>T</margin> **I have treated** a matter so difficult and subtle, never before addressed by others—at least not with the exactness that anyone can see I have applied here. And although in some places it may seem that a greater precision could be desired, I have nevertheless done this by design, sometimes only hinting at certain things and at other times even omitting them. This is because some points were so clear and easy in themselves that they required no lengthy discourse; others, without cluttering the pages in vain, could easily be noticed and understood by the readers themselves, even those of less than average intellect. Beyond this, to further illustrate these matters and place them, in a sense, before the eyes of the readers while treating each part of this science, I have always mentioned as examples some who were excellent in that specific area, so that readers would know whom they ought to imitate. I well know that there were many others worthy of being celebrated and proposed as examples for imitation, such as

<margin>Ag</margin> **Lorenzetto**, **Passerotto**, and **Somachino** of Bologna <note>original: "Lorenzetto, il Passerotto, il Somachino Bolognesi." Referring to Lorenzo Lotti, Bartolomeo Passerotti, and Orazio Samacchini, prominent Mannerist painters.</note>;
<margin>Ag</margin> **Andrea Schiavone** <note>original: "Andrea Schiauone." A Venetian school painter known for his loose, painterly style.</note>;
<margin>Ag</margin> **Giovanni Battista Simoleo**;
<margin>Ap</margin> **Simone Peterzano** <note>original: "Simon Petenzano." A Bergamasque painter active in Milan, famous today as the teacher of Caravaggio.</note>;
<margin>Ar</margin> **Palmetta** of Venice <note>original: "il Palmetta Venetiani." Likely referring to Palma il Giovane.</note>;
<margin>Ar</margin> **Raffaellino da Reggio** <note>original: "Rafael da Regio."</note>;
<margin>Ab</margin> **Romolo of Florence** <note>original: "Romolo Fiorentino." Likely Romolo del Tadda.</note>;
<margin>Ab</margin> **Bonifacio** and **Battista** of Verona <note>original: "Bonifacio, & Battista Veronesi." Bonifacio de' Pitati and Battista Zelotti.</note>;
<margin>Ab</margin> **Lattanzio of Brescia** <note>original: "Lantantio Bressano." Referring to Lattanzio Gambara.</note>;
<margin>Ar</margin> **Ambrogio Borgognone** and
<margin>Ac</margin> **Pietro Rizzo** of Milan <note>original: "Ambrogio Borgognone, & Pietro Rizzo Milanesi." Borgognone was a major early Renaissance Lombard painter; Pietro Rizzo is a nickname for Giampietrino, a pupil of Leonardo da Vinci.</note>;
<margin>Ab</margin> the **Campi** of Cremona <note>original: "i Campi Cremonesi." A family of influential painters including Giulio, Antonio, and Bernardino Campi.</note>;
<margin>Am</margin> **Bernardo Soiaro** <note>original: "Bernardo Soiaro." Also known as Bernardino Gatti.</note>, along with the two **Magni** brothers of Pavia <note>original: "duoi fratelli dei Maini Pauesi." Giacomo and Giovanni-Pietro de' Magni.</note>;
<margin>Al</margin> and many others, both foreigners and Italians. Since I mention painters in this treatise not to write their <term>biographies</term> <note>original: "vite." A nod to Giorgio Vasari’s famous "Lives," distinguishing this theoretical work from a historical one.</note> but for the sake of example, it was enough for me to name a few—especially those who, being already deceased, could be remembered without provoking envy. Furthermore, naming a great number of authors often diminishes the reputation of the art; for if excellence is seen as something easily achieved by so many, the art is held in lower esteem. It also detracts from those few craftsmen who are truly excellent, who alone should possess praise and glory, rather than having it shared with so many others.

In this entire work, when I have dealt with the parts most specific to this art—such as <term>lights</term> and <term>colors</term>—I have used an ordinary and familiar way of speaking without any ornament, even inserting many words that are less approved and not found in the usage of the <term>Tuscans</term> <note>Lomazzo, a Milanese, is defending his use of regional or technical vocabulary over the prestigious literary dialect of Florence (Tuscan), which was the standard for "high" literature.</note>. This is because my primary goal was to be understood, judging that anyone who teaches an art should seek clarity and ease rather than ornament and elegance of style. Thus, he said well who stated that:

> *The matter itself refuses to be adorned, being satisfied simply to be taught.* <note>original: "Ornari res ipsa negat contenta doceri." A quote from the Roman poet Manilius (*Astronomica* 3.39), often used to justify a plain, instructional style in technical writing.</note>

And if there is any art that does not admit the ornament of words, and which is difficult

<meta>This page continues Lomazzo’s concluding reflections from Book Seven. He moves from listing the masters of the art to justifying his plain, technical prose style, citing his physical limitations—specifically his blindness—as the reason he focused on substance over literary elegance.</meta>

to be explained, without doubt it is painting; so much so that I fear that in many places, although I have labored greatly to simplify matters, I will not be easily understood. But as for the less "approved" words <note>Lomazzo is defending his use of technical jargon and "vulgar" studio terms rather than the refined Tuscan literary language of the period.</note>, they are so specific to this art, and consequently so meaningful among painters, that they could in no way be omitted if I wished to be understood. For it was not possible to signify the same meaning with any other single word, and attempting to describe them with many words would have served to entangle the subjects rather than explain them. 

But even if this art had been more capable of literary ornaments, I could in no way have satisfied the ears of those "delicate" critics. Because in the little time that was granted to me by God to be able to work—being, as everyone knows, rendered little less than useless in the flower of my years by the loss of my sight in the thirtieth year of my age <note>Giovan Paolo Lomazzo (1538–1592) was a productive painter until he went blind in 1571. He then turned to writing massive, influential treatises on art theory from memory.</note>—it was not possible for me to have painted as much as is typically done, and to have speculated and observed as much in this profession as is seen gathered in these books, while also finding time to curate a collection of the choicest words from the *Canzoniere* of **Petrarch** or the *Decameron* of **Boccaccio** <note>Petrarch and Boccaccio were the gold standards for "high" literary Italian in the 16th century.</note>. 

Scholars, then, valuing the substance of things more than a sweet sound that flatters the ear, should not fail to occasionally spend a spare hour reading this treatise. Without doubt, they will gain profit and honor from it by observing those <term>precepts</term> <note>Technical rules or instructions for creating art.</note> they will have learned here. They will praise me—if not for my genius, at least for my diligence—and for this most honest desire I have had to benefit the world, and for the effort I have made to achieve it. This I shall consider a most honorable and complete reward for so many of my long nights and labors.

### The end of the seventh, and final book.

# S

**S***alaino the Milanese, painter, disciple of Leonardo.* <note>Gian Giacomo Caprotti, known as "Salai" (c. 1480–1524), Leonardo da Vinci's long-time pupil and companion.</note>
*San Marino, universal architect.* <note>Likely referring to Giovanni Battista Belluzzi, a military architect from San Marino.</note>
*Saint Luke, eminent painter and sculptor.* <note>According to Christian tradition, the Evangelist Luke was the first to paint the portrait of the Virgin Mary.</note>
*Scyllis the Cretan, sculptor.* <note>An early Greek sculptor from the 6th century BCE, often paired with Dipoenus.</note>
*Scipione Gaetano, painter.* <note>Scipione Pulzone (c. 1544–1598), a leading portraitist in Counter-Reformation Rome.</note>
*Scipione Delfinone, Milanese embroiderer.* <note>Member of a famous family of Milanese artisans specializing in silk and gold embroidery.</note>
*Scopas, very rare ancient sculptor.* <note>Scopas of Paros (c. 395–350 BCE), a famous Greek architect and sculptor of the Temple of Athena Alea.</note>
~~*Sebastiano Serlio of Bologna, painter and architect.*~~ <note>Author of a highly influential architectural treatise; this entry has been struck through by a later hand.</note>
*Sebordanet the German, painter and engraver of prints.* <note>Possibly a reference to a Northern engraver like Sebald Beham.</note>
*Serapion, ancient and bizarre painter.* <note>A Roman-era painter mentioned by Pliny the Elder as a painter of scenery.</note>
~~*Silvio of Lucca, sculptor.*~~ <note>Silvio Cosini, a sculptor who assisted Michelangelo in the Medici Chapel.</note>
*Simone Memmi of Siena, singular painter, disciple of Giotto.* <note>Known today as Simone Martini (c. 1284–1344); "Memmi" was actually the surname of his brother-in-law, Lippo Memmi.</note>
*Simone Peterzano of Venice, practical and delightful painter, disciple of Titian.* <note>Best known today as the teacher of Caravaggio.</note>
*Socrates, ancient and rare sculptor and painter.*
*Socrates the Athenian, most clear Philosopher and stonecutter.* <note>Historical tradition holds that the philosopher Socrates followed his father Sophroniscus into the craft of stonecutting before turning to philosophy.</note>
*Socrates, ancient sculptor.*
~~*Sostratus, principal architect of the tower on the island of Pharos.*~~ <note>Sostratus of Cnidus, the architect of the Lighthouse of Alexandria, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.</note>
*Sofonisba Anguissola of Cremona, prompt female painter, disciple of Bernardino Campi.* <note>One of the first female artists to achieve international fame, serving at the court of Philip II of Spain.</note>
*Stefano Scoto the Milanese, painter, and master of Gaudenzio along with Pietro Perugino.* <note>A master of the Lombard school; "Gaudenzio" is Gaudenzio Ferrari.</note>
*Sthennis, ancient statue-maker.* <note>A Greek sculptor of the 4th century BCE mentioned by Pliny.</note>

# ON THE CRAFTSMEN

**T** *Taddeo Zuccaro of Sant'Angelo in Vado, a valiant painter and brother of Federico.* <note>Taddeo Zuccaro (1529–1566) was a leading Roman Mannerist; his brother Federico became even more famous internationally.</note>
*Telephanes of Sicyon, painter.* <note>An early Greek painter mentioned by Pliny the Elder as one of the inventors of line drawing.</note>
*Telephanes of Phocis, a sculptor who wrote about art.*
<margin>X</margin>
*Tenodorus, an ancient sculptor.*
*Theodore of Haarlem, a rare Flemish painter.* <note>Likely Dirck Barendsz (1534–1592), who studied in Venice and brought the Italian style to the Netherlands.</note>
<margin>X</margin>
*Theon, an ancient painter.*
*Ctesibius, engineer and inventor of hydraulic organs.* <note>A Greek inventor in Alexandria (3rd century BCE) known as the father of pneumatics.</note>
*Chersiphron, the supreme architect of the Temple of Diana at Ephesus.*
*Ctesiphon, a sculptor who wrote about art.*
<margin>S-shaped mark</margin>
*Chersiphron of Knossos, a marvelous military architect.*
*Tiburzio Maino of Pavia, a principal sculptor of small wooden figures and brother of Agnolo.*
*Timagoras of Chalcis, a painter who composed verses on painting.*
*Timanthes of Cyprus, an illustrious painter.* <note>Famous in antiquity for his "Sacrifice of Iphigenia," where he veiled the father's face because his grief was too great to depict.</note>
*Timomachus, an ancient painter and sculptor.*
*Timotheus, an ancient and prized sculptor.*
*Timoteo Viti of Urbino, a celebrated painter and disciple of Raphael.* <note>Viti (1469–1523) actually influenced the young Raphael before later becoming his assistant.</note>
*Tyndareus, an ancient sculptor.*
*Titian Vecellio of Cadore, a singular painter and Knight. 27.* <note>Titian (c. 1488–1576), the greatest master of the Venetian school; the number 27 likely refers to a page or entry number in the main text.</note>
*Tommaso della Porta of Porlezza, a rare sculptor in imitating antiquity and marvelous with masks.* <note>The della Porta family were renowned Lombard sculptors and architects in Rome; "counterfeiting" or imitating the antique was a highly valued skill for restoration and creating new works in the classical style.</note>
*Troso of Monza, a sharp painter.*
*Taurianus, an ancient sculptor.*
*Turpilius of Venice, who was the first painter to paint with the left hand, and a Roman Knight.* <note>Mentioned by Pliny; a rare example of a Roman aristocrat who practiced painting.</note>

*Vincenzo Civerchio of Milan, a painter and master of Bernardo Zenale.*
*Vincenzo of Brescia, painter.*

*Virgil Solis, German painter and copperplate engraver.* <note>Virgil Solis (1514–1562) was a highly prolific Nuremberg printmaker whose designs were used by craftsmen across Europe.</note>
*Witelo the Thuringian-Pole, great master of perspective.* <note>Witelo (c. 1230–after 1280) was a friar and scientist whose work on optics and "perspectiva" was a standard text for centuries.</note>
*Vitello, writer and mathematician.*
*Vitruvius Pollio, primary and universal architect.* <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the 1st-century BCE Roman author of "De architectura," the foundational text for Renaissance architecture.</note>

# X
*Xenocrates, painter and statuary maker, who wrote about his arts, a disciple of Eutychrates.* <note>Xenocrates of Sicyon (3rd century BCE) is regarded as one of the first art historians for his technical writings on sculpture and painting.</note>

---

# Z
*Zenodorus the Tuscan, great statuary maker and sculptor.* <note>Zenodorus (1st century CE) was famous for creating the massive Colossus of Nero in Rome.</note>
*Zeuxis of Heraclea, most excellent painter and modeller.* <note>Zeuxis (5th century BCE) was a legendary Greek painter known for his extreme realism; he famously painted grapes so lifelike that birds flew down to peck at them.</note>

### This Chapter should be placed in the sixth book after chapter 16 on page 328.

## On the art of extending the view as much as one wishes, and likewise on making *the apparatuses for stage scenery with the aforementioned Geometric square.*

### Chapter XVII.

To understand the art of extending the view as much as you wish, it is necessary that you always know the distance from yourself to the <term>facade</term> <note>original: "facciata"; here referring to the picture plane or the front surface being painted</note>, because according to that distance you will come to know how much the proportions diminish. But at the very least, you should ensure that the space is not less than four <term>braccia</term> <note>original: "braccia"; an Italian unit of measurement roughly equal to the length of an arm, approximately 23–27 inches</note>. I place this before your eyes with an example: place yourself in a wide area, for example four *braccia* away from the facade you wish to paint. To extend the view as much as you want by diminishing the proportions that enter the facade, you will take a compass and mark the four *braccia* that are between you and the facade; this line you shall call the **line of sight**, which goes exactly to the base of the facade at a right angle.

Behind this will follow the **line of proportion or level**. On this line, you will again mark the four *braccia* with the compass. Now, wishing to diminish this proportion, you will place four other parts—which you shall call *braccia*—within the first *braccio* next to the facade of proportion. By multiplying them in the proportion, four times four makes sixteen; and that is the number of *braccia* from which you are viewing the facade.

Coming then to the <term>Geometric square</term> <note>original: "quadro Geometrico"; a grid or instrument used for calculating perspective</note>, you will set it perpendicular to the facade and draw the line of sight, on which you will mark the exact four *braccia* from the compass. At the end of that, you will draw another *braccio* at a level, like the one of proportion above that contains four; by joining the fourth line to this, a square is created four *braccia* high and one *braccio* wide (which contains four). Now, moving to your eye arranged for seeing, you will draw a line to the first *braccio* diminished in the proportion and you will <term>intersect</term> <note>original: "interfecherai"; the point where a line of sight crosses the vertical plane of the image</note> it on the facade. You will do the same for the second, third, and fourth *braccia*, intersecting them all on the facade, where you will pull them all at a right angle toward yourself. Then, in the place where you wish to set the point or the end of your eye, you will draw the four *braccia* marked on the line of sight brought to the line of seeing—as I said in the other chapter—from you to the facade, and there you wi-

<summary>This page introduces technical instructions for using a "Geometric square" to calculate perspective and distance in architectural painting and stage design. It explains how to establish a line of sight and use proportions to simulate depth on a flat surface.</summary>
<keywords>perspective, Geometric square, braccia, stage scenery, proportions, line of sight, technical drawing, optics</keywords>

--- Page 747 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical instruction from Chapter XVII regarding the Geometric square and the rules of perspective. The text picks up from the previous page's discussion on how to use these tools to create the illusion of depth.</meta>

...you will see the four <term>braccia</term> <note>original: "braccia"; an Italian unit of measurement roughly equal to the length of an arm, approximately 23–27 inches</note> diminish gracefully in perspective, <margin>+</margin>
And returning to the proportion—that is, to the three *braccia* that remain—
you will divide each of those *braccia* into four, which will total twelve. You shall place them beneath the Geometric squares just like the first one, and then <margin>+</margin>
draw them with lines toward your eye, intersecting them on the <term>facade</term> <note>original: "facciata"; the front surface of the work or the picture plane</note>.
Afterward, by drawing them at a right angle from that facade above the **line of sight**,
you will find the sixteen *braccia* diminish in perspective according to the number of the four *braccia* that stand between you and the facade. Likewise, you can increase and multiply the views as much as you wish, because we know for certain that among the greatest masters of perspective, as soon as the **floor plans** are made, the nature of the building is judged—both its height and its depth—in all parts that can be seen. 

But if you also wish to draw the floor plans of figures, columns, trees, and whatever else you desire, you shall draw a diagonal line from below the foot of the facade that forms a small corner with the proportion. The further this line descends, the more the proportions diminish (as will be explained), and the closer it comes, the larger they become. Therefore, by marking the plans of whatever you wish on those diagonal lines so they enter the facade, you will come up from those points marked on the diagonal lines at a right angle to the line of proportion, into the proportion itself. You will then draw those points—marked in the proportion of the diagonal plans and transferred to it—toward your eye; and where they intersect the lines of the facade, you shall mark them, for these are the depths that enter into the facade. 

As for the widths, lengths, or oblique parts of the members, or whatever has been transferred, you will mark them for the eye on the **line of sight** and bring them to the point with lines. Then, by drawing the intersections of the plans (transported from the proportion to the eye) at a right angle to the facade into those lines, you can raise the heights of the figures, columns, and whatever you wish, making the parts enter slightly into the facade. If these were viewed from such a distance, they would appear consistent and equal. Note, however, that if they are made with good <term>chiaroscuro</term> <note>original: "chiaro & scuro"; the use of strong contrasts between light and dark to create the illusion of three-dimensional volume</note>, those many tangles and errors committed by painters because of these distant views will be removed, and they will turn out pleasingly. 

Therefore, you can see how great the difficulty of this art is, both from this and from the preceding and following chapters. I hold that the ancients observed this method, such as <term>Calamis</term> <note>A Greek sculptor of the 5th century BC known for his refined style</note> and <term>Lysippus</term> <note>A famous Greek sculptor of the 4th century BC who developed a new system of proportions for the human body</note> in their bas-reliefs, as <term>Trajan's Column</term> <note>A Roman triumphal column in Rome, famous for its spiral relief depicting the Dacian Wars</note> and others even more ancient bear witness, and among the moderns, Buona- <margin>narotti</margin> <note>The text cuts off here, referring to Michelangelo Buonarroti</note>

<summary>This page provides technical instructions for calculating the diminishment of objects in perspective using diagonal lines and floor plans. The author emphasizes the importance of chiaroscuro and cites ancient masters like Lysippus and modern ones like Michelangelo as practitioners of these methods.</summary>
<keywords>perspective, geometry, braccia, floor plans, chiaroscuro, Calamis, Lysippus, Trajan's Column, Michelangelo Buonarroti, technical drawing</keywords>

--- Page 748 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on perspective and the "facade" or picture plane from Chapter XVII, specifically addressing how optical distance affects the representation of figures in both painting and sculpture.</meta>

...[Sanso]vatti, <note>original: "zatti"; likely referring to Jacopo Sansovino (1486–1570), a renowned architect and sculptor</note> and **Baccio Bandinelli**, <note>A prominent Mannerist sculptor and rival of Michelangelo</note> and other wonders in this art, such as our **Fontana**. <note>original: "Fontana"; likely Domenico Fontana (1543–1607), the architect famous for his work on St. Peter’s Basilica and the relocation of the Vatican obelisk</note> In this same way, the buildings and stage scenery <note>original: "apparati de le scene"; temporary structures used for theatrical performances or festivals</note> raised in the rear sections can be constructed, so that through the long view, the scenery does not appear disproportionate to the eyes of the viewers, whether in painting or in **low relief**. <term>Low relief</term> <note>original: "basso rilieuo"; sculpture where the figures project only slightly from the background</note> 

But there is this difficulty in painting: the figures arranged on the **facade** <note>the surface of the painting</note> cannot appear correctly to our sight unless they are viewed from as far away as they are represented to be. For it is clearly known that our eye does not see any part up close except that which is directly presented to it; but then, by pulling the body further away, one sees the surrounding parts more clearly than what is seen bluntly up close—even though the closer object seems larger to you than those that appear smaller. 

Thus, it is necessary to diligently examine and understand this rule of **perspective**, because we see many who are excellent in art who wish to portray nudes and draperies up close for figures that are to be placed far away. Not understanding the *art of seeing*, they remain stuck in these abuses of theirs, because the figures they have portrayed still appear as if they are up close. They do not know how to discern that lines spread out more rapidly from a distance, while up close they rise and fall bluntly. 

From this, it is also seen that if those who portray from life <note>original: "ritrattori del naturale"</note> stand too near the figure they are portraying, even if they do it excellently, others who see it will say that such a painting does not resemble the natural subject. And this happens because the painter stays close while portraying, whereas those skilled in perspective stand as far from the natural subject as a person is tall—or even further if possible. This ensures that the rays from the eyes receive the parts of the **portrait** softly, in such a way, however, that the eye of the subject and the eye of the painter are in a straight line. And this difficulty is not found in **sculpture**; because in sculpture all the parts are measured and checked with a compass <note>original: "compassano"; using a divider or compass to ensure mathematical proportion</note> according to the art of the one who knows how to work.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of perspective and the "facade" (picture plane) from the previous chapter. The text specifically addresses how a painter or sculptor must manipulate light (lumi) and shadow (oscuri) to compensate for the way the human eye perceives objects at a distance.</meta>

...consists of reflections of light, and other elements which are all distant displays; in this manner, the structure of the lights will be seen, along with the rear parts. Although these may appear distant, they should not for that reason be obscured or darkened in their appearance; instead, let them be seen at that point almost as a glimmer <note>original: "barlume"; a faint, shimmering, or flickering light</note>. 

But those who are fond of technical challenges in painting or sculpture do not want figures on the **facade** <term>facade</term> <note>original: "facciata"; in this context, the flat surface of the painting or the foremost plane of a relief</note> to appear to our sight unless they are accompanied by a representation of enlargement. This ensures that the darkness of one part is not seen right next to another—unless the painter intends for a distant body to appear more pronounced. However, if one captures more than what is seen appearing obscurely, the darkness must be enlarged for that reason, and thus it will appear clearer. The same must be done with the whites, as is clearly evident. 

For if we see objects very close to one another, they tend to remain large in appearance. Regarding figures placed at a distance: they should not be fully defined when viewed, so that they fade away <note>original: "s'ammortisi"; to deaden or soften the edges of a figure so it recedes into the background</note> in that manner. The truth is that lights appear more separated from a distance, while the dark areas seem to draw closer together. If a light is twice the size of the interior, it reveals itself very clearly to the eye from nature, even if it is far away. 

For this reason, regarding faces seen from afar, it is said that they will be perceived from the very start. This occurs because the painter, in handling the difficult dark tones, should not be seen [meaning the brushwork is hidden]; in understanding it in this way, the lights become denser. Therefore, one part of the body's enlargement may not be seen, and the painter does not enlarge it in that way. Those parts that ought to recede are not seen, so that the forward-facing part appears more clearly. Such is the art of those who work in this field; and the opposite effect is seen in **lighthouses**. <note>original: "fari"; likely referring to the way a lighthouse beam remains distinct over vast distances compared to smaller lights.</note>
